L3: records with a wrongly typed known field ( "metadata": null or a list, object or array content , list mimetype , boolean content ) no longer crash the import with a traceback or store "1" . L4: a high-cardinality key's example is stored apart from its enumerated values , so it is no longer written back as a bogus curated values: [id-0] ; a stale values from an earlier export heals on the next convert and export. C1: following the guard's advice ( arkiv convert x.db x ) now clears it; a full db-to-directory export records the directory and resets the unexported-writes counter. C5: a UTF-8 byte order mark no longer drops the first record of a JSONL file, in parse_jsonl , in the bundle readers, and in arkiv detect and arkiv fix (which keeps the mark when it rewrites the file). C6: zip packing no longer fails on a member of 2 GiB or more ( pack_bundle declares each member's size up front so zipfile switches to zip64 for members over 2 GiB), and write_bundle and pack_bundle write atomically, so a failure leaves no partial bundle behind. C7: corrupt, truncated, or encrypted bundles, and files that are not the archive their extension claims (a non-zip named .zip ), report a clean ValueError instead of a traceback ( zlib.error , NotImplementedError , RuntimeError , EOFError , BadZipFile , tarfile.ReadError ), in unpack
title: queelius/arkiv: arkiv 0.4.1

summary: Reliable video perception over bandwidth-constrained wireless links requires transmitting information that the receiver cannot already recover from its evolving scene representation. This paper introduces WorldGT, a world-model-guided semantic packet transmission framework that prioritizes information according to its contribution to the receiver's perception. A shared feature-space world model predicts the receiver's scene state through affine motion compensation and learned residual displacement, while sender-side verification identifies reusable predictions. An acknowledgment-synchronized receiver twin estimates task-impact scores through two counterfactual evaluations, guiding packet selection and unequal error protection over LDPC-coded wireless channels. A compact 3-bit feature representation increases spatial coverage under stringent bandwidth constraints, while predictive fallback sustains perception during packet outages. Experiments on KITTI and VisDrone under Rayleigh fading and AWGN demonstrate substantial gains in low-SNR conditions. On KITTI at a 4.13% reference bandwidth budget, WorldGT achieves 47.5% J&F at 0 dB Rayleigh SNR, outperforming H.264 by 11.3 percentage points. Controlled ablations show that world-model prediction contributes up to 8.7 points under Rayleigh fading. Object-detection experiments further demonstrate the transferability of receiver-relative predictive transmission across visual perception tasks. These results establish world-model-guided, receiver-state-aware transmission as an effective approach to robust video perception under severe communication constraints.
title: Guess and Send: World-Model-Guided Semantic Packet Transmission for Robust Video Perception

summary: We consider the open-loop optimal control of a dynamical system whose state is described by a time-dependent matrix $X(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. Gradient-based optimization methods may incur substantial computational and memory costs, particularly for large-scale systems and fine temporal discretizations. To alleviate this computational burden, we develop a mathematical framework to use Dynamical Low Rank Approximations (DLRA) in optimal control problems. We study two distinct paradigms: the first one, called Optimize-then-Project (OtP), first derives the optimality system and then approximates both the state and adjoint equations using DLRA. The second one, called Project-then-Optimize (PtO), first replaces the state equation with its DLR approximation, and then derives the optimality conditions for the resulting optimization problem. The two approaches differ fundamentally concerning the role of the adjoint variable. In OtP, the adjoint variable evolves on the manifold of fixed rank matrices, whereas in PtO, the adjoint variable belongs to the tangent space to the fixed-rank manifold at the evolving state variable. This latter formulation leads to a covariant ODE describing the dynamics of the adjoint variable as the underlying tangent space evolves in time. For both approaches we establish rigorous error estimates for the approximated gradients, identifying how their accuracy depends on the low-rank approximations of initial and terminal conditions, the components of the state and adjoint vector fields normal to the relevant tangent spaces, the stability properties of the dynamics, and the manifold curvature. PtO further requires tailored time discretization strategies for the adjoint covariant ODE, which we show to be robust against small singular values of the state variable. To illustrate the framework, we apply these methods to the optimal control of a random parabolic PDE.
title: Dynamical low-rank approximations for the optimal control of matrix ODEs

summary: Training modern AI models has become increasingly expensive, and updating deployed models can alter their internal feature representations, affecting applications built upon them. In retrieval systems, such updates often require complete gallery re-indexing, a computationally expensive process at scale. Existing backward-compatibility methods enable direct comparison of representations from updated and earlier models, avoiding re-indexing. However, they typically require compatibility-specific training, learned mapping functions, or architectural modifications, and often depend explicitly on the previous model. We propose hyperspherical simplex representations derived from softmax outputs and logits for backward-compatible retrieval across independently trained models. They leverage the simplex structure induced by softmax cross-entropy training with one-hot labels as a common geometric reference across model updates. Since this reference depends on the number of classes, adding new ones expands the simplex, misaligning existing class prototypes with their earlier counterparts. We therefore derive a deterministic linear transformation to restore their alignment. Our theoretical analysis of the formal backward-compatibility definition identifies two geometric conditions under which its inequalities hold in expectation, assuming von Mises--Fisher class distributions with increasing concentration across updates. Aligned regular-simplex representations satisfy these conditions, providing a theoretical basis for the proposed representations under the stated assumptions. Without using additional compatibility-specific losses, learned mappings, or architectural modifications, the proposed representations achieve competitive results on standard compatibility benchmarks, including expanded class sets, more expressive architectures, and independently trained models from public repositories.
title: Hyperspherical Simplex Representations for Backward-Compatible Retrieval

summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have seen broad adoption, but their biases are still far less examined than those of standard LLMs, creating possible social harms when deployed in real-world settings. Prior efforts to extend bias analyses from LLMs into the multi-modal space either cover only a few bias categories or do not ensure that the groups being compared are clearly addressed by visual cues in the images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Melange, a wide-ranging synthetic visual benchmark covering seven categories for assessing social biases in MLLMs. It is grounded in the widely used language-only BBQ dataset (Bias Benchmark for Question Answering) from BigBench, carefully extending its constructed contexts via controlled generation of visual scenarios so the target attributes appear visually and clearly. To maximize reliability, our generated images pass through two stages of validation: automated screening using visual question answering (VQA) and subsequent manual inspection by human annotators. By systematically evaluating 23 open-source MLLMs across three matched evaluation settings---text-only, image-only, and image-with-context---Melange isolates the fairness effect of the input modality. Switching from text to vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average, a gap that varies by model family rather than by scale alone. A perception control confirms that this gap is not an artifact of visual comprehension: models identify the depicted attributes at 90--95\% accuracy yet still fail to abstain. When models do commit to a biased answer, polarity-aware stereotype alignment shows they choose the human-stereotypical response roughly three-quarters of the time.
title: Melange: A Synthetic Visual Bias Benchmark for Multi-modal Large Language Models

summary: Residual-based causal discovery assumes that each variable is generated from its parents and an independent noise source. It estimates this noise and tests its independence from candidate causes. For identifiable functions such as additive-noise models (ANMs) and the broader class of location-scale noise models (LSNMs), this principle identifies the causal direction, as only the causal model admits this independence. Existing LSNM methods rely on parametric assumptions to obtain standardized residuals, risking model misspecification. In contrast, the RESIT-framework allows for nonparametric estimation of residuals to iteratively identify sink nodes, but was proposed for ANMs. To close this gap, we propose Loscar, an extension of RESIT to LSNMs that estimates the conditional mean and scale via quantile regression, enabling pretrained tabular foundation models as plug-in estimators. We compare it with a feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) variant, which is consistent given suitable basis functions. Across bivariate and multivariate causal-discovery benchmarks, in-context quantile regression substantially outperforms FGLS with flexible function classes, particularly for multivariate causes.
title: Residual-Based Causal Discovery via Pretrained In-Context Quantile Regression

summary: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.
title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity

summary: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for multi-step reasoning, yet obtaining reliable process labels remains a central bottleneck. Existing approaches typically rely on human annotation, rollout-based estimation, or auxiliary verification. In this work, we explore a different source of process supervision natively exposed by Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: expert routing. We show that simple routing statistics provide an intrinsic process-confidence signal that is competitive with conventional output-logit confidence. Building on this observation, we construct routing confidence by combining overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation, and introduce RoCo-Rethink, which identifies the least confident reasoning step and selectively regenerates the subsequent trajectory. We further introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM. Across multiple MoE architectures and diverse reasoning tasks, both RoCo-Rethink and RoCo-PRM consistently outperform strong baselines, while RoCo-PRM transfers effectively across both model architectures and tasks. Our findings suggest that expert routing is more than a computational dispatch mechanism: it provides an architecture-native source of process supervision for reasoning.
title: A Strong MoE Is All You Need for Process Supervision

summary: In this work, we assess the recently introduced spin-adapted TDA for spin-flip-down excitations (XSF-TDA) [Mol. Phys. e2631735 (2026)] as a practical approach to this problem. Starting from a high-spin restricted open-shell Kohn--Sham reference, XSF-TDA generates spin-adapted low-spin roots arising from open--open (OO), core--open (CO), open--virtual (OV), and core--virtual (CV) types of spin-flip-down excitations. Across four application sets comprising 243 benchmark cases, XSF-TDA substantially reduces the systematic positive bias observed for TDA and unrestricted spin-flip TDA (USF-TDA). With the B3LYP functional, XSF-TDA reduces the equal-set-weighted macro-MAE relative to USF-TDA from 0.252 eV (0.158 eV) to 0.102~eV (0.056~eV) with the ALDA0 (multicollinear) kernel. Its accuracy is competitive with state-specific $Δ$DFT and quasiparticle-energy DFT (QE-DFT), while being able to provide deeper mechanistic insight through the response vector. In particular, spin-adapted CV configurations provide selected higher-excitation character that strengthens the OO--CV dynamical-spin-polarization channel, which preferentially stabilizes the singlet states. We also identify an INVEST emitter with appreciable OO--OV mixing, suggesting a possible additional contribution to singlet stabilization when the CV contribution is small. The XSF-TDA method therefore provides practical singlet--triplet gap predictions together with interpretable state analysis for the screening and mechanistic understanding of MR-TADF and INVEST emitters.
title: Spin-Adapted Spin-Flip Tamm-Dancoff Approximation (XSF-TDA) for Singlet-Triplet Gaps in MR-TADF and INVEST Emitters

summary: Suitability maps guide perennial-crop expansion but are rarely converted into units that planners can allocate, tested for robustness to analyst choices or checked against presence records. We assessed land suitability for macadamia ( Macadamia integrifolia ) in four provinces of northwestern Vietnam, where a national programme targets 75,000–95,000 ha by 2030, using twelve FAO-rated criteria weighted by fuzzy AHP under baseline and 2041–2070 climates (five CMIP6 models, two scenarios). We delineated plantable zones: contiguous blocks of at least 1000 ha that keep a suitability index of 0.75 or more in all eleven runs and lie outside forest-planning land on slopes of at most 20°. Before the minimum-area rule, this land forms more than 100,000 patches, and projected changes in suitable area changed sign at high thresholds. Delineation produced 89 zones covering 346,945 ha, whose location changed little across weight sets (Jaccard ≥ 0.78), largely because the exclusion masks fix where zones can lie. Of 88 presence records not used to set class limits, 69% lay within 3 km of a zone, against 39% of the region, also after spatial thinning; mask-only zones did as well, so the agreement reflects the masks and cannot test the index ranking. With no heat or drought criterion, warming relaxes the cold limit, but the best low-lying zones decline most. The zones cover 3.7–4.6 times the 2030 target, yet half their area carries tree cover, a quarter is cropland and grassland alone falls short of it, so land availability is the likely constraint (SDGs 15 and 2).
title: Climate-robust plantable zones for macadamia outside forest-planning land in northwestern Vietnam

summary: This archive contains the code used for the experiments of the paper "AICAT: an AI tool for hierarchical cell-type annotation" (Dailin Gan, Siyuan Zhang and Jun Li), as used for the revised manuscript (release v1.0.0-revision). Contents: code/Build_Agent holds AICAT as run for the benchmark of 238 samples, with preprocessing, the LLM evaluator and the organisation of results and figures. code/GPTCelltype holds the GPTCelltype runs. code/Revision holds the experiments and analyses added in the revision: ablation, comparison with CASSIA and ScType, marker perturbation, repeated runs, runtime and cost, blinded re-scoring, statistics, figures and tables. code/process_data holds early GTEx processing scripts. requirements.txt records the Python environment. See code/README.md for details. The processed data are available on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.16739980). The installable AICAT package is aicat-annotator (PyPI; https://github.com/RavenGan/AICAT). To run the code, set the environment variable OPENAI_API_KEY; no API key is stored in the code. The third-party ScType scripts and database (GPL-3.0) are not included; code/Revision/external/sctype/SOURCE.md gives the exact source and checksums.
title: AICAT: code for the benchmark and revision experiments

summary: Reproduction package for the manuscript "Vehicle-to-Grid Scheduling for City-Scale Electric Vehicle Fleets: A Three-Stage Peak-Shaving Algorithm with State-of-Charge Recovery" (submitted to Energy). Contents: Codes/: three-stage V2G algorithm, LCVF baseline, exact charging-only model (Gurobi C API) and experiment runners Datasets/: conventional load profiles of Campo Grande (MS, Brazil) and preprocessed EV fleets (Boulder B1–B4, Norway N1) Results/: results of the 768 instances per technique (V2G, LCVF, exact) and the consolidated analysis See README.md for requirements and instructions to analyse the stored results or rerun the experiments.
title: Reproduction package for "Vehicle-to-Grid Scheduling for City-Scale Electric Vehicle Fleets: A Three-Stage Peak-Shaving Algorithm with State-of-Charge Recovery"
Do Sentinel-2 vegetation indices improve forecasts of Phenacoccus solenopsis on okra? A two-season retrospective benchmark study

summary: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents

summary: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model

summary: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.
title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing

summary: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models

summary: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.
title: Stochastic Pruning of the DPO Computation Graph: 1.4x Faster Training and Lower Peak Memory

summary: We are the first to give a certified rule for whether unseen data belong in a pretrained model's context or its weights, built on an exact law for their information value. That value, the code length saved on held-out queries, equals in expectation the bits stored about the query, plus a prior repair, minus a decoding loss, for any model, architecture, dataset and task. The law's ceilings certify the choice from one measurement, and an anytime-valid test makes it from held-out queries, with error controlled whenever it stops. Every certificate the ceilings issue on a trained transformer, TabPFN, an occupancy network and a stereo network is correct. The test picks TabPFN over XGBoost and a trained surrogate over an in-context learner on airfoil pressure, calls the better of GPT-2's cache and fine-tune in 61,948 of 64,000 query streams over 32 comparisons, and errs in at most 3.3% of null streams. The law also diagnoses when learning in context helps and when it does not. Deleting part of a context is held-out validation of that part in any model, and adding parts one at a time traces the learning curve in context: one patch that sees a shape feature cuts an occupancy network's code length there a hundredfold, while eight that miss it nearly double it, and one camera that sees the surface beats four in a stereo network. Ranked by this label-free valuation, a kriging learner's three best support cars beat four drawn at random, and on a yes-or-no claim the valuation recovers a published evidence adjudicator, with AUROC 0.91.
title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning

summary: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.
title: ChronoSynth: Constraint-Aware Question Synthesis over Temporal Knowledge Graphs

summary: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.
title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience

summary: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.
title: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling

summary: Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills. Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground. We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution. The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model. At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43-46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.
title: Compressing Onboard Language Models for Space Robots under a Behavioral-Fidelity Requirement

summary: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts

summary: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.
title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.
title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs

summary: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.
title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents

summary: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.
title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents

summary: A transformer MLP gives each hidden channel two roles: a reader that decides when the channel responds, and a writer that decides what it adds back to the residual stream. Read as a key--value memory, the layer can be measured one factor set at a time: the pairing of readers to writers is carried only by their shared index, invisible to any quantity computed from one factor set alone. Yet training couples the two factors through their joint update, so we ask what reading them together shows. The block supplies the joint instrument: the MLP writes back into the very stream it reads, so the exact Jacobian of its update is square, and its agreement with its own transpose resolves into reader--writer terms whose inner products give each channel, read as a couple, a signed pairing coordinate. Ranked by this coordinate, each block we measure has a small core of strongly coupled channels; where initialization gives either sign equally, the core is nearly all opposed: each writer points against the direction its reader responds to. This opposed core recurs from the smallest models trained from scratch to released checkpoints; its sign is in place within a few percent of training and holds while the coupling grows. Read as couples, most channels return their contribution against the reader that fired it, and the readers of later blocks take it up; few show in the logits. Training holds the couples in place: flipping the opposed writers moves the output toward common tokens, and a writer permuted onto another reader regrows to fit that reader while the reader stays.
title: Reader--Writer Coupling in Transformer MLPs

summary: World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it. Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold. Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models. In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.
title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models

summary: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.
title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use

summary: Evangelou, Stanković, Kevrekidis and Transtrum compared analytic and data-driven assessments of parameter identifiability for the infinite-bus synchronous generator. Fisher information with the manifold boundary approximation method (MBAM), and output diffusion maps with geometric harmonics, report the same six identifiable parameters on the late window $t \in [3, 5]\text{ s}$, and both place the inertia $H$ and the damping $D$ among the unidentifiable ones. We explain this result from the geometry of the dynamics rather than from that of the parameter-to-data map. The rotor swing is a fast fibre that has collapsed onto a two-dimensional normally attracting invariant manifold (NAIM) of the transient fluxes before the window opens. The zeroth-order NAIM is exactly independent of $H$, $D$, $T_{d0}''$ and $T_{q0}''$, four of the five MBAM limits. We prove, under stated smoothness and rank conditions, that each of the four limits is a boundary of the model manifold at a distance equal, to first order in the parameter, to its current profiled speed. The same analysis predicts how identifiability changes with the experiment: neither a larger initial speed deviation nor a load change restores $H$ or $D$ in the late window, whereas the early window $[0, 2]\text{ s}$ makes $H$ the best-determined parameter. Evaluated in a physical metric fixed by synchrophasor accuracy limits, the late window identifies five parameters rather than six and the early window nine. The spiked-covariance structure of the linearised trajectory map explains why the principal components of whitened, sampled trajectories reproduce the prior-scaled Fisher spectrum, and regression on those components attains the Fisher-predicted recovery error in 113 of 114 parameter--scenario pairs.
title: Why the Swing Parameters Are Sloppy

summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.
title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence

summary: Passive time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) localization is well suited for tracking non-cooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that do not report their positions. However, its accuracy degrades under the mixed line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) propagation that is typical of low-altitude flight. In this paper, we develop NLOS-aware Cramér--Rao lower bounds (CRLBs) and an empirically calibrated measurement model for TDOA-based UAV localization, and we evaluate both with measurements from five UAV flights on the Aerial Experimentation and Research Platform for Advanced Wireless (AERPAW). The analysis yields an identifiability condition that relates the number of sensors to the number of NLOS links, together with a bias-induced error floor that a wider bandwidth cannot remove. The model parameters are estimated by matching simulated and measured error distributions. Experimental results show that the error depends most strongly on the number of sensors in LOS, while a higher altitude and a wider bandwidth lower the median error. Relocating a sensor that is always in NLOS into the open flight area can lower the median horizontal bound by two orders of magnitude if the relocated sensor is in LOS. The fitted model reproduces the median errors of the 2.5 MHz and 5 MHz flights but underestimates the heaviest error tails. Finally, rejecting outlier fixes lowers the error far more than Kalman or particle filtering, because the remaining error is dominated by bias.
title: NLOS-Aware TDOA-Based UAV Localization: Cramér-Rao Bounds, Measurement Modeling, and Experimental Validation

summary: Flexible intelligent metasurfaces (FIMs) create geometry-dependent array responses that provide spatial diversity but complicate multiuser channel estimation. This paper studies uplink estimation using pilot observations collected under multiple prescribed and calibrated morphing configurations. Each user contributes a matrix--vector block that couples its diagonal reference-array response with its morphing-dependent phases, while its third-mode vector is the known pilot scaled by the complex channel gain. We develop a pilot-constrained structured block term decomposition (BTD) estimator whose alternating least-squares updates exploit both the known pilot directions and the diagonal spatial factors. The undeformed configuration sets the columnwise scaling convention, and a unit first-entry normalization assigns the remaining block scale to the channel gain. Matching the recovered factors to the calibrated spatial--morphing manifold then yields the physical angles and configuration-dependent channels. We characterize the rank conditions for unique conditional least-squares updates, distinguish these conditions from global factor and physical-angle identifiability, and summarize the training, coherence-time, and computational requirements. Simulations show accurate two-dimensional angle and channel recovery in the tested settings, equal total pilot-symbol overhead in rigid-panel comparisons, improved steering-vector estimates as morphing diversity increases, and degradation as user loading or pilot correlation increases.
title: Multiuser Channel Estimation in FIM Systems: A Structured Block Term Decomposition Approach

summary: This record contains the anonymised data, codebook and supplementary material (Online Resource 1) for the article "Two kinds of content in one score: provision items and motivation items are near-independent in a Turkish adaptation of a zero-waste scale". Files: - Dataset.csv: responses of 495 university students and staff to the 32-item Turkish adaptation of a zero-waste scale (5-point Likert, 1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree), banded demographic variables, and four careless-responding flags. The variable in_analytic_sample = 1 marks the 455 respondents retained in the analytic sample. - Codebook.csv: definition of every variable, the published and retained factor allocation of each item, item provenance, and the English and Turkish (as administered) item wording. - Supplementary material.docx: Online Resource 1, Tables S1–S18 (careless-responding screens, parallel analysis, confirmatory model comparisons, group comparisons, sensitivity and equivalence analyses, demographic profile and item provenance). Respondent identifiers are sequential numbers assigned for this deposit and have no link to any person.
title: Dataset and supplementary material for: Two kinds of content in one score: provision items and motivation items are near-independent in a Turkish adaptation of a zero-waste scale

summary: This package contains the code, data, model outputs and results supporting the study on nighttime heat assessment of uncooled ResStock homes. It includes the timestamp-alignment analysis, the 357-home natural-ventilation gate decomposition and fixed-setpoint sensitivity (20-25 C), the paired three-day versus seven-day sensitivity simulations, the bldg445337 humidity-bypass check, and a one-command reproduction script. The package reproduces the paper's main statistics. The MF5+ upper-tail diagnosis requires external ResStock state metadata as described in the included provenance files. All materials are released under CC BY 4.0.
title: Nighttime heat assessment of uncooled ResStock homes: data and code for reproduction

summary: Code, raw and processed data, production sources, figure scripts, provenance and verification for temporal filtering, dispersive stiffness, compacton collisions, corrected generalized-alpha damping experiments, Jacobian scaling, robustness screens, coherent-core benchmarks and accuracy-cost tradeoffs.
title: Reproducibility code and data for Temporal filtering of dispersive stiffness in compacton collisions: coherent-scattering benchmarks and accuracy–cost tradeoffs

summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.
title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

summary: We study joint moments of characteristic polynomials and their second derivatives for Haar-distributed matrices from the unitary symplectic and orthogonal groups. We establish their large-$N$ asymptotics throughout the full admissible range of the moment parameters and identify the limiting coefficients probabilistically in terms of the first inverse power sum of the Bessel point process. This extends the corresponding results of Assiotis, Gunes, Keating, and Wei [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc., 132 (2026), e70136] to the full admissible parameter range. Throughout this full range, we also express these limits in terms of a distinguished solution of the $σ$-Painlevé III' equation. Our approach reduces the problem to singular inverse-power statistics of the Jacobi unitary ensemble and combines their finite-$N$ $σ$-Painlevé V representation with a refined Riemann-Hilbert analysis yielding precise small-$x$ asymptotics and uniform derivative estimates for the finite-$N$ correction term. A key ingredient in the probabilistic identification is a kernel-based proof that the rescaled first inverse power sum of the Jacobi ensemble converges in distribution to its Bessel point process counterpart.
title: Painlevé representations for joint moments of characteristic polynomials from the orthogonal and unitary symplectic groups

summary: The iron-based ferromagnetic materials have emerged as a promising system for spintronics due to their high Curie temperatures and significant anomalous Hall effect (AHE) driven by Berry curvature. While there have been investigations into the epitaxial growth of non-layered iron-based ferromagnetic materials, the realization of high-quality single crystal thin films continues to be a formidable obstacle. Meanwhile, the issues such as grain boundary scattering further hinder their characterization and application. Here, we report the first chemical vapor deposition (CVD) synthesis of single-crystalline cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge nanoplates. This compound represents a substantial departure from the conventional hexagonal phases typically observed in the Fe-Ge system. Structural characterizations confirm the cubic lattice and stoichiometric purity of the crystals. Structural analysis identifies a strong epitaxial effect, resulting in a giant compressive strain of ~4.16% at the interface that relaxes gradually toward the surface. The second-harmonic generation (SHG) signals might further reveal that such interfacial strain disrupted the inherent centro-symmetry of the cubic phase. SQUID magnetometry shows robust room-temperature ferromagnetism and clear magnetic anisotropy. Magneto-transport measurements reveal a robust AHE that remains stable at temperatures far exceeding room temperature. The scaling observed between the anomalous Hall resistance and longitudinal resistance strongly suggests that this effect is dominated by the intrinsic Berry curvature mechanism. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the huge epitaxial strain induces band reconstructions and creates dense spin-orbit coupling gaps near the Fermi level, effectively doubling the anomalous Hall conductivity to match our experimental observations.
title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge Nanoplates Grown by Chemical Vapor Deposition

summary: Driven by recent advancements in hearing assistive devices, target speaker extraction (TSE) in multi-talker environments has drawn significant attention. To address this, hearing technologies identify attention using neural signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG) to guide TSE, enabling neuro-steered auditory attention decoding. However, most existing techniques rely on time-frequency masking, which suffers from low fidelity in spectro-temporally overlapping regions and is often restricted to narrowband audio. In contrast, we introduce NeuroCodec, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative EEG-guided TSE framework operating in the latent space of a neural audio codec. Specifically, NeuroCodec models spatial EEG dependencies via graph convolutions and fuses cross-modal EEG and speech representations through attention mechanisms and Mamba-based temporal modeling. We further introduce a six-phase training curriculum that progressively incorporates latent reconstruction, multi-scale spectral, and adversarial objectives to ensure stable, high-fidelity speech generation. Experiments on the public Cocktail Party and KUL datasets show NeuroCodec outperforms baselines, across several perceptual metrics. A listening experiment with 20 participants validated that NeuroCodec offers greater perceptual accuracy, achieving a mean score of 82.24 compared with 49.63 for M3ANet. Additionally, the proposed method is seen to enable 44.1 kHz reconstruction with spectral content extending up to 20 kHz, further supporting the perceptual results. Finally, we extend NeuroCodec with a causal streaming formulation suited for real-time processing, providing a basis for hearing assistive devices.
title: NeuroCodec: EEG-Guided Latent-Domain Generative Model for High-Fidelity Target Speaker Extraction

summary: We explore the inverse problem of determining the reaction coefficient $q(x',t)$ in the time-fractional diffusion equation ${}^CD_t u-Lu+q(x',t)u=f$ in $\mathbb{R}^n\times(0,T]$, $x=(x',x_n)$, $0<α<1$, from the trace of the solution on the hyperplane $\{x_n=0\}$. Here ${}^CD_t$ is the Gerasimov--Caputo derivative and $L$ is a uniformly elliptic second-order operator with variable, $x_n$-independent coefficients and without zero-order term. For $L=Δ$ this problem was studied in dimensions $n=1,2,3$ by methods based on pointwise bounds of the kernels, which are not available for $n\ge4$. Our approach relies on the Eidelman--Kochubei fundamental solution: although its singularity on the diagonal depends on the dimension, we show that it satisfies integral bounds of the same form for all $n\ge1$. Using these bounds, we prove existence, uniqueness and stability of regular solutions of the direct problem with a Hölder continuous reaction coefficient. Without assuming additional smoothness of the solution, we show that the inverse problem is equivalent to a closed system of integral equations for $q$ and the derivatives $\partial_{x_n}u$, $\partial^2_{x_n}u$. For the inverse problem we establish a conditional Lipschitz stability estimate on the whole time interval and global uniqueness in every dimension, and prove local existence of a solution. In the case $a_{in}\equiv0$, $b_n\equiv0$ we obtain a stability estimate with explicit constants, which reduces to the known estimates for the Laplacian. An explicit two-dimensional example with a mixed coefficient and a normal drift shows that the hypotheses of the main theorems are compatible and that the corresponding terms in the trace condition cannot be omitted.
title: Recovering the reaction coefficient in a time-fractional diffusion equation with variable coefficients in any spatial dimension

summary: Conservatism in distributed stability certification is often treated as a limitation of the certificate itself, motivating richer Lyapunov functions, tighter relaxations, or stronger optimization. But a more fundamental limitation may arise from the reporting interface: once information is compressed, physically different systems can become indistinguishable. If stable and unstable systems produce the same report, no sound method can separate them. This paper asks where this information limit lies and how much additional information is needed to move it. We model information as an information structure that partitions admissible systems into information fibers. The strongest sound certificate for a fiber is determined by its smallest stability margin, yielding a method-independent benchmark. This separates total conservatism into information-induced and method-induced parts and characterizes information order, task sufficiency, and the stability value of additional information. Three network-node studies show that network-spectrum, scalar/eigenvalue-only passivity, and independent-local reports respectively lose network--node alignment, local directional alignment, and cross-node relation. They show that critical missing information is often relational rather than dimensional. We then move from diagnosis to information design. An information-conservatism frontier gives the smallest irreducible conservatism achievable under a prescribed budget, while its inverse gives the minimum information required for a target conservatism. A witness-pair characterization turns this into a weighted covering problem. Besides, a local sensitivity law provides a computable approximation and identifies valuable unresolved quantities. The framework indicates whether conservatism should be reduced by improving the certificate or enriching the information.
title: Information-Induced Conservatism Frontier of Distributed Stability Certificates

summary: We present \textit{ab initio} no-core shell-model calculations of the electric dipole ($E1$) polarizabilities and photoabsorption cross sections of the $A=3$ mirror nuclei $^3$H and $^3$He using the Daejeon16 nucleon-nucleon interaction. The polarizabilities are obtained by direct summation over discretized continuum states in the harmonic-oscillator basis, while the same spectral information is used to reconstruct the cross sections. This work provides the first extension of the approach from the spin-zero $^4$He to nonzero-spin nuclei by calculating the $1/2^-$ and $3/2^-$ final-state contributions separately and demonstrating their model-space convergence. In both nuclei, the $3/2^-$ contribution is approximately twice the $1/2^-$ contribution. After quantifying finite-basis and excitation-energy-truncation uncertainties, we identify a clear difference between the mirror polarizabilities, induced entirely by the Coulomb interaction because the Daejeon16 interaction is isospin symmetric. The reconstructed cross sections remain stable under variations of the inversion parameters of the Lorentz integral transform and exhibit the same angular-momentum hierarchy. These results extend the discretized-continuum approach to integrated and energy-resolved $E1$ observables in nonzero-spin nuclei with multiple final-state angular momenta.
title: \textit{Ab initio} no-core shell model calculations of the electric dipole polarizabilities and photoabsorption cross sections of the $A=3$ mirror nuclei

summary: The Vertex Silicon Plane (VSP), installed close to the target in BM@N Run 9, can extend the tracking acceptance of the central tracking system toward larger polar angles. Using Monte Carlo simulations of Xe+Sn collisions at 3 AGeV, we reconstruct short tracklets from the primary vertex, one VSP hit, and hits in the first two Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) stations. These tracklets extend the reconstructed primary-proton coverage toward midrapidity and higher transverse momenta. For the 10-30% centrality interval of the independent validation dataset, the conditional reconstruction efficiency for reconstructible high-$p_T$ primary protons after BDT selection is 67.0%, while the tracklet purity reaches 86.5%. For $p_T>1.2$ GeV/c, the VSP-assisted tracklets increase the number of reconstructed primary protons by 17.5% relative to standard BM@N tracking. Of these additional protons, 84.6% lie within $|y|<0.3$, where the relative reconstruction gain reaches 45.5%. The added acceptance is concentrated in the high-$p_T$, near-midrapidity region relevant for identified-proton observables. Its use in data requires particle identification in the same region.
title: Monte Carlo study of extending the BM@N tracking acceptance toward midrapidity with the Vertex Silicon Plane

summary: We consider uplink multiuser channel estimation for a generalized flexible intelligent metasurface at the base station, under narrowband far-field propagation and a twin-time-scale mechanical protocol: on the slow time-scale the panel translates rigidly over a planar grid, while on the fast time-scale the surface morphs along its normal direction. From orthogonal multiuser pilots, we show that each user's channel admits a fourth-order canonical polyadic tensor structure. We develop two complementary estimators: alternating least squares factorization followed by paired rotational-invariance wavevector extraction, and a tensor spatial-smoothing multiple signal classification estimator that preserves the multilinear array manifold. Both share a minimum description length front-end for automatic tensor-rank detection. We derive Kruskal identifiability conditions that relate the numbers of elements, morphing states and grid positions to the maximum number of recoverable multipath components, and show that the tensor model reconstructs the channel at panel configurations beyond the training grid. This prediction capability drives a configuration-selective multiuser transmit precoder that searches the entire motion grid without additional pilot overhead. Numerical results confirm the identifiability limits and show that, once the model order is resolved, the configuration search makes the same choice from estimated as from perfect channel state information. The reconfiguration gain over a fixed panel of identical aperture and training budget grows with the user load, and fast morphing proves valuable for conditioning the tensor factorization rather than as a source of beamforming gain.
title: Training-Efficient Channel Estimation for the Multiuser Uplink Relying on Generalized Flexible Intelligent Metasurfaces

summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.
title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty

summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies

summary: Understanding failures of autonomous systems is challenging, particularly when their behavior depends on black-box components such as neural networks. In this work, we make a distinction between two objectives of failure analysis: reproduction, which seeks to identify conditions sufficient to reproduce an observed failure, and avoidance, which seeks to identify the changes required to prevent it. Previous work on causal explanations of system failures is based on the concept of sufficient explanations and naturally supports reproduction. Nevertheless, we observe that it does not address the problem of avoiding the failure. In this paper, we introduce and formalize the concept of necessary explanations for system analysis as the correct formalism for failure avoidance. We place necessary explanations in the framework of actual causality and show that, together with sufficient explanations, they provide a unified causal framework for addressing both objectives of failure analysis. We present an efficient approximation algorithm for generating necessary explanations based on the notion of causal responsibility. We evaluate the efficiency of our approach across multiple environments. We demonstrate the practical utility of necessary explanations for failure avoidance through counterfactual generation and show that it outperforms existing methods.
title: Sufficient and Necessary Causal Explanations for the Analysis of Autonomous Systems

summary: Diffusion language models generate by iteratively denoising a masked sequence under bidirectional attention, without the strict left-to-right commitment of autoregressive decoding. Whether this difference affects how reliably they remain grounded in structured inputs is largely unexplored. We study this question in table-to-text generation using ToTTo, where highlighted source cells make factual grounding directly testable. We compare the masked diffusion models MDLM and LLaDA with GPT-2 and GPT-Neo under an identical retrieval-based few-shot protocol, together with a QLoRA-adapted LLaDA, and we score reference similarity and source grounding as separate axes. The two pull apart. Within LLaDA, additional demonstrations raise BLEU from 11.3 to 22.0 while NLI entailment against the source table falls from 0.78 to 0.52; QLoRA reaches the best BLEU of the study, 24.15, and grounds no better for it. Manual annotation shows the failure modes differ in kind: the autoregressive baselines tend to wander off the table, while LLaDA-based models more often stay on topic and swap out individual entities. Reference-based metrics alone are insufficient to assess faithfulness in table-to-text generation.
title: A Diagnostic Study of Faithfulness in Diffusion Language Models for Table-to-Text Generation

summary: Experimental outputs for manuscript "Beyond Viewpoint Affinity: Measuring Political Bias in LLMs as a Failure of Epistemic Consistency" Political bias in large language models is often measured by treating responses to political questionnaires as evidence of ideological preference. This approach can conflate bias with differences in evidential support: asymmetric viewpoint preferences are not necessarily biased if one side is better supported by the available evidence. We explore a different facet of political bias: failures of epistemic consistency, in which models apply different evidentiary or evaluative standards to substantively equivalent items that carry different political cues. We operationalize this definition in two sets of experimental tasks. In person-attribution tasks, models evaluate nonpolitical items—such as mathematical proofs, logical arguments, or artistic artifacts---while only the political identity of the person associated with the item changes. In politicized-context tasks, models judge politically framed items, such as research designs, news articles, or policy outcomes, while partisan sources, group identities, or the left–right valence of the substantive outcome change. Across thirty LLMs, person-attribution tasks yield only modest left-leaning asymmetry—and this bias shrinks toward zero in more capable models. By contrast, politicized-context tasks yield large left-leaning asymmetries that do not shrink with model capability. Debiasing interventions---such as increasing reasoning effort, system prompts that emphasize epistemic rigor, and explicit instructions to ignore specific political cues—mitigate bias, but only partially. These results suggest that current LLMs show little bias based on an individual’s political identity when evaluating nonpolitical or politically orthogonal items. However, on politicized-context tasks, LLMs are persistently biased by task-irrelevant political cues, even when the relevant evidence is objectively assessable or held constant across political variants. Note: A previous version of the  experimental_results  archive contained partial and incomplete outputs for the legacy OpenAI model  gpt-4-0613 from 2023 . These results were not included in the analyses reported in the paper. The run was stopped partway through after we observed that this older model was incurring excessive API costs. As of April 2026, the input/output costs per 1M tokens of gpt-4-0613 were 30\$ and 60\$ respectively (between one and several orders of magnitude higher than newer OpenAI models used in the study, see: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4).  Completing the full benchmark for  gpt-4-0613 would have caused the project to exceed its compute budget, so we created a new version of the experimental outputs archive with those incomplete files for gpt-4-0613 removed. In the code repository (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/llms_epistemic_consistency-D133/README.md) associated with this experimental output there is the following bug for the Debiasing interventions using system prompts ("centrist" and "epistemically rigorous") experiment, which does not affect the experimental results but affects one field of the meta information saved to the CSV files  In vpei/epistemic_consistency/experiment_types.py, all six run_model functions build a payload dict before the API call: payload = {     "system_prompt": system_prompt,   # ← saves the BASE prompt only       ... } messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}, ...] tasks.append((payload, make_llm_request_async(model_name, messages, ...))) Then inside make_llm_request_async → prepare_request_params() (llm_requests_v3.py:309–314), the system_prompt_prefix (EPISTEMICALLY_RIGOROUS_LLM_SYSTEM_PROMPT) is prepended to the system message after the payload is already constructed. So: - LLM API receives: EPISTEMICALLY_RIGORO
