summary: Features GM-rPIE and GM-MAGPIE reconstruction Added geometric-mean rPIE and multigrid MAGPIE reconstruction through MAGPIEOptions and Reconstructors.MAGPIE . Set reconstructor_options.multigrid_levels = 1 for GM-rPIE or a larger valid depth for GM-MAGPIE. Added joint synthesis of object and shared-probe updates from random minibatches, with native gradient-based position correction and post-epoch constraints. Each additional multigrid level halves both spatial dimensions using 2-by-2 block averaging. The initial implementation supports a single object slice, a single coherent shared probe, matching object/probe/detector sampling, and patch-based object sampling. Both object and probe are updated on every minibatch. Setup validates the supported configuration, multigrid depth, and initial guesses, including the requirement for nonzero amplitude at every object pixel. Full-object sampling for near-field ptychography Added ForwardModelOptions.shift_operator with ShiftOperators.AUTO , PATCH , and FULL_OBJECT . The default AUTO selects full-object sampling when the propagation distance is finite and both probe dimensions strictly exceed 80% of the corresponding object dimensions on the probe pixel grid. Set PATCH to explicitly select patch extraction and placement. Added periodic shifting of complete object slices, followed by a fixed center crop or zero-padding to match the probe shape. Fourier, bilinear, and nearest interpolation are supported, with matching additive adjoints. Features crossing an object boundary wrap to the opposite side. Integrated full-object sampling into AD, BH, DM, LSQML, PIE, and RAAR reconstruction, including object/probe resampling, illumination maps, and position derivatives. Fourier or bilinear interpolation supports gradient-based position refinement; nearest interpolation has zero position derivatives almost everywhere. DM and RAAR use stabilized normalized-adjoint updates for full-object sampling. These are approximate projections for fractional interpolation, so convergence can differ from patch sampling. Bug fixes Corrected the adjoint of image shifting with replicated edge padding and applied the matching padding to analytical probe updates, preserving contributions from boundary pixels. Corrected the object smoothness kernel by placing its central weight at the center of the 3-by-3 stencil. Clarified that smoothing acts on the real and imaginary components of each object slice. Corrected support-based object position origins to use ceil(size / 2) - 0.5 , fixing inconsistent centering for odd object sizes. Fixed a probe-position update crash when clip_update_magnitude_by_mad is disabled and a user-specified update limit is configured. Updated probe rescaling and object-preconditioner initialization to account for the detector propagator's intensity normalization. rescale_probe() and get_probe_renormalization_factor() now accept a propagator argument, retaining the unnormalized far-field Fourier transform as the default. Added ptychi.propagate.get_intensity_scaling_factor() for converting between source- and detector-plane intensity sums under lossless propagation. Added setuptools as an explicit runtime dependency.

summary: Supplementary data for "OpenScientist: evaluating an open agentic AI co-scientist to accelerate biomedical discovery." This dataset contains research logs, knowledge states, provenance files, and generated figures for seven case studies spanning neurodegenerative disease transcriptomics, multiple myeloma genomics, survival proteomics, drug side effect analysis, and more. Each case study includes the full agent iteration log, configuration, and final report. Input datasets are included for three case studies where data sharing is permitted: case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics), case study 4 (multiple myeloma RNA-seq), and case study 7 (drug side effect frequencies from clinical trials).  Version 2 (August 2026) adds supplementary material for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics): 60 additional independent runs of the same question and dataset, comparing three agent/model configurations — Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8, and the omp harness with Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 — each run 10 times online and 10 times in a fully air-gapped configuration with no network access and literature served from a local 40-million-article MEDLINE mirror. Files: ..._supplemental_online_30runs_data.tar.gz and ..._supplemental_airgapped_30runs_data.tar.gz each contain 30 runs with reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), all generated figures, per-iteration transcripts, the exact prompt, and full version/commit provenance. ..._supplemental_60runs_metrics.csv gives per-run runtime, tool-call counts, literature searches, findings recorded and token usage for all 60 runs. Version 3 (September 2026) adds two further supplementary sets for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics). ..._supplemental_reproducibility_10runs_data.tar.gz contains 10 independent runs of the same question on Claude Opus 4.6, all run on 2026-03-08 with byte-identical inputs (the research question and the input .h5ad were SHA-256 verified identical across all 10) and a 10-iteration budget. Each run includes the report (Markdown, PDF, HTML), knowledge_state.json with structured findings and literature list, per-iteration transcripts, and the job UUID. These runs quantify run-to-run variability under fixed inputs. ..._supplemental_genomic_skill_comparison_data.tar.gz contains 30 runs — 15 using the original genomics Agent Skill and 15 using a revised version — with the two skill definitions included alongside the jobs. The revised skill adds explicit guidance on donor-level pseudobulk aggregation and mixed-effect modelling; the paired arms allow the effect of that guidance on the analysis the agent chooses to be assessed directly. Each run includes reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), per-iteration provenance transcripts, and container logs. Version 4 (October 2026) adds the run sets generated for the second revision of the manuscript, renumbers the case-study files to match the revised manuscript (the suvorexant proteomics analysis is now Case Study 5; neurofibromatosis is Case Study 6, drug side effects Case Study 7, and the CSF Aβ42/40 prediction model Case Study 8), and adds RUNS_MANIFEST.csv , which maps every job in this record to its experiment, supplementary table and row label. Run IDs quoted in the supplementary tables are the first 8 hexadecimal characters of the job ID. New archives, all for Case Study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics; same research question and input file as the existing archives, OpenScientist commit fac6971, Claude Opus 4.6, run 2026-10-18 with a 10-iteration budget): ..._supplemental_iteration_controls_10runs_data.tar.gz (10 replicate runs on unmodified code; Experiment 4 and the control arm of the two ablations), ..._supplemental_knowledge_state_ablation_10runs_data.tar.gz (10 runs in which the knowledge-state summary and outline were withheld from the agent; Experiment 5; the patched orchestrator file is included as ..._knowledge_state_ablation_iteration.py.patched ), and ..._supp

summary: This record holds the data and analysis code underlying the manuscript “Temperature Response of Intrinsic Viscosity in Methacrylate and Hydrocarbon Viscosity Modifiers: A Harmonized Analysis of Published Data” (submitted for publication). The manuscript is not included here. The deposit contains: (1) Supplementary_Dataset_S1.xlsx, the harmonized evidence workbook of 32 worksheets, holding the source registry, the lineage audit, the intrinsic-viscosity observations with chemistry and architecture codes and molecular-weight provenance flags, the per-system temperature slopes, the direct-compatibility records with multiplicity weights, the chemistry-by-architecture coding table, the wax-window analysis, and all model outputs, with source-level provenance on every quantitative record; (2) Supplementary_Dataset_S2_Figure_Data.xlsx, giving the input and plotted values for every figure; (3) Supplementary_Software_S1.zip, the complete Python analysis pipeline with README.md, requirements.txt and MANIFEST.txt, which reads only the two workbooks and regenerates every reported table and figure; and (4) README.md and LICENSE.txt for the record. To reproduce: download all files into one folder, unzip Supplementary_Software_S1.zip, install the packages listed in requirements.txt, and run the following command from inside the Supplementary_Software_S1 folder: python reproduce_all.py --data ../Supplementary_Dataset_S1.xlsx --figdata ../Supplementary_Dataset_S2_Figure_Data.xlsx --out results The pipeline regenerates the one-stage mixed-effects model with publication and system random effects (methacrylate-minus-ethylene-propylene temperature interaction of +0.646 ln units per 100 °C, 95% CI 0.433 to 0.858), the system-slope regressions with wild cluster bootstrap inference (+0.775, p = 0.005), the wax cut-off sensitivity scan, the multiplicity-weighted cross-study compatibility model with chance-level comparisons, the domain-restricted ordinal phase model, and Figures 1–5 and S1. All resampling uses seed 20260918. A full run takes about one hour; adding --bootstrap 500 --reml-bootstrap 49 gives a fast check with identical point estimates. The study is a secondary analysis of published data; no new experiments were performed. Values in the exact-value core were taken from tables or explicit numerical statements in the cited sources, and figure-derived values are excluded from that core. Architecture is recorded as reported by the source authors and is not a measured quantity. The analysis code was prepared with the assistance of a large language model (Claude, Anthropic); all outputs and analytical decisions were checked by the author. Contact: Ziyad T. AL-Malki, Polymer Research Center, University of Basrah, Iraq ( ziyad.falak@uobasrah.edu.iq ; ORCID 0000-0002-5137-6660).
title: Supporting data and code for "Temperature Response of Intrinsic Viscosity in Methacrylate and Hydrocarbon Viscosity Modifiers: A Harmonized Analysis of Published Data"

summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). The pooled robustness estimate (Δ = 0.25 → 0.46; d = 0.68; the primary main-wave cohort gives Δ = 0.24 → 0.45, d = 0.67) rests on that single item and, in an exploratory country split, on the UK sample, and it falls to d = 0.09 once the item is removed. A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. The orchestration-receipt component returned a registered, inconclusive null. The three com
title: Architectural Trust: Why Consumer Trust in Agentic Commerce Migrates from AI Models to Verifiable Architecture

summary: la versione 5  documenta riprende la versione 1 e la versione 3 e la versione 4  chiude il ciclo aperto dalla V4 e ne sostituisce integralmente i risultati numerici. Il documento riporta cinque punti fisici verificati sul modello a 240 nm (P1–P5), uno studio sistematico della scala da 1 nm a 1 m (S1–S4), la caratteriz zazione in microgravità e per tre classi di materiale (SP1–SP5), la simulazione dei fluidi con i due rotori come ostacoli (F1–F2) e il regime di vuoto profondo con assenza di attrito (V1–V5). La coppia ottica è trattata con un solo modello, il momento angolare ceduto dal fascio: τ = Pass/ωott = Fλ/2π = 2.610×10−24 N·m, cioè 108volte menodellimiteafasciointero P/ωott = 2.824×10−22 N·m, che coincide con la τmax dichiarata nella V4 (2.826×10−22). Poiché Per = τ/kT, il criterio di determinismo si riduce a un rapporto di potenze: Per = Pass/15.16 µW. Con 1 µW e l’intercettazione reale dello 0.924 % si ottiene 6.10×10−4 a 240 nm, 1.93×10−14 a 1 nm e 6.60×10−2 a 1 m: il dispositivo è termicamente limitato a ogni scala, e la soglia Per = 1 richiede 1.64 mW. A 1 GHz la configurazione in rameè strutturalmente impossibile(limite 72.6MHz). Nelvuotoprofondononesisteregimestazionario: esisteuntempocritico di rottura, che la scala governa (30.53 s a 240 nm, 2.538×1024 s a 1 m, un fattore 8.3×1022), mentre il materiale governa la velocità di rottura (31.909) e l’energia immagazzinata (250). Nessuna validazione sperimentale è rivendicata: ogni cifra è prodotta dagli script in Appendice A. Document version 5 build s upon versions 1, 3, and 4; it concludes the cycle initiated by version 4 and entirely replaces its numerical results. The document presents: five physical points verified on the 240 nm model (P1–P5); a systematic study across scales ranging from 1 nm to 1 m (S1–S4); characterization in microgravity for three classes of materials (SP1–SP5); fluid simulations with the two rotors acting as obstacles (F1–F2); and the deep-vacuum regime in the absence of friction (V1–V5). Optical torque is addressed using a single model—the angular momentum transferred by the beam: τ = Pass/ωott = Fλ/2π = 2.610×10⁻²⁴ N·m. This value is 10⁸ times smaller than the limit for a full beam (P/ωott = 2.824×10⁻²² N·m), which aligns with the τmax stated in version 4 (2.826×10⁻²²). Since Per = τ/kT, the criterion for determinism simplifies to a ratio of powers: Per = Pass/15.16 µW. With an input of 1 µW and an actual interception rate of 0.924%, the resulting values are 6.10×10⁻⁴ at 240 nm, 1.93×10⁻¹⁴ at 1 nm, and 6.60×10⁻² at 1 m. The device is thus thermally limited at every scale, and reaching the threshold of Per = 1 requires 1.64 mW. At 1 GHz, the copper-based configuration is structurally impossible (the limit is 72.6 MHz). In a high vacuum, no steady state exists; instead, there is a critical time to failure, which is governed by the scale (30.53 s at 240 nm, 2.538×10²⁴ s at 1 m—a factor of 8.3×10²²), while the material determines the rate of failure (31.909) and the stored energy (250). No experimental validation is claimed: every figure is generated by the scripts in Appendix A.

summary: Supplementary material for the paper "Business-Rule Admissibility in Process-Based Business Simulation" (Yan Fang, University of Southern California). It holds what is needed to check and reproduce the paper's results without the simulation framework: the study firm's handbook and the model's prose; the rule sets R (104 rules) and R0 (82 rules), each rule with the passage it formalises and its SQL query; the specification of every re-injected defect; the protocols of the pre-registered replication, the control rule set, the further mutants and the robust indicator score, with the hashes they froze; the instructions given to each agent and path-level records of each agent's file access; the scripts that apply the rules and compute the indicators, event-log distances and tables; and the databases and change histories of all 430 simulation runs. The simulation framework (NAILU) and the model's intermediate representation are proprietary to Aurite AI and are not included. Files: README.md (contents, and how to reproduce the tables), SHA256SUMS (the hash of every file), materials.zip, and three archives of runs (exploratory seeds 1–10; confirmatory seeds 11–30; further mutants, seeds 11–30). Unzip all archives into one folder next to README.md and SHA256SUMS; sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS then verifies the package.
title: Supplementary material: Business-Rule Admissibility in Process-Based Business Simulation

summary: This paper resolves the foundational deadlock of classical General Relativity metric engineering—namely, the requirement for unphysical, stellar-scale quantities of negative energy in models such as the Alcubierre warp drive. The bottleneck is shown to stem directly from the standard treatment of spacetime as an incompressible, geometrically rigid continuum. By reformulating the problem within Quantum Modified General Relativity (QMOGER) and Gordon’s optical metric, the vacuum is modeled as an active, compressible, barotropic superfluid. Consequently, the energy threshold required for propulsive metric modulation is governed by the polarizability of the quantum electrodynamic (QED) electron-positron vacuum rather than Planck-scale geometric stiffness, reducing the required energy barrier by more than twenty orders of magnitude. Key Mechanisms: Pressure-Driven Dynamic Casimir Effect: Rather than introducing exotic negative mass, the system leverages relativistic optical phase modulation driven by ultra-short laser bursts. Non-adiabatic boundary modulation converts virtual vacuum fluctuations into real photons, generating multi-megabar non-equilibrium radiation pressure spikes and steep spatial gradients while keeping total integrated pulse energy minimal. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) Structural Stabilization: To prevent three-dimensional turbulent enstrophy cascades from tearing the metric envelope apart, an external toroidal magnetic field is applied. At high interaction parameters, field-parallel velocity gradients are extinguished by anisotropic Joule dissipation, collapsing the flow into a quasi-two-dimensional regime. This eliminates vortex stretching and triggers an inverse energy cascade, causing microscopic injected energy to naturally self-organize into a stable, macroscopic warp envelope. Nonlinear QED Dielectric Phase Transition: Incorporating the Heisenberg–Euler effective Lagrangian under high magnetic fields, the vacuum exhibits intensity-dependent birefringence. At a critical relative intensity threshold, the vacuum undergoes a sharp dielectric phase transition that initiates direct macroscopic momentum coupling between the electromagnetic field and the vacuum substrate. Conclusion & Experimental Relevance: The manuscript replaces astronomical negative-mass speculation with concrete non-equilibrium quantum optical and magnetohydrodynamic processes. It provides closed tensor field equations, complete dimensional consistency, and a realistic experimental roadmap testable at high-intensity petawatt laser and high-field superconducting magnet facilities.
title: COMPRESSIBLE SPACETIME, NONLINEAR OPTICS, AND RELATIVISTIC METRIC ENGINEERING

summary: LaTeX source, figures, check program and Lean 4 file of the paper Weak-Type Endpoint Bounds for Bochner-Riesz Means in Every Dimension by Deep Bhattacharjee. At the critical index lambda(p) = n(1/p - 1/2) - 1/2, the Bochner-Riesz means (1 - |xi|^a/t^a)^lambda_+ in every dimension n >= 2 map L^p to weak L^p for 1 < p < 2n/(n+1), uniformly in t, and converge in weak L^p (Theorem A); they have (p,q) sparse bounds for (n-1)p/(n+1-2p) < q < p', which is sharp on the critical side of the trapezoid of Beltran, Roos and Seeger except at its corner (Theorem B); and they map L^p(w) to weak L^p(w) for every A_1 weight w in RH_sigma when 1 < p < 1 + (n-1)/(n+1)(1 - 1/sigma) (Theorem C), a range that by the self-improvement of reverse Hoelder inequalities includes its right end point. For n >= 3 these follow from OpenAI's preprint 'Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation' (25 October 2026), which proves the local smoothing and Bochner-Riesz conjectures, through the conditional theorems of Tao and of Beltran, Roos and Seeger. The paper reproduces OpenAI's argument and the epsilon-removal of Beltran, Roos and Seeger in full, with credit, and then applies their sparse domination theorem and the weighted theorem of Frey and Nieraeth. The Python program checks the algebraic identities and exponent computations; the Lean file proves the exponent arithmetic and the quaternion identities. No statement of the paper depends on them.
title: Source and verification code for the paper Weak-Type Endpoint Bounds for Bochner-Riesz Means in Every Dimension

summary: CrysPy is a Python library for the analysis of polarized and unpolarized neutron diffraction and X-ray diffraction data of powders and single crystals: nuclear and magnetic structure refinement, local magnetic susceptibility, and spin and magnetization density reconstruction by the maximum entropy method.
title: CrysPy: crystallographic library for polarized and unpolarized neutron diffraction data analysis

summary: An open coordination layer for AI research, experimentation and reproducibility. Connecting existing tools through bounded agent tasks, provenance, evaluation receipts and verifiable workflows, with an initial focus on open-model research.
title: DerekWiner/alvearium-commons

summary: Early-warning models in learning analytics can identify learners at risk of failure or withdrawal, but the resulting alerts are often only weakly connected to inspectable learning evidence. A risk score may indicate that intervention is needed without showing which traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the alert. This paper introduces an incremental Learner Digital Twin for evidence-grounded early warning, implemented as a lightweight knowledge graph. The twin is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying learning traces and assessment records, and it serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as an explanation-grounding substrate. Predictive features are derived through graph-mediated queries, while features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records are represented as queryable graph entities. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol. The results show that graph-mediated feature extraction preserves the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints. Generated alerts are materialized as evidence chains linking risk decisions to feature attributions, evidence items, and raw platform records. The study shows that early-warning prediction can be routed through a semantic and provenance-aware representation while preserving predictive performance and adding traceability, verifiability, and evidence-grounded explanation.
title: An Incremental Knowledge-Graph Learner Digital Twin for Evidence-Grounded Early Warning

summary: Security pipelines often fuse several data sources and protect a downstream model with a cross-source anomaly detector. Such detectors are usually judged by their clean false-positive rate and by how well they catch random corruption. Neither metric captures an adversary who controls some sources and targets a specific downstream decision. We propose a threat-quantification score, the \emph{task-conditioned visibility margin}, defined as the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task. The margin has a closed form, takes about $85\,μ$s per certificate, yields a minimum-evidence attack, and identifies task-relevant directions the detector cannot see. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector that flags 82.8\% of random single-channel corruptions is first-order blind on 64.7\% of task/subset pairs in an audit of one- to four-channel subsets. Task-conditioned manipulations cause more than twice as many falsely reassuring errors as generic stealthy ones, and more of them evade the alarm on four of five splits, mainly at small budgets. Used to prioritize audits on held-out subsets, the margin finds a median of four verified failures in ten checks, compared with none for random order and two for alarm-based ranking, and performs comparably to the task-gradient baseline. It also ranks vulnerable configurations of the learned GDN and TranAD detectors and of a five-source crop-yield panel.
title: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors

summary: Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents. These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE). PCE distils task records and modification histories from the population into a population block, which captures recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of previously attempted modifications to guide improvements to a selected parent's harness. Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points. In our evaluation, PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by one-third on SWE-bench and closes it on Polyglot. These results suggest that treating the population as evidence--not merely as candidates for selection--provides a complementary principle for agent evolution.
title: The View from Nowhere: Population-Centered Agent Evolution

summary: The landscape of software evolution is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift in the era of Large Language Models. As industrial software engineering increasingly transitions toward design-driven code generation, the bottleneck of evolution has shifted from writing code to maintaining deterministic consistency between multi-source design assets and the generated code. When a design asset changes, LLM agents currently lack a deterministic impact boundary to identify which code must be evolved, leading to two failure modes: hallucinating missing changes or breaking unrelated code. Probabilistic approaches, such as semantic retrieval or text-based diffing, fail to capture the structural ripple effects across highly interconnected design dependencies. We propose a paradigm shift from probabilistic semantic retrieval to deterministic structural constraints. We formalize the design assets as a Knowledge Graph and organize them into a content-addressed Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph. Our key insight reveals a topological isomorphism between the logical ripple effect of a design change and the content hash propagation within the DAG. By leveraging this, we transform ambiguous impact analysis into verifiable structural operations. Through a two-phase diffing process, we extract a precise causal chain that defines the exact modification boundary. This boundary enables deterministic context injection, providing the LLM agent with strictly scoped code and design updates, thereby fundamentally guaranteeing evolution safety. As a by-product, the KG serves as an agent-queryable knowledge base for natural language design retrieval. Early deployment on a large-scale industrial payment platform demonstrates that our mechanism successfully computes the exact impact boundary and generates incremental code modifications that meet the expected design changes.
title: From Ripple to Boundary: Deterministic Impact Boundaries for LLM-Based Software Evolution

summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

summary: Benchmarks for verifiable code generation usually test a proof against one fixed implementation. We ask whether the same proof remains valid after a program refactoring that preserves behavior. We introduce RefactorProof, which derives 458 Lean-certified variants from the 185 VERINA tasks that compile in our pinned environment while holding the specification and evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. VERINA supplies reference proofs for 46 tasks, all from its basic split; the primary model-versus-reference comparisons further match on 21-25 short, non-recursive tasks. Structural refactorings expose substantial brittleness across proof sources: task-normalized structural PSR is 4.3% for the supplied references and 13.3-26.8% for the specialized provers. On the matched tasks, specialized prover proofs nevertheless have higher overall unchanged-proof survival than the supplied reference artifacts: +15.6 points for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, +18.8 for Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and +20.3 for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B; all three 95% CIs exclude zero. The ordering persists after excluding universally survived T1 variants, under family-balanced aggregation, and under alternative deployable valid-proof selection rules. However, unchanged-proof failure is not the same as high repair cost: predefined one-identifier edits repair 51/54 eligible reference structural failures and 58/85 eligible prover failures. RefactorProof therefore measures unchanged-proof stability under program refactoring, not the cost of maintaining a proof after it breaks.
title: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation

summary: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning uses offline pretraining to accelerate subsequent online learning. While many methods assume the offline dataset remains available throughout fine-tuning, there are many settings where this is not the case. Prior work attributes failures in this setting primarily to critic recalibration under distribution shift. We identify a complementary actor-side failure: once the offline data disappears, continued behavioral cloning (BC) no longer preserves the offline behavior distribution and instead refits the behavioral model to the agent's limited, and nonstationary, online experience. We demonstrate that stopping online behavioral fitting while preserving the pretrained expressive prior substantially improves no-retention fine-tuning across implicit flow Q-learning (IFQL), flow Q-learning (FQL), and action-chunked RL (QC) on seven OGBench domains. We trace this failure to a behavioral feedback loop: continuing online behavioral cloning rapidly erases the pretrained prior, inducing representational collapse and action diversity loss that starves the critic of useful exploration. Freezing the prior breaks this cycle, preserving offline coverage while allowing value learning to drive continuous improvement.
title: Freeze, Don't Clone: Fine-Tuning with Expressive Policies Without Retaining Offline Data

summary: This repository provides the source code, simulation datasets, computational benchmarks, numerical results, and reproducibility materials supporting Paper I of the Principle of Representation Integration for Stable Models (PRISM-M), prepared for the Journal of Computational Neuroscience . PRISM-M V4 is a minimal recurrent computational framework organized around five functional operations: Extraction, Compression, Integration, Stabilization, and Prediction/Action (ECISP). The implementation uses a single independently evolving recurrent state, with finite-precision quantization and explicitly defined information-processing transformations. The framework is intended to examine the functional organization of information processing, contextual integration, and memory stabilization within established recurrent and state-space dynamics. The repository includes the frozen V4 implementation, mathematical definitions, parameter configurations, experimental protocols, random seeds, simulation trajectories, statistical analyses, and comparative benchmarks involving autoregressive models (ARX), Kalman filtering, and recurrent neural networks. The deposited materials document the original parameter-landscape and stability analyses, targeted perturbation experiments, memory-retention studies (M1–M5), and additional computational experiments (V1–V5) evaluating noise robustness, adaptability, recovery, interference resistance, and information recoverability. Additional validation materials include information-matched representation controls, intrinsic-noise sensitivity analyses, and mathematical verification of contraction and perturbation equivalence. These retrospective analyses are distinguished from the original experimental protocols. The repository also contains the numerical datasets, figure files, supplementary materials, execution instructions, software dependencies, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks associated with Figures 1–6 and Supplementary Figures S1–S4. Computational reproduction and numerical verification have been performed for the principal analyses. Complete automated regeneration of all final publication artwork and independent cross-platform verification remain outside the scope of the completed checks. The purpose of this deposit is to facilitate independent evaluation, computational reproduction, and further investigation of the PRISM-M V4 framework. The model is a theoretical computational implementation and does not constitute direct biological validation or demonstrate a new class of recurrent dynamics.
title: PRISM-M V4: Source Code, Simulation Data, Computational Benchmarks, and Reproducibility Materials for Paper I

summary: American states already hold the constitutional authority to check, prosecute, and outlast a captured federal government. The architecture has always been there. Scholarship on federalism and democratic backsliding has accurately described why subnational opposition to authoritarian federal measures tends to fail: states deploy individual tools in isolation, get outmaneuvered, and lose. What that scholarship has not provided is a unified taxonomy of the tools themselves or the recognition that they constitute an architecture that, when assembled deliberately and deployed concurrently, produces something qualitatively different from any single tool applied alone. Each of these postures has existed throughout American constitutional history. What the literature has never provided is the recognition that they constitute discrete categorical tiers within a single deployable architecture. This paper names and maps that taxonomy across five tiers. Tier Zero is cooperative federalism, the assumed ground state requiring no deliberation. Tier One, uncooperative federalism, describes governments withholding cooperation from federal enforcement, a category Bulman-Pozen and Gerken named in 2009. Tier Two, soft secession, describes states building parallel institutional and financial capacity that reduces dependence on federal partnership and builds resilience against federal mismanagement, corruption, and captured law. Tier Three, oppositional federalism, describes governmental actors at any level using sovereign powers offensively to confront and impose direct personal costs on federal officials and institutions, including through criminal prosecution under state law for offenses that are unpardonable by a corrupt federal executive. Tier Four is constitutional non-compliance, the condition at which states actively do the thing the federal government has prohibited, constructing competing legal regimes that directly contradict specific federal law as a matter of explicit state policy, with documented historical precedent across the political spectrum. The architecture is tier-modular, domain-modular, and actor-modular. A mayor, a city council, a state attorney general, a governor, or a state legislature can move from Tier Zero directly to Tier Three in a single session without prerequisites; any tier is independently deployable without activating the others; and any governmental actor can occupy different tiers simultaneously across different policy domains. Full concurrent deployment produces the constitutional infrastructure specifically suited to the failure mode the existing literature identifies but has not prescribed for: authoritarian federal capture by actors engaged in the systematic dismantling of democratic governance and the rule of law. The doctrinal foundation draws on dual sovereignty, the anti-commandeering doctrine, intergovernmental immunity, and the Tenth Amendment's structural reservation of sovereign authority to the states, doctrines consistently applied across two and a half centuries of American constitutional law because they reflect the Constitution's design rather than any particular political moment. Notably, the anti-commandeering doctrine at the architecture's foundation was built by conservative jurisprudence for entirely different purposes. Justice Scalia wrote Printz to protect states from federal gun control mandates. The doctrine he articulated does not ask which political faction is deploying it. They enable every tier of this framework, from refusing federal cooperation to prosecuting federal officials, without federal permission, federal oversight, or presidential interference. The framework does not conflict with the Supremacy Clause, which governs conflicts between state and federal regulatory regimes and has never been understood to immunize federal officials from state criminal liability for conduct that violates state law, to compel states to assist federal enforcement, or to displace the paralle
title: THE CONSTITUTIONAL ARCHITECTURE OF STATE OPPOSITION

summary: Reproducible finite-sample analysis of append-only copying in conformal calibration. The project contains five public regression benchmarks, three fixed model families, 30 random splits, six copying mechanisms, three coverage targets, independent score simulations, and exhaustive rank checks. It compares rowwise, source-ID, copy-budget, and effective-sample-size calibration, and quantifies coverage-width trade-offs under incomplete provenance.
title: How Copies Break Conformal Prediction

summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.
title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?

summary: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

summary: Log messages are employed to identify anomalies in IoT systems and have been widely used across many applications. To enable collaboration among infrastructures belonging to different organizations, federated log anomaly detection has been thoroughly investigated for this purpose, often assuming the availability of ground truth log templates. However, this is typically not the case, as it is still necessary to depend on log parsers to extract log templates at inference time, while the design and deployment of such parsers in distributed environments remains largely an open problem. To this end, we report on an empirical investigation of distributed parsing and its key challenges, providing insights and lessons learned towards closing the gap between research and application. To further refine and contextualize the resulting benchmarks, we examine and introduce new metrics that provide a more comprehensive view for evaluating distributed parsers and how they behave in distributed environments. We propose a set of lessons learned and recommendations to support the design, deployment, and evaluation of distributed parsers. In particular, we evaluate the performance of five distinct parsing algorithms in combination with aggregation techniques that allow a unified agreement of event-template mappings across all participating clients, a prerequisite for federated log anomaly detection. In total, 6,720 distinct distributed configurations were tested for this purpose.
title: Too many clients spoil the logs: distributed parsing, aggregation techniques and metrics

summary: Machine learning recommendations are often evaluated one model at a time, despite deployment across interconnected decision makers. For continuous NPK fertilizer prescriptions, correlated errors can aggregate across farms and generate systemic costs. A model of shared and farm-specific recommendation errors links expected social loss to model adoption shares; the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index characterizes concentration effects when common model errors are independent and predictive risks are equal. A covariance-generalized formulation captures the dependence between model families. A two-model threshold characterizes when privately optimal monoculture is socially dominated, and a convex portfolio rule limits average private predictive regret. Nine model families across five Moroccan cereal systems provide a benchmark-based calibration. Under illustrative parameters and a 10% regret cap, accuracy-constrained diversification lowers modeled social loss in all five systems by 10.89-41.53% (mean 19.41%). Uniform allocation reduces modeled loss in this setting, but breaches the regret cap in every crop. Correlation sensitivity shows that highly dependent model errors attenuate the benefits of diversification. These counterfactual outcomes are not estimates of agronomic or monetary welfare; the framework identifies adoption architecture and error dependence as ecosystem-level evaluation variables.
title: Algorithmic Monoculture in Machine Learning-based Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendation

summary: Generative recommendation (GR) represents items as semantic identifiers (SIDs) and autoregressively generates the next item's SID from interaction history. However, most methods assign the same SID length to all items despite highly unequal interaction frequencies. This uniform design repeatedly incurs the cost of fine-grained codes for popular items, while shortening codes to reduce this cost also compresses the semantic representations of long-tail items. Inspired by the compact forms of frequent expressions in natural language, we propose JevRec to encode items as variable-length words and generate the next item from interaction context. Linguistic encoding retains frequency-dependent semantic prefixes from shared codebooks, producing shorter SIDs for popular items and richer descriptions for long-tail items. Yet predicting a sequence-level length and generating token-level content impose different optimization requirements that may conflict under a shared output head. Our Jev-like decision modeling component therefore predicts a length distribution with a dedicated head and generates content conditioned on length through a separate head while sharing the interaction-history representation. Experiments on three public datasets show that JevRec outperforms all compared baselines across the evaluated recommendation metrics. Further analyses show lower training and inference time than TIGER and reduced gradient conflict between length and content prediction.
title: JevRec: Linguistic Encoding with Jev-like Decision Modeling for LLM-based Generative Recommendation

summary: Optimizing discrete allocation weights across competing segments of a shared budget is a fundamental challenge in resource-constrained, sequential decision-making environments. In practice, this optimization is often hindered by delayed, noisy, and aggregate feedback, alongside strict operational constraints on how frequently weights can be adjusted. Because of the resulting combinatorial action space and extreme data sparsity, classical multi-armed bandit algorithms that evaluate arms independently are rendered highly inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we propose a segmentation-agnostic approach utilizing Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (GP-UCB) algorithms. By placing a Gaussian Process prior on the reward function, our method effectively shares information across neighboring configurations, drastically reducing the necessary exploration horizon. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theoretical bandit research and production-scale deployment. We first introduce a high-fidelity synthetic simulator to evaluate various kernel configurations under stationary, drifting, and reactive environments, identifying a composite Matérn + Linear kernel as the most robust choice for overcoming local noise and global shifts. Finally, we validate our findings through a large-scale Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) in a live production environment. Our empirical results demonstrate that the GP-UCB approach delivers a statistically significant efficiency lift compared to a standard $\varepsilon$-greedy baseline, offering a highly practical solution for real-world black-box lever optimization.
title: Gaussian Process Bandits for Constraint Black Box Lever Optimization

summary: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding

summary: This work investigates how site-specific digital twins (DTs) can support wireless localization using simplified distributed infrastructure. We propose PRISM (Probabilistic Refinement using Inverse learning and a Site-specific Model), a DT-guided probabilistic localization scheme with single-antenna access points (APs). Localization is formulated as a probabilistic inverse problem in which a conditional proposal distribution over UE locations is learned from multi-node channel impulse responses (CIRs). The proposal generates candidate locations, with its spread regularized during training and DT consistency used to reweight candidates and refine the estimate at inference. The DT serves as an approximate forward-consistency model, avoiding assumptions of exact channel fidelity or differentiability with respect to user position. Numerical experiments demonstrate gains over data-driven and classical fingerprinting benchmarks, while achieving a median error of approximately $0.7$ m using 10 single-antenna APs. Without retraining, PRISM remains effective under degraded inference-time DT features. PRISM also yields uncertainty estimates from its proposal covariance, with empirical $χ^2$ calibration approaching ideal behavior as APs increase.
title: Digital Twin-Guided Wireless Localization via Probabilistic Inverse Learning

summary: We propose HiLo-RD (High-to-Low Budget Representation Distillation) to improve masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) under a limited generation budget. Unlike autoregressive models, MDLMs choose both what to generate and where to commit it. This creates two coupled challenges: predicting useful content before reasoning is complete, and deciding when to fix answer tokens that shape later predictions. We identify budget-induced premature commitment: even when a correct solution fits, the model can fix answer fragments near the window boundary before resolving intermediate steps. These fragments become context for later predictions and redirect subsequent reasoning. Existing post-training methods do not directly transfer the stronger trajectories that the same model follows with a larger window. HiLo-RD addresses this gap by (1) pairing large-window teacher states with cropped small-window views and (2) matching their hidden representations at committed positions. This supervision guides both token prediction and commitment order without an external teacher. Across mathematics benchmarks, HiLo-RD improves low-budget accuracy and shortens responses; these gains extend to code generation without code-domain training. On GSM8K, accuracy rises by 9.4 percentage points as mean readable length falls by about 25%. Attention diagnostics and fixed-budget order interventions support the proposed mechanism. Together, these results show that large-window reasoning can improve small-window decoding.
title: HiLo-RD: Cross-Budget Self-Distillation for Masked Diffusion Language Models

summary: Generative planners are often evaluated by the trajectories they can generate, although closed-loop driving ultimately depends on the single candidate committed to control. We identify this mismatch as the sample-to-execution gap and show that improving proposal quality alone can worsen the executed decision. Here, we introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent proposal-to-execution framework that couples candidate generation, trajectory selection, and subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics. Intent-Guided Diffusion Proposal (IGD) assigns hypothesis responsibility and shapes trajectories with execution-conditioned supervision. Execution-Grounded Selection (EGS) learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility, commits one trajectory to control, and returns it as context for the next planning cycle. Across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, ExecDiffuser achieves leading closed-loop performance against strong state-of-the-art baselines. Under a unified five-seed protocol, it obtains an average score of 85.62, improving over Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive by 4.02 and 1.31 points, respectively. On NAVSIM, it achieves 92.6 PDMS under the official evaluation pipeline. Matched counterfactual analysis further shows that ExecDiffuser more reliably converts strong candidates into committed decisions, while prefix interventions confirm that this advantage persists after physical execution and subsequent replanning.
title: ExecDiffuser: Closing the Sample-to-Execution Gap in Diffusion Planning

summary: In this paper, we propose a model-based boosting approach for fitting structured additive distributional copula regression models with bivariate responses, focusing particularly on the joint modeling of claim frequency and claim severity. The proposed approach is based on generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which extend the general idea of GAMs by allowing multiple parameters of a response distribution, rather than only its conditional mean, to depend on covariates. The model is therefore intrinsically interpretable at the level of its additive predictors, providing greater transparency and auditability than black-box alternatives. We evaluate the proposed framework using synthetic and real-world data. We demonstrate its ability to recover the underlying covariate effects and dependence structure, identify informative variables, and achieve competitive predictive performance relative to benchmark models. We also illustrate how the fitted model can be interpreted.
title: Joint Distributional Copula Regression for Insurance Claim Frequency and Severity via Boosting

summary: System One (decision) models return small structured answers, but can retain host dispatch, GPU launch overhead and full-vocabulary projection. We present DFIP (Decision-Focused Inference Path), an empirical systems study of established inference techniques in PPLX-Decider, Liquid d1-3B, Clef-Flash and GLiNER2.5-Decide. Selective CUDA graph replay, candidate-token projection and schema-compatible length-aware batching are applied at compatible model boundaries. We compare resident requests with stronger native baselines, audit exposed answers and measure changing arrivals. With optional native Qwen kernels installed, short Boolean resident speedups over strengthened native are 2.47x for Decider across five containers and 1.45x for Clef across four of five planned containers; Clef's fifth fails in native preflight. Liquid is effectively tied with released compilation; replay supplies most of its eager-baseline gain, while projection alone adds little full-request benefit. In a one-worker GLiNER follow-up, length-aware batching is 1.40x faster than compiled native FIFO batching on a diverse resident trace, but has worse arrival p95. Decider and Clef audits cover 3,024 decisions per model and preserve all 1,112 returned choices, while Clef changes scores, probabilities and serving confidence thresholds. Diverse external arrivals reverse fixed-shape replay gains and expose overload losses and a replay-path CUDA error. The results identify workload-specific acceleration and its limits, rather than a universal optimizer or production readiness.
title: DFIP: Decision-Focused Inference Path for System One Models

summary: Gradient-based data attribution has become an important tool for high-quality data selection in the instruction fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), as it estimates the contribution of training examples through their influence on model optimization. However, we find that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from surface-form bias: minor changes to semantically irrelevant details, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content remains unchanged. To address this issue, we propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (CIGA), a robust framework for instruction data selection. CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, thereby reducing formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. CIGA also reduces attribution cost, offering a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.
title: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution

summary: Borrowed Youth and the Geography of Production Investment explains how country demographic trajectories and multinational organisation jointly determine the continuity of labour-based location advantage. Opening access, local cohort succession and international recruitment supply distinct services over a production commitment. Under common tenure and the stated site conditions, the preferred host switches at most once as planned operating life increases. Home-linked recruitment, shared foreign arrangements and admission institutions change the country comparison. Public article and replication, version 3.21.0, 28 October 2026. The article develops its argument within JIBS debates on location advantages, human-capital mobility, cross-border coordination and investment commitment. It distinguishes host rankings across project horizons from later relocation decisions. The original formal results, empirical estimates, uncertainty, six figures and editable tables are retained. No new mechanism estimate is claimed. The manuscript contains 9,953 counted words, a 196-word abstract, 22 full substantive text pages before references, 40 total pages, six figures and three tables. The online appendix has 122 pages. Regression tables retain three-decimal p-values, p<0.001 for smaller probabilities, no significance stars and explicit economic magnitudes. Start with README.txt. The current manuscript, appendix and complete LaTeX are directly downloadable. Three verified current ZIP blocks and their restoration helper combine with the nine complementary frozen base archives to reconstruct the exact 1,839-file replication tree and verify 1,838 checksum entries. The publication_reporting module reconstructs the current source and bibliography from frozen editorial inputs after reproducing the statistical tables. The held country and multinational panels establish neither joint support nor a familywise contradiction for positive service pricing and rotation. The reference-fee envelope supplies conditional exclusions and non-exclusions. Licensed WRDS observations are excluded; subscriber queries and aggregate outputs are supplied. Third-party Lyons dissertation and journal-article PDFs are not republished; factual coding, original repository links, bibliographic sources and reconstruction instructions are supplied. The exact AI declaration is: ChatGPT and Codex (OpenAI) were used in October 2026 for coding help, literature search, and red teaming and review. Reviewer payloads exclude author identifiers; public repository metadata provides attribution. Original work is CC BY 4.0; third-party rights remain. This public deposit is not a journal submission or acceptance.
title: Borrowed Youth and the Geography of Production Investment: Article and Replication Materials

summary: A linter for JSON, I-JSON, JSONC, JWCC (HuJSON), JSON5 and JSON Lines. It reports syntax errors, duplicate keys, each dialect's rules and JSON Schema errors, all with exact positions. The schema comes from --schema, a config file or a file's own $schema. On a terminal, each problem shows as a code frame, and --color controls the color. It also writes SARIF for GitHub code scanning and JSON for scripts and editors. A playground runs it in the browser as WebAssembly. It ships as a pre-commit hook, PyPI wheels, Rust crates, release binaries and a GitHub Action. The repository includes a conformance matrix of JSON5, JSONC, JWCC and JSON Lines parsers.
title: jsonvet

summary: An open framework for building a multi-year, research-intensive summer program that brings high school students from traditionally excluded and low-income backgrounds into life sciences research labs. Includes a step-by-step setup guide, templates, and matched pre/post assessment surveys with an analysis script.
title: LiNC Replication Toolkit: Linking high school students to research experiences in the life sciences

summary: Enterprise email security protects employees behind a corporate mail gateway. The people most exposed to employment and support-impersonation scams - students and early-career job seekers - are contacted inside consumer platforms, where no gateway sees the message. We present a dependency-free, explainable detector that works at the level of the individual message and its sender, and a public benchmark for comparing such detectors under cheap adversarial transformation. The detector has four layers: (1) deterministic lookalike checks built on Unicode UTS #39 confusable skeletons, mixed-script detection, bounded edit distance, and brand-agnostic detection of a domain hidden inside a link host; (2) a logistic-regression sender scorer over 23 named features trained on a synthetic generator spanning eight brands (holdout F1 0.987); (3) a message-intent classifier, with a rule baseline and a prompt-injection-hardened LLM wrapper, that receives structured sender facts from the first two layers and whose impersonation verdicts are discounted deterministically only when the sender is verified or unremarkable, nothing sensitive is asked, links stay under the sender's control, and the body does not claim the platform's authority; and (4) a 76-message, brand-parametric benchmark with ten label-preserving adversarial variants and three model-paraphrased corpora, scored on per-layer recall, false-positive rate, injection hijack rate, and latency. On a paraphrased corpus frozen before a single evaluation, all three Layer 3 backends reach recall 1.00 in the fused pipeline, at FPR 0.03 for the rule baseline and Gemma 3 27B and 0.10 for Llama 3.1 8B, against 0.83/0.03, 1.00/0.07 and 1.00/0.47 for the same backends unfused: the sender layers are worth 17 points of recall to the rules and 37 points of FPR to the small model. The 8B model obeyed an appended injection on 6 of 46 attacks, each caught only by a deterministic overrule; the 27B model obeyed none. Three findings fall out: UTS #39 skeletons do not fold Cyrillic U+0442 or Greek U+03BA to ASCII, so skeleton equality alone misses a mixed-script brand lookalike; regex intent cues lose 33 points of recall to a single confusable glyph unless text is confusable-folded first; and negation must be handled at clause level with an exception for conditionals. Code, weights, corpora, and per-message verdict dumps are released under the MIT license.
title: Message-Level Detection of Support-Team and Recruiter Impersonation on Consumer Platforms: A Layered Detector and Adversarial Benchmark

summary: Python toolkit for the RoSE dataset, including three trained phase pickers (EQT-RoSE, PhaseNet-RoSE, and RED-PAN-60s), their benchmark code, and the magnitude calculation code and calibration tables. Catalog, pick, waveform, and StationXML files are not included. The related dataset record, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23153183 (all versions), is restricted while third-party redistribution rights are reviewed.
title: RoSE — Romanian SEismic Dataset Toolkit

summary: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation

summary: Autonomous agents increasingly depend on harnesses that govern interaction, memory, tools, and execution around large language models (LLMs). While recent work has begun to evolve these harnesses from execution experience, the supervision used to guide evolution often remains relatively static, making it difficult to track changing behavioral weaknesses across rounds and potentially limiting generalization to unseen tasks. To address this issue, we propose RuHarness, a rubric--harness co-evolution framework for continual agent self-improvement. RuHarness continually discovers and reassesses behavioral criteria from execution trajectories, prioritizes the most relevant unresolved weaknesses, and uses them to guide targeted harness updates while keeping the task objective fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse agent tasks and backbone models show that RuHarness outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, particularly on unseen held-out tasks. Further analyses show that adaptive rubric prioritization tracks shifting weaknesses and supports more sustained improvement and stable generalization across evolution rounds.
title: When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement

summary: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.
title: Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training

summary: Personalized spoken agents must identify speakers before accessing user-specific memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume correctly attributed histories. We argue that voiceprints are observations of identity, not identities themselves, and formulate online speaker-memory construction to maintain persistent user entities as acoustic evidence evolves. We introduce EvoSpeakerMem, a training-free layer for causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory writes and retrieval through a replaceable text-memory backend. We also construct LoCoMo-ID, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal SMIIP-TV, genuine-probe rejection under a frozen near-enrollment threshold rises from 29.8% to 55.6% over approximately one year. On LoCoMo-ID speaker-sensitive queries, gated updating improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions, respectively, with no wrong-user authorizations. The advantage persists in the four-speaker test. Yet reducing fragmentation and improving QA can coexist with incorrect cross-user links, revealing a fragmentation--contamination trade-off that QA alone cannot capture.
title: From Voiceprints to User Entities: Online Speaker-Memory Construction for Multi-User Spoken Agents

summary: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory.
