Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.
title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information

summary: AI agents have made substantial progress in domains where they have a non-trivial amount of time to deliberate between actions, such as mathematics, software engineering, and performing tasks on desktop applications. It is less clear how such models fare in settings that demand real-time interaction, such as playing a video game or operating a physical device. In these settings, the environment state may evolve as the agent is reasoning, or even as the underlying model is performing a forward pass. To gain insight into the real-time interaction capabilities of vision-language agents, we introduce Gym-Anything-RT. Our key idea is to construct visual minigames that demand a portfolio of capabilities required for interactive real-time settings. Gym-Anything-RT uses an agentic pipeline to automatically generate such environments based on a taxonomy of six capabilities required for real-time interaction, including the ability to perceive the environment and act under an evolving environment state. A key feature of Gym-Anything-RT is that it allows for controlled comparison of real-time interaction capabilities: we can run the same minigame in real time, or pause or slow down the environment to relax the requirement for real-time actions. We use Gym-Anything-RT to construct 100 real-time minigames and evaluate AI agents on them. We find large capability gaps in real-time interaction. For example, GPT-6 Astra (xHigh) achieves a pass rate of only 9.0% on the real-time minigames, which rises to 75.0% when the environment is paused. We also identify intriguing behaviors by the most powerful frontier agents: for instance, when given the ability to write code, these agents write code that bypasses the need to perceive and act in real time. We publicly release Gym-Anything-RT and the generated minigames to spur further research on AI agents in real-time interactive settings.
title: Gym-Anything-RT: Scaling Real-Time Environments for Vision-Language Agents

summary: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.
title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning

summary: In survival studies, right censoring often prevents the observation of subjects' complete outcomes, complicating inference about the underlying distribution. Evaluating whether a given distribution adequately fits right-censored data is therefore essential. However, guidance on the relative performance of available goodness-of-fit tests under different data conditions remains limited. In this work, we present a comparative assessment of three classical goodness-of-fit tests adapted for right-censored data: Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, and Cramér-von Mises. Through an extensive simulation study, we investigate how factors such as the proportion of right-censored observations, sample size, and distributional symmetry influence the statistical power of each test. All procedures were implemented using the R package GofCens, and power estimates were obtained from extensive replicated simulations. The results identify the settings in which each test exhibits superior performance, providing practical, evidence-based recommendations for test selection in survival analysis. These recommendations are summarized as user-oriented guidelines and complemented by a concise graphical cheat sheet, enabling practitioners to quickly identify the most suitable test for their specific application.
title: Practical Guidelines for Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Right-Censored Data

summary: We examine conditional charged-multiplicity fluctuations at fixed multiparton interaction (MPI) count in retained PYTHIA proton-proton samples at centre-of-mass energies of 2.76, 7, and 13 TeV. Charged particles satisfy |eta| < 0.8 and 0.15 < pT < 20 GeV/c. In the historical colour-reconnection (CR)-labelled baseline samples, the CR-ON conditional mean is smaller by a larger fraction than the standard deviation: the absolute width is smaller, while the coefficient of variation is larger in every retained matched MPI bin. Effective lifetime/decay settings and their per-run correspondence are unverified for this baseline, so these comparisons do not establish that CR alone causes the observed differences or their energy dependence. A separately documented 13 TeV comparison using the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) CP5 tune, with equal non-CR physics settings and particle data across the ON/OFF pair, exhibits the same absolute-versus-relative width ordering. Retained independent Monash and A14 samples also show this pattern, subject to historical production-record limitations. A comparison with mean-transverse-momentum data from A Large Ion Collider Experiment (ALICE) and simulated activity estimators provides final-state context within the stated particle-definition and provenance limits.
title: Color-Reconnection Effects on the nMPI-Nch Conditional Multiplicity Fluctuations in PYTHIA 8 pp Collisions

summary: Face swapping transfers a source identity onto a target image while preserving the target's pose, expression, hair, and lighting. The most realistic current methods are diffusion-based, but they need many network evaluations per image. GAN-based methods are fast, yet trained from scratch they must learn realism from the adversarial signal alone and produce visibly weaker results. We present ALADDIN (Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping), a one-step face swapper obtained by initialising the generator from a pre-trained multi-step flow-matching model and training it adversarially under identity and target-preservation constraints. We expose a controllable trade-off between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by training a student model with triplet pseudo-label supervision. We additionally identify a bias in the standard evaluation protocol, which favours methods trained against the same identity encoder used to score them, and re-evaluate all baselines with an independent one. ALADDIN is state-of-the-art among one-step methods in realism and target preservation at comparable identity transfer, and matches the best multi-step model with 28 times fewer network evaluations and an order of magnitude fewer training pairs.
title: ALADDIN: Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping

summary: This repository accompanies the manuscript "Early hypernatremia identifies a reproducible, graded excess of in-hospital mortality after acute brain injury: a two-database cohort study." The study included 11,332 adult patients with acute brain injury from two independent intensive care databases: 4,325 patients from 140 hospitals in the eICU Collaborative Research Database (version 2.0) and 7,007 patients from MIMIC-IV (version 3.1). A total of 1,369 in-hospital deaths occurred after the 24-hour landmark. The analytical workflow covers cohort identification, first-24-hour sodium exposure classification, covariate preparation, multiple imputation, adjusted logistic regression, standardized absolute risk estimation, independent replication, and sensitivity analyses. Additional analyses examine sodium concentration gradients, detection timing, osmotherapy context, and extended adjustment. This version extends the previously archived eICU analysis (version 0.1.0) to support the expanded two-database study. No patient-level records, patient identifiers, access credentials, or restricted clinical data are redistributed. Reproduction requires independent authorized access to eICU and MIMIC-IV through PhysioNet and compliance with the applicable data use agreements.
title: Analysis code for early hypernatremia and in-hospital mortality after acute brain injury: eICU and MIMIC-IV cohorts

summary: Data, coding materials, raw language-model output, analysis script and figures for the article "Whole-of-society defence under the test of war: which rules Ukraine's preparedness statutes could settle in advance, 2022–2026" (version 1.1.0 of the deposit; the article is under review). The dataset covers all 877 provisions (paragraphs of the official consolidated text) of Law No. 389-VIII on the legal regime of martial law, Law No. 4765-VI on compulsory alienation of property and Law No. 3543-XII on mobilisation, as published on 5 October 2026. Each provision carries its functional class (powers; decision-making authority; burden-sharing; enforcement; organisational), its addressee (citizens; enterprises; state bodies; mixed; none), whether it existed on 23 February 2022, and whether it was amended by a separate act, located in an article restated in full, or added during the war, together with the amending acts named in the editorial notes before and after 24 February 2022. Version 1.1.0 adds the addressee variable, a control corpus of 430 provisions of Cabinet of Ministers Resolutions No. 76 (2023, reservation of employees) and No. 998 (2012, compensation for requisitioned property) coded with the same scheme, the list of amending resolutions of Resolution No. 76, official series of recorded offences under Articles 336 and 337 of the Criminal Code from the Office of the Prosecutor General (Form 1, data.gov.ua), other series on enforcement, reservation and opinion polls with sources, and the chronology of change by half-year. All Ukrainian text fields in the data files carry English translations in parallel columns. The coding was produced by a large language model in independent runs under rules fixed in advance and verified by two authors; the deposit includes the exact prompts, the input files, the raw output of every run (including two excluded pilot runs and the adjudicating runs), the authors' rule decisions, and English renderings of the coding instructions. The script analysis/reproduce.py reproduces every number reported in the article. Supplementary files give the amendments tabled to Bill No. 10449 by member of parliament and the economic series used for context.
title: Replication package: Whole-of-society defence under the test of war: which rules Ukraine's preparedness statutes could settle in advance, 2022–2026

summary: Borrowed Youth and the Geography of Production Investment explains how country demographic trajectories and multinational organisation determine the continuity of labour-based location advantage. Opening access, local cohort succession and recruitment provide different dated services over committed production capital. Home-linked routes, shared foreign arrangements and admission institutions change host rankings. Completed public article and replication, version 3.24.0, 28 October 2026. This version clarifies when costly capital redeployment makes workforce renewal consequential, how recruitment expansion can induce admission-policy feedback, and how legal permission differs from operational staffing. It explains that negative conditional allocation coefficients are not causal effects of hiring. Total and average service weights are linked as I=A*K and J=A*Q; independent integration and optimisation verify the eighteen-year break-even coefficient 638.9660, reported as 638.97. The held engineering-life manufacturing analysis uses 317 observations from 32 firms in nine hosts, with independent BEA production-machinery lives and an identical 299-observation duration comparison. The rotation contrast remains -110.25 (95 percent interval -520.28 to 299.78; positive-direction p=0.724). Joint positive service pricing and rotation are unestablished (p=0.763); familywise contradiction is also unestablished (p=0.712). These are observational allocations; intended plant life and delivered recruitment are not observed. No estimate, uncertainty interval or probability is changed by this final revision. The documented twenty-year JLR host appraisal supplies a EUR106-226 million strategic hurdle after disclosed delay and aid adjustments. Its recruitment component is unobserved. The five-percent continuous-discount reference annuity is EUR8.38-17.88 million per year; JLR's internal rate is redacted. The article preserves other strategic factors and excludes double counting labour already priced in financial cash flows. The manuscript contains 9,992 counted words, a 180-word abstract and 23 full substantive text pages before references. The main PDF has 41 pages and six figures; the appendix has 126 pages. Regression tables retain three-decimal probabilities, no significance stars and explicit economic magnitudes. All earlier estimates, proofs, figures and the complete appendix are retained. Start with README.txt. Current manuscript, appendix and complete LaTeX are directly downloadable. Three verified current ZIP blocks, their restoration helper and nine frozen complementary base archives reconstruct the exact 1,858-file replication tree, verified by 1,857 checksum entries. Public aggregate inference reconstructs without WRDS; full reestimation uses saved licensed inputs obtained by the supplied subscriber queries. No new data were acquired. title: Borrowed Youth and the Geography of Production Investment: Article and Replication Materials

summary: Peanut is one of affordable nutrition rich leguminous crops. This experimental study evaluated the response of peanut,  Arachis hypogaea and soil properties to the application of ten (10) treatments with three replication such as T 1 -unfertilization, 10 t ha -1 of CM-chicken manure (T 2 ), CM-Biochar(T 3 ), GM-Goat manure(T 4 ), NPK -60-60-60 kg ha -1 (T 5 ), dolomite -1 t ha -1 (T 6 ), and T 7 (T 2 + dolomite), T 8 (T 3 + dolomite), T 9  (T 4 + dolomite) and T 10 (T 5 + dolomite) in RCB design. Comparison of means revealed there is no significant difference on plant height, number of leaves, girth size diameter and no. of pods and weight of nodules but there is significant difference in the weight of pods, number of nodules, dry weight of roots and shoot provide by ANOVA test. However, there is an increase inplant height, number of leaves, girth size diameter observed treatments with either chicken manure or biochar with dolomite. Further, chicken manure increase in number and weight of pods and weight of nodules while number of nodules, dry matter of shoot and root observed higher in chicken manure biochar alone and/or with dolomite and also improve soil characteristics. Furthermore, soil analysis revealed heavy soil texture, 0.6-0.7 % SOM, Soil pH range 5.3-6.2 i.e. moderately to slightly acidic, P low to medium, K is low amount but relatively improve than initial. Furthermore, soil amended with chicken manure increases growth and yield of peanut Arachis hypogaea L. published by the International Journal of Biosciences | IJB
title: Growth and yield response of peanut, (Arachis hypogaea L.) and soil characteristics with application of inorganic and organic fertilizer and dolomite addition

summary: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.
title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time

summary: GUI memory should preserve the results of past actions and learn reusable operations. This is difficult in long-horizon workflows, where agents must use information across applications and useful operations are interleaved with failed attempts. We introduce Task Advancement Memory (TAM), which defines task advancement as verified task progress, and supports ongoing task execution and learns reusable operations. During execution, Task Advancement State represents how verified task progress changes the remaining goals, allowing the agent to build on earlier achievements across applications. After each task, advancement supervision identifies and abstracts the interactions that produced a verified local result. The learned operations preserve the relation between required inputs, expected outcomes, and verification conditions. This retains locally successful operations from both successful and failed tasks. On MobileWorld GUI-only tasks, Advancement State alone raises success from 12.0% to 28.2%. Full TAM achieves a 17.6% relative gain in task success over the strongest evaluated baseline and reduces lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%. On SPA-Bench, TAM achieves state-of-the-art task success in the single-app English Level 3 setting.
title: From Interaction to Capability: Task Advancement as State and Supervision for GUI Agents

summary: Visual world models increasingly support spatial reasoning by generating RGB views of unobserved states. However, RGB has become the default interface largely because it is well suited for visual generation, rather than necessarily being the most effective representation for downstream reasoning. Different spatial questions may benefit from different representations of the same imagined state: top-down geometry can facilitate global distance comparisons, while panoramic views provide broader context for reasoning about open space. To isolate the role of representation in spatial imagination, we introduce ImagiRep, a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions spanning seven question types across two settings, Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration, providing oracle RGB and six alternative representations (e.g., depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry) of the same unobserved state. This controlled comparison reveals that even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, and different questions benefit from different representations. Similar trends hold for representations derived from world-model-estimated states. Notably, estimated RGB alone can mislead spatial reasoning, while alternative representations retain complementary benefits. Building on these findings, we introduce GEARS, a lightweight test-time strategy for adaptive representation selection, outperforming existing spatial imagination methods and showing that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.
title: Representing the Unseen: Rethinking Visual Imagination for Spatial Reasoning

summary: Accurate acquisition of full channel state information (CSI) is essential for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) wireless systems, while dense pilot-based estimation incurs substantial overhead. Directly minimizing the prediction error over raw CSI coefficients is fragile in realistic propagation environments, since small-scale fading, mobility, local scattering, and small spatial perturbations can induce large phase-sensitive variations. Nevertheless, wireless channels contain strong spatial, temporal, and frequency-domain correlations that can be more predictably represented in a latent propagation-field domain. Motivated by this observation, we propose a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA)-inspired field world model, defined as a latent predictive model of the wireless propagation field, for sparse-pilot channel reconstruction. The model maps CSI observations into latent time-frequency tokens, predicts masked or future latent field states from historical multi-band context, and fuses the predicted latent prior with sparse noisy current pilots to reconstruct the full MIMO-OFDM channel. Ray-tracing experiments show that the proposed method improves normalized mean square error (NMSE) over pilot-only and direct reconstruction baselines, supporting latent field prediction as an effective prior for sparse-pilot channel acquisition.
title: JEPA-Inspired Latent Field Prediction for Sparse-Pilot MIMO-OFDM Channel Reconstruction

summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.
title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data

summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations

summary: Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory, motivating low-bit weight quantization for efficient deployment. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates. We propose CoS-VQ (Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization), which preserves low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The key challenge is scale-induced coupling: the optimal scale depends on the entire codeword combination and, in turn, changes candidate rankings across positions, so pointwise updates can stall even after scale re-optimization. CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and constructs a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it identifies finitely many representative intervals for joint index--scale updates without exhaustively enumerating codeword combinations. On Qwen3.8-27B, CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks. Ablations from the same initialization further show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement, highlighting joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality. The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/Cos_VQ.
title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models

summary: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.
title: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Embedding Scaling in Vision-Language Models

summary: Proactive LLM agents anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history. Existing approaches emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories, providing limited support for validating recurring behavioral regularities and assessing their applicability to the current event. We propose Proactive Memory (ProactMem), which organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities. Trajectory facts are checked against source events, and regularities are assessed through historical replay before being matched to current conditions. We also construct ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark covering three application scopes, where agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On ProactiveStream, ProactMem achieves an overall effectiveness (F1) of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ProactMem-5351/.
title: Proactive Memory for Event-Driven LLM Agents

summary: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.
title: As the Story Unfolds: Watching a Film and Identifying Characters as a Human Does

summary: Thomson scattering (TS) is a key diagnostic for inferring plasma parameters from scattered power spectra, but its interpretation depends strongly on assumptions about the underlying velocity distribution functions (VDFs). Conventional analyses typically assume Maxwellian distributions, which can be invalid in high-energy-density and laboratory astrophysics plasmas where collisionless, multi-population dynamics produce non-thermal features. In such cases, Maxwellian models may reproduce observed spectra while yielding inaccurate or misleading plasma parameters. We present a generalized TS analysis framework that represents species-specific VDFs in flexible, physically motivated bases and so reconstructs complex, non-equilibrium distributions. To explore the resulting high-dimensional parameter space, we build the forward model from differentiable operations and optimize the VDF parameters by gradient descent. We apply the method to synthetic TS spectra generated from particle-in-cell simulations of a collisionless shock with interacting hydrogen and carbon populations. Immediately upstream of the shock, where the plasma is most non-thermal, the flexible bases cut the mean normalized ion VDF residual from 38.7% for a Maxwellian model to 20.3% and 20.5%, with correspondingly improved time-resolved plasma parameters. We also introduce a systematic method of uncertainty quantification that reveals degeneracies between ion species, highlighting the importance of both flexible VDF modeling and a statistical mapping of the solution space for this inherently ill-posed inversion problem.
title: Recovering Non-Maxwellian Velocity Distribution Functions from Collective Thomson Scattering Spectra Using Generalized Basis Representations

summary: For each time $t$, the regression function $m_t(x)=E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]$ of an outcome on contemporaneous covariates can be regarded as a field on covariate space. We study how this field evolves when the covariates of individual units move as a diffusion and the outcome attached to each unit changes according to its own dynamics. Under mild regularity we show that $m_t$ satisfies a second-order evolution equation whose diffusion term is $\frac12\mathrm{tr}(Σ\nabla^2 m_t)$, the trace of the Hessian of the regression function weighted by the instantaneous covariance $Σ$ of the covariate increments, whose transport term is the drift of the time-reversed covariate process, and whose source term is the conditional mean rate of change of the outcome. The equation is a regression-theoretic reading of a classical transport law, and it yields a Feynman-Kac representation of $m_t$ along reversed covariate paths. We connect the Hessian appearing in the equation to the Hessian estimated by quadratic regression (under Gaussian design the best quadratic approximation has Hessian $E[\nabla^2 m(X)]$ exactly) and to the leading bias of kernel smoothers. For binary outcomes governed by bistable replicator dynamics with imitation among units with similar covariates, the closed equation is of Nagumo type, its planar travelling fronts are exactly logistic in $(x,t)$, and a single logistic regression of the outcome on covariates and time identifies the ratio of diffusion to reaction and the direction of invasion. We discuss identification under panel versus repeated cross-sectional designs and a two-stage estimation strategy, and we illustrate the results with simulations.
title: Regression Functions as Fields on Covariate Space: Evolution Equations, the Hessian, and Identification

summary: We develop a multifidelity black-box variational inference (MF-BBVI) approach for PDE-constrained Bayesian inverse problems in which forward solves are expensive and PDE gradients are unavailable. The method is built on score-function estimators for the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which avoid differentiation through the PDE model but are known to suffer from high variance. To address this high variance, we employ multifidelity approximate control-variate estimators that combine a small number of high-fidelity samples with a larger number of low-fidelity samples to reduce estimator variance and the number of high-fidelity evaluations required for optimization. We further develop a PDE-derivative-free second-order optimization strategy based on both gradient and Hessian score-function estimators. For low-fidelity model generation, we propose an on-the-fly strategy that builds and adaptively updates a reduced-order model (ROM) as the variational distribution evolves throughout the optimization. We investigate strategies for adapting the ROM and estimating the approximate control-variate gains, examining tradeoffs between estimator bias, variance reduction, and computational cost. The resulting approach facilitates derivative-free variational inference for large-scale inverse problems through a reduction in overall computational cost. We demonstrate the method on four numerical examples: a linear benchmark with an exact posterior and three PDE-constrained inverse problems.
title: Multifidelity variational inference for derivative-free PDE-constrained inverse problems

summary: We present a survey of approaches to Bayesian inference with simulator forward models, focusing on settings with prohibitively expensive simulators. In this domain, Bayesian optimization-based methods have emerged as the most promising approach. We unify existing methods into a general framework, enabling consistent reasoning about shared algorithmic structure across the fragmented literature. Within this framework, we identify the primary design choices and perform a systematic empirical comparison of their effects on inference efficiency in terms of required simulation budget. A key result of our study is that inference efficiency is often dominated by the choice of surrogate-model response variable, as it directly governs the complexity of the modeled function. Specifically, we demonstrate that the prevalent scalar log-likelihood is a poor response variable, as it discards crucial information. Based on this insight, we introduce the concept of custom \emph{proxy variables}: transformations of simulator outputs engineered to retain more information and provide smoother response surfaces, substantially improving inference efficiency over standard response variables. We provide actionable guidance and a numerically robust Julia package to facilitate practical adoption of Bayesian optimization for simulator inverse problems.
title: Bayesian Inference of Expensive Simulators: Survey and Comparison of Design Choices

summary: Abstract: This paper investigates the computational mathematics of Fs-subsets within the refined framework of Complete Boolean algebras. Using computable homomorphisms, we establish key mathematical properties such as the Fs-De Morgan laws and structural projections. Finally, we discuss practical applications of those computational paradigms in multicriteria decision-making fuzzy soft topology.
title: Computational Mathematics and Structural Properties of Images of Fs-Subsets under an Fs-set Function

summary: According to the overall findings, young adults experiencing difficulties with emotion regulation (suppressing emotions, being unable to understand what they are feeling) have significantly higher levels of social anxiety and anxiety. It was found that young adults who manage their emotions using ‘Cognitive Restructuring’ (the ability to view situations from a positive or flexible perspective) feel much more at ease in social settings and experience reduced anxiety levels.A strong, negative (inverse) correlation has been found between young adults’ general self-efficacy (belief in oneself/confidence in one’s ability to succeed) and their levels of social anxiety. In other words, the higher a young person’s self-efficacy belief—that ‘I can cope with this situation’—the less they fear being humiliated or excluded (social anxiety) when entering social settings. A direct link has been found between young adults’ levels of social anxiety and their emotion regulation skills. The results of the analysis and research confirm that emotion regulation skills are a key variable in predicting anxiety in social settings.
tags: Social Anxiety, Self-Efficacy, Emotional Regulation, Young Adults, Psychological Resilience.
title: The Relationship Between Levels of Social Anxiety, Self-Efficacy and Emotion Regulation Skills in Young Adults

summary: This software release presents the formally verified mathematical developments of Matthew J. Hall’s Chronos Time-First Reconstruction through version 439 , extending the previously published v410 release. The Chronos Time-First framework investigates time as a foundational element of physical evolution and develops a mathematical reconstruction connecting temporal change, nonlinear field dynamics, spatial geometry, and established gravitational physics. The reconstruction is independent of the previously investigated universal constant χ. The underlying development constructs a short-time continuum solution of a 55-component nonlinear Fourier evolution system using Galerkin approximations. Archived Lean proofs establish gravitational constraint preservation, reconstruction of a four-dimensional Lorentzian coordinate spacetime satisfying the Einstein–scalar field equations, scalar stress-energy conservation, and independently derived geometric Bianchi identities. The formal development also includes one-sided endpoint curvature and field-equation results within the constructed physical interval. The v411–v439 update substantially extends the mathematical treatment of physical change as a clock. The Change readout is constructed from specified spatial expansion observables associated with selected solutions of the original nonlinear evolution system. Its initial behavior is derived from the governing source equations. After normalization, the readout has zero initial value and unit right derivative, establishing a mathematically precise relationship between accumulated change and elapsed evolution time near the initial instant. The newly verified developments establish several additional properties: Near-origin clock calibration: The normalized Change readout divided by elapsed evolution time approaches unity as time approaches zero from the positive direction. Cross-solution agreement: Change clocks associated with different admissible selected solutions exhibit matching first-order behavior near the initial instant. Ordered temporal events: Scale-separated event schedules produce strictly ordered clock readings, including an explicitly constructed infinite event sequence approaching the origin. Discrete temporal reconstruction: Under the specified separation conditions, clock readings uniquely identify events within the permitted event sets. Finite-schedule separation bounds: The formal development establishes positive minimum gaps between distinct scheduled event readings across finite families. Robust event identification: The latest results prove that observations subject to sufficiently bounded errors remain closer to their correct nominal event readings than to competing readings. This establishes unique nearest-event decoding within the formally specified finite schedules. Together, these results provide a verified mathematical pathway from nonlinear geometric evolution to normalized temporal change, cross-solution calibration, ordered event measurements, and robust discrete event identification. The cumulative verification inventory increased from 5,153 audited declarations at v410 to 5,531 at v439 , including 171 newly introduced named public theorem declarations across the intervening source modules. The Lean verification records report successful incremental compilation, kernel and dependency checks, and cumulative axiom audits using Lean 4.34.0-rc2 and pinned Mathlib dependencies. The reported axioms are limited to propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound . The release does not claim a new, complete clean-source rebuild of the entire historical project. The results establish mathematical properties under explicitly stated hypotheses. Remaining research obligations include global nonlinear continuation and uniqueness, unrestricted continuous-time clock injectivity, invariant probe selection, practical numerical decoding, experimentally calibrated error bounds, and identification of the early
title: Chronos Time-First: Lean-Verified Einstein-Scalar Evolution and Local Calibration of a Geometric Change Readout

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. When two copies of a system, one hotter and one cooler, relax in the same bath, the Markovian Mpemba effect is a crossing of their distances from equilibrium. This package gives a sufficient test that rules out such crossings at every time: if the dynamics and its time reverse preserve the cone of observables with nondecreasing arithmetic prefix means, cooling Gibbs preparations stay ordered for relative entropy (both orientations), squared Hellinger and Rényi divergences of order 0<α≤2, including for common schedules of noncommuting stages. For complete-graph bosonic population rates with common coupling, the test holds for every spectrum and bath temperature exactly when the spontaneous jump weight is concave; Ohmic baths with large enough cutoff, Drude–Lorentz and sub-Ohmic weights qualify on explicit ranges, super-Ohmic weights do not. A certified super-Ohmic example (J=d 3 ) shows an actual relative-entropy crossing. Limits: an exact five-state cone-preserving example has a brief total-variation reversal, and for every N≥4 there are N-level systems with a slow-mode inversion although no proper induced subsystem shows one. The archive contains the 27-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), exact rational and interval certificates, a reproduction runner, semantic negative controls, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs, exact certificates, internal AI-assisted review only (not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); the closest antecedent (Avitan et al. 2026) already excludes the slow-mode effect for Ohmic and sub-Ohmic spectra. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Thermal ordering under Markovian relaxation: a finite-time criterion and its limits

summary: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.
title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction

summary: Technical artifacts supporting the manuscript "AnxietyVRET: Reproducible Technical Evaluation of an Ontology-Driven, Safety-Aware, and FHIR-Oriented Architecture for Traceable GAD-Oriented Virtual Reality Exposure Workflows". The package contains the corrected and versioned AnxietyVRET OWL 2 DL ontology with embedded SWRL rules, the corrected example ABox, deterministic boundary-test scripts and outputs, ten executable SPARQL competency-question queries, computational-benchmark scripts and logs, eight representative HL7 FHIR R5 JSON resources with structural-validation output, the AnxietyVRET-to-FHIR mapping crosswalk, semantic-preservation materials, and provenance-reconstruction scripts and outputs. No independently collected clinical patient dataset is included. See README.md for reproduction instructions.
title: AnxietyVRET reproducibility package: corrected ontology, example ABox, validation scripts, benchmark logs, and representative FHIR R5 resources

summary: DIGITAL TWINS OF VOLITION, BIOELECTRICITY AND NANOSENSING ACUPUNCTURE AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition developing a falsifiable engineering architecture for synchronizing prospective task labels, authorized noninvasive EEG/EMG records, and the physical state of an isolated needle-emulator on a nonliving phantom. The principal question is whether a frozen digital twin improves independently verified prediction of event time, signal and surrogate-device state under deliberately hidden cross-sensor clock delays. The central candidate relation is x[k+1]=A x[k]+B u[k]+w[k], z[k]=C x[k]+v[k]. This is an established mathematical modeling form, not an original biological law or evidence of private thought decoding. The framework treats timebase skew, cue leakage, repeated EEG-window contamination, model discrepancy, shared calibration covariance and hidden actuator latency as explicit challengers. A strong ordinary baseline includes prospective persistence, linear autoregression, calibrated Kalman models and time/cue-only prediction, evaluated on entirely held-out acquisition episodes and unseen days. Thirty differentiated physical and mathematical plates connect state observability, clock drift, covariance propagation, prediction intervals, source ablation, independent actuator safety and external validation to their respective experiments. Across 82 scientific chapters and 410 separately paginated studies, the book develops signal identity, calibration, synchronization, latent-state recovery, prospective prediction, blind falsification, hardware interlocks and second-site replication. Two hundred detailed Research Gates, printed with prominent deep-navy questions on individual pages, lead future investigators through unknown perturbations, strong countermodels, measurable disconfirmation, hard stops and successor evidence packages. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose scientifically distinguishable instruments and paths for revision. The three STARLI author mother volumes contribute method ancestry on sensing identity, functional requalification and sample-to-signal provenance. Eleven separately identified published method references support classical state estimation, EEG algorithm benchmarking, clock synchronization, leakage prevention, cross-subject validation and digital-twin qualification. Those sources do not constitute experimental evidence for the new architecture. All proposed experiments remain unperformed: the volume does not establish clinical acupuncture, autonomous microneedle treatment, volition-to-actuation efficacy or regulatory authorization. Safe early validation is restricted to consent-scoped archived or noninvasive data, inert bench devices and independently calibrated reference instruments. summary: QIGONG BREATHING AND INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE NEUROFEEDBACK COUPLING AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition that constructs a falsifiable, explicitly nonclinical research program joining measured breathing tasks, cardiorespiratory and EEG feedback, and isolated microscale actuator surrogates. The central problem is not whether breathing changes heart-rate variability - that has established ordinary physiological explanations - but whether a proposed feedback architecture adds independently measurable predictive or benchtop-control value after breathing rate, phase, expectancy, ordinary cardiorespiratory dynamics, sensor calibration, stimulus timing and strong conventional controllers have been fairly matched. The primary hypothesis is deliberately narrow. A prospective factorial design separates a preregistered breathing condition from an isolated, non-human phantom-drive condition. Its interaction term, order effects, washout, hierarchical sampling units, pressure-related mechanisms and full-episode denominators are subjected to masked scheduling, matched sham sensory cues, covariance-aware uncertainty and independent laboratory reconstruction. Any apparent signal explained by paced breathing or cue entrainment is treated as a legitimate negative result. A bench interaction is not evidence of physiological effects from actual acupuncture in a person. Thirty mathematically differentiated research plates address factorial contrasts, hierarchical estimands, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, ECG event genealogy, pressure-respiration transfer, spectral coherence, lag and phase, multiple comparisons, uncertainty covariance, causal identification, feedback latency, safe-state projection, isolated charge and thermal constraints, abstention and provenance. Across 82 chapters and 410 separately paginated scientific investigations, the book examines operational breathing definitions, reference instruments, EEG and ECG artifacts, blinded feedback protocols, mechanical and electrical phantoms, strong ordinary competitors, statistics, safety vetoes and reproducible handoff. Two hundred full-page Research Gates place their complete falsifiable research question in large deep-navy type, followed by an independently measurable outcome, adverse experiment, conventional physical rival and stopping rule. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose distinct successor objects ranging from calibration bridges and sham credibility tests to independent hardware vetoes, covariance sentinels, multisite reference capsules and protected null-result archives. An accompanying Excel index links formulas, chapters, Gates, candidate objects, citations and explicit evidence limitations. This work reports no executed integrated experiments, in-human needling, electrical stimulation, clinical efficacy, diagnosis or regulatory authorization. Its three STARLI mother-volume DOIs establish author research-method ancestry. Thirteen separately identified external research and metrology DOIs support established measurement, breathing physiology, neurofeedback reporting, uncertainty and statistical methodology, not the novel combined hypothesis. The 777-page layout, formula-clearance checks and 200 Gate color checks were automated; recurring editorial phrasing remains and full independent scientific peer review has not taken place. summary: BIOELECTRIC FEEDBACK AND PERSONALIZED INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE CONTROL AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page prospective nonclinical research monograph on the boundary between measured bioelectric variability, personalized feedback algorithms, and genuinely verified safe closed-loop operation on inert phantoms and isolated bench hardware. Its primary question is whether a controller calibrated on limited reference data retains a meaningful improvement for entirely unseen simulated individuals while meeting hard, independently witnessed limits. The governing design separates physiological sensing, identification of individual model parameters, selection of feedback commands, and observed physical outcomes. The inherited objective is corrected to a unit-consistent normalized tracking loss and separately measured bench-output burden; no mathematical optimum can compensate a failed hardware veto, force cap, thermal boundary, or missing permission record. A synthetic dummy-output budget is explicitly not a clinical stimulation dose or therapeutic recommendation. Thirty differentiated mathematical plates explore covariance-aware metrology, personal and hierarchical system identification, robust model predictive control, posterior coverage, safe-set feasibility, population shift, abstention, actuator latency, thermal loading, physical isolation, state-space reachability, distributional tail risk and independent requalification. Each plate states construction assumptions, native units, blind tests, stop conditions and a crosswalk to relevant chapters and successor gates. Eighty-two chapters, each with five separately paginated studies, develop electrode and reference calibration, timebase reliability, individual parameter uncertainty, adversarial new-person transfer, fair PID and classical MPC comparisons, closed-loop constraints, sham feedback, safety engineering and handoff to an unrelated laboratory. Two hundred full-page Research Gates are designed as distinctly falsifiable future entry points, including blind reconstruction, strong conventional rivals and external adversarial continuation. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose different metrology tools, decision records, baseline devices or smaller successor theories that can survive disproof of the larger control claim. The three author mother-volume version DOIs are M1 10.5281/zenodo.23480803, M2 10.5281/zenodo.23486020 and M3 10.5281/zenodo.23318840. Separately identified published external DOI studies on neural decoding, population generalization, system identification, control and neurostimulation provide context only: none demonstrates this F47 integrated apparatus. This is a Research Working Edition, not an executed laboratory study, clinical trial, review approval or evidence of therapeutic benefit. Future human stimulation, puncture, clinical research and patient-facing equipment require their own independent regulatory and ethics program. summary: At the start of 1984 Britain still had a large deep coal industry; by the end of 1994 almost all of it had gone, and the last deep mine closed in 2015. Do the towns that grew up around the pits still look different from other towns, and does it matter when their pit closed? I compile a list of 196 deep mines working at the start of 1984 from the Northern Mine Research Society's tables of National Coal Board collieries and Wikipedia's colliery lists, with closure years and locations from OpenStreetMap, Wikidata and OS Open Names. 167 (85%) closed by the end of 1994, with a peak of 32 in 1985. Linking the pits to the ONS built-up areas of 2022, I find 209 pit towns of 2,000 to 100,000 people in England and Wales. Compared with towns of the same size in the same region that had no pit, in Census 2021 they have 2.0 percentage points more adults long-term sick or disabled (a comparison-town median of 2.9%), 3.2 points more adults inactive for reasons other than retirement or study, 6.5 points more in routine or semi-routine work, 8.0 points fewer in managerial or professional work and about £5,900 a year lower mean household income, but the same share in work. Towns with older collieries show about half the gap. Among pit towns, the year the last pit closed makes no clear difference. Because the coalfields differed from other places long before 1984 and no earlier baseline is used, these are associations, not effects of the closures. Interactive version: https://tristan-hotham.github.io/pit-closures/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/pit-closures . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/28/pit-closures/ .
title: Did the Pits Closing Still Show? Britain's Coalfield Towns, 1984 to 2021

summary: This record provides the research data and supporting documentation for the revised systematic review “Tactile and Physical Interaction Problems in In-Vehicle Infotainment Systems: A Systematic Literature Review”. The current corpus comprises 342 eligible reports assessed using 34 operational codes across seven categories, yielding 11,628 report–code decisions: 3,635 positive, 7,677 negative and 316 unresolved. The materials are organised into eight editable Word volumes, each with a linked table of contents: Methods and Figures: supplementary sections S1–S12, review methods, operational codebook, PRISMA crosswalk, Figures 1–2 and a source-to-volume index. Corpus and Eligibility: the complete bibliography, bibliographic provenance, retrieval records and eligibility decisions. Characterisation and Appraisal: report characteristics and MMAT domain-level appraisals. Coding Evidence: all 11,628 coding decisions, source-page locators and supporting rationales. Synthesis and Decision Changes: synthesis matrices, coverage and overlap bounds, sensitivity analyses, historical-to-current decision comparisons and Figures 3–5. Historical Citation Screening: historical citation metadata and title-and-abstract screening decisions. Historical Full-Text Eligibility: historical reviewer assessments, eligibility decisions and consensus records. Historical Coding and Reproducibility: historical calibration, independent coding, adjudication and reliability records, together with package documentation and verification-script texts. The current 342-report evidence base is distinguished from the earlier 228-report archive. Historical-to-current linkage covers 5,916 decision pairs for 174 retained reports. Historical independent ratings and consensus decisions remain separate from the authors’ joint source verification conducted from 13 to 23 October 2026. Tables are presented as editable Word content. Repeated wording is retained through linked value keys, and verification scripts are reproduced as editable text in Volume 8. Five updated figures are embedded in the relevant volumes. Copyrighted primary publications and extended verbatim source quotations are not redistributed. Bibliographic identifiers, source-page locators and paraphrased rationales support traceability. Computational consistency checks do not, by themselves, establish scientific validity.
title: Research Data and Reproducibility Materials for "Tactile and Physical Interaction Problems in In-Vehicle Infotainment Systems: A Systematic Literature Review"

summary: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.
title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions

summary: AI agents no longer act alone: they cooperate, coordinate and compete within and between groups, increasingly alongside humans who are in, on or out of ``the loop''. Whether such mixed groups can govern themselves is an open question about machine behaviour and human-computer interaction that needs a testbed for hybrid institutions. We present Megabike, a multi-agent simulator and serious game with interdependent arenas for common-pool resource management, cooperative survival and constitutional choice. Riders sharing a megabike must agree their arrangements for steering, pedalling and distributing resources, and their political regime, while negotiating with rival bikes and avoiding an existential threat. Every rule is enforced by the simulator, every action is logged, and any seat can be taken by a human or a machine, so governance can be studied under well-defined metrics. We demonstrate Megabike with forty sessions in which language-model riders with cooperative, lazy, subversive or opposing dispositions chose regimes, elected leaders and expelled one another. The results show that different combinations of agent archetypes could produce unexpected and counterproductive outcomes. We conclude with extensions for systematic experiments mixing human and computational agents.
title: A Serious-Game Testbed for Self-Governing Human-Machine Institutions

summary: Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.
title: LM-DSB: A Lightweight Multi-agent System for Automated Daily Safety Bulletin Generation in Construction

summary: Electric vehicle (EV) charging stations integrating photovoltaic (PV) generation, battery storage, and bidirectional grid exchange must coordinate access to limited chargers with energy supply while considering both energy cost and carbon emissions. This paper proposes a solver-free greedy heuristic (SFGH) for dynamic vehicle scheduling (VS) and a twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) controller for carbon-aware energy dispatch (ED). SFGH assigns EVs according to reductions in service delays, and TD3 controls battery operation to balance energy costs and carbon emissions while meeting the resulting charging demand. The model allows both PV and battery exports, accounting for export revenue and carbon credits. Simulations on year-long case studies show that SFGH--TD3 achieves the lowest accumulated service delay, energy cost, and carbon emissions among the evaluated heuristic and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) configurations.
title: Electric Vehicle Scheduling and Carbon-Aware Energy Dispatch for Charging Stations

summary: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems
title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations

summary: Independently developed autonomous agents, such as autonomous vehicles, must guarantee joint compatibility, such as safety and task-completion requirements, when they operate in a shared environment. Existing methods require a centrally designed specification, or interaction mechanism before any agent is deployed. However, such centralized design is unrealistic when agent designs are confidential to their developers, and it is not flexible enough to accommodate future agent designs. We study a bi-level structure in which a regulator coordinates developers by publishing seed agents, and each developer independently tests its agent to ensure that it is compatible with every seed-compatible agent, a property we call future-proofness. Under this structure, joint compatibility is guaranteed for any agents that are designed and tested independently, without any coordination with each other. In this work, we first formulate compatibility for general multi-agent systems and show why it is not trivially implied by seed-compatibility. We then characterize the future-proof agents as the closure of the seed and show that this closure is monotone in the seed. Finally, we study a class of executable tests that involve interaction with the seed alone, and we ask to what extent such tests can distinguish the future-proof agents.
title: Compatibility and future-proof testing for multi-agent systems

summary: Language-model agents increasingly coordinate in large groups, and current agent protocols focus on delivering messages. For these agents, however, the scarce resource is not delivery but reading: every message costs tokens, and the context is finite. Current infrastructure works by push: the sender decides when a message enters the recipient's context, so the recipient reads in arrival order and drops the oldest messages once its context is full. We study the alternative, pull, in which messages wait in an inbox outside the context and the recipient's own rules decide what it reads and keeps. We argue that the inbox is a coordination primitive: each agent sets its rules privately, and those rules decide whether other agents' requests reach it. In simulated societies of up to 16,000 agents, with every decision an LLM judgment, we report three findings. First, push fails as an agent takes part in more coordination at once: an agent leading 20 negotiations with a full memory proposes options already rejected 97% of the time, because it has dropped the oldest replies. Second, an inbox is necessary under heavy, noisy traffic. Where first come, first read misses every request, an inbox that first reads messages carrying a refundable deposit still finds about 60% of the agents a request needs, at every size from 1,000 to 16,000. On a real email network, losses compound: when half the agents adopt such an inbox, forwarded search recovers only 5% of full adoption, against 42% for one-hop search. Third, an inbox comprises four decisions (what to read, what to keep, what a sender pays, and what a reply may say), and the best rule for each depends on the traffic and the agent's role. Multi-agent coordination under load requires an inbox layer designed for the traffic each agent receives.
title: The Inbox as a Coordination Primitive for LLM Agent Societies

summary: TRUSTWORTHY MANUFACTURING AND DIGITAL QUALITY PASSPORTS FOR BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT Manufacturing Evidence x Digital Traceability x Quality Release This 770-page Research Working Edition develops a falsification-oriented, nonclinical architecture for proving whether every biomedical micro/nanorobot product or batch can be linked to sufficient material, tool, model, process, test and failure evidence for an independent team to reconstruct its release rationale. It distinguishes record completeness from product qualification and treats physical identity, typed provenance, signature status, version compatibility, raw functional evidence, uncertainty, recall and retirement as separate scientific objects. DOI-linked publications support component methods and boundaries; they do not validate the integrated F25 system. summary: This release provides R code, processed data, analysis outputs, and documentation supporting an exploratory investigation of a candidate circRNA–miRNA–mRNA network associated with triple-negative breast cancer recurrence. The package includes differential expression analyses, paired expression comparisons, probe aggregation sensitivity analyses, multiple-testing assessments, descriptive ROC analysis, and archived network and functional annotation results. Input provenance, software session information, and instructions for running the R script are provided. The analyses draw on publicly available GEO datasets GSE154255, GSE38167, GSE101123, GSE182471, and GSE43502. The proposed network represents a computational hypothesis requiring independent clinical and experimental validation. Patient-level survival analysis and direct circRNA–miRNA binding validation are outside the reproducible scope of this package.

title: TNBC ceRNA Network: R Code, Data and Figures

summary: Version 1.2 (28 October 2026) adds a notice on the arithmetic precision of the split‑Gibbs runs (NOTICE_v1.2.md), with the check behind it (TF32_CHECK.md, tf32_check_files.zip). DP1’s split‑Gibbs runs used reduced‑precision (TF32) matrix products, which a later like‑for‑like check found shift that sampler’s estimates, while its predictions ran in full float32. The split‑Gibbs null result therefore has a further candidate explanation that DP1 cannot separate. DPS is unaffected. No file of earlier versions has changed. A pre-specified pilot testing whether a blindness-risk score computed before any target data are seen ranks the realised blindness (undetected and uncovered error) of diffusion-prior inference on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access. Study DP-A: weak attenuation (F = 32,000), 240 errors × 20 bases. Study DP-B: bounded-reach control, 120 errors × 20 bases. Two samplers: split-Gibbs plug-and-play (primary) and diffusion posterior sampling (secondary). It follows the learned (VAE) pilot, arXiv:2610.28155 (reproducibility package doi:10.5281/zenodo.23392686). The analysis plan, decision rules and fixed result sentences were approved by the author, and predictions and calibration were committed by SHA-256 hash, before any trial. The plan was not lodged with an external registry, so the study is described as pre-specified; the files named PREREG_… are that plan (their names, and the word "pre-registered" inside the hashed plan and the dated log, are kept unchanged so that the recorded hashes still match). Version 1.1 (26 October 2026) adds a post-hoc check of the linear response used by the blindness-risk score, specified in a dated plan and approved before any computation (response_check_plan_v1.md, response_check.py, response_check_results.json, RESPONSE_CHECK.md). Under the plan’s pre-specified reading, the response was not adequate for either sampler in either study, so the null result for the learned score does not separate the learned prior from this approximation. summary: This is the second annual account of BR implementation and biosecurity under the D4.1 Biosecurity Measures Plan. It updates the ante-operam position reported in D4.3 and focuses on the physical construction pathway, the materials and equipment used, and the controls that limited the risk of transferring non-indigenous species (NIS), pathogens or associated organisms during BLR deployment. Permitting and design: the EIA process concluded positively in July 2025, and the executive project was adopted by the Municipality of Ravenna on 26 August 2025. Construction materials: netting and geotextile were new, while limestone was sourced from a quarry. The physical structure was therefore not assembled from previously used marine materials. BLR design: the executive design uses 5.00 x 2.00 x 0.30/0.60 m modular wire-mesh mattresses filled with 100/200 mm limestone, arranged in macro-blocks over an approximately 100 x 48 m footprint (4,800 m²). Local logistics: mattresses were assembled in the Port of Ravenna, approximately 7 nautical miles from the receiving site. The barge used for deployment operated only on local Emilia-Romagna coastal works and was not used at other sites during the LIFE NatuReef work period. Diving operations: support divers worked only at the project site or in its immediate vicinity during the period; equipment was washed between different jobs. NIS baseline: Jassa slatteryi, Paranthura japonica, Ruditapes philippinarum and Callinectes sapidus were already documented in the area before BLR deployment and remain the appropriate baseline for post-construction interpretation.
title: 2nd annual report on BRs implementation and biosecurity. Deliverable 4.4 of the LIFE NatuReef project: Nature-based reef solution for coastal protection and marine biodiversity enhancement. LIFE22-NAT-IT-LIFE-NatuReef/101113742
