The resulting log-determinant penalty is incorporated into regularized variable projection, which eliminates the image variables by minimization. Under periodic boundary conditions and assuming the matrices involved admit a joint spectral decomposition, we show that a sufficiently large determinant weight rules out the no-blur solution as a local minimizer. We also characterize the regularizer's behavior as the auxiliary regularization scale tends to zero or infinity. We solve the reduced problem with a quasi-Newton method that evaluates the objective and its derivatives in the Fourier domain. In experiments with Gaussian, defocus, and motion blur, the proposed prior improves image and blur recovery over Gaussian marginalization across several settings, with determinant weights computed from the true image. A single-sample experiment illustrates how to automatically choose parameters from the data using a conditional generalized cross-validation criterion.
title: Marginalization-Based Regularization for Separable Nonlinear Least Squares Problems with Applications to Semi-Blind Deblurring

summary: Payment fraud causes financial losses and undermines users' trust in web payment services. Although fraud detection is a critical defense for payment security, complex and diverse fraudulent behaviors can still evade detection. Generating fraud samples for data augmentation can broaden detectors' coverage of different fraud patterns. However, existing methods matching the distribution of transaction attributes alone do not ensure that generated sequences preserve the sequential relationships among transaction choices, payment feedback, and subsequent behavioral adjustments. To this end, we propose PaySeqGen, an interpretable inverse reinforcement learning framework that reconstructs fraud behavior policies from fraudsters' observed payment trajectories. We design a mechanism for constructing candidate actions to support plausible payment sequence generation while enabling exploration. The framework also learns interpretable behavioral rewards that capture fraudsters' preferences across different transaction contexts. By alternating between reward learning and policy optimization, the framework reconstructs policies that generate new fraud sequences for detector augmentation and learns interpretable rewards supporting sequential fraud-pattern analysis in real trajectories. Experiments in real-world payment scenarios at Ant International, a leading global digital payment provider, show that PaySeqGen outperforms state-of-the-art generative augmentation methods. Reward-based trajectory analysis also identifies fraud patterns of practical value, helping analyst locating suspicious segments and examine multistep fraud tactics. Evaluation in the deployed system of online payment further confirms its effectiveness.
title: Reconstructing Fraudulent Strategies in Online Payments via Interpretable Inverse Reinforcement Learning

summary: We study forward and inverse problems for weakly viscous nonlocal wave equations with elastic term $(-Δ)^s u$ and dissipative term $(-Δ)^r\partial_tu$, where $0\leq r<s$. For time-dependent potentials in suitable $L^\infty(0,T;L^p(Ω))$ classes, we establish finite energy well-posedness, strong continuity in time, and an energy identity by parabolic regularization and time-regularization arguments. Under explicit nonlocality and nonresonance assumptions on the fractional orders, we prove Runge approximation in $L^2(0,T;\widetilde H^r(Ω))$ and hence in $L^2(Ω\times(0,T))$. As an application, partial exterior Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements uniquely determine the potential in all three exponent regimes of the Runge theorem, including integer elastic orders with noninteger dissipative orders. The recovery argument combines equality of solutions with the same exterior input, unique continuation or the entanglement principle, and a single Lebesgue-space Runge approximation. It applies to the full admissible potential class, without spatial boundedness, sign, or smallness assumptions.
title: Weakly viscous nonlocal wave equations: forward theory, Lebesgue Runge approximation, and inverse problems

summary: The Onsager--Machlup functional of a probability measure is a generalisation of the negative logarithm of the probability density function, defined precisely using the ratios of masses of balls in the limit of vanishing radius. It plays an important role in several areas of applied mathematics because its minimisers can be understood as modes of the measure. We show that the Onsager--Machlup functional of the angular central Gaussian measure on the unit sphere of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space---i.e., the radial projection of a centred Gaussian measure with covariance operator $C$---is constant on the finite-dimensional sphere spanned by the eigenvectors of leading eigenvalue under $C$, and takes the value $+\infty$ elsewhere. We discuss the consequences of this extreme concentration of mass for maximum a posteriori estimation in Bayesian inverse problems with an angular central Gaussian prior.
title: On the Onsager--Machlup functional of the infinite-dimensional angular central Gaussian distribution and related measures

summary: Latent diffusion and flow matching models are ubiquitous in state-of-the-art generative video models. While highly effective, relying on pretrained autoencoders to compress the data into a lower-dimensional latent space also comes with drawbacks. First, training proceeds in two stages: autoencoder pretraining, with compression and reconstruction objectives, followed by latent generative model training, precluding fully end-to-end training. Second, autoencoders also lead to an inherent loss of signal, and the trade-off between reconstruction quality and generative performance in the latent space is still an active area of research. In this paper we explore the viability of generative video models directly in pixel space. We analyze recent approaches in pixel-space generative modeling of images that rely on basic transformer designs, and identify several shortcomings that limit their effectiveness for the high-dimensional pixel-space video generation. To overcome these limitations, we propose a UNet-like transformer architecture along with improvements to the training recipe and sampling strategy. We conduct controlled experiments, training latent and pixel-space models from scratch on Kinetics-600. For the standard frames-to-video task at 128 resolution, our U-JiT model improves generative FVD by 27% over prior state-of-the-art results, and by 14% against the JiT pixel-space baseline. Scaling to higher 256 resolution, we find the improvement over pixel-space and latent-based models grows as we increase the spatiotemporal compression rate up to $64 \times 64 \times 8$. Finally, we find that U-JiT improves per-frame FID by 27% over latent models and 61% over pixel-space models on class-to-video generation, with respectively 9% and 56% reduction in FVD.
title: Pixel-space video generation with U-JiT

summary: We develop a numerical framework to efficiently simulate the cyclic voltammetry models based on discontinuous Galerkin (DG) spatial discretization combined with linearly implicit Euler time integration. The method is applied to two electrochemical mechanisms: a heterogeneous electron-transfer (ET) reaction and an electron-transfer reaction coupled with a catalytic chemical step (EC'). The governing time-dependent reaction-diffusion equations are expressed in dimensionless form and discretized in space using locally defined orthonormal Legendre polynomial basis functions. This discretization leads to a system of ordinary differential equations that is subsequently advanced in time using the linearly implicit Euler method. The resulting solver, denoted $\text{DG}_{\text{Impl}}$, is evaluated through numerical experiments and compared with MATLAB's $pdepe$ solver in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The numerical results demonstrate the convergence of $\text{DG}_{\text{Impl}}$ with respect to spatial and temporal discretizations and show that the method accurately reproduces the voltammetric responses of both ET and EC' mechanisms. For a prescribed relative error, $\text{DG}_{\text{Impl}}$ requires less computational time than $pdepe$ in the numerical experiments considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DG formulation for the forward simulation of cyclic voltammetry models and provide a numerical foundation for subsequent adjoint-based parameter-estimation and inverse-problem formulations.
title: A Discontinuous Galerkin Framework for Efficient Simulation of Cyclic Voltammetry Models

summary: This article connects demographic renewal with multinational recruitment control and the operating life of committed capital. Its host-choice argument engages resource bundling and global staffing, with explicit conditions for shared recruitment, competition and border disruption. Version 3.65.0 adds a Bayesian decision analysis to the Nitra–Puebla staffing appraisal. Under the existing flat-margin, equal-offer-odds benchmark, choosing Nitra after losing the whole UK route carries an expected loss from choosing the wrong host of EUR0.14–1.00 million. Losing only intakes after year fourteen reduces that expected loss to about EUR2,000–15,000. Nitra retains the higher expected value in these reference comparisons. Appendix K11 derives the decision rule, reports alternative priors and provides two independent integrations of 312 specifications. These are conditional public-information appraisals before capital commitment, not realised JLR losses or evidence about its internal contracts. Existing Bayesian panel estimates, demographic inputs, propositions and eight figures are retained. The article distinguishes the measured population-access specification from the recruitment-control mechanism and explains common tenure through the timing of workforce replacement. No observations or regressions are added. Start with Main_Manuscript_ANONYMOUS.pdf, Online_Appendix_ANONYMOUS.pdf and README.txt. Compilable sources, public inputs, code, figure files and aggregate outputs are supplied. The current replication overlay and nine frozen base archives restore the complete permitted replication. Licensed WRDS rows require subscriber access; queries and reconstruction instructions are supplied. Editor-only cover and title pages are excluded.
title: Borrowed Youth: Demographic Change and Multinational Location Advantage — Article and Replication Materials

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A Markov chain sampler estimates averages from one long trajectory; its accuracy is the long-run (asymptotic) variance of the time average. Adding a target-preserving rotation (a nonreversible perturbation) to overdamped Langevin samplers is known to help every observable. For kinetic (underdamped) Langevin samplers with friction γ, Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis (J. Stat. Phys. 2017) proved a local improvement for linear and quadratic observables of a Gaussian target when γ > √2 and conjectured it for every square-integrable observable. Results (exact stationary Gaussian dynamics, matched position and momentum rotations, position observables). (1) Every square-integrable observable's long-run variance never increases with rotation strength if and only if γ ≥ √2, endpoint included: a global form of the conjecture. The mechanism: the oscillator's power spectrum S(ξ) = 2γ/(ξ 4 + (γ 2 − 2)ξ 2 + 1) is single-peaked exactly when there is no resonance, rotation shifts the spectrum, and convolution keeps single peaks single. (2) The literal second-derivative form holds exactly on an explicit weighted Hermite class containing all polynomials; rough observables have sharper cusps. (3) Below the threshold, for every friction, even observables still improve at every rotation strength, only finitely many odd Hermite degrees can be hurt, and one finite rotation strength improves every observable. (4) Sharp large-rotation rates (uniform constant √(2π/e); slower for incommensurate rotation speeds). (5) For noncommuting stiffness K and friction Γ: ordering iff Γ 3 − ΓK − KΓ ≽ 0; the least safe friction (2K) 1/2 is a safety boundary, not an optimal friction; two coupled replicas make the criterion apply to any Gaussian target. (6) Fixed horizons and regular sampling can reverse the ordering; independent Poisson sampling preserves it. Scope. Gaussian targets only; no claim about numerical cost or discretised integrators (Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis found small friction best in practice). Classical ingredients (Breuer–Major Hermite identities, closure of symmetric unimodality under convolution, the convolution-power variance formula of Maini 2026) are credited, not claimed. Priority holds within a bounded literature search. Archive: manuscript (Markdown source, generated LaTeX and PDF), three deterministic verification scripts with their JSON reports, figure, extension notes, novelty reports, frozen targets, rating-free internal review record, bibliography with registry records, CI and SHA-256 manifests. Assurance: internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Sharp variance ordering for rotating Gaussian samplers

summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) model signals as continuous functions from coordinates to values, but their performance depends strongly on how spectral capacity is allocated. Yet most Quantum INR (QINR) architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks. We introduce the Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM), a memory coupled quantum INR in which sequential hybrid data reuploading layers (bands) communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register. Each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back, so later bands can build on the computation of earlier ones. When memory read and write layers are input independent, we prove that the memory state forms an operator valued Fourier series whose support is contained in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra. Downstream bands then condition their Fourier coefficients on the spectral content stored by earlier bands, and the memory coupling creates no new primitive frequencies. This theory motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed prefix of the model. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.
title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations

summary: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.
title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware

summary: Radio Frequency (RF) jamming threatens fifth-generation (5G) networks. Open Radio Access Network (Open RAN) telemetry enables jamming detection without dedicated spectrum monitoring equipment, but labeled attack data are rarely available across deployments, motivating unsupervised detectors. Comparing such detectors across algorithmic families, however, remains difficult without ground-truth labels. This paper benchmarks statistical and reconstruction-based unsupervised jamming detectors using a symmetric evaluation interface that combines detection confidence and temporal interval coherence into a detector-independent composite score. We compare a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) detector against Vanilla, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) baselines on Key Performance Indicator (KPI) telemetry from ten heterogeneous 5G environments with fixed and variable jamming bursts and dynamic jammer gains. Under leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation, SEM achieves a mean composite score of 0.906, compared with 0.688 for the best autoencoder (AE) per fold. Ground-truth validation yields a mean F1-score of 0.918 for SEM, compared with 0.521 for the best AE variant. The composite ranks SEM first in all environments, consistent with F1 rankings. However, in both within-trace and cross-trace evaluation, it fails for detectors that flag far fewer samples than the jamming prevalence, indicating that rankings are reliable only when detection rate matches the expected prevalence.
title: Benchmarking Unsupervised Jamming Detection in 5G Open RAN

summary: Automatic tools can now generate whole-brain MRI parcellations at cohort scale, but generated-label releases often provide little evidence about which cases are reliable enough to reuse. We introduce OpenBrain, a confidence-aware release of 35,838 provenance-verified OpenNeuro T1w cases from 607 source datasets. OpenBrain is organized as an auditable case-record release rather than a directory of standalone segmentation files: each record links a primary parcellation, two committee parcellations, source/license provenance, raw QC-7 measurements, percentile risks, a combined risk score R, and a confidence tier. QC-7 is a reference-free reliability panel over label geometry, image-label consistency, and committee disagreement, so users can filter, weight, audit, or re-threshold generated labels without rerunning inference. We evaluate this released evidence under a frozen protocol. Across external cohorts, lower QC-7 risk corresponds to higher generated-label quality; in fixed-budget training, lower-risk selections improve paired macro Dice over random selection by +3.2 to +3.7 percentage points. OpenBrain also exposes raw axes, committee outputs, provenance, and datasheet documentation, so confidence claims remain inspectable after download. It does not turn generated labels into manual annotations or clinical-grade segmentations. Its contribution is a large open generated-parcellation substrate, a reusable case-level risk-evidence layer, and an external validation protocol for release-time QC. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/lanqz7766/OpenBrain. Code: https://github.com/lanqz7766/openbrain.
title: OpenBrain: An Auditable Generated-Label Release for Whole-Brain MRI Parcellation

summary: Self-assembly enables complex structures to emerge from simple building blocks through local interaction rules. Are some structures intrinsically easier to design, that is, do they admit more sets of assembly rules than others? And, can this be predicted from their geometry? We address these questions using a three-dimensional polycube model with programmable face-to-face binding, defining a structure's assembly rule probability as the chance that a randomly chosen rule set produces it. For polycubes, this probability decreases exponentially with assembly complexity, the minimum information required to specify a structure's assembly rules. Intuitively, this follows because structures with low assembly complexity are generated not only by minimal rule sets but also by numerous more elaborate ones, and so arise disproportionately often. Symmetry can reduce assembly complexity by allowing the same building blocks and local interactions to be reused across different parts of a structure. Indeed, we find that the highest probability structures come from a tiny subset of highly symmetric structures. However, symmetry alone does not determine assembly complexity. Structures with the same symmetry can differ substantially in the amount of assembly information they require, depending on how effectively their global symmetry can be exploited by local growth rules. Overall, our results link information, symmetry, and assembly rule probability and suggest that identifying which geometric features permit rule reuse is central to designing minimal programmable self-assembling systems.
title: How symmetry and complexity shape three-dimensional programmable self-assembly

summary: This paper presents a novel SAT encoding designed to represent a sequence of At-Most-K cardinality constraints arranged in a ladder-like structure, referred to as the Ladder AMK constraint. These AMK constraints feature a ladder-like arrangement, with shared common variables in the center and two variables differing at the beginning and the end. The proposed encoding first decomposes the sequence of AMK constraints into separated blocks, then encodes each block as a whole rather than encoding each AMK constraint individually. This approach improves the efficiency of constraint solving in SAT solvers by significantly reducing the size of the encoding, precisely the number of variables, and the generated clauses required. To achieve this, the encoding employs Sequential Counter to encode each block and constructs clauses that link adjacent blocks, ensuring equivalence with the input constraints. Compared to the previously proposed encoding that uses BDD for Ladder AMO constraint, our encoding requires fewer variables and clauses. Our study is the first study that develops SAT encoding for Ladder AMK constraints with k>1. Experimental results on single Ladder AMO and Ladder AMK constraints indicate that our encoding significantly enhances both the size of the encoding and the efficiency of solving time compared to existing encodings. Furthermore, by evaluating on the two real-world combinatorial problems, namely Anti-bandwidth Problem and Nurse Rostering Problem, we found that the proposed encoding surpasses alternative encodings, as well as more advanced Constraint Programming and Mixed Integer Programming solvers. In summary, the SAT encoding technique presented in this paper provides a more efficient method for encoding sequence constraint, specifically Ladder AMK constraint, which could enhance the effectiveness of SAT solving for various problems involving this type of constraint.
title: SAT Encoding for Set of At-Most-K Cardinality Constraints with Ladder Shape

summary: This repository provides the research data, model outputs, analysis scripts, and supporting materials associated with the study “Beyond Architecture: Optimization and Hydrologic Regime Reveal Performance Headroom in Deep-Learning Rainfall–Runoff Modelling.” The study investigates how hyperparameter optimization, hydrological regime information, and ensemble design influence the predictive performance of deep-learning rainfall–runoff models across 531 CAMELS-US catchments. The repository supports the evaluation of regional modelling strategies, hydrologically informed ensembles, configuration-level contributions, and sensitivity analyses. Contents of this release Original research materials: Ten files retained from earlier versions of the dataset, including model archives, predictions, metrics, catchment attributes, and supporting data. 2026 revision analyses: CAMELS_US_Revision_2026_Analysis_Data_v3_additions.zip , containing the additional analysis materials and results underlying the current study, including Top-10 and hydrologically informed ensemble diagnostics, Top-18 sensitivity comparisons, and supporting figure and table resources. Additional Top-18 experiments: CAMELS_US_Top18_Additional8_Raw_10Seed_v3.zip , containing the archived outputs and supporting experiment artifacts for eight additional model configurations evaluated over ten random seeds (80 runs). Version and provenance note This is version 3 of the CAMELS-US research deposit. The files inherited from earlier dataset releases are retained unchanged for provenance and continuity, while the two additional archives document the analyses and experiments introduced in the 2026 release. The version history of the deposit is maintained through Zenodo.
title: Beyond Architecture: Optimization and Hydrologic Regime Reveal Performance Headroom in Deep-Learning Rainfall–Runoff Modelling

summary: Between 2010 and 2023, Niger faced escalating security and governance crises that culminated in the military coup of 26 July 2023. Conventional accounts often describe this trajectory in terms of state fragility, treating institutional weakness primarily as a deficit requiring technical reform. This article instead critically examines the explanatory value of Frantz Fanon's theory of postcolonial crisis in The Wretched of the Earth. Drawing on historical scholarship, empirical studies and policy reports, it develops five propositions concerning the inherited colonial state, the intermediary national bourgeoisie, the political marginalisation of the masses, neocolonial dependence, and the failure to transform national consciousness into social consciousness. Each proposition is assessed against developments in Niger between 2010 and 2023. The analysis finds that Fanon offers particular insight into elite intermediation, unequal access to state resources and externally mediated political power. Nevertheless, his framework gives insufficient attention to the relative autonomy of customary and religious authorities, transnational armed organisations and contemporary security partnerships. The 2023 coup further complicates his account by showing how military actors can appropriate the language of national liberation without demonstrating a corresponding commitment to social transformation. The article argues that Fanon's work remains valuable as a critical diagnosis of historically produced political relations, but should not be treated as a deterministic explanation of Niger's institutional trajectory.
title: Postcolonial Crisis and State Fragility in Niger, 2010–2023:A Critical Interrogation of Frantz Fanon's Theory

summary: Code, derived data and result files for Differentiable Neuro-Fuzzy Reasoning (DNFR), a path-based link predictor that learns degree-aware edge memberships, a Schweizer–Sklar t-norm per metapath and metapath reliabilities, and aggregates paths by noisy-OR, used as an instrument for a controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs. Tasks: drug repurposing in Hetionet v1.0 and PrimeKG, disease–symptom prediction in Hetionet and in the graded health knowledge graph of Rotmensch et al. (2017), and a secondary test on a NHANES fuzzy relation, under leave-dyad-out random and disease-centred splits. Comparators: fixed t-norms, component ablations, restarts of the t-norm parameter, DWPC with logistic regression (with and without degree and prior features), a degree-preserving edge prior, popularity, AnyBURL, truncated and soft-thresholded SVD and knowledge graph embeddings. Version v3.0-rev3 (third revision) adds DNFR 2.0, four refinements tested one at a time and in combination (overlap-aware aggregation, Gumbel-softmax operator choice, an information-content hub discount and membership annealing), a fixed t-norm selected on validation data, a converged L-BFGS profile of the t-norm parameter, an unbounded parameterisation, a compact NBFNet baseline, an exact edge-level Shapley attribution of the explanations, a mechanistic classification of the drug-repurposing explanations, a sparsity variant that keeps the target relation, and 10 leave-dyad-out splits for the main comparisons on Hetionet compound–treats–disease, Hetionet disease–symptom and the graded health knowledge graph. Version 1.1.0 (second revision) added a profile analysis of the t-norm parameter, training without early stopping, additional splits, equivalence tests, the edge prior, share-matched and edge-level explanation tests, unit tests and the script that builds the manuscript from the statistics files. Includes per-query ranks for every method and split, trained models, path explanations, and the statistics files from which every number in the manuscript is read. Hetionet and PrimeKG are downloaded by download_data.py with MD5 checks.
title: Code and derived results for: Which parts of a neuro-fuzzy path reasoner should be learned? A controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs, with four refinements (DNFR 2.0)

summary: This dataset contains the raw and processed experimental data associated with the study "Eco-Friendly and Large-Scale Fabrication of Microelectronic Silk-Based Enzymatic Biosensors". The collection includes measurements related to silk fibroin film fabrication and characterization, electron-beam lithography process optimization, nanostructure dimensional analysis, and enzymatic activity assays of horseradish peroxidase immobilized within silk fibroin matrices. Raw instrument outputs, processed datasets, statistical analyses, and metadata describing experimental conditions are provided to ensure transparency and reproducibility. The dataset supports the development of environmentally friendly microfabrication strategies for enzyme-based bioelectronic devices and may be reused for studies involving silk fibroin processing, enzyme immobilization, biopolymer lithography, and microelectronic biosensor fabrication
title: Replication Data for Eco-Friendly and Large-Scale Fabrication of Microelectronic Silk-Based Enzymatic Biosensors

summary: SimilCode Benchmark is a controlled dataset of 120 source-code pairs in C# and Java (15 reference programs per language, four similarity categories: identical, functional, structural and different) for evaluating source-code similarity detectors in programming education. It includes the raw results of a replicated evaluation of four commercial large language models (GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5; 1,440 evaluations, three replicas per pair and model) and the outputs of Moss, JPlag and Dolos on the same pairs; a classification of the pairs by code-clone type; a second run with 84 copies of the reference programs rewritten with generative AI (by a local open-weight model and by commercial models), verified by execution and scored together with independent solutions to the same exercises (1,368 LLM evaluations and the three detectors), including the refusals of the generators; an analysis of how well each dimensional score of the language models, their weighted global score and a derivation score that excludes functional similarity separate copies from independent solutions; the validation corpus and predictions of the Big O estimator of SimilCode; and scripts that reproduce the reported numbers without calling any API. Contents, protocol and reproduction instructions: see README.md, CHANGELOG.md and copias_ia/README_COPIAS_IA.md in the archived repository.
title: SimilCode Benchmark: A Dual-Language Source-Code Similarity Dataset for the Evaluation of AI-Based Detectors

summary: Saigon300 is a semi-synthetic benchmark for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (VRPTW) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Version 1.0.0 archives 56 instances with 300 customers and one depot each: C1 (9), C2 (8), R1 (12), R2 (11), RC1 (8), and RC2 (8). The package contains eight shared asymmetric OSRM distance/duration matrices, instance files, BIH verification and OR-Tools code, figures, and recorded experimental outputs. Matrix units are metres and seconds; the routing profile is car. Source metadata reports an OpenStreetMap snapshot dated 2026-05-26. This deposit is an unchanged snapshot of public repository commit 555ac7d2eb9d2af402bdb23f9633e3af435d8ab4: https://github.com/ltlong-SGU/Saigon300-VRPTW . ZIP integrity and node IDs 0..300 for all 56 instance files have been checked. This is not a new solver experiment or full independent replication. Authors: Le Tan Long and Phan Tan Quoc (Saigon University); Do Phan Thuan (Ho Chi Minh City University of Industry and Trade), as stated in the source metadata. Original source licences are retained: CC BY 4.0 for the dataset; source metadata separately declares MIT for code. Upstream rights remain applicable to OpenStreetMap/OSRM-derived components; OpenStreetMap attribution: https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright . This dataset deposit is separate from the accepted Saigon300 camera-ready paper, which is not included.
title: Saigon300: A VRPTW Benchmark Dataset for Urban Delivery in Ho Chi Minh City

summary: Abstract Water balance penalties may improve numerical closure while reallocating error among unobserved ‎fluxes. We investigate this compensation and the limits of selecting a penalty for annual flood ‎prediction. Forty-five trained synthetic LSTMs isolate forcing, exchange, and initialization ‎disturbances. Thirty-five matched regional models and five accounting references use 89 quality-quality-‎screened CAMELS-AUS catchments, partitioned into 54 for development, 15 for selector validation, ‎and 20 for confirmation. Under 40% precipitation underestimation, fixed and bounded penalties ‎reduce estimated evapotranspiration below 1% of generating truth in all eight held-out synthetic ‎catchments. A historically selected rule lowers confirmation-normalized annual-maximum error ‎from 2.29 to 2.21, a 3.54% point reduction. The original conditional interval barely excludes zero, ‎and river-region sign randomization gives p = 0.0625. A post hoc 100,000-draw analysis retains a ‎near-zero upper endpoint, with numerical sub-batches still reaching or crossing zero. Direct paired ‎comparisons with simpler alternatives all span zero; the selector does not establish added predictive ‎value. Its seven active catchments occupy only five regions. Recovery of the original final archive ‎verifies the selection lock, completed fit records, and hashes of all 40 real/reference prediction files. ‎These findings support a controlled latent-compensation mechanism and a reproducible limitation ‎of selective regularization, while leaving real-catchment process attribution and robust predictive ‎superiority unresolved. ‎ Keywords: rainfall-runoff modeling; water balance; annual flood maxima; model misspecification; ‎spatial transfer; uncertainty
title: Ayad-Kathim-Hussein/Prof.-Dr.-Ayad-K.-H.-Alkhafaji: Why selective mass penalties do not reliably improve annual flood maxima: An 89-‎catchment diagnostic with recovered provenance

summary: Fractal Geometry and the Verifiability of Electronic Election Results: Limits of Identification and a Multiscale Framework for Analyzing Tabulation This record contains an integrated research article (preprint; not peer reviewed) that asks a deliberately narrow question: under what conditions can fractal and multiscale methods applied to the published tabulation of a two-candidate election yield useful statistical evidence of irregularity, and under what conditions can no such method identify the origin of the data? The paper is addressed equally to those who read smoothness in a tabulation curve as a certificate of integrity and to those who read any irregularity as proof of manipulation; it argues that both readings mistake arithmetic and model specification for evidence. The analysis separates five stages of the electoral chain (voter choice, machine record, transmission, tabulation, publication) and three research questions that are routinely conflated: whether the order in which precincts are reported is atypical, whether precinct-level results are atypical relative to an explicit reference model, and whether published results agree with independently preserved records. Three elementary propositions formalize what tabulation data can and cannot show. The cumulative vote share is mechanically damped as the count grows, so late smoothness is a property of weighted averaging rather than a sign of control. Two scenarios that induce the same distribution over the observable data cannot be separated by any test confined to those data, with discriminating power bounded by their total variation distance. And a class of proportional vote transfers leaves every increment-based statistic (first differences, centered CUSUM, zero-mean wavelet contrasts) unchanged while shifting the cumulative margin by 2δN_k. A fully synthetic experiment models 256 precincts in 16 regions with correlated regional preferences and geographically dependent reporting times, and compares four two-sided detectors (level test, centered CUSUM, multiscale scan and Haar contrast over windows of 4 to 128 precincts), each calibrated separately on 2,000 null elections and evaluated on 1,500 independent elections per scenario. Under the correct null, alert rates lie between 4.1% and 5.7%. With a 4% transfer concentrated in a block of 51 precincts, the Haar contrast alerts in 94.0% of replicates (Wilson 95% interval 92.7%–95.1%); with a diffuse 0.8% transfer across all 256 precincts, moving approximately the same number of votes (608 versus 612 on average), it alerts in 4.5%, indistinguishable from the null. A legitimate regional preference shift omitted from the reference model produces Haar alerts in 57.7% of elections in which no vote was transferred, and a deliberately homogeneous reference that ignores geography drives three of the four detectors to 100% false alerts. Sensitivity depends on the shape of the alteration and on the specification of the reference model, not on the volume of votes moved. The limits of these findings are stated explicitly. The reference model is an oracle known to the simulator; all data are synthetic; the experiment was not preregistered; detection delay and localization accuracy were not systematically evaluated; no actual election is analyzed, and nothing in the paper certifies or refutes the integrity of any election. A p-value is not a probability of fraud, and the absence of an alert cannot certify the absence of manipulation. The paper closes with a protocol for future application to real tabulation records, covering data provenance and chronology, preregistration, a global multiscale statistic with Monte Carlo calibration, nonfractal comparators at equal false-alert rates, adversarial and benign alternatives, and robustness checks, and situates the discussion within software independence and the cast-as-intended, recorded-as-cast and tallied-as-recorded framework of election verifiability. title: Fractal Geometry and the Verifiability of Electronic Election Results

summary: This dataset provides the CLIMA-CARE Preprocessed Source Data Repository, version 2.0.0 , developed within WP2 of the CLIMA-CARE project. It contains the harmonized environmental, territorial, demographic, socioeconomic, mobility, population, land use, and settlement datasets used as input to the CLIMA-CARE Data Loading Module. The original source data have been preprocessed to ensure compatibility with the project analytical framework. Depending on the dataset, preprocessing includes spatial reprojection, area-weighted transfer to the CLIMA-CARE reference grid, spatial aggregation or disaggregation, downscaling, temporal transformation, recoding, and derivation of indicators or summary metrics. The common spatial reference is the LMB0A grid , composed of hexagonal cells with 1 km diameter in EPSG:32632 . Version 2.0.0 consolidates the previously available source datasets with revised NDVI, OMI NO₂, WUSTL PM₂.₅, and MODIS land-cover products, together with additional ESA LST, WUSTL surface NO₂, and ERA5 and ERA5-Land monthly products. The release also includes spatial representativeness datasets describing the relationship between the native spatial support of selected source products and the CLIMA-CARE reference grid. The package includes the preprocessed data files together with the reference grid, the operational data dictionary, structured metadata describing provenance, spatial and temporal characteristics, preprocessing, and field-level definitions, and source-specific licensing information. Daily, monthly, long-term, yearly, static, and spatial representativeness products are included according to the characteristics of each source dataset. This release provides a transparent, reproducible, and versioned input repository for the CLIMA-CARE processing workflow. The data package is designed for use with the CLIMA-CARE Data Loading Module and for independent reuse where compatible with the applicable licensing conditions. The repository incorporates data derived from multiple third-party sources subject to different licences and attribution requirements. The applicable conditions for each dataset family are documented in the accompanying licensing file. Use of the CLIMA-CARE package and derived products must acknowledge the original CLIMA-CARE release and reference the specific version and DOI.
title: CLIMACARE_02DAT_02PRE_PreprocessedDataset_v2.0.0

summary: Effective pandemic preparedness depends on the ability to identify, access and reuse health data across borders rapidly. This requires knowing what data and capabilities exist, how infrastructures are governed, which standards they use, and under what conditions data can be accessed or analysed. This work is central to the BE READY European Partnership for Pandemic Preparedness, which aims to strengthen Europe's capacity to coordinate research and respond to emerging infectious disease threats. Comparable, machine-actionable implementation metadata can help BE READY connect existing infrastructures, identify interoperability and governance barriers, and guide strategic investment. This presentation was delivered at the Research Data Alliance (RDA) Plenary 27, hosted by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), under the theme "Shaping a global open research commons." It examines how fragmented health data infrastructures can become part of a connected, interoperable and sustainable global research ecosystem. The presentation reports two outputs from the RDA Health Data Commons GORC Profile Working Group. The first is the pilot of an implementation metadata survey and profile, building on the RDA Global Open Research Commons (GORC) International Model and FAIR, CARE and TRUST principles. The profile captures technical, legal, governance and equity characteristics of health data commons. Two national biomedical data infrastructures had piloted the survey. The second output is a scoping review of 47 health data infrastructures across 26 countries, described in 74 publications. The review identifies significant reporting gaps in the characteristics needed for interoperability and reuse. Metadata standards were reported for nine infrastructures, APIs for six, identifiers and provenance for two each, and machine-actionable permissions for none. Seven infrastructures supported federated analysis, while three described federated governance. Twenty-one reported legal or governance barriers. Only three described benefit-sharing arrangements, and none reported benefits returned to patients or communities. Just 10 papers reported empirical evidence. These findings reflect gaps in published reporting, which may differ from actual implementation. The RDA Working Group proposes refinements to the GORC International Model covering omics and bioimaging provenance, federated data reuse, and benefit sharing. It also proposes publishing implementation metadata as a living, queryable knowledge graph, supported by a community of practice among health data commons operators. For BE READY, this approach provides a foundation for understanding which European health data capabilities can be mobilised together during a health emergency, what barriers prevent their reuse, and where investment is most needed. More broadly, this work contributes to the RDA P27 ambition of shaping a global open research commons by transforming fragmented infrastructures into a connected, discoverable and interoperable ecosystem that supports research, pandemic preparedness and public health.
title: Federated Reuse of Participant-Level Data across Health Data Commons: Evidence, Insights, & Future Directions

summary: RaMa-Scene Explorer traces the supply chains behind consumption using EXIOBASE v3.3.sm data for 2011. It maps where greenhouse-gas emissions, employment and metal-ore extraction occur across 49 countries and regions, grouped into 15 industry sections. Readers can trace a footprint, inspect its flows and compare 155 published scenarios. Custom scenarios compute on the reader's device, in WebAssembly, or through an optional RaMa-Scene job API. The model changes monetary final demand or inputs per unit of output, with prices and other coefficients fixed. The results describe the 2011 economy, not forecasts. Methods, assumptions, provenance and numerical checks accompany the results. The code is MIT-licensed; derived EXIOBASE data is shared under CC BY 4.0.
title: RaMa-Scene Explorer

summary: This archive contains the Python code, raw numerical results and figure-generation scripts accompanying the paper "An Alternated Inertial Method for Bilevel Split Variational Inequalities Beyond Monotonicity and Lipschitz Continuity" by N. T. T. Thuy and P. T. Hieu (submitted to Optimization, Taylor & Francis, 2026). The paper studies the bilevel split variational inequality problem with multiple output sets (BSVIP-MOS) governed by non-monotone, possibly non-Lipschitz operators, and proposes AISE-VS, an alternated inertial subgradient-extragradient method with a look-ahead self-adaptive stepsize, a split correction and a viscosity step, together with an Armijo line-search variant (AISE-VS-LS) that dispenses with the stepsize conditions. The archive reproduces every table and figure of the paper: - numerical certification of the assumptions (Table 1); - Experiment 1: a certified non-quasimonotone benchmark with skew-type operators, 20 starting points (Table 2, Fig. 1); - Experiment 2: a Hölder (non-Lipschitz) benchmark, self-adaptive rule versus line search, up to 2×10^5 iterations (Table 3, Fig. 2); - Experiment 3: a trade-network instance built from BACI-VI-Bench (year 2022 and a study over 2017–2024) with an independently certified reference solution (Table 4, Fig. 3); - long-run convergence (Fig. 4) and a look-ahead ablation (Fig. 5). The package contains the source code (src/), the raw results behind all tables and figures (results/), the figures (figures/), a README.md that maps each table and figure to the command that regenerates it, run_quick.sh (smoke test) and run_all.sh (full reproduction). Seeds are fixed (global seed 2024). Requirements: Python 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib. The BACI-VI-Bench dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20607238), derived from CEPII-BACI, is NOT redistributed here; it must be downloaded separately to rerun Experiment 3 (see README). Experiments 1 and 2 are fully synthetic. Version 1.0.1. This version adds the scripts (verification/, run by run_verification.sh) and logs (results/verification/) of the additional checks reported in the revised manuscript. The source code in src/ and all tables and figures are unchanged from version 1.0.0. The checks are: (i) an independent recomputation of the reference solution x† for 2017–2024 with an interior-point solver (CVXPY/Clarabel), compared with the stored x†; (ii) the marginal residual of the stored x†; (iii) an a-posteriori check that every point at which the operators are evaluated stays in the region where the extended operator coincides with the original one; and  (iv) the number of times the restart criterion is examined and the number of times it is activated in Experiments 1–3, including two runs of 10^5 iterations. The logs of one complete run are summarised in results/verification/SUMMARY.md; the version history is in CHANGELOG.md.  Check (i) additionally requires cvxpy (requirements-verification.txt); the other checks need only the packages of requirements.txt.
title: AISE-VS for bilevel split variational inequalities with multiple output sets: code and raw results

summary: Abstract   Objective : In a previous study, the author used a Cox proportional hazards regression model to analyze the relationships between emergency transport data for heatstroke cases in Tokyo in 2025, meteorological factors, and urban aerosols, thereby identifying factors that alter the risk of heatstroke in an urban environment. While the analysis suggested a positive correlation between PM2.5 concentrations and the risk of heatstroke, this association was not statistically significant. The present study reports the results of an analysis that integrates data from 2023, 2024, and 2025. Method : Analysis was performed using a Cox proportional hazards regression model in which ambient temperature was incorporated as a parameter of the baseline hazard function . Result and Discussion : The results of the Cox proportional hazards regression analysis identified atmospheric pressure and relative humidity as positive predictors. Furthermore, an increase in PM2.5 levels was found to be statistically significantly associated with an elevated risk of heatstroke. Conversely, duration of sunshine, PM10 levels, and the cumulative number of days since June 1st were identified as negative predictors. PM2.5 contains numerous substances derived from combustion, which generate free radicals that are harmful to the human cardiopulmonary system. Consequently, it is thought that PM2.5 may increase the risk of heatstroke. In the present study, which integrated data from 2023, 2024, and 2025, PM2.5 concentration was identified as a statistically significant positive modifying factor. It should be noted, however, that while this study demonstrates an association, it does not establish a causal relationship.   Conclusion: Further research was conducted on the relationship between PM2.5 and the risk of heatstroke, utilizing a larger number of cases. PM2.5 showed a positive correlation with the risk of heatstroke, and this association was statistically significant.
tags: Keywords: heatstroke; Cox proportional hazards regression; meteorological factors; urban aerosols; PM10; PM2.5
title: Meteorological factors and urban aerosols associated with emergency transport of heatstroke cases

summary: IberCloud-L is a dataset of 1,094 Landsat patches annotated for cloud and cloud shadow segmentation in four classes. It covers Landsat 5, 7, 8 and 9 imagery over the Iberian Peninsula, including Cantabrian, Mediterranean and southern coastal regions, an inland region and a mountainous region in the Pyrenees, with contrasting cloud regimes. The images are Landsat Collection 2 top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance downloaded via Google Earth Engine. Annotations were produced in two stages. A model trained on CloudSEN12 generated initial masks, which an expert annotator then reviewed and corrected manually. Landsat 7 scenes affected by the Scan Line Corrector failure (after May 2003) were excluded. This dataset accompanies the article “NIMBUS: A multisensor cloud segmentation model for Sentinel-2 and Landsat coastal monitoring using RGB imagery”. Files train.zip val.zip test.zip Format Bands 1–3: RGB Band 4: GT mask (0 = clear sky, 1 = thick cloud, 2 = thin cloud, 3 = cloud shadow)
title: IberCloud-L

summary: What are the capacity limits of a bounded observer’s epistemic activity, and what constructions attain those limits? This technical and philosophical companion connects preservation, acquisition and discovery, construction, certification, adoption, continuation and revision, with resource accounting, self-application and coverage throughout. The full connected capacity characterization remains OPEN. Interim technical revision r7t, 4 November 2026. This corrected successor improves the reader’s guide, lifecycle explanation, prior-work comparisons and model-to-system discussion. It preserves the published finite-Fourier orbit-separating construction with its explicit nonzero-reference condition, arithmetic-cost model and conditioning limits. Orientation is an explanatory atlas, not a proof premise. Exact results, assumptions and review evidence govern mathematical claims. The revision qualifies empirical-verification and identifiability statements by their evidence models; separates expected, probabilistic and worst-case guarantees; and distinguishes imported mathematics from unresolved transfer obligations. Historical cases and dated internal AI-agent trials illustrate the lens without establishing universal performance or research novelty. It separates native builder controls from generated-application behavior, passing local checks from authorized outcomes, and prospective tests from completed observations. Review is internal and AI-assisted, not external peer review or whole-program mathematical acceptance. Earlier versions and dated evidence cutoffs are preserved. This is an explanatory and corrective edition, not a claim that the full research program is complete. The manuscript retains its review-candidate designation. This record contains the manuscript, not a standalone proof-reproduction package.
title: The Missing Distinction: The Connected Capacity of a Bounded Observer

summary: Proposals document accompanying the talk "Digital therapeutics: state of the art in Italy" (SIFO 2026 National Congress, Rome, 6 November 2026). It is a proposals paper, kept separate from the Supplementary Information of the talk, which contains the data and analyses. Each paragraph is tagged as Data, Analysis or Proposal, so that sourced facts, the author's inferences and the author's opinions can be told apart. The starting point is the "efficacy without use" problem: digital therapeutics (DTx) that work in controlled settings are abandoned early in real life. Trial dropout ranges from about 19% to 48%, real-world abandonment reaches a median of 70% within 100 days, and human contact is the best-documented protective factor, although only as an association. The paper notes that most usage data concern health apps in general, not DTx as defined by ISO/TR 11147:2023, and that we found no post-marketing usage data for DTx. The bill S. 1918, as approved by the Italian Chamber of Deputies on 27 May 2026, defines digital therapies and their assessment, but in our reading it does not mention prescription or dispensation. The step between prescription and intake is therefore undefined. We propose three distinct activities with three actors: prescription (prescriber), dispensation (a health mediator distinct from the prescriber) and intake (patient). We distinguish software and procedural "digital excipients", to be described in HTA dossiers and assessed on use endpoints, separately from the clinical endpoint of the active function. Health mediation comprises five acts: verify, explain, activate, control, and vigilance, delivered at three levels of intensity proportional to risk. We propose the term "dispensazione", with an explicit definition, and discuss its legal risks. As mediator we propose a specialised DTx pharmacist in the pharmaceutical services of the local health authorities, working remote-first from regional or inter-ASL hubs, with in-person dispensation when needed and with other professionals as co-mediators. An illustrative sizing, built on German activation data, suggests that a few dozen full-time pharmacists would suffice in the first years. Evidence for the model is limited: a Danish routine-care programme with psychologist support shows that human mediation is feasible at scale, but not that it improves outcomes. We propose a comparative pilot with retention at 12 weeks as primary endpoint, and state what result would lead to revising or withdrawing the proposal. Conflicts of interest and the use of an AI model (Claude, Anthropic) for analysis and drafting are declared in the document. The Italian version is published on the website of the Associazione TendenzeSaluteSanità.
title: Analysis and Proposal for the Dispensation of Digital Therapeutics in Italy

summary: Source, programs and Lean 4 certificate of the paper Yang–Mills Mass Gap Follows from One Cube, by Deep Bhattacharjee, Ushashi Bhattacharya, James Montgomery Lockwood and Tristan Romanov (Hexagon preprint 2610.00341). The gauge of four-dimensional lattice Yang–Mills theory is fixed on a period-two field of straight lines that meets every plaquette in exactly one link. At fixed lattice spacing this gives a unique free-boundary state, reflection positivity, exponential clustering and an explicit transfer-matrix gap: for SU(2) up to beta_W = 0.348 through plaquette blocks with constants proved by hand, and for SU(3) up to beta_W = 0.52 through plaquette blocks with constants proved by hand, and for every compact simple group G when N|beta| < 2 kappa_G/29, with kappa_G the least Ricci curvature. A Dobrushin–Shlosman condition on one cube of fixed physical size, uniform along the continuum tuning, gives a mass gap in physical units in every continuum limit, also for observables smoothed by the gradient flow; the paper proves what that cube estimate needs and which Osterwalder–Schrader properties a limit of the flowed fields has. Towards the estimate it labels the blocks of Balaban's averages, proves that the weight of bad islands factorises through kernels on the good layers between them with cross-ratios exponentially small in the widths of the layers, gives the explicit coupling past which bad islands and their clusters are rarer than their entropy, and controls one step of the block map on the large fields and on the calm small fields. It also reduces the cube estimate to an averaged condition, proves that this condition descends to block variables and climbs one scale under a split inequality, proves that inequality at strong coupling and on each finite torus, reduces the condition at the coarsest scale to Dobrushin bounds on the single-link coefficients of the laws of the block variables, which one step of the block map contracts and which gauge covariance excludes at weak coupling, and states the conditional chain for every compact simple group. Lean 4 (Mathlib) checks the combinatorics of the line field and the block gauge, the finite arithmetic of the perturbation propositions and the chain of rational bounds of the SU(2) blocks; the ball-arithmetic programs (python-flint), which no proof uses, are included. The averaged covariance of the labels, the effective action across all scales and a nontrivial continuum limit are not proved; the Clay Millennium problem is open. The archive also keeps the sources of two earlier papers of the project in tex/ and strong-coupling/prd/.
title: Yang–Mills Mass Gap Follows from One Cube

summary: This replication package accompanies the paper “Code-to-Prompt-to-Code: An Empirical Study of Prompt Recovery, Adaptation, and Structural Drift.” It contains everything needed to reproduce the study’s results. A Jupyter notebook reproduces the main tables, the statistical tests, and the RQ1 and RQ2 plots. The analysis/ folder contains scripts for the additional analyses (effect of the repair loop, prompt-level measures, change coverage of adapted prompts with bootstrap confidence intervals, a data-leakage check based on git blame , and repository statistics) and for the final versions of the RQ2 figures. Two further scripts recompute the CodeSage similarity scores. The data/ folder contains the 200 sampled real-world Python functions, 8,400 prompt-recovery records (7 information levels, 2 models, 3 repetitions), 2,400 prompt-adaptation records (400 modifications across 6 modification types, 2 prompt-adapting models, 3 repetitions), and precomputed CodeSage similarity scores for both research questions. The figures/ folder holds the generated plots. The README maps each table and figure in the paper to the notebook cell or script that produces it.
title: Replication Package -- Code-to-Prompt-to-Code: An Empirical Study of Prompt Recovery, Adaptation, and Structural Drift

summary: This study presents the results of portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) analysis of a pale grey-bluish ceramic brush washer. Two measurements were obtained from the vessel: one from the side wall and one from the glazed base. The analytical results demonstrate an exceptionally high degree of compositional consistency between both measurement locations. Major and trace element concentrations are virtually identical, indicating that the vessel is covered by a single homogeneous glaze and shows no evidence of secondary glazing, restoration, or later surface modification. The glaze is characterized by elevated silica and calcium concentrations, a strong predominance of lime over alkali fluxes, extremely low titanium content, negligible lead concentrations, and the complete absence of artificial coloring agents. Comparison with published analytical studies of Southern Song Guan kilns from Jiaotanxiao, Laohudong, and Wansongling demonstrates close correspondence in major technological parameters, including high-calcium glaze chemistry, iron-based coloration, low titanium values, and lead-free high-temperature firing technology. The analytical data define a coherent high-fired lime glaze system colored exclusively by iron and closely aligned with the archaeometric characteristics of Southern Song Guan ware. Keywords: Guan ware, Southern Song Dynasty, brush washer, celadon, XRF analysis, archaeometry, lime glaze, Chinese ceramics, high-fired glaze technology. 1. Introduction Guan ware (官窑) occupies a distinguished position among the imperial ceramic productions of the Southern Song Dynasty. One of the defining technological characteristics of Southern Song Guan ceramics is the use of high-fired lime-rich glazes producing subtle grey-blue, grey-green, and jade-like surface tones. These visual effects were achieved through carefully controlled glaze compositions and reducing firing atmospheres rather than through the addition of artificial pigments. Archaeometric investigations conducted on kiln materials from Jiaotanxiao, Laohudong, and Wansongling have established a characteristic technological profile for Guan glazes, including elevated calcium concentrations, low titanium content, iron-controlled coloration, and the absence of lead-based flux systems. The present study examines the glaze chemistry of a pale grey-bluish brush washer and compares the analytical results with published archaeometric data from Southern Song Guan kiln sites. 2. Description of the Object The investigated object is a glazed ceramic brush washer. Visual examination reveals: a uniform monochrome glaze; pale grey-bluish coloration; absence of painted decoration; absence of localized artificial color effects; soft vitreous surface luster; visually homogeneous glaze coverage across the entire vessel. The glaze extends continuously over both the body and the base of the vessel. The analytical target images demonstrate excellent contact between the instrument window and the glaze surface, resulting in high-quality measurements. 3. Materials and Methods The analysis was conducted using a Geochem (3-Beam) Extra portable X-ray fluorescence spectrometer. Measurement conditions: acquisition time: 30 seconds; non-destructive in situ analysis; Geochem analytical mode. Two analytical locations were examined: ID 1 – Side Wall Glazed side surface of the vessel. ID 2 – Base Glazed lower surface of the vessel. The lightweight-element index (LE) ranged between approximately 45% and 46%, indicating excellent analytical conditions and high confidence in the elemental results. 4. XRF Results Table 1. summary: Nonlinear root-finding, analytic signal extrapolation, and Marchenko inverse scattering share a common mathematical bottleneck: the inversion of ill-posed linear or linearized operators that suffer from spectral clustering, numerical instability, and spurious pole proliferation in unconstrained continuous spaces. Projecting these systems onto the maximal class-number-one Heegner modular curve establishes a unique factorization domain that eliminates fractional holonomy phase slips, preventing branch-cut bifurcations and suppressing spurious pole-zero doublets. Truncating the singular modulus expansion at its principal term provides an analytical starting anchor that strictly satisfies Smale point-estimate convergence criteria, placing the system directly within the quadratic attraction basin and reaching machine precision in a single iteration. In analytic continuation, the modular coordinate under the maximal discriminant is suppressed well below double-precision machine epsilon, truncating out-of-band noise and bypassing the Runge phenomenon without empirical regularization parameters. For high-dimensional networks and discretized scattering kernels, operator preconditioning via Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak Ramanujan graph Laplacians enforces a uniform spectral gap derived from the Deligne bound on Hecke operators. This holds the condition number on the invariant zero-mean subspace to a small, constant bound, ensuring that both the Newton Jacobian update and the Marchenko integral equation converge in very few Krylov iterations regardless of network scale.
title: Arithmetic Operator Inversion: Resolving Nonlinear Root-Finding, Analytic Extrapolation, and Inverse Scattering via Heegner Modular Uniformization and Ramanujan Preconditioning

summary: Audited research compendium supporting the evaluation of Big Five league representation as a candidate squad-composition performance indicator for FIFA World Cup knockout progression from 1998 to 2026. The release contains 1,584 first-knockout starting-eleven records nested within 144 team-tournaments across eight men’s World Cups and 48 national teams. The analytical framework evaluates three linked properties: discrimination between levels of format-harmonised knockout progression; incremental information beyond pre-tournament World Football Elo; and transportability of any increment to World Cup editions and national teams excluded from model estimation. The 1998–2010 historical extension preserves the frozen exposure, outcome and model definitions established for 2014–2026. Historical starter status derives from the Fjelstul World Cup Database and was cross-checked against RSSSF match details. Club affiliation and top-division status were adjudicated using tournament squad records and season-specific domestic-league reference files. The 2014–2026 subset retains the completed provenance audit, including 505 re-checked starter records, 13 starter-name corrections, 45 club-affiliation checks and seven Big Five reclassifications. Analyses include tournament-adjusted ordinal and cut-point models, AICc comparison with Akaike weights, 5,000 national-team cluster-bootstrap samples with bias-corrected and accelerated intervals, leave-one-edition-out validation, leave-one-national-team-out validation, a strict 2026 temporal and tournament-format holdout, and a predictive cluster bootstrap that refits both competing models within every fold and resample. Additional checks address collinearity, edition adjustment and dependence through within-edition permutation testing and an edition-level block bootstrap. Big Five representation was associated with deeper knockout progression before adjustment for Elo, but this association attenuated after adjustment. Model comparisons and held-out evaluations did not establish a stable, transportable increment beyond prior team strength. These findings concern the predictive information provided by current league representation; they do not distinguish the mechanisms through which players enter elite leagues or develop within them. Version 5.2.0 updates presentation and documentation only. Figure 1 presents the relationship between Big Five representation and Elo alongside the four primary ordinal-model estimates. Figure 2 displays the held-out difference in ignorance score between the joint Big Five + Elo model and Elo alone for each World Cup edition, together with the equal-edition mean and its 95% BCa interval. The former supplementary interval figure was removed; its underlying estimates remain available in the deposited machine-readable results. No data, frozen definition, model specification, inferential estimate, predictive score, random seed or substantive conclusion changed from v5.1.0. The estimand is knockout progression conditional on qualification for the knockout stage. These observational data do not identify a causal effect of Big Five employment, estimate the long-term developmental return to elite-league exposure or address group-stage qualification. The compendium includes analytical data, provenance records, analysis code, machine-readable results and publication-ready figures. The derivative dataset is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, with attribution to the Fjelstul World Cup Database.
title: Big Five representation, Elo and FIFA World Cup knockout progression, 1998–2026: audited data and reproducibility materials

summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.
title: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles with Recursively Feasible Control Barrier Functions

summary: Open-Source Moon: A Technical Framework for Intelligent Development of Extraterrestrial Bodies Based on Sensor Dispersal and Golden Consensus Abstract: The exploration and development of the Moon and other celestial bodies currently depend heavily on State-led, integrated space missions that are costly, slow, and difficult for the public to join. To address this situation, this paper proposes “Open-Source Moon”, a technical framework that applies the open-source philosophy to the intelligent development of extraterrestrial bodies. The framework treats the Moon as a large developer platform that all of humankind can program collectively. Following the progressive principle of “information first, from the outside in, from sensing to action”, it transforms the Moon layer by layer into a “smart planet” that can be programmed as a whole, and it organizes global participation through open-source protocols and the contribution-securing mechanism of “Golden Consensus”: massive numbers of low-cost, standardized micro sensors are first dispersed over the lunar surface to form a distributed sensing network whose nodes are beacons and hotspots; delay-tolerant networking (DTN) and a predictive compensation mechanism then overcome the one-way communication delay of about 1.28 s; and a small-machine cooperation ecosystem, LEGO-style combination of medium-sized machines, and finally unmanned factories and lunar computing carry the staged evolution from sensors to a “smart planet”. Based on the self-similar allocation principle and the Schelling focal point, which secure and incentivize decentralized contributions, a “Golden Consensus” system founded on the golden ratio ( φ ≈ 1.618) is proposed: explorers receive 61.8% of the development-rights return (of which a further 2.8% is set aside as a “common allocation” for public facilities), and 38.2% is designated as socially shared. A model with 880 000 cornerstone nodes is set up, in which a distributed ledger establishes ownership of contributions and keeps tamper-proof records. Verifiable engineering models of network coverage, link budget, energy budget, and delay compensation are established, and the compatibility of this approach with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, as well as the general applicability of extending it to other celestial bodies such as Mercury and Mars, is demonstrated. This study provides a feasible technical route and governance framework for public participation in the development of extraterrestrial bodies. Keywords: Lunar Landing; Human Lunar Landing ; Open-Source Moon; sensor network; smart planet; Golden Consensus; delay-tolerant networking; lunar development; citizen science; Outer Space Treaty; Human Spaceflight 1. Introduction 1.1. Background and Motivation For more than half a century, the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies has taken the form mainly of large, integrated, State-led missions. After Apollo 17 in 1972, crewed spaceflight remained confined to near-Earth orbit for a long time, until Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby (without landing) in April 2026 [1]. On 22 February 2024, the Odysseus lander of Intuitive Machines achieved the first soft landing on the Moon by a commercial spacecraft [2], marking the beginning of the era of commercial lunar landings. However, the development and launch cost of a single mission is still on the order of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of US dollars, and most of the failure risk is concentrated in the powered-descent and landing phases. From the soft landing of Chang’e-3 in 2013 to June 2025, there were 14 soft-landing attempts on the lunar surface worldwide (Table 4): six full successes, three partial successes (in which the attitude or mission capability was impaired after landing), and five failures. According to public reports retrieved for this study, no new lunar landing attempt had occurred

summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.
title: MELITE — Multi-Model Supervised Learning Evaluator

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule
