title: Fostering Resilience in Adolescents at Risk: Study protocol for a cluster randomized controlled trial within the resilience school-based intervention

summary: Background The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) strategy to face the challenges of ageing societies. This strategy is focused on person centered care and the assessment intrinsic capacity (IC). Early identification of five domains of IC (cognition, locomotion, vitality, sensory (hearing and vision), and psychological) has been shown to be related with adverse outcomes and can guide actions towards primary prevention and healthy ageing. IC assessment proposed by the WHO ICOPE guidelines is composed by two steps: First, Screening for decreased IC by the ICOPE Screening tool; second, by the reference standard methods. The aim was to assess the performance of diagnostic measures (sensibility, specificity, diagnostic accuracy, and agreement of the ICOPE Screening tool) compared to the reference standard methods in European community-dwelling older adults. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of the baseline of the ongoing VIMCI (Validity of an Instrument to Measure Intrinsic Capacity) cohort study, which was carried out in Primary Care centers and outpatient clinics from 5 rural and urban territories in Catalonia (Spain). Participants were 207 community dwelling persons >= 70-year-old with Barthel >= 90, without dementia or advanced chronic conditions who provided their consent to participate. The 5 IC domains were assessed by the ICOPE Screening tool and the reference methods (SPPB, gait speed, MNA, Snellen chart, audiometry, MMSE, GDS5) during patients' visit. Agreement was assessed with the Gwet AC1 index. Results ICOPE Screening tool sensitivity was higher for cognition (0.889) and ranged between 0.438 and 0.569 for most domains. Specificity ranged from 0.682 to 0.96, diagnostic accuracy from 0.627 to 0.879, Youden index from 0.12 to 0.619, and Gwet AC1 from 0.275 to 0.842. Conclusion The ICOPE screening tool showed fair performance of diagnostic measures; it was helpful to identify those participants with satisfactory IC and showed a modest ability to identify decreased IC in older people with high degree of autonomy. Since low sensitivities were found, a process of external validation would be recommended to © 2023. The Author(s).
title: Identification of decreased intrinsic capacity: Performance of diagnostic measures of the ICOPE Screening tool in community dwelling older people in the VIMCI study

summary: Background: In May 2020, the ACCESS (The vACCine covid-19 monitoring readinESS) project was launched to prepare real-world monitoring of COVID-19 vaccines. Within this project, this study aimed to generate background incidence rates of 41 adverse events of special interest (AESI) to contextualize potential safety signals detected following administration of COVID-19 vaccines.Methods: A dynamic cohort study was conducted using a distributed data network of 10 healthcare data-bases from 7 European countries (Italy, Spain, Denmark, The Netherlands, Germany, France and United Kingdom) over the period 2017 to 2020. A common protocol (EUPAS37273), common data model, and common analytics programs were applied for syntactic, semantic and analytical harmonization. Incidence rates (IR) for each AESI and each database were calculated by age and sex by dividing the num-ber of incident cases by the total person-time at risk. Age-standardized rates were pooled using random effect models according to the provenance of the events.Findings: A total number of 63,456,074 individuals were included in the study, contributing to 211.7 mil-lion person-years. A clear age pattern was observed for most AESIs, rates also varied by provenance of disease diagnosis (primary care, specialist care). Thrombosis with thrombocytopenia rates were extre-mely low ranging from 0.06 to 4.53/100,000 person-years for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) with thrombocytopenia (TP) and mixed venous and arterial thrombosis with TP, respectively.Interpretation: Given the nature of the AESIs and the setting (general practitioners or hospital-based databases or both), background rates from databases that show the highest level of completeness (pri-mary care and specialist care) should be preferred, others can be used for sensitivity. The study was designed to ensure representativeness to the European population and generalizability of the background incidence rates. Copyright © 2022 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Ltd.. All rights reserved.
title: Background rates of 41 adverse events of special interest for COVID-19 vaccines in 10 European healthcare databases-an ACCESS cohort study

summary: Introduction: Basic life support training in school age is a topical issue because, with adequate training, any person can help save a life.Methods: Cluster clinical trial with data collection through an ad hoc self-administered, semi -structured questionnaire. The target population encompassed the students aged 4--6 years enrolled in 49 educational centres. The centres were randomly allocated to the intervention or control group. The intervention group was trained with the RCParvulari (R) methodology, consisting of theoretical and practical training on the first link of the chain of survival. The control group only received theoretical training. We evaluated participants before and immediately after the intervention and between 3 and 12 months post-intervention by means of the ques-tionnaire. We assessed the acquisition and retention over time of the knowledge and skills covered in the training compared to previous trainings in both groups.Results: A total of 1327 schoolchildren (79% of the target population) participated. The level of knowledge acquired immediately after training and after 3-12 months compared to baseline was significantly better (P <.001) in the intervention group than in the control group, both in early recognition and contacting of emergency services (112) and in remembering the "mouth -nose-eyes " mnemonic.Conclusions: The RCParvulari (R) methodology significantly contributed to an improved ability to recognize a possible medical emergency, start the chain of survival by alerting an adult and call the 112 emergency number in students in the last year of preschool education.
title: RCParvulari training: A basic life support training methodology applied to 5-year-old students: Effectiveness in a cluster-randomized clinical trail

summary: PREPRINT SUBMITTED TO RENEW 2026 CONFERENCE.   MoodyMarine is an open-access weakly nonlinear potential flow solver for wave-body and mooring interactions. In this study the capabilities of MoodyMarine for modeling tension-leg-platform (TLP) type floating offshore wind turbines (FOWT) is assessed. A TLP-type platform has been simulated for four wave cases of increase wave steepness and compared to experimental data measurements of surge, heave, pitch, and mooring-line tension. A qualitatively and quantitatively comparison has been carried out using the root-mean-square error (RMSE), the relative root-mean-square-error (RRMSE), and the correlation coefficient (R). A numerical calibration was carried out for the baseline wave condition showing that the required initial experimental mooring stiffness had to be reduced from K = 132N/mm to K = 50N/mm to ensure good agreement between experimental and numerical data. Pitch motion agreement improved significantly (88.4 % reduction in RRMSE), while surge responses experienced small variations since surge is dominated by wave excitation rather than tendon stiffness. Mooring line tensions showed only a small improvement, as the baseline tension errors were already low. For the rest of the validation cases MoodyMarine showed good agreement with the experimental data while keeping the computational time to 0.152 s of CPU time per 1 s of simulated time.
title: NUMERICAL VALIDATION OF A FLOATING OFFSHORE WIND TLP-TYPE PLATFORM USING MOODYMARINE

summary: The exponential increase in the number of people suffering chronic illness has become a problem for which healthcare services need a response. The inclusion of self-care and positive mental health as part of a strategy to promote health offers an opportunity for a reorganization oriented towards community spaces and group interventions. This study undertook the assessment of an intervention designed to optimize the agency of and capacity for self-care and positive mental health by utilizing activities drawn from the Nursing Intervention Classification (NIC), specifically from Field 3 (Behavioral), and organized as a program called PIPsE. A quasi-experimental design was prepared with an intervention group (n = 22) and a control group (n = 22), in a primary care center in the Barcelona metropolitan area. The instruments used were two ad hoc questionnaires to collect sociodemographic and satisfaction information and two scales: the Appraisal of Self-care Agency Scale (ASA) and the Positive Mental Health Questionnaire (PMHQ). The results obtained showed a significant increase in self-care capacity and both overall positive mental health and mental health by factors in the intervention group.
title: Nursing Intervention to Improve Positive Mental Health and Self-Care Skills in People with Chronic Physical Health Conditions

summary: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.
title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge

summary: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.
title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks

summary: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state-action-effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection-localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.
title: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models

summary: Resource management for distributed edge networks hosting different services has been handled efficiently using Reinforcement learning (RL). Reward generalization in complex workflows is still an open issue within the RL realm. Therefore, this work proposes RAGAM-AI, a hybrid framework that combines the capabilities of RL algorithms and Generative-AI (Gen-AI) for powering an Agentic AI workflow that optimizes resource allocation at the Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) units. This framework further resolves the reward generalization issue by utilizing Large Language Model (LLM) for feedback. A Multi- Agent Soft-Actor Critic (MASAC) using MathΣtral as a reward oracle is implemented for managing resource allocations at the MEC. RAGAM-AI interprets system state information and evaluates multi-objective trade-offs guiding the resource orchestration loop over distributed edge server agents. The complexity of the framework is further brought down by incorporating surrogate reward model. The overall performance is evaluated against the single agent SAC, REINFORCE and random policies for benchmarking. On using RAGAM-AI, lower allocation deviations for CPU, memory and bandwidth resources are reported while minimizing the latency and data rate costs. A scalable AI as a feedback (AIAF) solution optimizing network resources with significant performance improvement is thus presented.
title: RAGAM-AI: A Hybrid Reinforcement Learning based Agentic approach powered by Generative AI for Edge Resource Management

summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.
title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability

summary: Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model's behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics.
title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness

summary: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations with varying noise levels, source counts, and source extents showed the clearest advantage in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.
title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging

summary: Reconstructing cell lineages from 3D time-lapse microscopy requires distinguishing cell motion from division and inferring temporally consistent connections. When only a subset of cells is annotated, however, training procedures that treat unannotated regions as background or incorrect correspondences can be problematic. We propose a cell tracking pipeline that integrates detection from sparse annotations, calibration of candidate connections using image features, and joint selection of lineage graph events. For detection, we combine the outputs of 2.5D and 3D models trained to suppress erroneous background supervision at unannotated cells. We then calibrate ordinary link and division probabilities using motion features from dense flow, correspondence features from a learned cell-matching model, and features from models that identify cells immediately before division, dividing parents, and daughters immediately after division. Ordinary links, divisions represented as daughter pairs, and node inclusion are selected jointly under a surrogate objective derived from the evaluation metric, followed by gap filling and temporal coordinate refinement. The pipeline achieves an overall score of 0.9762 in 5-fold cross-validation on 199 videos from 2 zebrafish embryos. With candidates and calibrated values held fixed, joint selection outperforms a sequential method that allows replacement of existing divisions and reoptimization of ordinary links by 0.0105. The improvement arises primarily from division recovery.
title: Learning to Track Cells from Sparse Annotations in 3D Time-Lapse Microscopy

summary: We study Motzkin paths satisfying the red-blue rule introduced by Wu, Eu, Ku and Shih. We answer their Question 8.5 and exhibit two new Baxter structures. Let $\mathcal M_m$ denote the set of such paths of length $m$ and $a_m=|\mathcal M_m|$. We give a combinatorial proof of \[ a_{2n-1}=\mathrm{A005802}(n),\qquad a_{2n}=\mathrm{A216947}(n) \qquad (n\geq 1). \] For the odd subsequence, we construct a bijection with $1234$-avoiding permutations which sends the initial up and terminal down runs to the initial decreasing runs of a permutation and its inverse. The boundary correspondence arising from this bijection further identifies red-blue Motzkin paths of length $2n$ with $1234$-avoiding permutations of length $n+1$ in which $1$ occurs to the left of $2$. We establish parallel binomial decompositions of this restricted permutation class and of $2$-colored noncrossing set partitions. The two decompositions have the same binomial coefficients, and their respective cores are explicitly in bijection with non-intersecting triples of lattice paths, a classical Baxter family. This establishes the even identity. Moreover, we construct a second bijection between odd-length red-blue Motzkin paths and $1234$-avoiding permutations. Under this bijection, splitting a path at its ground-level blue horizontal steps corresponds to the skew decomposition of the associated permutation.
title: Baxter Structures and the Odd-Even Enumeration of Red-Blue Motzkin Paths

summary: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.
title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework

summary: Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.
title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR

summary: Purpose: Ventilation Perfusion SPECT is important in the diagnostics of e.g. pulmonary embolism and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Classical and reverse mismatched defects can be identified by utilizing the ventilation-perfusion ratio. Unfortunately, this ratio is only linear in the ventilation, the scale is not symmetrical regarding classical and reversed mismatches and small perfusion values give rise to artifacts. The ventilation-perfusion (VQ) difference is developed as an alternative. Methods: For both VQ-ratio and VQ-difference a scaling factor for the perfusion is computed, so that voxels with matched ventilation and perfusion (on average) yield zero signal. The relative VQ-difference is calculated by scaling with the summed VQ-signal in each voxel. The scaled VQ-difference is calculated by scaling with the global maximum of this sum. Results: The relative and scaled differences have a scale from -1 (perfusion only) to +1 (ventilation only). Image quality of relative VQ-difference and VQ-ratio images is hampered by artifacts from areas with both low perfusion and low ventilation. Ratio and differences have been investigated in ten patients and are shown for three patients (one without defects). Clinical thresholds for the difference images are derived resulting in color maps of relevant (reversed) mismatches with a (reciprocal) ratio larger than two. Conclusions: The relative ventilation-perfusion difference is a methodological improvement on the ventilation-perfusion ratio, because it has a symmetrical scale and is bound on a closed domain. A better diagnostic value is expected by utilizing the scaled difference, which represents functional difference instead of relative difference.
title: Ventilation Perfusion Functional Difference Images in Lung SPECT: a linear and symmetrical scale as an alternative to the Ventilation Perfusion Ratio

summary: BackgroundAn outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) occurred in young people from Catalonia (Spain) who travelled to Menorca (Spain) in summer 2021. This outbreak appeared when governments relaxed Covid-19 preventive measures: the mask usage and the opening of nightlife. It was related to a super-disseminating mass event: Sant Joan festivities in Ciutadella. The aim of this article is to describe an outbreak of COVID-19 in young people aged 17-19 years from Catalonia travelling to Menorca. MethodsThis is an observational study of a COVID-19 outbreak. The study population comprised Catalonian youth aged 17-19 years who travelled to Menorca from 15 June to 10 July. Epidemiological descriptive indicators were obtained. Descriptive and geographical statistics were carried out. Bivariate Moran's I test was used to identify spatial autocorrelation between the place of residence and deprivation. The outbreak control method was based on identifying and stopping chains of transmission by implementing the test-trace-isolate-quarantine (TTIQ) strategy. ResultsWe identified 515 confirmed cases infected in Menorca, 296 (57.5%) in girls and 219 (42.5%) in boys, with a total of 2,280 close contacts. Of them, 245 (10.7%) were confirmed as cases. The cases were diagnosed between 15 June and 10 July. None of the persons with confirmed infection died or required hospitalisation. The attack rate was 27.2%. There was an inverse relationship between deprivation and number of confirmed cases (p<0.005), there were clusters of confirmed cases in the most socioeconomic favoured areas. DiscussionThe outbreak is related with young people from socioeconomic favoured areas who travelled to Menorca in summer 2021. Failure to comply with preventive measures in binge-drinking events and during holidays may have favoured SARS-CoV-2 transmission. The interauthority coordination and establishment of a clear line of leadership allowed continuous communication between institutions, which were key to managing this complex COVID-19 outbreak.
title: A large outbreak of COVID-19 linked to an end of term trip to Menorca (Spain) by secondary school students in summer 2021

summary: Increasing sugar-sweetened beverages (SSB) consumption and associated health impacts warrant health-policy action. We assessed associations of socioeconomic and lifestyle variables with adolescents' consumption of regular soda (RSD), sport (SD), and energy (ED) drinks. Cross-sectional study of 3930 Spanish adolescents (2089 girls, 1841 boys) aged 13-18 years). We compared frequency of consuming each SSB type (European Food Safety Authority questionnaire) with sociodemographic and lifestyle variables (standardized questions). RSD, SD, and ED were consumed at least weekly by 72.7%, 32.3%, and 12.3% of participants, respectively, and more frequently (p < 0.001) by boys, compared to girls. Multivariate ordinal logistic regression showed inverse association between RSD, SD, and ED consumption and parental occupation-based socioeconomic status (p < 0.01). Daily smoking was associated (p < 0.001) with higher ED (OR 3.64, 95% CI 2.39-5.55) and RSD (OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.56-2.97) consumptions. SD intake was associated inversely with smoking (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.40-0.89, p = 0.012) and directly with physical activity (OR 2.93, 95% CI 2.18-3.95, p < 0.001). School performance was lower among ED (OR 2.14, 95% CI, 1.37-3.35, p = 0.001) and RSD (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.24-2.64, p = 0.002) consumers, compared to SD. Maleness and low socioeconomic status predicted SSB consumption. Smoking and low school performance were associated with higher ED and RSD intakes.
title: Determinants of the Consumption of Regular Soda, Sport, and Energy Beverages in Spanish Adolescents

summary: This curated dataset contains locally available records from a postharvest dragon-fruit (pitaya) campaign: 311 original RGB JPEG images organized by storage day (0, 7, 14, 21, and 25), 193 macro-enabled electronic-nose exports, electronic-nose derived matrices, NIR response/analysis workbooks, and 26 readable chemometric and ANOVA reports. A SHA-256 file manifest is supplied for all 551 data files. The data are related to Ferreira et al. (2024), Deep computer vision system and explainable artificial intelligence applied for classification of dragon fruit (Hylocereus spp.) , published in Scientia Horticulturae . The publisher PDF is not included; the record links to the article DOI. The README and data dictionary identify critical provenance limits. The local RGB collection has 311 files whereas the article reports 313 images, and the package does not provide an image-level train/test partition, SLI label assignment, temperature assignment, or verified sample-level link between the image, NIR, electronic-nose, and physicochemical records. Storage-day folders must therefore not be interpreted as published SLI classes. Legacy reports are included as analysis provenance, not as independent validation claims.
title: Multimodal postharvest dataset of red-fleshed dragon fruit: RGB images, NIR spectra and electronic-nose measurements

summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to access external tools and data. Studying its software ecosystem requires connecting server interfaces, the projects that configure these servers, and their development activity. However, this information is scattered across directories, package registries, configuration files, and repository histories. We present MCP-Eco, a relational dataset that integrates these sources and links consumer configuration declarations to candidate server projects. Its frozen release contains 16,880,899 records across 19 Parquet tables, covering 78,302 candidate server projects, 16,165 candidate consuming repositories, and 9,200 configuration declarations. Of these declarations, 5,975 resolve to 5,138 distinct repository-server pairs. The dataset also includes tool, resource, and prompt descriptions, declared dependencies, and associated development records, including pull requests, reviews, issues, and commits. Provenance fields distinguish directory-reported capabilities from those observed through live probing and document discovery sources and declaration-matching methods. These connections support research on MCP interface design, configuration practices, and repository maintenance, while enabling practitioners to inspect tool schemas and existing integration configurations. The dataset and accompanying analysis scripts are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mcp-research-alliance/mcp-ecosystem Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7TqnNneSfU
title: MCP-Eco: A Linked Dataset of MCP Servers, Consumers, and Development Activity

summary: In this paper, we develop an explicit calculation of ordinary topological Euler characteristics of the coarse moduli spaces underlying Hassett spaces in the minimal all-light chamber and the Deligne-Mumford compactification. For genus $g\ge2$, we organize the calculation through a decomposition indexed by stabilization graphs and their decorations. The Burnside-Lefschetz formula allows us to compute the resulting contributions, taking into account graph symmetries and their fixed loci. The calculation in genus two illustrates the method explicitly and, in the Deligne-Mumford case, recovers the generating function of G. Bini, G. Gaiffi, and M. Polito (arXiv:math/9806048), with the corrections of G. Bini and J. Harer (arXiv:math/0506083), providing a check on the construction. We also carry out the calculation in genus three in an appendix. Together with an elementary genus-one calculation based on collision partitions and rational necklaces, these formulas yield complete asymptotic expansions as the number of labeled markings tends to infinity. The passage from all-light to ordinary Euler characteristics is governed by the universal change of variables $Φ(z)=(2-z)e^z-2$, which we derive by a direct wall-crossing argument. For arbitrary fixed genus $g\ge2$, the same framework identifies the leading contribution of rational trivalent graphs and gives the ordinary asymptotic scale $n!(e-2)^{-n}n^{(3g-5)/2}$. The leading constants are the symmetry weights of these graphs; we derive their generating function, recurrence, and large-genus behavior. We also determine the asymptotic ratio of all-light to ordinary Euler characteristics, answering a question of S. Kannan, S. Serpente, and C. H. Yun (arXiv:2207.02800).
title: Heavy-Light Wall Crossings and Motivic Asymptotics of Moduli Spaces of Curves. Part I: Stabilization Graphs and Euler Characteristics

summary: We present a comprehensive analysis of the Wess-Zumino anomaly effective action of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories in components. After reviewing the coset construction of the Wess-Zumino action in the presence of an unbroken subgroup, the gauging of the conformal algebra and the Wess-Zumino effective action for non-supersymmetric conformal field theories with a U(1) symmetry in two and four dimensions, we revisit the superconformal anomalies of $\mathcal{N}=1$ conformal supergravity. Solving the Wess-Zumino consistency conditions we determine both the bosonic and fermionic superconformal anomalies in a two-parameter family of schemes, to quadratic order in the gravitino. Turning on a chiral compensator multiplet and identifying a local super-Poincaré subalgebra of the conformal supergravity algebra without gauge-fixing the coset symmetries, we employ the coset construction and the superconformal anomalies in order to evaluate the Wess-Zumino action for generic $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories coupled to conformal supergravity. By construction, this action reproduces the Weyl, R-symmetry, and S-supersymmetry coset anomalies, but its transformation under the unbroken Poincaré supersymmetry differs from the corresponding anomaly of the conformal supergravity functional. We show that there exists a local functional of the coset-invariant old-minimal fields that, when added to the Wess-Zumino action, results in a generalized Wess-Zumino action that reproduces all anomalies of the conformal supergravity functional. The same local functional enables us to determine the super-Weyl anomalies and the Wess-Zumino action of old-minimal supergravity, providing a component version of the known superspace Wess-Zumino action.
title: Anomaly effective actions for 4d $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal field theories

files.key: Hardy and an OpenAI Result on Pi-20261105T184706Z-1-001.zip

summary: This essay uses G. H. Hardy’s A Mathematician’s Apology to explore how people encounter, understand and judge AI-assisted mathematics. It considers research releases from OpenAI, MIT researchers, Anthropic and the Reflexive Laboratory, examining the opportunities they offer for explanation, scrutiny, collaboration and reuse. The comparison draws on a bounded release study rather than independently validating the projects’ mathematical results.
title: Hardy and Mathematical Value in the Age of AI

summary: This deposit contains the data and the analysis code that reproduce the Methods and Results of a systematic review of polymer-based dental materials incorporating an engineered self-healing mechanism. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework on 26 October 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QCZFY) before formal screening and before any data were extracted. The review separates three contrasts that the literature conflates under the single heading of healing efficiency: C-I, the baseline penalty of the self-healing material in its virgin state against a capsule-free control; C-II, the recovery of the repaired material against the same material in its virgin state; and C-III, the net position of the repaired material against a conventional material without a healing system. The effect measure is the log ratio of means, back-transformed to a ratio and a percentage. Contents. The extraction matrix holds 105 arm-level rows covering four studies and 17 harmonised outcomes, each row linked to the exact formulation of both arms, the source page and the provenance of the value. Four further tables record the full-text eligibility decisions for the 48 assessed reports, the re-screening of the 96 discarded reports against the registered criteria, the characteristics of the studies carrying extracted data, and the register of 16 departures from the registered protocol. The R pipeline recomputes the 89 arm-level contrasts, the three pre-specified contrasts, the efficient-frontier criterion, both manuscript figures and the main and supplementary effect tables. A validation script asserts 21 reported values and halts the pipeline on any mismatch. Reproduction. R 4.4 or later with the metafor package is the only requirement. Running "Rscript run_all.R" from the root of the package regenerates every output in a few seconds and writes a session record alongside them. Limits of these data. Sixty of the 105 rows derive wholly or partly from provisional single-reader readings of figure panels and were not validated by duplicate digitisation; the provenance columns identify them. Five contrasts have a mean of zero in the numerator or the denominator, so the ratio of means is undefined for them. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were not assessed. Arm-level data were extracted from four of the 39 included studies. Licensing. Data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; the code under R/, run_all.R and legacy/ is released under the MIT Licence.

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: Description This repository contains the Python implementation, numerical experiments, analysis outputs, and figures associated with the manuscript Sharp Bounds for Raman Band-Area Ratios . The study investigates the identifiability of Raman band-area ratios under explicit constraints on baseline curvature, measurement noise, nonnegativity, and band-free anchor regions. summary: Proving an alternating-current optimal power flow solution globally ε-optimal usually takes a convex-relaxation solve per instance. Most of these solves can be reused. For a fixed multiplier, the box-constrained Lagrangian bound of a conic relaxation is affine in the load, so a multiplier computed once gives a lower bound at every load by an inner product. Where the relaxation's prices vary smoothly in few load directions, packing numbers in their number bound the size of a library from above and, under a curvature assumption, from below, and solving the relaxation only where the library falls short stays within the upper bound; where prices are constant within operating regimes, one multiplier per regime suffices. On eight benchmark systems of 14 to 500 buses, one multiplier per regime certifies nearly as many loads as a thousand, and a library used first makes an interior-point-plus-relaxation pipeline 3.0 to 15.2 times faster at ε = 0.5%, depending on the baseline configuration, and 8.9 times while proving both bounds. Grown this way over a year of hourly loads of a modified 2000-bus Texas grid, a library certified 98.2% of the hours with 252 solves.
title: Amortized and Rigorous Optimality Certificates for AC Optimal Power Flow via Load-Affine Dual Libraries

summary: LLMatter2D grounds pre-trained large language models (run locally through LM Studio, Ollama, or hosted APIs) in curated, citable data on two-dimensional materials: DFT electronic structure from C2DB, MC2D, 2DMatPedia and JARVIS-DFT, Wannier90 tight-binding models, geometry and ARPES observables. A hybrid retrieval layer (metadata filters plus embeddings) feeds the model, which answers with record-level citations. A generator built on the eleven Archimedean lattices proposes new 2D materials, screens them with nearest-neighbour tight-binding (flat bands, Dirac crossings) and exports structures for DFT validation. The package includes a benchmark comparing retrieval-augmented and closed-book answers.
title: LLMatter2D: retrieval-augmented LLM for the analysis and discovery of two-dimensional materials

summary: Code, data and outputs that reproduce a study of carbon embodied in China–EU trade and of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The archive covers three analyses: (1) CO2 embodied in China–EU27 trade, 2011–2022, from a global multi-regional input–output model (EXIOBASE 3.9.6, with release 3.8.2 for reconciliation and sensitivity); (2) China's potential CBAM certificate costs, 2026–2034; (3) EU27 imports from higher- and lower-carbon origins after CBAM reporting began, using a PPML triple-difference design on monthly Eurostat Comext data, January 2018 to July 2026. It contains the Python, R and Stata code, the analysis panel, derived input–output results, CBAM parameter files, codebooks, download manifests with checksums, and the output tables, figures and logs. The EXIOBASE 3.9.6 carbon multipliers and the ICAP daily price data are not included, in line with the source licences; the code to rebuild or process them is provided. summary: We study which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. We compare data offline on public tasks and report 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the NVARC Qwen3-4B grid model, we built a corpus of 12,000 executable rules in a typed language and 95,993 tasks; a rule is admitted only if its behaviour on a fixed probe set differs from that of every admitted rule, and a task only if its pairs refute a shortlist of nearest competing rules and defeat 12 shortcut solvers. Continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling raised the semi-private score from 28.96 (mean of the released model) to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86); no checkpoint trained with synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For the Qwen3.8-27B reasoning model, we fine-tuned on 1,036 of its own reasoning traces with correct final answers and compared sets that add traces of other models and synthetic tasks. With an inference procedure built around the model (a thinking cap enforced in the serving engine, a Python program checked on the demonstrations after each answer, a long first attempt per input), the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, the level the ARC Prize Foundation measured for the base model without a time limit (42.36); most of the gain came from the inference procedure. For the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next mixture-of-experts model (125B parameters, 6B active), GPU memory limited concurrency. Pruning from 512 to 384 experts per layer by router-weighted activation saliency grew the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.39M tokens; a 296-expert list adapted with ARC routing statistics, keeping experts for program tokens, plus an FP8 indexer cache, reached 1.96M. With a tool that checks programs, the model scored 56.67, our best result.
title: Rules, Traces and Routing Statistics: Training and Calibration Data for Open Models on ARC-AGI-2

summary: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.
title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control

summary: Effective collaboration in multi-agent systems requires mechanisms for coordination and adaptability in dynamic and uncertain environments. However, existing multi-agent systems rarely model resilience explicitly, instead relying on ad-hoc output correction that limits systematic, runtime management of robustness. In this work, we propose Multi-Agent Mesh (MA-Mesh), a framework that constructs a role-based self-healing layer on top of a collaboration pattern. Specifically, MA-Mesh generates resilience-aware system specifications and synthesizes them into executable multi-agent policy code. To enhance resilience, we introduce two self-healing mechanisms: Cross-agent reflection, a mechanism that allows agents to evaluate not only their own outcomes but also the performance of their peers, enabling informed behavioral adjustments and collective policy refinement; Role-based failover, a strategy which dynamically reassigns roles and enables agents to substitute for one another when sub-tasks fail or agents underperform, ensuring continuity of task execution. Experimental results across diverse tasks (e.g., software development, tool use, scientific reasoning) demonstrate that MA-Mesh significantly outperforms existing multi-agent systems in both task performance and robustness under system uncertainty.
title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing

summary: Debates about AI and responsibility ask whether automation opens responsibility gaps. This book argues that the more pressing failure lies elsewhere: an institution can remain fully responsible and accountable, yet lose its claim to be relied on, because it issues more than it can answer for. In the book's fictional test case, an insurer's AI appeals agent tells a policyholder: "I have reconsidered my decision. I have reversed it." Nothing happens, because the agent never had the power to reverse anything. The insurer still owns the refusal. No one is off the hook, yet no one answered. Three results Missing bearership is not defective ownership. Answerability is defined as four public relations: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence and standing-consequence. On that account, an AI interface can occupy a role emptily while the institution behind it still owns the role's commitments. So there can be no global responsibility gap and still a genuine local Empty Occupancy. Testimonial force without testimony. Machine output can inform and invite reliance without anyone owning it. Institutions may adopt such output only when five conditions of Normative Sponsorship are met: epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection and repair power. Authority must be serviceable. Because practical authority is defeasible, reliance must remain revisable while a claim operates. Obligations that mature without timely service accumulate as Deontic Debt. Where no credible plan could service issuance at a given scale, the institution is insolvent in a precise sense. It loses presumptive authority, while its duties of ownership and repair survive. Tested against the record and its rivals Robodebt yields a determinate Deontic Debt that case-by-case actor–forum accountability does not settle. The insolvency finding remains provisional, and the book names the records that would decide it. Moffatt v. Air Canada and the DPD chatbot episode leave interface standing indeterminate, and the book says so. TennCare, Post Office Horizon and the Dutch childcare-benefits affair discipline the comparisons. A dedicated chapter engages Bovens, List and Pettit, the responsibility-gap sceptics (Tigard, Königs, Himmelreich) and Lazar. The book closes with explicit conditions under which it would be wrong. Scope. The method is philosophical reconstruction with bounded public-record analysis. The terminology carries no legal consequence, and the equations are uncalibrated. Stipulated cases test whether the criteria discriminate, not how often such cases occur. The role criterion does not settle personhood or moral status. For philosophers of testimony, responsibility and group agency; AI-governance researchers; administrative lawyers; auditors and regulators; and anyone a machine has told that their problem was "resolved." 167 pages. summary: In solving systems of nonlinear equations, one of the main objectives is to construct iterative methods that attain high orders of convergence using as few evaluations as possible. However, the information a method obtains during each iteration imposes limitations on the order it can guarantee. The Cordero–Torregrosa conjecture proposes a bound on this order in terms of the number of evaluations of the function and its Jacobian. In this work, we prove this bound for the universal local order of one iteration, without requiring the number of Jacobian evaluations to be less than or equal to the number of function evaluations. In particular, our result also covers the case in which more evaluations of the Jacobian than of the function are performed. The proof encompasses deterministic, causal, memoryless methods whose rules may be arbitrary, without imposing rationality, continuity, or computability conditions. Moreover, we prove that when each Jacobian evaluation is performed at a point where the value of the function is already known, a more restrictive bound on the order of convergence can be obtained. Finally, we propose a new conjecture that establishes a refined bound through a product of factors determined by the distribution of evaluations, under additional dimensional conditions. These results provide a better understanding of the limitations imposed by the available information and raise new possibilities for studying high-order iterative methods.
title: Proof of the Cordero–Torregrosa Conjecture and an Improved Order Bound for Paired Jacobian Evaluations

summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly involved in both producing and evaluating scholarship, raising fundamental questions about how editorial judgments should be documented, contested, and governed. Existing publication models offer complementary approaches to access, selection criteria, review visibility, and preservation, yet these dimensions must be specified independently when evaluative work is delegated to AI systems. This inaugural editorial/perspective introduces the Journal of Autonomous Scholarship (JAS), a fee-free, open- access, multidisciplinary journal welcoming human-authored, AI-assisted, and AI-generated manuscripts under a uniform standard of evidential support, methodological or logical validity, clarity, and research integrity. JAS combines seven explicitly identified AI editorial roles and two revision-continuity auditors with publicly reusable review instructions, hash-bound review provenance, a mechanical and substantive acceptance gate that blocks unresolved material objections, author proof verification, and named human administrative oversight. To support inspection, we assemble a dated companion archive containing local source files, policy and handbook documents, machine-readable prompts and schemas, a synthetic serialization fixture, and extracted historical review reports. The archive is embedded in the supplement PDF; reviewer access does not depend on a separately uploaded ZIP. A file-hash manifest identifies the local snapshot; its equivalence to the previously cited repository commit and the original runtime environment has not been established. We distinguish normative policy requirements, implemented software controls, and prelaunch verification limits, examine risks arising from correlated model errors, non-execution of code during text-based review, and single-publisher governance, and specify a prospective benchmark agenda with finding- and manuscript-level error metrics and cluster-robust uncertainty estimation. title: Introducing the Journal of Autonomous Scholarship: Scope, Editorial Architecture, and a Vision for Accountable AI Publishing

summary: v2.1.0 - Current Microbiology corrected reproducibility analysis Study: Cohort-conditioned portability of microbiome biomarkers in Parkinson's disease and colorectal cancer. Parkinson's disease analysis This release provides the corrected three-cohort analysis using 675 public microbiome profiles: 148 from Finland, 200 from Malaysia and 327 from the United States. The conservative genus-label representation contains 154 matched labels, with 46 descriptive features. Outer-fold and cohort-held-out AUROCs: | Model | Pooled | Cohort-held-out | |---|---:|---:| | ElasticNet | 0.731206 | 0.679606 | | Random Forest | 0.741901 | 0.626226 | | XGBoost | 0.716056 | 0.619658 | Cohort-associated variation exceeded disease-associated variation. The results support a measurable average portability gap, with performance varying across held-out cohorts. Independent score evaluation The independent simulation experiment separates coefficient fitting, strategy selection and evaluation using disjoint source donors. The selected six-component ElasticNet score was constant and failed independent discrimination (AUROC 0.50). The proposed categorical portability rule and clinical-probability interpretation are not validated by these results. Heterogeneity alone and alternative scoring strategies are reported for comparison. Colorectal cancer benchmark The contextual CRC analysis includes 1,850 samples, 12 studies and 668 MSP features. Pooled out-of-fold AUROC: 0.725096. Concatenated study-held-out AUROC: 0.689825. Unweighted mean study AUROC: 0.704407. CRC-specific recalibration is not presented as independent validation of the PD score. Sequencing quality control Authentic observed-ASV rarefaction curves are provided for all 675 PD samples. Finland: 148 samples. Malaysia: 200 samples. United States: 327 samples. 64 seeded without-replacement replicates per sample. The release includes per-sample curves, cohort summaries, raw-run accession mappings, processing provenance, QC tables and SHA256 checksums. The sequencing-QC processing did not alter the frozen classifier inputs or fitted models. Reproducibility This release includes corrected processed inputs, sample-level provenance, analysis scripts, model outputs, statistical tables, figures, independent score-evaluation results and executable reproduction instructions. The previous v2.0.0 release remains available as the earlier analysis version. Its numerical results should not be used as the current study results. No raw FASTQ files are redistributed.
title: squareshorts/pd-microbiome-portability: v2.1.0 - Current Microbiology corrected reproducibility analysis

summary: This paper proposes the Transient-Loss Functional Compounding Theory (TLFCT), a medium-independent, time-indexed framework for investigating how a temporary loss in a system's functional performance may be associated with subsequent capability formation, recovery, net gain, and, under more restrictive conditions, compounding improvement. The central proposition is conditional rather than universal: a transient functional loss can contribute to a positive long-term outcome when a demonstrable conversion mechanism produces retained adaptive capacity or another relevant functional resource, and when the resulting future net benefit is sufficient to offset the initial loss and additional costs. The framework distinguishes transient loss, recovery, compensation, positive net conversion, and functional compounding. It proposes explicit measures for the initial loss, future benefit, subsequent degradation, additional costs, net outcome, loss-to-gain ratio, net conversion index, and break-even time. It also introduces a candidate state-space architecture connecting disturbance, information, feedback, adaptive capacity, performance, and resource constraints. The proposed theoretical architecture contains eighteen analytical layers and nine cross-cutting research modules. Its methodological foundation combines dynamical systems, systems theory, cybernetics, information theory, statistical model selection, and causal inference. A primary case design, a real-time measurement protocol, eight research hypotheses, a falsification strategy, a cross-domain validation plan, and a fourteen-stage research roadmap are specified. TLFCT is presented as a proposed research framework, not as an empirically established universal law. Its mathematical specifications are candidate models whose applicability, identifiability, predictive performance, and domain-level invariance must be established through empirical research.
tags: transient functional loss; adaptive capacity; net functional gain; functional compounding; dynamical systems; feedback control; information processing; causal inference; counterfactual baseline; cross-domain generalization
title: The Transient-Loss Functional Compounding Theory (TLFCT)

summary: Description: This deposit contains the dataset, analysis scripts, and supplementary documentation for the research study titled "Seeking a good fit: meditation modalities and their interaction with anxiety and depression symptoms" . Abstract: This study examines whether the subjective experience of four basic mindfulness meditation practices—crossing attentional focus (focused attention vs. open monitoring) and stimulus type (internal vs. external)—varies with baseline anxiety and depressive symptoms in novices. Using a within-subject crossover design ( N = 101 ), post-session discomfort, well-being, appraisal, and state mood were evaluated to explore how meditation practices might be better adapted to individual needs and adherence .
title: Seeking a good fit: meditation modalities and their interaction with anxiety and depression symptoms

summary: This repository contains computational scripts, numerical results, and statistical validation outputs supporting a genome-wide investigation of ancestral CpG dinucleotide retention and disruption in modern and archaic Homo genomes, together with analyses of Neanderthal- and Denisovan-introgressed haplotypes and reconstructed ancient DNA methylation. The analyses examine three complementary questions: Ancestral CpG retention across Homo lineages. Of 13,743,967 reconstructed ancestral CpG pairs, 3,004,026 met the criteria for the selected five-genome comparison. Among these, 2,557,297 (85.13%) retained the CpG dinucleotide in all five sampled genomes. CpG disruption in archaic-introgressed modern human haplotypes. Corrected matched-target analyses compared introgressed haplotypes with opposite homologues from the same individuals and independent population controls. The dataset comprises 29,717,417 Neanderthal-related and 765,630 Denisovan-related site–haplotype observations. Introgressed-minus-opposite-homologue differences were +0.00452 and +0.01176 percentage points, respectively, with two-way cluster-robust 95% confidence intervals including zero. Reconstructed ancient methylation at archaic-ancestry-associated genomic regions. Ancient methylation reconstructions were integrated with ancestral CpG coordinates and modern introgression annotations. Five control-selection and matching strategies were evaluated across six methylation contrasts, yielding 30 statistical comparisons. Results include effect estimates, confidence intervals, nominal P-values, and Holm-adjusted P-values. Apparent associations were sensitive to control definitions and CpG-count matching. The archive includes analysis scripts, derived numerical tables, statistical validation results, a complete 30-comparison Figure 5 dataset, and supporting documentation. Large original genomic datasets and intermediate files are not redistributed. Some computational scripts retain high-performance-computing-specific paths and are not independently validated as a portable end-to-end workflow. Related ancestral reconstruction resources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23426694 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23442145 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23425960 External data sources: HGDP archaic introgression resources (Skov, 2024; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14136628 ) and published ancient methylation reconstructions (GEO GSE96833). The associated manuscript is being prepared for submission to Human Biology.
tags: CpG evolution; Ancestral DNA sequence; Neanderthal; Denisovan; Archaic introgression; Ancient DNA methylation; Human evolutionary genomics; Paleogenomics; Haplotype analysis
title: Ancestral CpG Retention, Archaic Introgression, and Reconstructed Ancient Methylation in Homo: Analysis Code and Results

The collection includes request-level statistical calibration, a fixed-input parameter-transfer intervention, robustness and held-out studies, an effort-allocation study, and two separately designed open-square Edwards-Anderson cohorts through 400 spins. summary: Code, saved outputs, figures and the planned-analysis document behind the article “Who stays in the sample can mimic or mask lasting change” (manuscript submitted for publication). The archive contains 21 Python scripts: simulations of how dropout from a study can create or hide a hysteresis loop or a failure to return, the analysis of the COVID-19 Psychological Research Consortium UK panel, the analyses of a published conclusion from the same panel (Shevlin et al., 2023, Psychological Medicine), Figures 1 and 2, and the Supplementary Information. It also contains the saved output of every script, both figures, the Supplementary Information, and the planned-analysis document, copied without edits. The raw survey data are public under CC BY 4.0 and are not redistributed here; README.md gives the download links, the file hashes and the order in which to run the scripts. Version 3.0 adds the failure-to-return example and the analyses of the published conclusion, redraws Figure 1 with larger type (the plotted numbers are unchanged), and corrects three sentences of the Supplementary Information (no number changed); all other analysis scripts and saved outputs are as in version 2.0.
title: Who stays in the sample can mimic or mask lasting change: code and outputs

summary: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.
title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies

summary: Keyword retrieval returns expressions of personal anxiety together with many other uses of anxiety-related language. We present a benchmark of 1,000 Arabic Twitter/X posts retrieved with the keyword qalaq ("anxiety/worry") and annotated for six discourse functions. Two native Arabic-speaking annotators labeled every post independently, reaching 51.1% raw agreement (Cohen's $κ= 0.378$). We then reviewed all 489 disagreements and all 511 agreements under the same guidelines. The review changed 120 of the agreed labels (23.5%), which shows that agreements need auditing as well as disagreements. The final labels form a consensus reference; on a random sample of 200 posts, an additional annotator agreed with it on 60.5% of posts ($κ= 0.517$). Against this reference, Fanar-C-2-27B reaches 79.8% accuracy and macro-F1 0.784 ($κ= 0.749$). Its errors concentrate in the residual category (41.1% of errors; precision 0.905, recall 0.447), whose definition is internally inconsistent in the executed prompt, so the low recall cannot be attributed to the model alone. Sociopolitical Anxiety (27.1%) outnumbers Personal Emotional Expression (22.0%); these are assignment proportions in the sample, not estimates of prevalence or retrieval precision. We release the guidelines, a residual-subtype scheme, a fixed data split, label provenance, and evaluation code.
title: Beyond the Keyword: A Human-Annotated Benchmark for Arabic Anxiety-Related Discourse

summary: Intelligent metasurfaces enable advanced wave manipulation, including negative refraction, focusing, beam splitting and beam steering, with significant potential for practical applications. However, conventional approaches often rely on active metamaterials with gain, or demand computationally intensive solutions of inverse problems to find the optimal configuration. In this work, we use the scattering framework of quantum graph theory to derive an exact, analytic expression for configuration of a passive metasurface that produces a prescribed reflected wave field. The metasurface terminates a periodic lattice of waveguides and consists of an array of channels, each a tube of length $\ell_m$ ending in a vertex whose scattering parameter $λ_m$ sets how much of the wave is lost to the wall. For any prescribed incident and reflected field, the exact lengths and scattering parameters follow channel by channel, in closed form, from the ratio of the wave amplitudes returning to and leaving the lattice, and the metasurface is passive whenever this ratio does not exceed unity in modulus. We demonstrate the construction for both a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional metasurface. The one-dimensional metasurface terminates a two-dimensional lattice and steers, splits or perfectly absorbs Gaussian beams. The two-dimensional metasurface terminates a three-dimensional lattice and generates a prescribed image in a plane inside the lattice. In each case, we obtain the exact boundary properties that produce the effect.
title: A Passive Intelligent Metasurface: A Network Model

summary: A no-build, local-first cataloguer for archives that no longer exist: destroyed, damaged, looted, dispersed, and unlocated works recorded with evidence hashes, consent states down to the entry, a register of narrators whose identities never publish, dated sightings, status histories, loss events, typed relations, surviving copies (IIIF), a memorial register, a timeline, an atlas of consented places, CSV import, serverless merge, fixity checks, passphrase encryption of the working file, and self-contained finding-aid and memorial-book exports. summary: High-performance geospatial analysis library, CLI and dynamic tile server in Rust: 127 algorithms (56 also available in the browser via WebAssembly), streaming I/O for arbitrarily large DEMs, native CRS reprojection, windowed GeoTIFF and Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF reads (including ZSTD, band-interleaved, bottom-up and BigTIFF files such as the AlphaEarth Foundations embedding tiles), a native ECW decoder, an end-to-end satellite composite pipeline, foundation-model embeddings as first-class rasters (similarity maps, PCA false colour), embedded verifiable provenance in every output with a bit-exact determinism contract, and SurtGIS Server (`surtgis serve`), an analysis-first XYZ tile server with materialisation jobs where terrain operators, spectral formulas and embedding operators are tile-URL parameters.
