summary: Current research in the food industry highlights the importance of alternative protein sources in the context of global population growth and the need to reduce the negative impact of raising animals, producing animal proteins, on the environment. Plant proteins represent a sustainable, affordable and beneficial option for health, with high potential to replace animal proteins in the food industry. Plant sources rich in protein include legumes, cereals, pseudocereals, oilseeds, green leaves, algae and, more recently, insects. They differ considerably in protein content and amino acid profile, and their strategic combination can ensure a balanced intake of essential nutrients. Legumes offer high protein content, but are deficient in sulfur amino acids. Cereals, although lower in protein, bring technological benefits and can complement the amino acids missing from legumes. Pseudocereals have a higher nutritional value than conventional cereals, while green leaves and algae offer a high proteins intake and compounds with antioxidant potential, although they require advanced technologies to overcome extraction limitations. Extraction methods play a decisive role in the yield and quality of plant proteins. Conventional techniques are efficient but can cause denaturation and provide low yields. On the other hand, emerging methods allow the recovery of proteins in larger quantities, preserving their functional and technological properties.
title: Plant-based proteins: sources, extraction methods and functional perspectives for the sustainable food industry

summary: Replication package for a staged empirical study of whether a dependency upgrade changes the conclusions of machine-learning comparisons. Quick check, with no experiments required: python3 paper/verify_results.py and python3 postreview/verify_postreview.py --zip VersionShift_replication.zip . The attached VersionShift_replication.zip (SHA-256 5eb716b64c21ded6f979b0b1610bb68aee46ad2f24889a0d3b133bd430c6ff7d) is the frozen original-study archive that the post-review kits require. The OpenML-CC18 datasets are not redistributed. The scripts rebuild them from OpenML and check them against the frozen hashes.

title: When a Library Upgrade Changes the Verdict: Default-Configuration Drift and the Stability of Machine-Learning Comparisons

summary: Photonic Neural Networks (PNNs) are projected to be the next-generation AI platform, driving significant advances in compute energy and area efficiency by leveraging light’s parallelism across space, wavelength, and time. Here we present a Photonic Integrated Tensor Core (PITC) architecture that combines an Arrayed Waveguide Grating Router (AWGR)-enabled PNN with a SiGe electro-absorption modulator (EAM) array following a chiplet-based silicon photonic (SiPho) accelerator setup for multi-wavelength data and weight encoding. The 8×8 PITC architectural layout, was experimentally validated in two AI benchmark workloads at 20 Gbaud, successfully classifying the IRIS and MNIST datasets yielding Cohen’s kappa-scores of 0.8438 and 0.7421, respectively.
title: A Time-Space-Wavelength Multiplexed Photonic Tensor Core using WDM SiGe EAM array chiplets

summary: Code accompanying the paper Benchmarking DFT and Machine Learning Potentials for Heat of Formation and Combustion of High-Energy Materials . For a target molecule the script enumerates isodesmic reactions against a curated library of small reference species and ranks them. Bond conservation is encoded as bond signatures (bond order together with the hybridisation and aromaticity of the connected atoms) and solved with a linear programming solver under random cost-vector perturbations, so that many distinct valid schemes are found. A secondary ring-breaking relaxation is applied where strict conservation is impossible for fused ring systems. Candidates are ranked by an IsoScore that balances chemical simplicity, Tanimoto structural similarity to the reference library, and stoichiometric cost. The repository contains the generator, the input file with the twenty high-energy materials of the benchmark set, and a README.
title: Automated isodesmic reaction generator for high-energy materials

summary: Simultaneous tolerance certification asks whether every component of a dense latent vector lies within its prescribed range. This preprint studies noisy unit-norm linear measurements under pathwise resource budgets, with tolerances calibrated to a fixed prior membership probability. For independent Gaussian priors, every fixed linear channel is uniformly asymptotically equivalent, for the membership decision, to a coordinate-precision design at no greater total precision. A marked Poisson limit characterizes the complete family of feasible limiting experiments. The resulting allocation theory gives exact Brier-optimal designs and proves that every classification-optimal allocation has zero plus at most one positive normalized precision level. The global classification problem therefore reduces to a one-dimensional coverage choice. At low budgets, no allocation is most informative for every decision loss. At fixed row precision, adaptive screening yields a squared-logarithmic reduction in the order of measurements required for prescribed positive decision gain. For classification, sharp high-accuracy constants distinguish the inverse-square risk dependence of fixed designs from the logarithmic dependence of adaptive acquisition. Bounded-spectrum Gaussian dependence preserves the fixed-design frontier. Matching resource orders extend to exponential-power priors, including Laplace and lighter tails. A frozen Gaussian simulation, combined with certified deterministic bounds, establishes a finite-dimensional advantage over all fixed linear designs under the same affine acquisition budget, with one-sided 95% Monte Carlo confidence. This record contains the preprint, proof supplement, editable LaTeX sources, and a reproducibility archive with programs, experimental protocols, and saved results. The manuscript and proof supplement are licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0; original software is licensed under MIT. Third-party components retain their own licenses.
title: Simultaneous Tolerance Certification: Limit Experiments and Sharp Resource Laws

summary: Research code accompanying the paper Data-proximal null-space networks for inverse problems by Jürgen Frikel, Simon Göppel and Markus Haltmeier. summary: Version 5: Documentation corrections only; code, data, and results are unchanged from v4. Version 4  adds the analyses of the second revision: time-ordered and cross-project evaluation, structured label noise, a drop-one process-feature ablation, a Random Forest hyperparameter check, and label-provenance analyses (results/r2_experiments/), with the per-row revision metadata and commit dates they need. All Java runners now read the datasets from a configurable data directory (JML_DATA_DIR). Everything in v3 is otherwise unchanged; the audit labels are the same as in v3. Version 3. Supersedes version 2 (distributed as package v1.1) and version 1 (package v1.0). Prepared for the revised submission to Science of Computer Programming. Figures from earlier versions should not be cited. Manual validation re-run with a two-rater protocol. Estimated commit-level SZZ label precision is now  49.5% (197/398) with inter-rater agreement Cohen's κ = 0.799 , replacing the 29.2% reported in versions 1 and 2, which came from a single-rater audit with no documented agreement statistic. Per-project precision: Kafka 57.1%, Gson 48.5%, Commons-IO 42.9%. Both raters' blind passes, the disagreement-resolution record for the 10 conflicting cases, and a per-instance false-positive taxonomy of all 201 false positives are included. The labelling question changed, so labels are not directly comparable across versions. The is_valid_fix column has been renamed is_true_bic . The earlier audit recorded whether a candidate was itself a valid fix; the current audit records whether the candidate introduced the defect that its traced fix later repaired. These are different questions, and the resulting labels cannot be compared row by row with earlier versions. A central claim has been withdrawn. Earlier versions of the paper argued that feature-engineering quality has a stronger influence on predictive performance than label purity. A label-noise sensitivity experiment, included here, does not support that claim: adding 20 percentage points of label noise erases more MCC than the entire static-to-hybrid feature-engineering gain, in every project. The claim has been removed from the manuscript and replaced with the measured finding that process features hold a consistent advantage over static features at the observed noise level, while performance remains sensitive to further label degradation. Ablation and significance results re-derived from logged runs. All values now come from 270 independently seeded 10-fold cross-validation runs (30 seeds × 3 projects × 3 feature sets), with per-seed raw results, runner scripts and exact seeds included. The reported Hybrid-over-Static improvement on Commons-IO is 55%, not the 128% stated previously; Static-only MCC on Commons-IO is +0.166, not negative. Statistical testing is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test paired by seed with Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni correction over nine comparisons per metric. MCC replaces F1 as the primary metric, and class prevalence, trivial baselines and confusion matrices are now reported. Prevalence differs by a factor of ~2.7 across the three projects (55.4% / 44.9% / 20.9%), so F1 is not comparable across them; all trivial baselines have MCC = 0. The reported pipeline does not use SMOTE. A direct comparison, included here, shows no benefit in any project and a measurable cost on Commons-IO. SMOTE remains available as a configuration option in the framework. Runtime and energy figures are measured, not extrapolated: 30.6 minutes wall-clock across all three projects for the reported configuration, with per-phase timings and logs. New in this version: the label-noise sensitivity sweep; an AGE-feature ablation; confusion matrices and specificity per project and feature set; a Process-versus-Static significance test; a read-only exporter for the SZZ fix-to-BIC mapping, which the original pipeline did not persist; and a replication configuration annotated with the exact s

summary: Se estudia la variante del algoritmo de Collatz que aplica 3m+1 a los impares congruentes con 1 módulo 4 y 3m−1 a los congruentes con 3 módulo 4, introducida por el autor en 2019. La regla equivale a elegir, entre 3m−1 y 3m+1, el término divisible por 4, de modo que cada paso impar va seguido al menos de dos divisiones por 2. Se demuestra que la distancia al punto fijo 1 se contrae al menos en el factor 3/4 en cada transición entre impares. De ello se siguen la convergencia a 1 de toda órbita, una cota explícita para el número de términos impares y una cota logarítmica para la longitud total de la trayectoria. Se establecen dos acoplamientos exactos. El primero relaciona, en un solo paso, la variante con la aplicación de Collatz acelerada y sitúa su diferencia en una única valuación 2-ádica. El segundo la relaciona con la permutación considerada por Collatz en 1932: sobre cada impar, la inversa de la permutación realiza en un paso el resultado de tres pasos elementales de la variante, y los retornos impares de ambos sistemas difieren en una potencia de 3 determinada por la valuación 2-ádica del paso. Se demuestra que el retorno impar de la permutación es biyectivo y que la variante se obtiene suprimiendo los factores de 3 de su resultado, y se precisa que esta factorización no es una conjugación. Se señalan además obstáculos a la conjugación de la variante con la aplicación de Collatz y con el retorno de la permutación. El resultado central es de naturaleza simbólica. El lenguaje de paridades de la variante es exactamente el conjunto de palabras binarias que evitan el factor 11, con entropía topológica igual al logaritmo de la razón áurea, y la densidad de las clases residuales que realizan cada palabra viene dada por una medida de Markov explícita y no uniforme. Ello contrasta con el teorema de paridades de Terras y Lagarias para la aplicación de Collatz, donde todas las palabras se realizan con la misma densidad. Se plantea como problema abierto la geometría de las clases residuales asociadas a cada palabra, con datos de enumeración exhaustiva. El escrito discute con precisión qué no se sigue de estos resultados acerca de la conjetura de Collatz, y propone controles positivos y negativos para evaluar argumentos generales. Los enunciados efectivos se han comprobado computacionalmente, y el suplemento contiene el programa en Python que reproduce esas comprobaciones con aritmética entera, junto con sus resultados. Versión 2. Se añaden un índice, las referencias a los escritos del autor sobre la permutación de Collatz de 1932 y sobre los filtros bilaterales de los mínimos de sus órbitas, y un suplemento computacional formado por el programa de verificación, un resumen de sus resultados y la tabla de las pruebas sobre las clases residuales. La sección de verificación numérica se reescribe para describir ese suplemento.
title: Una variación en el algoritmo de la conjetura de Collatz.

summary: The KV cache is the bottleneck of long-context LLM inference.  Every modern serving system —  vLLM, SGLang, Mooncake  — is, at its core, a memory manager for the cache that grows one token at a time as the model decodes.  PagedAttention, RadixAttention , and the various  prefix caching  schemes each solve a piece of the problem, but none of them is  lock-free , none of them is  position-keyed , and none of them uses  structural sharing  to handle both beam-search branching and multi-tenant prefix sharing at the same time. This book introduces the  persistent rope  — a single data structure that does all of these things, derived from two pieces of prior art that were never combined before: the  persistent vector  (which gives the rope its branching semantics) and the  Bw-tree  (which gives the rope its lock-free properties). The book is a design document and API reference for the rope, written for engineers who build serving systems, GPU kernels, and lock-free data structures.  It is  not  a benchmark paper,  not  a tutorial, and  not  a complete serving system. The Python reference implementation is  correct but not lock-free ; the  lock-free Rust port is scaffolded in the repository  and described in detail in Chapter 22. The book covers the design (Ch 1–9), the Python reference (Ch 10–11), the verification (Ch 12–14), the public API (Ch 15–19), and the honest framing of what works, what doesn't, and what's left for future work (Ch 20–23). The appendices include a full  glossary, references, and index . Read it in order if you want to understand the design end-to-end; jump to Chapters 10–19 if you want to use the Python reference; read Chapter 22 if you're planning the Rust port.
title: The Persistent Rope: Position-Keyed Indexing for the LLM KV Cache

summary: This record accompanies Working Paper No. 9 of the Independent FAIR Evaluation Series of the ATLAS Framework , entitled Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation . The study examines the concentration of computational AACF susceptibility profiles derived from frozen PaccMann and DRPreter predictions for 95 unique registered configurations across 970 matched cancer cell-line profiles . Scores are transformed into normalized weights using a softmax transformation favouring lower AACF indices, with fixed model-specific reference scales. Profile characterization includes Shannon entropy, normalized entropy, effective configuration counts, and leading configuration weights. The evaluation addresses five normalization-scale multipliers, the effect of retaining 97 registered labels instead of 95 unique configurations, lineage comparisons covering 953 profiles in 21 groups, and variability across ten DRPreter checkpoints. It also distinguishes entropy calculated after median index aggregation from the median of checkpoint-wise entropies. At the reference scales, median normalized entropy was 0.9346 for PaccMann and 0.9528 for the DRPreter median consensus . These aggregate differences coexisted with weak cross-model agreement in cell-line entropy rankings ( Spearman ρ = −0.0788 ) and only six shared profiles among the 97 most concentrated profiles identified by each model. Normalization and checkpoint aggregation affected concentration summaries and rankings, demonstrating that entropy requires an explicitly specified computational representation. The accompanying computational materials document the six-stage workflow through analysis scripts, frozen input resources, configuration and profile mappings, normalization policies, numerical tables and arrays, saved bootstrap draws, and provenance and validation records. A README explains the directory structure, principal outputs, reproduction workflow, and interpretation limits. Resources inherited from ATLAS Working Papers 06–08 retain their upstream licensing and attribution requirements. The final technical audit recorded 2,363 passed checks and no failed checks , reviewing 206 distinct files in the selected analysis chain. This audit supports technical consistency and traceability within the implemented checks; it does not constitute independent experimental or clinical validation. The results establish entropy as a conditional descriptor of computational profile concentration . They do not establish therapeutic efficacy, measured mixture responses, biological mechanisms, or malignant-versus-normal selectivity. The materials support transparent inspection, reanalysis, and further methodological evaluation of the ATLAS framework.
title: Entropy of ATLAS AACF Susceptibility Profiles across Cancer Cell Lines: Dependence on Model, Normalization Scale, and Checkpoint Aggregation

summary: Resilience in psychology and public health is usually assessed through recovery or maintained functioning, outcomes that do not reveal whether desirable states have become self-maintaining or still depend on external support. Drawing on coerced-regime theory from social-ecological systems research, we develop aided mental health resilience (AMHR), a framework for desirable mental health states established or maintained through external inputs of resources, organisation, political capital and trust. We make three contributions. First, we frame population mental health as a dimension of social-ecological system states and define the external maintenance subsidy required to sustain desirable conditions. Second, using a dialectical reading of regime change, we distinguish reversion, permanent subsidy and sublation, in which the function initially supplied by aid becomes reproduced through reorganised capacities, practices or institutions. Displacement of harm is treated as a cross-cutting failure mode. Four cases illustrate these dynamics and their limits. Third, drawing on strange loop ethics, we argue that paradoxical outcomes should trigger review not only of intervention instruments but also of the premises that define desirable states and authorise intervention. We outline disconfirmation conditions and a research agenda centred on longitudinal evaluation, subsidy accounting, displacement monitoring and recursive premise review.
title: Aided mental health resilience: governing desirable states that cannot sustain themselves

summary: This paper establishes the mathematical and methodological foundations of the GCT-STL research program on the P versus NP problem, using the decision Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP_dec) as a canonical NP-complete representative and its polynomial reduction to 3-SAT with an exact materialized 3-CNF artifact. The framework organizes nine provenance-controlled descriptors (D1–D9) across three computational-information domains: semantic/geometric (S), temporal/computational (T), and logical/syntactic (L). These descriptors form the canonical raw Valiant–González tensorial signature (R0), supported by explicit SourceMap and Provenance Bundle contracts and three foundational entropy results. Paper I-A situates R0 within a branched four-representation architecture: R1 is a componentwise logarithmic scale complement, R2 is the canonical entropic/information representation, and R3 is the exact-envelope normalized representation. The Full STL Tensorial Coupling Principle remains an open and falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established obstruction theorem. The logical-complexity architecture distinguishes the internal classes P_STL and NP_STL and the conditional F1–F4 route toward the classical P versus NP problem. F1 and F2 remain open mathematical obligations. Empirical robustness, tensorial diagnostics, and candidate obstructions do not constitute universal computational lower bounds. Accordingly, Paper I-A does not prove P ≠ NP. It establishes the representational, logical, methodological, and formal-certification foundations for subsequent research within the GCT-STL program.
title: Three-Dimensional Entropic Domains for TSP Complexity via 3-SAT: Foundations of the GCT-STL Research Program on P versus NP

summary: This deliverable presents practical and adaptable protocols for scaling citizen science initiatives, developed through a user-centred design (UCD) process informed by co-design and validation workshops, interviews with citizen science experts, researchers, and practitioners, and a literature review. Rather than proposing a single, one-size-fits-all model, the protocols are organised around five CROPS scaling strategies: institutional scaling (driving policy and governance change), expansion and replication scaling (extending reach and participation), transformative change scaling (influencing values, attitudes, and behaviours), downscaling (reducing scope while maintaining impact), and combined scaling (pursuing multiple pathways simultaneously). These strategies reflect a multidimensional understanding of scaling that extends beyond geographic or numerical growth. To support projects in deciding whether and how to scale, the deliverable also highlights the CROPS Scalability Framework, a diagnostic tool built around nine constructs relating to the intrinsic characteristics of a project, the scaling process itself, and the target context. This is complemented by a six-step Strategic Scaling Decision process that helps projects determine whether scaling is not only feasible but strategically appropriate. In this deliverable, the protocols are first presented through concise, visually structured informative briefs, providing accessible overviews of guidance for each scaling strategy. These are followed by more detailed guidance, including summary tables of protocols, pillars, and objectives, illustrative examples, and practical dos and don'ts. Additional resources, tools, and guidelines support implementation. The protocols are designed to be adopted in full or in part, depending on a project's context, resources, and objectives, and are intended to remain useful not only for scaling but also for the design of new citizen science initiatives from the outset. Ethical considerations, including privacy, inclusivity, fairness, and transparency, are treated as a cross-cutting requirement throughout. The primary audience for the protocols is the citizen science practitioner community, represented through personas developed as part of the UCD process, alongside researchers, policymakers, EU and international organisation representatives, and other stakeholders engaged in scaling citizen science, particularly in relation to the Horizon Europe EU Missions. The CROPS protocols are intended as an evolving, non-prescriptive resource rather than a definitive model for scaling. Their value lies in providing a structured basis for reflection, planning, and decision-making, while recognising that successful scaling also depends on a broader enabling ecosystem of institutional readiness, sustainable funding, and supportive technical and policy infrastructure. The methodology underpinning protocol development, including persona creation and the wider UCD process, is described in detail in Section 7 and the accompanying annexes.
title: D3.1: User-centred Design Protocols for Scaling Citizen Science

summary: tc-cwi is a lightweight Python toolbox for Environmental and Operational Condition (EoC) compensation in ultrasonic Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) using Coda Wave Interferometry (CWI) and the Time-Stretching method . summary: This record contains the experimental datasets supporting the technical Key Performance Indicator (KPI) evaluation of the DETO-XR (Dynamic Edge Tracking Optimization for XR) use case developed within the 6G-PATH (6G Pilots and Trials Through Europe) project, Open Call 2. DETO-XR investigates a distributed edge–cloud architecture combining environment sensing, Multiple Object Tracking (MOT), GPU-accelerated cloud processing, and remote rendering for interactive Mixed Reality applications. The proposed MOT-as-a-Service (MOTaaS) concept enables multiple independent tracking sessions to access shared cloud processing resources. The dataset provides raw measurement traces, processed results, experimental configurations, and verification scripts covering five technical KPIs: Dataset Description KPI-1: Frame Drop Streaks HoloLens 2 client-side video-selection telemetry collected during 5G experiments, including a selected stable operating interval and a supplementary retrospective 30 Hz frame-availability analysis. KPI-2: Jitter Buffer and Frame Availability Evaluation of video-frame availability with a configured 30 ms jitter buffer, including per-stream frame-selection events, timestamped records, and full measurement-stage context. KPI-3: Pose Staleness Comparative experiments evaluating a tracking pose-staleness proxy using different cloud-based object-detection configurations. KPI-4: GPU Duty-Cycle Reduction GPU utilization measurements comparing continuous object detection with periodic detection refresh, supporting the evaluation of computational resource efficiency. KPI-5: Concurrent MOT Sessions Application traces and GPU monitoring data collected during experiments with one, two, and three concurrent MOT sessions sharing GPU-backed cloud services. The experiments were conducted between 18 October and 4 November 2026 , including measurements associated with the 6G-INCOGNICO experimentation environment in Greece. Dataset Organization Each KPI is documented in a dedicated directory containing the relevant raw and processed measurement data. The archive also includes: Detailed README files explaining the experimental setup, measurement methodology, and interpretation of results. A data dictionary describing measurement fields, timestamps, and derived metrics. Source provenance information and mappings between reported KPI results and supporting evidence. SHA-256 checksums and Python verification scripts supporting data integrity and reproducibility. Measurement Scope The KPI-1/KPI-2 dataset includes a retrospectively selected 5G operating interval evaluated using a 30 Hz frame-availability model, together with the original 13-minute measurement-stage records. The alternative frame-availability metric is distinct from native 60 Hz display-frame-loss measurements and does not establish full-run compliance with the original KPI targets. Similarly, KPI-3 uses a model-based pose-staleness proxy rather than direct HoloLens display measurements, while KPI-4 and KPI-5 evaluate specific GPU utilization and concurrency configurations. The datasets are intended to support reproducible performance evaluation, independent analysis, and further research into distributed object tracking, cloud-assisted XR applications, and efficient GPU resource utilization. summary: This paper develops a scale-spanning account of latent vibration and frequency manifestation within Extended Classical Mechanics (ECM). It examines the relationship between complete latent vibration, the negative and positive displacement domains around the manifestable origin, and the eligibility of positive displacement for progression towards physical manifestation. The development distinguishes the complete latent-vibration interval from the directed displacement associated with manifestation, establishing the proposed Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck threshold relationships in terms of the Planck length. The analysis further develops phase-dependent frequency relations below the Planck threshold and considers the proposed frequency increments associated with the Pre-Latent and Pre-Planck domains. It then presents a state-dependent sequence of energy–frequency transformations across latent, phase, and manifested states, including the reverse progression associated with dissolution. Within this framework, frequency and displacement are treated as related physical parameters whose coefficients depend on the corresponding phase domain. The paper also distinguishes the phase-state potential-energy mass representation from the mass contribution associated with the manifested domain. It formulates the effective-mass relationship and separates this ECM representation from the distinct dark-energy-related mass representation. Taken together, these developments present an integrated theoretical description of latent vibration, manifestation eligibility, threshold transitions, energy–frequency relations, and mass-state transformations within the proposed ECM framework.
title: Complete Latent Vibration and Frequency Manifestation Eligibility in Extended Classical Mechanics

summary: Nicomachean Algorethics: Principles, Limits and Verification of Human and Artificial Transformative Decision-Making This monograph develops a philosophical and formal framework for examining the legitimacy, responsibility and verifiability of transformative decisions made by human agents, institutions and artificial systems. Drawing on Aristotelian practical philosophy, contemporary ethics, epistemology, decision theory and the challenges of artificial intelligence governance, Nicomachean Algorethics addresses a fundamental question: under what conditions may an agent legitimately make decisions that transform the lives, opportunities and futures of others? The proposed framework is organised around twelve normative laws and a Recognition Matrix designed to distinguish technical possibility, epistemic justification, normative admissibility and legitimate authority. Rather than attempting to calculate or optimise the Good, the framework investigates the conditions under which decisions may be justified, contested, corrected or withheld. Particular attention is given to uncertainty, the limitations of representation, delegated authority, corrigibility, reversibility, capability preservation, the distribution of responsibility, value pluralism and the prevention of harm. The work introduces formal definitions, mathematical formulations, verification contracts and operational procedures intended to make normative assumptions and decision-making constraints explicit. Its methodological approach distinguishes conceptual arguments, formal propositions, computational verification, illustrative examples and empirical claims, without treating these different forms of evidence as interchangeable. The monograph also examines recognition as a philosophical and practical problem, investigating the relationship between distinction, otherness, interpretation and responsibility in human and artificial decision-making. Through theoretical analysis and selected case studies, it explores how artificial systems and institutions may improve not only their decisions but also their capacity to identify, explain and correct errors. The work comprises twenty-three chapters, an epilogue and five technical appendices addressing verification contracts, retrospective analysis, comparative protocols, canonical terminology and formal mechanisation. Nicomachean Algorethics is intended as a contribution to moral philosophy, philosophy of technology, artificial intelligence ethics and the interdisciplinary study of responsible decision-making. Its central thesis is that responsibility requires more than selecting among available alternatives: it requires recognising who may be affected, what authority may legitimately be exercised and which possibilities must remain open to others and to future generations.

title: NICOMACHEAN ALGORETHICS - Principles, Limits, and Verification of Transformative Decision-Making by Humans and Artificial Systems

summary: Visual geo-localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in GNSS-denied environments remains challenging due to the lack of datasets with trajectory continuity, broad scene and geographic coverage, multimodal UAV imagery, wide altitude and geometric variation, and sufficient scale. Here we present UAV-VisLoc, a dataset for UAV geo-localization through image retrieval between UAV imagery and geo-referenced satellite tiles. UAV-VisLoc contains 14,998 UAV images organized into 30 flight trajectories, spanning six continents and seven scene types. The dataset preserves contiguous observations along each trajectory, enabling trajectory-level studies under realistic sequential flight conditions. It includes RGB and Infrared UAV imagery and covers altitudes from 160 to 2,500 m. The dataset comprises 21 real UAV flights collected across multiple provinces in China and 9 synthetic flights built from OpenAerialMap imagery for regions outside China. The dataset also provides image-level flight metadata and more than 120,000 geo-referenced satellite tiles. Baseline retrieval experiments and accompanying scripts are provided to validate data organization, ground-truth annotations, and benchmark usability under diverse real-world conditions.
title: UAV-VisLoc: A Large-scale UAV Dataset with Continuous Trajectories for Visual Geo-localization

summary: This paper examines the effectiveness of Uzbekistan's tax reforms in reducing the shadow economy. Drawing on macroeconomic indicators, firm-level data, and econometric estimates, the analysis reports model-based shadow-economy estimates of approximately 38.9–39.6% of GDP for 2025, alongside reductions in statutory tax rates. The reported average firm-level tax burden was 27.3%, compared with a macroeconomic indicator of 18.3%. Econometric findings suggest a conditional tax-burden benchmark of 19–20% of GDP. The study concludes that sustainable formalization may be supported by tax-rate optimization, equitable taxation, simplified compliance procedures, improved VAT administration, and effective institutional enforcement. summary: This Zenodo repository contains the data for the following article: Molecular Signatures of Pressure-Induced Phase Transitions in a Lipid Bilayer (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcb.5c08607) by Yanna Gautier, Guillaume Stirnemann, and Jérôme Hénin   Abstract: Understanding how lipid bilayers respond to pressure is essential for interpreting the coupling between membrane proteins and their native environments. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics to examine the pressure–temperature behavior of model membranes composed of dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) or its cis-unsaturated analogue Δ9-cis-PC. Within the studied range (288–308 K, 1–2000 bar), DMPC undergoes a liquid–gel transition, while Δ9-cis-PC remains fluid due to unsaturation. The CHARMM36 force field reproduces experimental boundaries with high fidelity: simulated DMPC transitions fall within 5–10 K and 100–300 bar of experimental values, and Δ9-cis-PC exhibits no transition. Hysteresis is modest but most pronounced when starting from low-temperature gels; we propose a split-phase simulation protocol that alleviates the hysteresis problem. We identify the area per lipid, bilayer thickness, and acyl-chain gauche fractions as sensitive phase markers; among these, the gauche fraction provides the most robust signature. Simulations indicate that an interdigitated gel is the equilibrium structure under finite-size conditions, and we propose a novel metric to quantify the extent of this phenomenon. However, at low temperature and high pressure, interdigitation decreases, consistent with the experimental lamellar gel phase. This long-lived interdigitation critically impacts standard order parameters, specifically, area per lipid and membrane thickness. Finally, we discuss in detail how finite-size effects influence phase transition and interdigitation. Overall, these results underscore the accuracy of modern force fields and highlight how simulations are essential to mechanistically complement experimental studies of pressure-sensitive membranes. Keywords : Molecular Dynamics, DMPC, lipid phase transition, high pressure, phase diagram   Detailed content of the repository: The directories contain the all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulation data generated for the different systems and simulation protocols investigated in this study. All atoms are retained in the trajectory files. To limit the overall size of the repository, the trajectories have been subsampled, with one frame retained for every three frames. DRPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic Δ9-cis-PC bilayer, which was used as the control system. Pressure_temperature_ramp : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure file (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer subjected to a pressure and temperature ramp. These simulations were performed for comparison with the pressure and temperature jump simulations used as reference. DMPC_Large_Small_Bilayers : Contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for periodic DMPC bilayers with different system sizes, corresponding to twice and half the size of the reference bilayer, respectively. The reference system consists of 57 DMPC molecules per leaflet. DMPC : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations used to construct the DMPC phase diagram. The directory is organized into subdirectories, with one folder per simulation replicate.  gel_to_fluid_simulations : contains the trajectory files (.xtc) and corresponding structure files (.pdb) for the periodic DMPC bilayer simulations performed to investigate the gel-to-fluid phase transition. The transition, starting from final gel phase configurations obtained from the DMPC simulations, was induced by independently varying either the pressure or the temperature
title: Molecular Signatures of Pressure-Induced Phase Transitions in a Lipid Bilayer

summary: This archive contains the complete, reproducible analysis pipeline accompanying the article by Bentounsi, Achour and Boufaida, currently under review. Purpose Clinical datasets often present expert labels as if they applied a published guideline. This work proposes an audit method that (i) measures the gap between a guideline-derived reference rule base and the expert labels, (ii) attributes the disagreements to an implicit criterion (Algorithm 1), and (iii) tests whether that criterion can be reconstructed out of sample, using an explicit acceptance criterion: an agreement gain of at least 5 points over the majority baseline, the same rule selected in at least 4 of 5 folds, and a family-wise permutation p-value below 0.01. The method is applied to an Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) dataset (270 records, six labels) and replicated on the UCI Cardiotocography dataset (2,126 segments) against the FIGO 2015 guideline. Contents src/ : Python modules (thresholds and protocol constants, data loading with hash check, generated rule trace, rules–expert gap and Algorithm 1, threshold and interval enumerations with permutation tests, learning control and Shapley attribution, cardiotocography replication, robustness analyses, figures). results/ : every result file used in the manuscript (CSV, TXT, JSON). figures/ : Figures 1–5 (PDF and PNG). tests/ : pytest suite (equivalence of fast and direct enumerations, regression tests on the published tables, checks of the FIGO rule base, and a test that every key figure of the manuscript matches the recomputed results). PROTOCOL.md : analysis protocol, including Amendment 1 for the replication.  PROTOCOL2.sha256 records the hash of Protocol 2. run_all.sh , requirements.txt (pinned versions with hashes, Python 3.13). Data (not redistributed) The input datasets are not included and must be downloaded from their original sources; the code refuses to run on any other version of the files. ABPM: Douibi K, Benabid MM, Settouti N, Chikh MA. Data for: An analysis of Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) . Mendeley Data, V1, 2017. https://doi.org/10.17632/y4dh3b3tfx.1 . File ABPM-dataset.arff , SHA-256 0ea0a53c86bd2564117913fe99dd6699579fc03b23acd118c0b33822db911e07 . Cardiotocography: Campos D, Bernardes J. Cardiotocography . UCI Machine Learning Repository, 2000. https://doi.org/10.24432/C51S4N . File CTG.xls , SHA-256 d6aa62e82625e59f9d5b05bc8fc52af9ea67bdf2a23f1faca8511d5618fcb421 . Reproduction Place both files in data/raw/ , then run: python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt ./run_all.sh The script verifies the dataset hashes, runs all modules, regenerates every result file and figure, and runs the test suite (about twelve minutes on an ordinary laptop). All randomness uses a fixed seed (0); the rule trace is deterministic. Licence Code released under the MIT licence. The datasets remain under the terms set by their authors.

summary: Description This record contains the data, code and source data supporting a Mendelian randomization (MR) study of smoking and obesity traits, with DNA methylation (CpG sites) and gut microbial features (species and pathways) as candidate mediators. Files Processed and formatted GWAS summary statistics (instrumental variables and outcome data) used in the analyses. Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx : sources of the original GWAS summary statistics (also listed in Table S1 of the article). Codes.zip : R code for instrument selection, two-sample MR and sensitivity analyses, mediation analysis, colocalization and the figures, with a README describing each script and the run order, software versions and R session information. Source_data.zip : source data underlying the main and supplementary figures. Fstatistic.zip : F statistics of the instrumental variables in the MR analyses. Data sources The uploaded data are processed and formatted versions of publicly available GWAS summary statistics; the original sources are listed in Public GWAS Summary Statistics Sources.xlsx . Ethical approval and informed consent were obtained by the original GWAS studies. Methods Instrumental variables were selected at P < 5 × 10⁻⁸ for smoking and obesity traits, P < 1 × 10⁻⁵ (effect allele frequency > 0.01) for gut microbial features, and P < 1 × 10⁻⁸ (cis, within 1 Mb) or P < 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ (trans) for methylation quantitative trait loci of CpG sites (GoDMC). Variants were clumped at r² < 0.001 within 10,000 kb windows using PLINK with the 1000 Genomes European reference panel, and instruments with F < 10 were excluded. The multiplicative random-effects inverse-variance weighted method (Wald ratio for single-SNP instruments) was used as the primary MR method. Sensitivity analyses included the fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted method, MR-Egger, weighted median, simple and weighted mode, Cochran’s Q test, the MR-Egger intercept test, MR-PRESSO and the Steiger directionality test. Reverse causation was assessed by MR in the reverse direction. Indirect associations were estimated by two-step MR using the product-of-coefficients method with delta-method standard errors. Colocalization was assessed with coloc (p1 = p2 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, p12 = 1 × 10⁻⁵) within ±1 Mb windows and with HyPrColoc for three traits (prior.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, prior.c = 0.02).  Acknowledgements We thank UK Biobank ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ ), GSCAN ( https://genome.psych.umn.edu/index.php/GSCAN ), the GIANT consortium ( https://giant-consortium.web.broadinstitute.org/index.php/GIANT_consortium ), GERA ( https://cg.bsc.es/gera_summary_stats/ ), GoDMC ( http://mqtldb.godmc.org.uk/about ), the Dutch Microbiome Project ( https://dutchmicrobiomeproject.molgeniscloud.org/menu/main/home ), the IEU OpenGWAS project ( https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/ ) and the GWAS Catalog ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/ ) for providing the publicly available genetic data used in this research. We acknowledge the research teams, participants and consortia behind these datasets for their commitment to open science.
title: Causal Relationships Between Smoking and Obesity Mediated by Epigenetic Modifications and Altered Gut Microbiota

summary: Urban design relies on judgments about existing and anticipated needs, while the available evidence ranges from lived experience and historical records to geospatial observation, statistical estimation, and computational simulation. Contemporary developments in geospatial artificial intelligence, agent-based modeling, urban digital twins, and computational search expand the means of inquiry while raising questions about inferential validity and methodological compatibility. This paper develops a question-guided framework for identifying and evaluating candidate urban needs through the reconstruction of spatial, temporal, social, ecological, and infrastructural relations. Two complementary inquiry pathways are distinguished: hypothesis-driven assessment of specified candidate needs and exploratory search for candidates emerging from observed or simulated relational patterns. Both pathways are connected to explicit procedures of evidential appraisal, causal examination where identifiable, participatory scrutiny, and post-intervention evaluation. A provisional formal interface is proposed in which generative–relational (GR) subjects have question-dependent spacetime-supported representations, heterogeneous evidence is linked by category-theoretic constructions, and selected event structures are encoded through algebraic-topological invariants of labeled two-complexes. Evolutionary updates of these representations and spin-foam-inspired cellular initializations are considered as exploratory modeling options, with the physical meaning of quantum-gravity spin foams kept separate from urban research. The framework is intended to guide methodological comparison and further model development; its empirical adequacy requires case-specific operationalization and validation.
title: Identifying and Evaluating Urban Needs Through Relational Reconstruction: A Preliminary Generative and Evolutionary Formal Model in an Algebraic Framework

summary: The World on Record Index (TWR) — version 1.2.0 Released 9 November 2026. Concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23997606 resolves to the latest version. What is new: the sector layer 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 published one score per country-year. This release adds  goal_level  — one score per country-year  per SDG goal  — so the measure can say  what  a government stopped reporting, not only that it reported less. Sixteen goals are scored.  Goal 7 is not : it has three series, too few to identify a factor. That is a structural fact about the goal, not a judgement on it. Each goal is a  separate  unidimensional 2PL fit on that goal's own series, drawn from the same 524 that build the overall index. A goal's score therefore owes nothing to the other fifteen, and both layers sit on the same scale. The layer is not a restatement of the overall index. Across the sixteen goals a median of  64%  of the variation in goal-level reporting is not explained by a country's overall level — from 18% for goal 17 to 99.9% for goal 15. What it is checked against Check Result Convergence 16 of 16 goals, 19–73 EM cycles each Reliability 0.772–0.953, median  0.844 ; every goal above 0.70 Median posterior SD 0.338 (overall index: 0.114) Bootstrap, 500 replicates 0 failed replicates ; sampling SD is 7–42% of the posterior SE, median 13% Held-out series Fit on 70% of a goal's series, predict the held-out 30%: median AUC  0.725  against a per-series permutation null at  0.500 The bootstrap result means the published standard errors are  conservative  — they already cover item-parameter uncertainty with room to spare. Report the posterior SE, not the bootstrap SD. The held-out test is the first direct check that a goal score predicts reporting it was not fitted on. Thirteen of sixteen goals score 0.649 or better. The three weakest — goal 17 (0.618), goal 15 (0.526) and goal 6 (0.479) — are precisely the three already set apart on content grounds, which the test did not know. Disclose, do not gate Every goal fitted is published.  Nothing is excluded for imprecision, and 0.70 (Nunnally) is reported as a reference point, not applied as a cut. Each goal ships with four numbers a reader can weigh it by: reliability  — 0.772 to 0.953 se_median  — the typical error bar on that goal's scores weight_top5_pct  — how concentrated the score is in its five heaviest series weight_agency_pct  — how much of the score rests on series the custodian agency produces rather than the country Two goals carry  release = hold_content . The hold is on  content  grounds and for  different reasons , never on precision: Goal 6  is largely satellite measurement of lakes, wetlands and river flow. "Reported" there mostly records whether an agency published a dataset, not a country's choice. Goal 15  is overwhelmingly country-produced, but a third of its series are treaty and policy instruments (Nagoya Protocol, Aichi targets, NBSAP), which may track commitment status rather than reporting effort. An error bar cannot warn a reader about either, so the flag travels with the data. Both goals are published in full. Known limitations Weight concentration.  Within a goal, small groups of series that are always reported together can carry much of the score — in goal 10 the five heaviest series carry 80%, in goal 1 75%. These groups are near-duplicates that the variant rule does not collapse, because they are not reported identically: in goal 1, India, Sri Lanka and Malaysia report the education and health breakdowns but never the aggregate, every year from 2015 to 2023. Collapsing them would erase those reporting choices, so they are disclosed in  weight_top5_pct  instead. Modelling the dependence directly is deferred. Provenance.   weight_agency_pct  records h
title: The World on Record: statistical reporting across countries, policy sectors, and time

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Total Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. summary: Did the places that lost most men in the First World War turn to Labour? The question runs through accounts of Labour's replacement of the Liberals, and studies of Italy and Germany link local war losses to post-war radicalism, but its link to party support has not been tested for Britain, where there is no record of deaths, or map of seats, at constituency level. I link 717,287 First World War names on community memorials in the Imperial War Museums' War Memorials Register, counted once per place, to every Great Britain constituency contest from 1906 to 1924, using 176 county and borough units as a common geography, and test hypotheses fixed before any outcome model was run. Contrary to the radicalisation hypothesis, a one standard deviation higher memorial rate (22 names per 1,000 electors of 1918) is associated with a 2.9 percentage point smaller Labour gain between December 1910 and 1918 (95% CI 0.1 to 5.7; p=0.040; Holm-adjusted across four primary outcomes p=0.16; N=131). The gap widens to 4.8 points by 1922, mirrored by Liberal resilience, and is not present in pre-war changes in six placebo tests. All 21 robustness variants give negative estimates, but only 8 have intervals excluding zero. Exploratory analysis points to where Labour fielded candidates. The design is correlational: recorded losses track volunteering and occupational structure, for which no data exist here. The data do not support a larger Labour advance where recorded losses were heavier; the negative association itself is modest and should be treated as suggestive. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/war-dead-labour/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/war-dead-labour . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/war-dead-labour/ . Sources: Imperial War Museums War Memorials Register (non-commercial reuse); general election results from UK Parliament (Open Parliament Licence v3.0), matched to Wikidata; ONS boundaries (OGL v3). Text, figures and derived data CC BY-NC 4.0 (the register's terms); code MIT.
title: The War Dead and the Rise of Labour: First World War Memorial Names and the British Vote, 1910 to 1924

summary: CRISPR-TRIAGE is an open-science computational biology research archive evaluating parameter-efficient off-target prioritization under budget-constrained experimental validation budgets (K <= 50). This package contains the complete trained model checkpoints, multi-seed training pipelines (5 random seeds), biophysical feature extractors, pre-registered baseline models (LightGBM GBDT, Pairwise 1D-CNN, Logistic Regression, crispAI architecture), and evaluation results across two external cellular benchmarks (Listgarten 2018 GUIDE-seq and K562 cellular compilation). Key Scientific Findings & Methodological Disclosure: Algorithmic Parity with Gradient Boosted Trees: On the deduplicated independent cellular benchmark (K562 retrospective multi-assay compilation from DeepCRISPR / Yang et al. 2023; 11 guides, 16,172 unique candidate pairs, 110 confirmed positive guide-target sequence pairs without genomic coordinates), standard gradient boosting (LightGBM GBDT) trained on 15 simple biophysical mismatch features achieves Macro Recall@20 = 0.6350 vs 0.6416 for CRISPR-TRIAGE (margin +0.0066 / +0.66%; paired Wilcoxon W = 18.0, p = 1.0000; 95% bootstrap CI [-0.0979, +0.0900]). LightGBM runs 2.39x faster with 0 neural parameters. While lack of statistically significant superiority does not prove biological equivalence or disprove neural-network utility, the empirical evidence failed to reject the null hypothesis of no difference vs LightGBM under available statistical power. Multi-Seed Volatility in CRISPR Modeling: Retraining across 5 independent random seeds reveals substantial Macro Recall@20 fluctuations (+-6.5% standard deviation on identical data), demonstrating that single-seed reporting in the CRISPR machine-learning literature frequently reflects random seed-selection noise rather than genuine algorithmic superiority. Dataset Deduplication Importance: Forensic auditing documented the impact of 1,613 duplicate candidate rows (and 2 duplicate confirmed positive sites) in the K562 compilation, showing how uncleaned duplicates distort evaluation metrics. Two-Tier Reproducibility Scope: Tier 1 (Saved-Model Inference & K562 Cellular Benchmark Reproduction): 100% self-contained in this archive. All 5 trained seed weights, baselines, scalers, predictions, metric summaries, and the K562 cellular cohort execute fully offline without internet access. Tier 2 (Full Retraining on Primary Assay Datasets): Full retraining from raw sequence reads and complete Listgarten raw dataset reproduction requires separately downloading the 4 un-subsampled raw assay datasets (>20MB each), registered with authoritative accessions and cryptographic SHA256 checksums in DATA_MANIFEST.csv. Licensing, Provenance & Third-Party Rights: CRISPR-TRIAGE code, models, and documentation are licensed under the permissive MIT License. The crispAI architecture code (src/crispai_official/) is under MIT License (Copyright 2023 Furkan Ozden; reference: Özden & Minary, NAR 2024). Pretrained third-party weights for crispAI are omitted from the archive to ensure compliance with conflicting upstream documentation, with archive extraction utilities provided for the authors' official Zenodo records (13335960 / 12609337). Bundled K562 benchmark datasets are distributed under CC BY 4.0 (Yang et al. CSBJ 2023; Chuai et al. Genome Biol 2018). Raw CFD scoring lookup matrices (Doench et al. 2016 Supplementary Table 19) are strictly omitted from the release archive for third-party rights compliance; tested user-side acquisition and verification utilities are provided via scripts/download_cfd_matrices.py. See the root LICENSE file for full details.
title: CRISPR-TRIAGE: Evaluation of Parameter-Efficient Bi-Modal Off-Target Prioritization Under Budget-Constrained Screening

summary: Hobsbawm and Rudé argued that parliamentary enclosure helped to cause the Swing riots of 1830; Caprettini and Voth showed that threshing machines mattered. I link 5,375 places named in 4,104 enclosure Acts to the parishes in Caprettini and Voth's data (79% of places named in Acts of 1790 to 1830 linked) and test, in a model specified in advance with county fixed effects and their controls, whether recent enclosure predicts unrest in 9,674 parishes. As planned, parishes named in an Act of 1790 to 1830 were 2.7 percentage points more likely to see an incident (95% CI 0.2 to 5.3; mean 14.5%). Three findings argue against a grievance reading. Parishes enclosed only before 1790 show the same gap (3.1 points); stricter linking rules shrink it to between 0.7 and 1.7 points; and in exploratory models that add parish area, a control the plan omitted, it disappears (-0.8 points, 95% CI -3.2 to 1.5); larger parishes were both more often enclosed and more likely to record any incident. The planned estimate is therefore not robust evidence that recent parliamentary enclosure predicted where Swing broke out. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/enclosure-swing/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/enclosure-swing . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/enclosure-swing/ . Sources: Caprettini and Voth (2020) replication data (openICPSR 117044, CC BY 4.0); Chronological Tables of Private and Local Acts, legislation.gov.uk (Open Government Licence v3.0); Wikidata (CC0). Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: Enclosure and the Swing Riots: A Pre-specified Parish-level Test of the Grievance Hypothesis, England and Wales, 1830 to 1831

summary: LOADX (workLOad Assessment in Dual-task eXecution) is a multimodal dataset developed to support research on physical and mental workload estimation during single- and dual-task activities. The dataset contains synchronized physiological, kinematic, task-related, and subjective data collected from 20 participants performing a structured experimental protocol designed to elicit different combinations of physical and cognitive demand. The protocol includes 16 experimental conditions: three physical tasks, three cognitive tasks, nine dual-task combinations, and one resting baseline. The physical tasks consist of repeated shoulder flexion–extension, marching in place, and squats. The cognitive tasks include a Stroop test, a 2-back working-memory task, and backward counting by seven. Each active condition lasted 90 seconds and was followed by a resting interval. Physiological data were acquired using wearable sensors and include raw electrocardiographic signals, raw respiratory waveforms, heart rate, inter-beat interval, respiratory rate, galvanic skin response, and triaxial acceleration. Full-body kinematic data were collected using a contactless vision-based monitoring system based on MediaPipe Pose, providing the three-dimensional coordinates of 33 anatomical landmarks. All acquisition streams share a common temporal reference, enabling the alignment of physiological signals, body movements, task execution, and workload annotations. After each experimental condition, participants rated their perceived physical and mental demand using selected dimensions of the NASA Task Load Index. The dataset therefore includes task-level Physical Demand and Mental Demand scores, which can be used as subjective workload annotations for supervised learning, correlation analysis, clustering, and validation of multimodal workload-estimation methods. The dataset is organized into one folder for each participant, identified through an anonymized numerical code such as S01, S02, and so forth. Each participant folder contains: Sxx.csv: synchronized physiological, kinematic, task-related, and subjective data; Sxx_ecg.csv: raw ECG waveform; Sxx_breath.csv: raw respiratory waveform; Sxx_nasa.xlsx: task-level NASA-TLX Physical Demand and Mental Demand ratings. LOADX can support research on multimodal workload assessment, physiological and movement-signal processing, sensor fusion, feature extraction, task recognition, modality-ablation analysis, subject-independent validation, and the development of adaptive human–machine interaction systems. The inclusion of physical-only, cognitive-only, and dual-task conditions enables the investigation of how physical and mental demands interact and how they are reflected in complementary sensing modalities. LOADX should be considered a structured multimodal research dataset rather than a population-level normative dataset. Inter-individual variability was intentionally retained to support the investigation of personalized and subject-independent workload-estimation approaches.
title: LOADX Dataset: workLOad Assessment in Dual-task eXecution through multimodal monitoring

summary: VCAB-Wild characterizes the functionality and observable security properties of deployed web applications created with Lovable, an AI application builder. It covers all 7,937 distinct *.lovable.app hosts indexed by Common Crawl in CC-MAIN-2026-39. For each host it records reachability, ten building blocks identified in public client code, and four categories of non-intrusive exposure indicators: database readability with the application's public key (row counts only), secret-key strings in public code (type only), public source maps and security headers. A random subset of 500 hosts carries application-type labels from two LLM annotators with adjudication and a 50-host human check. The release includes a keyed development/test split, three reference tasks with a scoring tool, SHA-256 fingerprints for snapshot reconstruction, and all collection and analysis code. Host names are withheld; the key linking records to hosts is available from the author under a non-disclosure agreement. Data: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT. Part of the Vibe-Coded App Benchmark (VCAB).
title: VCAB-Wild: A dataset of 7,937 deployed vibe-coded web applications with building-block annotations, non-intrusive data-exposure measurements and reference tasks for security evaluation

summary: Factoring and supply chain finance (SCF) allow firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to obtain liquidity against receivables and other trade assets, but they expose financiers to the credit risk of suppliers, buyers and their relationships. This study maps the scientific literature on credit risk management in factoring and SCF through a bibliometric analysis. A Scopus search conducted on 12 October 2026 and screening following the PRISMA 2020 flow yielded 288 articles and reviews published between 1995 and 2025. Performance analysis was combined with science mapping in VOSviewer, including keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship and co-citation analyses of references and sources. The results show that the field has grown rapidly since 2019, with 87.2% of the documents published in 2019–2025. China dominates research output, while studies from the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy attain higher normalised impact, and operations management and operational research journals are the main publication venues. Three research streams are identified: analytical operations–finance models of risk allocation in capital-constrained supply chains, conceptual and empirical research on SCF adoption and reverse factoring, and machine learning-based credit risk assessment of SMEs. Research attention has shifted from traditional factoring and receivables financing towards SCF, machine learning, blockchain and, most recently, artificial intelligence and sustainability. The accounting, financial reporting and internal control dimensions of these arrangements, the allocation of risk among multiple financiers, and evidence from under-represented regions emerge as the main gaps.
tags: factoring, supply chain finance, credit risk management, reverse factoring, bibliometric analysis, VOSviewer.
title: CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT IN FACTORING AND SUPPLY CHAIN FINANCE: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF SCIENTIFIC PUBLICATIONS

summary: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.
title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

summary: LLMs excel at language tasks, but long-meeting QFS remains difficult due to complex speaker dynamics, sparse key information, and limited data. Meetings involve disfluencies, long transcripts and complex discourse. QFS have high risk of information omission, hallucination, even for advanced models such as GPT-4-mini and Gemini. Existing end-to-end methods compress retrieval, evidence extraction, and summary generation into a single pass, failing to handle the complex reasoning required for targeted meeting summaries. We propose ReSUM, a modular multi-LLM framework coordinated by a planner that orchestrates retrieval and summarization agents. By distilling teacher reasoning into query- and plan-conditioned retrievers and summarizers, ReSUM enhances long-context robustness, minimizes irrelevant exploration, and generates more faithful and comprehensive query-focused summaries. Experiments show consistent gains on query-focused meeting summarization benchmarks.
title: ReSUM: Reasoning-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Query-Focused Summarization

summary: Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances. To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control. A graph neural network represents the pieces, their target poses, and their spatial relationships, and predicts translational and angular velocities for each component. Per-agent proximal policy optimization with a centralized graph critic directly learns motion and temporal coordination within a single feedback policy. We study this formulation through planar Tangram assembly, where pieces must slide and rotate into a given configuration while remaining on the assembly surface. Procedural generation of target configurations and randomized initial arrangements support training and evaluation across diverse assembly problems. Our experiments isolate the roles of relational structure and multi-agent optimization, and compare learned control with sampling-based planning. We demonstrate concurrent assembly in simulation and transfer the policy to sequential execution on a real robot, as our object-centric formulation decouples learned assembly coordination from low-level physical control. Project page: https://tangrambench.org/
title: It Takes Two to Tangram: Multi-Agent Object Centric Reinforcement Learning for Assembly

summary: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation

summary: Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.
title: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL

summary: Version 1.0.0 research artifact for JISA-N03. The archive provides selected original packet captures, native command/state observations, independent receiver records, retained failure evidence and standard-library Python scripts for offline reanalysis of packet-size validation under different probe orders. The first qualification retains six trials, twelve related phases, sixty service probes, forty-five intact receiver records and twelve separate capture fences. The follow-up retains twelve fresh histories, twenty-four service transfers, seventeen intact receiver records and twelve separate fences. Its designed pairs distinguish TCP-before-UDP from UDP-before-TCP in routed IPv4 and IPv4-in-IPv4 paths, with correct-static-limit and blocked-feedback controls. The default offline command verifies selected input bytes and regenerates reported structures and three figure sources using 27 scientific comparisons. One realization per designed order cell, bounded observations and shared parsing do not establish population reliability, an exclusive kernel/cache cause, a new discovery protocol or a selector advantage. Original data, documentation and figures are licensed CC BY 4.0. Original Python scripts are separately MIT licensed. Third-party tools retain their own licenses and executables are not redistributed. No manuscript, reference-paper library, internal editorial/AI history, governance, cache or access credential is included.
title: Probe-order effects on packet-size validation in routed and encapsulated Linux paths: research artifact

summary: Overview The Earth Surface Anomaly dataset (v1.0) is a five-class, event-grouped Sentinel-2 benchmark for immediate disaster and surface-anomaly detection. It contains 622 samples grouped into 46 event or spatiotemporal observation units (17 source-named/inventory units and 29 observation groups, 2017–2025, globally distributed): 129 fire, 58 flood-context, 54 landslide, 204 crop-residue-burning and 177 retrogressive-thaw-slump samples. 595 samples carry source polygon-derived binary masks; 27 carry weak point inventories only; all 54 landslide samples include pre/post paired observations. Industrial heat sources (208 candidates) are excluded from this release and 17 visually ambiguous candidates are withheld, both enumerated in quality/excluded_samples.csv . Sample structure Each sample ( data/CODE/EVENT/SAMPLE/ ) provides a six-band Sentinel-2 L2A chip (declared bands B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, B12; aligned grid spacing does not imply native 10 m for every band), a 0/1 binary mask, RGB/NIR/SWIR previews, annotation.json and measured facts.json (CRS, transform, WGS84 bounds, geometry statistics, spectral indices, SHA256 checksums). Annotation-conditioned vision-language tasks (4–6 per sample depending on label strength and pairing) cover event classification, factual captioning, spatial reasoning, visual grounding, spectral comparison, and for suitable samples temporal reasoning and label provenance. Splits Group splits are precomputed: default splits/event_disjoint (443/102/77 train/val/test) and inherited splits/site_disjoint (433/114/75). Event-disjointness does not guarantee site-disjointness (1 measured case); use site_disjoint when required. Never randomly split patches from the same event. Screening and quality All 639 non-industrial candidates underwent AI-assisted visual screening of RGB, SWIR and target crops with review sheets and per-sample geometry/text audits retained in the release ( quality/ , visual_review.csv ). This is not independent expert pixel adjudication, field validation, or new external verification of every event identity. Limitations (documented in README, README_zh and DATA_DICTIONARY) Flood-context masks often follow existing river channels; no paired baseline establishes incremental inundation. Fire annotations can cover smoke, scars or hotspots and are not universally burned-area boundaries. Crop-residue burning is a source label; imagery alone does not establish fuel identity. Thaw mechanism/onset and landslide onset cannot be established from the supplied views alone. Point inventories (27 samples) are weak localization, not segmentation truth; polygon provenance does not guarantee exact pixel boundaries. Radiometric scale/offset and the inherited non-landslide band mapping have not been independently traced to every source product; facts.json indices are stored-DN calculations, not validated physical reflectance. External event-match references in index/external_verification_ledger.csv were not newly re-verified during release preparation. License and third-party terms CC BY 4.0 applies to the project-original annotations, revisions and documentation. Sentinel/Copernicus imagery is used under modified-data attribution terms and COOLR landslide inventories retain their original conditions; see LICENSE , licenses/ and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . No ESA or European Union endorsement is implied. Access The metadata and preview figures of this record are public. The files are distributed on an approved-request basis: use the Request access button on this record page and state your affiliation and intended use; requests are reviewed by the authors. The dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0 for research use, subject to the third-party imagery conditions listed in licenses/ and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Citation Zhao, W., & Wang, Q. (2026). Earth Surface Anomaly Dataset (v1.0): Five-Class Event-Grouped Sentinel-2 Observations for Immediate Disaster and Surface-Anomaly Detection . Zenodo. https:
title: Earth Surface Anomaly Dataset (v1.0): Five-Class Event-Grouped Sentinel-2 Observations for Immediate Disaster and Surface-Anomaly Detection

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Total Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed.
