The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.
title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation

summary: Sampling only part of the data reduces the cost of each iteration in an inverse problem, but can make reconstruction updates unreliable. We study stochastic multilevel sampling, which computes updates on a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of correction spaces. The guiding idea is that a small sample may support a reliable coarse-grid update even when it provides insufficient information for a fine-grid update. For quadratic objectives, we identify conditions under which corrections computed from sampled data decrease the full-data objective. In small-batch experiments with computed tomography and periodic deblurring, the stochastic multilevel method improves reconstruction accuracy over matched single-level methods. In an increasingly ill-conditioned CT refinement with a fixed number of projection angles, the single-level error increases as the image dimension grows, whereas a deep hierarchy maintains or improves accuracy and outperforms full-data single-level optimization at the same number of forward and adjoint applications. The gains persist across the tested local solvers and strengthen with deeper hierarchies. A separate known-probe ptychography study provides complementary evidence for the benefit of hierarchical corrections for nonlinear inverse problems.
title: Stochastic Multilevel Sampling for Inverse Problems via Coarse-Space Identifiability

summary: We present a class of numerical collocation methods to solve a typical inverse problem that arises in the stress-controlled rheology of complex fluids with pronounced history-dependent response, where the relation between stress and flow rate is given by an integral constitutive equation as the material law. We demonstrate the method by calculating the creep response of a nontrivial model of a shear-thinning viscoelastic fluid where a stress overshoot in rate-controlled startup flow leads to ``sudden yielding'' in stress-controlled creep. Our method is able to address the long-time behavior of the model, distinguishing the amorphous solid from the stress-induced yielded fluid, and from the in-between case of infinite deformation that never achieves a stationary shear rate (proper creep). To this end, we implement a method with flexible time-stepping, and prove uniqueness of the solution and convergence of the methods for a broad class of highly viscoelastic non-linear rheological laws in integral form.
title: Nonlinear integral equations for stress-controlled rheology: Collocation methods for Volterra equations with functional kernels

summary: Natural systems are often composed of processes evolving on multiple timescales and coupled through complex interaction networks. Inferring such networks is especially challenging when timescales are widely separated, since resolving the fastest processes while accurately sampling the slowest ones is generally prohibitive. In this work, we propose a framework to reconstruct a multiscale interaction tree by combining a rescaled version of the mutual information rate, its conditional counterpart, and the ordering of timescales. We derive an exact theory for stationary Gaussian processes, finding that these measures identify directly connected processes, with the asymptotic mutual information rate distinguishing fast-to-slow from slow-to-fast couplings. We show that this reconstruction can be achieved from the spectral matrix and illustrate its robustness to finite trajectory lengths, moderate timescale separation, and weak nonlinearities. Our work paves the way for exploiting the presence of multiple timescales in real-world systems as a source of structural identifiability rather than an obstacle to network inference.
title: Resolving the backbone of multiscale interactions through mutual information rates

summary: Functional dependencies are used to flag erroneous cells, but without error labels the value of these flags is unknown. Dependency strength cannot settle it, because identical data and flags can have positive value in one clean state and negative value in another. We treat this value as partially identified and certify a fixed detector when its value is positive in every clean state compatible with the observation under an error model and budget. The largest such budget is the certification radius. For a detector that flags departures from the unique mode of each class, the worst case reduces to a 0/1 knapsack over class flips, yielding sharp bounds on true positives and the exact radius in polynomial time. Allowing bounded legitimate exceptions in the clean data, we derive an exact threshold for the existence of a positive certificate and compute the radius with the same knapsack. Across five relations and 21,981 candidate dependencies, rules with nearly equal $g_3$ and flag rate can have certification margins differing tenfold. Error injection confirms sound certification and shows that, at equal error counts, changing the organization of errors reverses certification outcomes for every tested rule.
title: Certifying the Error-Detection Value of Functional Dependencies without Ground Truth

summary: Multi-view anomaly detection is crucial for industrial inspection to identify defects hidden from single viewpoints. Yet, despite their strong success in single-view applications, reconstruction-based methods remain largely underexplored in multi-view settings. A key challenge in extending these methods lies in generating view-consistent pseudo-anomalies. To address this, we propose PAR, a reconstruction-based framework for enhanced multi-view anomaly detection. First, we introduce a feature perturbation strategy coupled with a consensus aggregation module that integrates these perturbed features across viewpoints to mitigate view-inconsistent anomalies and construct highly aligned pseudo-anomaly representations. Second, we employ a view-specialized multi-decoder architecture; by assigning a dedicated decoder to each view, we increase the model's representational complexity, enabling the generation of highly feasible, localized anomaly maps rather than less precise, view-agnostic reconstructions. Last, we incorporate Fourier attention into the decoders to emphasize global frequency-domain structures over local token evidence, effectively preventing identity mapping. Extensive experiments on the Real-IAD dataset demonstrate that PAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in sample-level, image-level, and pixel-level anomaly detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/SpatialAILab/PAR_mvad.
title: Perturb, Aggregate then Reconstruct: Consensus Aggregation and Fourier-Attended Multi-Decoders for Reconstruction-based Multi-View Anomaly Detection

summary: Scientific research has long been driven by substantial human effort, from reviewing prior work and identifying research gaps to designing specific solutions. Recent advances in harness-based agent systems have given rise to increasingly capable Auto Researchers, which can autonomously carry out these tasks and, increasingly, entire end-to-end research workflows. Yet despite their rapidly growing capabilities, how closely the research decisions and outputs produced by auto researchers align with those of human experts remains underexplored. We investigate this gap through the lens of research reconstruction and study: Given comparable research context, how similar are the research decisions and outputs produced by Auto Researchers to those of human researchers in AI research? To answer this question, we introduce AutoResearcher-Human Research Similarity (AutoHRS), a stage-wise evaluation framework for assessing how faithfully auto researchers reconstruct human research artifacts across different stages of the scientific workflow. Using 152 ICLR oral papers as our corpus, we generate 456 research trajectories spanning different stages of the research process. Applying AutoHRS to these trajectories, we find that current Auto Researchers frequently fail to recover key research decisions and their resulting artifacts across multiple stages of the research process.
title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?

summary: Companion manuscript: *Multi-Source Data Assimilation for Regional Ionospheric Reconstruction Using GNSS, Ionosonde and Radio Occultation Observations*
title: Multi-Source Data Assimilation

summary: Combining video generation, dynamic reconstruction and monocular SLAM requires consistent coordinates, explicit handling of missing outputs and predictable memory use. We present AcrossVAM3.0, an offline system that converts text, images or monocular RGB video into a versioned point representation. Frozen components run sequentially on one GPU; map corrections update cameras, points and trajectories together. The coordination layer adds no neural parameters. Three fresh input-mode runs completed with a maximum sampled task-process-tree GPU footprint of 17.14 GB. In a frozen 16-scene video suite, every scene yielded a 4D reconstruction and 15 yielded a non-empty SLAM map. Strict cross-window matching reduced local surface error but lost long-range track coverage on TAP-Vid-DAVIS. We therefore developed multi-hypothesis adaptive surface chaining (MHAC), which retains several candidate matches and an explicit missing state. After selection on disjoint development data, MHAC improved Average Jaccard over a position-only baseline by 0.1394 on a frozen ten-video holdout (95% bootstrap interval [0.1074,0.1689]). Across 265 RoboTAP videos, the mean paired gain was 0.0610 ([0.0510,0.0715]), with 215 wins, one tie and 49 losses. These results support resource-bounded scene construction and an external tracking gain under the tested protocol. They do not establish metric scale, semantic identity or high-fidelity novel-view rendering.
title: ACROSSVAM3.0: Resource-Bounded 4D Scene Construction and Adaptive Surface Association

summary: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.
title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity

summary: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.
title: Self-Indexing Latent Memories for Access-Aware Continual Instruction Tuning of LLMs

summary: Learning neural solvers for spatiotemporal partial differential equations (PDEs) under real-world constraints remains a key challenge in scientific machine learning, especially for inverse tasks with sparse and noisy boundary observations. We present the Aletheia dataset, the first 3D benchmark for learning data-driven solvers in the context of nondestructive testing (NDT). The dataset simulates eddy-current-induced heating in conductive solids and models the resulting transient heat propagation governed by the heat equation. Aletheia contains over 4,700 high-resolution samples across 10 excitation frequencies (1-100,kHz), each providing volumetric heat source and temperature fields over time. It supports both forward prediction of temperature evolution and inverse reconstruction of internal heat sources or defects from surface infrared measurements. Real infrared thermography data from cracked rail specimens are included for calibration and comparison. We define four canonical tasks on both regular and irregular grids and benchmark them using various neural operators. Aletheia establishes a unified platform for evaluating neural PDE solvers under realistic NDT conditions, enabling progress in reliable, data-driven inverse modeling. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://github.com/sherlock-0327/ALETHEIA.
title: ALETHEIA: A Multi-Frequency Eddy Current Pulsed Thermography Dataset for Neural Operator Learning in Nondestructive Testing

summary: Low-bit post-training quantization reduces language-model memory but can sharply degrade downstream task accuracy. Calibration usually relies on generic text, but when task-informed data recover accuracy and which quantizers benefit remain poorly understood. We introduce FragCal-DC, which supplements generic text with training documents from task families with low retention of full-precision accuracy in a two-bit scan. We use a two- to four-bit sweep to locate functional regimes and four-seed calibration comparisons to evaluate six data-dependent methods across six dense models (1.7B-8B) and ten tasks. At their lowest tested functional bit widths, iterative SignRound V2 and OmniQuant improve at two bits, whereas single-pass GPTQ and AWQ show small mean responses at three bits. At two bits, SignRound V2 gains 1.83 percentage points in mean ten-task accuracy over generic-text calibration across six models. At 70 billion parameters, GPTQ and SignRound V2 both improve at two bits, with functional generic-calibration baselines. For two-bit SignRound V2, task-level controls show that recovery concentrates on families included in calibration, while incorrect answer designations retain about 90% of the mean accuracy gain. Changes in reconstruction error do not consistently track accuracy gains. These findings support task-informed calibration as a design principle for preserving downstream accuracy in low-bit quantization.
title: When Calibration Data Matter in Sub-4-Bit Language Model Quantization

summary: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.
title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations

summary: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.
title: PARIS: A multi-agent LLM framework for end-to-end, PRISMA-guided systematic literature reviews with pre-synthesis corpus quality assessment

summary: Recent systems such as the eBPF Certificate Framework (BCF) and Proof-Carrying BPF address the imprecision in the Linux eBPF verifier with proof-carrying code. When the verifier's abstract domains cannot prove a safety condition, an in-kernel proof checker checks an untrusted user-space refutation proof. A single bug in this checker can compromise the security of the entire kernel. While formalizing BCF's in-kernel checker, we discovered 13 bugs such as unsound rewrite rules, silently unchecked proof steps, and memory safety errors. We demonstrate that forged certificates can trick the kernel to accept arbitrary unsafe eBPF programs. To address this problem, we propose Keel, a formally verified in-kernel proof checker for the Linux eBPF verifier. First, we specify the checker as a pure functional program in Lean and prove its soundness against bit-vector semantics. We decouple the steps of the proof certificate checker from the mathematical rewrite rules, which enables us to extend the rewrite rules without the need to change the checker. Second, we implement the checker in EmbC, a deeply embedded C fragment, and prove that our C implementation refines the functional specification without undefined behavior or memory leaks. Third, using an amortized potential argument, we prove linear time and memory bounds for the C checker. Keel is correct-by-construction while also being faster than the BCF checker inside the kernel, 1.3X in total and 2.0X on the slowest 1.4% of certificates.
title: Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF

summary: The Retriangulation of Great Britain, begun in 1936, left thousands of concrete pillars on British hilltops and gave the country its National Grid. Treating the Ordnance Survey's legacy station list as data, this paper asks four questions, pre-specified in a written plan: how the network is laid out, when it was built, how much is recorded destroyed, and whether a modern open terrain model reproduces the rule that neighbouring stations of the same order must be intervisible. Grouping 31,521 mark records into 24,433 stations (6,573 pillars), I find a clear hierarchy of spacing (median nearest same-order distance 19.6 km for primary stations, 7.1 km for secondary and 4.3 km for third-order pillars), primaries far more regular than random points (Clark and Evans ratio 1.54 against 1.02 to 1.17), and 99.0% of pillars dated 1936 to 1962. Over Terrain Tiles (zoom 9), with curvature and refraction, 228 of 240 nearest-neighbour primary lines are clear (95.0%, 95% CI 91.5 to 97.1), against 16.6% when both ends are moved 1 km and 10.9% for random land pairs of the same lengths. Of the 12 failures, 8 involve a structure without a recorded height and 3 a station observed from a steel tower; one is unexplained. The result depends on using surveyed station heights: with the terrain model's own heights at the ends, only 67.1% of lines are clear, because the model sits a median 22 m below surveyed pillar tops. Pillars are far less often recorded destroyed (6.3%) than other marks. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/trig-network/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/trig-network . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/trig-network/ . Sources: Ordnance Survey legacy triangulation station list (contains OS data, Crown copyright and database right 2018, used under the Open Government Licence v3.0, via the trigpoints R package); Terrain Tiles (AWS Open Data; Mapzen: SRTM and GMTED2010 courtesy of the USGS, EU-DEM produced using Copernicus data, ETOPO1 NOAA); OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL); ONS boundaries (OGL v3.0). Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0, except that OS station fields remain under the Open Government Licence v3.0 and the OSM-derived file osm_points.csv is ODbL; code MIT.
title: The Trig Pillar Network: Geometry, Construction, Survival and Intervisibility of the Ordnance Survey Retriangulation of Great Britain

summary: In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to space-filling input design for nonlinear system identification, in which an agent learns a control policy that actively drives the system to explore its state space. Classical input design, developed mainly for linear models, minimises the covariance of the estimated parameters. For nonlinear black-box models, however, the dominant error is the bias induced by the model structure over the region of interest, which motivates space-filling strategies that seek to cover the system state space. Existing space-filling approaches rely on predefined input signal classes and require solving explicit optimisation problems. Unlike these methods, the proposed approach requires no input class to be selected and no frequency band to be tuned for the system at hand, satisfies and amplitude bound by construction, and adapts to varying initial conditions through its observation-based policy without re-optimisation. The learned excitation signals exhibit physically meaningful behaviours, such as resonance excitation and amplitude modulation. The approach is evaluated against tuned swept sine and crest-factor-optimised multisine excitations, and against a state-of-the-art space-filling multisine design, on two nonlinear benchmark systems: a mass-spring-damper with nonlinear stiffness and a Van der Pol oscillator. Under the same amplitude bound, the learned policy achieves the best overall space-filling performance on both systems and distributes its samples more uniformly than the state-of-the-art design.
title: Space-Filling Input Design for Nonlinear System Identification: A Reinforcement Learning Approach

summary: Post-Temporal Physics and the SPARC Galaxy Rotation Data — An Independently Audited Empirical Benchmark A Fourteen-Year Foundational Research Program Reaches a Reproducible Empirical Milestone Post-Temporal Physics (PTP) originated in 2012 as a foundational scientific research program investigating whether physical existence, persistence, causality, interaction, and observable behavior could be reconstructed from principles more primitive than conventional continuous spacetime and geometric descriptions. Its development has involved fourteen years of theoretical investigation, mathematical construction, physical analysis, and successive reformulations aimed at establishing a coherent alternative framework for understanding physical law. The research initially progressed through a substantial transitional program encompassing twenty native physics sectoral expansions (18 Transitonal Sectoral Expansions have not been released due to sever dual-use concern). These investigations explored the implications of the developing theory across multiple physical sectors and exposed the mathematical requirements of constructing a unified foundational system. The subsequent development of Ledgeral Mathematics provided a dedicated finite mathematical architecture through which the physical theory could be reconstructed with explicitly defined primitive objects, operations, admissibility conditions, and verification procedures. This progression culminated in the consolidated formulation of Post-Temporal Physics: The Finite Ledgeral Reconstruction of Existence, Persistence, and Physical Law , supported by Ledgeral Mathematics: A Finite Algebra of Recursion, Admissibility, Projection, and Survivor Structure and the companion Applied Ledgeral Mathematics research program and their respective sectoral and subsectoral expansions. Within this architecture, physical standing is described through finite retained records, admissibility, recursion, projection, survivor formation, residue accounting, and auditable relationships. Conventional physical quantities are admitted through specified recovery procedures, while continuum spacetime and geometric structures are not assigned primitive status within the native formulation. The present empirical release represents a significant milestone in this long-term undertaking. It establishes a reproducible astronomical benchmark through which a specified observational recovery prescription associated with the Post-Temporal Physics research program is evaluated against measured galaxy rotation behavior.   The Empirical Investigation The investigation uses observational data from the SPARC database, originally assembled by Lelli, McGaugh, and Schombert. SPARC provides measured galaxy rotation curves and baryonic mass models suitable for examining the relationship between observed circular velocities and the gravitational contribution attributed to measured baryonic matter. The analysis retains 3,269 usable radial observational records from 163 galaxies. A galaxy-level training and testing procedure separates 114 galaxies, containing 2,216 radial records, from 49 withheld galaxies containing 1,053 observational measurements. A single characteristic acceleration scale is calibrated using the designated training population. The resulting observational recovery prescription is subsequently evaluated against the withheld galaxies without additional galaxy-specific calibration of the principal fitted scale. The recovered predictions achieve a root-mean-square velocity error of approximately 22.91 kilometers per second, compared with approximately 57.52 kilometers per second for the specified fixed baryon-only reference. This corresponds to an approximately 60.2 percent reduction in RMS prediction error. At the individual galaxy level, the tested prescription improves predictive accuracy relative to the baryon-only reference in 45 of the 49 withheld galaxies. Additional analysis across 200 galaxy-level
title: Post-Temporal Physics and the SPARC Galaxy Rotation Data: An Independently Audited Empirical Benchmark

summary: Purpose: The aim of this study was to define whether a gesture similarity index (GSI) based on muscle synergies extracted by a wearable device (REMO, Morecognition Ltd, Turin, Italy) provides the same information of clinical outcome measures, after specific training of hand function. The secondary aim was to define whether specific hand tasks could be considered as target tasks for hand function assessment, after stroke.  Methods: REMO is a wearable composed of 8 surface-electromyography (sEMG) sensors able to detect forearm muscles activation in real-time. The acquisition protocol consisted of bilateral execution of wrist and hand movements of the Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA-Hand, maximum score 24 points) using REMO. Then, we applied the Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) algorithm to extract muscle synergies from the sEMG signals. We calculated the GSI which represents the mathematical distance between the muscle synergies extracted from a group of elderly-healthy subjects (as reference model) and from the patient's performance (the lowest distance represented the maximum similarity, GSI=100%). Stroke survivors were assessed before (T0) and after (T1) a specific hand training of 15 sessions (1 hour each, 5 time/week, 3 weeks) (ClinicalTrial.gov ID NCT05815368). After randomization, the patients underwent to a task-specific training (control group, CG) or biofeedback training using REMO (experimental group, EG). We compared the FMA-Hand and GSI results before and after the training, and we calculated Spearman's correlation to investigate the relationship between the level of FMA-Hand and the GSI index.  Results: We collected data from a control group of 4 elderly-healthy subjects (age 74±6.3) and a group of 14 people with diagnosis of stroke (age 64.7±13.8). Overall patients showed a significant hand motor recovery (FMA-Hand: T0=11.8 ± 3.0; T1=15.7 ± 3.7; p=0.002). Based on GSI results, data showed a statistically significant improvement in wrist circumduction movements (T0= 82% ± 4.5%; T1= 85.4% ± 4.3%; p=0.048). No differences between groups were found both in FMA-Hand and in GSI analysis. Then, at the baseline, correlation analysis showed a positive significant correlation between FMA-Hand and GSI value in circumduction movement (r=0.54; p=0.046).  Conclusion(s): The results showed that a specific hand motor training induced a significant improvement in patients’ functional level. GSI results showed that wrist circumduction could be a target movement to describe motor recovery after stroke. Future perspectives will include a wider data collection to confirm the results.
title: Gesture similarity index based on muscle synergies model describing hand recovery after stroke: preliminary results of a randomised controlled trial

summary: Original paper authored by Geng Niu, Yi Wang, Yang Zhou, & Xu Gan. DOI: 10.1057/s41267-024-00692-9. The authors have made a replication repository available at https://osf.io/upg2w/?view_only=b8687df7582b4b3394f0e542ed8c68d9. The component you are viewing now is empty.
title: Family Ties and Corporate Tax Avoidance

summary: Golden simulation baseline v17 for the ALMASim CI regression gate (MADIV-28), from workflow run 42800271858 at commit 5e76dc3a6aaba8e6477f5f0e036f02e0e34d187c. Reason: MADIV-28: The simulated samples observe the whole time on source (#555). The tier-1 baseline is unchanged (v16). Test data, not a software release.
title: astromadiv/ALMASim: CI golden baselines v17

summary: Voters often see a candidate's face before learning about the candidate's political positions. Building on evidence that rapid visual impressions predict electoral outcomes, we examine how time pressure and information costs shape political learning and whether these constraints produce distinct patterns of scrutiny for women candidates. We conduct a preregistered three-arm online visual conjoint experiment using photographs and political information drawn from Colombian electoral data. Respondents are randomly assigned to make these choices under a nine-second deadline, an effort cost for accessing political information, or an unconstrained baseline. Candidate pairings, task order, and left-right placement are randomized within respondents. The experiment measures recorded candidate selection, candidate-specific information acquisition, and decision time. Working paper (work in progress). The oTree implementation is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24089204.
title: Faces or Facts? Experimental Evidence on Time Pressure, Information Costs, and Gender Bias in Electoral Choice

summary: How much of Great Britain lay within a day's travel of London, and how did that change between the coaching era and today? I build a multimodal network model on a 2 km grid for five dates (1750, the 1830s, 1850, 1910 and today) from historical GIS of the turnpike roads of England and Wales and the railways of 1851, a reconstruction of the 1910 rail network, and OpenStreetMap. Coach speeds are fitted to scheduled times of London coach services in 1836 (136 destinations) and to twelve cited journeys of 1739 to 1764; train speeds come from published averages; every era is tested on journeys it was not fitted to. The 1830s model reproduces the 1837 mail-coach timetable with a median absolute error of 12%. The 1750 model fails the error threshold set in advance (28% against 25%), so its map is a rough sketch. The 1850 and 1910 models use average train speeds and are slower than documented expresses by a median 46% and 34%, on four and six journeys, so their areas are lower bounds. Leaving Charing Cross at dawn, twelve hours of travel reached 5% of Great Britain's land in 1750, 19% in the 1830s, at least 47% in 1850, at least 72% in 1910 and 97% today. The largest gain per year came between the 1830s and 1850, when the first railways multiplied the area within a day by at least 2.5 in about fifteen years. The surfaces and code are released for reuse. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/day-from-london/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/day-from-london . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/day-from-london/. Sources: turnpike roads and London coach services of 1819 and 1836 (Rosevear, Bogart, Shaw-Taylor and Satchell, openICPSR 195126 and 195128; derived results only); 1851 England, Wales and Scotland rail lines (Satchell et al., UK Data Service ReShare SN 852991, CC BY 4.0); OpenStreetMap contributors via OpenFreeMap (ODbL); train speeds from Leunig (2006). Text, figures and derived data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: A Day from London: One-Day Travel Reach across Great Britain in 1750, the 1830s, 1850, 1910 and Today, from a Calibrated Historical Network Model

summary: This study investigates the inverse domination number and inverse total domination number of Sierpiński Star graphs, contributing to the broader study of domination theory in graph theory. Domination parameters play an important role in understanding graph structures and have practical applications in areas such as computer networks, communication systems, and network security, where efficient selection of primary and backup nodes is essential. Building on previous studies of inverse domination and inverse total domination in various graph classes, this research focuses on the distinctive structural properties of Sierpiński Star graphs, which are constructed based on the Sierpiński triangle. The study examines the relationships between domination sets, inverse dominating sets, and inverse total dominating sets within these graphs. Through mathematical analysis and graph-theoretic techniques, it seeks to establish the corresponding inverse domination parameters and provide results that extend existing knowledge of domination in specially structured graphs. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of domination theory and provide a foundation for further investigations of inverse domination parameters in fractal-related graph structures.
title: COMPUTING INVERSE DOMINATION AND INVERSE TOTAL DOMINATION NUMBERS OF SIERPIŃSKI STAR GRAPHS

summary: This paper examines the concept of permission within the set-theoretical approach to the logical theory of normative systems. Drawing on Alchourrón and Bulygin’s expressive conception of norms, and Žarnić’s formal reconstruction of von Wright’s later deontic logic, the study argues that the standard interpretation of permission as the derogation of a command fails to capture its pragmatic function. Building on a distinction between prescriptive and descriptive uses of deontic language, the paper develops an alternative reinterpretation of the set-theoretical framework in which permission is treated as an autonomous prescriptive speech act. Within this model, the relations among obligation, prohibition, and permission are expressed through two sets—commanded and permitted act-propositions—and then two perfection properties of ideal normative systems are identified—inner consistency and relational consistency. Finally, the analysis reveals that the notion of permission is even more ambiguous than the literature has so far acknowledged, distinguishing four types—normative, weak (negative), unilateral positive, and bilateral positive—and shows that the principle “Obligation implies permission” is valid only under specific interpretations of positive permission.
title: Four concepts of permission

summary: The development of deep learning-based medical AI depends on high-quality annotated data. Yet, dataset creation remains constrained by the need for expert radiologist annotations, limiting curated datasets to relatively small cohorts. To overcome this limitation, recent efforts increasingly aggregate disparate public datasets into large-scale dataset collections. However, combining datasets at scale often obscures data provenance, introducing substantial risks of reuse propagation, unintended leakage, bias amplification and distorted data distributions. In this work, we study these problems on a massive collection of 565k 3D radiological images across 1034 public datasets and provide practical resources to address them. Firstly, we formalize dataset collections as a distinct paradigm in medical image analysis and characterize their structural challenges, including reuse propagation, duplication, and provenance fragmentation. Secondly, we perform a large-scale empirical study of duplication on this collection and demonstrate extensive exact and near-duplicate reuse across public datasets via perceptual hashing and manual tracing, identifying a lower bound of 118k duplicate pairs. We make the perceptual hashes publicly accessible for comparison through our website, providing researchers with a standardized reference for identifying potential overlaps and shared provenance. Thirdly, since hashing alone cannot detect all duplicates, we introduce MAP (Metadata for Aggregation and Provenance), a lightweight, portable metadata profile for documenting provenance, known overlaps, and deduplication decisions in dataset collections. Our contributions help dataset collections shift from coarse aggregations to reliable and provenance-aware data scaling mechanisms in medical image analysis. A web tool supporting our work is available at https://mic-dct.dkfz.de/.
title: Dataset Collections: Challenges of Large-Scale Data Aggregation in 3D Medical Image Datasets

summary: The ocean environment is inherently unpredictable, posing significant challenges for the reliable operation of marine energy converters (MECs). A critical step in the design of any WEC is identifying the scenarios that may lead to system failure. One common failure mode in marine energy devices occurs at system joints, such as mechanical hinges, where excessive loads or unfavorable configurations can lead to malfunction or structural breakdown [1]. A typical approach for identifying such failure modes is to perform high-fidelity simulations in which a MEC is subjected to a broad range of loading conditions, including irregular multidirectional waves and slamming events [2]. However, this approach can be prohibitively time consuming. Additionally, identifying high-risk scenarios becomes more difficult as system complexity grows, particularly for MECs, which span a wide range of configurations that complicate the identification of representative conditions. Importantly, MECs failure depends not only on load magnitude, but also on the system configuration at the moment wave forces act.
title: Rapid Identification of Potential Failure Scenarios in Marine Energy Systems

summary: A tape of $n$ cells over three values — equivalently, two-bit cells read through their sum — is read by two headers that enclose a window; at each step a fixed rule, given the window's content and the geometry, chooses one of eight actions: move a header inward or outward, trim a cell from the left, the right or both, or halt. The cost is the number of cell reads, the state is $O(\log n)$ bits, and the question is how the cost must grow with $n$ for each rule. On the evidence the rules fall into three classes — fully linear, semi-linear and superlinear — separated by a worst-case cost and a mean cost. All three are populated: four natural rules are fully linear, one construction is semi-linear ($e=\Theta(n)$ with $g=\Theta(n^2)$), and the remaining seventeen are superlinear. The paper separates the length of a walk from the number of cells it reads, shows the length is a property of the rule rather than of the model, gives machines for every rule in the catalogue, arranges their costs on a ladder from $n^{1/2}$ to $n^3$, and states exactly which rungs are proved, which are conditional and which are conjectural. Negative results included: the certificate bound does not compose (on one tape per-query certificates sum to $1{,}285{,}703$ cells while their union has $1{,}020$), and a bound on the rule's output transfers to the walk only after multiplication by the fraction of queries at which the answer can change the action, measured at $0.104$ and falling like $n^{-0.99}$.
title: A memoryless two-header tape machine: what a window costs, and why two lower-bound techniques fail

summary: Enterprise adoption of agentic systems is often framed as a problem of agent reasoning, tool use, retrieval, or memory. This paper investigates an additional architectural problem: preparing heterogeneous enterprise knowledge into task-appropriate representations that agents can interpret, reuse, and govern. We propose Cognitive Preparation as an explicit architectural lifecycle between authoritative enterprise knowledge and agent execution, with a Cognitive Preparation Compiler (CPC) coordinating representation decisions, compilation, validation, provenance binding, temporal constraints, and publication through a reusable Cognitive Substrate. The contribution is positioned at the architectural and methodological level; no novelty is claimed for ontologies, symbolic predicates, memory mechanisms, provenance, temporal models, or knowledge compilation individually. Recent 2026 preprints on precomputed agent-memory views and enterprise context engineering further narrow the novelty boundary and are treated as close, non-peer-reviewed prior art. We report a staged prototype evaluation implemented in Ver.Test9 on a Ver.Test8 runtime foundation. Deterministic tests examine selected lifecycle controls, while exploratory LLM-assisted evaluations (T17–T22) examine controlled reuse of synthetic operational knowledge through deterministic retrieval. The results provide implementation-level feasibility evidence and preliminary observations of scoped procedural knowledge reuse, including provider- and operation-specific applicability, temporal validity, and version precedence. They do not establish general performance superiority, validated adaptive representation selection, transfer between genuinely independent agents, autonomous learning, production readiness, or economic break-even. The five research questions are retained, with preliminary support strongest for controlled knowledge reuse; preparation effectiveness and evolution receive partial evidence, while adaptive representation selection and reuse economics remain open.
title: Cognitive Preparation for Agentic Enterprise Systems: A Knowledge Compilation Architecture and Preliminary Evaluation

summary: Local bus mileage in England outside London has fallen by more than a quarter since 2005, and debate about rural buses relies mostly on counts of routes cut or money spent. This paper measures what remains, place by place. Using the complete set of regional timetables published through the Bus Open Data Service, I count departures on one weekday, one Saturday and one Sunday at 251,790 English bus stops and relate them to 15,012 villages from Wikidata and to all 33,755 small areas (LSOAs). 32.6% of villages have no stop with a weekday bus within 800 m, and 41.4% have no stop with four or more weekday departures. 61.5% have no bus from 19:00 and 67.8% none on Sunday; only 29.8% have a usable weekday service, an evening bus and a Sunday bus. 10.5% of England's population, 6.0 million people, live in small areas without a usable weekday bus, 72% of them in rural areas. In a pre-specified model with rurality and region held fixed, more deprived areas are less likely to lack a usable bus (odds ratio 0.68 per standard deviation, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.78) and areas with older populations more likely (odds ratio 1.28, 1.19 to 1.38). A planned falsification test fails, so these associations partly reflect rural differences the official classification does not capture. The results give a reproducible baseline for measuring rural bus provision. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/bus-deserts/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/bus-deserts . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/bus-deserts/ . Sources: Department for Transport, Bus Open Data Service regional GTFS timetables (Open Government Licence v3.0); Wikidata (CC0); English Indices of Deprivation 2025, MHCLG (OGL v3.0); ONS 2021 Rural Urban Classification and LSOA 2021 boundaries via the geographr R package (OGL v3.0); ONS region and country boundaries (OGL v3.0). Text, figures and data CC BY 4.0; code MIT.
title: Bus Deserts: Villages Without a Usable Bus, the Last Bus Home and Who Lives Beyond the Network in England

summary: We present a calibrated search for a coincident plasma enhancement associated with the binary neutron star merger GW170817 using Wind/WAVES quasi-thermal noise measurements.   Using electron density fit_n_e from the WIND_WAVES_QTNFIT dataset via NASA CDAWeb HAPI, we compare a ±60 s window around the GW170817 merger time to 1000 control windows on the same day.   We find a mean density of 10.01 cm^-3 at the event (N=21), versus 10.57 ± 0.83 cm^-3 in controls, yielding z = -0.67, p = 0.50, consistent with no excess.   This null result calibrates the method, establishes the background distribution for radio-plasma searches, and sets the baseline for a targeted search in Jovian decametric emission in Paper 2.   Data: NASA CDAWeb HAPI, WIND_WAVES_QTNFIT, 2017-08-17 10:00-15:00 UTC, 3425 valid points after cleaning fill value -1e31. Method: Event window ±60s around GPS 1187008882.43 (2017-08-17 12:41:04.43 UTC) vs 1000 random control windows on the same day. Reproduction: Run reproduce_paper1.py - it downloads the data from HAPI, cleans it, computes the statistics and regenerates Figure 1. Files: paper1.pdf, reproduce_paper1.py, figure1_wind_lightcurve.png
title: Limits on Plasma Density Enhancement Coincident with GW170817 from Wind/WAVES QTN Measurements

summary: The Hydraulic and Electric Reverse Osmosis Wave Energy Converter (HERO WEC) is a 3-kW point-absorber WEC designed to desalinate ocean water using breakwater wave energy. In its electrical configuration, a permanent magnet synchronous generator produces three-phase "wild AC" power that is rectified and regulated by a charge controller to charge a battery bank and power a reverse-osmosis pump. Wave energy presents a uniquely challenging environment for power electronics: energy delivery is pulsed, irregular, and characterized by high peak-to-average power ratios. The HERO WEC originally used an off-the-shelf buck converter charge controller designed for wind, solar, and hydropower. Field deployments to North Carolina revealed two critical limitations: (1) a 32 V cut-in voltage that rendered the controller inoperable during low-energy wave states, and (2) severe current overshoot in energetic waves that exceeded commanded current and threatened system survivability. Together, these constraints produced only a narrow operational window and average battery power of tens of watts, far below the controller’s 1.8 kW rating. This work describes the redesign of the charge controller to address these limitations and expand the operational range of the WEC.
title: Custom Charge Controller Design and Validation for Wave Energy Conversion

summary: This dataset contains experimental data supporting the reproducibility of side-channel-assisted secret-key reconstruction attacks against HQC. It provides the vectors used to construct soft spectra from side-channel-derived error-weight estimates for two attack scenarios: Chosen-Ciphertext Attack (CCA) and Known-Ciphertext Attack (KCA). The corresponding estimated error weights, as well as the C implementations of the soft-spectrum construction and secret-key reconstruction algorithms (Simulated Annealing and Depth-First Search), are available in the accompanying GitHub repository. The dataset does not contain raw side-channel traces. Instead, it provides the intermediate experimental data required to reproduce the soft-spectrum-based key-recovery experiments and evaluate reconstruction success rates as a function of the number of observations. The files should be placed in the appropriate data/cca/ and data/kca/ directories of the GitHub repository, as described in its README.
title: Experimental Side-Channel Data for HQC Secret-Key Reconstruction

summary: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.
title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery

summary: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.
title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels

summary: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) have emerged as generative models guaranteeing tractable probabilistic inference. However, tractability comes at the price of larger model sizes than in other generative models. As such, to scale PCs to high-dimensional data such as images, previous work has devised several parameter sharing techniques as well as fast evaluation protocols that consider learning PCs on independent image patches. In this work, we revisit this practice to highlight a surprising learnability issue: models that assume independence counterintuitively can yield better likelihoods than models that do not. To break this apparent bottleneck and to scale PCs further, we introduce a recursive parameter sharing construction (RePA) that fosters efficiency without assuming independence. We show empirically that RePA can greatly reduce time and memory consumption while yielding competitive likelihoods. Inspired by these results, we further generalize the approach to data modalities that do not inherently exhibit patch-structure (NoPA), such as tabular data, showing similar efficiency improvements, with marginal changes in likelihoods and sample quality on seven tabular datasets. Code available at https://github.com/april-tools/RePA.
title: Patching Up Circuit Learning via Parameter Sharing

summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.
title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs

summary: This repository provides the data, scripts, intermediate products, numerical outputs and documentation supporting the manuscript “Monitoring habitat conservation status and assessing biodiversity: The Dehesa case”. It implements a reproducible framework combining Earth observation, probability sampling and model-assisted estimation to monitor dehesa conservation status, carbon stocks and change, and biodiversity. The repository is organised into two Earth observation preprocessing modules and six numerical examples: EO Sentinel: processing of wet- and dry-season Sentinel-2 imagery and construction of the 10 m auxiliary pixel database. EO LiDAR: processing and validation of PNOA LiDAR data and construction of the reviewed LiDAR candidate-tree dataset. Numerical Example 1: tree condition and temporal change. Numerical Example 2: grassland condition and temporal change. Numerical Example 3: shrubland condition and temporal change. Numerical Example 4: integrated woody carbon-stock accounting, with annual herbaceous biomass-carbon flows reported separately. Numerical Example 5: herbaceous composition and biodiversity. Numerical Example 6: bird composition and biodiversity. After downloading and extracting the archive, readers should begin with the top-level README.md. Each module also contains a README describing its purpose, inputs, analytical workflow, scripts, expected outputs, validation checks and limitations. The module READMEs document the provenance of the Earth observation source data included in the archive and identify any additional inputs needed to run the workflows. The numerical examples illustrate the methods presented in the manuscript and its supplementary materials. Some example data are simulated or use proxies, as specified in the corresponding documentation. The repository is intended to facilitate peer review, reproducibility and adaptation of the monitoring framework to other dehesa areas.
title: Monitoring habitat conservation status and assessing biodiversity: The Dehesa case

summary: The discovery rate p a of Cuckoo Search sets how much of each solution the abandonment operator rebuilds, and many variants tune it with schedules or online controllers. Using one shared implementation, paired seeds and 70 problem instances (classical functions at D = 10, 30 and 50, shifted-rotated functions, and CEC-2017 F1 and F3–F20 at D = 30 and 50), we show that the best constant p a ranges from 0.02 to 0.80. Much of this dependence reflects separability: rotating the classical functions raises the best level on 6 of 8, as the crossover-rate theory of differential evolution predicts. Early progress is an unreliable guide: the best level after 10% of the budget differs from the best final level on 12 of 35 functions, and on the classical functions choosing it raises the final error a median 12.4-fold. Keeping a spread of rates across the nests avoids this choice. A random per-nest spread alone improves on the default on 13 of 19 CEC-2017 functions at D = 30; self-adaptive (SA- p a ) and success-history (SH- p a ) per-nest rates improve on it on 54 and 47 of 70 instances, with 3 and 5 losses (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests). On CEC-2017 their median error is 0.93 (D = 30) and 1.13 (D = 50) times that of the best constant chosen in hindsight, against 1.76 and 1.67 for the default. The gains vanish at D = 10, and Cuckoo Search remains well behind jDE.
tags: Cuckoo search; Parameter control; Self-adaptation; Discovery rate; Rotation invariance; Separability; Benchmarking
title: A spread of rates, not a schedule: population-level heterogeneity in the discovery rate of Cuckoo Search

summary: EXTRARNAS — Datasets, Software Outputs, and Analysis Scripts Companion material for the CIBB 2026 short paper and an extended manuscript under submission This repository contains research data, RNA annotation outputs, curated references, analysis scripts, and supplementary documentation associated with EXTRARNAS. It supports the original CIBB 2026 short paper, “EXTRARNAS: A Framework for Extracting RNA Structures with Multiple Tools,” and the extended manuscript “EXTRARNAS: Standardized RNA Structure Annotation and Cross-Tool Comparison” (currently under submission). What is new in this version The extended study analyzes eight RNA structures containing triple-helix motifs using seven tools: RNAView, MC-Annotate, RNApolis Annotator, FR3D, X3DNA-DSSR, Barnaba, and BPNet. The archive includes the full tool outputs, standardized BPSEQ/BPSEQE representations, curated structural references, and quantitative comparisons with the references and among the annotators. The extension experiments used EXTRARNAS v1.1.0. The accompanying manifest documents Docker image IDs, tool versions, Git revisions, checksums, and analysis dependencies. The licensed X3DNA-DSSR executable is not redistributed. Repository contents ·   experiment_triple_helices_extension/ — complete eight-structure dataset, seven-annotator outputs, BPSEQ/BPSEQE files, curated references, analysis scripts, quantitative results, figures, and reproducibility instructions. ·   experiment_triple_helices_extension/software_environment/ — version and execution-environment manifest. ·   experiment_triple_helices/ — original CIBB 2026 experiment using three annotators, retained unchanged. ·   additional-experiments/5s-pseudoknot-batch/ — historical batch-processing experiment on 20 5S RNA structures; not included in the extended study’s quantitative evaluation. ·   documentation_CIBB2026/ and README.md — archived original documentation and current repository-wide guide. Reference annotations and reproducibility For the extended study, the PAN2 reference sequence was corrected to match the 3D model and the published structure figure; the original reference remains in the historical material for provenance. Exact cWH Hoogsteen-pair recovery is evaluated against a non-exhaustive curated reference and therefore reported as recovery/recall only, not precision or F1. The included scripts reproduce the raw quantitative comparison results from archived annotation outputs without rerunning the seven tools. Full workflow reproduction additionally requires a compatible software environment and separately licensed components. The original CIBB 2026 experiments were generated with EXTRARNAS v1.0.1-cibb2026. Software repository: https://github.com/bdslab/EXTRARNAS Software DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21238912 Dataset DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21246054
title: EXTRARNAS: Data, Results and Analysis Scripts
