summary: Purpose This record documents a two-sample summary-data Mendelian randomization study designed to test whether genetic liability to cirrhosis, and to liver fibrosis, is causally related to cardiovascular disease. People with fibrotic liver disease carry a substantial excess of cardiovascular events, but whether that excess reflects a direct vascular effect of fibrosis or the metabolic disturbance that accompanies it is difficult to separate in observational data, where both are entangled with shared risk factors and with reverse causation. The study uses common genetic variants as instruments to break that entanglement, and asks two questions in sequence: whether the exposure is causally associated with five cardiovascular outcomes, and, if the association is absent or heterogeneous, which component of the exposure carries such association as exists. Contents The deposit holds the complete analytical record rather than selected outputs. It comprises 44 analysis scripts; 6 typesetting scripts retained for transparency but not runnable in isolation; 105 analysis-ready input files derived from public summary statistics, including a rebuilt LD score panel; 56 result files, one per analysis; the thirteen numbered tables of the companion article as CSV, with a companion legends file; Figures 1–3 as submitted; and a manifest giving dataset provenance for each of the eleven source datasets, a file-level inventory with SHA-256 checksums, a crosswalk between pipeline and article table numbering, and the recorded software environment. ANALYSIS_PLAN.md is the English rendering of the study protocol, together with a record of how each provision was implemented and a twelve-item register of departures from that protocol. Two of those departures, and two analyses added after first submission, are documented there rather than left implicit in the code. Methods Instruments were constructed from eleven public datasets — ten studies from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog and one FinnGen release — for cirrhosis liability as the primary exposure and liver fibrosis as the replication exposure, against coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ischaemic stroke and arterial stiffness, with four metabolic traits considered as candidate mediators. Estimates were obtained from six estimators: inverse-variance weighted with multiplicative random effects, MR-Egger with SIMEX correction, weighted median, weighted mode, MR-PRESSO and the contamination mixture. These are read alongside Cochran's Q and I²_GX, leave-one-out analysis, reverse-direction Mendelian randomization, overlap correction by MRlap, multivariable Mendelian randomization with conditional F statistics, two-step mediation, stratification by each variant's effect on LDL cholesterol, and colocalisation by coloc.abf . A positive control, LDL cholesterol against coronary disease, is included to show that the pipeline recovers a known effect. Use Three entry points are supported, at increasing cost. A published estimate can be checked from the deposited harmonised per-variant effects alone, without any download, by passing four columns to the estimator functions in mrlib.py . Every numbered table can be regenerated from the deposited results with a single script; the regenerated sources for the two tables carrying the primary estimates were verified byte-identical to those that produced the submitted tables. A full re-run from raw data is possible once the third-party summary statistics are placed under data/ in accordance with the registry in datasets.py , from which the driver run_all.py executes the stages in order. Every stochastic estimator is seeded and its resampling counts are fixed, so a re-run reproduces the deposited numbers exactly rather than within Monte Carlo error. Reuse and value The deposit is constructed to be reusable beyond the study that produced it. mrlib.py implements each estimator from its published description and is self-contained, so
title: Genetic Liability to Cirrhosis and Cardiovascular Disease: A Mendelian Randomization Study of Dyslipidemia, Not Fibrosis

summary: Overview Songdo Vision OBB is the oriented bounding box (OBB) counterpart of the Songdo Vision dataset. It provides the same 5,419 high-resolution 4K RGB frames (3840×2160) captured over the Songdo International Business District, South Korea , with every one of the 274,190 vehicle annotations expressed as a rotated rectangle instead of an axis-aligned box, across the same four classes : Car (including vans and light-duty vehicles) Bus Truck Motorcycle Horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) are a poor fit for high-altitude bird's-eye-view (BeV) imagery, where vehicles appear at arbitrary in-plane orientations. A diagonally traveling or parked vehicle fills a small fraction of its axis-aligned box, and the rest is road surface, lane markings, or a neighboring vehicle. Songdo Vision OBB replaces those boxes with tight oriented ones, so the dataset can serve as a benchmark for oriented aerial vehicle detection and as a source of vehicle heading for downstream traffic analysis. The images are byte-identical to those of Songdo Vision, and the annotations are derived one-to-one from Songdo Vision v2 , so the two records can be used together or interchangeably. Alongside the converted annotations, the release ships the 50 manually annotated OBB frames that were used to tune and validate the conversion. A full dataset card with usage instructions and download guidance is available on Hugging Face . 📌 Citation: if you use this dataset in your work, please cite the paper that introduces it, which is the preferred citation: Robert Fonod, Nikolas Geroliminis (2026). Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes. arXiv: XXXX.XXXXX. Please also cite the article behind the imagery and the source annotations [1] . BibTeX entries for both, and the dataset's own archival citation, are in Citation & Attribution. 🔗 Related datasets: the source HBB annotations are Songdo Vision v2: 10.5281/zenodo.21728430 . For precisely georeferenced vehicle trajectories extracted from the same large-scale multi-drone experiment, see Songdo Traffic (latest version): 10.5281/zenodo.13828383 . The benchmark paper that introduces this dataset annotates its own data at the conversion settings selected here: see its software, stabilo-benchmark ( 10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX , GitHub: rfonod/stabilo-benchmark ), and its data record ( 10.5281/zenodo.23623540 ). 🛠️ Conversion tool: the oriented boxes were produced with HBB2OBB v1.10.0 ( 10.5281/zenodo.22664151 , GitHub: rfonod/hbb2obb ), the exact version recorded in each subset's PROVENANCE.txt . See How the OBBs Were Produced. Motivation Axis-aligned boxes discard orientation, which in aerial imagery is both information the sensor genuinely captured and information downstream tasks need: Loose spatial support. A vehicle at 45° occupies roughly half of its axis-aligned box; the remainder is background that a detector must learn to ignore, and that an instance-level consumer cannot separate from the vehicle. Neighbor bleed. In dense parking rows and at intersection approaches, the axis-aligned box of one diagonally oriented vehicle routinely overlaps, and sometimes fully contains, its neighbors. Songdo Vision v2 documents 104 such pairs at IoU 0.3 to 0.5 that are correct yet unavoidable with HBBs. No heading. Vehicle orientation has to be inferred from tracking, which is fragile for stationary or slow-moving vehicles. Cost of re-annotation. Producing OBBs by hand at this scale, roughly 274k instances, is not practical. Songdo Vision OBB addresses this by converting the existing, human-verified HBBs into OBBs with a segmentation-based method, rather than by re-annotating from scratch. Every OBB inherits the class label and the provenance of the HBB it came from, so the annotation quality work done for Songdo Vision v2 carries over intact. Dataset Composition The dataset keeps the training (80%) and test (20%) split of Songdo Vision, frame for frame. Conversion is one-to-one, so
title: Songdo Vision OBB: Oriented Bounding-Box Vehicle Annotations from High-Altitude BeV Drone Imagery in a Smart City

summary: Human dermo-epidermal skin equivalents (DE) comprising  in vitro  expanded autologous keratinocytes and fibroblasts are a good option for massive burn treatment. However, the lengthy expansion time required to obtain sufficient surface to cover an extensive burn together with the challenging surgical procedure limits their clinical use. The integration of DE and biodegradable scaffolds has been proposed in an effort to enhance their mechanical properties. Here, it is shown that poly(hydroxybutyrate) electrospun scaffolds (PHB) present good biocompatibility both  in vitro  and  in vivo  and are superior to poly-ε-caprolactone electrospun scaffolds as a substrate for skin reconstruction. Implantation of PHB scaffolds in healthy rats polarized macrophages to an M2-type that promoted constructive  in vivo remodelling. Moreover, implantation of DE-PHB composites in a NOD/SCID mouse xenograft model resulted in engraftment accompanied by an increase in angiogenesis that favoured the survival of the human graft. Thus, PHB scaffolds are an attractive substrate for further exploration in skin reconstruction procedures, probably due in part to their greater angiogenic and M2 macrophage polarization properties
tags: poly(hydroxybutyrate); electrospinning; skin equivalents; human skin xenograft
title: Electrospun poly(hydroxybutyrate) scaffolds promote engraftment of human skin equivalents via macrophage M2 polarization and angiogenesis

summary: Run records, analysis of record and code of the component study reported in the appendix "Design, Provenance and Component Study of KAYROS" of the PhD thesis of Florian Rascoussier, "Improving Anytime Resolution of Large-Scale VRPTW and its Time-Dependent Extension" (ED SPIN, IMT Atlantique and INSA Lyon). Every table, figure and number of the component-study section of that appendix is computed from the files of this dataset. KAYROS is an exact and anytime solver for the time-dependent vehicle routing problem with time windows (TDVRPTW) under the Duration objective. Its exact mode is a branch-price-and-cut derived from the open-source solver of Lera-Romero, Miranda-Bront and Soulignac (Networks, 2020), and its heuristic mode is an iterated local search. The study asks 3 questions: whether the exact mode of KAYROS still performs as the solver it comes from once embedded, repaired and extended, what the open LP backend HiGHS costs compared with CPLEX, and what the heuristic and exact modes bring to each other. Design. The panel is the complete set of 56 Dabia et al. (2013) TDVRPTW instances with 100 customers, as distributed by MAMUT-routing. The 5 arms are the repaired baseline (the solver of Lera-Romero et al. at its public commit cabc56a plus 3 patches, with CPLEX 12.10), the exact mode of KAYROS 1.7.0 alone with CPLEX, the same with HiGHS 1.14.0, the heuristic mode of KAYROS alone, and the full solver (15 s of heuristic search, then the warm-started exact mode with CPLEX). Each arm runs 5 trials on each instance, 1,400 runs in total, each with 7,200 s from process launch, one pinned core and an address space limited to 16 GiB, with 10 concurrent runs per node on the grvingt cluster of the Grid'5000 testbed. The heuristic and full arms use 5 paired seeds. KAYROS runs used commit 25d8f0088337b9667956f07fe365c749def9894f of https://github.com/0nyr/kayros , released as version 1.7.0. The sources of the repaired baseline are also public, as the tag component-study-as-run of https://github.com/0nyr/lera-tdvrptw-bpc-repaired . Contents. cells/ holds one directory per run with the run summary (cell.json), the timestamped stream of incumbents, lower bounds and closures (events.jsonl), the native solver result (native.json, absent for the 185 runs ended by the memory limit or killed after the budget), the solver standard error (stderr.log) and the claim record (claim.json). plan.json is the plan of the 1,400 runs, runners/ the runner and job logs, scripts/ the frozen runner scripts. analysis/ holds the analysis of record (final-summary.json, which re-checks every route set with the reference checker mamut-routing-lib 0.11.0), the main and per-instance tables, and a comparison of the proofs with the stored optimality certificates. code/ holds the experiment harness, the analysis scripts, the frozen best-known-solution snapshot used as reference, the script that produces the tables and figures of the appendix, and the 3 patches of the baseline. The bundled README.md decodes the layout, the record fields, the acceptance rule of a proof and the integrity hashes. Main results. Accepted proofs: 165 of 280 runs for the repaired baseline, 172 for the exact mode of KAYROS with CPLEX, 135 with HiGHS (5 proofs rejected because a priced column fails the checker), 171 for the full solver, and none for the heuristic arm, which cannot prove optimality. Restricted mean time to proof: 3,295.0 s, 3,181.3 s, 4,256.3 s and 3,197.5 s. Mean anytime score: 0.37914, 0.35880, 0.49777, 0.00238 for the heuristic arm and 0.00644 for the full solver. 177 runs end at the memory limit, on 13 instances that no arm proves. Limits. The baseline is the repaired solver, not the published one. The pricing changes of KAYROS 1.7.0 were selected on this same panel. The panel is one family at one size, run on one machine type. The proofs are computational closures of single runs, checked for consistency, and not independent certificates. The records keep their original Grid
title: Component Study of KAYROS on the Dabia2013 TDVRPTW Instances with 100 Customers: Run Records and Analysis

summary: Code, data and model outputs of the study "Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference". The study fine-tunes small language models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Phi-4-mini-instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) to estimate twelve structural properties of a graph from its text serialization, and maps where this generalizes and where it fails: across graph sizes, graph families, vertex numberings, serializations and real-world domains. Files graph-structural-inference-slm.zip - the code of the study: generation of every evaluation set, fine-tuning, constrained-decoding evaluation, audits, statistical analyses and the scripts that produce every table and figure of the article, together with every model prediction (one record per graph and evaluation). Code under the MIT licence, predictions under CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-evaluation-sets.zip - 10,320 synthetic evaluation graphs (twelve size ranges beyond the training size and a second size series up to 300 vertices, seven further graph families, renumbered copies, seven serializations, and the test graphs rewired with every vertex degree kept) and two further samples of 1,200 training graphs, with exact labels, provenance and checksums. CC BY 4.0. graph-structural-inference-slm-adapters-main.zip - the 18 LoRA adapters behind the in-distribution results (three base models, adjacency list and edge list, seeds 42, 43 and 44), with their base models, seeds and checksums. Each adapter is subject to the licence of its base model (Llama 3.2 Community License, MIT, Qwen Research License). Built with Llama. Built with Qwen. The training and test graphs of the study are those of the TinyGraphEstimator dataset. The real-world datasets (ENZYMES, IMDB-BINARY, NCI1, ogbg-moltox21) are not redistributed: the code rebuilds the sets of the study from their original sources.
title: Generalization Boundaries of Small Language Models for Graph Structural Inference: code, predictions, evaluation sets and fine-tuned adapters

summary: Code, runner kits and measurements of ParityRT, a method for comparing hardware ray tracing cost across Apple GPUs (Metal) and PC GPUs (Vulkan). One renderer runs the same workloads on both APIs through inline ray queries in compute passes, times every ray-traced effect as its own pass, and withholds timings from any backend that fails the image-parity, ray-count and depth-correctness gates. The record holds the source code (C++20 engine, Slang shaders, scenes, workload files, analysis scripts), runner kits for macOS and Windows, and the 18 result bundles of the measurements: an Apple M5 (fanless), an Apple M5 Max and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti as measured devices, and an AMD Radeon 660M, an Intel Arc 140T, an Intel Arc (Core Ultra 7 155H) and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2050 as validation-only devices run by outside runners. DATA_README.md describes every file and how to re-analyse the bundles. Computer names and home-folder paths are redacted.
title: ParityRT: a cross-vendor hardware ray tracing benchmark for Metal and Vulkan GPUs: code, runner kits and result bundles

summary: Version 3.1 (12 November 2026) of "The Standard Model and gravity as effective LdGS". The Standard Model and gravity as a reference effective theory with a matching programme toward a single Landau–de Gennes–Skyrme (LdGS) tensor field. Version 3.0 established the reading used throughout (classical configurations as leading order, quantized ensembles as physical objects, experiment as the final judge), milestones stated by experiment across atomic, nuclear, particle, gravity and cosmology, and atomic-scale bounds on LdGS-specific effects. New in 3.1: • First steps toward a derived hadronic action: the winding field and the record frame form an SO(4) frame with the hidden-local-symmetry parametrization (a composite connection, not yet a dynamical ρ); unfitted soliton numbers with physical meson inputs reproduce the known soliton systematics; a parent-induced vector response computed, with the timelike control showing what remains to be calculated (pole, residue, decay vertex). • A corrected account of the native Card C: the record enters the matter tensor and couples to the winding field through an exact positive cross term of order 1/230, with a coefficient-free ablation defined. • External replication through frozen packets (manifests, SHA-256 checksums, plans before numbers): the string tension of the fractional-charge strand with its width and stress profile against archived lattice data is the first LdGS-specific test, taken by an external team; then the W multi-baryon pipeline and the photon-point comparison with and without the record. • Reviews by several AI systems folded in, including corrections of earlier statements, recorded in the version history. Sharpest external test remains the rank-two seesaw's Σmν = 58.69 meV (normal ordering, m1 = 0), at the edge of DESI's Bayesian ΛCDM limits and in tension with its Feldman–Cousins limit, as every oscillation-compatible spectrum is. Version 4.0 is reserved for the first native LdGS prediction confirmed against data it was not fitted to, in any domain. AI-assisted research: computations and reviews by several AI systems (Claude, ChatGPT/Sol and others), contributions listed in the paper; hypotheses and responsibility are the author's. Not externally peer reviewed. Source, scripts, frozen-packet definitions and review documents are in the accompanying archive.
tags: LdGS, Standard Model, effective field theory, topological solitons, Landau-de Gennes, khronometric gravity, Lorentz violation, Koide formula, neutrino mass, black hole shadow
title: The Standard Model and gravity as effective LdGS: toward a complete non-perturbative picture

summary: This repository provides data and Python code supporting the manuscript “Estimating Depth-Integrated Suspended-Sediment Flux During Floods Using Hyperspectral CCTV.” The study combines hyperspectral estimates of surface suspended-sediment concentration (SSC) and image-derived surface velocity with a Rouse–flux model to estimate depth-integrated sediment transport per unit channel width. The archive includes: SSC training data and models: 342 matchups for the unified model, comprising 127 baseline observations and 215 flood observations, and 211 matchups for the tracer model. Reflectance data, concentration targets, feature-selection information, model parameters, and code for model fitting and 5-fold cross-validation are provided. Vertical-profile and flux data: Processed SSC and velocity profiles from 27 field casts, together with code for vertical-profile reconstruction and flux correction. Camera-input comparisons: Nine comparison records, including seven with paired camera-derived SSC and velocity estimates. STIV example: One preprocessed space-time image from a flood observation, with code for surface-velocity estimation. Summary results for all nine STIV validation scans are also included. Supporting information: Hourly hydrological data, archived comparison results, a data dictionary, dependency specifications, and numerical reproduction checks. The archive starts from processed observation tables and a preprocessed space-time image. Raw hyperspectral cubes and complete spatial SSC, velocity, and flux maps are outside its scope. The tracer training table preserves the original processed concentration target and provides all-size LISST concentration separately. Target definitions, wavelength conventions, evaluation procedures, and calibration dependencies are documented in the accompanying files. Run python run_all.py to execute the included analyses and reproduction checks. See README.txt for installation and usage instructions and DATA_DICTIONARY.txt for variable definitions and units. Data, documentation, and results are provided under CC BY 4.0 , and Python code is provided under the MIT License . Please cite this dataset and the associated paper when using these materials.
title: Data and code for HISST-FLUX: estimating depth-averaged suspended-sediment flux using hyperspectral CCTV

summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) presents significant clinical heterogeneity in cognitive decline. Neuroimaging profiles and peripheral biomarkers, such as plasma oxidative stress biomarkers could provide information on AD progression. This study evaluates the contribution of baseline neuroimaging features and plasma lipid peroxidation biomarkers to modelling cognitive decline trajectories in early AD. Data were collected from patients with early AD (n = 195), and they were neuropsychologically evaluated to assess their progression. Baseline data included demographics, neuropsychological evaluations, neuroimaging measures and plasma lipid peroxidation levels. Follow-up neuropsychological evaluations were conducted biennially. Individual cognitive decline trajectories were estimated using MMSE and CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. Multivariate modelling and hierarchical clustering analyses were applied to identify prognostic signatures and patient subgroups. Baseline neuroimaging variables showed significant associations with longitudinal cognitive trajectories, as reflected in MMSE and CDR Sum of Boxes slopes, whereas plasma lipid peroxidation biomarkers did not. Multivariate models based on neuroimaging features demonstrated substantial predictive contribution (conditional R 2 0.825 for MMSE and 0.808 for CDR Sum of Boxes). Hierarchical clustering identified four distinct groups, primarily driven by left Koedam scores, enlarged perivascular spaces, and Fazekas scores. These clusters were significantly associated with differential rates of cognitive decline, particularly for MMSE. In conclusion, structural neuroimaging measures at baseline are robust indicators of cognitive decline in early AD, supporting its utility for individualized prognosis in early AD.
title: Baseline Neuroimaging profiles and predictive modelling for early Alzheimer disease diagnosis

summary: Industrial motors are widely used in manufacturing plants, pumps, conveyors, compressors and other industrial equipment. Unexpected motor failure can interrupt production, increase maintenance costs and create safety risks. Routine maintenance and reactive repair may not identify developing faults early enough. This project presents an embedded-system-based predictive maintenance system for industrial motors that monitors operating parameters and provides early warnings when abnormal conditions are detected. The proposed system uses an ESP32 microcontroller with a DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, an SW-420 vibration sensor and an ACS712 current sensor. Sensor readings are processed by the controller to identify conditions such as excessive temperature, abnormal vibration and unusual current consumption. An LCD with an I2C interface displays the operating status, while LEDs and a buzzer provide local fault alerts. The ESP32 can also transmit readings to an IoT dashboard for remote monitoring. An AI prediction layer can be added by collecting labelled operating data and training a classification or anomaly-detection model to estimate motor condition. In a small-scale implementation, threshold-based alerts provide the baseline, while the AI model can be evaluated separately using recorded data. The project demonstrates how embedded sensing, IoT communication and data-driven analysis can support condition monitoring and reduce unplanned downtime. The system is intended as an educational demonstrator and requires industrial-grade sensors, isolation and validation before deployment on production equipment.
title: Predictive maintenance for industrial motors using embedded system

summary: Abstract : Background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global public-health problem and an important cause of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality. Although nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy has substantially improved management, antiviral resistance-associated mutations may occasionally be detected before treatment exposure. Objective: To systematically determine the prevalence and distribution of established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations among treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection and to estimate the pooled prevalence of patients carrying at least one established primary resistance mutation. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using a patient-level endpoint defined as the presence of at least one established primary antiviral resistance-associated mutation in a unique treatment-naïve patient. Secondary or compensatory mutations were not counted as primary resistance when occurring alone. Studies using highly sensitive assays, including mutation-specific PCR and next-generation sequencing, were considered separately where appropriate. The review was structured according to PRISMA 2020. Results: The current primary quantitative dataset comprised 42 cohorts involving 9,811 evaluable treatment-naïve participants, of whom 417 carried at least one qualifying primary resistance-associated mutation, giving a crude prevalence of 4.25%. The current random-effects synthesis estimated an overall pooled prevalence of 1.80% (95% CI, 1.04–3.09%). Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I²=93.3%; τ²=2.541; Q=616.02). The approximate 95% prediction interval was 0.08–30.41%. Conclusion: Naturally occurring primary antiviral resistance-associated mutations are detectable in a minority of treatment-naïve patients with chronic HBV infection, but reported prevalence varies substantially according to population, geography, genotype, study design, and assay sensitivity. The pooled estimate should therefore not be interpreted as a universal prevalence applicable to every clinical setting.

title: Prevalence and Distribution of Naturally Occurring Antiviral Resistance-Associated Mutations in Treatment-Naïve Chronic Hepatitis B: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Protein sequences change over time due to the accumulation of mutations in the genes that encode them. Nonetheless, accurately identifying the most probable evolutionary pathways and more efficient trajectories between an ancestral and a derived sequence remains a challenge. This difficulty stems from a limited understanding of the critical factors that drive the evolutionary process. This study aims to address this issue by validating a newly proposed mechanistic model (grounded on the principle of least action) for analyzing protein evolution, using beta-lactamase as an empirically characterized evolutionary model. The initial findings indicate that, after accounting for how mutations and the context-dependent interactions between them (epistasis) affect protein stability and, hence, the kinetics of protein folding, a resort to the principle of least action allows us to simultaneously identify the most probable pathways and the most efficient trajectories swiftly and accurately. These findings also suggest that the most probable evolutionary protein pathways are the ones that exhibit the most efficient trajectories. All in all, our study addresses several unanswered questions regarding the main factors that govern how protein evolves at the molecular level (under constant selection pressure) and outlines directions for future research in key fields such as directed evolution and ancestral sequence reconstruction.
title: Analyzing \b{eta}-Lactamase Evolution from the Principle of Least Action Perspective

summary: Assuming that mutation and fixation processes are reversible Markov processes, we prove that the equilibrium ensemble of sequences obeys a Boltzmann distribution with $\exp(4N_e m(1 - 1/(2N)))$, where $m$ is Malthusian fitness and $N_e$ and $N$ are effective and actual population sizes. On the other hand, the probability distribution of sequences with maximum entropy that satisfies a given amino acid composition at each site and a given pairwise amino acid frequency at each site pair is a Boltzmann distribution with $\exp(-ψ_N)$, where $ψ_N$ is represented as the sum of one body and pairwise potentials. A protein folding theory indicates that homologous sequences obey a canonical ensemble characterized by $\exp(-ΔG_{ND}/k_B T_s)$ or by $\exp(- G_{N}/k_B T_s)$ if an amino acid composition is kept constant, where $ΔG_{ND} \equiv G_N - G_D$, $G_N$ and $G_D$ are the native and denatured free energies, and $T_s$ is selective temperature. Thus, $4N_e m (1 - 1/(2N))$, $-Δψ_{ND}$, and $-ΔG_{ND}/k_B T_s$ must be equivalent to each other. Based on the analysis of the changes ($Δψ_N$) of $ψ_N$ due to single nucleotide nonsynonymous substitutions, $T_s$, and then glass transition temperature $T_g$, and $ΔG_{ND}$ are estimated with reasonable values for 14 protein domains. In addition, approximating the probability density function (PDF) of $Δψ_N$ by a log-normal distribution, PDFs of $Δψ_N$ and $K_a/K_s$, which is the ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate per site, in all and in fixed mutants are estimated. It is confirmed that $T_s$ negatively correlates with the mean of $K_a/K_s$. Stabilizing mutations are significantly fixed by positive selection, and balance with destabilizing mutations fixed by random drift. Supporting the nearly neutral theory, neutral selection is not significant.
title: Selection originating from protein stability/foldability: Relationships between protein folding free energy, sequence ensemble, and fitness

summary: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Data governance (access rules, purpose limits, obligations, and claims about what data means) is enforced where data is stored and served, but derived data rarely inherits it. Query results, aggregates, and reports written by large language models (LLMs) leave the system that governed their inputs, and downstream consumers cannot tell which rules still bind them. TN represents a value together with its source policies. A calculation on governed inputs produces another governed value carrying their policies. Signed claims retain their original authors and subjects. Each receiving endpoint verifies the policies bound to the result and decides the proposed use under its own authorities and keys. An analyst joins two tables to prepare a financial report. The query filters on companies.active and returns the selected amounts. Although the active flag is absent from the result, those amounts carry the internal-use policy on companies. A dataframe aggregate computed from them inherits that policy. When an application supplies a governed value to an inference server, the server puts its policies and claims in the model's prompt before the model can request a protected field. Immediately before generation, the runtime checks that the scheduled input tokens and settings match the task it authorized. TN is a wire protocol for exchanging governed values between applications. Its adapters let developers use ordinary SQL queries, Polars expressions, Python operators, and calls to an inference server. As long as the application passes governed values through these interfaces, the adapters package each result with its policies and claims automatically. In our evaluation, Qwen3-4B generated an HTML report from data queried in SQL, aggregated in Polars, and formatted in Python. The report retained the source policies and original claims.
title: TN: Data Governance That Travels Through SQL, Dataframe, and LLM Pipelines

summary: Fibonacci -Spiral Nanophotonic Cavity and Symmetry-Modulated Ly Lattice Quantum Key Distribution C. J Tully and collaborators Ly-Design Engine / NOUS-ONE Lattice Continuity Project https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332   13 November 2026 We present a dual construction that maps the linear amino-acid sequence of Gen4_Variant_04 onto a Fibonacci -spiral coordinate matrix for a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) nanophotonic cavity and embeds the same algebraic grading into a high-dimensional quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol. The cavity uses a base lattice pitch and selectively etches air holes at the five basic residues (K, R, H), targeting a localized resonance near . The QKD protocol encodes blocks into one of five cyclic algebraic sectors , applies non-commutative forward and inverse matrices, and employs center-invariant checking states protected by the golden-ratio operator . Intercept-resend attacks by the designated party Eav produce detectable deviations from the degree-conservation law modulo 5. The resulting GDSII stream is provided for mask fabrication, and the protocol is ready for numerical evaluation of the quantum bit error rate under Eav’s attack.
title: Fibonacci -Spiral Nanophotonic Cavity and Symmetry-Modulated Ly Lattice Quantum Key Distribution

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FHR File Converter

The fingerprint is meaningful only if competing explanations such as abiotic acid treatment, biomass-associated peaks and analytical drift cannot reproduce its claimed transformation. F037: Enzymes can reveal, transform, and destroy Fermentation can liberate an existing phenolic from a plant cell wall, hydrolyze a glycoside into an aglycone or convert a released compound into smaller downstream products. These are different processes with different mass ledgers. A purified beta-glucosidase may alter a named glycosidic bond, but a crude culture may also change pH, solvent exposure and degradation simultaneously. One should preserve absolute parent moles, identified intermediate moles, product moles and the unrecovered fraction. Reaction rates require independent enzyme activity and defensible substrate concentration; saturation models should not be trusted when particle diffusion or enzyme inactivation dominates. The scientific success is not the largest product peak. It is the ability to identify which molecular bond changed, where its atoms went and which comparator could recreate that pattern without the proposed enzyme. A polymer chain may shorten through hydrolase cleavage, become compact through ionic screening, associate with a peptide, or be replaced by newly produced microbial exopolysaccharide. All can generate contradictory relationships between apparent molar mass, diffusivity and the feel of a gel. Size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, monomer composition, linkage analysis and calibrated wet-state rheology ask different questions. Even SEC-MALS requires attention to aggregates, optical parameters and sample recovery. A claim about botanical polymer remodeling should not be made when the measured high-mass fraction originates from microbial material. The pathway from polymer molecular structure to a future carrier must be preserved rather than simplified into a claim that all fermentation increases hydration. DLS size and polydispersity describe a scattering-weighted population, not the chemical identity of material inside the droplet. Free cargo, micelle-bound cargo, vessel-wall loss, carrier-associated cargo and degraded cargo need separate inventories. Residual enzymes can weaken a shell while fermentation acids alter emulsifier charge, so a formulation that looks stable on preparation day can change after storage. Release tests must distinguish actual molecular diffusion from dialysis membrane retention. A useful crossover experiment tests the same chemically named cargo both with and without the carrier, matching total mass and vehicle conditions. The model asks whether a reproducible material state was formed, not whether a new cosmetic product has already been proven. Biogenic amines, solvent residues, unintended microbial metabolites, active residual enzymes, contamination and extraction impurities need explicit risk-based decisions. Microfiltration removes some physical particles, but dissolved hazards can pass through untouched. Adsorption may reduce a hazard while destroying the named botanical cargo; purification must therefore have an identifiable mass balance and a noncompensatory safety gate. Dark extracts can interfere with reconstructed epidermis assays and should be subjected to validated blanks. OECD TG 439 concerns a defined irritation hazard and is not human tolerance or product efficacy proof. The Ben Cao Gang Mu tradition invites care in preparation, provenance and proportion; scientific inheritance requires that care to be expressed as testable identities, transparent failures and safe stopping conditions.

summary: A companion paper argued that biological memory is a record that is rewritten by its own consultation, and wrote this as a readout-write channel that preserves the index of a record and revises its content. That treatment assumed the codes addressing different records do not overlap, which is the one assumption the distributed, superposed memories of the holographic lineage never make. We relax it. In a mushroom-body layer where odour codes overlap, every write has the same form, addressed by the code of the record being read, and one line of algebra gives an identity: the change a revision of record a produces in the readout of record b is the code overlap times the change it produces in a. Because training is a write of that form too, the fraction of a revision that transfers to b and the fraction of training that generalises to b are the same number, and it cancels. The prediction has no free parameter and no measurement of overlap: transfer of revision equals generalisation of training. Four consequences follow. Leakage splits into a term set by mean overlap and a term set by the fluctuation in overlap that does not fall with sparseness, so there is a floor at a coding level of 1/√N, about two per cent in the fly. Trading read noise against leakage gives an optimal coding level that falls as the revision load rises. Leakage inherits the window of the companion paper, so a record can be protected by timing alone. And in the quantum layer, index invariance turns out to be a conservation law, one charge per record, belonging to an abelian symmetry of the channel; overlap breaks that symmetry, and the index charge moves only at second order in the overlap while content moves at first, so the objectivity result degrades more slowly than the content does. We then show that the two classic results that look like confinement, synapse-specific reconsolidation and the protection of indirectly reactivated memories, are both compatible with leakage, because neither tests two records that share synapses. The fly is where that case can be tested, and we give the experiment, its controls and its power.   Spanish version included in this record: "Lo que toca una revisión: reescritura en la lectura en una memoria superpuesta". The English version is the reference text.
title: What a Revision Touches: Rewrite-on-Read in a Superposed Memory

summary: This is a big release, jam-packed with lots of new features in our GUI, a more streamlined saving interface, and many new kinematic measures. [!important] This release contains minor breaking changes to the saving functions, to the nan_policy options of path metrics, and to the default behaviour of filter_by_confidence() . Please read the notes below before updating. To update movement to the latest version, see the update guide . What's Changed ⚡️ Highlight: Edit pose tracks in the GUI Pose estimation models often produce errors, such as mis-localised keypoints or false-positive detections in the background. movement.filtering offers several post-processing options, but not all errors can be dealt with automatically. You can now correct these stubborn errors by hand, directly in the movement GUI. This feature is the result of @anna-teruel's Google Summer of Code 2026 project . A huge thank you to Anna for designing and building it, and congratulations on joining the movement team! We're also grateful to @sfmig, who co-mentored the project and made the GUI's layer callbacks and frame slider more robust. Thanks also to @SahilKumar75 and @devanshc777 for contributing the reset controls and a re-export fix. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/10cba1ff-998b-4931-842a-0a84d5be940e Once you load tracked data into the GUI, you can: Move keypoints by dragging them to the correct position, or remove them altogether. See which frames you have edited on the edit timeline , optionally split by individual, and click on it to jump to an edited frame. Reset edits in the current frame or across all frames. Save the corrected dataset in movement 's native netCDF format, and load it again later to pick up where you left off. The tracks layer stays in sync with the edited keypoints, and edited keypoints are shown as rings. The saved dataset has an additional boolean edited data variable, which records which keypoints were edited by hand. You can use it in your analysis, for example to report how many keypoints were corrected. See the Edit tracked data section of the GUI guide for details. What's next? Editing currently works one frame at a time and supports moving and removing keypoints in poses datasets, with saving to netCDF only. Planned extensions include: editing across a range of frames, addition of missing keypoints, correction of identity swaps between individuals or keypoints, support for editing bounding boxes datasets, and saving to third-party formats. [!WARNING] The confidence of edited keypoints is set to NaN , since the model's score no longer applies. To make sure your corrections survive filtering, filter_by_confidence() now keeps points with NaN confidence by default. This also applies to data proofread in other tools (e.g. SLEAP). Previously, such points were dropped. To restore the old behaviour, set keep_points_with_nan_confidence=False . summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative learning on Internet of Things (IoTs) without sharing raw data, yet deployment remains challenging due to Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) local distributions, intermittent participation, and evolving environmental conditions. Resource-constrained devices such as zero-energy devices (ZEDs) further require communication-efficient training and lightweight models. This work examines whether tiny Machine Learning (tinyML) -oriented FL , hereafter Lightweight Federated Learning (LWFL) , is practical under these constraints. We evaluate three LWFL aggregators ( FedAvg , FedNova, and FAdamGC ) under heterogeneous non-IID settings with client participation rates of 10%, 90%, and 100%. To reduce communication overhead, we apply three Quantization/Compression (Q/C) schemes to client–server payloads. We also study two distribution-shift scenarios: intra-dataset distribution (intraDD) (redistribution of class subsets among clients) and interdataset distribution (inter-DD) (label space replaced by a disjoint dataset). Under extreme heterogeneity (three clients, one shared class), every aggregator roughly doubles the heldout accuracy of the Local baseline (Local) , with FedNova highest and the spread among aggregators below 0 . 013 . With 20 clients, even simple averaging is competitive. All FL methods converge to high accuracy. FAdamGC performs best at 10% participation due to drift correction but degrades sharply under inter-DD . FedNova attains the highest accuracy in the two most demanding conditions, extreme heterogeneity and interDD shift, and stays within 0 . 016 of the best method under sparse participation, lossy communication, and intra-DD shift. Q/C methods reduce payload size with negligible accuracy loss, among which quantization offers the best balance of simplicity, speed, and fidelity. Overall, the results show LWFL , particularly FedNova with compression, can deliver robust and adaptive learning in resource-constrained environments.
title: Lightweight Federated Learning for Environmental Resiliency in TinyML-IoT Ecosystems

summary: KenyaESG is a sentence-level dataset for three independent binary ESG classification tasks (Environmental, Social, Governance) built from the annual, integrated, and sustainability reports of firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), 2010–2024, combined with reference sentences from Schimanski et al. (2024). For each pillar, the dataset provides a fine-tuning set of 3,900 sentences and a disjoint held-out human evaluation set of 300 sentences. Each evaluation sentence carries the judgments of two independent annotators and an adjudicated reference label. Training and evaluation sentences share no sentence (exact match after normalisation), which prevents leakage. Version 2 (November 2026) changes: (1) the evaluation sets were extended from 100 to 300 sentences per pillar, the 200 new sentences being drawn at random from Kenyan reports outside the training pool and balanced across sectors; (2) all Kenya-sourced training labels were re-read against an explicit, meaning-based annotation guideline (45 E, 80 S and 124 G labels changed, all documented); (3) an adjudicated evaluation label was added, with agreement between the adjudicated label and annotators A/B of κ = 0.79/0.81 (E), 0.66/0.68 (S) and 0.70/0.72 (G); (4) the companion models were retrained, reaching F1 against the adjudicated label of 0.926 (E), 0.886 (S) and 0.918 (G); (5) precision, recall, confusion matrices, bootstrap confidence intervals and full training details are reported in the dataset card. Training labels for the Kenya-sourced sentences are keyword-derived and reviewed, not fully manually annotated, so the human-annotated evaluation sets are the appropriate benchmark for performance estimates. The dataset captures disclosure intensity rather than disclosure quality. The corpus is predominantly English but retains a small number of Swahili and OCR-degraded sentences, reflecting the original NSE reports. Company names and personal names have been masked in the text field ([COMPANY] and [PERSON]) in line with the anonymisation principles of the Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019) and Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR). Masking is semi-automatic and not guaranteed to be exhaustive. A small number of false-positive masks on common words (e.g. “equity”, “equality”, “Standard”) were subsequently restored, as documented in the correction log. The dataset must not be used to attempt re-identification of individuals or firms. Files: three training sets (KenyaESG_train_environmental_v2.xlsx, KenyaESG_train_social_v2.xlsx, KenyaESG_train_governance_v2.xlsx); three evaluation sets (KenyaESG_evaluation_environmental_final.xlsx, KenyaESG_evaluation_social_final.xlsx, KenyaESG_evaluation_governance_final.xlsx); the list of revised labels (KenyaESG_train_v2_changes.xlsx); the dataset card (KenyaESG_dataset_card.pdf); the correction log (KenyaESG_correction_log.txt). The dataset is also available on the Hugging Face Hub (DOI 10.57967/hf/11590). The companion fine-tuned classifiers (version 2) are KenyaESG-RoBERTa-env (DOI 10.57967/hf/11591), -soc (10.57967/hf/11592) and -gov (10.57967/hf/11593). Licensed under Apache-2.0. Companion working paper: Agossa, J. (2026). Pricing the Cost of Compliance: Equity Reactions to Mandatory ESG Disclosure in Kenya. SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6933338
title: KenyaESG: A Sentence-level ESG Disclosure Classification Dataset for Nairobi Securities Exchange Corporate Reports

summary: Eleven burnt areas from Copernicus Emergency Management Service (EMS) Rapid Mapping activations for forest fires in 2025 (Spain, Greece, Montenegro). Each area of interest (AOI) pairs a pre-event Sentinel-2 L1C image (bands B2, B3, B4, B8) with a post-event Sentinel-1 GRD image (VV, VH, dB) and the EMS burnt-area map as reference, on a common 10 m UTM grid, with a validity mask and the reason of every excluded pixel. The benchmark was built for heterogeneous (optical-to-SAR) change detection: 18.9 million evaluated pixels, 11.9 % burnt (3.7 % to 32.5 % per AOI), 3 to 14 days between the two images. See README.md for the file layout, the selection rules and the known limitations. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025. Contains modified Copernicus Service information 2025. Burnt-area references derived from Copernicus Emergency Management Service (© 2025 European Union) Rapid Mapping products; the per-AOI product citations are listed in ATTRIBUTION.txt.
title: EMS Wildfires 2025: a pre-event optical / post-event SAR burnt-area benchmark

summary: This versioned research dataset accompanies the manuscript "Does Downhole Seismic Information Add Value to Pressuremeter-Modulus Prediction? Borehole-Held-Out Evidence from Isfahan Metro Line 2". It contains a coordinate-free, pseudonymized cohort of 41 support-matched Ménard pressuremeter and downhole seismic analytical observations from 21 borehole groups on Isfahan Metro Line 2, a data dictionary, retained out-of-borehole model predictions, scripts that independently reconstruct B0–B3 nested grouped predictions, whole-borehole bootstrap calculations, and secondary robustness diagnostics. The dataset field Es_MPa denotes the Ménard pressuremeter modulus E_m in MPa, as explicitly confirmed by the responsible author; original computational field names are retained for traceability. B4-CA is supplied as a frozen-output sensitivity, not a fully reconstructed original fitting pipeline. Positive controls are synthetic and clearly distinguished from empirical observations. The package does not contain original third-party geotechnical reports, direct borehole coordinates, unmasked site identifiers, source workbooks, or external-site/Tabriz data. There is no calibrated tunnel-settlement finite-element prediction or demonstrated independent-site transportability in this archive. Data, derived results and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; original code files under the MIT License.
title: Isfahan Metro Line 2: pseudonymized pressuremeter–downhole seismic benchmark and reproducibility code

summary: Changes since v1.0.0 Optimizer (MATLAB HSSR_Optimizer.m and Python optimizer.py) Fixed the Akaike information criterion used to choose between the normal and gamma regression models (2k - 2 log-likelihood). Responses fitted with the gamma (log-link) model are now back-transformed before the desirability is computed, so that all responses are on the scale of the measurements. title: HSSR-SLOPE: PPG waveform reconstruction and beat detection for heart rate variability analysis

summary: This repository provides analysis code, aggregate results and supporting documentation for the manuscript “Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana.” The study uses Ghana Living Standards Survey Round 7 (GLSS 7), conducted in 2016/17, to examine associations between earnings, observable employment conditions and employment-change intentions across Ghana’s ten survey-era regions. Employment-change intentions distinguish wanting to change jobs, take an additional job or change current-job conditions. The materials include Stata scripts for survey-weighted earnings, job-quality, binary-logit and multinomial-logit models; regional interaction analyses; and Python scripts for data construction and machine-learning prediction. The repository also contains aggregate statistical tables, figures, variable documentation, sample-construction summaries, reproduction instructions and file checksums. Respondent-level survey data and individual prediction records are excluded. Researchers must obtain the underlying GLSS 7 data from the Ghana Statistical Service under its applicable access conditions. The supplied code and results are preserved without re-estimation. Reproduction requirements and outstanding limitations including unavailable original software-version information and two inventory files required for raw-data reconstruction are documented in the package. The findings describe conditional associations and predictive relationships, not causal effects.
title: Replication Materials for Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana

summary: BOTANICAL NANOEMULSIONS: OIL-PHASE CHEMISTRY, NANODROPLET DISTRIBUTIONS, SURFACTANT EXPOSURE, THERMAL STABILITY AND SKIN COMPATIBILITY Integrated Scientific Technical Notebook | Botanical Family 10 | F046-F050 | November 2026 Author: White Rainbow Epoch / 33 x STARLI Five botanical nanoemulsion mechanisms, one traceable evidence chain F046 authenticates botanical oil identity and distinguishes oil composition from apparent emulsification performance. F047 challenges scattering-derived mean sizes using population tails, independent droplet counts and volume-weighted oil ledgers. F048 distinguishes adsorbed interface coverage from free surfactant exposure and micellar assemblies. F049 examines hysteresis, Ostwald ripening, oxidation and real-time stability rather than extrapolating accelerated cycling without qualification. F050 specifies vehicle-controlled, interference-aware nonclinical skin compatibility studies with independent stop conditions. No study has been executed and no product-specific efficacy, full safety or regulatory authorization is claimed. The eighty-two chapters move through three differentiated modes: origin and mechanism, metrology and uncertainty, then a rival mechanism and inheritable refusal. The PDF presents six successive folios per chapter: research object, constitutive physics, qualified measurement, counterfactual, cross-flagship coupling, and independent successor proof. The notebook condenses this progression into 246 connected but distinct technical sections, and it is not a substitute for the quantitative primary atlas. The user-supplied 200-topic outline specifies F046 through F050 but contains no original equations or measured data. We therefore derive thirty NEW candidate mathematical models and twelve cross-stage sensitivity surfaces, all strictly hypothetical. Normalized chart axes are dimensionless synthetic coordinates; they are not measured particle diameters, chemical rates, surface doses or tissue viability. External reviews and standards provide general scientific or analytical context, not verification of this imagined formulation. Why the oil is a chemical population rather than one cosmetic ingredient A botanical oil is a mixture with a species identity, an extraction route, a volatile fraction, minor components, oxidation products and a changing solvent history. A nanoemulsion can appear stable while the molecule used to justify its name has migrated, evaporated or degraded. We should then ask whether the oil-phase polarity, viscosity and interfacial tension jointly create droplets or merely change the apparent particle reading. The question is an engineering proposal. It is not a claim that any one plant extract has produced a safer or more effective cosmetic. It exists through competition among free-energy cost, oil composition, interface coverage and imposed mixing work. The user-supplied 200-topic outline specifies F046 through F050 but contains no original equations or measured data. We therefore derive thirty NEW candidate mathematical models and twelve cross-stage sensitivity surfaces, all strictly hypothetical. External reviews and standards provide general scientific or analytical context, not verification of this imagined formulation. Why the oil is a chemical population rather than one cosmetic ingredient A botanical oil is a mixture with a species identity, an extraction route, a volatile fraction, minor components, oxidation products and a changing solvent history. A nanoemulsion can appear stable while the molecule used to justify its name has migrated, evaporated or degraded. Scientific accountability begins before the homogenizer is switched on: the botanical species and marker compounds need independent authentication. We should then ask whether the oil-phase polarity, viscosity and interfacial tension jointly create droplets or merely change the apparent particle reading. The question is an engineering proposal. It is not a claim that any one plant extract has produced a safer or more effective cosmetic. F046: From oil chemistry to an accountable oil-water interface A droplet cannot be defined by a photograph alone. It exists through competition among free-energy cost, oil composition, interface coverage and imposed mixing work. A low-energy phase inversion route and an energy-intensive emulsification process may produce similar early hydrodynamic diameters while leaving different residues, oxygen histories and molecular degradation. The experimental challenge is to keep an oil chemical ledger and a process energy ledger simultaneously. A strong oil-matched control can reveal that supposed botanical superiority originated in a residual cosolvent or in surfactant concentration. An independent laboratory must be able to identify the same marker molecules before accepting the morphology. F047: A mean radius is a poor description of a diverse droplet world An intensity-weighted DLS peak can be ruled by a small number of large scatterers. Number-weighted counts and volume-weighted oil fractions answer different questions. The same mean hydrodynamic diameter can belong to two populations with different rare large-droplet tails, different oil mass distribution and different stability trajectories. This is why the tenth family refuses a one-number specification. A richer experiment defines the droplet population at the moment of collection, after a controlled dilution, and after thermal aging. An unblinded analyst can always find the prettiest distribution. A credible research method should make a high-tail or poorly fitting distribution visible even when it defeats the preferred recipe. F048: The useful interface and the hazardous excess may coexist A surfactant occupies the oil-water interface, exchanges with water and may assemble into micelles at concentrations above its relevant critical aggregation threshold. Shrinking droplets increases total interface area. Yet simply adding more surfactant can increase the bioavailable free fraction without ensuring superior film coverage. A formulation might therefore look beautiful and remain unsuitable for a qualified reconstructed epidermis comparison. The laboratory must measure adsorbed, dissolved, micellar, degraded and container-associated amounts. Co-solvent and preservative must enter the competition as separate interventions. A safe-looking numerical stability frontier cannot overrule a failed nonclinical exposure gate. F049: Temperature is a history, not just a number on a shelf Heating and cooling can rearrange interfacial films, drive oil oxidation, change phase densities, reveal cloud transitions and make small droplets feed large ones by differential solubility. A single elevated-temperature hold cannot be treated as a certificate of ambient shelf life. Repeated heating-cooling loops can generate hysteresis even when they return to an identical endpoint temperature. The mechanistic rivals include droplet coalescence, reversible flocculation, Ostwald ripening, packaging sorption and loss of the original botanical marker. Each produces a different laboratory question. At least one independent real-time lot is needed to test whether accelerated aging forecasts actual storage behavior. F050: Nonclinical skin compatibility is an evidence contract A reconstructed human epidermis model is a defined surrogate, not a human wearer. Botanical pigments, reducing molecules and surfactants can distort common viability assays. The proper design uses a matched oil-and-surfactant vehicle, an independent exposure dose per tissue area, qualified tissue integrity, color interference controls and noncompensatory refusal conditions. A lower cytokine concentration can arise from fewer living cells. A higher local skin-associated chemical signal may arise from barrier injury or unwashed surface material. Even a fully qualified irritation hazard test cannot rule out sensitization, repeated-use intolerance or clinical treatment effects. All these boundaries should be visible on the first reading.

summary: Coal Mine Overburden Waste (CMOW) material in the coal mining industry possesses serious environmental risk through the leaching of hazardous and toxic heavy metals along with geotechnical constraints because of the low strength. Hence, the primary objective of the present study is to examine the efficacy of Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation (MICP) technique to immobilize the metal ions present in the CMOW and simultaneously to investigate the enhancement in the Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS). Leaching tests along with highly advanced Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) have been performed to examine the immobilization potential of MICP treated CMOW samples. ICP-MS analysis indicated that MICP treatment resulted in more than 90% immobilisation of several investigated metal ions, based on comparison of their initial concentrations in untreated CMOW obtained by direct digestion with their concentrations detected in the leachate following MICP treatment. However, the extent of immobilization was more pronounced in metals due to changes in the pH, controlling precipitation of calcite and thereby ionic exchange.   Further, UCS test of CMOW has achieved significant improvement in the average strength i.e., 437.76 kPa, 324.46 kPa and 141.83 kPa due to corresponding average precipitation of calcite is 7.46%, 6.06%, and 4.15% and thereby enhancement in particles bonding using bacterial strains (SP79, SP77 and SP78), respectively. Further, PFC(2D) based discrete element modelling was performed by calibrating particle-scale stiffness, friction, and parallel-bond strength parameters to reproduce the experimental stress–strain response of the MICP-treated CMOW samples, with UCS deviations of less than 4% for all three bacterial strains. The calibrated models further captured the development of bond failure and localized fracture patterns, which are consistent with the strain localization and shear-band evolution observed using Digital Image Correlation (DIC). This pronounces that the process is switched to localized brittle failure as cementation increased. In addition, FESEM examination has confirmed the presence of calcite between the particles, validating the results of XRD analysis. Finally, MICP technique is established to be used for heavy metal ions immobilization and improvement in strength of CMOW materials.
title: Metal Ions Immobilization and Strength Behaviour of Coal Mine Overburden Waste Materials Treated with Microbial Induced Calcite Precipitate Technique – Experimental and DEM Analyses

summary: Technical Report S-A-R-v2.2-ORIGIN traces the historical genealogy and software engineering architecture of Curriculum-as-Code (CaC) across three distinct generations (2018–2026) and establishes the canonical S-A-R Standard v2.2 (Scalable / Auditable / Repeatable) reference architecture deployed across higher education and clinical kinesiology / nutrition cohorts. Generation 1 (2018–2020) originated in network infrastructure emulation (NRE Labs / Antidote Kubernetes container laboratories), proving that interactive technical instruction could be version-controlled in Git and compiled reproducibly. Generation 2 (2021–2024) adapted plain-text Single Sources of Truth (Markdown / LaTeX), early GitHub AI Co-Pilot workflows, Python federal data APIs, and Continuous Integration (CI/CD) pipelines to public planning and open textbooks—demonstrating version control and accessible HTML generation while remaining limited to flat document trees without pedagogical graph semantics or civil-rights compliance gates. Generation 3 (2025–2026, S-A-R Standard v2.2 — originated by Alan Lee Pruitt at Webcognita LLC and Arizona Western College) advances Curriculum-as-Code from flat Docs-as-Code into neuro-symbolic clinical pedagogy and upstream Compliance-as-Code. The architecture unites: (1) a 3,265-node DOM GraphRAG knowledge graph preserving heading hierarchy, learning outcomes, and primary federal Sources of Truth (HHS PAGA 2018 2nd Ed., 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, ACSM 12th Ed., NASM OPT, and U.S. DOL ETA Advisory TEN No. 07-25 AI Literacy); (2) W3C PROV-O SHA-256 cryptographic provenance receipts and W3C SKOS bilingual (English / Norteño-Spanish) clinical ontologies; (3) automated pre-commit ADA Title II (28 CFR Part 35), WCAG 2.2 AA (9:1 Double-Contrast Guard), and WCAG 3.0 APCA accessibility linters verified at 0 open issues across 419+ production Canvas LMS pages; and (4) air-gapped Apple Silicon Edge AI inference preserving 100% FERPA and HIPAA data sovereignty under The Centaur Protocol and The Clinical Framing Protocol (Pattern / Rule / Solve).   Canonical Web Edition: https://alanpruitt.com/curriculum-as-code/ Institutional & Federal Partner Portal: https://www.webcognita.com/
title: From Infrastructure Automation to Clinical Pedagogy: The Origin and Evolution of Curriculum-as-Code (2018–2026)

summary: This record contains the Python analysis scripts, generated CSV data files, and environment specification used in the manuscript "Feasibility Bounds and Uncertainty Breakdown Near the Effectiveness Limit in Shell-and-Tube Exchangers" by Majid Esfandiari and Mustafa Omranshobi. Contents: - run_analysis.py: generates the agreement loci and area fractions (Fig. 2, Tables 1–3) - verify_levelA.py: verifies the effectiveness relation against the numerical ODE solution (Table 4) - uncertainty_compare.py: performs the Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis (Tables 6–9, Fig. 3) - ntu_crossflow_screening.py: compares cross-flow effectiveness relations for the Kang et al. measured case (Table 10) - fthx_model_margins.py: calculates the loose bounds from the reported effectiveness range - fig1.py: generates the schematic of the one-shell-pass/two-tube-pass exchanger (Fig. 1) - Generated CSV files corresponding to the tables and figures in the manuscript - requirements.txt: Python package versions - README.md: brief instructions for reproducing the results The Monte Carlo analysis uses 4 × 10^5 realizations per point with seed 7. This record is deposited to support reproducibility; the manuscript itself is not included in this record.

title: Analysis code and generated data for "Feasibility Bounds and Uncertainty Breakdown Near the Effectiveness Limit in Shell-and-Tube Exchangers"

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Total Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. summary: Background: Gut microbiota modulation is a candidate adjunct for childhood obesity therapy, but the metabolic effects of sequential antibiotic–synbiotic strategies remain unknown. Objectives: To evaluate whether rifaximin followed by a synbiotic improves glucose metabolism, inflammation, oxidative stress, and endotoxemia beyond lifestyle modification (LSM) in prepubertal children with obesity and insulin resistance. Methods: In this open-label, randomized proof-of-mechanism pilot trial, 32 prepubertal children with obesity and acanthosis nigricans received 21 days of LSM alone, LSM plus synbiotic, or LSM plus rifaximin followed by synbiotic; 30 completed the trial. Glycemic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, and endotoxemia markers were assessed before and after treatment. Results: HOMA-IR, the primary outcome, fell by 30–44% in all arms without between-arm differences (sequential regimen vs LSM: ratio 0.86; 95% CI 0.54 to 1.36), and adiposity and lipids also improved similarly. Among secondary outcomes, the sequential regimen reduced 2-hour glucose more than LSM (−0.79 mmol/L; 95% CI −1.28 to −0.29) and synbiotic (−0.74 mmol/L; 95% CI −1.26 to −0.22), with similar results for glucose area under the curve, and reduced C-reactive protein, TNF-α, formazan, and carbonyl groups more than both. Lipopolysaccharide fell similarly in all arms. In exploratory analyses, biomarker changes were not associated with the glycemic response independently of treatment, and the glycemic effect was attenuated in children with greater baseline severity. Conclusions: Adding rifaximin followed by a synbiotic to LSM did not reduce HOMA-IR beyond LSM alone, but it improved postprandial glucose handling and lowered markers of inflammation and protein oxidation. This sequential approach to microbiota modulation should be tested as an early metabolic intervention for childhood obesity in longer, adequately powered trials that characterize the microbiota.
title: Sequential rifaximin-synbiotic therapy, inflammation, oxidative stress and glucose tolerance in prepubertal children with obesity and insulin resistance: a randomized proof-of-mechanism pilot trial

summary: This dataset contains hydrological model inputs, simulation outputs, spatial data, analysis code and reproducibility materials for the Mandena coastal mineral-sand mining basin near Taolagnaro, southeastern Madagascar. The SWAT+ simulation period covers 1987–2022, including a warm-up period of 1987–1992. The principal analysis covers 1993–2022, with an additional analysis window ending in 2020. Auxiliary source datasets may extend beyond these periods. The archive includes basin, mining-area, reference-area and hydrological response unit geometries; elevation, land-cover and soil-class rasters; meteorological inputs and rainfall-processing materials; model configuration files; annual and monthly hydrological outputs; scenario definitions; numerical results; scientific figures; and documentation describing data structures, model formulations and analytical methods. Source materials for the independent evapotranspiration comparison include MODIS MOD16A2GF Collection 061 data and associated quality and spatial-support information. The experiment registry defines 35 simulation configurations. These include standard and coupled surface–soil water formulations, static composite parameter-perturbation scenarios, individual parameter-family experiments, rainfall-forcing alternatives, identity experiments and dated synthetic interventions. The parameter families are curve number, overland roughness, leaf area, biomass, residue cover and soil available water capacity. Perturbations target a documented selection of 158 hydrological response units. The dated synthetic intermediate intervention begins on 1 January 2008. Temporal analyses examine simulated mining–reference contrasts using BACI-style and interrupted time-series formulations. The baseline uses static land-cover and soil configurations; its temporal contrasts describe outputs from that configuration. Dated interventions are imposed numerical experiments rather than reconstructions of historical mining disturbance. The analytical materials include annual step, trend, segmented and ramp regressions; alternative breakpoint and pre-intervention placebo analyses; heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent inference; confidence intervals and Holm multiplicity adjustments; monthly and quarterly analyses; conditional detectability and minimum-detectable-effect calculations; block-bootstrap experiments; residual and influence diagnostics; and sensitivity to reference selection, spatial support, analysis period, forcing and parameter configuration. Spatial analyses document polygon coverage, HRU intersections, shared supports, the representativeness of selected HRUs, and differences in configured soil, vegetation and terrain characteristics. Water-balance diagnostics include annual export-based assessments and high-precision daily coupled-budget checks for the documented diagnostic period. Evapotranspiration comparisons report results under alternative quality and spatial-support filters. The archive provides model source code, Windows AMD64 executables, Python analysis scripts, offline dependency wheels for Python 3.12, experiment-specific inputs and outputs, file inventories, checksum manifests and execution instructions. The main entry point supports file-integrity verification, simulation execution and analysis regeneration. Reproducibility testing completed all 35 registered simulation configurations and confirmed numerical agreement for three designated summary tables using an absolute tolerance of 10⁻⁶ and a relative tolerance of 10⁻⁹. Author-created data and documentation are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. The MIT licence applies to the robust-statistics component identified in the archive. Third-party data, model components and software dependencies retain their respective licences, attribution requirements and copyright notices.
title: Mandena hydrological simulations, data and analysis

summary: Code, trained models and run data behind every number, table and figure of the article "Matching forecast horizons to actuator dynamics in data-driven supervisory control of wastewater treatment" (D. Voipan and M. Barbu, submitted to the Journal of Process Control). The plant is the open-source bsm2-python implementation (v0.0.16) of Benchmark Simulation Model No. 2 with its official 609-day influent; no other data are needed. Contents - analysis/: recomputes the paper from the included run data. verify.py recomputes every reported value and fails on any drift; make_supp_tables.py and figures/make_figures.py regenerate the supplementary tables and the figures. Requires only NumPy and Matplotlib. - code/: the closed-loop driver, surrogate and policy training, screening experiments and scenario generation, with the launch scripts that record the exact flags of every reported run. - checkpoints/: the trained surrogates and policies the paper reports, including the sixteen arms of the ablation grid. - runs/: the raw full-year runs reduced by the analysis, and the logs of the runs the paper uses. Reproducibility The headline closed-loop results were re-run from this archive alone, in a clean directory, with the commands given in README.md: the recommended release schedule gives 0.2638888889 equivalent days of ammonia violation and the learned schedule with the measured balance target (seed 123) 0.5951388889, both identical to the values in the paper. Environment: Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.3.1 (CUDA 11.8), mamba-ssm 2.2.2, bsm2-python 0.0.16, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.15.3, pandas 2.3.3.
title: Code, trained models and run data for "Matching forecast horizons to actuator dynamics in data-driven supervisory control of wastewater treatment"

summary: Code used for the manuscript "EDMORE: Workflow-Constrained LLM Agents for Automated 4D-STEM Ptychography in the SEM" (M. Zhao, A. Gladyshev, J. Müller, S. Shabih, C. T. Koch).
