QUANTUM OPTIMIZATION FOR REHABILITATION CONTROL AT THE LIMIT FAMILY 11 | F051-F055 | SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK A connected argument through 82 chapters: Mechanism / Measurement / Refutation Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI | White Rainbow Era | 2026 SCIENTIFIC STATUS: Prospective, nonclinical, falsifiable research architecture. No patient trial, tested quantum supremacy, demonstrated stroke recovery, or qualified medical device is claimed. THE OTHER SIDE OF THE CONTROL MONOGRAPH The technical notebook is not a glossary pasted below the research monograph. It is a second argumentative surface. The monograph states exactly what can be tested, with candidate equations, independent measurements and research gates. The notebook asks why the experiment deserves construction, which competing explanation should be taken most seriously and how an unsuccessful first generation could become a stronger foundation for someone else. This difference is a methodological commitment rather than a claim of novel experimental results. Family eleven begins from an uncomfortable contrast between optimization and authority. A method may compute a more attractive control input, but no numerical attractiveness can authorize an illegal actuator command. The physical and ethical permission envelope must be defined outside the optimizer, and a safe fallback must remain available when the proposed method is late, uncertain, energy-depleted or dependent on inaccessible backend infrastructure. The most important output of a difficult trial may be an unambiguous refusal. The five flagship mechanisms form a causal chain without becoming duplicates. F051 asks what it means to optimize permitted control gains fairly. F052 places the optimizer inside the receding-horizon control clock. F053 asks whether progressively less assistance can maintain a fixed mechanical task, while refusing to equate phantom success with human recovery. F054 requires energy and latency to be counted across acquisition, computation, communication and actuation. F055 tests whether every scientific conclusion remains subordinate to command legality, independent vetoes and serious classical rivals. This lineage comes from two distinct source studies and the author-supplied STARLI forty-family research DNA blueprint. The four-dimensional microrobotics source supplies material history, force generation, responsive structures and safety concerns. The BCI-stroke atlas supplies intention observability, minimally necessary assistance, withdrawal and the crucial distinction between assisted motion and restored independent function. These source relationships are not evidence that a fused 4D, quantum, BCI and clinical treatment platform exists. Five-stage parallel spacetime reasoning is a public name for a disciplined research workflow. Physical origin asks what the bench is permitted to do. Mathematical evolution asks which candidate model and parameters represent it. Counterfactual branching makes the ordinary baseline and hidden confounder genuine competitors. Extreme extrapolation applies bounded adversarial inputs, where the correct output may be stop. Evidence convergence leaves both a reconstructable result and an open Research Gate. These stages are viewpoints on one research contract, not literal physical parallel worlds. A 4D actuator can return to its familiar geometry and still lose force. A quantum optimizer can return a lower cost and still arrive after the legal deadline. A minimally assisted movement can succeed while a person would remain dependent on the device. A smooth average can hide a rare illegal command. Those four asymmetries explain why this research must separate shape, computation, mechanical assistance, function and safety, and why none of these outcomes can be imported into the others without a new experiment. The wisdom of stopping is the opposite of indifference. It means ending a research round when the testable contract is complete, the strongest rival has been confronted, the permission gates have been audited and the next laboratory can reconstruct the adverse case. When further parameter search no longer distinguishes the mechanism from the rival, additional polished prose or training calls do not create new evidence. The unresolved difference becomes an explicit research door for future investigators. FIVE INDEPENDENT FLAGSHIP RESEARCH CONTRACTS F051 | Quantum-Assisted Post-Stroke Rehabilitation Control Optimization at the Limit The core candidate mechanism is control gain search under hard actuator and state constraints. Its measurable endpoint is angle tracking error and total tuning-to-command cost. The leading alternative says benefit is produced by extra search, hidden preprocessing or the classical controller. The preregistered blind competition would blind-swap candidate gain vectors on identical nonhuman control traces. A fully observed test requires encoder angle [rad], actuator command, output torque [N m], motor work [J], gain-search calls and full wall time [ms] and resource-equivalent comparison with tuned robust PID/LQR, constrained SQP, CMA-ES and mixed-integer gain search with identical runs and CPU/GPU ledger. Each result must be classified as tested observation, source-derived background, synthetic mathematical illustration or unverified hypothesis. No single flagship may import a clinical efficacy conclusion from its neighboring research question. F052 | Quantum-Assisted Model Predictive Control for Rehabilitation Robots at the Limit The core candidate mechanism is finite-horizon constrained optimization with receding-horizon deadlines. Its measurable endpoint is closed-loop error, solver completion percentile and deadline violation. The leading alternative says a solver-only benchmark ignores compilation, upload, readout and communication. The preregistered blind competition would conceal horizon changes and impose actuator-relevant controller deadlines. A fully observed test requires state estimator [rad,rad/s], solver input/output timestamp [ms], horizon [steps], safety margin and fallback event and resource-equivalent comparison with well-tuned conventional MPC, SQP, mixed-integer solvers, warm starts and robust tube MPC on identical task clocks. Each result must be classified as tested observation, source-derived background, synthetic mathematical illustration or unverified hypothesis. No single flagship may import a clinical efficacy conclusion from its neighboring research question. F053 | Quantum Optimization for Minimum Necessary Assistance at the Limit The core candidate mechanism is assistance-minimizing policy with a fixed task-feasibility envelope. Its measurable endpoint is minimum delivered force and unassisted phantom-task feasibility. The leading alternative says a more forceful actuator makes the task look easier without reducing dependence. The preregistered blind competition would blindly taper physical assistance and test device-off task feasibility. A fully observed test requires independent load cell [N], motion target error [rad], assisted/unassisted phantom condition and residual passive force and resource-equivalent comparison with a fixed-gain assistive policy, optimal classical assistance scheduler and a fully disengaged zero-assistance phantom control. Each result must be classified as tested observation, source-derived background, synthetic mathematical illustration or unverified hypothesis. No single flagship may import a clinical efficacy conclusion from its neighboring research question. F054 | Energy-Latency Tradeoffs in Quantum Rehabilitation Control at the Limit The core candidate mechanism is energy-constrained compute-actuation scheduling and deadline-aware fallback. Its measurable endpoint is joules per safe episode, wall latency and feasible trajectory fraction. The leading alternative says external service electricity or device idle consumption disappears from cost. The preregistered blind competition would inject finite battery, network stalls and safe-stop events in randomized order. A fully observed test requires electrical energy [J], power [W], battery state [J], acquisition and network timestamp [ms], safe-stop trace and resource-equivalent comparison with energy-aware classical MPC, local deterministic fallback and measured on-device scheduling with the same task energy budget. Each result must be classified as tested observation, source-derived background, synthetic mathematical illustration or unverified hypothesis. No single flagship may import a clinical efficacy conclusion from its neighboring research question. F055 | Safety-Constrained Quantum Rehabilitation Control Against Classical Baselines at the Limit The core candidate mechanism is noncompensatory command legality with paired quantum-classical evaluation. Its measurable endpoint is illegal commands, veto timing, safety margin and matched-cost task error. The leading alternative says rare forbidden states are omitted while average performance improves. The preregistered blind competition would inject hidden infeasible states and verify fail-silent refusal before actuation. A fully observed test requires command legality indicator, independent hardware veto timestamp [ms], state margin, source version and paired baseline results and resource-equivalent comparison with independently certified physical interlock, robust classical MPC, rule-based veto and cost-matched quantum candidates. Each result must be classified as tested observation, source-derived background, synthetic mathematical illustration or unverified hypothesis. summary: Many high-stakes AI failures trace to the training data rather than the model, yet teams still treat pre-training data validation as a checklist and rarely wire its signals to a go/no-go decision or to a governance framework. We study the detectability boundary of that validation: what a pre-training data-readiness gate catches, what it misses, and why a flagged source is often not blocked. We reuse a validation gate from a prior single-domain system and generalize it across three high-stakes domains (healthcare, finance, and government) on the real MIMIC-IV, SEC EDGAR, and CMS Open Payments datasets, injecting controlled defects across simulated sources. A composite readiness score detects 0.76 of degraded sources (95% CI [0.74, 0.76]) but withholds only 0.42; the 0.34 gap (95% CI [0.32, 0.35]) traces to a single averaging step, and we show it is fixable but privacy-sensitive. The grid is small by design (six sources per domain, two degraded, five seeds), so the intervals describe this controlled setting, not field variability. We map the privacy-utility curve of validating on differentially private summaries, prove a blind spot for symmetric label noise on balanced targets, and add a confident-learning label detector that runs on DP-noised summaries and keeps its recall down to epsilon = 0.1. We compare against Great Expectations and Deequ, measure how poorly thresholds port across domains, and map the gate to the NIST AI RMF MEASURE function. We report the negatives, among them a near-chance inter-rater reliability on fine-grained incident coding. What is new is the integration of production incidents, a private benchmarked gate, and a governance mapping, not any one of those parts.
title: Detection Is Not Action: The Detectability Boundary of Pre-training Data-Readiness Gating

summary: This record contains supplementary research materials supporting the manuscript entitled "Evaluating Out-of-Fold Weighted Soft Voting for Network Intrusion Detection: Benefits and Limitations of Classifier Fusion" (Manuscript ID: MJCSC-D-26-00018R3), submitted to the Mesopotamian Journal of Computer Science. The study evaluates training-derived optimized weighted soft voting for multiclass network intrusion detection using Decision Tree (DT-Gini), Random Forest variants (RF-Gini and RF-Entropy), and XGBoost. The primary evaluation uses a prepared CICIDS2017 development subset comprising 78,437 observations and 15 traffic classes. An additional dataset-specific evaluation uses a prepared CICIoT2023 subset comprising 99,327 observations, 34 traffic classes, and 39 numerical predictors. The experimental framework includes data preprocessing, mutual information-based feature selection, training-only minority-class oversampling, stratified outer cross-validation, and inner out-of-fold optimization of classifier fusion weights. The supplementary materials are intended to support verification of the reported experimental configurations and results. The original complete source-scanning log and sampling-run metadata for CICIoT2023 are unavailable; therefore, exact independent reconstruction of the original sampling run has not been established. These materials accompany the third-round revised manuscript submitted to the journal.

summary: This paper studies all-to-all broadcast scheduling for underwater swarms with collision-resilient physical layers that can decode asynchronously overlapping packets. Propagation-aware collision-free schedulers coordinate packet arrivals but do not account for this reception capability. We first design a data-driven neural reception model that captures per-interferer power and timing effects. The model improves prediction accuracy over SINR baselines while admitting an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. The resulting neural-network-embedded MILP (NN-MILP) optimizes transmission times while explicitly encoding schedule-dependent overlaps and the predictor's inference, enabling globally optimal scheduling for small-scale instances. For larger networks, a two-stage ant colony optimization (ACO) heuristic combines low-cost transmission-order search with neural-aware timing refinement. Simulation results show that ACO shortens broadcast rounds compared with existing schedulers. It approaches the NN-MILP optimum on small-scale instances while supporting larger networks at substantially lower computational cost.
title: Collision-Resilient All-to-All Broadcast Scheduling in Underwater Acoustic Networks

summary: Accurate future channel state information (CSI) is essential for underwater acoustic (UWA) communication because delays associated with signal propagation, feedback, scheduling, and transceiver reconfiguration can render currently available CSI outdated. However, most existing predictors estimate only the next channel state and obtain multi-step forecasts through recursive rollout, which causes prediction errors to accumulate as the multipath structure evolves. The scarcity of sea-trial measurements further limits reliable model training. To address these challenges, we propose LLM4UACP, a dual-domain, structure-preserving framework that adapts a pretrained Transformer for few-shot multi-step UWA channel prediction. LLM4UACP extracts complementary features from the channel impulse response (CIR) and channel frequency response (CFR), aligns them through Fourier-consistent fusion, and encodes the fused representation as delay-time tokens. A pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone is adapted through Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict multiple future CIRs in a single forward pass, thereby avoiding the error accumulation associated with recursive prediction. Experiments on the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels show that LLM4UACP achieves normalized mean squared error (NMSE) values of 0.0411 and 0.0399, corresponding to reductions of 88.53% and 85.15%, respectively, relative to the most recent baseline. With only 0.11M trainable parameters, LLM4UACP maintains robust performance across varying prediction horizons and observation-window lengths, limited-data settings, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios.
title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer

summary: Grid mismatch in wideband channel estimation leaves structured cancellation residuals after strong-path subtraction. These residuals generate spurious correlation peaks or mask weak arrivals, turning continuous parameter errors into path-count errors. We propose RC-SAGE-Brent, a residual-closed-loop estimator that jointly refines continuous delay-scale parameters and corrects the unknown-order path set. Within each feedback cycle, ambiguity-constrained alternating Brent searches suppress strong-path cancellation residuals. Candidate validation, resolution-constrained pruning, and full-domain residual redetection then revise the active path set. For linear frequency modulation (LFM) probes, an observable signal-to-residual ratio adaptively scales the model-order penalty to mitigate overestimation caused by delay-scale coupling. Theoretical analysis links off-grid parameter errors to local cancellation-residual curvature and weak-path detectability. Factorial ablations, paired comparisons against standard sparse and off-grid estimators, and measured channel replay demonstrate improved path-set recovery and waveform reconstruction while delineating the operational boundaries of the method.
title: Residual-Closed-Loop SAGE-Brent Estimation for Unknown-Order Wideband Underwater Acoustic Channels

summary: The proliferation of maritime activities has spurred the emergence of numerous computation-intensive and delay-sensitive marine applications and services. Given the inherent rationality, selfish nature, and limited computational abilities of marine devices, devising effective strategies to incentivize their participation in task processing become a critical challenge. In this paper, we investigate the satellite-assisted marine multi-access edge computing (MEC) and propose a two-tier task offloading scheme through a hybrid Stackelberg-Bargaining game approach to enhance offloading efficiency and maximize the utility of marine devices. Specifically, for the underwater acoustic communication, we consider the scenario where multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), managed by maritime autonomous surface ships (MASSs), upload their collected data using non-orthogonal multiple access(NOMA) to optimize channel utilization. For the data transmission above the sea surface, we consider the scenario where a low earth orbit satellite (LEOS) functions as a space edge server to provide computing services, and MASS offloads workloads to LEOS through frequency division multiple access(FDMA) to prevent co-channel interference. we define the utility of AUVs, MASSs and LEOSs, and model the offloading process between AUVs and MASSs as a Stackelberg game, while representing the offloading interaction between MASSs and LEOSs as a Bargaining game. Additionally, we propose efficient algorithms to optimize AUV offloading strategies and MASS pricing strategies, while refining the bidding strategies for both MASSs and LEOSs. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms significantly outperform benchmark schemes in achieving optimal solutions.
title: Two-Tier Task Offloading for Satellite-Assisted Marine Networks: A Hybrid Stackelberg-Bargaining Game Approach

summary: Underwater acoustic communication faces challenges such as limited available bandwidth and complex channel environments, which impose demanding requirements on efficient image transmission and reliable reconstruction. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a generative image communication framework based on cross-modal semantic successive refinement. At the transmitter, text descriptions, compact bottleneck features, and visual side information compressed by residual vector quantization are transmitted. At the receiver, text and bottleneck features are first fused to predict a base estimate of the intermediate visual representation. The received RVQ indices are then used to recover supplementary visual information and perform residual correction, followed by image reconstruction using a one-step Pixel Mean Flow model. During training, a CLIP-based text-image semantic consistency constraint is introduced to preserve the semantic correspondence between generated results and the original text descriptions. During transmission, protection resources are allocated according to the importance of different information branches and RVQ quantization stages. Simulations using COCO 2017 images and measured underwater acoustic channel records from Watermark show that text and bottleneck features provide complementary semantic and structural conditions, RVQ visual side information further improves reconstruction quality, and layered unequal error protection helps improve recovery at low SNRs. Code-rate allocation experiments reveal a tradeoff between the reliability of fundamental conditions and visual-detail reconstruction under a limited visual-feature coding budget, providing guidance for allocating protection resources in underwater acoustic image transmission.
title: Cross-Modal Semantic Successive Refinement for Generative Image Communication over Underwater Acoustic Channels

summary: Acoustic holography in the megahertz range can impact applications from manufacturing and non-destructive testing to transcranial ultrasound. Designing lens topologies for complex holograms in the sub-megahertz to low-megahertz regime most relevant to transcranial therapy is difficult because wave propagation through an acoustically thick lens cannot be ignored. Here we show that the heterogeneous angular spectrum approach (HASA), which admits in-plane varying speed-of-sound maps and supports rapid differentiable optimization with the Adam optimizer, can generate three-dimensional lens topologies directly. With it we quantify the failure of the thin-element approximation (TEA) at these frequencies, where lenses enter an acoustically thick regime (thickness L much greater than the wavelength) governed by refractive walk-off, and we introduce a dimensionless refractive walk-off number Nw that defines a frequency-dependent operating regime. Topology optimization outperformed TEA-based design in all 45 configurations tested, with the largest structural gains at or below 1 MHz; for high-numerical-aperture designs the fidelity at 1 MHz matched that at 2 MHz, while structural similarity was highest at 0.5 MHz. The sub-megahertz to low-megahertz window is therefore a favorable operating regime for high-fidelity transcranial holography rather than one to be avoided. Free-field hydrophone measurements of 3D-printed lenses reproduced the designed patterns, and because the framework also accounts for aberration in heterogeneous media, patient-specific lenses corrected skull-induced aberration in simulation and ex vivo experiment, generalized across skull segments, and shaped volumetric beams through the human skull. Together these results provide a framework for designing simple, economical, and high-performance ultrasound systems.
title: Differentiable topology optimization for high-fidelity acoustic holography beyond the thin-element approximation

summary: We propose a Raspberry Pi-based underwater vessel classification system for edge deployment under limited connectivity, bandwidth and power in offshore acoustic surveillance. Using ShipsEar, we compare six classifiers on a Raspberry Pi 5 through a complete audio-to-prediction pipeline. We assess classification performance, processing latency, CPU utilisation, memory consumption and monitored power. Supporting experiments examine acoustic feature selection, statistical pooling and Transformer patch configurations. The two-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) achieved a mean macro-F1 of \textbf{(99.14 \textpm{} 0.32)\%} across five random seeds. The radial basis function support vector machine (RBF-SVM) achieved \textbf{98.83\%}, with a median end-to-end latency of 28.109~ms compared with 120.655~ms for the CNN. This favourable trade-off motivated RBF-SVM deployment on the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It maintained the same classification performance with a median end-to-end latency of \textbf{349.09~ms} and a sustained throughput of \textbf{2.962 classifications/s}, or \textbf{14.8} times the rate required for consecutive five-second audio segments.
title: Lightweight Underwater Acoustic Vessel Classification for Embedded Deployment

summary: Underwater acoustic passive detection is essential to maritime surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Existing detection systems typically collapse multichannel array observations into a binary decision or a scalar confidence score, offering limited insight into the physical evidence that supports or contradicts a target declaration. This limitation is acute at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where isolated spectral peaks and transient beamforming responses are inherently ambiguous and physically verifiable targets are characterized by an ensemble of coupled reinforcing cues. Building on the unified from-signals-to-evidence framework introduced in the companion Part I, this paper instantiates the framework for passive target detection. A physics-aware multichannel acoustic encoder encodes the array observations into complementary acoustic evidence tokens through a direction-guided architecture that combines minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) processing with time-frequency and fine-frequency representations. These tokens are combined with environmental priors and fed into a pretrained large language model (LLM) that evaluates target-present and noise-only hypotheses and generates a structured detection report detailing target presence, bearing, spectral-line locations, received SNR, range, and per-field confidence scores. A physics-parameterized data engine extended to realistic oceanic channels provides traceable supervision at both discrete-label and structured-description levels. Experiments under white-noise and mixed ocean-background conditions demonstrate reliable detection, accurate bearing estimation, and physically interpretable structured reports, validating the feasibility of evidence-grounded underwater acoustic detection.
title: From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part II: Passive Detection

summary: This preprint evaluates a reversible sample mapping that embeds 8-bit RGB values in the central half of a 9-bit sRGB code space before lossy JPEG XL encoding. The stored file includes a five-byte header that identifies the inverse mapping. The evaluation covers 41 previously unused CLIC Professional and DIV2K validation images at their original resolutions. Under common RGB PSNR and MS-SSIM floors and a single-thread encoding cap of 0.82 seconds per megapixel, the centered mapping reduced aggregate file size by 6.71% relative to direct JPEG XL at effort 6 (95% bootstrap interval: 3.85% to 9.86%). The centered files were 3.94% larger in aggregate than the tested AVIF files. Same-depth and transfer-function controls, together with libjxl coding counters, examine how the input representation affects the result.
title: Centered Sample-Range Remapping at JPEG XL Effort 6

But the bridge is only useful when we know what went into the decoder. An electrode voltage is a mixture of cortical, muscle, eye, reference and environmental processes. A task label may record what was instructed rather than what was imagined. A camera can record what moved but not what a person intended. This family treats those distinctions as independent scientific objects, not inconvenient details. The five flagship questions are coupled without being identical. F081 asks whether EEG adds information about spontaneous motor intention after cue clocks and residual muscle activity are accounted for. F082 distinguishes imagery, attempted movement and overt displacement with independent electromyographic and visual witnesses. F083 measures what remains stable across recording days. F084 resists the temptation to hide weak-signal and rare-class strata in a pooled score. F085 observes the safety consequences of false intention triggers during long periods of silence. The minimal platform is an anonymous, synthetic EEG-EMG-EOG task replayer with inert video coordinates, frozen event timestamps and a virtual command queue. The test generator can provide a hidden latent state to evaluate conditional identification. The model never sees that latent state during inference; it must work from the channels and timing evidence available at the specified decision moment. Cue onset may encode movement class because the task schedule is regular. Eye motion may precede an instruction. EMG can influence scalp electrodes before obvious displacement occurs. A test-day montage can reveal which session generated a signal. A preprocessing transform can learn the distribution or labels of the held-out partition. A fair protocol separates these shortcuts from useful cortical information with interventions that are physically or informationally interpretable. The real methodological enemy is the persuasive but under-identified success. A model can predict a motor class accurately without identifying voluntary intent. A classifier can distinguish imagery from actual movement using residual muscle activity, not imagination. A transfer algorithm can report stable day-to-day performance after silently adapting on test-day labels. A strong subgroup average can hide dangerous errors among weak signals. summary: We formulate a finite-core vorton representation of three-dimensional incompressible Navier– Stokes flow. Smooth divergence-free vorticity fields are represented by finite-core filamentary modes and studied in the limit of decreasing core scale. The singular vorton configuration is obtained strictly as a distributional concentration limit rather than imposed a priori as a singular solution. We prove dynamical equivalence by mapping the infinite-dimensional Navier–Stokes partial differential equations exactly onto the finite-dimensional ordinary differential equations of the discrete vorton ensemble. The passage through the nonlinear convective term is established via Mosco-type energy convergence and Aubin–Lions–Simon compactness. Topological reconnection supplies a microscopic writhe-to-twist transfer to regularize the ultraviolet limit, while a Fredholm boundary reconstruction controls wall interactions via weakly singular integral operators. The resulting framework proves that the continuum flow collapses onto an irreducible, compact geometric attractor, reducing global regularity to a uniform bound on vorticity and satisfying the Beale–Kato–Majda (BKM) criterion for global continuation.
title: RIGOROUS CONVERGENCE OF 3D NAVIER–STOKES TO A VORTON ATTRACTOR

summary: Routing-driven timely data collection in Underwater Acoustic Sensor Networks (UASNs) is crucial for marine environmental monitoring, disaster warning, and underwater resource exploration, etc. However, harsh underwater conditions, including high delays, limited bandwidth, and dynamic topologies, make efficient routing decisions challenging in UASNs. In this paper, we propose a smart interrupted routing scheme for UASNs to address dynamic underwater challenges. We first model underwater noise influences from real underwater routing features, e.g., turbulence and storms. We then propose a Software-Defined Networking (SDN)-based Interrupted Software-defined UASNs Reinforcement Learning (ISURL) framework, which ensures adaptive routing through dynamical failure handling (e.g., energy depletion of sensor nodes or link instability) and real-time interrupted recovery. Based on ISURL, we propose the MA-MAPPO algorithm, integrating multi-head attention mask mechanism with MAPPO to filter out infeasible actions and streamline training. Furthermore, to support interrupted data routing in UASNs, we introduce MA-MAPPO\_i, MA-MAPPO with interrupted policy, to enable smart interrupted routing decisions in UASNs. The evaluations demonstrate that our proposed routing scheme achieves exact underwater data routing decisions with faster convergence speed and lower routing delays than existing approaches.
title: Smart Interrupted Routing Based on Multi-head Attention Mask Mechanism-Driven MARL in Software-defined UASNs

Interpretability is especially vulnerable to beautiful output. Heatmaps, feature masks and counterfactual diagrams can look precise while merely expressing local correlation or an approximate post hoc surrogate. A serious explanatory claim tells the next investigator which feasible feature intervention will change the prediction and which independent witness can confirm it. A neural feature that was never intervened on cannot be declared causal from the color of a plot. Distribution shifts change the meaning of confidence. The familiar recording can be transformed by a new electrode montage, a different clock, an unknown class or missing-channel patterns. A detector that recognizes only the noise signatures on which it was trained may appear successful while failing precisely where a reliable refusal is needed. This is why F077 preserves selective risk, coverage, false acceptance and the full latency of the veto, not just aggregate classification accuracy. Leakage often survives a superficial audit. A synthetic source can be transformed into many nearly identical examples. The copied signals may receive new filenames, be presented as a different session or pass through a normalization fitted on the entire dataset. A high score on this partition does not demonstrate that the proposed quantum model has learned generalizable neural dynamics. F078 requires source ancestry, label availability at inference time, group balance and versioned data contracts before model comparison. Human authorization has a different grammar from prediction. A permission token may be valid for one task and forbidden for another; a model version may change while a previously signed policy does not. An operator may revoke consent after inference begins. These are not situations to be resolved by increasing confidence thresholds. A correct engineering design makes the action envelope an intersection of scope, role, time and safety, independently auditable after both successful and refused requests. In this book the commands remain inert simulations. Quantum performance remains an open empirical question for the present application. A systematic review of quantum machine learning in digital health, DOI 10.1038/s41746-025-01597-z, did not find a consistent empirical advantage over classical methods. That does not forbid the search for new architectures. It does require clean experiments. Encoding overhead, noisy operations, repeated runs, queueing, mitigation, hardware drift and classical tuning all belong to a practical utility comparison. A result below the preregistered benefit threshold must be allowed to stop the search. The five-stage parallel spacetime method organizes scientific uncertainty into origin questions, mathematical proposals, competing explanations, bounded stress worlds and independently reconstructable evidence. This phrase describes intellectual branches, not physical travel through alternative universes. The stages are most useful when a late counterfactual changes what we thought we knew at the beginning. No stage gives special permission to call a hypothesis established. A technical notebook does not repeat an entire research monograph line by line. It attempts to show why a researcher would care about an experiment, how instruments might mislead, and what interpretation could survive a fair adversary. Repeated concepts are welcome when their role deepens; recycled paragraphs masquerading as new research are not. This notebook uses Mechanism, Measurement and Refutation not as decorative labels but as obligations that make one another more exact. The research is deliberately nonclinical. It uses synthetic and authorized nonclinical proxies, inert test-bench decisions and invented stress scenarios. The proposal does not support diagnosis, implantation, robotic stroke rehabilitation or therapeutic claims. Clinical translation would require a separately approved, prospective, human-subject program with its own risk and endpoint design. Neither this document nor its figures can supply that evidence. The future reader may inherit much better hardware and different methods for causality, uncertainty or governance. If our circuits look primitive, the questions remain: what was actually measured, which part was guessed, where did the permission come from, what ordinary explanation could prevail, and who can reproduce the result? A living research civilization does not demand that its first equations remain sacred. It tries to leave an apparatus for self-correction. THE FIVE DISTINCT FLAGSHIP CONTRACTS F076 | Explainability of Quantum AI Models for Rehabilitation at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: test whether feature-level interventions change model explanations and predictions consistently under a frozen causal hypothesis. Declared primary observables: counterfactual fidelity [1], explanation stability [1], calibration gap [1], audit time [s]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that a saliency map follows correlated noise or a post hoc surrogate rather than the model decision. The concealed discriminating test should blindly perturb one neural feature while preserving its nuisance-correlated partner. Instrumental evidence: frozen synthetic EEG-like feature traces [normalized], plausible intervention support [1], explanation audit logs [1] and independent causal labels [1]. A strong baseline is feature ablation, sparse logistic models, calibrated gradient boosting and causally constrained classical surrogate explanations under identical data and access. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F077 | Out-of-Distribution Detection in Quantum Rehabilitation AI at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: detect unfamiliar EEG acquisition regimes and refuse unsupported inference before any simulated control action. Declared primary observables: OOD AUROC [1], selective risk [1], false-acceptance [1], refusal latency [s]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that shift scores measure recording artifacts or test-set tuning rather than genuinely unsupported states. The concealed discriminating test should hide a center-specific acquisition defect and replace a high-impairment synthetic test subgroup. Instrumental evidence: held-out sensor arrays [mV], acquisition timestamps [ms], unseen-site shift manifests, accept/reject flags [1] and dispatch times [s]. A strong baseline is deep ensemble and conformal selective prediction, classical density models and transparent acquisition-quality rules with equally tuned thresholds. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F078 | Data Leakage and Bias Control in Quantum Rehabilitation AI at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: separate individual/session/center provenance and audit false performance improvements across synthetic subgroups. Declared primary observables: leakage exposure fraction [1], subgroup calibration gap [1], false-positive disparity [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that participant overlap, batch identity or label timestamp leaks the holdout answer. The concealed discriminating test should plant blinded duplicate source fingerprints and evaluate a locked independent subgroup. Instrumental evidence: source genealogy hashes, session identifiers, timestamp manifests [ms], subgroup sizes [count] and sealed evaluation outcomes [1]. A strong baseline is grouped nested cross-validation, strict temporal split, classical feature leakage audits and equal-cost subgroup calibration analysis. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F079 | Human Oversight and Authorization of Quantum Rehabilitation Decisions at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: enforce a versioned authorization-policy intersection before any model suggestion can be executed in an inert test sandbox. Declared primary observables: unauthorized action rate [1], revocation latency [ms], false-denial rate [1], audit trail coverage [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that human consent is inferred from a stale token or a policy exception hidden in the interface. The concealed discriminating test should expire a synthetic authorization and revoke permission during an otherwise successful trial. Instrumental evidence: synthetic signed policy tokens, scope lists, version hashes, consent expiry clocks [ms] and complete inert action logs. A strong baseline is ordinary role-based access policy, signed consent records, deterministic fail-closed interlocks and human stop procedures. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. Declared primary observables: task utility gap [1], total wall time [s], energy [J], safety refusal error [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that encoding, queueing, mitigation or retraining overhead erases a solver-only apparent gain. summary: DjangoDefects is an inter-release defect prediction benchmark for Python, built from the full version history of the Django web framework. It covers 24 consecutive releases (1.0 to 5.2, September 2008 to April 2025). For every release it provides defect labels at four granularities, all derived from a single SZZ run: - File level: 20,442 file-release instances, 32.0% buggy - Method level: 169,744 function and method instances with their source code, 9.8% buggy - Line level: 14,917 buggy source lines - AST-node level: 5.38 M nodes from a full DFS traversal of each affected file's AST, with typed parent edges (ready to load as a graph), 1.29% buggy A source snapshot of every release is included. All file paths, method spans, line numbers and node spans refer to the code exactly as it shipped in that release. Construction. 5,585 closed, fixed Bug tickets from Django's Trac issue tracker were linked to 4,801 fix commits through Fixed #<ticket> references. Each fix was traced back to the commits that introduced the bug using SZZ Unleashed, with whitespace-insensitive blame and whitespace and comment filters, giving 6,306 bug records. Fixes that only add code, such as a missing check, change no existing line that blame could trace. Each one is attributed instead to the nearest code line above the insertion point. This adds 1,914 bug records, which label files and methods only. Releases are assigned by git ancestry rather than by date, which accounts for Django forking each stable branch months before the release tag. Buggy lines are located in each release snapshot by blame identity. Contents. - file_level.zip, method_level.zip, line_level.zip, ast_level.zip: one CSV per release - source_code.zip: every file under django/ at each release tag - code.zip: the pipeline that generated the dataset, the cached ticket-to-commit links, and instructions for reproducing it - README.md: full documentation, including schemas, statistics and threats to validity Intended uses. - Cross-version defect prediction at file and method level - Fine-grained defect localisation at line and AST-node level - Training models that use code structure, such as graph neural networks on the ASTs or code language models on method source Known limitations. - Labels for the most recent releases (about 5.0 to 5.2) are incomplete, because many of their bugs have not been reported or fixed yet. - File and method labels cover every release in which a bug is present. Line and node labels cover only the release that introduced it. - Labels from fixes that only add code are a heuristic. The anchor line can be older than the bug itself, so these bugs may start a few releases too early. They are marked label_source = added_only and can be filtered out. - See README.md §7 for the other threats to validity. Changes in 2.0.0. Fixes that only add code now label files and methods, which adds 746 buggy file-release instances and 2,474 buggy method-release instances. A new label_source column (removed / added_only) in the file- and method-level CSVs marks where each label comes from. Keeping only rows with label_source = removed reproduces the 1.0.0 labels exactly. The line, AST-node and source-code files are unchanged. Licence. The labels, documentation and code are released under CC BY 4.0. The included Django source code is © Django Software Foundation and individual contributors, redistributed under its BSD-3-Clause licence (LICENSE-DJANGO).
title: DjangoDefects: A Multi-Granularity SZZ-Labeled Defect Dataset for Python

summary: MDPSolver 0.12.0 Faster, with less memory : the transition probabilities are now stored in compressed sparse rows (CSR) and read by direct loops, and each sum is split over four partial sums. Large models given as arrays solve 9–12× faster end to end than with 0.11.0, with 3.4–4.6× less peak memory. On one thread, value iteration is 2.4–3.6× faster on models with many next states per state and action. Against pymdptoolbox, MDPSolver is now up to 719× faster with policy iteration, 407× with modified policy iteration and 6.2× with value iteration (see the wiki page Performance experiments ). New: NumPy arrays as input : every input format of mdp() accepts NumPy arrays, and lists still work. As arrays, every state has the same number of actions, and tranMatProbs / tranMatColumns pad state-action pairs with fewer entries with the probability 0. As lists, or in the elementwise formats, states may still have different numbers of actions. New: float32 transition probabilities : transition probabilities given as float32 are kept as float32, which takes 8 instead of 12 bytes per non-zero probability. Rounded to float32, the probabilities of a state and action sum to 1 only to within about 1e-7. That can take the solver more iterations, and limits the tolerance it can reach under the average reward criterion. New: NPY files : rewardsFromFile and tranMatFromFile read NumPy .npy files, recognised by the .npy extension, straight into the solver, so the model is never held in Python. The files hold the elementwise rows ( [state, action, reward] and [from_state, action, to_state, probability] ) as float64, float32, int64 or int32. A model with 1 billion non-zero transition probabilities loads in 19 seconds, instead of 9 minutes from CSV files, with the same peak memory. CSV files work as before. See the wiki page Loading models from NPY files . New: Python threads : solve() lets other Python threads run while it computes, so models in several threads are solved at the same time. Calls on one model object still run one at a time. Bug fix : CSV files with more than 2^31 (about 2.1 billion) lines overflowed the loader's line counter, which made errors name wrong line numbers. Outputs : getPolicy() and getValueVector() now return NumPy arrays (int64 and float64) instead of lists. Dependency : NumPy is now required, and pip installs it with MDPSolver. Results : values can differ from those of 0.11.0 in the last digits (relative differences up to about 1e-14), since the sums are now added in a different order. Policies and iteration counts were unchanged in our tests. Tests : two new unit tests cover NumPy arrays and Python threads, and the import test now covers .npy files. Documentation : the README has a new performance table, with models up to 1 billion non-zero transition probabilities, and the benchmark against pymdptoolbox was rerun with the newest versions of both packages. Backward compatible with 0.11.0, except for the outputs: code that compares getPolicy() or getValueVector() with a list, passes them to json.dumps , or uses list methods on them needs .tolist() , e.g. mdl.getPolicy().tolist() . Verified across Linux, Windows, and macOS before release.
title: areenberg/MDPSolver: MDPSolver v0.12.0 Release Notes

summary: This record is the replication package for the paper "New rules, old habits: across seven team sports, each league keeps its own way of using the rules" (Gustavo Pedro Ricou, Trinity College Dublin). It holds the paper and its supplement, the code that computes and checks every number they print, the hand-built evidence that no script can rebuild, and the result tables every number is computed from. Why the manuscript is archived here. The manuscript is archived with its code and data, not as a second place of publication, because the three are one object. Every number in the paper is computed from the archived result tables by the archived code, and the archived tests fail if the text and the tables disagree. So the version of record of the evidence includes the version of the text it supports, and a reader can check any sentence of the paper against the data behind it. The preprint is arXiv:2609.05584; this record is its data complement. Versions. Version v1.0.0 of this record held the first version of the preprint, a nine-sport paper on how playing time is allocated. Versions v2.0.0 and v2.0.1 hold its second version. Version v2.0.1 carries the same paper and the same numbers as v2.0.0. Its archive holds only the files the paper's builders and tests use. What the paper does. Studies of a rule change usually report one average effect. This paper asks whether a rule change reorders the leagues, in 101 leagues of seven sports. When football's substitution limit rose from three to five, the fourteen top leagues kept their order into the first season under five (rank correlation 0.89). That is about as firmly as from one ordinary season to the next. A prediction for twelve second tiers, written before their records were read, held (0.73), and they ranked like their own country's top league. Across rule changes in other sports, leagues kept their order in four of eight tests. In every sport measured, a league stayed near its place among its sport's leagues from season to season. So a rule change is best judged league by league, against each league's own seasons. What is in the files. source-v2.0.1.tar.gz : the manuscript and supplement sources with their generated tables, among them the audit of the pre-specification (paper_b/), and the files that the paper's builders and tests open, measured by a trace of their runs, as the tagged commit paper2-v2.0.1 holds them, unchanged. Those files are the pipeline's stages (src/), the tests (tests/), the builders (tools/), the hand-built evidence (data/manual/: the rule limits, the registers of pre-specified tests and an extract of the repository host's push log) and the plan of stages 361 to 368 (docs/). A README, the LICENSE, CITATION.cff and a checksum for every file (SHA256SUMS-source.txt) are added. derived-outputs-v2.0.1.tar.gz : the 156 result tables that the paper's builders and tests read, which are the minimum dataset needed to verify every claim, with a checksum for every table (SHA256SUMS-tables.txt). manuscript.pdf and supplement.pdf : the paper and its supplement, compiled from the tagged sources. SHA256SUMS.txt : the SHA-256 checksum of each of the four files above. The archives are built deterministically, with sorted entries, no owner and fixed timestamps. So a rebuild from the same tag gives the same bytes, and the checksums mean what they say. From the two archives alone, all of the paper's gate tests pass but one, which reads a third-party index of competitions that cannot be redistributed. Licence carve-out. Three different terms apply inside this record. The data compilation and the documentation are released under CC BY 4.0. The code is released under the MIT Licence, whose text is in LICENSE inside the source archive. The manuscript and supplement files (manuscript.pdf, supplement.pdf and the sources under paper_b/) are (c) the author and are expressly NOT released under CC BY, pending journal publication. The record's licence field reads CC BY 4.0 because Zenodo all
title: New rules, old habits: across seven team sports, each league keeps its own way of using the rules — replication package (code, derived tables and manuscript)

summary: Speaker representation learning is fundamental to speech processing tasks such as speaker verification and diarization. Although long-context speaker encoders can produce stable and discriminative embeddings, short-duration verification and diarization require finer-grained temporal representations. Short temporal contexts limit the available speaker evidence and make speaker identity difficult to disentangle from phonetic and acoustic variability. This creates a temporal resolution-representation reliability trade-off: speaker representations should maintain local within-speaker consistency, between-speaker discriminability and remain sensitive to speaker changes at fine temporal resolution. Accordingly, we propose a framework for reliable speaker representation learning at fine temporal resolution. FineSpeaker first constructs resolution-controllable frame-wise speaker representations through mean pooling over an adjustable n-frame window, enabling flexible control of representation granularity. It then introduces a speaker encoder with local temporal modeling that exploits short-range speaker context to improve the stability and discriminability of short-duration and frame-wise representations. Furthermore, we develop a generative disentanglement strategy for optimizing frame-level speaker representations, combining VAE-based probabilistic modeling with flow matching to characterize speaker-related variation and suppress non-speaker interference. Experiments demonstrate competitive full-utterance performance, improved fine-grained speaker verification on VoxCeleb and CN-Celeb, and strong zero-shot diarization results, highlighting the benefits of balancing temporal resolution and representation reliability.
title: FineSpeaker: Reliable Speaker Representation Learning at Fine Temporal Resolution

summary: This document describes the measurement setup, signal processing, data organization, and MATLAB file format of a database of acoustic responses measured on a Knowles Electronics Manikin for Acoustic Research (KEMAR) using the Hearpiece, a multi-microphone, multi-driver in-ear research device. The data include binaural room impulse responses (BRIRs) and Hearpiece driver responses, together with center-microphone room impulse responses and a loopback impulse response of the playback and recording system. The BRIRs cover two Hearpiece configurations, three room conditions, three independent insertions per configuration, and 24 horizontal source directions. The database supports reproducible research on binaural and hearing-device signal processing, with potential applications in speech enhancement, spatial filtering and source separation, dereverberation, active noise and occlusion control, and acoustic feedback cancellation. The database, MATLAB loading script, and technical documentation are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23667308.
title: The Hearpiece Database of Binaural Room Impulse Responses and Driver Responses on KEMAR

summary: This paper studies the capability of an object-centric audio representation to support multiple downstream tasks within a unified framework. The object-centric model is trained in a self-supervised setup using slot attention by reconstructing Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) patch embeddings from a set of latent slots. It is trained on synthetic audio mixtures, which provides controlled multi-source audio scenes. These slot representations are evaluated for the classification, detection, and separation of sound events by training task specific output layers. On the classification task, the model achieves an F1-score of 0.8, comparable to clip-level AST embeddings which achieve 0.7. For sound event detection, it reaches a macro F1-score of 0.7, outperforming clip-level AST embeddings at 0.4 and matching AST patch embeddings at 0.7, which encode finer time-frequency information. In source separation, it achieves an SI-SDR improvement (SI-SDRi) of 18.4 dB. Furthermore, in a zero-shot source separation setting, the model achieves an SI-SDRi of 14.5 dB. These results demonstrate that slot-based representations capture transferable and compositional structure in audio scenes, enabling generalization across tasks and datasets.
title: Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representation for Multi-Task Audio Analysis

summary: Video-queried sound separation (VQSS) aims to isolate a target sound from an audio mixture using its corresponding video as a query. However, scene-level video queries can become ambiguous when multiple sounding objects are visible, particularly when the target and interferer are semantically similar. We propose SelectSep, a target-selective VQSS framework that jointly uses text and a single click coordinate to specify the target source and instance without requiring segmentation at inference time. We adapt the visual encoder through target-feature distillation with text and click conditioning, and then fine-tune the separator using the adapted visual features. We also introduce an on-screen interference setting, where both the target and interferer are visible, to evaluate target selectivity. Experiments on standard benchmarks and the on-screen interference setting demonstrate consistent improvements in separation quality and target selectivity, particularly for mixtures containing semantically similar sources.
title: SelectSep: Target-Selective Video Queries for Audio Source Separation

summary: Many real-world signals are corrupted by localized, structured perturbations whose distribution is unknown: an intermittent background noise in a music recording, a watermark stamped on a photograph, a cast shadow. We study the task of recovering a clean signal $x$ from an observation $y$ containing such a localized out-of-distribution (OOD) corruption. We propose Support-guided OOD Removal with Diffusion, SORD, an iterative algorithm to recover $x$ using only two ingredients: a binary map of the corruption support and a single diffusion model pretrained on clean signals. SORD does not require any paired data or any statistical model of the corruption. We evaluate SORD on natural images and human faces with spatially localized corruptions including handwritten digits, other images, watermarks, and shadows, as well as audio recordings of different musical instruments with temporally localized corruptions including other instruments and human speech. SORD is competitive with, and often outperforms, posterior-sampling inpainting given the same diffusion prior and the same mask, source-separation baselines that require a separate diffusion model for each source, and, on several benchmarks, supervised networks trained on paired clean and corrupted signals. The code is released here: \href{https://github.com/voilalab/SORD}{https://github.com/voilalab/SORD}.
title: Support-guided OOD Removal with Diffusion

summary: Generative target speaker extraction (TSE) models achieve high-quality extraction, but suffer from considerably slow training convergence. Representation Alignment (REPA) accelerates diffusion transformer training by aligning hidden states with a pre-trained Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) teacher. However, existing alignment in the speech and audio domain operates at a single granularity. For TSE, frame-level alignment leaves the global, time-invariant characteristics of the target speech implicit, whereas utterance-level alignment leaves the time-varying content implicit, even though extracting the target requires both. We propose Multi-Granularity Representation Alignment (MG-REPA), aligning the hidden states with an SSL model at the frame level and a speaker verification model at the utterance level. We further apply temporal normalization to the frame-level target, removing its utterance-level statistics so that each branch concentrates on its granularity. On Libri2Mix, MG-REPA reaches the OVRL and PESQ of a MeanFlow-TSE baseline with $3.0\times$ and $2.1\times$ fewer epochs, respectively. Trained for 750 epochs, it is competitive with the published 2,000-epoch baseline on intrusive metrics while improving non-intrusive metrics. An ablation demonstrates that MG-REPA outperforms alignment at a single granularity.
title: MG-REPA: Multi-Granularity Representation Alignment for Generative Target Speaker Extraction

summary: Large self-supervised speech models provide powerful representations for speaker verification, but full fine-tuning is expensive. Most conventional adapters insert small trainable modules to modify the output of each layer, while keeping the original residual connections unchanged. Building on our preliminary study of manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections in speaker encoders, we explore parameter-efficient adaptation of both residual paths and feature selection across layers. We first propose a Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (MCRA), which splits the hidden dimensions of each Transformer residual state into N groups and uses a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix to exchange information among them. A learnable gate controls the balance between the original and mixed residual paths. The gate adds only one scalar parameter at each residual connection and initially favors the original path, allowing gradual adaptation. We further propose Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (FALA), an attention-based aggregation method that uses a single learned query shared across all utterances to compute layer weights separately for each speech frame. Because the layer representations depend on the input, the resulting weights vary across both utterances and frames, unlike the fixed weights of a conventional layer-weighted sum. Compared with a frozen WavLM baseline using a fixed layer-weighted sum, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb, with trainable adaptation parameters equivalent to only 0.0009% and 0.0016% of the WavLM-Large parameters, respectively.
title: Manifold-Constrained Residual Adaptation with Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation for Speaker Verification

summary: End-to-end neural diarization with vector clustering (EEND-VC) is a strong framework for long-form conversational diarization, where speaker embeddings are used to link local speaker decisions across windows. Conventional EEND-VC systems extract these embeddings by cutting out regions assigned to each local speaker, preferably using only non-overlapped speech. This works well when enough clean target-speaker speech is available, but it discards useful speaker evidence in overlapped regions and becomes unreliable when a local speaker appears mostly in overlap. We propose a speaker-activity-conditioned embedding extractor that adapts a pretrained WavLM-MHFA speaker verification model to extract target-speaker embeddings directly from full conversational windows. Inspired by the recently proposed diarization-conditioned Whisper (DiCoW) model for target-speaker ASR, frame-level diarization-dependent transformations inject local speaker-activity information into intermediate WavLM representations while preserving the pretrained initialization. Experiments on multiple conversational diarization benchmarks show that fine-tuning with limited real meeting data reduces speaker-confusion errors and improves EEND-VC diarization performance. The results further indicate that real conversational data provides an effective alternative to large-scale simulated-mixture training for diarization-aware speaker embedding extraction.
title: Learning Speaker-Activity-Conditioned WavLM Speaker Embeddings with Real Conversational Data

summary: Target speaker extraction (TSE) isolates a desired speaker from a multi-speaker mixture using cues that identify the target. Prior work has explored acoustic and textual cues, such as enrollment audio and different types of speaker descriptors, but typically relies on a single cue family. Yet no single cue is both broadly available and reliably discriminative. Moreover, most TSE systems adopt mask-prediction models, which are prone to audible artifacts and generalize poorly across acoustic conditions. To address these limitations, we propose PromptSep-Speaker, a generative TSE model based on latent diffusion that unifies four interchangeable cues: speaker temporal order, transcript, enrollment audio, and speaker caption. The generative formulation delivers higher separation quality and multi-modal prompting improves applicability across scenarios. To fully exploit each cue, we further introduce a frozen WavLM representation with an auxiliary alignment loss that supervises query-mixture cross-attention without extra labeling. Across four evaluation sets and a listening study, PromptSep-Speaker achieves state-of-the-art performance over TSE and universal source separation baselines, improving separation accuracy and quality across cue modalities.
title: PromptSep-Speaker: Generative Target Speaker Extraction via Multimodal Prompting and Semantic Alignment

summary: Drum beats are often conceptualized and produced as arrangements of repeated single-drum sound events or one-shots. Drum Analysis-by-Synthesis (AbS) models combine this structural assumption with reconstruction-based training to perform MIR tasks such as drum transcription, drum source separation, and one-shot extraction, offering a flexible alternative to more traditional task-specific supervision. However, leading AbS approaches struggle to generalize to a broad range of drum timbres (e.g., electronic drum kits), rely on high-quality paired audio-transcription training data, and do not model intra-class timbral variation within a single arrangement (e.g., multiple kick sounds). To overcome these limitations, we propose D-Composer, an autoregressive language modeling framework that decomposes drum recordings into labeled sound events and their onset times. In drum transcription and one-shot extraction tasks, D-Composer performs comparably to or better than a state-of-the-art AbS system and task-specific baselines while generalizing to a broader range of drum timbres. Our results demonstrate that when equipped with abundant synthetic data and compact acoustic token representations, language modeling provides a simple recipe for unifying transcription and sound event decomposition.
title: D-Composer: Language Modeling for Simultaneous Drum Transcription and Sound Event Decomposition

direction_title: Rowan / BBC1 protein structural confidence vs experimental stability falsification [FORWARD]
summary: The prediction of protein stability changes following single-point mutations plays a pivotal role in computational biology, particularly in areas like drug discovery, enzyme reengineering, and genetic disease analysis. Although deep-learning strategies have pushed the field forward, their use in standard workflows remains limited due to resource demands. Conversely, potential-like methods are fast, intuitive, and efficient. Yet, these typically estimate Gibbs free energy shifts without considering the free-energy variations in the unfolded protein state, an omission that may breach mass balance and diminish accuracy. This study shows that incorporating a mass-balance correction (MBC) to account for the unfolded state significantly enhances these methods. While many machine learning models partially model this balance, our analysis suggests that a refined representation of the unfolded state may improve the predictive performance.
title: Mass Balance Approximation of Unfolding Improves Potential-Like Methods for Protein Stability Predictions

direction_title: Rowan / BBC1 protein structural confidence vs experimental stability falsification [FORWARD]
summary: Understanding how residue variations affect protein stability is crucial for designing functional proteins and deciphering the molecular mechanisms underlying disease-related mutations. Recent advances in protein language models (PLMs) have revolutionized computational protein analysis, enabling, among other things, more accurate predictions of mutational effects. In this work, we introduce JanusDDG, a deep learning framework that leverages PLM-derived embeddings and a bidirectional cross-attention transformer architecture to predict $ΔΔG$ of single and multiple-residue mutations while simultaneously being constrained to respect fundamental thermodynamic properties, such as antisymmetry and transitivity. Unlike conventional self-attention, JanusDDG computes queries (Q) and values (V) as the difference between wild-type and mutant embeddings, while keys (K) alternate between the two. This cross-interleaved attention mechanism enables the model to capture mutation-induced perturbations while preserving essential contextual information. Experimental results show that JanusDDG achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting $ΔΔG$ from sequence alone, matching or exceeding the accuracy of structure-based methods for both single and multiple mutations. Code Availability:https://github.com/compbiomed-unito/JanusDDG
title: JanusDDG: A Thermodynamics-Compliant Model for Sequence-Based Protein Stability via Two-Fronts Multi-Head Attention

direction_title: Rowan / BBC1 protein structural confidence vs experimental stability falsification [FORWARD]
summary: Predicting the impact of single-point amino acid mutations on protein stability is essential for understanding disease mechanisms and advancing drug development. Protein stability, quantified by changes in Gibbs free energy ($ΔΔG$), is influenced by these mutations. However, the scarcity of data and the complexity of model interpretation pose challenges in accurately predicting stability changes. This study proposes the application of deep neural networks, leveraging transfer learning and fusing complementary information from different models, to create a feature-rich representation of the protein stability landscape. We developed four models, with our third model, ThermoMPNN+, demonstrating the best performance in predicting $ΔΔG$ values. This approach, which integrates diverse feature sets and embeddings through latent transfusion techniques, aims to refine $ΔΔG$ predictions and contribute to a deeper understanding of protein dynamics, potentially leading to advancements in disease research and drug discovery.
title: AlgoRxplorers | Precision in Mutation: Enhancing Drug Design with Advanced Protein Stability Prediction Tools

direction_title: Rowan / BBC1 protein structural confidence vs experimental stability falsification [FORWARD]
summary: Domain adaptation enables generalizable and efficient data-driven research. However, existing work has largely focused on domain adaptation for some intrinsically homogeneous target cohort, overlooking inherent heterogeneity within the target, which can exacerbate biases and unfairness in the presence of subgroups with imbalanced sample sizes. We develop a novel domain adaptation framework that addresses more complicated target data that consists of heterogeneous and data-sparse subgroups and lacks gold-standard label observations. Our method simultaneously handles high-dimensionality, covariate shift, and outcome model heterogeneity by combining a model-assisted debiasing step used for covariate shift correction with an adaptive knowledge-guided sparsification procedure used to mitigate the issue of sample disparity. We also introduce a new model selection strategy to avoid negative knowledge transfer in the absence of labels in the target data. Our method is theoretically justified for being robust to nuisance model misspecification and adaptive to heterogeneity between the subgroups. Numerical experiments and two real-world applications, including genetic risk modeling of type II diabetes and prediction of mutation-induced protein stability changes, demonstrate the practical advantages of our method.
title: Domain Adaptation Targeting Heterogeneous and Imbalanced Subgroups

summary: This record is the replication package for the paper "New rules, old habits: across seven team sports, each league keeps its own way of using the rules" (Gustavo Pedro Ricou, Trinity College Dublin). It holds the paper and its supplement, the code that computes and checks every number they print, the hand-built evidence that no script can rebuild, and the result tables every number is computed from. Why the manuscript is archived here. The manuscript is archived with its code and data, not as a second place of publication, because the three are one object. Every number in the paper is computed from the archived result tables by the archived code, and the archived tests fail if the text and the tables disagree. So the version of record of the evidence includes the version of the text it supports, and a reader can check any sentence of the paper against the data behind it. The preprint is arXiv:2609.05584; this record is its data complement. Versions. Version v1.0.0 of this record held the first version of the preprint, a nine-sport paper on how playing time is allocated. Versions v2.0.0 to v2.0.2 hold its second version. Version v2.0.2 carries the same results as v2.0.0 and v2.0.1, with small changes of wording. Its archive holds only the files the paper's builders and tests use. What the paper does. Studies of a rule change usually report one average effect. This paper asks whether a rule change reorders the leagues, in 101 leagues of seven sports. When football's substitution limit rose from three to five, the fourteen top leagues kept their order into the first season under five (rank correlation 0.89). That is about as firmly as from one ordinary season to the next. A prediction for twelve second tiers, written before their records were read, held (0.73), and they ranked like their own country's top league. Across rule changes in other sports, leagues kept their order in four of eight tests. In every sport measured, a league stayed near its place among its sport's leagues from season to season. So a rule change is best judged league by league, against each league's own seasons. What is in the files. source-v2.0.2.tar.gz : the manuscript and supplement sources with their generated tables, among them the audit of the pre-specification (paper_b/), and the files that the paper's builders and tests open, measured by a trace of their runs, as the tagged commit paper2-v2.0.2 holds them, unchanged. Those files are the pipeline's stages (src/), the tests (tests/), the builders (tools/), the hand-built evidence (data/manual/: the rule limits, the registers of pre-specified tests and an extract of the repository host's push log) and the plan of stages 361 to 368 (docs/). A README, the LICENSE, CITATION.cff and a checksum for every file (SHA256SUMS-source.txt) are added. derived-outputs-v2.0.2.tar.gz : the 156 result tables that the paper's builders and tests read, which are the minimum dataset needed to verify every claim, with a checksum for every table (SHA256SUMS-tables.txt). manuscript.pdf and supplement.pdf : the paper and its supplement, compiled from the tagged sources. SHA256SUMS.txt : the SHA-256 checksum of each of the four files above. The archives are built deterministically, with sorted entries, no owner and fixed timestamps. So a rebuild from the same tag gives the same bytes, and the checksums mean what they say. From the two archives alone, all of the paper's gate tests pass but one, which reads a third-party index of competitions that cannot be redistributed. Licence carve-out. Three different terms apply inside this record. The data compilation and the documentation are released under CC BY 4.0. The code is released under the MIT Licence, whose text is in LICENSE inside the source archive. The manuscript and supplement files (manuscript.pdf, supplement.pdf and the sources under paper_b/) are (c) the author and are expressly NOT released under CC BY, pending journal publication. The record's licence field reads CC BY
title: New rules, old habits: across seven team sports, each league keeps its own way of using the rules — replication package (code, derived tables and manuscript)

summary: We develop a counterfactual semantics based on reopening partial information states. Evaluation first removes enough stated content to leave the antecedent’s attributes unresolved, retaining what the chosen scope protects, then asserts the antecedent and considers the surviving consistent refinements. Would and might quantify over the admissible alternatives; a weighted extension supplies graded evaluations. The principal result concerns finite models with fully supported residues. When a conjunctive antecedent reopens each constituent attribute, adding a supported conjunct can remove the grounds of another conclusion. A four-attribute countermodel therefore violates Cautious Monotony, excluding any smooth preferential representation that preserves the evaluable verdicts. We also establish a sufficient nesting condition for Cut and exhibit its failure without that condition. The conjunctive reopening rule is an explicit interpretive commitment; its suitability for ordinary-language counterfactuals remains an empirical question. The account uses declared dependencies, scope restrictions, and priorities, while the quantitative extension assumes a weight kernel. Comparisons with belief revision, premise semantics, update semantics, and causal intervention identify the consequences of reopening an attribute rather than merely making its proposed value consistent with retained information.
title: Counterfactual Evaluation by Reopening Information States
