summary: Introduction Root system architecture (RSA) plays an important role in plant growth and development, influencing soil exploration, water and nutrient uptake, and interactions with the surrounding environment. However, characterising root systems under field conditions remains challenging due to their spatial complexity, below-ground location, and the cost and destructive nature of many root measurement techniques. DeepRootGen provides a computational framework for generating synthetic three-dimensional root system architectures using a stochastic, parameterised root simulation model. The model represents individual root organs and segments within a hierarchical graph, allowing their geometry, topology and spatial distribution to be analysed. The framework is intended to support the digital reconstruction of root systems using observational data collected from the field. By combining mechanistic assumptions about root development with statistical calibration and inference methods, DeepRootGen provides a means of investigating plausible root architectures consistent with available measurements. DeepRootGen has been developed with an emphasis on woody perennial root systems, including horticultural applications involving apple and grapevine rootstocks. The underlying simulator is parameterised to support different root system configurations and can be recalibrated for specific applications. Features and Functionality DeepRootGen provides the following functionality: Stochastic 3D root simulation: Generate synthetic root system architectures with configurable root numbers, lengths, diameters, branching behaviour and growth orientations. Hierarchical graph representation: Represent root organs and segments using explicit parent–child relationships, branching orders and segment identifiers. Root branching and development: Simulate primary and higher-order roots, including stochastic branching locations and configurable interbranch distances. Architectural analysis: Calculate summary statistics describing root length, diameter, branching patterns, orientation, spatial extent and root length density. Spatial aggregation: Aggregate simulated root segments onto three-dimensional soil voxel grids for comparison against field observations. Model calibration: Estimate root system parameters using optimisation and statistical discrepancy measures. Sensitivity analysis: Investigate the influence of model parameters on simulated architectural characteristics. Stochastic ensemble simulation: Generate multiple plausible root architectures under a common parameter configuration to investigate variability between realisations. Visualisation: Explore root architectures and summary statistics through interactive three-dimensional visualisations and statistical plots. Experiment management: Support reproducible simulation workflows, experiment tracking and model artefact management. The repository also contains infrastructure for simulation-based inference and generative modelling. The availability and configuration of individual inference workflows depend on the installed dependencies and repository revision. Model Overview DeepRootGen uses a stochastic root growth simulator to construct root system architectures from a configurable set of parameters. Root architecture generation A simulated root system consists of primary roots originating from the plant base, with lateral roots emerging from their parent organs according to the specified branching configuration. The model supports several aspects of root development: Number and arrangement of primary roots. Root organ lengths and diameters. Maximum branching order. Number and length of lateral roots. Stochastic variation in root growth. Interbranch distances and lateral-root attachment locations. Root growth orientation and gravitropism. Classification of structural and fine roots. Individual simulation runs may produce different architectures even when the input parameters are identical. R
title: DeepRootGen: Unlocking the 3D root architecture of perennial trees using deep learning

summary: Analysis package for a study of copy-specific assignment at the two 23S rRNA copies of Helicobacter pylori . The package contains the seventeen supplementary tables, the analysis and figure code, the recorded software versions, the reconstruction log for the long-read alignments, and a per-read phase-evidence table. What is reproducible. The six-criterion classification of 103 matched isolates is re-runnable and every verdict was re-derived from the counts with zero mismatches. The reference metadata for all cited works is captured from Europe PMC and every DOI was verified against its record. The figures are generated by script and each passes a programmatic overlap, clipping and text-on-line audit before export. The short-read counts at the two A2143 coordinates are reproduced from the archived alignment, whose header records the exact command and tool versions. What is not. The original NCBI query string and its date were not retained, so the cohort cannot be rebuilt verbatim; per-accession inclusion flags are given instead. The barrnap installation originally used on the analysis machine is missing a Perl module and does not run; the rRNA copy numbers were therefore archived values in earlier versions and are re-derived with barrnap 1.10.5 in this version. The original parameter sets for two of the three long-read procedures were not retained; those procedures were re-run and both original and re-run values are reported side by side and never pooled. One cell of the long-read table reproduces exactly; the others do not, and this is stated in the manuscript. Changes in version 4. The package matches the manuscript. All thirteen supplementary tables are present, including Supplementary Tables S12 and S13, which were absent from the previous version, and Supplementary Table S1 now carries the genome length and assembly level of all 1,483 retained genomes rather than leaving those columns empty. A new Supplementary Table S1b lists the seven excluded genomes that could be recovered from local storage, with their lengths; the genome-length window is 1.5 to 1.7 Mb and this version states the evidence that fixes its bounds. Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. The four control reference sequences are deposited under results/marker_control/. Changes in version 6. This version restores the complete file set. The previous version was published from an incomplete upload, so most of the figures, several of the supplementary tables and part of the analysis code were missing from that record. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files and this package has 134, so the package is now deposited as a single archive, hp23s_copy_assignment_package.zip , which holds every file at the path it occupies in the source repository; this README, the SHA-256 manifest and the archive of rRNA calls and copy sequences are additionally placed loose in the record. From version 10 the manuscript itself is not deposited, in the archive or loose. Every member of the archive is listed in SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256, and that manifest is regenerated here, which corrects the entry for this README (the previous manifest had been computed before the last edit of the file). DOI.txt now lists the version DOIs, and the data-availability sentence in the manuscript names the concept DOI rather than one version, so that it cannot point at a superseded record. Changes in version 7. This version is a manuscript round: the text is rebuilt from the same locked data by the same script, and no reported value changes. Three defects in the supplementary apparatus are correcte
title: Long reads assign a 23S rRNA resistance allele to one of the two copies in Helicobacter pylori; a complete short-read assembly does not

summary: Results-only supplement. On one synthetic calculation, the recorded request changes before admission under reduced buffer capacity. Four deterministic situations (input lengths 6 and 8, with or without a reservation) were evaluated under four controllers: 16 exact transfer outputs, not 16 independent situations. With two acquisition episodes and four controls, there are 22 episodes in all. The classical option using the same learned tree matched all four OASI trajectories. Transfer work units total 104 for OASI, 104 for the classical option, 100 for planning, and 100 for cache with replanning. These units are not execution time. No advantage specific to OASI is established. The included passive reader verifies the mathematical consistency of derived results, not the private receipt chain, the original execution, or independent replication. Original runtime and host telemetry are excluded. Not a general OS, production release, or hardware crash test. No institutional endorsement. The previous software versions and the associated article remain unchanged. Authorized license scope for this exact seal: Apache-2.0 for the new reader and tests; CC BY 4.0 for documentation and derived data. The preparation-time license proposal inside the immutable archive is superseded by this notice. Archive: oasi-operant-results.zip, 21,037 bytes, SHA-256 81f69fa10c884b61199025eab547a8445cf4c7951e96b3befa97ea93fba68ac3. One work unit is charged per successful admission, completed batch, produced record or additional content check actually performed in drift mode. The totals sum the four transfer episodes per arm, not all 22 episodes; they exclude two acquisition episodes (25 additional units), four controls, policy compilation, startup and CPU time. Observing a response before admission does not show that learning the rule rather than supplying the same tree conventionally was necessary.
title: OASI Operant Evidence: Bounded Host-Process Experiment and Passive Readback

summary: We present an analytical derivation of fundamental coupling constants and structural attractors emerging from a descending residual iteration function F(y,x) possessing a unique global fixed point y*(x) . Evaluating the first iteration term for specific membrane residues ( 155 and 185 ) yields pure, asymmetric numerical invariants--most notably 461.4331634036143, composed almost exclusively of the four digits {1, 3, 4, 6}--which directly link the inverse fine-structure constant alpha^{-1} approx 137.036 and the characteristic quark bounce frequency (925) to the 43.2 GeV signal. Through algebraic decomposition, we isolate the longitudinal attractor ( 323 ) governing transversal gravitational anchorage and membrane confinement from the transversal emission attractor ( 232 ), demonstrating how their balance generates a flat background (555) driven by the double-axis torsion gradient of charmonium. Finally, by applying discrete digit-suppression transformations ( 137.036 -> 137.360 and removal of the 036 residue), we map the transition to an antimatter-dominated dual system lacking inversion symmetry and derive a secondary four-digit invariant (2177.5711270036704), establishing arithmetically differentiated topological sets as the fundamental origin of the distinct interaction regimes.

summary: This version (v3.1.0-2021-2024) contains reproducibility materials for the 2021-2024 National Immunization Survey-Teen analysis of parent-reported clinician recommendation, preventive-care access, and insurance gaps in U.S. adolescent HPV vaccination. The provider-phase sample comprises 66,938 adolescents aged 13-17 years, and multivariable complete-case models comprise 60,338 adolescents. Relative to v3.0.0-2021-2024 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22796335), every statistical analysis script (01, 02, 04, 07, 08) and all 35 aggregate statistical and diagnostic tables are preserved byte-for-byte without refitting any models. This update upgrades script 06_ahp_figures.R, the PDF/SVG vector exports for Figures 1-3 and Supplementary Figure S1, and their companion aggregate figure source-data CSVs to match journal artwork conventions (adding the annual recommendation-stratified up-to-date panel to Figure 1, expanding Figure 2 to display both primary overall and insurance-stratified adjusted probabilities and differences, and adding private-insurance benchmark reference lines to Figure 3). The package includes six scientific R scripts, an optional public CDC downloader, a dependency checker, aggregate analysis and diagnostic tables (including 999 Rao-Wu stratified bootstrap replicates for two-stage inverse-probability complete-case weighting and complete six-category reason reporting), source data and PDF/SVG exports for three main figures and one supplementary figure, software session records, execution-verification files, and SHA-256 checksums. Primary adjusted recommendation-associated differences are 21.7 and 22.5 percentage points for initiation and up-to-date vaccination; IPCW sensitivity differences are 21.2 and 22.1 points. Script 01 reads source files for 2018-2024; script 04 restricts the analysis to 2021-2024 and uses annual provider weights divided by four. Run scripts in the order documented in the README: dependency check, 01, 04 with --skip-ipcw, 07 final 999 8, 08, and 06. Script 02 supplies analysis functions and should not be run as a standalone seven-year analysis. Raw CDC public-use files and individual-level processed extracts are not redistributed. Obtain public-use files and documentation from the CDC NIS-Teen data and documentation page . The package contains code and aggregate outputs only.
title: Reproducibility package for NIS-Teen HPV vaccination analysis, 2021-2024

summary: QCArchive records go public the moment a calculation finishes, carry provenance but no author, and are credited by citing the paper that produced them. A one-page contribution to Open physics data: what license and attribution terms should it carry? , a moderated discussion at SESAPS 2026 (Kennesaw State University, Nov 12–14, 2026). Drafted by the organizers from a 20-minute call and approved by the contributor. All contributions: https://det-lab.github.io/open-physics-data-terms-site/ Terms reported for the contributor's own releases: data: none; software: LGPL.
title: Compute locally, publish automatically: how QCArchive makes sharing a side effect of running the calculation

summary: The biological response of the body is a fundamental adaptation mechanism underlying the diagnosis and evaluation of the effectiveness of therapeutic interventions. Regardless of the registration methods used, whether instrumental or clinical, medical practice relies on an objective assessment of the response of the body's functional systems to internal and external stimuli. The article discusses the concept of biological response as a universal criterion combining the approaches of evidence-based and holistic medicine. An analytical review of scientific publications and theoretical concepts devoted to the physiology of adaptation and self-regulation of the body has been conducted. The study is based on an analysis of the theories of homeostasis, stress, and functional systems (W. Cannon, G. Selye, P.K. Anokhin, C. Pert), as well as modern concepts of neuroendocrine, autonomic, and immune regulation. Methods of biological response registration used in osteopathy, applied kinesiology, traditional Chinese medicine, and other holistic fields are considered. A universal sequence of biological response formation has been systematized, including afferent synthesis, assessment of compliance with the physiological norm, initiation of adaptive reactions, executive action, and reverse afferentation. It is shown that various diagnostic approaches use a single physiological feedback mechanism, differing mainly in the ways of registering the response. The modern physiological justification for holistic diagnostic methods, including muscle testing, osteopathic listening, and pulse diagnostics of traditional Chinese medicine, is presented. The data on the relationship of pulse wave characteristics with the state of the autonomic nervous system and hemodynamic parameters are considered. The biological response of the body is a universal diagnostic and therapeutic criterion reflecting the state of functional systems and the effectiveness of therapeutic interventions. The unity of the mechanisms of formation and registration of the biological response allows us to consider it as a methodological basis for the integration of evidence-based and holistic medicine. The use of feedback principles helps to increase the personalization, safety, and validity of diagnostic and therapeutic measures.
title: The Biological Response of the Body as a Universal Diagnostic and Therapeutic Tool

This flagship-specific design keeps the title from being an empty keyword bundle and ensures that future discoverability points readers to an actual falsifiable method. 05 | Five-Layer Nonclinical Testing from Batch Registry to Cross-Laboratory Transfer First register material lots, allowed sample identity and operator authority. Fourth conceal malformed samples and counterfactual lot assignments while independently collecting negative outcomes. Fifth hand an unedited archive to a second laboratory and require reconstruction of one success and one refusal. Its main independent observations are replay match fraction [1], unmatched evidence rate [1], version-transfer discrepancy [1], contrasted with classical laboratory information management with independently signed records and human audit. summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FAIR-bioHeaders Specification

summary: Obesity is a growing public health issue in New Zealand, increasing the risk of chronic diseases and exacerbating health disparities. Mobile health (mHealth) initiatives, such as smartphone apps, have showed promise in improving weight management and physical exercise. FatSecret, a popular software for tracking nutrition and activity, may help people lose weight, but its efficacy across ethnic groups and areas in New Zealand is uncertain. The primary goal is to determine the efficacy of the FatSecret app in promoting weight loss and boosting physical activity among overweight and obese people in New Zealand. The secondary purpose is to investigate potential differences in intervention effectiveness based on ethnicity (European, Māori, Asian, and Pacific Islanders) and living place (urban or rural). A two-arm, parallel, randomized controlled trial design will be used. Adult volunteers (aged 18–65 years, BMI ≥25 kg/m²) from various ethnic groups and areas in New Zealand will be recruited and randomly assigned 1:1 to the intervention or control group, stratified by ethnicity and region. The intervention group will receive a 12-week weight management and physical activity program given via the FatSecret app, while the control group will not use the app and will continue with their usual lifestyle. The primary outcome is the change in body weight between baseline and 12 weeks. Secondary objectives include changes in body fat percentage, waist circumference, physical activity level measured using established methods, and health-related quality of life. This randomized controlled trial will evaluate the FatSecret app’s effectiveness in promoting weight loss and physical activity among New Zealand’s overweight and obese individuals. The study design allows for the evaluation of potential differences in intervention effectiveness across ethnic groups and residential locations, which will inform the creation of culturally appropriate and geographically targeted mHealth therapies for obesity control. If proven effective, the FatSecret app might be widely promoted and integrated into national health policies to combat the obesity pandemic and minimize health disparities. Potential limitations include self-reported data for some outcomes and the short intervention duration. Version note: Author manuscript of a study protocol prepared for DIGIHLTH 705 at the University of Auckland, listed on ResearchGate on 29 May 2025: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/392166804. This is a protocol, not a report of completed trial results. This public archive copy removes the author’s student identifier and updates PDF metadata; the scientific text is otherwise unchanged.
title: Impact of the FatSecret App on Weight Management and Physical Activity among New Zealand Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial Protocol

summary: eglish version)This work presents a three-parameter mechanical-medium framework for the forward derivation of physical constants and characteristic scales within the Four-Forces–Quantum-Induction research program. The central objective is to determine how a minimal set of medium parameters can generate a hierarchy of microscopic and macroscopic physical quantities through a closed forward construction, rather than through post-hoc fitting to target observations. The current formulation includes an absolute-scale solution that no longer requires Newton’s gravitational constant as an external scale-setting calibration. Newton’s constant is instead used as a downstream consistency and round-trip closure test. The framework develops explicit relations among the characteristic medium density, elastic scale, viscosity-related input, characteristic radii, effective gravitational quantities, particle-scale structures, and derived observables. Strict NoAlias and NoDoubleCount rules are applied throughout to prevent numerically similar quantities or multiple readouts of the same physical inventory from being incorrectly identified or counted twice. An independent internal consistency test is provided by two routes to the model’s Hubble-equivalent scale. A global-field calculation and a local curvature or pressure-gradient calculation converge to approximately 67.33789544 km/s/Mpc. This quantity is reported as a model Hubble-equivalent scale. Its exact identification with the standard cosmological expansion rate H0 remains subject to a separate clock-identity condition and is therefore not assumed. The release also incorporates the current charge-conjugate electron-origin structure and the resulting birth-population asymmetry. The frozen current value is 6.117043204146319e-10. This result is treated as a theoretical output of the current model structure and is not presented as a new blind observational test. A strict theory-to-evidence firewall is maintained throughout the project. The workflow is: authority snapshot, declared inputs, forward operator, frozen prediction, external evidence, and statistical or qualitative score. Observational information is not permitted to modify a prediction after the prediction has been frozen. The empirical portfolio is intentionally reported with mixed outcomes. It includes compatible historical cross-checks, the Hubble-equivalent forward result with its explicit clock qualifier, cosmic-age consistency checks, an electron g-2 comparison that currently fails the frozen operator at high experimental precision, ring-laser results that remain retrospective rather than a new blind holdout, and prospective constant-drift predictions reserved for future evaluation. Compatible but non-discriminating tests are distinguished from genuinely discriminating evidence. The accompanying archive contains the English manuscript, validation and evidence status material, selected derivation records, Hubble-equivalent and asymmetry authority snapshots, provenance and reproducibility information, SHA256 manifests, and the sealed v4.43 historical authority package. This Zenodo release should therefore be interpreted as a frozen research record of the current theoretical construction, its absolute-scale closure, its derived cross-scale relations, and its explicitly classified empirical status. It is not a claim that every external observable has been successfully reproduced. Failed, conditional, prospective, and not-yet-opened evidence channels are retained explicitly as part of the scientific record.     预印本 — 未经同行评审。

summary: Modern AI assistants, agents, and decision-support systems increasingly rely on information beyond model parameters by retrieving documents, accessing memory, invoking tools, and combining external evidence. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is one prominent realization of this broader information-grounding paradigm. Yet external grounding does not by itself ensure trustworthiness. Systems can still fail under incomplete, noisy, conflicting, or misleading evidence, and these failures become harder to diagnose as retrieval, reasoning, memory, tool use, and generation interact. Existing evaluation frameworks measure important aspects of system quality, but do not necessarily ensure deliberate coverage of the conditions most likely to expose system vulnerabilities. We introduce PRISM as a methodology for systematic stress testing of retrieval-grounded AI through controlled synthetic data generation. Rather than treating evaluation data as a static benchmark, PRISM constructs and validates document and question-answer pairs designed to reproduce deployment-relevant failure conditions. Its 25 evaluation instruments are organized across ten diversity dimensions and eight thematic clusters, covering conditions such as fragmented or noisy evidence, lexical and semantic mismatch, unanswerable queries, and adversarial or epistemically unreliable content. Because these conditions are generated synthetically, they can reproduce relevant document and evidence characteristics without requiring access to proprietary or sensitive operational data. Stress conditions are also linked to concrete system choices to support targeted diagnosis. PRISM is expected to provide reproducible and traceable evaluation artifacts that help reveal vulnerabilities before deployment and distinguish failures originating from retrieval, evidence selection, generation, or abstention. Automated construction and validation are also intended to reduce the manual effort associated with human-curated evaluation sets while preserving the control, coverage, and consistency needed for systematic evaluation. More broadly, PRISM reframes evaluation as not only a measurement problem but also an experimental-design problem. By complementing existing metrics, human evaluation, observability, and post-deployment monitoring, it contributes toward more systematic pre-deployment assessment of increasingly agentic, retrieval-grounded AI systems.
title: Toward Trustworthy Retrieval-Grounded AI through Synthetic Stress Testing

summary: SideCow-VSS is a side-view dairy cow video semantic segmentation dataset developed to support computer vision research in precision livestock farming. The original study describes 921 five-second video clips with dense pixel-level annotations, sampled at 10 frames per second under real dairy farm conditions. The annotations were generated using a semi-automated pipeline involving YOLOv11, SAM2, and manual verification. This version (v1.0.0) provides the currently available JPEG frames and PNG segmentation annotation files, organized into the original training, validation, and testing splits. The release contains 46,024 JPEG files and 46,024 PNG files, distributed as follows: Training: 32,177 JPEG files and 32,177 PNG files. Validation: 6,897 JPEG files and 6,897 PNG files. Testing: 6,950 JPEG files and 6,950 PNG files. The dataset supports semantic segmentation of dairy cows and background regions. The original data partitions and available files are preserved without reconstructing missing frames. For details of dataset construction, annotation methodology, and benchmarking, please refer to the associated publication: Yao, L., Liu, J., Hong, W., Kong, F., Fan, Z., Lei, L., & Li, X. (2025). summary: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.
title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems

summary: Tools that claim to detect emerging research topics are rarely judged on their own lists. Our main contribution is a protocol that makes such judgement possible. A bet freezes four things before its verdict can be known: the date of the photograph, the population of candidates, the verdict rule, and the comparison with chance drawn among the same candidates. The list has a fixed length, is read on two axes (champions and failures) against a computed ceiling, and is sealed by cryptographic fingerprint; sealing proves that a list existed at a date, not that it is right. A topic is a champion if its yearly volume of records triples within three years and reaches 100, a failure if it falls by 30%. We apply the protocol to one detector on PubMed/MEDLINE, in three separate blocks. On a retrospective benchmark (2017-2022), chance among the candidates yields 26.7 champions and 15.1 failures out of 120 slots; the detector yields 85 and 3, and under nine pre-registered variants of the verdict rule its champions stay between 2.5 and 5.0 times chance, with no more failures. The detector was developed with these verdicts known, and its specification is not published. Prospective validation rests on six sealed bets, judged in early 2029 and early 2030; only bets 5 and 6 test exactly the instrument of the benchmark. A secondary, exploratory study applies the same judge to eight research funders: under exact name matching, which may disadvantage grant texts, the detector's lists are more concentrated in future champions than the twenty topics named in the most grants of each funder (70.8% against 20.8% to 35.8%, chance 22.3%). We document data defects, negative results and the limits of each comparison.
title: Sealed bets on emerging research topics: a protocol for judging early detection, applied to a detector and to eight research funders

summary: Capability benchmarks measure what large language models can do, but not whether their recommendations remain appropriate as decision conditions change. This paper proposes a trajectory-based measurement framework and prospective validation protocol for artificial wisdom, defined behaviorally as context-sensitive regulation of judgment. Versioned reference specifications determine admissible responses and transition materiality before evaluation. Seven stage-level criteria assess judgment under current conditions, while two transition components assess material-update adequacy and commitment-preserving stability. Stability requires prior adequacy; switching within registered commitment classes is permitted, and persistent error earns no stability credit. A nine-component profile is primary, with a secondary bottleneck score and separate critical-failure reporting. Three simplified simulations examine precision, bottleneck estimation, and sensitivity to model-family count. A single-criterion simulation met its precision criteria at 24 scenarios per domain. Near a bottleneck tie, the estimated minimum had a downward bias of 0.55 points at that size. A simplified incremental-prediction simulation detected a Brier improvement of 0.027 with probabilities of .508 and .742 using eight and twelve families, respectively; it does not establish power for the operational protocol. An exploratory predecessor-rubric study comprising 71 evaluation records illustrates aggregation sensitivity but does not validate the proposed instrument. The twelve-family target remains provisional pending feasibility assessment and calibration of the complete analysis. Whether the profile predicts independent decision outcomes beyond capability remains an open empirical question.
title: Evaluating Artificial Wisdom (AW): A Trajectory-Based Framework for Context-Sensitive Decision Regulation

summary: Objective: Choosing between noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS) and invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for acute respiratory failure is a time-sensitive decision. Although guidelines provide population-level guidance, it remains unclear who benefits more from NIRS than IMV. The standard outcome, ventilator-free days at 28 days (VFD-28), scores death and prolonged ventilation equally, and current estimators do not distinguish between them. We developed and validated a censoring-aware Digital Twin framework for Individualized Treatment Effects of Non-Invasive Respiratory Support (DINIRS) to estimate individualized treatment effects (ITEs) that capture both mortality and ventilation duration. Materials and Methods: We emulated a target trial in 5,336 MIMIC-IV patients and trained DINIRS on 23 baseline clinical variables measured during the first 24 ICU hours. A transformer encoder with a survival attention gate decomposed VFD-28 into survival probability and conditional ventilation duration. A cross-fitted, doubly robust learner estimated ITEs. We externally validated DINIRS in 2,540 patients from the multi-site eICU-CRD dataset without retraining. Results: The DINIRS policy achieved a mean benefit of 2.07 ventilator-free days per patient (207 per 100 patients) compared with observed practice. Predicted NIRS benefit was higher among patients with less organ dysfunction (88.4% versus 49.0%) and persisted across hypoxemia severity. External validation reproduced this pattern. Discussion: The NIRS benefit stemmed from shorter ventilation among survivors rather than from reduced mortality, indicating that avoiding intubation-associated complications was the primary mechanism. Conclusion: Prospective validation is needed before these estimates inform treatment decisions. The decomposition framework can be extended beyond respiratory support to any zero-inflated composite outcome.
title: A Digital Twin for Individualized Treatment Effects of Non-Invasive Respiratory Support Strategies (DINIRS)

summary: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with increased risks of stroke, heart failure, and mortality. Recent ECG foundation models offer transferable representations for automated AF detection. However, their relative effectiveness remains unclear because existing studies use different datasets, preprocessing procedures, classifiers, and validation protocols. This study presents FOUND-AF, a unified, leakage-controlled, and deployment-oriented benchmarking framework that evaluates the quality of pretrained ECG representations under identical experimental conditions. Nine publicly available foundation models from five families, including HuBERT-ECG, CLEF, ST-MEM, ECG-JEPA, and ECGFounder, were evaluated across four heterogeneous ECG datasets, namely AFDB, CinC2017, CPSC2021, and LTAFDB. All models were used as frozen feature extractors with standardized preprocessing, model-native resampling, a fixed XGBoost classifier, and recording-level grouped cross-validation. The evaluation included classification metrics, receiver operating characteristic analysis, paired recording-level bootstrap comparisons with Holm correction, embedding-space visualization, and computational efficiency profiling. The ECGFounder model consistently achieved the strongest overall performance across datasets while offering a favorable trade-off between accuracy, model size, inference time, and memory usage. FOUND-AF therefore provides a reproducible framework for selecting ECG foundation models and demonstrates that compact, clinically pretrained encoders can support robust and computationally efficient AF detection across heterogeneous acquisition settings.
title: FOUND-AF: Benchmarking ECG Foundation Models for Atrial Fibrillation Detection

summary: Large language model research agents can connect literature retrieval, analysis code, and manuscript preparation, but coherent output does not establish scientific validity. We developed Plato-Bio, a biology-routed extension of the open Plato/Denario architecture that couples explicit workflow states with provenance records, citation checks, claim-to-evidence links, scoped file writes, and publication gates. A source audit identified and repaired three defects that could distort evaluation: loss of task domain in the default factory, omission of declared method signals from scoring, and evidence sidecars that lacked the drafted-claim denominator. On the current clean revision, the full Python suite completed with 931 passes, six skips, and no failures or errors; targeted biology, genomics, evidence/citation, and adversarial-safety suites likewise completed without failure. We evaluated two narrow use cases. In a frozen historical rediscovery task, independent pre-1986 literature bridges ranked the later-studied relation between fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon first; TF-IDF ranked it second and corpus frequency third. This single curated task measures retrospective ranking, not prospective discovery. In a separate comparison of AlphaFold models with experimental structures for 15 human proteins, 11 targets had high-confidence-core C-alpha RMSD below 1 Angstrom (median 0.501 Angstrom). Four targets exceeded 2 Angstrom, and confidence masking reduced the SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Angstrom over 74 residues. The workflow emitted 27 traceable discrepancy regions, all retained as unvalidated hypotheses. Plato-Bio therefore provides reproducible software contracts and auditable screening baselines; broader claims of agent efficacy or biological novelty require preregistered evaluation, independent review, and prospective validation.
title: Plato-Bio: verification-first biological novelty screening with temporal rediscovery and structural benchmarks

summary: Tuning of gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) is a major bottleneck for scaling spin qubit technologies. We present a deep learning (DL) driven, semantic-segmentation pipeline that performs charge auto-tuning by locating transition lines in full charge stability diagrams (CSDs) and returns gate voltage targets for the single charge regime. We assemble and manually annotate a large, heterogeneous dataset of 1015 experimental CSDs measured from silicon QD devices, spanning nine design geometries, multiple wafers, and fabrication runs. A U-Net style convolutional neural network (CNN) with a MobileNetV2 encoder is trained and validated through five-fold group cross validation. Our model achieves an overall offline tuning success of 80.0% in locating the single-charge regime, with peak performance exceeding 88% for some designs. We analyze dominant failure modes and propose targeted mitigations. Finally, wide-range diagram segmentation also naturally enables scalable physic-based feature extraction that can feed back to fabrication and design workflows and outline a roadmap for real-time integration in a cryogenic wafer prober. Overall, our results show that neural network (NN) based wide-diagram segmentation is a practical step toward automated, high-throughput charge tuning for silicon QD qubits.
title: Automatic Charge State Tuning of 300 mm FDSOI Quantum Dots Using Neural Network Segmentation of Charge Stability Diagram

summary: Camera images are ubiquitous in machine learning research. They also play a central role in the delivery of important services spanning medicine and environmental surveying. However, the application of machine learning models in these domains has been limited because of robustness concerns. A primary failure mode are performance drops due to differences between the training and deployment data. While there are methods to prospectively validate the robustness of machine learning models to such dataset drifts, existing approaches do not account for explicit models of the primary object of interest: the data. This limits our ability to study and understand the relationship between data generation and downstream machine learning model performance in a physically accurate manner. In this study, we demonstrate how to overcome this limitation by pairing traditional machine learning with physical optics to obtain explicit and differentiable data models. We demonstrate how such data models can be constructed for image data and used to control downstream machine learning model performance related to dataset drift. The findings are distilled into three applications. First, drift synthesis enables the controlled generation of physically faithful drift test cases to power model selection and targeted generalization. Second, the gradient connection between machine learning task model and data model allows advanced, precise tolerancing of task model sensitivity to changes in the data generation. These drift forensics can be used to precisely specify the acceptable data environments in which a task model may be run. Third, drift optimization opens up the possibility to create drifts that can help the task model learn better faster, effectively optimizing the data generating process itself. A guide to access the open code and datasets is available at https://github.com/aiaudit-org/raw2logit.
title: Data Models for Dataset Drift Controls in Machine Learning With Optical Images

summary: Conformal selection promises distribution-free, finite-sample control of the error rate of a decision, and has been proposed as a safety layer for machine-learning CRISPR guide design. We ask whether such a certificate is attainable from the validated off-target data that exist. The constraint is arithmetic: a conformal p-value cannot fall below one divided by the calibration cohort size plus one, so a Benjamini-Hochberg selection certifies a single candidate only when that cohort is at least the candidate pool size divided by the tolerated error rate. Public cohorts supply ten validated guides, whereas a pool of two thousand at a ten percent error rate needs twenty thousand; the accepted set is consequently empty in over ninety-six percent of splits. Two benchmarking findings explain why this went unnoticed. The standard CIRCLE-seq file lists ten guides under eighty on-target strings, so grouping cross-validation on the sequence column trains and tests on one guide; corrected, pair-level discrimination and per-guide fidelity collapse. With that leakage removed, a training-free position-weight score and a bare count of near-match genomic sites are not beaten by a trained oracle. We give the corrected protocol, the baselines a new model must beat, and the cohort size a certified pipeline needs.
title: What Conformal Selection Can Certify in CRISPR Off-Target Design:Benchmark Leakage, Free Baselines, and a Finite-Sample Cohort Requirement

summary: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). The stability term was lower at the savanna site (0.39) than at the zoo (0.65-0.67), showing that it penalises the natural diel cycle of bird activity. Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation provide a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.
title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can benefit from more sophisticated retrieval, but extra retrieval may be unnecessary for many questions and gains in evidence retrieval may not translate into faithful or correct answers. We study a cost-aware, two-action retrieval policy that chooses between a dense-retrieval-plus-reranking baseline and a hybrid lexical--dense retriever. Rather than classifying baseline retrieval as simply successful or unsuccessful, we estimate the question-specific incremental evidence-retrieval benefit of hybrid retrieval using features available before the routing decision. A regularized linear model and decision threshold are selected using document-grouped cross-validation and frozen prior to held-out evaluation. On 60 previously unseen QASPER training-split articles (188 questions, 169 evidence-evaluable), the policy triggers hybrid retrieval on 46 questions (24.5\%) and obtains the same evidence Hit@10 as always-hybrid retrieval (78.70\%, versus 76.92\% for always-keep). Paired, paper-cluster bootstrap intervals do not establish a reliable utility advantage. We further compare generated answers from a 4-bit Qwen3-4B model under the three retrieval policies. Provisional answer-level assessments show no clear correctness or faithfulness improvement after partial review, despite the evidence-retrieval result. The generation assessments remain model-assisted and lack independent human validation. These results expose an important distinction between retrieving relevant evidence efficiently and improving the reliability of the generated answer. The work is presented as a reproducible empirical study, not a claim of statistically established answer-quality superiority.
title: When Is Additional Retrieval Worthwhile? A Cost-Aware Study of Evidence Gain and Answer Reliability in RAG

summary: Training-time explanation regularization is often evaluated by whether saliency maps become more concentrated within annotated regions. We argue that this criterion alone is insufficient: transformation consistency, lesion localization, and faithfulness to the classifier are distinct properties and should be evaluated separately, particularly in medical imaging. We examine this distinction through a case study of Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency (CGC) in three-class brain tumor MRI classification. Using a single-channel ResNet-50 with five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation, we compare a cross-entropy baseline with CGC. CGC changes overall Pointing Game (PG) from $27.24\%$ to $36.02\%$ and Relevance Mass Accuracy (RMA) from $11.17\%$ to $18.01\%$, while classification accuracy changes from $93.63\%$ to $94.87\%$. Perturbation-based faithfulness metrics show inconsistent changes: Insertion Area Under the Curve (IAUC) changes from $0.73$ to $0.78$, whereas Deletion Area Under the Curve (DAUC) favors the baseline ($0.36$ versus $0.41$; lower is better), and overall Iterative Removal Of Features (IROF) is $0.57$ for both models. These results support our position that improved spatial agreement with pathology should not be interpreted as a general improvement in explanation faithfulness. We therefore recommend property-specific evaluation in which the property targeted by the explanation objective, spatial agreement with reference regions, and model reliance are measured and reported separately.
title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.

summary: The study examines the physiological adaptation of boxers to mid-altitude conditions (1,800‒2,200 m above sea level) and substantiates the need to individualize training loads based on functional markers: blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), heart rate (HR), lactate levels, and maximum oxygen consumption (VO2). The article presents the results of a pedagogical experiment involving 24 qualified boxers (CMS and MS), divided into control and experimental groups. The experimental methodology included real-time monitoring of functional markers and real-time adjustment of the weekly microcycle. Following a 4-week high-altitude training camp, the experimental group demonstrated a significant increase in VO2 by 6.8%, hemoglobin concentration by 4.3%, and an improvement in the heart rate recovery index by 34.4% compared to the control group (p<0.05). The obtained data demonstrate the high efficiency of an individualized approach to load planning in midaltitude areas and are recommended for use in the training of highly qualified athletes.
title: Individualization of Boxing Training Loads in Middle-Altitude Conditions Based on Functional Adaptation Markers.

summary: Presents the results of an experimental study on the effectiveness of computer biomechanical analysis in improving the technical training of qualified wrestlers. The aim of the study was to determine the effect of an integrated biomechanical throw-assessment system on athletes' competitive performance. Thirty-two wrestlers (Masters of Sport and Candidates for Master of Sport) participated in the pedagogical experiment and were divided into a control group (n=16) and an experimental group (n=16). The experiment lasted six months. The control group trained according to the standard programme, while the experimental group additionally used a hardware-software complex for three-dimensional biomechanical motion analysis based on inertial sensors and computer video modelling. Kinematic and dynamic parameters of the key throw elements were recorded: joint angular velocities, trajectory of the overall centre of mass, and the temporal force-transfer profile. As a result of the experimental methodology, athletes in the experimental group showed a significant improvement in biomechanical movement coordination (p<0.05); the effectiveness of technical actions in competitions increased: the throw execution rate rose from 38.4% to 56.7%, and the judges' technical score from 6.1 to 7.8 points. It was established that systematic feedback through computer biomechanical data forms a more stable motor stereotype and accelerates the correction of technical errors. The data obtained confirm the feasibility of introducing computer biomechanical technologies into the training system for qualified wrestlers.
title: Effectiveness of Computerized Biomechanical Assessment of Throwing Technique in Qualified Wrestlers

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.
title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation

summary: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.
title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions

summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.
title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code

summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for graph understanding and decision-making, while System One models such as Jev select directly from supplied options. However, the capabilities of System One models on graph-related tasks remain unclear. We introduce GraphDecisionBench, a model-independent benchmark that combines structural task profiles, matched graph-text input contrasts and heuristic-proposal controls to diagnose graph decision performance. We evaluate Jev and related choice-based models alongside language-model baselines, covering fourteen model-interface configurations. Jev's results illustrate the benchmark's central distinctions: accurate adjacency recognition does not guarantee broader structural correctness, joint graph-text input does not consistently improve prediction, and feasible construction does not establish high solution quality. Its task contracts, candidate interfaces and scoring rules support comparison across native selectors and language-model adapters. Code and aggregate results are available at https://github.com/VictorYXL/GraphDecisionBench.
title: GraphDecisionBench: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks

summary: We develop a price-based framework for stochastic portfolio theory in which trading strategies are generated from nominal price weights and evaluated relative to a price-weighted benchmark. Stock splits and reverse splits induce jumps in the generating weights without changing the value of existing investments. In a semimartingale market with predictable adjustment events, we incorporate the corresponding share adjustments into the self-financing condition and construct additively and multiplicatively generated strategies with explicit jump-corrected wealth decompositions. For additive generation, an entropy-based example exhibits relative wealth tending to $-\infty$ almost surely under repeated splits, demonstrating why the usual argument for long-horizon relative arbitrage does not extend directly. We also show that advance adjustment information alone provides no model-free guarantee of improved performance for functionally generated portfolios. For multiplicative generation, wealth-preserving restarts retain the classical portfolio allocation evaluated at the current price weights. We also establish a correspondence with the capitalization-based framework that preserves absolute wealth and yields a strategy-independent benchmark conversion. We illustrate the framework using daily NYSE data, comparing price- and capitalization-weighted benchmarks and the corresponding diversity-weighted portfolios across price- and capitalization-selected universes.
title: A Price-Based Framework for Stochastic Portfolio Theory

summary: We present a systematic study of the quantum phase transition from a Dirac semimetal to an antiferromagnetic Mott insulator in the honeycomb-lattice Hubbard model, using finite-temperature auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) simulations. Given the dynamical critical exponent $z=1$ at criticality, we scale the inverse temperature $β$ with the linear system size $L$, i.e., $βt=L$ (with $t$ as the hopping amplitude), to approach the thermodynamic and zero-temperature limits simultaneously. On the algorithmic front, we generalize the fast Fourier transform in path propagation to multi-sublattice systems and employ the delayed update technique in configuration updates to accelerate the AFQMC simulations. These advances enable us to access unprecedented system sizes of up to $3528$ sites (with $L=42$ and $βt = 42$). We additionally use twist-averaged boundary conditions to reduce the finite-size effects in computed observables. On the physical side, we determine the Dirac quantum criticality via finite-size scaling analysis of the spin correlations and off-diagonal single-particle Green's function, and locate the critical point at $U_c/t=3.731(4)$ with the critical exponents $ν=1.097(7)$, $η_φ=0.72(2)$ and $η_ψ=0.155(6)$. We further corroborate the critical point by examining several relevant quantities, including the quasiparticle weight, Fermi-liquid parameter, charge compressibility, $U$-derivative of double occupancy, and fidelity susceptibility. Our work establishes an independent benchmark for the chiral Heisenberg Gross-Neveu-Yukawa criticality in the honeycomb Hubbard model, offering a complementary perspective to previous ground-state simulations.
title: Finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo study of Dirac quantum criticality: Algorithmic advances and comprehensive analysis

summary: Many existing Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions on mobile devices rely on an extensive collection of sensitive data, raising privacy concerns and often requiring storage for both context and model improvement. Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) aims to address this by emphasizing mobile device integration and a privacy-first design. The central claim of PCC is that it does not store any user data and that user input and user accounts are unlinkable. While most of the PCC system specifications are public, compiled binaries add a layer of opaqueness. There are no reproducible builds, and there are no symbols within those binaries, creating potential discrepancies between the specification and what is shipped to the user. Additionally, the underlying models and interfaces for querying PCC are not openly accessible, limiting academic evaluation of model properties, such as accuracy. This poses a challenge in assessing whether a privacy-preserving approach like PCC is actually trustworthy while also providing high-quality answers. We are the first to reverse-engineer the PCC implementation on mobile devices to evaluate privacy aspects and to open its non-public interfaces on local devices to support custom PCC queries. We demonstrate this level of access beyond Apple's intended use cases by independently benchmarking the PCC model. We enable future research by making our PCC benchmarking framework publicly available.
title: Unlocking Apple's Private Cloud Compute: An Analysis of Privacy-Preserving Artificial Intelligence

summary: This paper presents our submission to the ACMMM25 - Grand Challenge on Multimedia Verification. We developed a multi-agent verification system that combines Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with specialized verification tools to detect multimedia misinformation. Our system operates through six stages: raw data processing, planning, information extraction, deep research, evidence collection, and report generation. The core Deep Researcher Agent employs four tools: reverse image search, metadata analysis, fact-checking databases, and verified news processing that extracts spatial, temporal, attribution, and motivational context. We demonstrate our approach on a challenge dataset sample involving complex multimedia content. Our system successfully verified content authenticity, extracted precise geolocation and timing information, and traced source attribution across multiple platforms, effectively addressing real-world multimedia verification scenarios.
title: Multimedia Verification Through Multi-Agent Deep Research Multimodal Large Language Models

summary: We develop and validate a one-dimensional electron-ion two-fluid model, self-consistently coupled to Maxwell equations, for magnetosonic structures generated by a moving charged source. The model is independently benchmarked against kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations to assess its ability to reproduce electrostatic and electromagnetic responses. In the zero-magnetic-field limit, the electrostatic precursor structures are validated using the Korteweg--de Vries amplitude--width invariant. For a finite magnetic field, the frequency and propagation speed of the far wake are consistent with the low-frequency fast-magnetosonic branch, providing a linear benchmark for the electromagnetic response. The model reproduces the transition from a wake-dominated regime to localized forward precursors as the source velocity exceeds the magnetosonic speed, and to source-locked pinned structures at higher velocities. Independent PIC simulations recover the principal features of these regimes, supporting the validity of the two-fluid description for the parameters considered. By retaining separate electron and ion dynamics, electron inertia, and charge-separation effects, the validated model provides a framework for investigating source-driven plasma-wave structures across a broader range of plasma conditions and source-magnetic-field geometries, with potential applications to interpreting plasma-wave signatures associated with moving charged objects in space plasmas.
title: Magnetosonic Solitons Driven by a Moving Charged Source: Two-Fluid Modeling and PIC Validation

summary: This version extends the previously archived replication package for within-project and cross-project just-in-time software defect prediction. C5: Sensitivity analyses examining SHAP evaluation sample size and background selection. C6: A descriptive simulation of defect-oriented commit review prioritization. C7: External validation using six historical Kamei projects, comprising 960 model records and corresponding global SHAP feature-importance vectors. The C7 source-provenance audit confirmed that SHA-256 fingerprints, input summaries, and temporal training/test splits matched the archived experimental records for all six projects. All 36 crosschecks passed. This verification does not constitute independent retraining of all models. The findings concern the sensitivity of global SHAP feature rankings to training conditions. They do not establish causal effects, explanation correctness, or demonstrated benefits to software developers. The archive contains experimental outputs, analysis scripts, figures, and reproducibility documentation. Original third-party ApacheJIT and Kamei datasets are not redistributed. summary: Supporting code and data for the exploratory ETV4 case study “Sequence and family context shape ETV4 representations in protein language models”. The deposit contains 711 biological/control activation arrays from ESM-2 650M, ESM-2 3B and ProFam, 71 numerical-qualification arrays with receipts, and a versioned repository snapshot containing processed results, input sequences and prompts, fixed readout masks and configurations, analysis and figure-generation code, provenance and supplementary information. summary: We present the first mechanised formalisation of Romanov's Triplet Logic (TLS) in the Rocq proof assistant. TLS is a combinatorial framework originally motivated by Boolean satisfiability, based on triplet structures and a filter that we call Simple Vertex Intersection (SVI). We formalise the core of TLS, including its translation from 3-CNF, the clearing procedure, and the SVI algorithm. For the well-formed sliding-window fragment, we prove explicit polynomial-time bounds for the filter stages and verify the translation and intersection operations. Our main contribution is a precise correctness boundary: for general formulas, SVI non-emptiness is necessary but not sufficient for satisfiability; for aligned structures, we prove a full bi-implication, extended to systems of structures. We also formalise the grouped-window translation and provide a formal counterexample to its completeness. We introduce VFR (Verified Filter for Romanov's triplet logic), an extracted OCaml prototype that implements a verified decision procedure for the sliding-window fragment and a sound filter for general 3-CNF, with a Python runtime and Docker packaging. Benchmarks corroborate the predicted behaviour, and the complete toolchain is available as a curated Zenodo artifact. The Rocq development comprises over 23,000 lines of code, with 424 proved lemmas and no unproved assumptions.
title: Formal Verification of Romanov's Triplet Logic: A Verified Filter for Sliding-window 3-CNF with Application to Structured Formulas

summary: We present JOR-Bench, a collection of five Japanese-language benchmarks for evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to formulate and solve operations research (OR) problems. Each benchmark is a Japanese translation of an existing English benchmark: IndustryOR, MAMO Complex LP, NL4OPT, OptiBench, and OptMATH, covering 1,319 problems spanning linear programming, mixed-integer programming, non-linear programming, and combinatorial optimization. JOR-Bench is a solver-independent benchmark that can be used with any solver or programming language, and consists of pairs of Japanese problem statements and expected numerical answers. We evaluate seven LLMs, including multilingual general-purpose models and Japanese-specialized models, on both the original English and the new Japanese versions, and compare performance across languages. For the main evaluation, we standardize execution with the Python interface to OR-Tools to make model outputs comparable and reproducible with open-source software. Our results show that OR formulation ability is largely language-neutral for strong multilingual models; the overall average accuracy difference between English and Japanese is only $-0.3$ pp. Yet error analysis reveals subtle cross-lingual differences, including a pragmatic disambiguation failure in some domains that causes models to output decision-variable values instead of the objective value when the prompt is in Japanese.
title: JOR-Bench: Japanese Operations Research Benchmarks for Large Language Models

summary: Reusable robot skills are becoming the basic units through which embodied agents turn open-ended instructions into long-horizon physical behavior. We argue that, while foundation models have collapsed the cost of creating these skills, the cost of trusting them has not. Existing skill-evolution loops refine skills through execution feedback, unit tests, environment reward, or LLM self-critique, but these signals provide only trace-level evidence: they show that a skill worked on sampled executions, not that skill-induced plans satisfy temporal safety contracts under untested conditions. We introduce VASO, a framework for verification-guided self-evolution of LLM-generated robot skill contracts. In VASO, each skill is represented as a semantic contract with two coupled interfaces: a formal interface that aligns robot states, observations, and control commands with logical propositions for model checking, and a planner-facing interface that guides executable behavior generation. A model checker first filters logically inconsistent skill contracts, then verifies plans induced by the skill against global and local temporal specifications. When verification fails, VASO translates the counterexample trace into a textual gradient that updates the reusable skill contract while keeping foundation-model weights frozen. On Clearpath Jackal and PX4 quadcopter tasks, VASO reaches 97.2% formal-specification compliance using fewer than 100 optimization samples, outperforming execution-feedback, prompt-optimization, and fine-tuning baselines. To our knowledge, VASO is the first framework that closes the loop between formal verification and self-evolving LLM-generated skills for physical AI agents: formal counterexamples become optimization feedback for reusable robot skill contracts, rather than merely verifying one-off plans, tuning planner prompts, or fine-tuning model weights.
title: VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents

summary: Mathematical reasoning demands two critical, complementary skills: constructing rigorous proofs for true statements and discovering counterexamples that disprove false ones. However, current AI efforts in mathematics focus almost exclusively on proof construction, often neglecting the equally important task of finding counterexamples. In this paper, we address this gap by fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to reason about and generate counterexamples. We formalize this task as formal counterexample generation, which requires LLMs not only to propose candidate counterexamples but also to produce formal proofs that can be automatically verified in the Lean 4 theorem prover. To enable effective learning, we introduce a symbolic mutation strategy that constructs candidate counterexample-generation tasks by systematically extracting theorems and removing selected hypotheses. Together with curated datasets, this strategy enables a multi-reward expert iteration framework that substantially enhances both the effectiveness and efficiency of training LLMs for counterexample generation and theorem proving. Experiments on three newly collected benchmarks validate the advantages of our approach, showing that the mutation strategy and training framework yield substantial performance gains.
title: Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with Large Language Models
