summary: Hydrogen threatens the structural integrity of metals and thus predicting hydrogen-material interactions is key to unlocking the role of hydrogen in the energy transition. Quantifying the interplay between material deformation and hydrogen diffusion ahead of cracks and other stress concentrators is key to the prediction and prevention of hydrogen-assisted failures. In this work, a generalised theoretical and computational framework is presented that for the first time encompasses: (i) stress-assisted diffusion, (ii) hydrogen trapping due to multiple trap types, rigorously accounting for the rate of creation of dislocation trap sites, (iii) hydrogen transport through dislocations, (iv) equilibrium (Oriani) and non-equilibrium (McNabb-Foster) trapping kinetics, (v) hydrogen-induced softening, and (vi) hydrogen uptake, considering the role of hydrostatic stresses and local electrochemistry. Particular emphasis is placed on the numerical implementation in COMSOL Multiphysics, releasing the relevant models and discussing stability, discretisation and solver details. Each of the elements of the framework is independently benchmarked against results from the literature and implications for the prediction of hydrogen-assisted fractures are discussed. The second part of this work (Part II) shows how these crack tip predictions can be combined with crack growth simulations.
title: A COMSOL framework for predicting hydrogen embrittlement -- Part I: coupled hydrogen transport

summary: We study the performance of sequential contention resolution and matching algorithms on random graphs with vanishing edge probabilities. When the edges of the graph are processed in an adversarially-chosen order, we derive a new OCRS that is $0.382$-selectable, attaining the "independence benchmark" from the literature under the vanishing edge probabilities assumption. Complementary to this positive result, we show that no OCRS can be more than $0.390$-selectable, significantly improving upon the upper bound of $0.428$ from the literature. We also derive negative results that are specialized to bipartite graphs or subfamilies of OCRSs. Meanwhile, when the edges of the graph are processed in a uniformly random order, we show that the simple greedy contention resolution scheme which accepts all active and feasible edges is $1/2$-selectable. This result is tight due to a known upper bound. We then show that when the algorithm can choose the processing order, a slight tweak to the random order---give each vertex a random priority and process edges in lexicographic order---results in a strictly better contention resolution scheme that is $1-\ln(2-1/e)\approx0.510$-selectable. Moreover, we show that this bound is tight over any sequential contention resolution scheme, even one which may adaptively choose the order in which it processes edges. This provides a separation from the $0.544$ upper bound for offline contention resolution implied by the classic result of Karp and Sipser. Our positive results also apply to online matching on $1$-uniform random graphs with vanishing (non-identical) edge probabilities, extending and unifying some results from the random graphs literature.
title: Online Matching and Contention Resolution for Edge Arrivals with Vanishing Probabilities

summary: We introduce an automated, formal, counterexample-based approach to synthesise Barrier Certificates (BC) for the safety verification of continuous and hybrid dynamical models. The approach is underpinned by an inductive framework: this is structured as a sequential loop between a learner, which manipulates a candidate BC structured as a neural network, and a sound verifier, which either certifies the candidate's validity or generates counter-examples to further guide the learner. We compare the approach against state-of-the-art techniques, over polynomial and non-polynomial dynamical models: the outcomes show that we can synthesise sound BCs up to two orders of magnitude faster, with in particular a stark speedup on the verification engine (up to five orders less), whilst needing a far smaller data set (up to three orders less) for the learning part. Beyond improvements over the state of the art, we further challenge the new approach on a hybrid dynamical model and on larger-dimensional models, and showcase the numerical robustness of our algorithms and codebase.
title: Automated and Formal Synthesis of Neural Barrier Certificates for Dynamical Models

summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 42 examines why enterprise artificial intelligence strategy is moving beyond the assumption that one general-purpose model should serve every workload. The paper argues that model selection is increasingly an intelligence-allocation decision involving capability, cost, latency, governance, data restrictions, decision authority and measurable business outcomes. As enterprise AI expands across routine classification, specialised extraction, complex reasoning, multimodal production and consequential decisions, different categories of work require different execution approaches. The paper distinguishes model selection, inference tiering, model routing, policy-controlled routing and outcome verification. It proposes that enterprises should first determine whether generative inference is required, define the minimum capability needed, apply mandatory eligibility constraints, select an appropriate execution route, establish escalation conditions and verify whether the completed outcome meets a predetermined business acceptance standard. Six author-developed frameworks structure this operating model. The AI Workload Classification framework divides work into deterministic, routine language, specialised, complex reasoning and consequential-decision categories. The Model Routing Matrix separates mandatory policy constraints from economic and performance preferences. The Capability-Cost Frontier evaluates eligible models against verified acceptance and complete delivery cost. The Model Escalation Ladder defines structured movement from deterministic execution through compact, specialised and frontier intelligence to human authority. Minimum Sufficient Intelligence identifies the least expensive eligible intelligence capable of satisfying the complete business requirement. Cost per Accepted Outcome, or CPAO, measures total attributable workflow delivery cost against completed business outcomes that satisfy defined acceptance standards. The analysis also challenges the assumption that sophisticated routing automatically produces superior economics. Evidence from LLMRouterBench shows strong model complementarity while demonstrating that several routing approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines. The paper therefore argues that routing complexity requires evidence of incremental value rather than being treated as an architectural objective in itself. Commercial case studies examine three different intelligence-allocation mechanisms. Sword Health illustrates central gateway control, provider portability, policy enforcement and cost attribution. Forethought demonstrates how specialised deployment, multi-model endpoints and serverless inference affect AI infrastructure economics. gimmefy illustrates multimodel execution across different marketing modalities and provider capabilities. The cases are treated separately because their reported outcomes rely on different commercial baselines and measurement approaches. The paper proposes a 90-day evaluation path based on workload classification, baseline measurement, shadow testing, controlled deployment and an explicit investment decision. Leadership measurement should focus on accepted outcome rate, cost per accepted outcome, realised business value, consequential errors, latency distribution, policy compliance, escalation and rework, and model substitution readiness. The central argument is that enterprise advantage will come from disciplined allocation of intelligence rather than maximising model capability or model count. The appropriate question is which intelligence should handle each workload, under what authority, and at what verified cost of successful execution. The AI Workload Classification framework, Model Routing Matrix, Capability-Cost Frontier, Model Escalation Ladder, Minimum Sufficient Intelligence principle and Cost per Accepted Outcome framework are author-developed analytical constructs. summary: Herrero García, José Luis. “La reivindicación marroquí y la soberanía española sobre Ceuta y Melilla.” Boletín CODESEL , vol. 2, no. 11, Oct. 2026, pp. 1–15. ISSN 3045-7750 LEGAL REVIEW The territorial claims advanced by the Kingdom of Morocco concerning Ceuta, Melilla and the remaining Spanish territories in North Africa constitute a particularly complex controversy at the intersection of international public law, historical sovereignty, territorial integrity, decolonisation and European security. Although these claims are frequently presented through the political vocabulary of colonial restitution and national reunification, their historical and legal foundations require examination beyond the geographical proximity of the disputed territories or the nationalist narratives surrounding Morocco's independence. In this extensive historical and juridical study, José Luis Herrero García undertakes a systematic examination of Moroccan territorial revisionism and the legal continuity of Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. His principal argument challenges the doctrine of Greater Morocco by distinguishing premodern religious allegiances, dynastic dominion and military expansion from the legal characteristics of territorial sovereignty under contemporary international law. Through the combined analysis of medieval political formations, historical treaties, constitutional provisions, international judicial reasoning and European institutional practice, the article develops a comprehensive interpretation of the historical and legal circumstances supporting Spain's position. The significance of the study extends beyond the bilateral dispute, raising fundamental questions concerning the construction of historical territorial titles, the stability of international borders and the limitations imposed by international law upon irredentist claims. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 43 examines the governance and evidence requirements that arise when artificial intelligence influences consequential business decisions. The paper defines a decision chain of custody as a controlled, verifiable record connecting the information used, systems involved, applicable policies, delegated authority, approvals, execution and preserved evidence behind an AI-influenced decision. Its central operating test is independent reconstruction: an authorised reviewer should be able to determine what happened, which authority permitted the action and how the resulting business state was verified without relying on the original operator's memory. The analysis distinguishes decision custody from related concepts including accuracy, explainability, data lineage, observability and content provenance. It argues that these controls answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable forms of transparency. Content provenance might identify the history of a digital asset, for example, while providing no evidence that a user held authority to approve a payment or that the resulting transaction was correctly executed. The paper proposes eight linked evidence domains for consequential AI-influenced decisions: information received, intelligence used, rules applied, tools invoked, state changed, authority held, outcome approved and evidence preserved. These domains connect through a shared decision identifier and are intended to preserve relationships between initial inputs, policy evaluation, delegated authority, approval, execution and verified outcome. Particular attention is given to the moment of commitment, when an AI-generated recommendation becomes an external or financial business action. The paper argues that approvals must remain linked to the material terms ultimately executed. Changes to amount, recipient, purpose or other material conditions require a defined re-evaluation path rather than reliance on an earlier approval. The paper also addresses delegation across multiple agents and systems, retry behaviour, transaction reconciliation, evidence integrity, retention, human oversight and supplier evidence obligations. It distinguishes reconstruction from reproduction and outcome verification, noting that exact reproduction of stochastic model output is neither always possible nor necessary for reconstructing observable system behaviour. Three cases illustrate different dimensions of the argument. IBM provides company-reported evidence of reduced data-clearance processing time within an integrated governance programme. HSBC demonstrates large-scale financial-crime detection alongside explainable and auditable investigative outputs. AstraZeneca provides published evidence concerning the organisational scope and challenges of ethics-based AI auditing. None of these cases is presented as proof of a complete decision-custody architecture. The paper proposes consequence-based evidence requirements, independent reconstruction tests, explicit stop conditions for missing authority or mandatory evidence, supplier acceptance tests and measurable indicators including reconstruction pass rate, authority coverage, approval match, outcome reconciliation and preservation verification. The chapter concludes that auditability after an AI-influenced decision is becoming as important as intelligence before the decision. Enterprises expanding autonomous authority should first demonstrate that completed consequential decisions can be independently reconstructed from preserved evidence with clear ownership, valid authority and verified outcomes. The eight-domain decision record, consequence-based evidence model, reconstruction tests and associated management controls are author-developed conceptual frameworks informed by established provenance, AI governance, legal and assurance sources. They are not externally validated standards or universal legal requirements.
title: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 43: Every AI Decision Needs a Chain of Custody

summary: Abstract This integrative research synthesis develops a candidate relational architecture across quantum foundations, physical history, persistent organization, relational time, and the recovery problem for spacetime. Its method is unification by decomposition : constraint, weighting, singular factualization, and retention are treated as distinct operations with distinct evidential burdens. Key Analyses & Framework Quantum Foundations & Entanglement: The double slit separates coherent alternatives, receiver-defined effects, Born weighting, and the $n = 1$ record. The Sorkin hierarchy and reconstruction literature delimit what is already formally known and leave open the physical motivation for second-order weighting. Entanglement is analyzed through a missing-loss audit: spatial routing, operational differentiation, and dynamical decoupling do not by themselves demonstrate ontological severance of a nonfactorizable joint state. Ontology & Event-Factualization: Primitive factualization is treated as a technical event-ontology posit, with fundamental agency as a stronger interpretive hypothesis (alongside objective stochasticity, Bohmian completion, Everettian branching, and collapse dynamics as comparison classes). A present-state coherence veto prevents absolute factualization while coherence-bearing degrees of freedom remain causally accessible to future interactions in which their phase relation can again matter. Retained factual consequences provide the bridge to physical history, memory, differential persistence, and increasingly organized agency. Downstream Physics & Empirical Testing: Transition and stabilization are treated as relational roles of one field-energy reality rather than new substances. The synthesis incorporates a fully exposed prospective transition-stabilization kill test in a driven liquid-to-vapor system and preserves planetary, gravitational, and spacetime extensions as explicitly conditional research branches. Methodological Stance: No universal master equation is claimed. The program is a structured ontology, audit, and research architecture whose modules must earn mathematical or empirical closure independently. Philosophical Extensions (Dual-Aspect Hypothesis): A further dual-aspect factualist hypothesis, with a panexperiential extension, distinguishes the publicly accessible objective face of factual processes from a minimally subjective first-person-like aspect associated with irreducible factual resolution. This is presented as a stronger ontological interpretation, not as an experimentally established consequence. It does not identify an elementary subjective aspect with a subject, mind, or consciousness. Complex biological agency is treated as potentially nested and hierarchically integrated, while the combination of elementary subjective loci into a unified subject is left as an explicit unresolved problem.

summary: A negative and methodological result on Edward Elgar's Dorabella cipher (87 arc symbols, 14 July 1897). Thirty decipherment hypotheses were each tested against shuffled-symbol nulls and enciphered-English controls; all were ruled out or disfavoured. About 10% drawing slips reduce a standard substitution solver from 97% to about 57% accuracy on 87-letter controls, so earlier "not English" verdicts do not cover a carelessly drawn cipher; a slip-tolerant solver places Dorabella above all shuffles but below all English controls. Neighbouring arcs that are 180° flips of each other are strongly over-represented (27 of 86 against 12.6 expected, p ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵). The cipher is not solved. AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) was used in transcription, decipherment, checking and drafting, under the author's direction; it is disclosed in the text. No archival images are reproduced.
title: Elgar's Dorabella cipher (14 July 1897): thirty hypothesis tests with shuffled and enciphered controls, a slip-tolerance loophole, and an excess of opposed neighbouring arcs

Distribution-shift evaluation: Results under increased electricity demand (+20%), reduced photovoltaic (PV) generation (−30%), increased electricity tariffs (+50%), and combined perturbations. Ablation analysis: Comparisons among RSE-AS, Economic-Only, Fixed attenuation, Adaptive attenuation, and unmodified SAC actions. summary: The rapid growth of blockchain networks has raised concerns about their environmental sustainability, yet existing assessments are fragmented and often rely on problematic metrics or unverifiable self-reported data. This article addresses these gaps by combining quantitative measures of annual energy consumption and carbon emissions with a qualitative assessment of sustainability initiatives. Using data from the Crypto Carbon Ratings Institute (CCRI) and corporate sustainability reports, we evaluate Bitcoin, Ethereum, Binance Chain, XRP, Cardano, Solana, Dogecoin, Polygon, and Polkadot, and benchmark their operational footprints against those of Visa and Mastercard as representatives of traditional payment systems. Results show wide variation in sustainability performance: Proof-of-Stake networks exhibit substantially lower energy use and carbon intensity than Proof-of-Work systems, while transparency and reporting practices differ significantly across projects. This research contributes to the sustainability discourse by providing one of the first systematic comparisons between blockchain networks and incumbent payment systems, identifying methodological challenges in sustainability accounting, and advancing policy recommendations for standardized reporting, third-party verification, and energy-efficient design. This is the published version of: Mabrouk, H., Paul, L., & Wild, D. (2026). Sustainability Metrics and Disclosure Alignment in Blockchain Networks. Blockchain and Cryptocurrency, 4(1), 1–9. IFSA Publishing, S. L. Originally published on 23 March 2026. Original article: https://bc-ifsa-journal.com/p_bc_21.html Deposited under the journal’s Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license (CC BY 4.0).
title: Sustainability Metrics and Disclosure Alignment in Blockchain Networks

summary: Data and code that reproduce every number, table and figure in the manuscript "What Do Indonesian Artificial Intelligence Courses Teach That Industry Asks For? A Multi-University Curriculum Audit That Accounts for Lecturer Disagreement" (submitted to Computer Applications in Engineering Education). The study compares 953 course learning outcomes from 71 AI-related courses at 19 Indonesian universities with 840 requirement sentences from 51 AI job postings. A multilingual sentence-embedding model (paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2) finds the closest match in both directions, and similarity is converted into the probability that a lecturer would accept the match, using judgements from four faculty validators and a lead researcher, under six judgement standards and three calibration curve shapes. Curriculum relevance, demand coverage and their harmonic mean (alignment) are reported for the corpus, universities, Bloom levels, AI-relevance tiers, courses and skills, with cluster-bootstrap intervals, size controls, cross-validation of the calibration curves and a verb-swap check. Contents: paper4_replication.zip holds the anonymised data (universities coded U01 to U19, courses C01 to C71), the expert labels (cosine similarity, labels and job-statement group only; the texts of the judged pairs are not included), one Google Colab script (code/paper4_replication.py) and a README that maps each output file to the table or figure it produces. paper4_results.zip holds the outputs of the published run, and similarity_matrix.npy the 953 x 840 cosine similarity matrix. Raw validator forms contain personal data and are not released.
title: Replication package for: What Do Indonesian Artificial Intelligence Courses Teach That Industry Asks For? A Multi-University Curriculum Audit That Accounts for Lecturer Disagreement

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: for every preorder that contains no “crown”, the support polynomial of its preorder polytope is the h-polynomial of a flag simplicial sphere, which settles the flag form of a 2026 conjecture of Athanasiadis and Chapoton for that class. The release also identifies the gamma-coefficients as counts of matchable pairs (found at the same time, independently, by Y. Zhong) and proves two Ehrhart conjectures from the same paper. The objects. A preorder is a way of ranking things in which ties are allowed. Athanasiadis and Chapoton (arXiv:2605.26916) attached to each preorder τ on n elements a lattice polytope Q τ : its integer points are the ways of putting nonnegative whole-number loads on the elements so that no downward-closed group carries more than its own size. Counting these points by how many loads are nonzero gives a polynomial H τ (t). For the chain 1 < 2 < 3 the counts are 1, 6, 6, 1, and 1 + 6t + 6t 2 + t 3 = (1+t) 3 + 3t(1+t); the 3 counts the three ways to pick one element and one strictly above it. The conjectures. Athanasiadis and Chapoton conjectured that H τ always looks like the h-polynomial of a sphere: palindromic, unimodal, gamma-positive (a nonnegative combination of t j (1+t) n−2j ) and realised by a simplicial, even a flag simplicial, polytope. They also conjectured several Ehrhart identities. Gal conjectured that flag spheres always have gamma-positive h-polynomials, so families that are both gamma-positive and realised by flag spheres are natural test cases. Results. (1) The gamma-coefficient γ j counts ordered pairs of disjoint j-element sets that can be matched upwards in τ; this proves gamma-positivity (their Conjecture 5.2). Y. Zhong (arXiv:2611.16858, 12 November 2026) obtained the same formula independently and concurrently, by the same route. (2) New here: if τ contains no crown (2k ≥ 6 elements joined in a closed zig-zag), then H τ is the h-polynomial of the boundary of an n-dimensional flag simplicial polytope (Conjecture 5.1(d) for this class). The class includes all arbors (Chapoton’s original setting), compositions, width-two posets, series–parallel and interval orders, and every preorder with at most five blocks. The proof builds a quadratic Gröbner basis for a root polytope, adapting Ohsugi–Hibi and Ohsugi–Tsuchiya; the new step is to pull a special simplex first. For preorders with a crown, the two polytopes used here have no flag regular unimodular triangulation, and the six-element crown is the smallest open case. (3) Matrix Ehrhart–zeta duality (Conjecture 4.2) and double Ehrhart reciprocity (Conjecture 7.2) hold for every preorder; the descent formula (Conjecture 4.4) and the zeta value Z(P τ , −1) = (−1) n #max(P τ ) follow. Also: a simplicial-polytope realisation for every preorder (Conjecture 5.1(c)), an explicit reflexive polytope with Ehrhart numerator H τ , and a table of the status of every conjecture in the originating paper (Conjecture 5.4 was proved by Dai et al., Conjecture 6.3 by Luo, and Conjecture 5.3 is false by Patel’s example). Limits. The flag result covers crown-free preorders only. Several of the Ehrhart proofs are short applications of standard tools (Postnikov’s lattice-point formula, Ehrhart–Macdonald reciprocity, Athanasiadis’s special-simplex theorem). Magic positivity, Conjectures 6.2, 8.1 and 8.2 and the q-form of Conjecture 4.9 remain open. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); exact Python checks with a runner that compares every output byte for byte in normal and python -O mode (all 355 labelled four-element preorders and smaller ones, 24 seeded preorders at each size 5–8, 689 small bipartite graphs, 560 matrix-duality cases, 390 preorders for the corollaries); flag-sphere checks on 570 crown-free preorders and Macaulay2 Gröbner-basis certificates for 461
title: Preorder polytopes: matching endpoint pairs, flag spheres and the Athanasiadis–Chapoton conjectures

summary: This record contains two complementary reproducibility packages supporting the manuscript "Mean Squared Error of 3 x 3 Median Filtering for Two-Dimensional Ising Images: Local Determinant Representation and Denoising Improvement Boundaries" by Jun Tsuzurugi. The filtering-examples package contains one reproducibly generated 256 x 256 free-boundary Ising image at K = 0.40, independent pixel-flip noise at p = 0.10 and 0.30, a single simultaneous 3 x 3 median-filtering pass, saved arrays, measured sample mean squared errors, thermalization diagnostics, and plotting code. These images are illustrative single-sample results, not estimates of infinite-lattice expected risk. The near-critical finite-size package contains deterministic central-pixel mean squared errors for free-boundary square lattices of side length 15, 31, and 63 at K = Kc +/- 0.005 and flip probabilities 0.10 and 0.20, compared with infinite-lattice references. It includes code, numerical tables, figures, convergence checks, validation records, and provenance. Numerical checks are empirical and do not constitute rigorous error bounds or a critical-exponent analysis. These additional materials supplement the original computational reproducibility archive at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22987387. Both uploaded ZIPs preserve their original contents and provenance. Historical manuscript references remain unchanged: the filtering package includes original-submission and R1_4 records; the near-critical package includes R1_6 records and manuscript text extracted for source checking. This deposit does not claim a fresh verification against a later manuscript revision. No scientific calculations were rerun during deposit preparation. summary: Experimental data from tests on timber–concrete composite beam–floor slab joints, carried out at PEMADE (Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Lugo Campus) with the project's own test procedure within the FrameTCC project. Three specimens were tested (J1–J3), each representing the intersection of two floor slab sections on a beam. Each test comprised two load cycles, loading to failure and unloading. The first cycle of J2 is not discussed in the related manuscript. For each record (the unloading of J1 is in a separate record, so there are ten), the dataset provides the time series of applied load, actuator stroke, the vertical displacement at mid-length measured by two transducers and the slip between the flanges of the floor slabs and the flange of the beam measured by four transducers, sampled at intervals of about 0.28 s, as CSV files (10 files). It also includes the processing workbook of each record, the maximum load of each record, the mass and failure mode of each specimen and 15 selected photographs with descriptions, five per specimen. It also contains nine digital image correlation (DIC) projects (created with GOM Software 2017), described in dic.csv together with the free software that can open them, and the calibration report of the DIC system. The results are discussed in the manuscript «Continuity effect over beams of timber-concrete composite floor slabs» (under review; doi:10.5281/zenodo.24142933).
title: FrameTCC 4.1 – Tests on timber–concrete composite beam–floor slab joints: test data and DIC

summary: Experimental data from axial compression tests on supports, carried out at CITEEC (Universidade da Coruña) with the project's own test procedure, within the FrameTCC project. Twenty-three supports were tested in two series. Series 1 (1.35 m long): reinforced concrete reference supports RC-1 and RC-2, and timber–concrete composite supports TCC-N-1 to TCC-N-4. Series 2 (1.45 m long): timber box-section supports of birch plywood PLY-P, PLY-N and PLY-S (three each), and timber–concrete composite supports TCC-P and TCC-S (four each). The suffix of the timber and composite supports gives the connection type: P plain, S slots and N notches. All channels were recorded at 5 Hz. RC-1, RC-2 and TCC-N-1 were instrumented with the pressure of two hydraulic jacks, four displacement transducers (LVDT) and four strain gauges; the other supports, with the force and displacement of the press and four strain gauges. The strain gauges measure the shortening of the timber boards and, internally, of the steel bars. The dataset includes 24 CSV files: one per support, plus a short record of TCC-N-3 taken after failure. The results are discussed in the manuscript «Axially loaded timber-concrete composite supports» (under review; doi:10.5281/zenodo.24143983). The package follows the FrameTCC data standard v7: a README, metadata files (test, specimens, channels, publications, SHA-256 manifest and changelog), the converted test data as CSV files and the other files described above. Time is given relative to the start of each acquisition; no calendar dates are included. Original acquisition files are kept unmodified by the project and are not published.
title: FrameTCC 3.1 – Axial compression tests on timber–concrete composite, timber box-section and reinforced concrete supports: test data

summary: Experimental data from four-point bending tests on cross-laminated timber–concrete composite floors, carried out at PEMADE (Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Lugo Campus) following EN 408 within the FrameTCC project. Three floor elements were tested (F1–F3), 6.10 m long with a span of 6.00 m. F1 and F2 were loaded to failure; F3 was loaded twice up to 60 kN without failure (F3a and F3b) and was then used in the long-term test of dataset 2.4, so there are four records. For each record, the dataset provides the time series of applied load, actuator stroke, mid-span deflection, local deflection over 1500 mm and the slip between concrete and timber at both ends, sampled at intervals of about 0.28 s, as CSV files (4 files). It also includes the processing workbook of each record, the values obtained (maximum load, loads and readings at two load levels, and local and global bending stiffness), the failure mode of F1 and F2 and 15 selected photographs with descriptions, at least four per floor. It also contains the digital image correlation (DIC) projects of F1, F2 and F3a (created with GOM Software 2017; the second cycle of F3 was not recorded with DIC), described in dic.csv together with the free software that can open them, and the calibration report of the DIC system. The results are discussed in Martín-Gutiérrez, Suárez-Riestra and Otero-Chans (2026), Structures 88, 111857 (doi:10.1016/j.istruc.2026.111857). The package follows the FrameTCC data standard v7: a README, metadata files (test, specimens, channels, publications, SHA-256 manifest and changelog), the converted test data as CSV files and the other files described above. Time is given relative to the start of each acquisition; no calendar dates are included. Original acquisition files are kept unmodified by the project and are not published.
title: FrameTCC 2.2 – Four-point bending tests on cross-laminated timber–concrete composite floors (EN 408): test data and DIC

summary: Experimental data from bending tests on short I-beams with a cross-laminated timber (CLT) web, carried out at PEMADE (Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Lugo Campus) within the FrameTCC project, following a procedure based on EN 13377. Four beams were tested (B1–B4). For each beam, the dataset provides the time series of applied load, actuator stroke, mid-span deflection, local deflection over 400 mm and the slip between the lower flange and the web at both beam ends, sampled at intervals of about 0.25 s, as CSV files (4 files). It also includes the processing workbook, the values obtained for each beam (maximum load and shear force, and load and deflection at 10 % and 40 % of the mean maximum load), the failure mode of each beam and 15 selected photographs with descriptions, of the assembly and of the tests. The package follows the FrameTCC data standard v7: a README, metadata files (test, specimens, channels, publications, SHA-256 manifest and changelog), the converted test data as CSV files and the other files described above. Time is given relative to the start of each acquisition; no calendar dates are included. Original acquisition files are kept unmodified by the project and are not published.
title: FrameTCC 2.1 – Bending tests on short I-beams with cross-laminated timber web (based on EN 13377): test data

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-six entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963), converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2000) for a peak wavelength and chromophore the caller states, and gives the distance between two colours in units of receptor noise by the model of Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), for a noise the caller states. summary: Gridded density fields and cosmic-web class masks used to train and test DeepVoid , a 3D U-Net that labels each cell of a simulated volume as void, wall, filament or halo. These grids are derived from simulation data produced and released by others: the IllustrisTNG project (TNG300-3-Dark) and the Bolshoi simulation (via the CosmoSim database). We only gridded the particles and halos and computed the class masks. Please credit the simulations as listed below whenever you use these files. All grids cover the full periodic simulation box at redshift 0, with axis order (x, y, z) and lengths in h -1 Mpc. File Contents tng300-3-dark_dm_n512.npz TNG300-3-Dark, dark-matter density from all particles; 512 3 cells in a 205 h -1 Mpc box tng300-3-dark_tweb_n512.npz T-web classes from that density (0 void, 1 wall, 2 filament, 3 halo): effective smoothing 1 h -1 Mpc, eigenvalue threshold 0.65 tng300-3-dark_subhalos_L{3,5,7,10}_n512.npz Mass density of the most massive subhalos, selected so that their mean separation is 3, 5, 7 or 10 h -1 Mpc. The subhalos are from the TNG group catalogs, found by the Subfind algorithm bolshoi_dm_n640.npz Bolshoi, dark-matter density from all 2048 3 particles (mean separation 0.122 h -1 Mpc); 640 3 cells in a 250 h -1 Mpc box bolshoi_tweb_n640.npz T-web classes from that density: effective smoothing 1 h -1 Mpc, eigenvalue threshold 0.65 bolshoi_halos_L{3,5,7,10}_n640.npz Bolshoi halos at mean separations of 3, 5, 7 or 10 h -1 Mpc, found by the Bound Density Maxima (BDM) halo finder MANIFEST.txt Size and SHA-256 checksum of every file   Format. Each .npz opens with NumPy alone: np.load("tng300-3-dark_dm_n512.npz")["data"] . data holds the values (uint8 for class masks, float32 otherwise); header is a JSON string with the box size and the file's provenance; fvol_header keeps the header of the file the grid was converted from. The conversion is lossless: each original file can be rebuilt byte for byte as fvol_header followed by data as float32, and its SHA-256 checksum is stored in header under source_sha256 . Cosmologies. TNG300: Ω m = 0.3089, Ω Λ = 0.6911, Ω b = 0.0486, σ 8 = 0.8159, n s = 0.9667, h = 0.6774. Bolshoi: Ω m = 0.27, Ω Λ = 0.73, Ω b = 0.0469, σ 8 = 0.82, n s = 0.95, h = 0.70. Credit IllustrisTNG. summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: for 1 < p < 2 this paper finds the exact Schatten-norm constant for sums of matrix moduli when there are at least as many matrices as the matrix size, gives a new general upper bound ((1+√m)/2) 1−1/p , and certifies in exact arithmetic that rank-one matrices do not give the answer to Lee’s two-matrix problem. The question. For numbers, |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b|. A matrix A has a natural absolute value |A| = (A*A) 1/2 , but for matrices the size of a sum can exceed the size of the sum of the absolute values. Measuring size by the Schatten p-norm (p = 1 is the trace norm, p = 2 the Frobenius norm), one asks for the smallest constant c with ‖A 1 +…+A m ‖ p ≤ c ‖|A 1 |+…+|A m |‖ p . What was known. Eun-Young Lee (2010, 2012) asked for the best constant for two matrices. Lin and Zhang (2022) settled p = 2; Tang and Zhang extended the question to m matrices and conjectured a formula; Qiu (2026) proved it for p ≥ 2; below p = 2 the formula fails, by counterexamples of Zeng, Liu and Ratnavelu, of Pang and of Qiu, all built from rank-one matrices. The survey of Bourin and Zhang (2026) lists the range 1 < p < 2 as open. Results (1 < p < 2, n-by-n matrices). (1) When m ≥ n the best constant is an explicit one-variable maximum D p,n ; it depends only on the rank of the sum of the moduli, every equality case is classified, and for m < n the constant is strictly smaller. Consequently the best constant for rank-one summands is D p,min(m,n) in every dimension. (2) The best constant is log-convex in 1/p, so interpolating between p = 1 and p = 2 gives the dimension-free bound ((1+√m)/2) 1−1/p , better than the previous m (p−1)/(2p) for every m ≥ 2 (for two matrices at p = 3/2: 1.0648 instead of 1.1225, while the true value is at least 1.0364). (3) For two 3-by-3 matrices a computer-assisted proof in exact rational and interval arithmetic shows that the best rank-one value is beaten at nine exponents between 11/10 and 17/10. How. The sum is written as a product of two block matrices and Hölder’s inequality is applied; the problem reduces to comparing two Rényi entropies of the spectrum, whose extremal shape is one large eigenvalue and the rest equal. This extends T. Zhang’s Frobenius-norm argument; the matching examples are Pang’s, with a re-tuned parameter. Limits. The exact constant for two matrices of arbitrary size (Lee’s problem) for 1 < p < 2 remains open, as does the case m < n; the interpolation bound is not sharp; the certified excess over the rank-one value is tiny (about 10 −5 to 10 −7 ) and covers nine specific exponents, not an interval. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF) with Figure 1; the certificate script certify_rank_gap.py with its exact rational witnesses; verify_schatten.py (128 numerical checks of the scalar constant, equality families, adversarial searches, the bounds table and asymptotics, with negative controls); the figure script; recorded outputs; the bibliography from registry records; a machine-readable index; a research-gate record; a rating-free review summary; a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Assurance. Written proofs, except one computer-assisted proof in exact arithmetic (Proposition 2.5). Internal AI-assisted review only (five reviewer roles, an adversarial review and audit by a second AI model, a clean replay, a re-review and a proof audit): not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Sharp constants for sums of matrix moduli when 1<p<2

summary: The Brina Gap measures the difference between the growth a company can self-finance and the growth its market price already assumes.  Its fundamental arm is the sustainable-growth ceiling,  g f  = ROIC × Reinvestment Rate; its pricing arm is the market-implied growth  g *, recovered from a reverse discounted-cash-flow on enterprise value. Both come from public filings, so the Gap makes the market's embedded growth expectation explicit — mechanically, reproducibly, and without an analyst's private valuation. Stated in growth units, it is the only kind of valuation claim that can be checked against what firms later deliver —  and it checks out. On the complete point-in-time S&P 500 (2010–2024, survivorship-free), the market-implied growth  g * genuinely tracks the growth firms subsequently realize (correlation ≈ 0.4–0.5, nearly unbiased at the 10-year horizon) and is robust across independent recovery methods (Spearman 0.73–1.00).  The Brina Gap is a detector of over-extrapolated growth expectations:  the market systematically over-extrapolates growth — the calibration slope sits below one at every horizon — and the median firm priced for high growth under-delivers what its price implies (≈ 26% priced in vs ≈ 22% realized).  Head-to-head against the classical Margin of Safety, the Gap is mechanical and falsifiable where the Margin of Safety is not, nearly orthogonal to it in cross-section, and more accurate on the one directional test both can take (+3.9 points, p ≈ .004; the Gap's expensive-side calls were correct 58.9% of the time on the full universe).  Among all pure valuation metrics tested — book-to-market, earnings yield, EPV, the Margin of Safety — the Brina Gap ranks first, and it is the only one whose central claim can be verified at all.  Its practical form is the  Brina Matrix , which crosses the Gap's pricing read with fundamental quality and yields one rule that survives every specification tested:  "cheap" is only a bargain when quality is high — cheap plus low quality is the value trap, the worst-performing cell in the sample. We are equally explicit about the limits: the fundamental arm is a conservative anchor, not a forecast; and the Gap — like every metric in the companion audit, the Margin of Safety included — is not a standalone return signal, which is exactly what efficiency logic predicts for any transparent, filings-based measure, in the most pricing-hostile decade on record. Data and code are published: a per-call outcomes file and a one-command verifier reproduce every headline number (see below). Verify the headline numbers yourself (added in v3.0.1). directional_outcomes_v3.0.csv lists all 1,504 directional calls on the complete point-in-time S&P 500, 2010–2024, delisted and acquired firms included (CRSP-style). Running python3 verify_headline_claims.py (Python standard library only) recomputes: • Stocks the Brina Gap clearly flagged as priced too high trailed the S&P 500 over the next five years in 546 of 927 cases (58.9%; a coin flip gives 50%). Exact one-sided binomial p = 3.3×10⁻⁸: if the warnings were coin flips, a record this good would come up about once in 30 million tries. • On the same 1,504 calls the classic Margin of Safety scored 50.9% (chance); the Gap 54.8%: +3.9 points, year-clustered bootstrap p = 0.0038. • Value Trap calls: 59.5% (207 of 348). The Gap's "cheap" calls were at chance (48.2%), as the paper reports. The paper claims no standalone return edge (over every stock, sign only: 52.4%). See README_VERIFY.md. Two parts:  Part I — the paper (the construct, its theory, the validity battery, the Brina Matrix); Part II — the complete empirical record (directional tests, robustness, failure modes, pre-registered refinements).  Supersedes v1.0 and v2.0; their d
title: The Brina Gap: A Framework for Identifying Growth Mispricing in Equity Markets

summary: A law $F$ with mean $\mu$ is $n$-completely mixable if there are $n$ random variables with law $F$ whose sum is almost surely $n\mu$. Wang proved that such a law satisfies a family of inequalities between the norms of the positive and negative parts of $X-t$ and $X-s$, where $X\sim F$ and $s=(n\mu-t)/(n-1)$, for every threshold $t$ and every law-determined norm, and asked when these inequalities are also sufficient (Open Problem 4 in his 2015 survey). We show that for bounded $F$ the whole family is equivalent to the single convex-order condition $X-\mu\cx-(n-1)(X-\mu)$, and that the same holds for integrable $F$ if the norms are required to have the Fatou property. The inequalities do not imply $n$-complete mixability: for $n=3$ the analytic density $\frac1{10}+\frac{27}{10}(2x-1)^2$ on $[0,1]$ satisfies all of them and is not $3$-completely mixable, and for $n=3$ and $n=4$ there are counterexamples with densities bounded away from zero on $[0,1]$ and with $C^\infty$ densities, the one for $n=4$ not symmetric. A Bernoulli$(p)$ law satisfies the inequalities exactly when $1/n\le p\le1-1/n$, while it is $n$-completely mixable exactly when $np$ is an integer. For $n=2$ the inequalities are equivalent to symmetry, hence to $2$-complete mixability, for every integrable law. For $n=3$ the examples refine the symmetric non-mixable laws of Yin and Zhu, and the reduction explains why those laws satisfy the inequalities.
title: Law-determined norm inequalities do not imply complete mixability

summary: Replication package for the working paper "Precision Matters: Anti-Corruption Campaigns, Targeted Crackdowns, and Sector Returns in China's Stock Market" (Xuanyuan Li, 2026). The package contains: (1) four hand-verified event libraries — 31 general anti-corruption campaign events (2012–2026), 12 sector-targeted interventions, 12 local-flagship case-study events, and 14 positive policy tools — every date anchored to an official primary source (CCDI, NDRC, MIIT, NPC, SAMR); (2) a 152-month hand-compiled CCDI eight-point-regulation enforcement series (2013-09 to 2026-09) with per-month source anchors and the December 2019 coverage-revision flag; (3) Sina hfq-adjusted daily return panels for the sector proxies and the CSI 300 benchmark; (4) all analysis scripts (Python 3.11, pandas/numpy): event-study grids, monthly enforcement-intensity regressions, exact permutation / cluster-bootstrap / sign-test inference, index-proxy robustness, and a beta-adjusted market-model replication with Newey-West lag sensitivity; (5) the manuscript (Markdown and Word), cover letter, and title page. Run the scripts from the package root; README.md gives replication steps and data-source conventions. All paper results are reproducible from the cached CSVs without network access. Inference note: policy events of this precision are scarce by construction; the paper reports exact permutation tests as primary evidence and discloses that the beta-adjusted replication weakens the headline targeted-intervention spread (p = 0.073).
title: Replication package for: Precision Matters: Anti-Corruption Campaigns, Targeted Crackdowns, and Sector Returns in China's Stock Market

summary: Replication code for a study of battery storage investment prioritisation across five campuses of a merged public technical university in Taiwan, under a contract-capacity time-of-use tariff. The code recovers tariff parameters from billing records, jointly optimises storage size, contracted capacity and time-of-use dispatch for each site-year by linear programming with a genetic-algorithm benchmark, and values storage against an administratively optimised counterfactual so that contract reductions obtainable without capital expenditure are not credited to storage. The institutional billing records analysed in the paper are not included, having been obtained under a data use agreement that does not permit redistribution; a synthetic panel with the same schema is provided so the code runs out of the box.
title: Analysis code for: Visible in kilowatts, invisible in money — contract capacity, storage and investment priorities under a Taiwanese demand-charge tariff

summary: Measurement data and analysis code for maximum independent set (MIS) written as a single penalty (QUBO) objective and run on quantum annealers (D-Wave Advantage_system6 and Advantage2_system1) and gate-model processors (IBM Heron r3 and Nighthawk r2) through a QAOA circuit. The deposit contains: measurement count histograms of every executed circuit and annealer read set, with the executed angles, compiled depth, two-qubit gate counts and physical layouts; job ledgers and submission plans; the calibration snapshot each gate-model batch ran under; noiseless state-vector results for the same circuits; the instance generator (every instance is a pure function of size, fill fraction and seed) for king-lattice graphs, random 3-regular graphs, Erdős–Rényi graphs and heavy-hex induced subgraphs; the analysed tables; four hardware jobs whose predictions and criteria were written before submission, with the written designs and plan hashes; and the analysis scripts. reproduce.py recomputes derived quantities from the deposited tables offline. Account identifiers and budget statements were removed; the redactions are listed. The record is one zip archive ( zenodo_deposit.zip , directory structure preserved) with the README.md and a SHA-256 checksum list of every archived file alongside. title: Measurement data and analysis code: maximum independent set under a penalty objective on quantum annealers and gate-model processors

files.key: Coffee and Scheirer 2026 - Feature Fusion for Computational Intertextuality Detection in Tesserae V6 - preprint v1.pdf

summary: Computational detection of intertextuality has so far used individual features such as word n-grams, edit distance, or word embeddings to identify text reuse or allusion, with only limited efforts to combine two such features for improved detection. This article presents Tesserae V6, a freely available platform that searches, weights, and combines into a single fused score ten distinct signals: shared headwords; a single shared headword; identical surface forms; character-trigram sound similarity; near-identical strings by edit distance; shared meaning by sentence embedding; curated cross-headword synonym pairs; matching dependency-tree patterns at shared headwords; identical dependency frames without any shared word; and shared rare words. The fused score also incorporates word-rarity weighting from corpus-wide frequencies. On the founding Lucan–Vergil benchmark, the previous V3 lexical baseline recovered about 27% of known parallels. Against five commentator-attested benchmarks comprising 862 parallel passages from Latin epic, the new fused V6 system recovered 91.5% in its full ranked output. Of the top distinct results for the Lucan–Vergil comparison, 79% (34 of 43) are meaningful instances of intertextuality. The platform was built by a classicist directing a sequence of AI coding assistants in natural language, with no traditional programming, and with each stage of development checked against the same benchmarks. The platform is available at https://tesserae.caset.buffalo.edu . This preprint has not been peer reviewed.
title: Feature Fusion for Computational Intertextuality Detection in Tesserae V6

summary: MakeCOO is a Wolfram Language command-line package that constructs a stoichiometric matrix from reaction definitions. It represents each reversible reaction as separate forward and reverse records and constructs a matrix with chemical species as rows and directed reactions as columns. It also exports the species list and directed reaction table. This archive contains MakeCOO version 0.3.0, the version used to construct the stoichiometric matrix in the anaerobic Mn(II) oxidation case study. It includes the source code, documentation, example inputs and tests, and the shared Utils/IO.wl file. The software is distributed under the MIT License. If you use MakeCOO in research, please cite the accompanying article by Mayumi Seto and Yuya Tsukamoto in Geomicrobiology Journal ( https://doi.org/10.1080/01490451.2026.2762317 ).
title: MakeCOO: Stoichiometric matrix construction from reaction definitions

summary: Supplementary materials (v5.3.0) for: Design-based null audits: what two decades of pronoun-production experiments could and could not detect This package supports a design-based statistical audit of the predictability literature on pronoun production (story-continuation paradigm, 1994–2023). The audit asks whether the designs that produced this literature's null results were capable of detecting the effects they tested, via (i) a re-extraction of all eligible effect sizes on the log-odds-ratio scale with quasi-separation screening, (ii) design-by-design minimum-detectable-effect (MDE₈₀) simulation under each study's own published parameters, and (iii) power-contour guidance for future designs. Package structure: Online Resource 1 (search & PRISMA screening), Online Resource 2 (effect-size extraction workbook with provenance and separation flags), Online Resource 3 (publication-bias diagnostics: Egger regression and contour-enhanced funnel plots), audit data and figures (MDE table, power grid, Figures 1–3), seeded simulation code (Python authoritative + R re-implementation, plus separation-screening and power-grid tools), and the superseded original OSF materials of the companion meta-analysis. Relation to other materials: The correlation-based meta-analytic dataset audited and superseded by this re-extraction is archived in the OSF project osf.io/gx5ad ("Referential Predictability in Pronoun Production: Evidence from Meta-Analysis and Simulation for a Generalized Bayesian Model"). Version note (v5.3.0): BRM submission-readiness revision of v5.2.1 — data unchanged; adds separation flag column, contour-enhanced funnel plots with generation script, bit-exact power-grid code (verified against the shipped grid), separation-screening tool, requirements.txt and sessionInfo() records. Egger-test p-values in the manuscript should read .020 (subjecthood) and .312 (thematic role); see Online Resource 3 README. All simulations are seeded (20260825 / 20260827).
title: Design-based null audits: what two decades of pronoun-production experiments could and could not detect (supplementary materials, v5.3.0)

summary: Receive → Give-Forward as the Substrate-Invariant Atom of a Reciprocity Economy This paper discloses a design criterion for peer-to-peer gift, reciprocity and gratitude systems (pay-it-forward schemes, time banks, complementary currencies, peer-recognition ledgers): classify each transfer by where the recipient's next transfer goes — onward to a third party (generalized reciprocity: a gift that circulates) or back to its source in a return that settles the account (balanced reciprocity: an exchange). With it come a six-way taxonomy of gift flows by relational scope, a bounded relay subclass that preserves provenance, and a three-tier classification of transferable value by hoardability that predicts how much lifecycle machinery each kind requires. The criterion is applied to HeartBank, which is, on its surface, many mechanisms: a family-scale money economy, an adult-scale time economy, a line of physical gratitude artifacts, a matchmaking instrument, an autonomous AI successor, a planetary balancing game. This paper makes a reductive claim about all of them. There is exactly one atomic operation underneath the entire institution: give as a gift, not as exchange — whose circulation form, and the form every network product implements, is receive a gift, then give it forward — never back. The claim has three dimensions of invariance. The operation is invariant across currency : the thing received-and-forwarded can be money (a re-tip), time (funded presence), a physical object (a passed artifact), or a gene (a trait selected and propagated), and the operation is structurally identical in each. It is invariant across scale : it runs at the level of a person (one self-thank forwarded), a family (a circulating object), a civilization (a synchronized annual disbursement), and a species (kindness propagated by mate choice). And it is invariant across substrate : it is the same operation whether it executes in software, in the hand, or in biology. The biological cases (the gene, the species, the biological substrate) are resemblances rather than instances by the sameness criterion of §9.8; the invariance claimed is across money, time and object, from person to civilization, in the digital and physical substrates. We then locate the operation's load-bearing constraint — forward, not back — as the boundary this corpus draws, against Mauss's obligation to reciprocate, between the gift (which circulates and binds) and the commodity (which is exchanged and clears the relation): a return back to the giver is what converts a gift into a trade and dissolves the bond it was meant to create. This has an immediate consequence for HeartBank's wordmark. "Circulation, not accumulation" has been read as a description of a state the institution is in; we show it is better read as a specification of an operation the institution performs — the public line is the atom, compressed to three words. We then map the broader space of which forward-circulation is one case: the gift-topology map , six relational-scope topologies (self-directed, dyadic-reciprocal, group-circulation, open forward-chain, commons/place-anchored, across-time), each realized by one product in the physical line, the truest invariant being give-as-gift (not exchange) with forward its circulation topology. Finally we show the atom is the corpus's unifying spine — upstream of the Treasury re-tip, the Chronicle hour, the physical artifacts, the matchmaking instrument, and the species-scale propagation thesis — and we ground it in the four brahmavihāra design lens, where the gift is the accessible foundation that the immeasurables are cultivated from . §9 is unusually large because the claim is unusually strong and unusually unproven: the invariance is asserted across many domains from the design of a single project (n=1), it is at constant risk of over-unification (collapsing genuinely different operations under one flattering word), and forward is demonstrably not the right topology for tw
title: The Gift Operation

summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. Keywords: proof of personhood, proof of humanity, sybil resistance, decentralized identity, AI-content trust, open identity protocol, recipient-side filtering, BLE-Nearby proximity, blockchain consensus, AI alignment, defensive publication. --- Provenance. This paper is part of the THonly research corpus, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The canonical version is at https://thonly.org/research/b-poh-humanity-layer-ai-native-internet . Its SHA-256 is d9d9a6d7bced60a5c39ba39079426a240024416799b1219b1d536173833df670 , independently timestamped to the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps and signed under RFC 3161 by three trust authorities, one of them eIDAS-qualified. AI co-authorship is disclosed. Miss Aquarius is the consistent name used for the AI collaboration across all venues. Miss Aquarius co-authored this paper; Zenodo lists no AI tool as a creator, so Miss Aquarius is named here rather than among the creators.
title: B-PoH℠ as Humanity Layer for the AI-Native Internet: An Open Proof-of-Personhood Protocol with Four Optional Layered Proofs and Recipient-Side Filters

summary: For every integer p>=4, a previously constructed symmetric numerical semigroup ring R_p and rigid two-generated monomial ideal determine a conductor ideal T_p whose special fiber C_p = F(T_p) is one-dimensional Cohen-Macaulay, generated in degree one by 10p monomials, with multiplicity 24p. Taking the imported offset bases as input, we prove that C_p ≅ k[xy^a : a ∈ G_p] ⊆ k[x,y]/(y^24p), that its defining ideal J_p is primary to the ideal of positive offsets, with nilpotency index 24p, and that Proj(C_p) is a saturated length-24p curvilinear fat point, locally Gorenstein although the coordinate ring has Cohen-Macaulay type 10p+1. The Kähler differentials split by characteristic. We then determine the reduced Gröbner basis for graded reverse lexicographic order with X_0 last. Its degree profile is (50p^2-17p, 5p-1, p-2) and no minimal leading monomial contains X_0, which gives a flat Cohen-Macaulay monomial degeneration. The quadratic part, the stabilization of the staircase, the absence of elements in degree five and higher, the absence of X_0 from the leading monomials and the flatness are derived from derived imported input; the imported relation type three is machine-verified. The cubic and quartic classification, for all p, is machine-verified and not derived: 16 Presburger obligations are decided unsatisfiable by Z3 and by cvc5 on identical queries, with no checked proof object. Exact sweeps at every p=4,...,300, an independent clique recomputation and negative controls validate the formulas. The results concern the conductor fiber cones of this explicit family; they do not assert that arbitrary monomial fiber cones are primary, curvilinear, Cohen-Macaulay or locally Gorenstein. Source code, compact artifacts, premise hashes and proofs: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
title: Curvilinear Geometry, Primary Structure, and a Gröbner Degeneration of Conductor Fiber Cones in a Huneke–Wiegand Family

summary: The widespread application of inductive loads in today ‘s power distribution systems where power factor (PF) correction has become an integral requirement, has led to power factor degradation as a serious problem and requires correction for more efficient power distribution. In this paper, an innovative AI based Adaptive PF correction scheme is proposed to integrate conventional PF correction capacitor bank compensation with an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) based predictor-controller for dynamic reactive power compensation. A detailed MATLAB/Simulink 3–phase distribution system-based model has been evolved which yields operational data sets for ANN training and testing with different loading conditions. Proposed ANN predictor-controllers are trained with back-propagation algorithm applying MSE (Mean Squared Error) function as a network performance measure. The network prediction accuracy 96.9 to 97.8% and the generalization capability has been established through comprehensive results analysis. The proposed architecture significantly decreases the reactive power demand by approximately 77%, apparent power consumption by 28.1% and the dynamic response by 3 times compared to fixed capacitor compensation method. Moreover, the (PF) is maintained between 0.95–0.96, confirming its effectiveness for real-time adaptive power factor correction in modern distribution systems.
title: AI-Based Adaptive Power Factor Correction for Reactive Power Reduction in Distribution Systems

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Proof of the Mogilnykh–Vorob’ev–Valyuzhenich conjecture, the exact Rényi minimum for sampling without replacement, and the hypergeometric tail problem from n = 4k. The question. Pick k of n given real numbers at random, without replacement, and add them. How concentrated can that random sum be? The paper answers three classical forms of this question exactly: how often the sum can be exactly zero, how small its entropy can be, and how rarely it can be nonnegative. Results. (1) Zero sums. If the numbers add up to zero and are not all zero, at least 2·C(n−2, k−1) of the k-subsets have a nonzero sum whenever k ≥ 5 and n ≥ 2k+1, and only the pattern (1, −1, 0, …, 0), up to scaling and reordering, attains this. This is the smallest support of an eigenfunction in the first nontrivial eigenspace of the Johnson graph, and proves Conjecture 1 of Mogilnykh, Vorob’ev and Valyuzhenich (2018), who had checked it by computer for n ≤ 600. A formula with all equality cases is given for every n and k, including the case (1, 1, −1, −1, 0) at n = 5, k = 2 that earlier classifications missed (Theorem 1.1). (2) Entropy. The minimum Rényi entropy of the sum is found for every finite order, answering a question of Ai, Kuželka and Pelekis (2026): one outlier is optimal except at half-sampling (n = 2k), where two outliers win above an explicit order α k (α 2 = 2, about 1.386k for large k). So the universal Bernoulli lower bound holds exactly for orders up to 2 (Theorems 1.2 and 1.3, Corollary 1.4). (3) Tails. For two-valued populations, the probability that the sum is at least its mean is at least k/n whenever n ≥ 4k, with a single outlier the unique minimiser for n > 4k (Theorem 1.5); Ai and Pelekis (2026) had n ≥ 8k. The proof uses a 2026 lemma of Ai, Karagiannis, Kuželka and Pelekis. Consequently the Aydinian–Blinovsky conjecture (that two-valued populations are the worst case) would imply the Manickam–Miklós–Singhi conjecture for all n ≥ 4k. This does not prove the Manickam–Miklós–Singhi conjecture, and below 4k a single outlier is not always the worst case. (4) Exact analogues over Abelian groups, where elements of order two change the answer at half-sampling (Theorem 1.6), and a small-ball inequality for sampling without replacement; a known incidence-rank result is re-derived. Limits. Real numbers only for the zero-sum theorem (it fails over Z 2 , Z 3 and Z 5 ); first Johnson eigenspace only; the tail problem below n = 4k is open. Finite computer checks corroborate but do not replace the written proofs. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); five standard-library Python scripts of exact finite checks (each runs in seconds and exits nonzero on any failure, also under python -O) with their recorded outputs; a claim ledger and prior-art note; the bibliography from registry records; a machine-readable index; a research-gate record; a rating-free review summary; a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Assurance. Complete written proofs for every result. Internal AI-assisted review only (five reviewer roles, an adversarial review and an audit by a second AI model, clean replays, a re-review and a proof audit): not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Fixed-size subset sums: sharp support, Rényi entropy and tail bounds

summary: Supplementary note to arXiv:2611.08310 and arXiv:2610.19779. A fingerprint of coherent noise built from a stabilizer code is only as informative as the recovery gates that produce it, and every fixed choice of those gates is blind somewhere. This note isolates what can nevertheless be guaranteed, and states it as a worst-case floor rather than an average improvement. Two elementary facts about Fisher information make the guarantee exact. Because information matrices add, the identifiable set of a collection of designs is the union of theirs, so running several designs in parallel can never cost a direction that any member sees. Because the inverse of a sum is Loewner-dominated by the inverse of any summand, splitting a fixed shot budget over S designs can never cost more than sqrt(S) in standard deviation, that is, S in shots. The premium is therefore fixed in advance and independent of the working point, while the gain is not. Both statements are certified over the 64-design space of the three-qubit repetition code, under the 48- and 112-component fingerprints: the Loewner inequality is evaluated rather than assumed at every point tested, the worst case over 300 working points is 1.25 against the certified sqrt(2) = 1.4142, the bound is attained to five figures at one structured point, and at the worst points of the individual designs the parallel pair sits below the better single design by factors of 2.6 to 9.5. Two three-gate placements suffice; a third adds 3.5 to 11.5 per cent. The floor buys recoverability and worst-case precision, and it buys nothing else: it does not buy accuracy under common-mode calibration bias, and it does not repair a model degeneracy that no design can see. Contents: the two propositions with proofs, the cost corollary, the numerical certification (five tables, one figure), the relation to the two companion papers, and a reproduction map. The archive repro_v1.0.zip in this record contains the seven scripts, four data files, the figure and a self-test that re-derives every quoted number; run python scripts/selftest.py from the archive root and compare against MANIFEST.sha256. Companion papers: arXiv:2611.08310 (recovery gates as a resource) and arXiv:2610.19779 (coherent-noise identifiability).
tags: quantum process tomography; coherent noise; stabilizer codes; repetition code; recovery gates; Fisher information; parameter identifiability; Cramer-Rao bound; metrology; quantum error correction
title: A Hard Worst-Case Floor for All-Parameter Recoverability in Three-Qubit Coherent-Noise Fingerprinting

summary: Contemporary speculative fiction unsettles anthropocentric assumptions about language, intelligence and the production of knowledge. This article compares Laline Paull’s The Bees (2014) to Ray Nayler's The Mountain in the Sea (2022) and The Tusks of Extinction (2024), exploring how the novels represent the conditions under which non-human knowledge is produced, recognized and transmitted. Drawing on biosemiotics and critical posthumanism in conversation with Andrew Lopez's account of epistemic injustice towards non-human animals, it develops a comparative framework based on recognition, access and continuity. The key argument is that the novels depict epistemic harm not merely as a failure to interpret non-human signs but as the institutional restriction of the very environments and social relations through which practical knowledge can flow. In Paull's hive caste is the source of authority which controls access to sensory information; in Nayler's oceanic enclave corporate power turns scientific attention into a potential tool of appropriation; and in the de-extinction narrative, biological restoration is simply not enough without the recovery of the skills that are socially transmitted. The novels are not being read as descriptions of actual animal species. Rather they are being used as a lens through which to examine the political and ethical dimensions of human authority over other ways of knowing. The article makes a contribution to contemporary literary studies by linking multispecies representation to the distribution and preservation of epistemic goods.
tags: Biosemiotics; critical posthumanism; epistemic injustice; nonhuman communication; collective knowledge; multispecies justice; contemporary speculative fiction
title: Sign Systems and Shared Worlds: Nonhuman Communication, Collective Knowledge and Epistemic Justice in Contemporary Speculative Fiction

summary: Enterprise database systems face data-loss risks that come from operational errors, system failures and security incidents. MySQL binary logs give tools for data replication and point-in-time recovery, yet many organizations do not use them fully for recovery. This study proposes an automated, schema-aware MySQL binary-log recovery framework that integrates log discovery, dependency-aware recovery planning, database reconstruction, and validation into a unified enterprise restoration pipeline. The framework explains how to read binary-log formats, how to run recovery steps automatically and how to use performance-boosting tactics learned from well-known recovery models such as ARIES write-ahead logging, log-structured storage and event sourcing. The framework was tested in four failure scenarios and compared with the usual backup-and-restore approach. In those tests, the recovery time dropped by about 65%, meaning the framework needed only about one-third of the baseline time. A real-world check compared each recovered field to the printed reference invoice: 99.7% of the fields matched exactly, and every financial total was correct. The only error was a single non-financial field. This work gives reusable tools for people who care about database reliability, and it offers a clear map of failure types and a step-by-step method for bringing MySQL databases back to life. The proposed approach differs from conventional binary-log recovery methods by providing an end-to-end automated workflow with schema awareness and independent validation of recovered data.
title: Advanced MySQL Binary Log-Based Data Recovery
