summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The paper also discloses one application-facing composition of the per-action passkey press, the presence call (§3.8): an identity provider confirms to an app, for one named action and in the provider's own closed wording, that the holder of a person's passkey pressed it, for a person the app already knows by its own pairwise identifier, and keeps nothing; §12.1 reports the novelty census that scopes that claim to the composition alone. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. Keywords: proof of personhood, proof of humanity, sybil resistance, decentralized identity, AI-content trust, open identity protocol, recipient-side filtering, BLE-Nearby proximity, blockchain consensus, AI alignment, per-action passkey confirmation, pairwise subject identifier, WebAuthn user verification, defensive publication. --- Provenance. Its SHA-256 is 26ba7ff48f047fef035d7248ba97c5c86fb1538b839a66410b2be44ea72b8816 , independently timestamped to the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps and signed under RFC 3161 by three trust authorities, one of them eIDAS-qualified. title: B-PoH℠ as Humanity Layer for the AI-Native Internet: An Open Proof-of-Personhood Protocol with Four Optional Layered Proofs and Recipient-Side Filters

summary: We study in-context learning of scalar linear regression by L untied linear-attention layers, each with a trainable key scalar k_i and query scalar q_i. For every depth L and prompt length n, population gradient flow on the 2L factors is bounded and converges to a critical point, every critical point that is not a global minimizer has a negative Hessian eigenvalue, and the flow reaches a global minimizer from all initializations outside a Lebesgue null set, for instance almost surely under Gaussian initialization. The trained network performs L gradient descent steps on the prompt's least-squares loss, with step sizes k_iq_i the reciprocals of the zeros of a rescaled Laguerre polynomial L_L^(n/2), and its risk is $2^LL!/\prod_{j=1}^{L}(n+2j)$. Initializations with k_i = -q_i in some layer converge to a critical point that is not a minimizer, so the null set is not empty.
title: Gradient flow for deep factored scalar linear attention learns multi-step gradient descent

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-nine entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters, gives the absorbance template of a visual pigment of Govardovskii et al. (2000) for a peak wavelength and chromophore the caller states, and gives the distance between two colours in units of receptor noise by the model of Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), for a noise the caller states. Without a water type, it gives Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001) or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013), the remote sensing reflectance from a and bb (Gordon et al. 1988; Lee et al. 2002), and the Secchi depth from Kd and that reflectance (Lee et al. 2015), and inverts the reflectance to the absorption and backscattering coefficients by the quasi-analytical algorithm, in the version of IOCCG Report 5 (2006), checked against that report's published statistics, and as QAA_v6, checked against its author's spreadsheet. summary: Pre-registration of an exploratory analysis, deposited before any race/ethnicity-specific outcome was estimated. We will examine racial/ethnic differences in first-molar dental sealant prevalence among US children aged 6–11 years using NHANES (1999–2004, 2011–2016, and 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic file; 2005–2010 cycles are excluded because tooth-level sealant codes are unavailable). Outcome: presence of a sealant on ≥1 permanent first molar among children with ≥1 assessable first molar. Comparison: non-Hispanic Black and Mexican American children versus non-Hispanic White children. Planned estimands are survey-weighted prevalence and absolute differences (percentage points) by period, change in the absolute gap between 1999–2004 and 2017–2020.3 (Holm-adjusted for the two primary contrasts), and attenuation of the gap after adjustment for age, sex, and income rank (poverty-income ratio), alongside a parallel income-gradient (slope index of inequality) comparison. Variance is estimated by Taylor linearization; attenuation uses a Rao-Wu bootstrap. Status. Exploratory: the hypotheses were formed after the authors had analysed overall (non-race-specific) prevalence and income inequality in the same data for a separate study. Published race-specific estimates for 2011–2014 exist (CDC Vital Signs, 2016), so the 2011–2014 direction is a replication rather than a confirmation; the change in racial/ethnic gaps since 1999–2004 is the new question. Race-specific outcomes had not been computed at the time of registration. Files: preregistration document (Markdown and PDF), version 1.0.
title: Racial/ethnic disparities in first-molar sealant prevalence among US children, 1999–2020: exploratory analysis pre-registration

summary: CHASE-AML is a synthetic banking benchmark comprising 33,176,605 settled transactions and 500,000 registered accounts. It combines persistent account activity with 26 standalone suspicious typologies and annotated single-path and branching laundering cases. Case, path, parent-transaction and stage information connects transfers so transaction rankings and the reach of alerts across cases can be evaluated separately. The package contains the full 36-column canonical transaction export and a 13-column core export of the same rows, opening and closing synthetic ledger snapshots, a data dictionary and file checksums. No customer banking records, paper-specific evaluation files, generator or evaluation code, trained policies or fitted models are included.
title: CHASE-AML: A Lifecycle-Aware Synthetic Banking Dataset for Anti-Money Laundering Research

summary: This dataset is version 1.1.0 of the P1 complete derived transcriptomic resource for mapping and comparing human pluripotent stem cell-derived beta-cell differentiation across published protocols. It contains 100 sample or time-point analysis units, an S0-S6 stage ontology with S7-S9 reserved, a 2,552-gene shared cost space, optimal-transport stage coordinates with 20 retrospectively exported reference-centroid bootstrap draws, five-axis/46-gene Maturity Fidelity Index scores with 16 sensitivity versions, a 25-module concordance atlas, gene- and module-level variance components, constructed reliability descriptors, provenance records, analysis-code snapshots, and two application workflows. Applications and evidence boundaries. The internal GSE158617 example uses 38 samples in a retrospective, in-sample interface demonstration and is not independent validation. The external GSE203264 application uses 35 wild-type samples and a rebuilt P1-compatible 2,550-gene reference. Its non-monotonic D35 result concerns unsorted, compositionally heterogeneous SC-islets and is not validation of the unmodified 2,552-gene model or a pure beta-cell accuracy result. Reliability values are constructed descriptors, not absolute dataset-quality scores or significance ranks. MFI values are within-matrix relative profiles, not absolute cross-protocol maturity measures. No in vivo developmental tiers, validated benchmark accuracy, clinical validity, or universal generalization are claimed. Reproduction scope. The package supplies package-local verification for the two application workflows and the external diagnostics. The analysis-code and provenance snapshots support inspection and traceability but are not represented as a relocatable clean-room rebuild of every manuscript display item. The reference-centroid draws are a retrospective deterministic reconstruction from frozen training inputs, not an original frozen cache. Source data and governance. GSE270220 and GSE275610 remain sealed and contributed to no statistic. The associated pilot-informed preregistration and execution governance records are identified through the related OSF project; private OSF access tokens are neither included nor required for the packaged application checks. summary: For hedge fund research reviewers, this report examines checks for selective reporting when a registered study is closed. At the author’s research service, the proposed use is review of research records before their conclusions enter an evaluation; no product integration or saving in review time has been measured. This report makes no claim of originality.   Checking whether a study followed its pre-registration requires comparing the report with the plan. This report tests one method for that comparison. A research record is kept in a fixed JSON format (registration, hash commitment, event log, closure), and seven mechanical rejection rules, R1 to R7, each target one selective-reporting defect taken from Arnott, Harvey and Markowitz (2019) and Harvey and Liu (2015). The comparison arm gives the same information, rendered as plain text, to a general-purpose language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) with one fixed instruction. The test plan, its thresholds and its decision order were frozen, with a local SHA-256 hash, before any code, record or label existed. For each of two cohorts a separate model session generated 33 synthetic records, 12 valid and 21 with one injected defect, without seeing the rules, and labels were locked before either arm ran. In the first (in-sample) cohort the rules flagged 21 of 21 defective records and rejected 0 of 12 valid ones. The language model also flagged 21 of 21 but rejected 6 of 12 valid records, which disqualifies it under the plan. In the second (out-of-sample) cohort the rules again scored 21 of 21 with 0 of 12 rejected, and the language model scored 17 of 21 with 0 of 12. The gap of 4 is below the pre-registered margin of 5. The pre-registered verdict for both cohorts is therefore "compared, threshold not met", and the report makes no claim that the rules add detection. A reduced rule set (R1, R2 and R7 only) missed 12 of 21 defects in both cohorts and is refuted. No confidence intervals are reported, because the plan forbids them: the records are constructed counterexamples, not a sample from any population.   Deposit version: Working paper, version 1.2 (2026-11-12). Author: Peilun Cai. The manuscript is an English typeset presentation of the same experiment; no new experiment or result was introduced. summary: Data and code for the paper "Label-efficient plant disease classification with vision foundation models: a leakage-controlled benchmark" by Harshvardhan Rai and Ravi Shankar Singh (Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology (Banaras Hindu University), Varanasi, India), submitted to the Journal of Plant Diseases and Protection. Code repository: https://github.com/harshvardhanrai-iitbhucse/plant_peft (version v1.0, also archived here as plant_peft_code_v1.zip). WHAT THIS DEPOSIT CONTAINS This deposit holds the derived data needed to check and reuse the results. It contains no images and no model weights; the images come from three public datasets and must be obtained from their original sources under their own licences. The data archive plant_peft_data_v1.zip contains: - splits/: the train/validation/test assignment of every image with its perceptual hash (pHash); the near-duplicate groups (Hamming distance ≤ 4) used to keep duplicates within one split; the cross-class duplicate list for the pigeon-pea dataset; and the manual audit of the 236 PlantDoc test images (photograph, plain background, text slide, collage). - results/: results.jsonl, one line per training run with its full configuration (model, method, learning rate, seed, data fraction) and validation and test metrics; the efficiency measurements (GMACs, latency, memory); per-class PlantDoc results. - runs/: for each run, the test-set predictions and labels as NumPy arrays, in the order of the test split in splits/, with small log and configuration files. - tables/ and figures/: every table and figure of the paper, as generated by the scripts from the files above. SOURCE DATASETS (NOT REDISTRIBUTED) - PlantVillage (Hughes and Salathé 2015), colour images; the 15 pepper, potato and tomato classes. - PlantDoc (Singh et al. 2020), official train/test split, 27 classes. - Pigeon-pea leaf dataset (Rajput and Doddamani 2024, Mendeley Data, version 1). The repository README describes how to prepare them. HOW TO REPRODUCE THE PAPER'S NUMBERS 1. Unpack plant_peft_code_v1.zip, or clone the repository at tag v1.0. 2. Obtain the three datasets and build the caches as described in the repository README. 3. Place splits/, results/ and runs/ from the data archive in the repository root. 4. Run python scripts/make_tables.py and python scripts/make_figures.py; they regenerate every table and figure from results/ and runs/ without any training. 5. To re-train a configuration, follow the repository README; each line of results.jsonl stores the full configuration of its run. PROTOCOL Splits are grouped by near-duplicate (pHash Hamming distance ≤ 4), so a duplicate never crosses the train/test boundary. Checkpoints are selected on validation data only. Every configuration is run with five seeds. Comparisons use a paired bootstrap over test images (10,000 resamples) with Holm correction within pre-registered families. LICENCE The derived data (splits, audits, logs, predictions, tables, figures) are released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT licence. The source images keep the licences of their original datasets. CITATION If you use these splits or audits, please cite the paper (reference to be added on publication) and this deposit (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24195419).
title: Data and code for: Label-efficient plant disease classification with vision foundation models: a leakage-controlled benchmark

summary: Conditional event studies often judge a result against placebo dates drawn at random. When the selecting state persists and forward returns overlap, that placebo is miscalibrated. In an exploratory simulation with 1,024 days, three event masks, 20-day overlapping outcomes and 1,000 replicates per scenario, a true null was rejected at nominal 5% in 30.8% of replicates by the first clustered mask (Wilson 95% interval 28.0–33.7) and in 79.1% (76.5–81.5) by the test across all three masks. Circular mask shifts, White’s Reality Check, Hansen’s SPA and Romano–Wolf stepdown came much closer to 5% but exceeded it in several cells, up to 15.5% for restricted shifts under a variance regime. The mechanism is old; this note proposes no new method and no new theorem, and gives one benchmark in one design. This deposit candidate awaits independent review of the publication-only changes. No new experiment, data or result is introduced.
title: When Random-Day Placebos Fail: Persistent Event States and Overlapping Returns

summary: A hedge fund researcher needs to know whether a reported event contrast depends on the control used to judge it. This study compares downside-reversal, 52-week-high-breakout and reported-volume-event masks on 20 admitted, existing long-history equity series. The application is a replayable check of the evidence attached to these conditions, rather than a return forecast. The revised protocol, code and source hashes were locked before these market outcomes were computed. No method passed every registered calibration cell, so this study makes no confirmatory market claim. The historical sample is conditional on the available cached histories and contains survival and selection bias. Differences between control distributions do not identify an amount of true economic overstatement. During the preparation of this work the author used Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) to write analysis code and draft text. After using these tools, the author reviewed and edited the content as needed, verified every number and citation against the replication package, and takes full responsibility for the content of the publication.
title: Control choice in price-and-volume event studies: reference geometry, costs, and calibration

summary: Analysis package for a study of copy-specific assignment at the two 23S rRNA copies of Helicobacter pylori . The package contains the eighteen supplementary tables, the analysis and figure code, the recorded software versions, the reconstruction log for the long-read alignments, and a per-read phase-evidence table. What is reproducible. The six-criterion classification of 103 matched isolates is re-runnable and every verdict was re-derived from the counts with zero mismatches. The reference metadata for all cited works is captured from Europe PMC and every DOI was verified against its record. The figures are generated by script and each passes a programmatic overlap, clipping and text-on-line audit before export. The short-read counts at the two A2143 coordinates are reproduced from the archived alignment, whose header records the exact command and tool versions. What is not. The original NCBI query string and its date were not retained, so the cohort cannot be rebuilt verbatim; per-accession inclusion flags are given instead. The barrnap installation originally used on the analysis machine is missing a Perl module and does not run; the rRNA copy numbers were therefore archived values in earlier versions and are re-derived with barrnap 1.10.5 in this version. The original parameter sets for two of the three long-read procedures were not retained; those procedures were re-run and both original and re-run values are reported side by side and never pooled. One cell of the long-read table reproduces exactly; the others do not, and this is stated in the manuscript. Changes in version 4. The package matches the manuscript. All thirteen supplementary tables are present, including Supplementary Tables S12 and S13, which were absent from the previous version, and Supplementary Table S1 now carries the genome length and assembly level of all 1,483 retained genomes rather than leaving those columns empty. A new Supplementary Table S1b lists the seven excluded genomes that could be recovered from local storage, with their lengths; the genome-length window is 1.5 to 1.7 Mb and this version states the evidence that fixes its bounds. Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. The four control reference sequences are deposited under results/marker_control/. Changes in version 6. This version restores the complete file set. The previous version was published from an incomplete upload, so most of the figures, several of the supplementary tables and part of the analysis code were missing from that record. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files and this package has 134, so the package is now deposited as a single archive, hp23s_copy_assignment_package.zip , which holds every file at the path it occupies in the source repository; this README, the SHA-256 manifest and the archive of rRNA calls and copy sequences are additionally placed loose in the record. From version 10 the manuscript itself is not deposited, in the archive or loose. Every member of the archive is listed in SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256, and that manifest is regenerated here, which corrects the entry for this README (the previous manifest had been computed before the last edit of the file). DOI.txt now lists the version DOIs, and the data-availability sentence in the manuscript names the concept DOI rather than one version, so that it cannot point at a superseded record. Changes in version 7. This version is a manuscript round: the text is rebuilt from the same locked data by the same script, and no reported value changes. Three defects in the supplementary apparatus are corrected
title: Long reads assign a 23S rRNA resistance allele to one of the two copies in Helicobacter pylori; a complete short-read assembly does not

summary: AiMat-Suite is the integrated, verifiable software framework developed for the doctoral thesis of A. O. Marcelo Júnior (PPGECM/UFC, LAMEFF). It chains, in a single system: (i) U-Net (ResNet-34) segmentation of fibre networks in optical photographs of chitosan/sisal films; (ii) automatic geometry and meshing (CalculiX cgx: S4 shells for the matrix, B32 beams for the fibres, translational MPC tie) and linear-elastic FE solution (CalculiX ccx); (iii) physics-informed and operator-learning surrogates (SharedPINN/Cascade PINN with Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation; Kuramoto-reservoir DeepONet with a Poisson-coupled nodal solver); (iv) a differentiable Rietveld engine for XRD with calibrated uncertainty and a declared domain of validity; (v) a material-card module that turns raw EMIC/Instron tensile curves into FE material cards with declared estimators, bootstrap confidence intervals and a load-regime check. Version 3.1.1 is the thesis reference release. The platform was developed in two stages: the aiMat MVP (2023–2025), which automated the image → model → simulation chain and produced the 2025 Materials Research papers, and AiMat-Suite (2026), which adds an operator-verification module (digitisation-invariance criterion), material cards built from tensile curves, the X-ray diffraction module, image-conditioned surrogates and zero-shot transfer to 217 microstructures. In AiMat-Suite the FE deck generator uses the translational fibre–matrix tie ( areampc 123 ), the choice supported by the digitisation-invariance criterion; matrix E = 13.67 MPa / ν = 0.35 from the tested plasticised film; fibre E = 9.3 GPa (sensitivity 31 GPa) / ν = 0.153; line load q = 1.75 kN/m applied as F = q·L_edge in N; static linear analysis; *NODE FILE, OUTPUT=2D . The provenance of every parameter is recorded in packages/fem/src/aiMat/calculix/materials.py . The MVP protocol (six-DOF tie, MVP material cards and load) is kept as legacy to reproduce the 2025 papers. packages/fem/reexecucao_v13/ contains the full re-execution of microstructures M1–M6 (decks, displacement fields, SHA-256 hashes) and of 220 image-derived microstructures, plus a test that rebuilds and solves M1 with ccx (E_eff within 0.5 % of the deposited value). The suite ships 170 Python modules and 90 tests ( scripts/verify.sh ). Changes in 3.1.1. (i) The coupled nodal solver and reservoir-readout ablation used in Sections 5.5.3.3–5.5.3.4 of the thesis ( packages/newton_oir/oir/phase_field_coupled.py , phase_field_sparse.py , metrics.py , hybrid_readout.py and experiments/ex31_v62_ablation_full.py ) were missing from 3.1.0 and are restored unchanged from the repository history; (ii) re-executions of 30 Oct–1 Nov 2026 are added under packages/fem/reexecucao_v13/ : surrogates on the AiMat-Suite fields, normalisation by the image-derived fibre fraction, sensitivity to shell thickness and beam diameter, and a complementary re-execution (reservoir readouts, coupled solver, leave-one-out and Wilcoxon on the AiMat-Suite fields; 660 CalculiX runs of the 220 image-derived cases with pure matrix, 9.3 GPa and 31 GPa fibres); (iii) SHA-256 manifests are computed on the LF-normalised files as versioned. Erratum to 3.1.0: its description states 210 Python modules; the 3.1.0 archive contains 154 (verify.sh count). Dependencies: Python ≥ 3.10, numpy/scipy/scikit-image/opencv (core); PyTorch (segmentation, PINNs, DRX AI routes); JAX (Rietveld engine); CalculiX 2.17 (FE). Abaqus is required only by the optional XFEM module ( packages/fem/src/abaqus/ ) and is not part of the open-source chain. Licence: MIT (integration and packages/drx ); datasets under assets/ are CC-BY-4.0. Companion archive (15 Nov 2026). AiMat-Suite-v3.1.1-tese_complemento.zip adds the trained U-Net weights (ResNet-34 encoder; partition by photograph and by crop) and the script and CSV that reproduce Tables 4 and 5 of the thesis (fibre diameter and total length on predicted versus annotated masks, 13 photographs, at the photograph resolu
title: AiMat-Suite v3.1.1 — integrated framework for image-based characterisation of natural-fibre biocomposites: U-Net segmentation, automatic FE meshing and CalculiX simulation, physics-informed surrogates, differentiable Rietveld XRD engine (thesis reference release)

summary: Deep-research Numbers article on heart disease, explaining one disparity statistic with its definition, denominator, and limits. In the American Heart Association's 2025 Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics fact sheet (data 2017-2020), 58.9% of non-Hispanic Black men and 59.0% of non-Hispanic Black women aged 20 and older had cardiovascular disease counted as a four-component bundle (coronary heart disease, heart failure, stroke, and hypertension), versus about 49% of all U.S. adults; hypertension alone accounted for 57.5% of men and 58.4% of women, while coronary heart disease alone was 6.2% and 6.3%. The article contrasts the bundle with interview-survey diagnosed coronary disease (Black adults 4.1% vs. 5.0% overall, NHIS 2024, via HHS OMH), shows major cardiovascular mortality in 2022 at 301.0 versus 223.0 per 100,000 (ratio 1.35, wider than the prevalence ratio of about 1.20), and prints the sources' limits: no confidence intervals in the fact sheet, a rounded summary comparison, and 2017-2020 vintage. No supplement claim and no product are made; omega-3, garlic, and green tea trial effects are used only as a scale check, including the omega-3 null across 20 trials and 68,680 patients (Rizos 2012). Evidence grade: STRONG. Educational article from the Buddha Ayurvedic School of Medicine: https://buddha.hospital
title: 59 Percent: What the Cardiovascular Disease Number for Black Adults Actually Means

summary: Publishing a model or method does not finish the work of applied mathematics. Turning a mathematical idea into a reliable operational tool requires translation: assessment of how well a method behaves in theory and under real domain constraints, adaptation of both the mathematical formulation and the software to modern computing architectures, and adoption into sustained community use. Because every simplified model leaves a gap between idealized assumptions and reality, it carries applicability debt that an overlapping web of skills—uniting applied mathematicians, statisticians, domain specialists, and research software engineers—must manage. Generative AI and multi-agent harnesses have upset that balance. Large language models and coding agents make it cheap to generate candidate derivations, simulation code, and machine-checked proofs while leaving problem formulation and concrete domain verification tied to scarce human judgement. When automated generation outpaces translation, applicability debt goes unmanaged and pushes adoption toward unverified shortcuts, risking a crisis of application. At the same time, Australian science and innovation policy largely equates translation with commercial intellectual property and private data centres while overlooking research software and verification capacity inside public agencies, national facilities, and universities. Picking up in 2006—the fiftieth anniversary of the Australian Mathematical Society (Counting Australia In) and the birth year of the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) and the ACCESS Earth-system partnership—this monograph contrasts that post-war public compact at the Society's seventieth anniversary in 2026 against Ambitious Australia and Science 2035, where research software disappears from policy view and the 2016–2025 mathematical-sciences decadal plan has expired without a successor. Written for both public policymakers and working quantitative practitioners, this book examines how translation succeeds or short-circuits across two centuries of computational history, a twenty-year citation census of 112 works applying the EQ algorithm for equal-area sphere partitions, Research Software Engineer workforce audits, Earth-system and biomedical case studies, and invariants-first software verification (PyEQSP and GluCat). Benchmarking Australia against Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, and New Zealand across 18 chapters, 3 empirical appendices, and 750 verified primary sources (188 pages), it outlines practical, trade-off-aware opportunities across university assessment, service teaching, research software careers, scientific societies, sovereign infrastructure, and public-interest model verification ahead of the 2026–2028 national research and infrastructure renewals.
title: What does it take to apply mathematics in Australia today?

summary: Single-valued neutrosophic set theory is an important soft computing approach for resolving uncertainty and imprecision in decision-making. Several models have been established under the framework of single-valued neutrosophic sets for decision-making purposes. Single-valued neutrosophic relations, their max-min-max composition and a score-based use of this composition in medical diagnosis already exist in the literature; this paper revisits the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation in the framework of composite relations under fuzzy-set extensions, describes its algebraic properties, and applies it to two new healthcare problems. In this work, this composite relation on single-valued neutrosophic sets is presented. The numerical illustrations of the composite relation are given, and some of its algebraic properties are proved (inverse, monotonicity, associativity and distributivity over union), while it is shown by counterexamples that the composition is neither commutative nor distributive over intersection. In addition, the applications of the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation to medical healthcare services are considered to illustrate its use. Two medical healthcare applications are considered involving prediction of maternal outcome for a pregnant woman and the diagnosis of some common ailments. The examples are illustrative and use data adapted from earlier studies; no clinical validation is claimed.
title: Single-Valued Neutrosophic Composite Relation and Its Application to Healthcare Services

summary: Emissions figures in ship weather routing rest on regulatory and market data that change with new legal acts and markets. Maintaining them by hand is slow and prone to plausible errors. This paper presents the Data Steward, an agent built on a large language model that maintains these data in EcoRouter, a workbench for ship weather routing. The agent changes a value that calculations use only through an approved proposal. Deterministic tools take over the tasks that the model performs unreliably, such as reading area boundaries from legal texts, and checks run as workflows of small steps with an outcome for every item. The contribution to artificial intelligence is the design of an agent that maintains regulatory reference data under human control, together with a method for evaluating such an agent. The engineering application is the maintenance of the regulatory data on which a ship-routing tool computes emissions and regulatory costs. In a controlled test with 40 errors injected into the data that a full check covers, the Steward corrected 36 to 38 in three runs, against 20 to 28 for the same model alone with web search. In three full checks of the live data, 96 to 99 % of judged items were correct. A person who took no part in building EcoRouter found 57 of the 59 approved values correct. The results show that a commercial language model can maintain regulatory reference data with few errors once the tasks it performs unreliably are moved into deterministic code. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Version 1. The records of the tests are published as a dataset: 10.5281/zenodo.24251511. Use of AI: during the preparation of this work the author used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) in order to correct the text, check its grammar, to create the tables and figures from the author's records, and to check the statements about EcoRouter against its source code. The same assistant also helped to run tests 1 and 3, to judge their results against the acts and publishers, to prepare the person's sheet for test 2 and to aggregate the results of the three tests. It did only the tasks that the author gave it, under the author's control. The author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for it. Language models are also part of the research itself: Section 5 of the paper states which model the Data Steward ran on and which AI assistant judged its results.
title: A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence" by Jingyang Li (School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, China). This deposit contains the analysis code, the result files behind every number reported in the manuscript, the figure sources and the executed forced-choice log. The external eye-tracking arm re-analyses the public SensCogAR dataset archived at Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/45tjp); that archive declares no explicit data licence, so the raw records are not redistributed here, while the derived per-participant windows and metrics are included in data/real_ar_gaze/. The nine display devices used in the external-evidence arms are described by published measurements, each cited with its DOI in the manuscript, and the extracted parameters are recorded in data/panel_response_identification/. The target display panel and the human observers of the perceptual arm were not measured, so no raw panel or eye-tracker record exists for them. Contents: code/ (analysis, verification, simulation and figure scripts plus the LaTeX typesetting pipeline), data/ (the JSON, CSV and Markdown result files behind every number), manuscript_en_jsid_template.md (manuscript source), perceptual_experiment_protocol.md, AUDIT_citations.md, README.md, LICENSE.txt and CITATION.cff. Reproducing the results: ``` export JSID_MD='manuscript_en_jsid_template.md' python code/verify_manuscript_numbers.py    # CHECKED 404 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_tables_6_9.py           # TABLES 6-9 CHECKED 252 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_data_provenance.py      # per-device DOI and tau audit python code/verify_figure_resolution.py    # 600 dpi plate check ``` Licence: data and documentation CC BY 4.0; code MIT. Please cite the article above; a CITATION.cff file is included in this deposit.
title: Data and code for: Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence

summary: The records of the tests reported in the preprint "A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation" (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24250853). The Data Steward is an agent built on a large language model that keeps the emissions-regulation data of EcoRouter, a weather-routing tool, current. It proposes changes, and an administrator approves them. The files hold every message EcoRouter sent the agent and every answer, its proposals, the outcome of every item checked, and the judgement of each item and proposal against its act or publisher. - Test 1: three full checks of the live data, checks 1, 2 and 3. - Test 2: a person's check of the 59 values approved in test 1: the values, the instructions given to the person, the person's sheet, the key and the result. - Test 3: nine runs on a copy of the data with injected errors. A1 to A3 are the agent as built, B1 to B3 the same model alone with web search, and E1 to E3 a check of the EU ETS exemptions. Beside the runs: the answer key, the random draw of the errors with its seed, the changes that made the test copy, and the result of each run. - Severity: the rule that grades every wrong result as high, medium or small, the grade of each, and EcoRouter's value catalogue. E-mail addresses and names are replaced by codes. CONTENTS.md lists every file and the test it belongs to. The ZIP keeps the folder tree. These files are the output of the language-model agent evaluated in the paper, gpt-5.5 (version 2026-04-24) in Microsoft Foundry, and the judgements of its work, made by an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) under the author's control, as Section 5 of the paper describes. They are research data on that agent. Some proposals carry area boundaries from Marine Regions: Flanders Marine Institute (2026), MarineRegions.org, licensed under CC BY. Some carry place positions from OpenStreetMap: © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License, https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright.
title: Records of the tests of a language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool

summary: RideLab is a self-contained, browser-based platform for the design and teaching of active suspension control, for students, researchers, educators and engineers. It simulates a vehicle active suspension in real time and compares six controllers, PID, fuzzy logic, sliding mode, linear-quadratic regulator, model predictive control and a neural network, against a passive baseline on an ISO 8608 road, with live plots and a multi-indicator dashboard. An integrated adaptive AI tutor guides learners with missions, prediction questions and graded hints, and can be switched off for pure design work. The archive contains the toolbox, a Python reference engine, verification harnesses for the design tool and for the tutor, the road seeds and controller tunings, and the scripts that regenerate the published results and figures. How to use Option 1, use the toolbox: download RideLab.html and open it in any modern web browser (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox or Microsoft Edge). No installation or external dependencies are needed. Option 2, see the code and regenerate the results: download RideLab_v1.0.zip and unzip it. The toolbox is included as suspension_design_toolbox.html. To regenerate the results, follow README.md; the scripts need Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib, and the harnesses and timing script need Node.js. Generative AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) assisted in developing the software; the author verified all results against the reference engine. Access to the files is granted on request.
title: RideLab: a browser-based platform for the design and teaching of active suspension control

summary: This doctoral thesis, entitled Genomic Studies of Piscine Streptococci and Genome Assembly of Clariidae Catfishes (Siluriformes) for Aquaculture Enhancement, was prepared at the Faculty of Fisheries, Kasetsart University, Thailand, for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). The thesis integrates microbial comparative genomics, genome assembly, genome annotation, repeat and gene-family analysis, population genomics and chromosome evolution to develop genomic resources and analytical approaches relevant to aquaculture, fish health and genetic management. It comprises eight research chapters and a general discussion. Chapter 1 — Bighead catfish genome assembly. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of Clarias macrocephalus generated with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing. Chapter 2 — Streptococcus iniae comparative genomics and reverse vaccinology. The genome of strain SIKU01 and comparative analyses of 90 isolates used to prioritize candidate antigens. The candidates require experimental validation. Chapter 3 — F1 hybrid catfish genome annotation. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved assembly of the interspecific hybrid Clarias macrocephalus × Clarias gariepinus , with its protein-coding, non-coding, satellite and transposable-element annotation. Chapter 4 — Repetitive architecture of the two haplotypes. Tandem repeats, segmental duplications, gene-family clusters, the miR-430 array and the divergence of Gypsy and Helitron elements. Chapter 5 — Hatchery population genomics. Diversity, relatedness, family reconstruction, autozygosity, structural variation, polymorphic inversions and shared parents in a commercial C. gariepinus broodstock. Chapter 6 — Gene repertoire and divergence of the two parental haplotypes, on a phylogenomic framework of 17 catfish genomes. Chapter 7 — Composition of the 41 polymorphic inversions of C. gariepinus and deletion-based PCR markers for their arrangements. The markers were designed in silico and have not been tested in the laboratory. Chapter 8 — Fusion and fission between the karyotypes of the two species. Junctions are reported as intervals; no mechanism is resolved at any junction. Chapter 9 — General discussion and conclusion. Changes since the version of 2026-11-03: lists of tables and figures; Chapters 7 and 8 revised; five figures of the repeat analyses added to Chapters 3 and 4 (spacer types of the LG04 array, tandem repeats against chromosome ends, copy number by counting step, array structure of repeated loci, Gypsy and Helitron); new introductions of Chapters 6 and 7; Chapter 9 updated to the chapters. summary: We present an analytical derivation of fundamental coupling constants and structural attractors emerging from a descending residual iteration function F(y,x) possessing a unique global fixed point y*(x) . Evaluating the first iteration term for specific membrane residues ( 155 and 185 ) yields pure, asymmetric numerical invariants--most notably 461.4331634036143, composed almost exclusively of the four digits {1, 3, 4, 6}--which directly link the inverse fine-structure constant alpha^{-1} approx 137.036 and the characteristic quark bounce frequency (925) to the 43.2 GeV signal. Through algebraic decomposition, we isolate the longitudinal attractor ( 323 ) governing transversal gravitational anchorage and membrane confinement from the transversal emission attractor ( 232 ), demonstrating how their balance generates a flat background (555) driven by the double-axis torsion gradient of charmonium. Finally, by applying discrete digit-suppression transformations ( 137.036 -> 137.360 and removal of the 036 residue), we map the transition to an antimatter-dominated dual system lacking inversion symmetry and derive a secondary four-digit invariant (2177.5711270036704), establishing arithmetically differentiated topological sets as the fundamental origin of the distinct interaction regimes.

summary: Here are our trained ARPA format 4-gram language models. We evaluated each model by computing the average per-word perplexity on 36.6K words of conversational style text. Name                Size      Perplexity Tiny 25MB 90.1 Small 110MB 73.7 Medium 205MB 69.2 Large 662MB 63.3 Huge 4.9GB 59.1 The test set consisted of 4,567 sentences (36.6K words, 161K characters). The test set was a combination of: COMM - Sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (2.1K words). COMM2 - Crowdsourced sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (13K words). See our ASSETS 2013 paper . Specialists - Phrases suggested by AAC specialists. Taken from University of Nebraska-Lincoln from web pages that are no longer available (4.2K words). Enron mobile - Messages written by Enron employees on Blackberry mobile devices (18K words). The test set was in lowercase and included limited punctuation (apostrophes, commas, periods, exclamation points, and question marks). We excluded the sentence end word from our perplexity calculations. This was necessary since the models were trained only on sentences ending in a period, exclamation point, or question mark. But some test sentences do not have end-of-sentence punctuation, this led to the sentence end word being very improbable. There are also BerkeleyLM and KenLM versions of these models (see bottom of page). Training details Vocabulary. These models use a 100K vocabulary including an unknown word, and words for commas, periods, exclamation points, questions marks, sentence start <s> , and sentence end </s> . We first trained a unigram language model on each of our training sources. We only included words that were in a list of 697K English words we obtained via human edited dictionaries, including a February 2019 parse of Wiktionary. We converted all words to lowercase. We trained a linear mixture model using equal weights for each of the unigram models. Finally, we took the most probable 100K words as our vocabulary. Training data We used the following training sources: Amazon - Amazon review corpus (4.0B words). Common - Text of web pages from Common Crawl, Oct 2018 version (185B words). Blog - ICWSM 2009 Spinn3r Blog Dataset (599M words). Book - Books from Project Gutenberg (1.2B words). Email - Archived email messages from Apache lists, through Jan 2019 (167M words). Forum - Messages parsed from web forums (278M words). News - Newswire text from the one billion word language modeling benchmark (272M words). Reddit - Reddit corpus, Dec 2005 - May 2019 (82.0B words). Social - Social media data from the ICWSM 2011 Spinn3r blog data set (829M words). Subtitle - OpenSubtitles corpus (677M words). Twitter - Twitter messages sampled between Dec 2010 and Aug 2019 (18B words). Usenet - WestburyLAB reduced redundancy USENET corpus (2005-2011) (1.6B words). Wiki - Dump of Wikipedia including talk pages but not page history (1.5B words). Yelp - Yelp open dataset, 6.7M restaurant reviews (470M words). We dropped sentences where 20% or more of words were out-of-vocabulary (OOV) with respect our 698K word list. We wanted our models to learn across end-of-sentence punctuation words. After each parsed sentence from a training set, we concatenated another sentence from that training set with probability 0.5. We only concatenated sentences that came from the same apparent author (i.e. from the same tweet, blog post, web page, etc). Within each training set, we removed training sentences that occurred more than once. Data filtering We used cross-entropy difference selection to select a subset of sentences from each training set. summary: Sweet proteins — brazzein (54 aa), monellin (single-chain MNEI, 95 aa), and thaumatin I (207 aa) — elicit intense sweetness at the human TAS1R2/TAS1R3 heterodimeric receptor at concentrations orders of magnitude lower, by weight, than sucrose. Their utility in food and ingredient applications is constrained by thermolability (monellin), limited yield in plant expression hosts (brazzein), and receptor-binding geometry that makes rational mutagenesis difficult. We apply inverse folding with ESM-IF1 and ProteinMPNN to redesign all three sweet proteins under structural constraints that pin the established sweetness-contact residues and the disulfide geometry, while sampling the remaining sequence space for predicted thermostability and expression-host compatibility. For each protein, we generate 500 candidate sequences per method (1,000 per protein, 3,000 total), score each with ESM2 log-likelihood ratio and in-silico thermostability predictors, and report the top-20 designs per protein alongside matched random controls (sequences that do not pin the contact residues) to establish the baseline distribution. All designs are computational; no wet-lab validation was performed. Covered by U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. [P4 APPLICATION NUMBER]. Platform: platform.scovillesplice.farm The methods and constructs described herein are the subject of U.S. Provisional Patent Application Nos. 64/172,827 (filed October 9, 2026), 64/188,197 (filed October 30, 2026), 64/192,062 (filed November 5, 2026), and 64/199,105 (filed November 15, 2026).
title: Computational Redesign of Sweet Proteins via Inverse Folding: Brazzein, Monellin, and Thaumatin Variants with Pinned Sweetness-Contact Residues and Matched Random Controls

summary: This paper develops a mathematical framework for Quantum Information Holography (QIH), examining how nonlocal quantum information, phase relationships, interference, and holographic encoding can be represented through a unified information-processing architecture. The framework establishes formal relationships between quantum state vectors, angular frequency, the sum over histories, boundary encoding, and geodesic information addressing. It derives conditions for reversible reconstruction, matched quantum readout, and the preservation of information through successive phase-dependent transformations. The analysis further examines connections to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, relational geometry, quantum measurement, and the emergence of spacetime structure. It extends this framework to investigate the proposed role of biological information processing in the reconstruction of conscious experience. Mathematical definitions, conditional theorems, and explicit derivations distinguish established quantum-information results from the additional physical hypotheses concerning gravitation and consciousness, providing a foundation for further theoretical development and experimental investigation.
title: The Quantum Internet of Consciousness: The Universe Has an Address

summary: Version 1.0 — November 2026. Initial preprint deposit. Umami-Enriched Capsicum: Glutamate Accumulation via GAD1/GAD4 Knockout and GDH1 Overexpression Achieves IFI-U ≥ 800 in Ultra-High-SHU Cultivars Priyanca Iyengar Ford, Scoville Splice LLC · ORCID 0000-0003-0395-1752 Preprint · Scoville Splice Research Series · Paper 5 of 11 · 2026-11-01 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── OVERVIEW This paper describes a dual metabolic engineering strategy to accumulate free L-glutamate in the placental tissue of ultra-high-SHU Capsicum annuum cultivars, achieving an Iyengar Flavor Index for umami (IFI-U) of ≥ 800 without disrupting capsaicinoid biosynthesis. The strategy combines (1) CRISPR knockout of two fruit-specific glutamate decarboxylase isoforms (CaGAD1, CaGAD4) to block the GABA shunt, and (2) overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (AtGDH1) to increase net glutamate synthesis from the TCA cycle intermediate 2-oxoglutarate. This paper should be read alongside Paper 4 (Iyengar Flavor Index methodology), Paper 7 (Kokumi engineering, which shares the glutamate/N-metabolism pool), and Paper 1 (foundational capsaicinoid engineering, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23743695). ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── BIOLOGICAL BACKGROUND Free L-glutamate is the primary ligand for the umami taste receptor, metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1), which was identified as a taste receptor by Chaudhari et al. (2000, Nat Neurosci 3:113). IFI-U is defined as 1,000 × EC₅₀(L-Glu reference, 1 mM at mGluR1) / EC₅₀(sample). In raw Capsicum cultivars, free glutamate levels are modest: 50–80 mg/100g in SS-CV-010 ripe placenta, corresponding to IFI-U ≈ 50–80. The GABA shunt (Glutamate → GABA, catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase; GABA → succinate, via GABA-T + SSADH) represents the major glutamate sink in ripening fruit. Two fruit-expressed GAD isoforms were identified in C. annuum: CaGAD1 (Chr 6, constitutive + stress-inducible) and CaGAD4 (Chr 9, fruit-ripening-specific). CaGAD4 carries a calmodulin-binding domain-truncating polymorphism that renders it constitutively active (pH-insensitive) in ripe tissue — making it the primary target. Precedent: Kisaka et al. (1997, Plant Cell Physiol 38:255) demonstrated that expression of E. coli glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) in tomato increased free amino acid content 2–3×, with glutamate the primary beneficiary. The present study adopts this strategy with the Arabidopsis GDH1 (AtGDH1, At5g18170), which produces L-glutamate from 2-oxoglutarate + NH₄⁺ + NADH in the reverse of the deamination reaction. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: GAD CRISPR KNOCKOUT Targets: CaGAD1 and CaGAD4, simultaneous dual-gene knockout. Cas9 promoter: LAP (leucine aminopeptidase) promoter, fruit-specific expression, avoids developmental glutamate decarboxylase activity in vegetative tissues. LAP is expressed in wounded and ripening Capsicum fruit (Fowler et al. 1992, Plant Physiol 99:439). Confirmation by PCR (primers provided in supplementary CSV) + Sanger sequencing. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: AtGDH1 OVEREXPRESSION Gene: AtGDH1 (At5g18170, Arabidopsi

summary: High-dimensional sparse recipe formulation in process industries involves nonlinear association of various covariates, bounded by sparsity constraints and multi-criteria tolerances. Traditional physics-based classical methods (such as Kubelka-Munk) fail to generate sparse candidate recipes properly due to their simplified assumptions and industrial process variations. This study proposes a hybrid physics-informed uncertainty-aware framework that is structured into three modules: (a) Module A, a multi-target forward quality model; (b) Module B, a sparse inverse reconstructor; and (c) Module C, a feasibility-constrained ranking layer. Then it has been validated in an industrial textile dyeing context with recipe-grouped cross-validation under multi-illuminant quality assessment comprising process and production information, target reflectance, K/S values, and spectral descriptors. Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB) with spectral-only features ($R_λ$, K/S) and Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBDT) with recipe-process features outperforms other configurations with out-of-Fold MAE of 0.1655 and 0.1523 in the forward quality model. For inverse reconstruction, a component-wise median blend achieved a recipe-vector MAE of 0.0295. Exploratory conditional treatment effect (CATE) suggests an observational association that alkali adjustment reduces error for red and pale shades (CATE = -0.196). This framework provides a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool that minimizes costly laboratory trials across industrial formulation domains.
title: A Physics-Informed Hybrid Forward-Inverse Machine Learning Framework for High-Dimensional Sparse Recipe Reconstruction

summary: Co-design methods optimize a robot's body and controller jointly and judge the result by one number, the task reward of the fully optimized pair. That number cannot separate morphologies whose competence depends on the controller to very different degrees. We evaluate a morphology by restricting its controller instead, recording the task competence it retains under an explicitly declared, low-complexity controller family, environment, task and search budget. On three EvoGym locomotion tasks, task reward explains only $39\%$, $33\%$ and $10\%$ of the variance in this quantity, and geometric descriptors do not predict it under run-grouped cross-validation. The measurement is reliable across optimizer restarts (ICC$(2,k) = 0.956$--$0.986$) but depends on the declared family: phasing the drive by actuator index instead of position ranks the same morphologies at Spearman $0.50$--$0.63$ and reverses reward-matched pairs. As a second search objective the axis improved competence at matched task reward in $3$ of $5$ paired runs, short of a pre-registered bar of $4$. Used after an ordinary reward-only search instead, to choose within its top task-reward band, it selected a different body in all $8$ runs offering a choice, at a cost of at most $0.10$ reward units, and in $6$ of $8$ that body also scored higher under a held-out family. Restricted-control competence is therefore a reportable property of a co-designed morphology, interpretable only with the controller family that defines it.
title: Beyond Task Reward: A Controller-Restriction Protocol for Evaluating Embodiment-Dependent Competence

summary: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial malignancy, occurring in roughly 30% of patients with primary solid tumors and carrying a median survival near 5.9 months. Automated segmentation is critical for treatment planning and volumetric monitoring, but metastases are frequently small, numerous, and heterogeneous in size within a single patient. We compare a plain nnU-Net baseline, a Residual Encoder Large (ResEncL) variant, region-based training, and a Primus transformer model for BraTS-METS 2026 Task 1, using patient-grouped cross-validation to prevent leakage from the longitudinal UCSD subset. Primus (label-based) is our strongest individual model by aggregate DSC/NSD, achieving 0.710/0.761 (ET), 0.742/0.785 (TC), 0.683/0.689 (WT), and 0.531/0.436 (RC). ResEncL trails Primus on aggregate DSC/NSD but achieves substantially higher lesion-wise F1 (e.g. ET: 0.452 vs. 0.052); a probability-averaging ensemble of the two only partially preserves ResEncL's F1 advantage (ET lesion-wise F1: 0.064). We further report three postprocessing and label-reconstruction pitfalls we believe generalize beyond this challenge. Code is available at https://github.com/mahdiislam79/BraTS_METS_2026.
title: Brain Metastases Segmentation for BraTS 2026 Task 1: A Multi-Architecture Comparison

summary: Spatially resolved stress proxies and rate-based seismicity models are increasingly combined for regional earthquake forecasting, yet formally testing their non-redundancy remains largely unaddressed. We present the Nested-Permutation Alarm for Dual-Parameter Earthquake Forecasting (ANADEF) pipeline, integrating a stress-sensitive Gutenberg--Richter $b$-value field, estimated via a penalized 2D B-spline inversion, with a stationary background rate ($μ$) from space--time ETAS stochastic declustering. Applied to the Zagros Fold--Thrust Belt using an 18-year catalog ($n=40{,}731$, $M_{\mathrm{N}}\geq1.5$, 2006--2024) under a two-stage protocol with non-overlapping training (2006--2014) and target (2015--2024) windows, the model achieves, for $M_w\geq5.0$ ($N=55$), a retrospective Area Skill Score $S=0.69$ (95\% CI: 0.64--0.73), reducing alarmed area from $τ\approx0.38$ ($μ$-only) to $τ\approx0.28$ while retaining hit rate $ν=92.7\%$; since thresholds are calibrated on the evaluation catalog, these are in-sample, not out-of-sample, estimates. A nested permutation procedure re-optimizing thresholds within each null realization tests whether $b$-value adds information beyond $μ$, absorbing the optimization bias. Significance is null-model dependent: cell-wise randomization yields $p=0.012$, while a conservative spatial-structure-preserving null gives weaker, non-significant evidence ($p=0.057$)---incremental stress information is suggestive but not unambiguously established. Calibrated thresholds were frozen and applied to updated 2015--2024 fields, generating an unvalidated, forward-looking spatial alarm template for 2025--2029. These results establish a reproducible, statistically transparent methodology for testing, rather than assuming, complementarity between stress-sensitive and rate-based predictors, offering a candidate operational template pending prospective validation.
title: ANADEF: A Nested-Permutation Alarm for Dual-Parameter Earthquake Forecasting

summary: Performance claims in quantum technology are not properties of hardware alone. They are properties of a declared task, system boundary, normalization denominator, uncertainty or security convention, and comparator. We perform a cross-domain analysis spanning quantum computing, simulation, communication, sensing, clocks, randomness generation, and their enabling technologies. The analysis changes substantive conclusions in several representative cases. For the longest direct finite-key quantum key distribution case analyzed here, the same final key gives rates differing by a factor of $1.91$ when normalized by complete acquisition rather than transmission-active time. In Advanced LIGO, $6.1\,\mathrm{dB}$ peak quantum-noise reduction coexists with a $0.534$ coincident analysis-ready fraction, separating detector-level gain from delivered observing service. In quantum computation and photonic sampling, matching the observable, error tolerance, loss model, sample count, amortization, and classical hardware moves or reverses published crossover claims. Across domains, the recurring limits are correlated error, multiplicative interface loss, thermal and nonequilibrium occupation, calibration covariance, measurement efficiency, fabrication yield, and control latency. A quantum advantage is therefore established only for a fixed task and boundary when the accepted output outperforms the best documented alternative at matched accuracy, elapsed time, availability, and lifecycle cost. The resulting framework identifies the measurements required to convert component records into reproducible system capability. Credible progress is defined by reproduced logical workloads, prospectively validated simulations, repeater links outperforming direct transmission, long-duration calibrated sensors and clocks, integrated hardware with predictable yield and reliability.
title: Quantum Technologies: System-Level Performance and Validation Priorities

summary: We present Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory (AVCT), a theory-guided framework for deriving interpretable blood pressure (BP) predictors from photoplethysmography (PPG) attractor geometry. AVCT connects vascular dynamics, PPG observation, delay-coordinate reconstruction, and attractor descriptors within a unified framework for formulating testable hypotheses, without presupposing the physiological sufficiency of a particular low-dimensional feature set. We evaluate a LightGBM-based estimator using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV) across two complementary experimental settings. Experiment 1 comprises 46 ICU/surgical subjects from BIDMC and VitalDB, with ECG, PPG, and repeated reference BP measurements. The calibrated full model achieves systolic/diastolic BP (SBP/DBP) mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 2.05/1.67 mmHg, compared with 2.02/1.63 mmHg for the PPG-attractor-only model. Experiment 2 includes 217 ambulatory subjects from the PPG-BP dataset (651 PPG windows; one cuff-based BP reference per subject) and assesses cross-subject calibrated BP reconstruction rather than within-subject BP tracking. The PPG-attractor model achieves SBP/DBP MAEs of 1.98/0.96 mmHg. Across both cohorts, incorporating ECG-derived features provides no practically meaningful improvement in MAE. Calibration substantially reduces between-subject offset error, while morphological and dynamical descriptors contribute complementary predictive information. Although the reported numerical errors fall within commonly cited thresholds associated with AAMI/ISO and BHS criteria, these findings do not establish compliance with device-validation standards. Collectively, the results support AVCT as a mechanistically motivated representation framework for interpretable PPG-based BP estimation and provide a foundation for prospective validation using repeated reference BP measurements and smartphone-acquired PPG.
title: Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory: Formal Grounding and Empirical Validation for AAMI-Standard Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation from Smartphone Photoplethysmography

summary: Pre-registered evaluation exhibit on the UCI SECOM dataset (1567 rows, 590 features, 104 fail vs 1463 pass). The experiment tests whether the accuracy-optimal classifier misses more defects than a lower-accuracy alternative under an explicit error-cost matrix, and whether a cost-aligned decision threshold (p* = FP/(FP+FN)) reverses the accuracy ranking. The sealed design (seal.json, verified before run) uses RepeatedStratifiedKFold (10 folds x 3 repeats, 30 splits), stdlib-only validation, and deterministic artifact generation. The archive includes the pipeline and analysis code, the sealed experiment specification, per-fold records, the findings write-up, figures, and the data dictionary and methodology contract.
title: Classifier Cost Exhibit: Accuracy vs fail-class recall inversion under asymmetric error costs on UCI SECOM
