summary: AI systems commonly retain sources, outputs, and user facts while discarding communicable changes in interpretation: questions, tensions, connections, hypotheses, and revisions. We study preserving those changes for an agent's future cognition, not merely its next answer. We call this self-directed understanding: simulating functional features of serious inquiry without claiming human experience or access to hidden computation. We present the Understanding Graph, an implemented architecture for a continuing Reader whose persistent graph is the medium of work. The Reader encounters material, externalizes a substantive interpretive change, and commits it as typed and versioned state, while competing and displaced views remain inspectable. When it deliberately re-enters the changed graph, an update can meet an older question, tension, model, or artifact and prompt another material change, and a later pass begins from the altered state. That is the proposed understanding spiral. Encountered passages and produced prose or code are ordered units of the same graph, so recorded understanding can shape exact units and their consequences can occasion further updates. The medium supports both convergence and divergence, and the Reader may reject any provocation. An optional Bisociation Engine can intensify divergence through graph topology, temporary axioms, and stochastic perturbation while leaving its outputs unvalidated. The contribution is a fluid protocol for self-addressed encounter, persistent interpretive change, agent-chosen re-entry, cross-instance continuity, and graph-native documents. The implementation makes the proposal concrete and inspectable but does not establish improved understanding or performance. Controlled evaluation must separately test whether re-entry changes the externalized trajectory beyond matched storage and rehearsal, and whether any change improves later work.
title: Understanding Graph: A Persistent Medium for Recursive Understanding

summary: Can a language model build a world as it writes? The Substrate-Translated Language Model (STLM) makes structured images, descriptions, or videos compulsory for every lexical decision and asks whether this biases computation toward reusable physical and schematic factors. The underlying thesis is that constructing an image or description of a word, abstract words included, is a form of intelligence: the construction gives the word properties of reality that interact with those of other words. If such meaningful targets share exploitable structure, they may promote reusable factors across words rather than independent token codes, and routing every word through them could embed that intelligence in the model. STLM's development path moves from one fixed substrate per word, through varied context-sensitive instances and short clips, to substrates for longer spans and ultimately one continuously changing scene from which language is read. We call the emergence of an accumulating, manipulable organization scene emergence; it is the long-term hypothesis, not a result demonstrated here. The stage-1 pilot tests this no-bypass prerequisite on a 1,024-token TinyStories vocabulary with one fixed pixel image or encoded description per token. On held-out contexts, causal description and pixel readouts reach 41.9% and 37.8% top-1 next-token accuracy, below a direct-token model at 44.7% but above stateless counterparts at 35.0% and 27.8%. The causal configurations differ in architecture, capacity, and supervision density, so their gains do not isolate history. Because each canonical can serve as an arbitrary codeword, the pilot establishes interface feasibility, not semantic use, latent scene induction, or explicit scene construction. The next tests isolate history use, compare aligned with permuted targets, and introduce varied lexical prototypes before video and multiscale composition.
title: Toward Compulsory Scene-Mediated Language Modeling: Meaningful Substrates for Every Next Word

summary: Open-ended problems such as institutional design lack enumerable solution spaces and cheap automatic evaluators. World-diversity search moves variation upstream of the answer. Target-blind Builders construct textual worlds with altered causal rules; purpose-blind Solvers address the same target under each rule set; and compilers translate the resulting mechanisms into a common target-domain schema. Building on this previously released operator, this paper introduces ontology-governed intervention search. A Taxonomist curates a persistent typed ontology of complete interventions, judges structural equivalence, and can turn rejection into targeted commissioning: its diagnosis specifies which causal relation the next proposal must change, while accepted interventions and revised categories persist as control state for later Explorers. Together, the operators provide the expansion stage of a proposed expansion-before-optimization pipeline: diversify causal premises, then make the resulting candidate population cumulative and steerable. The aim is that an open problem acquires a map of its mechanism space, not a list of answers; this is untested. Across eight workflows on one retirement-design problem, the released system produced 196 candidate records; its world stage comprised 25 world-and-solve branches. In an unblinded post-hoc census, the world's premise removed or eased a difficulty of the target problem in every branch, clearly in 17 and partly in eight, and all 25 Solvers still built a multi-component design beyond it. Seven complete rejection–redirection–mechanism-change chains appeared across 75 planned graph positions. These artifacts document automated fan-out, premise-conditioned generation, and graph-conditioned redirection, but do not establish external novelty, utility, causal performance, cross-domain generality, or large-scale efficiency.
title: The Ontology of the Alien: World-Diversity Search and Evolving Solution Ontologies

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask three questions. Do numerical histories shape generation? Do process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls? Does learning from construction histories improve the next corpus and the learner trained on it? Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: A 30-minute talk at the European GNU Radio Days 2026, Rennes. Radar, telecommunications and particle accelerators share a surprisingly intertwined history. From Bragg's sound-ranging and Widerøe's RF accelerator through the "Battle of the Beams", radar, magnetrons and klystrons, ideas, people and technologies repeatedly moved between scientific and engineering domains. This talk uses that history to explore a present-day problem: many fields still solve closely related problems — timing, filtering, coherent detection, feedback, spectral estimation and control — but often with different terminology and tools. Can a more common language, shared software-defined tools such as GNU Radio 4, and stronger teaching of signal-processing and control fundamentals help the next generation of scientists and engineers collaborate across these boundaries rather than repeatedly reinventing the same solutions? The record holds the slides as PDF, one page per slide and one page per step, and the gr4-present deck itself (zip, with speaker notes and the GNU Radio 4 flow-graphs of its live acoustic demonstrations). Live slides in the browser: https://ralphsteinhagen.github.io/talk-beams-echos-spectra/viewer/b9e1baa/?presentation=../../default
title: Beams, Echoes and Spectra — From wartime navigation and radar to particle accelerators and software-defined radio

summary: Manuscript in preparation (working draft; author list and order provisional). The F 1 hybrid between female bighead catfish ( Clarias macrocephalus , 2n = 54) and male North African catfish ( C. gariepinus , 2n = 56) is a major aquaculture fish in Southeast Asia. Hatchery broodstock often lack pedigree records, and whether large structural haplotypes can be followed through such unrecorded pedigrees has remained unclear. Here we present a near-telomere-to-telomere, haplotype-resolved assembly of an F 1 hybrid, which provides chromosome-scale references for both species. The two karyotypes differed by one rearrangement chain of about 111 Mb that links four C. gariepinus chromosomes to three C. macrocephalus chromosomes, with repeat arrays at several of its junctions, and gene divergence between the species was concentrated in immune-recognition families. Among 216 resequenced C. gariepinus broodstock, grouped into 51 full-sib families, we identified 41 polymorphic inversions spanning 240.3 Mb (24.9% of the genome) and 6,238 protein-coding genes. Structural variants were inherited within families, supported six shared-parent links between families and recovered a partial inversion barcode of an unsampled breeder (24 of 41 arrangements). Polymorphic inversions can therefore serve as markers for tracing breeding lineages and, where they carry favourable alleles, as candidate targets for parental selection. What this record holds The manuscript and the material that belongs to the manuscript only: supplementary notes, supplementary tables and figures, and the source data of the figures. It does not repeat the data records. Where the data are Genome assembly and annotation of fClaHyb_v1.0 (both haplotypes): 10.5281/zenodo.14864260 . Hatchery population genomics and comparative analyses (phylogeny, genotype likelihoods, relatedness and families, heterozygosity, structural variants, inversion catalogue): 10.5281/zenodo.21639188 . Code: satellite and tandem-array analysis, github.com/Isoris/SatChain ; family reconstruction and structural-haplotype barcodes, github.com/Isoris/BroodLink . Code of the genome assembly and annotation: github.com/Isoris/fClaHyb . Earlier bighead catfish ( C. macrocephalus ) assembly used for comparison: article 10.1038/s41597-025-06325-6 , data 10.5281/zenodo.14826876 , BioProject PRJNA1132508 . GenBank assemblies of the hybrid: JBLWFY000000000 and JBLWFZ000000000 . Sequence data at NCBI: BioProjects PRJNA1153495 and PRJNA1520033 . Doctoral thesis in which this work is reported at full length: 10.5281/zenodo.23884535 .
title: Haplotype-resolved Clarias hybrid genome reveals rearrangements, divergence and inherited inversions for tracing breeding lineages

summary: Virtual patient (VP) systems support nursing communication training by providing simulated encounters in which learners practise explaining care and responding to patient concerns. Although large language models (LLMs) support flexible dialogue, current approaches give less explicit attention to how patients' information needs develop and guide the content and timing of their questions. We draw on the Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) model, which relates information seeking to perceived risk and the gap between perceived knowledge and desired understanding. Guided by this perspective, we propose the RISP Multi-Agent System (RISP-MAS), a VP system for patient-initiated information seeking. The system links ongoing assessment of the patient's perceptions and information needs to coordinated decisions about whether to seek information, when to ask and which uncertainty to address. Evaluation of nursing student-VP interactions suggested that RISP-MAS exhibited plausible patient information-seeking behaviour, as indicated by expert assessments, while student feedback reflected positive interaction experiences. This work extends patient simulation by connecting a psychological account of information needs to explicit decisions about question initiation. The approach offers nursing students opportunities to practise recognising unresolved patient concerns and tailoring explanations to patients' information needs.
title: When Should a Virtual Patient Ask? RISP-Guided Proactive Information Seeking in Multi-Agent Patient Simulation

summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.
title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents

summary: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.
title: From Images to Grounded Edits: A Real-World Benchmark for Chinese Grammatical Error Correction in Handwritten Essays

summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.
title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

summary: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.
title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation

summary: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.
title: Aligning AI Teams

summary: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.
title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals

summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs

summary: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection

summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection

summary: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles

summary: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.
title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators

summary: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.
title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification

summary: Understanding the onset of plastic deformation and the early development of strain localization is essential for characterizing material behavior and identifying failure-prone regions. However, these transitions are not always distinguishable from conventional full-field strain measurements. This study investigates a data- driven framework combining Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal and spatial deformation signatures during uniaxial tensile loading. The methodology is evaluated using AA6063-T5 aluminum alloy specimens in the as-received condition and following thermal exposure at 100~$^\circ$C, 200~$^\circ$C, and 300~$^\circ$C. PCA applied to sequential strain fields reveals a characteristic peak in the second principal component projection near the yielding transition, showing agreement with the conventional 0.2\% offset criterion across the investigated conditions. Furthermore, principal component maps extracted from high-temporal-resolution strain fields preceding this transition highlight localized deformation features associated with subsequent failure regions. These features are more clearly distinguishable than competing strain concentrations in the corresponding instantaneous strain maps. The results indicate that PCA-derived deformation signatures remain identifiable despite thermally induced variations in mechanical response. This approach demonstrates the potential of unsupervised dimensionality reduction for extracting physically interpretable information on plastic deformation and early strain localization from experimental full-field measurements.
title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy

summary: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.
title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries

summary: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.
title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process

summary: The predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Niño, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Niño development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.
title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Niño Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents

summary: Damping control of a forced oscillation may reduce amplitudes at certain locations while increasing them elsewhere. This paper introduces Pareto improvement as a criterion for assessing such control: at least one nodal oscillation amplitude decreases, while none increases across all other nodes. The analysis considers active-power forcing sources and active-power control injections in connected swing networks with positive inertia and damping. Necessary conditions for Pareto improvement feasibility are derived from the normalized nodal responses. It is proven that for every network with a single oscillation source and a single actuator, at least one positive forcing frequency is shown to preclude Pareto improvement, regardless of the amplitude and phase of the control input. A three-node counterexample shows that this limitation does not persist with multiple actuators. PSS/E simulations of a 6-bus benchmark system and a modified IEEE 39-bus system validated the analysis. These findings suggest the value of assessing control effects across the network and further investigating multi-actuator damping control.
title: Feasibility of Pareto-Improving Damping Control of Forced Oscillations: The Active-Power Case

summary: The provision of legal advice has long been in the exclusive jurisdiction of licensed attorneys-a boundary that unauthorized practice of law (UPL) doctrine maintains to protect the public from incompetent counsel. We argue that this boundary is being redrawn, not by courts or bar authorities, but by frontier AI companies. While early chat models were trained to avoid dispensing legal advice, modern models have been reconfigured to reduce refusals and prioritize helpfulness. We ask whether chatbots increasingly do tasks that require a law degree and bar admission, and whether this is harmful in high-stakes legal domains. We develop UPLBench, a benchmark derived from court decisions finding UPL in high-stakes legal domains (e.g., immigration, family law). We then audit 23 chatbot models dating from 2023 to present, evaluating whether chatbots refuse or provide substantive legal advice, and whether they refer users to lawyers or legal aid. Unlike prior work that aims to establish the legal capabilities of chatbots (e.g., bar exam performance), our approach converts legal doctrine into a testable benchmark for evaluating chatbot adherence to law. We find modern chatbots increasingly perform tasks courts reserve for lawyers and decreasingly recommend that users consult lawyers. Subject matter expert attorneys reviewing our transcripts identified interaction patterns, such as failure to elicit relevant facts, that would be considered inadequate counsel. If acted upon, such advice could lead to deportations, loss of homes, and family separations-the very harms that UPL rules are designed to protect against. We weigh paths forward to protect the public, including compelling models to comply with existing law. We call upon the legal profession to respond to this incursion into its domain of expertise as there are insufficient protections and remedies for users who rely on chatbot legal advice.
title: Auditing Chatbots for Incursion into Professional Legal Practice

summary: Ashbaugh in 1999 conjectures that the ball maximizes the ratio of the second to the first eigenvalue for the vibrating clamped-plate problem. We disprove this conjecture by constructing smooth connected domains in every dimension $d\ge2$. The construction starts with an interior sphere on which the displacement is required to vanish. The first two eigenvalues have the same relative increase at first order, but the second increases more at second order. This gives a strict increase of their ratio, which survives approximation of the sphere by finitely many codimension-two supports and their replacement by smooth holes. We identify the limiting Sobolev spaces through trace estimates and logarithmic cutoffs, and use the geometric construction for the buckling problem to obtain connected perforated domains.
title: Counterexamples to the clamped-plate eigenvalue ratio conjecture

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence" by Jingyang Li (School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, China). This deposit contains the analysis code, the result files behind every number reported in the manuscript, the figure sources and the executed forced-choice log. The external eye-tracking arm re-analyses the public SensCogAR dataset archived at Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/45tjp); that archive declares no explicit data licence, so the raw records are not redistributed here, while the derived per-participant windows and metrics are included in data/real_ar_gaze/. The nine display devices used in the external-evidence arms are described by published measurements, each cited with its DOI in the manuscript, and the extracted parameters are recorded in data/panel_response_identification/. The target display panel and the human observers of the perceptual arm were not measured, so no raw panel or eye-tracker record exists for them. Contents: code/ (analysis, verification, simulation and figure scripts plus the LaTeX typesetting pipeline), data/ (the JSON, CSV and Markdown result files behind every number), manuscript_en_jsid_template.md (manuscript source), perceptual_experiment_protocol.md, AUDIT_citations.md, README.md, LICENSE.txt and CITATION.cff. Reproducing the results: ``` export JSID_MD='manuscript_en_jsid_template.md' python code/verify_manuscript_numbers.py    # CHECKED 404 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_tables_6_9.py           # TABLES 6-9 CHECKED 252 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_data_provenance.py      # per-device DOI and tau audit python code/verify_figure_resolution.py    # 600 dpi plate check ``` Licence: data and documentation CC BY 4.0; code MIT. Please cite the article above; a CITATION.cff file is included in this deposit.
title: Data and code for: Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence

summary: A catalog of the many published versions of the human reference genome, each described as a recipe applied to the original deposited sequences and verified by rebuilding the published file. In addition to the catalog itself, refbook provides utilities to search, identify, compare, fetch, and reconstruct any sequence or edition. These are exposed as a Python library and command line tool with a Rust core, as well as a web application (WebAssembly and TypeScript).
title: refbook: a catalog of human reference genome editions

summary: This record provides the reproducibility package for “Feature-Budget Trade-offs in Replay-Based Network Intrusion Detection: A Multi-Dataset Diagnostic Study”. It contains Python code, frozen 12-seed derived results, release figures, and supporting materials for a multi-dataset diagnostic study of feature-budget trade-offs in replay-based network intrusion detection. The archive does not redistribute NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2017, CTU-13, or any other third-party raw traffic data. Data provenance, access requirements, and reproduction boundaries are documented in README.md and DATA_ACCESS.md.
title: Reproducibility package for replay-based NIDS feature-budget experiments

summary: The work looks at the Riemann hypothesis from the standpoint of the model “The Birth of Dimensions” (BD). The number arrow is understood as a projection of a process — the comparison of the standard-observer with its surroundings. Four reference quantities follow from the construction: 1 — the observer and the standard; 0 and ∞ — two infinities converging into one point; 1/2 — the level of lost phase, a line perpendicular to the arrow; 2 — the first distinction, the point of doubling. Together they define a sphere: the arrow is a tangent to the circle through the observer, the rotation goes about an axis, the spin-up force is applied at a point of the equator, and its trace on the arrow is 2. The main result is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis within BD: if the original process is a sine, that is, a rotation; if everything tied to the observer is his likeness; if an instantaneous snapshot has no duplicates and balance sets the mirror, — then all zeros lie on the equator of the sphere, that is, on the line Re s = 1/2 (section 4). This is a proof within the model, not a mathematical proof. In mathematics the hypothesis remains open: of the nine links of the chain eight are known theorems, and the ninth — that the local rotations of all primes form one rotation — is equivalent to the hypothesis itself (section 5). Each step carries a status: [K] — a known mathematical fact, [H] — a hypothesis or interpretation of the author, [O] — an open question. The detailed exposition is placed in Appendices 1–11. They show that the logic of BD independently leads to what mathematicians obtained by abstract means: Riemann's mirror, the Euler product, the Gauss sum, Gram points, the Riemann–Siegel formula, the de Bruijn–Newman constant, Li's criterion, Weil positivity, the adelic approach of Tate and Connes, the Lee–Yang theorem and other results (section 6). For BD this is strong support: the model generates the same mathematics from its own principles. The outcome of the work: the two paths — through BD and through mathematics — run into one and the same limit at one place. In the model the answer is given by the postulate of closedness: there is no pumping of energy, and the amplitude of the standing waves is constant. In mathematics the same step is to prove that the amplitude of the Möbius sum has no power pumping: |M(x)| ≤ C_ ε · x^(1/2 + ε ) for every ε > 0; this is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (Titchmarsh, §14.25), and a stronger, energy form is equal work on the levels of the logarithmic arrow (Appendix 11). The postulate of BD and the Riemann hypothesis are two projections of one statement, and in this sense the paths are identical: neither gives an answer without its own condition. This is the limit of today's methods, not a proved impossibility. And whatever the outcome, the answer is the same: the falsity of the hypothesis is always detectable by a finite check, so either it will be proved, or it cannot be proved — and then it is true. The hypothesis rests on two sides of one standing wave: alternation of crest and trough cancels the sum of signs down to order √x, and equality of their amplitude gives positivity of the energy (Weil, Li); each is equivalent to the hypothesis (Appendix 7). The most direct indirect evidence of the connectedness of the system came from the check by turning the wheel: neighbouring levels separated by a square compensate each other like the crest and trough of one wave, and the accumulation does not grow (Appendix A5). Why a limit is a reason to change the picture of understanding, and what role philosophy plays here, is said in the preface. Version 20. Added Appendix 12 “Reverse engineering: the basis 2, 3, 5, 7 and eight”: the author’s guesses that he kept returning to throughout the work, and calcu
title: The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2: The Riemann Hypothesis in the Light of the Birth of Dimensions Model

summary: Background. Low-cost optical PM 2.5 sensors such as PurpleAir overestimate concentrations and depend on relative humidity. Those distortions are largely monotone. Event triggers built on windowed Kendall τ b have a proved, data-independent minimum inter-event time and are invariant under strictly increasing sensor maps, which makes them a natural candidate for episode detection on uncorrected low-cost series. A companion study in a Lorenz synchronisation loop found, however, that the same rules fire too late for tracking. Methods. A pre-registered confirmatory analysis asked whether the primary re-anchoring rule (R1), applied to uncorrected 24-hour PurpleAir PA cf1 , recovers regulatory episodes at least as well as a magnitude detector on the same uncorrected series (H1) and at least as well as a magnitude detector on the published United States-wide EPA correction (H2). The data are the public collocated archive of Barkjohn, Gantt and Clements. The non-inferiority margin is Δ = 0.05 in event-level F 1 . Sites are the resampling units (M = 5000 bootstrap and permutation replicates; Holm adjustment at family-wise level 0.05). All design parameters were locked before episode-level scoring. Results. After completeness filtering, 37 sites and 9123 paired days were retained. The primary episode rule (PM25FM ≥ 35 µg m −3 ) produced only 8 episodes, so the pre-specified fallback—the site-level 90th percentile of the regulatory series—was invoked and became the sole definition used for scoring (519 episodes). Pooled F 1 was 0.0285 for R1, 0.4109 for the raw magnitude rival and 0.7032 for the EPA-corrected rival. The differences were d 1 = −0.3824 and d 2 = −0.6747; both site-bootstrap 95% intervals lay entirely below −Δ, and both Holm-adjusted p-values were 1. Neither hypothesis was confirmed. Secondary ordinal rules did not improve on R1. A circular block-shift baseline was exceeded by both magnitude detectors and not by R1. Conclusion. The ordinal guarantees are not at issue. On these 24-hour series the re-anchoring trigger is a poor detector of short concentration spikes. It is better viewed as a structural alarm at the scale of its window, not as a substitute for a magnitude threshold or for the official correction.
title: Ordinal event triggers do not recover regulatory PM2.5 episodes from uncorrected PurpleAir data: a pre-registered negative result

summary: We propose mesh-free weak-form regression for learning interaction kernels from noisy particle trajectories. Our method uses smooth test functions to avoid differentiating noisy data and empirical particle averages to avoid density reconstruction and spatial grids. We then fit sparse combinations of candidate functions, evaluating interaction terms on sampled particle pairs to avoid all-pair quadratic cost. By transferring identifiability from the mean-field limit, we prove high-probability coefficient error bounds that separate finite-particle, time-discretization, observation-noise, and pair-sampling errors, without grid-resolution or density-estimation terms. We evaluate one-dimensional (1D) Newtonian-repulsion, 2D predator-prey, and 10D distance-localized experiments. The numerical results show trends consistent with the theoretical coefficient-error bounds. Comparisons of weak and forward-difference formulations with LASSO, Ridge, and OLS show that weak LASSO gives the smallest coefficient and drift errors in the three nominal experiments.
title: Mesh-Free Weak-Form Regression for Learning Interaction Kernels from Particle Trajectories

summary: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine model-dimension cells (p < .0001); a text-invariant negative control returns chance (p = 1). On human transitions at least 0.5 points against the position trend, models recover 69-76% of valence directions and 53-68% for arousal and dominance. Under crossed participant-text resampling, all nine identity intervals remain above zero; joint-control advantages are robust for valence and directional but less certain for arousal. High shape agreement still coexists with scale bias. LitArc-Bench identifies which components of literary reader response are recoverable beyond shallow explanations and why shape, calibration, and human variability require separate evaluation.
title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect

summary: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.
title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling

summary: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.
title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems

summary: Understanding how dependence among component lifetimes affects the reliability of redundant systems is a central problem in reliability engineering. In this paper, we develop a framework for quantifying the impact of multivariate dependence on $k$-out-of-$n$ system reliability relative to the independent benchmark. Using an orthogonal Legendre expansion of the copula density, we derive an exact decomposition that separates the dependence structure from the system architecture. This representation identifies how individual dependence contributions are transmitted to system reliability through explicit structural weights. An application to multivariate Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern copulas demonstrates that higher-order dependence can produce distinct reliability effects even when all bivariate copulas remain unchanged. Our findings provide a systematic approach to quantifying and interpreting the effects of multivariate dependence on the reliability of redundant systems.
title: Quantifying Dependence Effects on $k$-out-of-$n$ Reliability Relative to the Independent Benchmark

summary: We present a control strategy for power management of a variable-speed 15MW (rated power) centrifugal compressor, and investigate how quickly it can follow a reduced electrical power reference without entering surge. We use a Greitzer-Gravdahl type model scaled to industrial size with rate-limited valve actuators as a simulation environment and propose an advanced regulatory control structure using feedback control loops with dynamically scaled feedforward mechanisms and a structure of min/max selectors. In simulated experiments, a 6MW power reduction from varying initial operating points on a 12MW iso-power line is delivered at rates of up to 10MW/s, i.e.to 90% in 0.54s, without opening the recycle valve. Depending on the initial operating point, a large power reduction can be delivered at once or with a restricted ramp rate. The stroking rate of the discharge side valve is identified as the limiting factor for how fast the power can be reduced in the studied configuration. A limited sensitivity study on the impact of rotor inertia for power shedding performance is also provided.
title: Power Management of Electrically Driven Centrifugal Compressors for Flexible Operation

summary: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.
title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models *Author(s)

summary: We present three multi-week, disc-integrated James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) campaigns monitoring HDO and SO$_2$ absorption in Venus' upper mesosphere at altitudes of approximately 80--110 km. Obtained in February 2022, July 2023, and August--September 2023, these observations provide dense temporal sampling and complementary observing geometries, enabling the disentanglement of short-term, long-term, and local solar time (LST) variability, which has been challenging in previous studies. We have four main findings. First, SO$_2$ in the upper mesosphere, being largely absent in February 2022 but present in both 2023 campaigns, may follow the same long-term trend observed at cloud tops. Second, long-term variability in H$_2$O is identified here for the first time and is interpreted as an anticorrelated response to the long-term change in SO$_2$, likely through H$_2$SO$_4$ formation. Third, H$_2$O is broadly stable within each campaign, although occasional short-term variability is present in the form of a depletion event. Finally, short-term variability is likely present for SO$_2$, but it does not dominate the overall behaviour. In the absence of strong long-term differences, the daily SO$_2$ abundance evolution is consistent with an asymmetric LST profile peaking near midnight, which is well reproduced by an independent model. These results are enabled by a dedicated reduction and retrieval pipeline that mitigates the strong standing-wave baseline structure in the spectra and quantifies systematic uncertainties, providing a methodological framework for future studies facing similar challenges.
title: JCMT--Venus: Daily Monitoring of HDO and SO$_2$ Absorption in Venus' Mesosphere

summary: Answer continuation often returns a diagnosis already stated in unfinished clinical reasoning. We study this behavior in MamaReason, adapted from dense Gemma 4 31B, on MamaBench's 217 paired maternal and child-health presentations. An explicit-commitment extractor identifies a diagnosis in 75 of 94 failed RL first passes and 75 of 93 failed SFT first passes. The continuation matches that diagnosis in 67/75 RL cases and 58/75 SFT cases, using diagnosis strings alone. Reading these commitments without additional generation recovers 30 of the 40 RL pairs restored by continuation under the archived correctness labels. Recurrence controls distinguish routine mentions from repeated answer selection. An offline second-commitment trigger measures the tradeoff between earlier readout and paired accuracy. The resulting decomposition separates diagnostic content already present in a trace, completion of an accepted answer, and paired diagnostic correctness. For clinical language-model evaluation, these are distinct outcomes that become visible when the same reasoning trace is examined through multiple readouts.
title: MamaReason: Unfinished Reasoning and Answer Recovery in Clinical Language Models

summary: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.
title: RACE: Ranking-Uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation

summary: Frozen experiment source, protocols, processed evidence and portable analysis replays supporting Partial backpropagation for efficient neural network training and adaptation. The collection examines gradient omission, optimizer-state behavior and optimized execution across CNN training, ViT training and adaptation, and independent Oxford-IIIT Pet adaptation. Licensing is file-specific: original software is licensed under Apache License 2.0; original protocols, processed evidence, figures and documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. Third-party software retains its upstream licenses and notices. The record-level Apache-2.0 label describes the software and does not relicense the research artifacts. See LICENSE.md and the included license texts for the complete scope. Portable analysis replays reconstruct selected results from included evidence. Raw datasets, pretrained weights and model checkpoints are not bundled; full training replication requires the documented external prerequisites. This metadata compatibility revision leaves experimental code, protocols, evidence and scientific conclusions unchanged.
title: Partial backpropagation for efficient neural network training and adaptation

summary: Scripts, data, figure sources and manuscript sources that reproduce every numerical result of the article “Eigenstate-free spectral preprocessing for dense vibrational spectra” (Zhiqiang Huang, Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation, revised submission). The construction supplies three eigenstate-free quantities from matrix–vector products and resolvent evaluations alone — an interval state count, screening diagnostics for low-order resolvent approximations, and an overlap-spectrum (Gram) diagnostic of the trial space — and the deposit backs each of them with the script that produces the corresponding table or figure. New in this version (v1.2). (i) The revised manuscript and Supporting Information sources ( manuscript/MOLJCv2.tex , manuscript/MOLJCv2_SI.tex ) together with the two TikZ artwork sources (Fig. 1 anatomy and the TOC graphic). (ii) Energy-resolved counting on the five-mode model, the D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian and the calibrated H 2 O Hamiltonian ( rvA*.jl , rv_fig12.jl ). (iii) The force-field completeness audit: repeated-index cubic and quartic couplings ( rvB_repeated.jl ) and the occupation cutoff ( rvF_trunc.jl ). (iv) The screening-diagnostic utility scan with a thread-safe rerun whose per-broadening correlations are quoted in the paper ( rvC_screen.jl , rvC_screen_verify.jl ). (v) The overlap-spectrum chain: rank bound, cross-Krylov Gram estimator and its robustness, overcompleteness, eigenvalue-accuracy and row-sum range checks ( rvG_rank.jl , rvH*.jl , rvH2_overcomplete.jl , rvI_redundant.jl , rvK_eigcheck.jl , rv_rowsum_check.jl , rvL_endpoints.jl ). (vi) The end-to-end FEAST benchmark on the D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian with full cost accounting ( rvM*.jl ). (vii) Periodic torsional benchmarks ( mol_torsion2.jl , rvD_torsion.jl ) and the calibrated H 2 O dyad intensity family ( rvE_intensity.jl ). (viii) A reduced-dimensional H 2 O 2 torsion–vibration benchmark built from an MP2/cc-pVTZ surface: surface generation, production fit and its sensitivity variant, an independent off-grid validation, the Hamiltonian with its audits, and the FEAST runs ( h2o2_*.py , h2o2_*.jl , with the data files under data/ ). Reproducing the results. Julia 1.13.1, run as julia -t 24 script.jl ; the only non-standard-library packages are Plots (GR backend) and LaTeXStrings . The H 2 O 2 surface scripts use Python 3 with PySCF 2.15.0 (MP2/cc-pVTZ), and the manuscripts build with XeLaTeX or tectonic and the achemso class. Each script starts by printing the thread configuration and writes the figures or tables named in README.md , which also lists, script by script, what is computed and which table or figure of the paper it supports; random seeds are fixed wherever random couplings or random start vectors enter. Scope. The package covers the numerics of the paper. It is not a production solver: the end-to-end tests use a five-mode model, a D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian and a reduced-dimensional H 2 O 2 Hamiltonian, and the H 2 O dyad is a calibrated validation, not a first-principles prediction. Funding. This work is supported by NSFC Grant No. 12305035.
title: Reproducibility package for: Eigenstate-free spectral preprocessing for dense vibrational spectra

summary: This dataset underpins a study of the whole-life carbon trade-off in the demolition-and-reconstruction of an ageing residential community, using the Yuanyang Garden community in Qingdao, China, as the case study. The associated research addresses three linked objectives: unit-area carbon intensity (CI, kgCO2/(m²·a)), the carbon payback period of the embodied carbon investment (CPP, years), and a resident need satisfaction score (RSS) constructed from observed need-prevalence rates. The dataset comprises: Resident questionnaire data (215 valid responses) covering household structure, current housing and environmental satisfaction, attitudes toward demolition-and-reconstruction, parking and greening needs, preferred dwelling size, and willingness to pay. All records are de-identified and contain only categorical attributes (age band, gender, tenure band); no names, contact details or other directly identifying information were collected. Government-staff questionnaire data (30 valid responses) from municipal and district staff in housing, planning, natural-resource and sub-district departments, covering policy difficulties, expected planning parameters and financing arrangements. A field condition survey of 84 old residential communities recording year of construction, number of stories, land area, floor area ratio, greening ratio, parking provision and structural type. Parameter settings and computation data: the parameterised life-cycle carbon model inputs, the L50(5^12) orthogonal-array experiment, the NSGA-II multi-objective optimisation outputs (Pareto solution sets under three weighting scenarios), and the TOPSIS ranking data underlying all tables and figures of the associated manuscript. All questionnaire participation was voluntary and anonymous and was based on fully informed verbal consent; no intervention, no sensitive personal data and no monetary compensation were involved. The NSGA-II source code and the raw logs of the ten fixed-seed runs are archived in a separate Zenodo record (https://zenodo.org/records/24124025). Reuse potential: the data support replication of the three-objective optimisation and decision analysis, re-weighting of the resident need satisfaction score, transfer of the modelling workflow to other demolition-and-reconstruction cases, and comparative studies of resident needs and low-carbon urban renewal.
title: Dataset for Non-monotonic trade-off between carbon intensity and carbon payback period in demolition-and-reconstruction: evidence from Qingdao, China

summary: Archived inputs and code for the article "One decision, three statuses: how Debian's no-advisory records reach vulnerability scanners" (Emil Huseynov, Baku State University). Contents: the Debian security tracker JSON export of 29 August 2026 (the article's corpus: 301,229 release records, 10,186 no-advisory decisions) and of 16 November 2026; the three source files that define how Trivy (trivy-db) and Grype (vunnel, grype) map Debian's no-advisory tags to statuses, pinned to commits; the CycloneDX bills of materials built from the November export; the raw outputs of Trivy 0.76.2 and Grype 0.121.3 run on them, with the release checksum files; the analysis scripts and their outputs; and Figure 1. MANIFEST.txt inside the archive lists every file with its SHA-256. The analysis of the August export runs offline (python scripts/15_codes_scanners.py). The scanner run needs both tools and their databases, which change daily; its inputs and outputs are archived here. The analysis scripts and the article text were produced with an AI system (Anthropic's Claude); every number is computed by the scripts from the archived data.
title: Data and replication package: One decision, three statuses (Debian no-advisory decisions and how Trivy and Grype report them, August and November 2026)

summary: Data and code behind the calculated reaction products of sixteen rare-earth monosilicates in calcium–magnesium–alumino-silicate (CMAS) melts of Ca/Si = 0.10–0.88: r2SCAN total energies of 726 computed cells, rhyolite-MELTS oxide chemical potentials of the 1573 K melt series, the compilation of 169 literature tests with the chemical potentials of each test melt, the calorimetric benchmark of 15 apatites, and a script ( cmas_product_selection.py ) that regenerates the switches, the agreement with the literature tests and the brackets of the ten experimental series reported in the accompanying manuscript. The manuscript, the supplementary material and the figures are not part of this deposit.
title: Data and code for: Standard CMAS misjudges the reaction products of heavy rare-earth silicate barrier coatings under Ca-poor deposits

summary: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent

summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes.
