When a filled crate is moved by the machine, an RGB image is automatically captured and analysed using a three-class detector that identifies ripe, semi-ripe, and unripe berries. The system operates locally on the existing CPU-only industrial computer and therefore requires neither continuous image processing nor dedicated GPU hardware. During field testing, 79 crate images containing 48,634 visible blueberries in manually verified reference annotations were evaluated. The vision system estimated an overall ripe-fruit fraction of 90.22%, compared with 90.97% determined manually. Per-image ripe-fruit estimates showed a mean absolute error of 0.935 percentage points and a Pearson correlation of r=0.967. Maturity estimates remained similar between the two sides of the harvester for which the light conditions varied despite poorer absolute counting performance under direct sunlight. All field events were processed within the available 14 s per-side crate interval. The proposed approach provides a practical means of quantifying one component of harvest selectivity while the machine is operating. Such information could support operator decision-making and, when combined with measurements of fruit recovery and losses, contribute to future feedback-based control of mechanical harvesting.
title: Event-Triggered Visual Perception for Real-Time Harvest Outcome Estimation in Mechanical Blueberry Harvesting

summary: Generative artificial intelligence complicates evidentiary assessment at the International Criminal Court by enabling fabricated audiovisual material and making authentic digital evidence easier to dismiss as fake. This article calls the latter problem synthetic doubt: an objection alleging that a digital item may be AI-generated or AI-manipulated. Existing scholarship addresses digital evidence, open-source investigations and deepfakes in the ICC context. Yet the question of when synthetic doubt should trigger enhanced reliability review under the Rome Statute, without displacing the prosecution's burden under article 66 or compromising article 67 fair-trial rights, remains underdeveloped. The article proposes a three-stage framework: a baseline authenticity and provenance showing by the proponent; a case-specific articulation threshold for the objector; and proportionate reliability review by the Chamber under articles 64 and 69(4). The framework treats AI-related provenance information and synthetic-media detector outputs as contextual rather than dispositive.
title: Synthetic Doubt and the Integrity of Digital Proof before the International Criminal Court

summary: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.
title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression

summary: Gaia has observed every detected source on the sky 50 to 100 times, each time through a window of about 1 by 2 arcseconds at a different scan angle. The resulting one-dimensional flux profiles to be released in Gaia DR4 encode the two-dimensional arrangement of nearby point sources at ~0.1 arcsecond resolution. Repeated observations also constrain their relative motion. We present a method to model the scene with a mixture of moving point sources. Complementing Gaia DPAC's source-environment reconstruction, our approach focuses on close, blended companions and models their relative motion. We first fit each window with a few point sources and obtain their along-scan positions. We then triangulate these positions from different scan angles to identify candidate sources on the sky. A joint forward model of all windows measures positions, fluxes, relative proper motions, and parallax differences, even for blended components. In simulations, we recover companions at separations smaller than the instrumental profile width. For a moving companion at ~75 mas separation with a flux ratio of ~0.2, we obtain a separation precision of ~0.1 mas and a relative proper-motion precision of ~0.1 mas/yr per component, even in a scene contaminated by a third source. These precisions assume a known instrumental profile and independent Gaussian noise. We also recover differential parallax for a chance-aligned source. Modeling nearby contaminants prevents significant biases. With a Gaia-like instrumental profile, sampling and scan law, we show a sensitivity of ~5 mag in contrast at separations of 50-150 mas, and we discuss its dependence on the color term of Gaia's line-spread function. The method could extend the census of close companions and provide relative astrometry, and so dynamical information, along short orbital arcs. External measurements could also guide retrospective searches in Gaia's windows.
title: Gaia as a 0.1 arcsec point-source survey across the sky: dynamical scene reconstruction from one-dimensional scans

summary: A conformal surface that alternates between sectoral low scattering and directive telemetry poses a shared-hardware inverse problem when both modes must use one finite passive impedance alphabet, although their spatial codebooks may differ. This paper formulates and solves that mixed continuous--discrete problem at the effective impedance-boundary level. Reference-centered Tikhonov preimages prescribe restricted radiation data; inverse-source null-space freedom then moves each current within its data-equivalent class toward impedance profiles quantizable by the same alphabet. A line-searched Gauss--Newton update, common-state assignment and projected-centroid updates, and exact forward refinement determine the currents, two codebooks, and one passive library. Data invariance, the current-to-impedance differential, the optimal state update, monotonic mismatch reduction, and a forward perturbation bound are derived. A full-mutual-coupling two-dimensional TM study of a $4λ_0$-diameter cylinder uses 64 physical cells and one shared eight-state library. On a 256-unknown validation model, the worst power ratio over $\pm10^{\circ}$ monostatic sectors and incidence angles from $-30^{\circ}$ to $30^{\circ}$ is $-11.6$~dB relative to a PEC cylinder; telemetry directivity is 13.1~dB with $-13.6$-dB peak sidelobes and a $1^{\circ}$ pointing error. A separate Fourier--Galerkin formulation, converged through 513 complex modes without reoptimization, gives $-11.36$~dB and 13.02~dB for the corresponding worst-sector and directivity metrics. The results establish feasibility at the effective impedance-boundary level; they do not establish unit-cell, bias-network, or platform-level realizability.
title: Shared-State Inverse Synthesis of Dual-Mode Conformal Metasurfaces for Low Scattering and Telemetry

summary: Abstracting a continuous-time Markov chain by grouping its states into blocks raises a fundamental question: which rates should the abstract chain use when states within a block have different exit rates and transition probabilities? We study harmonic-mean aggregation, which matches the mean waiting time and next-block distribution of a local experiment that uniformly selects a state within the block and observes its next jump. Equivalently, the abstract transition rates are averages of the concrete rates with inverse-exit-rate weights. Since the aggregation does not preserve reachability probabilities in general, we derive theoretical error bounds for time-bounded reachability. We decompose the error into a blockwise mean and centered-within-block deviations, and show that the rate mismatch has zero weighted mean. Exploiting this cancellation and differences between abstract reachability values, we obtain bounds valid at every time horizon through a linear comparison system with two quantities per block, without computing concrete reachability values. All results are formalized and proven in Lean 4.
title: Harmonic-Mean Aggregation of Continuous-Time Markov Chains with Reachability Error Bounds

summary: We study nonparametric instrumental variable regression when the outcome takes values in a separable Hilbert space $\mathbb{Y}$, for instance a curve, a density or the kernel mean embedding of a distribution. The structural function solves an ill-posed operator equation whose conditional expectation operator need not be injective, and whose solutions need not belong to the hypothesis space. We analyse a two-stage kernel estimator that extends kernel instrumental variable regression to $\mathbb{Y}$-valued outcomes and allows spectral regularisation in both stages, including Landweber iteration and Showalter's method in the second stage. We show that the second stage is a regularisation method in the Hilbert scale generated by the inverse of the kernel integral operator. This viewpoint identifies the solution towards which the estimator converges: the minimum-norm solution in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space in the well-specified case and, in the misspecified case, the unique solution in the range of the continuous extension of the projection operator associated to the well-specified setting. Under source conditions and link conditions expressed through general index functions, we derive non-asymptotic bounds in a scale of interpolation norms that hold with high probability in terms of the first-stage error, with or without identification and in the well- and misspecified settings. For polynomial link conditions, we recover the rate of scalar kernel instrumental regression and extend it to targets outside the hypothesis space; for exponential link conditions, we obtain logarithmic rates in the severely ill-posed regime.
title: Nonparametric Instrumental Kernel Regression: The Well- and Misspecified Setting Under General Link Conditions

summary: Design decisions shape software architecture, and writing them down preserves the reasons behind it. Architecture decision records (ADRs) capture them, each with its context, choice, and consequences. A decision can depend on earlier ones: reversing one of them would force its review. We call these its premises. Yet ADRs do not always name their premises. When a decision is reversed, engineers supersede its ADR and search by hand for what it affects. That search can miss ADRs resting on an unnamed premise. We frame this as premise recovery: given an ADR with identifiers masked, find its premises among earlier records. We collect 1,060 ADRs from 36 repositories and label 1,529 candidate pairs for 60 target ADRs. Two LLM annotators agree at \k{appa} = 0.859. An independent human annotator, blind to their labels, agrees with the stated/implicit tag on 30 of 32 premises (\k{appa} = 0.875). We compare 7 open-weight models with 2 baselines that use no LLM. Qwen3.8-27B reaches F1 0.756, against 0.466 for word overlap; 2 models added post hoc score similarly. On the 11 premises whose titles barely overlap the target, it finds 0.758, while word overlap finds none. Reasoning raises its recall of implicit premises but not its F1. Word overlap with as many predictions gains 69% as much. We find only 2 to 3 stale dependents, though we searched for unlinked ones in only 30 of 66 supersessions. Open models could thus suggest unwritten premises when a decision is reversed, with precision between 0.68 and 0.78.
title: Premise Recovery in Software Design: What Does This Decision Rest On?

summary: We present a transferable Density Functional Tight Binding (DFTB) model for bismuth with explicit spin-orbit coupling that enables exploration of the structural degrees of freedom governing topological properties with minimal computational resources. We have used our DFTB model to run high-throughput calculations at a scale that would be significantly more expensive with standard Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory (DFT) to determine a strain-buckling map of electronic and topological properties for bismuthene, where we identify regions of band gap closure and band inversion as a function of structural parameters. We show that our approach yields an accurate band structure for the rhombohedral phase, where small band gaps exist at or near time-reversal-invariant momentum (TRIM) points. We then demonstrate the transferability of our model to bismuth properties not included in our training data through determination of the rhombohedral phase phonon density of states and energetic ordering of additional bismuth solid phases. Finally, we have validated our topological predictions through comparison to DFT results for the optimized bilayer geometries, a band inversion order parameter, and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant as a function of monolayer unit cell length. Our efforts establish DFTB as a rigorous approach for topological characterization while yielding approximately three orders of magnitude increase in computational efficiency relative to DFT. Our model can thus serve as a computational tool for topological materials discovery by enabling large-scale computational screening to address the potentially complex relationship between physical-chemical properties and the resulting topological classification.
title: A Density Functional Tight Binding Model for Rapid Screening of Spin-Orbit-Coupling-Driven Topological Properties in Bismuth

summary: In this paper, we propose a method to recover simultaneously the shape and wavenumber of an object from noisy radar or sonar measurements. The physical problem is modeled in a bounded domain with the Helmholtz equation and appropriate transmission conditions. The approach relies on a Kohn-Vogelius formulation of the inverse problem and uses Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent combined with shape optimization techniques. To address the robustness of the method with respect to measurement noise, we are looking to minimize a convex combination of the expected value and variance, which we achieve by using a Karhunen-Lo{è}ve expansion. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through twodimensional numerical experiments.
title: Simultaneous reconstruction of an obstacle and its wavenumber for the Helmholtz equation: a robust optimization approach

summary: Recent experiments have established excitonic optical resonances as powerful probes and control knobs of moiré Chern ferromagnets. However, the microscopic nature of excitons formed on such interaction-driven, time-reversal-symmetry-broken ground states remains largely unexplored. In this paper, using a Gutzwiller plus Bethe-Salpeter equation framework, we investigate twisted bilayer MoTe2 at hole filling ν_h=1 and identify two near-infrared Chern-ferromagnet excitons (CFEs) selectively coupled to opposite circular polarizations. Strong electron-hole interactions markedly enhance their energy separation and drive a pronounced momentum-space reconstruction of the emergent X- state, beyond the quasiparticle-transition picture. We further find that this reconstruction enhances the interlayer electron-hole character of X-, giving rise to a giant quadratic Stark response. These findings reveal the nontrivial interplay between electron-electron correlations and electron-hole interactions underlying CFE formation, providing optical fingerprints of moiré Chern-ferromagnetic order and a microscopic basis for its optical control.
title: Moiré Excitons in a Chern Ferromagnet

summary: Solar tower power plants provide dispatchable, renewable energy by concentrating sunlight with thousands of mirrors, called heliostats, onto a central receiver. Efficient operation requires accurate modeling of the optical path from each heliostat to the receiver and compensation for manufacturing imperfections, kinematic misalignment, and material degradation that distort the flux distribution. Conventional ray tracers predict the flux from an assumed plant model but are limited to forward simulation. They cannot recover unknown plant parameters from measured flux nor directly optimize plant operation. We present artist, an open-source, FAIR4RS-compliant Python package implementing a fully differentiable digital twin of solar tower power plants. By making the optical pipeline, comprising heliostat surface representation, kinematics, blocking, and ray tracing, end to end differentiable, artist turns the digital twin from a passive forward model into an active physics-based tool for inverse modeling and data-driven optimization. The resulting gradient-based framework unifies tasks usually handled by separate solutions, such as reconstructing heliostat surfaces and kinematics from operational flux images without costly deflectometry, predicting irradiance at the receiver, and optimizing aim points to realize a desired receiver flux density distribution. Built on PyTorch, artist scales to real plants through GPU acceleration, a structure-of-arrays memory layout, and nested data parallelism. It interfaces with open data sources such as the PAINT database. We describe the software architecture, physical models, and optimization framework, and demonstrate the workflow on representative tasks. By integrating modeling, prediction, and optimization into a single open, interpretable package, artist provides a principled foundation for data-driven research toward autonomous solar tower operation.
title: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation

summary: When processor implementation details are unavailable, black-box microarchitectural reverse engineering helps security researchers identify hardware conditions related to security vulnerabilities. However, this process requires substantial manual effort to design experiments, develop test programs, and analyze results for each processor. We present ProcReverser, a multi-agent system that automates this process. ProcReverser uses execution feedback to improve experimental plans and test programs and identifies microarchitectural properties from measurements. We develop a comprehensive suite of property identification tasks focused on hardware mechanisms relevant to Spectre-class attacks, covering speculative execution, branch prediction, memory dependence, and cache behavior. We evaluate ProcReverser on the XuanTie C910, the gem5 RISC-V O3 CPU model, and the SiFive P550. ProcReverser achieves Pass@1 and Pass@5 scores of 81.3% and 93.8%, respectively, on C910, and 83.0% and 100.0% on gem5 O3. On the SiFive P550, ProcReverser further characterizes microarchitectural properties covered by the proposed task suite. These findings highlight the potential of automated microarchitectural reverse engineering to support processor vulnerability analysis and defense evaluation.
title: ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis

summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. We propose GEAR (Gated Expert Activation Reuse), which reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. In addition, we propose GEAR$^2$ to further recover what reuse cannot express with an ultra-lightweight residual. On five MoE LLMs from 16B to 106B parameters with 25% and 50% of experts pruned, GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting (up to 4 pp.) in terms of accuracy, and GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches (up to 2.75 pp.) in every setting on nine zero-shot benchmarks, with larger advantages (up to 2.72 pp. higher) under more aggressive pruning (up to 50%).
title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual

summary: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.
title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache

summary: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.
title: GaugeRoPE: RoPE-Compatible Executable Latent Attention
Reproduction archive for: Identifiability-Aware Detection under Graph-Model Inconsistency

summary: Bug fixes Fixed caching of timing properties in Scan and Kymo with recent cachetools versions, where using cachedmethod beneath @property could raise TypeError: Decorating class methods is not supported . The fix preserves read-only access and invalidation when the instance cache is cleared. Fixed timestamp mismatches in PiezoTrackingCalibration , PiezoForceDistance and force-baseline fitting/correction with ForceBaseLine by cropping native force and trap-position channels to their shared time range before matching sample rates. Only complete averaging blocks are retained. Incompatible sampling grids now raise an informative error suggesting native channels instead of manually downsampled data. Fixed potential complex-to-real casting warnings in the kymotracker geometry tests by explicitly taking the real parts of reference eigenvalues and eigenvectors for real symmetric matrices. Also corrected assertion failure messages in the candidate-direction test. These are test-only changes. The geometry implementation and tracking results are unchanged. Ensured Scan.export_video() and ImageStack.export_video() use a Python integer for the default stop-frame index, improving compatibility when the frame count is a NumPy integer. This silences some warnings that pop up during testing. Fixed alignment of values in calibration tables for ForceCalibrationItem and CalibrationResults with tabulate 0.10 by explicitly preserving whitespace, while retaining compatibility with older supported versions.

summary: Recent megajoule laser inertial confinement fusion (ICF) experiments have demonstrated thermonuclear target gain above unity, yet scaling pulsed laboratory ignition to commercial 1–20 Hz Inertial Fusion Energy (IFE) power plants remains obstructed by six coupled physics and engineering bottlenecks: hydrodynamic Rayleigh–Taylor (RT) and Richtmyer–Meshkov instabilities, core contamination from mechanical target support tents and fill tubes, parasitic cross-beam energy transfer (CBET) and stimulated Brillouin/Raman backscatter (SBS/SRS), critical-density reflection and solid gold cone vaporization in petawatt fast ignition, dielectric mirror blistering and positive plasma pulse dispersion, and the absence of non-destructive focal-plane phase diagnostics in high vacuum. This paper presents an integrated theoretical and reactor-engineering solution derived from the Lorentz Invariant / Localized Intrinsic Field Equilibrium (LIFE) framework, governed by the exact four-dimensional covariant divergence of the Maxwell stress-energy tensor (∂ μ T μν = 0). By arranging subsets of N beam ≥ 4 coherent laser beamlines into mutually orthogonal pairs with quadratic sinusoidal cross-beam phase modulation, directional wave operators annihilate longitudinal radiation-drag force densities (f x = f z ≡ 0) while enforcing strictly forward longitudinal Poynting transport (S x, S z ≥ 0), eliminating coherent backscatter and replacing chaotic CBET with deterministic transverse Poynting routing. Along the mutual orthogonal axis, optical-cycle averaging via the Jacobi–Anger Bessel expansion establishes a stationary three-dimensional ponderomotive restoring lattice with zero net volume momentum bias, enabling both stalk-free high-vacuum cryogenic pellet levitation and dynamic RT shear damping during implosion. For fast-ignition architectures, orthogonal precursor guide beams induce an effective curved optical metric (n eff = c/v g > 1) forming an exponentially self-confined slow-light channel I core (r) = I 0 exp(−k|r|) that guides petawatt ignitor pulses directly into the stagnated fuel core without solid gold cones. Combined with coating-free corrugated monolithic bulk tungsten negative-dispersion wall optics and sub-millisecond vacuum three-beam differential interferometric and dual-divergence (∇·E, ∇·H) electro-optic feedback, the LIFE architecture provides a non-invasive upgrade path for existing megajoule and petawatt laser facilities as well as next-generation commercial IFE power plants. Keywords: Laser Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF); Inertial Fusion Energy (IFE); Localized Intrinsic Field Equilibrium (LIFE); Fast Ignition; Rayleigh–Taylor Stabilization; Jacobi–Anger Ponderomotive Lattice; Cross-Beam Energy Transfer (CBET); Curved Optical Metric; Negative Group Delay Dispersion; Tungsten Plasma-Facing Optics PACS / PhySH: 52.57.-z (Laser inertial confinement); 52.57.Kk (Fast ignition of compressed cores); 52.38.-r (Laser-plasma interactions); 42.65.-k (Nonlinear optics); 52.35.Py (Macroscopic plasma instabilities) SSRN JEL Codes: Q42 (Alternative Energy Sources); O32 (Management of Technological Innovation and R&D); L94 (Electric Utilities); C61 (Optimization Techniques)
title: Three-Dimensional Synchro-Resonant Electromagnetic Confinement, Ponderomotive Rayleigh–Taylor Stabilization, and Cone-Free Slow-Light Fast Ignition in Multi-Beam Laser Fusion Reactors within the LIFE Framework

summary: AetherHuman is a candidate eleventh functional dimension of the Aether family. v2.0.0 is an architectural investigation of the human participation gap between governance authority (AetherGovern), identity (AetherIdentity), and runtime monitoring (AetherRuntime). Phase 2 (Hypothesis Review) is now complete. The independent external review was signed and authorized by Jonathan Rabe (AI | ML Engineer, Angeles University Foundation) on 2026-11-17, confirming the (E) Undetermined (interim) decision. Links: - Paper (v1.0.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24278322 - Figshare preprint: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.35038726 - GitHub: https://github.com/gitdeeper15/aetherhuman - GitHub Release v2.0.0: https://github.com/gitdeeper15/aetherhuman/releases/tag/v2.0.0 - GitLab: https://gitlab.com/gitdeeper15/aetherhuman - Codeberg: https://codeberg.org/gitdeeper15/aetherhuman - Bitbucket: https://bitbucket.org/gitdeeper15/aetherhuman - Website: https://aetherhuman.netlify.app What v2.0.0 contains: - 5 functions under investigation (Fn1–Fn5): Human Principal Representation, Authority Relation, Intervention Semantics, Accountability Chain, Human-Agent Boundary. - 4 failure conditions (H-F1–H-F4): Non-redundancy, Distinction from Govern + Identity + Runtime, Decentralizability, Observable benefit. - 2 propositions (P1–P2): Determinism of human intervention semantics, Irreducible human authority anchor. - External Independent Review (signed by Jonathan Rabe). - Architectural hypothesis, responsibility boundaries, falsification plan, independence decision, internal review, and investigation report. - Evaluation Design Protocol (addressing Sybil delegation & latency). - Adversarial Threat Model (AT-1 to AT-4). - 9 figures (Fig1–Fig9). - No implementation, no tests, no experiments. What v2.0.0 does not claim: - AetherHuman is not confirmed. - H-F1–H-F4 are not all "not falsified". - P1–P2 are not proven. - The architecture is not production-ready. - The gap is not genuine. No implementation has been evaluated. H-F1, H-F2, H-F3 are not falsified by argument; H-F2 is most fragile; H-F4 remains untested. P1–P2 remain proof sketches, not machine-checked. This is a research artifact, not a product.
title: AetherHuman: Human Participation in Autonomous Agent Ecosystems

summary: Kohn-Sham solver for isolated atoms using the finite-element discrete variable representation (FE-DVR). Pseudo-atoms with norm-conserving pseudopotentials in UPF format, including pseudopotentials without pseudo-atomic orbitals (e.g. SG15) All-electron atoms (non-relativistic), plus approximate scalar-relativistic (Koelling-Harmon) and ZORA treatments LDA and GGA functionals: PBE built in, all others via libxc Confined atomic orbitals with polarization functions for use as localized basis functions or projectors, exported on a logarithmic grid (Quantum ESPRESSO style), on the FE-DVR grid, or as spherical Bessel transforms; dipole matrix elements Photoemission : scattering phase shifts and dipole matrix elements to continuum states 🚀 Installation $ python3 -m pip install atomic_femdvr   The built-in exchange-correlation driver provides PBE. Other functionals (e.g. the LDA used for the NIST benchmark) need the libxc Python bindings, which are not on PyPI; see the installation guide . 💪 Getting started Calculations are defined by a JSON input file. A pseudo-atom with a confinement potential and polarization orbitals ( examples/Si_Pseudo.json ): { "control" : { "storage_dir" : " ./Si_pseudo " }, "sysparams" : { "element" : " Si " , "file_upf" : " ../tests/data/Si/Si.oncvpsp.upf " , "lmax" : 2 , "nmax" : 1 }, "dft" : { "xc_functional" : " PBE " , "mixing_scheme" : " anderson " , "alpha_mix" : 0.5 }, "confinement" : { "type" : " SoftStep " , "rc" : 20.0 , "ri_factor" : 0.5 , "polarization_mode" : " SoftCoul " }, "output" : { "output_wfc_qe" : true , "output_wfc_bessel" : true } }   $ cd examples $ atomic_femdvr pseudoatomic Si_Pseudo.json -t scf,nscf out   This solves the Kohn-Sham equations self-consistently ( scf ), computes two confined radial functions each for s, p and d ( nscf ), and writes them to out/ . All energies are in Hartree and all lengths in bohr. The all-electron solver is run with atomic_femdvr atomic (see examples/Ne_full.json ). See the documentation for the input reference, the method and the output formats. ✅ Validation All-electron : LDA eigenvalues agree with the NIST atomic reference data (Ne, to 2e-6 Ha). Pseudo-atoms : eigenvalues reproduce the all-electron reference energies stored by ONCVPSP in the UPF file to about 0.5 meV (Mo, Si). summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24314752 . Reviewer Report: Multi-Track Cognition Framework for Global Integrative Medicine Manuscript: "A Multi-Track Cognition Framework for Global Integrative Medicine: Breaking Paradigm Incommensurability Through System-Level Mapping Across Medical Systems" (G. Yang; Preprints.org , doi:10.20944/preprints202603.0470.v1, posted 5 March 2026) Type of report: Point-by-point reviewer report, prepared to help the author strengthen the work before journal submission. The manuscript proposes a computational "multi-track cognition" (MTC) framework that lets data from different medical systems (traditional Chinese medicine, biomedicine, Tibetan medicine, with others said to be addable) be compared and fused without forcing one system's vocabulary onto another. The author's stated aim is to move beyond format-level standardisation towards semantic alignment, and beyond single-point linear correspondence towards system-level mapping. Importance of the research area. Integrative medicine is widely practised and increasingly supported by health policy, including the World Health Organization's strategic work on traditional and complementary medicine. A persistent barrier to generating integrated evidence is that systems describe the patient and the intervention in different conceptual languages. Examples are pattern differentiation, nature and flavour, and meridian tropism on one side, and disease categories, biomarkers and molecular targets on the other. A general and extensible way to connect these descriptions would be useful for evidence synthesis, chronic-disease management and individualised care. The author appropriately targets semantic, and not merely syntactic, interoperability, which is a question that merits careful methodological work. Approach proposed. The framework has three layers (Figure 1; Section 2): 1. Cognitive tracks (Section 2.1). Each medical system has its own track with a native feature set, normalisation rules and a native "systemic effect" index. 2. Homeostatic representation network, HRN (Section 2.2). A directed acyclic graph of 28 laboratory indicators across eight physiological systems serves as the shared anchor. Its topology comes from literature and three expert physicians. Its parameters are learned with a Bayesian network on MIMIC-III. 3. System-level mapping (Section 2.3). A random forest, guided by three rules (cluster correspondence, network emergence, context dependence), is trained with a mean-squared-error loss to predict post-intervention changes in the HRN indicators. Performance is judged by Semantic Alignment Accuracy (SAA, the share of cases in which two mapped vectors reach cosine similarity ≥ 0.85), R², MAE and RMSE (Section 2.4). Evidence reported (Section 3). Four public datasets are used (Table 1), with a 70/30 split and 5-fold cross-validation. In the TCM–Western dual-track setting the framework reports SAA 91.27% and R² 0.852, against 59.13–76.58% SAA for three baselines (Table 2). A three-system extension adding Tibetan medicine reports SAA 86.34% and R² 0.821 (Section 3.4). Agreement with three clinical experts is reported as κ = 0.86, and a Lung–Spleen Qi Deficiency case illustrates the workflow (Section 3.5). The author concludes that the framework is lossless, general, and ready to support clinical integration. Strengths. The following strengths provide a sound basis for revision: • The problem is timely and clinically meaningful. • The modular idea, with track-specific components and one shared core, is attractive and in principle testable. • An outcome-level physiological anchor is a practical way to compare interventions that act through different theories. • The model, loss, hyperparameters and pseudo-code are stated explicitly, which allows scrutiny. • The author attempts expert annotation, effect sizes and a multi-system extension. •
title: PREreview of "A Multi-Track Cognition Framework for Global Integrative Medicine: Breaking Paradigm Incommensurability Through System-Level Mapping Across Medical Systems"

summary: Adding new parameters to the baseline distribution using the generated family concept has been one of the most commonly used techniques in recent years. The Median-based Unit Rayleigh (MBUR) is a one-parameter unit distribution. In this paper, the author added another parameter using the Topp_Loene generated family. The new approach not used previously in the literature is to use the Lomax distribution. The author truncated the Lomax distribution to obtain the unit-truncated Lomax distribution and used it as a generator to elaborate the unit-truncated Lomax-generated MBUR distribution. The derivations of the new generalized forms are discussed. The properties of both distributions, including the quantile function and raw moments, are discussed in detail.   The quantile functions can be expressed in a closed form, while the raw moments cannot be expressed in a closed form. Both distributions have bathtub-shaped, J-shaped, and increasing shape hazard rates. Real data analysis is performed to compare the fitness of both distributions.
title: Topp Leone Generated MBUR and Unit Truncated Lomax Generated MBUR Distributions: New Generalization of The MBUR Distribution

summary: Data and Stata code for a study of whether social capital predicts retained luxury imports. The outcome is imports less re-exports of four HS headings — 7113 jewellery, 9101 wristwatches with cases of precious metal, 4202 trunks, handbags and similar containers, and 3303 perfumes — scaled by population. Subtracting re-exports matters because entrepôt economies import these goods for onward shipment. The main regressor is the GSCI social capital dimension DIM_SC_30, a balanced annual series covering 247 countries. The full panel is 3,883 country-years across 184 countries, 2000–2023; the estimation sample with all controls is 3,241 country-years across 159 countries. A second, smaller panel uses the WVS/EVS Integrated Values Survey trust measure at wave level (86 country-waves, 36 OECD countries), with luxury imports averaged over a five-year window centred on each wave year. The package contains the UN Comtrade extract and the PowerShell script that produced it from the Comtrade public API, the World Bank control variables and their download script, the GSCI series, the Integrated Values Survey trust file, the Stata do-files and logs, and Figures 1–3. Code/Replication_Luxury_SocialCapital.do reproduces every table and figure in the paper. Nothing is interpolated: a country-year enters a panel only if it was observed. See README.md.
title: Social capital and retained luxury imports: replication data and Stata code for a global panel, 2000–2023

summary: We compared target-specific eight-point dose layouts for four withheld interior responses in 171 held-out Merck 4 × 4 drug-pair matrices, with (1,1) designated as the primary target. For the projection predictor, near-minus-far mean absolute error was −0.05772 at the primary target (95% pair-bootstrap interval −0.07163 to −0.04441) and −0.07085 for the four-target pair average (−0.07899 to −0.06262). Overall projection errors for near, far-plus-anchor and fixed random layouts were 0.0412, 0.1120 and 0.0773; on the same near inputs, the order-based predictors had lower average errors than the tested local interpolators, while projection showed no clear added benefit over the raw witness. A post-hoc Gaussian-process comparator showed no clear average difference from projection on the Merck near inputs, with optimizer-bound warnings in 293 of 684 fits.
title: Fixed-Budget Dose Layouts in Merck 4 × 4 Combination Matrices

summary: Two independent bulk RNA-sequencing datasets were generated using a zebrafish model of Dravet syndrome at 5 days post-fertilization (dpf). Dataset 1: Disease-associated transcriptional alterations Comparison of scn1lab−/− zebrafish with wild-type controls ( scn1lab+/+ ) to identify disease-associated changes in gene expression. scn1labvWT_metadata.txt scn1labvWT_unnormalised_counts.txt Dataset 2: Drug treatment and transcriptional response An independent dataset comprising scn1lab−/− zebrafish treated with sertraline, orphenadrine, brexpiprazole, fenfluramine, or DMSO. All treatment groups were compared against wild-type controls to investigate compound-induced transcriptional changes and their potential to reverse disease-associated gene expression signatures. scn1labvWT_treatment_metadata.txt scn1labvWT_treatment_unnormalised_counts.txt Data integration and batch correction Both datasets contain unnormalized gene-level RNA-sequencing counts and corresponding sample metadata. Although generated independently, the datasets can be analyzed jointly using appropriate batch correction or statistical models that account for dataset-specific effects. This enables integrated comparisons of disease-associated and treatment-induced transcriptional changes, provided that batch effects can be distinguished from the biological conditions of interest.
title: From molecular dysfunction to therapeutic discovery: Novel targets and drug repurposing candidates for Dravet syndrome

summary: The package contains four current Round-2 annotation sets covering the same 236 publicly documented B2B generative-AI use cases across 26 professional roles and five functional areas, yielding 944 coder–task records. The annotated dimensions are agency component, delegation degree, task structuredness and error criticality. Additional materials include a reduced, adapted extract of the original published task covariates; an earlier version of Coder 1’s delegation annotations for historical sensitivity analysis; Python analysis and validation scripts; aggregate results; supplementary tables; and documentation of variables, methods and provenance. Analyses cover inter-rater agreement, matched task comparisons, predictor-source substitution, role-cluster bootstrap uncertainty and exploratory logistic GEE models. The original task inventory is available in Mendeley Data under DOI 10.17632/vp6pxrbrpz.1. Its classifications serve as a comparison source, not as a fifth independent Round-2 coder. The earlier Coder 1 version is a historical sensitivity condition, not an additional independent evaluator. Coder identities are pseudonymised as C1–C4. Public task identifiers are retained to support reproducibility and linkage to the original dataset. Private linkage keys, original coding forms, personal declarations, task descriptions and the consolidated private research master are excluded. These annotations concern the interpretation of task descriptors. They do not establish observed organisational AI behaviour or verified operational autonomy. Uncertainty summaries are conditional on the 26 professional roles represented in the dataset.
title: Independent annotations of human–AI agency delegation in professional tasks: data and reproducibility code.

Do not extrapolate a verified laboratory entangled state to neural tissue without an independently validated transduction and state model. Bell tests and the locality boundary The CHSH inequality constrains a class of local hidden-variable models under specified assumptions. Hensen and colleagues used independently controlled electron spins in diamond; this is not a demonstration in human brains. The experiment must specify the settings, admissible trials, event ordering and outcome distribution. Ordinary correlation deserves the strongest defense A shared environment, clock, stimulus schedule or physiological rhythm can create cross-site association. F097 makes this ordinary explanation a serious predictive model rather than a weak nuisance adjustment. Measure independent reference channels, precommit preprocessing, retain dyad-level units and fit common-driver alternatives on training records only. A residual unexplained by measured covariates is uncertainty, not a unique indication of nonlocal causation. Negative expectation certifies entanglement for a trusted two-qubit measurement with established assumptions. The blueprint leaves the witness units unspecified. summary: This software record provides the source code and selected experimental artifacts associated with the research paper entitled "Blockchain-Anchored Data Continuity for Smart-City Digital Twins: A Dual-State Verification Framework." The project presents a hardware–software proof of concept for maintaining and verifying data continuity between IoT sensor records, a local hash-linked ledger, and a digital-twin-oriented dashboard. The prototype uses an ESP8266-based sensor node, a DHT11 temperature sensor, Python-based data acquisition, SQLite storage, SHA-256 record fingerprinting, and a Streamlit dashboard. The main contribution implemented in the software is a dual-state verification approach that distinguishes ledger integrity from source-record coverage. This distinction enables the detection of cases in which the ledger remains internally valid while one or more source records are not represented by corresponding ledger references. The released materials include: IoT data acquisition and database storage code. Local hash-linked ledger implementation. Source-to-ledger verification procedures. Six controlled data-tampering scenarios. Local verification performance measurement scripts. Digital Twin dashboard implementation. Solidity smart-contract and local EVM integration files. Experimental multi-replica demonstration and associated tests. The SQLite experimental database snapshot used in the study. The included baseline database contains 481 sensor records and 482 ledger blocks, including one genesis block. The verification experiments cover source-record consistency, hash-chain integrity, unique record association, and source-record coverage. The repository is intended to support inspection and reproduction of the software experiments described in the associated research paper. Results may vary depending on the execution environment, hardware, software dependencies, and database state. This release is a research proof of concept. It does not claim production-scale deployment, independent distributed consensus, sensor identity authentication, physical measurement accuracy, or full-scale urban digital-twin simulation. title: Blockchain-Anchored Data Continuity for Smart-City Digital Twins: A Dual-State Verification Framework

summary: The linear stability of solitary waves of the nonlinear Dirac equation in $1+1$ dimensions has resisted direct numerical computation because the discretized linearized operator produces eigenvalues that do not survive the continuum limit. We identify the mechanism as species doubling. Linearizing the complementary generalized Alexeeva--Barashenkov--Saxena (cABS) model about its exact solitary waves, we compute the spectrum of the stability operator with four lattice derivatives: the symmetric (naive) difference, the Wilson derivative, the SLAC derivative, and the chiral disordered derivative of Jacobs (1983). The naive derivative produces real unstable eigenvalues that are independent of the lattice spacing and carry their entire Fourier weight at the edge of the Brillouin zone; this doubler sector is the continuum stability operator evaluated at the spatially reflected profile $\psi_0(-x)$, which is not a stationary solution, so that its spectrum is that of a definite, wrong problem rather than numerical noise. The chiral disordered derivative, which lifts the doublers by a chirality-preserving, non-Hermitian mechanism, renders the stability operator non-Hermitian and is unusable for a real-time problem, in line with the symmetry-class criterion of arXiv:2611.05395. The Wilson and SLAC derivatives agree as $a\to0$ and isolate a third signature, complex quartets in the overlap of the two continuum branches with real parts proportional to $1/L$, which are finite-volume Krein collisions; a box-size sweep at every spectrally stable point confirms that none survives the infinite-volume limit. With these signatures separated, the physical spectrum is unambiguous and shows two instabilities. A real unstable eigenvalue is present wherever $dQ/d\omega>0$, equivalently wherever $E/Q$ decreases with $\omega$ (the two are the same statement, by $E'(\omega)=\omega Q'(\omega)$), which confirms the surmise of Khare, Cooper, Dawson and Saxena, identifies it with the Vakhitov--Kolokolov sign condition, and reconciles it with their non-relativistic result. The sign condition is sufficient but not necessary: at $q=1.1$ and small $\omega$, where $dQ/d\omega<0$, a complex quartet appears for $\kappa$ from about $1.4$ to beyond $2.4$, with a growth rate that rises from $0.06$ to $0.55$ across that range and a frequency between $1.3$ and $2.4$, converged in lattice spacing and box size up to $L=320$. It is an oscillatory instability confined to the window $1.05<q<1.15$, with growth rates up to $0.75$ at $q=1.075$: it marks the region where the scalar term nearly cancels the vector term. Solitary waves with $E/Q>1$ but no unstable eigenvalue exist, so $E/Q<1$ is a binding criterion, not a stability criterion. Below a threshold $\kappa_c(q)$, computable from the closed-form charge, equal to $1+0.49\sqrt{\epsilon}+O(\epsilon\ln\epsilon)$ near $q=1$, $\epsilon=(q-1)/q$, and to the non-relativistic value $2$ for $q\ge7$, every solitary wave is spectrally stable for all $0<\omega<m$.

title: Lattice doubling and the linear stability of solitary waves in the complementary generalized ABS model

summary: Teaching English for Specific Purposes (ESP) at specialized sports universities presents distinct pedagogical challenges, primarily due to student-athletes' rigorous training schedules, frequent competition travel, and heterogeneous baseline language proficiency. This study investigates the pedagogical efficacy of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven platforms and interactive digital tools into an ESP curriculum to enhance speaking fluency, domain-specific vocabulary acquisition, and learner autonomy among undergraduate sports students. A quasi-experimental study was conducted over one academic semester involving 64 second-year students divided into an experimental group ($n = 32$) and a control group ($n = 32$). While the control group received conventional textbook-based classroom instruction, the experimental group utilized AI conversational agents for simulated press conferences, automated speech recognition (ASR) tools for pronunciation feedback, and gamified digital platforms for sports terminology retention. Pre- and post-test assessments, alongside a post-intervention learner perception survey, demonstrated statistically significant improvements in the experimental group's oral proficiency, specialized lexical accuracy, and self-regulated learning engagement ($p < 0.001$). The findings indicate that AI-assisted and digital language environments offer flexible, personalized, and anxiety-reducing pathways that align effectively with the dynamic schedules and practical career needs of future sports professionals.
tags: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED); English for Specific Purposes (ESP); digital pedagogy; sports university; communicative competence; learner autonomy.
title: LEVERAGING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DIGITAL TOOLS TO ENHANCE ENGLISH FOR SPECIFIC PURPOSES (ESP) INSTRUCTION IN SPORTS UNIVERSITIES

summary: This database has eight zip files, each containing monthly netcdfs of daily 1/24-degree (~4 km) gridded counterfactual climate data for the western US. Variables represented are daily precipitation total (prec; mm), maximum and minimum temperature (tmax and tmin, respectively; degrees C), mean vapor pressure (hPa), mean 2-m wind velocity (m/s), mean downwelling solar and longwave radiation at the surfae (solar and longwave, respectively; W/m2), and surface pressure (hPa). The counterfactual dataset is meant to represent an alternative realization of the observed climate from 1951–2025 from which anthropogenic trends in background means and daily variances about those means have been removed. The observed climate dataset is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19636838. Anthropogenic trends in background means and daily variances are estimatated to be represented by a weighted mean of trends simulated by 24 CMIP6 climate models under the historical (1850–2014) and SSP2-4.5 (2015–2100) scenarios. Trends in background means and daily variances are assessed relative to a baseline period of 1851–1900 (1851–1910 for daily variances). Model trends are weighted based on a combination of performance and independence following the ClimWIP method, where performace is assessed as agreement with the observed linear trend in global mean surface temperature from 1961–2025 and independence is assessed based on inter-model differences in maps of historical climatological mean surface air temperature and sea-level pressure. The methods used to produce the observational dataset, CMIP6 model weightings, and the counterfactual dataset are described in a manuscript submitted to Earth System Science Data. This dataset will be made publicly available upon publication of the corresponding paper.
title: Couterfactual version of 1/24-degree gridded daily observed climate for the western United States after removal of CMIP6 trends in background means and daily variances, 1951–2025

summary: Positioning: PubMed stores scientific papers. ScientificClaims.org stores the evolving answers to scientific questions. The Scientific Claim Registry (SCR) is infrastructure for the memory of science — not its truth, consensus, or recommendations. It registers, it does not arbitrate . What v0.5 adds over v0.4: v0.4 made every evidence link independently verified. v0.5 is the first version in which the registry has been kept current by its own Layer 1 surveillance loop (retrieve → classify → dual-model verify → promote/corroborate → recompile → version), and it reports what that took, including where it failed. Growth through the loop, not manual curation. From v0.4 to v0.5 the lipedema pilot grew from 347 to 526 evidence claims and from 423 to 626 evidence records (895 question–claim links, 383 distinct DOIs) under the same 42 versioned questions. Sources: (1) an unattended weekly rotating contradiction sweep (R-AI-12), June–September 2026, pairing each topical retrieval with a null/negative/opposing-evidence pass; (2) a library-scale backfill re-running all 42 questions against the author’s curated lipedema library (4,563 structured records) plus Europe PMC. Verification across the registry: 614 verified, 5 disputed (kept and flagged), 7 unverified ; 19 records contradict the claim they sit under. Each changed answer received a new immutable version with a “what changed” note. Operational honesty. Unattended operation exposed failures a demo never shows, documented with the guarantees added: (a) eight silent weeks in which a missing LLM credential made every run fail while the rotation still advanced and logged the questions as swept — the rotation now advances only on successful runs, and a missing credential is a loud warning; (b) silently degraded semantic retrieval, now with keyword fallback and a self-started library service; (c) a malformed model response that discarded a whole run (atomic writes kept the registry intact), now parsed leniently on retry. A memory system that hides its own gaps contradicts its premise. Object model (unchanged). The scientific question (e.g. SQ-LIP-000007) is the primary navigable object. Underneath it, claims (SCR-LIP-000001) are structured, versioned units of evidence with an explicit role (supporting / contradicting / refines / context), PECO context, a GRADE rating, dated provenance, a change log, sentence-level provenance and an independent verification verdict. Prior-art honesty: SCR does not invent the claim primitive or persistent claim identity — nanopublications/Trusty URIs, micropublications, Wikidata, CIViC, ClinGen, Epistemonikos/PICO, SciFact, GRADE and MAGICapp already exist. The v0.5 contribution is evidence that a question-centric, verified, versioned registry can be maintained by its own loop, with the failure modes of unattended operation documented and guarded. Operated by the BIO (Biological Intelligence Observatory) research method.
title: Scientific Claim Registry (SCR): A Versioned Memory of How Scientific Answers Evolve — Framework v0.5: Unattended Layer 1 Surveillance at Library Scale, with Documented Failure Modes

summary: This deposit accompanies the study “ Balancing predictive accuracy and structural interpretability in airborne LiDAR biomass models of Mediterranean forests ”. It provides anonymised, analysis-ready forest inventory biomass responses, area-based and crown-based airborne LiDAR predictor tables, fixed outer and inner spatial cross-validation folds, R source code, allometric equation registries, selected derived tables, and a reference figure for Mediterranean forests in Castilla y León, Spain. The analysis combines PNOA-LiDAR data acquired in 2017-2019 with Fourth Spanish National Forest Inventory (IFN4) field observations from 2019. The deposited prepared data support reproduction of the nested spatial modelling, validation, and reporting stages. The archive includes an automated integrity validator, an executable workflow launcher, a column-level variable inventory, package versions, workflow documentation, and SHA-256 checksums. Raw IFN4 records, PNOA point clouds, corrected plot coordinates, original plot identifiers and the confidential identifier crosswalk are not redistributed. Scripts documenting raw-data preparation are included, but reconstruction from raw sources requires obtaining the original data from their official providers and complying with their licences. Corrected IFN4 plot coordinates and original keys have been removed. The public plot_uid is a release-specific anonymised sequential identifier. Code is provided under the MIT License. Author-created anonymised data, tables, figures and documentation are provided under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Conditions and attribution requirements of the source datasets remain applicable. PNOA attribution: Obra derivada de PNOA-LiDAR 2017-2019, CC BY 4.0, Instituto Geográfico Nacional/Centro Nacional de Información Geográfica (IGN/CNIG), Spain.

summary: This reproducibility package supports the study “Wearable Stress Models Across Sessions and Exercise Conditions: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation with Same-Session Controls.” The study developed wearable stress classification models using the WESAD dataset and externally evaluated them using the Wearable Device Dataset from Induced Stress and Structured Exercise Sessions, PhysioNet version 1.0.1. The package contains the analysis scripts, locked study protocols, Protocol Amendment v1.1, source manifests, integrity records, model settings, aggregate results, and analysis-freeze outputs used to produce the reported findings. It covers the 20-second primary analysis, the 30-second sensitivity analysis, external stress-versus-rest transport qualification, cross-session affective and exercise evaluation, same-session exercise-minus-final-rest comparisons, internally derived operating points, protocol-version checks, and self-report alignment analyses. summary: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.
title: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Analyzing whole-slide images (WSIs) requires combining evidence across tissue regions and spatial scales. Multi-agent systems offer a promising approach to this task. However, existing systems make limited use of molecular evidence, often select visually prominent but less representative regions while overlooking global context, and struggle to reuse experience from previous cases. To address these challenges, we present PathLoop, a self-evolving multi-agent framework that integrates omics data for evidence-grounded WSI analysis. Specifically, PathLoop coordinates visual and omics interpreters across slide, patch, and pixel levels, using molecular signals to guide region selection and combining local tissue details with global slide features. A judgment agent then checks the consistency of the collected evidence against Pathology-Wiki, a knowledge base built from 48 entries across 24 organ systems, and triggers re-examination when the evidence is inconsistent. To reuse past experience, a four-level memory stores reasoning trajectories, practical tips, skills, and tools to guide future cases, forming a loop of evidence collection, review, and memory update. We evaluate PathLoop on four TCGA cohorts with biomarker prediction, survival prediction, and subtype classification. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of PathLoop across these tasks and support its use for evidence-grounded WSI analysis.
title: PathLoop: Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Reasoning for Evidence-Grounded Whole-Slide Image Analysis

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24326466 . Overall assessment: Hollmann et al. present a study that addresses an enduring mystery in the field of HIV biology: how does HIV target only two copies into the viral particle during viral assembly at the membrane? The authors use biochemistry, negative stain electron microscopy, and cryogenic electron microscopy to show the structural basis for the selection of dimeric copies of the HIV RNA genome by the immature Gag protein during assembly of the virion. This approach provides compelling biophysical evidence for the main claim that RNA packaging by HIV Gag is selective for dimeric species. The author's system for preparation of smaller, soluble Gag:RNA species will be useful for many labs. This preprint review provides comments aimed to improve readability and boost support for the main claims of the study, detailed in the major and minor points below. Major points ● The introduction discusses the role of genome dimerization and packaging. A simple infection assay demonstrating that mutation of the dimerization nucleotide tract (as in Figure 2a) abolishes infection would experimentally validate the central claim that genome dimerization is a critical component of infection. ● In the first section of the results (corresponding to Figure 1a, Figure 2a, Figure S3a), dimerization mutants are described that impact assembly. However, it is unclear whether mutant truncates the dimerization tract from 10 nucleotides to four (shortening the ruler) or if the length is maintained but the sequence swapped with GAGA repeats. Adding language to clarify the mutation made and adding discussion of these findings in the results section to explain how the results demonstrate a molecular ruler function would increase credibility. ● In Figure 3c/e/g, the six helical bundle is depicted interacting with density corresponding to RNA. However, the density maps do not show which residues or nucleotides are critical for the contact. A sentence clarifying the limitation of their cryoEM analysis and explaining how the mutations performed in the RNAse activity assay (Figure 3j/k) provide orthogonal support would increase clarity. The authors might consider conducting focused classification of the six-helical bundle and the RNA density from their existing single-particle datasets (Figure S6) to resolve the molecular details of RNA binding. Minor points: ● The authors use HIV-related and structural biology jargon extensively. While this conveys expertise, it also is a major barrier to clearly understanding the main point of the paper for readers outside specific sub-fields of HIV biology. To make the paper more accessible to an audience outside of the narrow HIV field, the authors could consider simplifying the language and using simpler, shorter sentences and fewer abbreviations. ● Figure 1a: It is difficult to interpret which nucleotides belong to which monomer of the dimer. A color-coded linear diagram or schematic of a single 5' 350 nt section of the HIV genome would allow the readers to more easily interpret the figure. ● Figure 1a: It is unclear from the diagram in Figure 1 how the dimerization signal is hypothesized to function and which elements were included in the study. The authors could consider using non-overlapping color sets between the two panels. ● Figure 1c: The typical void volume for a Superdex 200 10/300 (used for the size exclusion chromatography in Figure 1c) is 8.5-9.5 mL. summary: Estimates each judge's confusion matrix, the class prevalence, and a posterior over every item's true label from a panel of imperfect judges labelling the same items, with no gold labels, via the Dawid-Skene model fitted by EM. Includes majority-vote baselines, Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa agreement diagnostics, bootstrap confidence intervals, and panel simulators for planning and failure-mode analysis. Validated on a real five-judge panel over 400 agent trajectories where estimated judge accuracies can be checked against construction-time gold labels, including an honest account of the correlated-judge failure mode.
title: judgepanel: estimating LLM-judge accuracy without gold labels

summary: This repository contains the replication materials supporting the manuscript "Forecasting U.S. Residential Property Prices: An Autometrics Approach with Indicator Saturation" by Shipra Aggarwal and Manish Aggarwal, submitted to Discover Analytics. The study applies Autometrics with impulse indicator saturation (IIS) and step indicator saturation (SIS) to quarterly U.S. real residential property prices (FRED series QUSR628BIS). The replication package includes archived data vintages, PcGive estimation outputs, forecasting results, Python analysis scripts, model specifications, methodological documentation, and supporting tables. The principal forecast evaluation covers 2013-Q3 to 2024-Q1, using models estimated through 2013-Q2. A separate robustness exercise uses a later data vintage and forecasts through 2026-Q1. The materials enable reproduction of the reported model estimates, forecasting accuracy measures, directional accuracy statistics, and forecast comparison tests. Data source: Bank for International Settlements (BIS), distributed through Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED), series QUSR628BIS. Associated manuscript: Forecasting U.S. Residential Property Prices: An Autometrics Approach with Indicator Saturation. Software used: OxMetrics/PcGive and Python. The README.md and METHODS.md files provide details of the replication procedure and software requirements.

summary: This dataset contains de-identified clinical, hematological, biochemical, questionnaire, and molecular data from a prospective longitudinal study investigating biological features associated with anxiety symptoms in medical students. The study included 33 medical students, classified into an anxiety-symptom group (n = 16) and a control group (n = 17) according to the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A). Clinical and biological measurements were collected at baseline and follow-up to explore changes associated with anxiety symptom severity over time. The dataset includes demographic characteristics, lifestyle-related variables, HAM-A total scores and symptom-domain assessments, hematological parameters (erythrocyte count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit), and serum cortisol concentrations. In addition, mitochondrial 7S RNA expression was evaluated by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in an exploratory subgroup of 10 participants (5 per group). The molecular dataset includes cycle threshold (Ct) values for mitochondrial 7S RNA and the reference gene RPLP0, as well as derived expression measurements calculated using the comparative 2⁻ΔΔCt method and log2 fold change transformation. The repository includes the complete clinical dataset, the RT-qPCR dataset, an Excel workbook containing the datasets, and a data dictionary describing the variables, units, and measurement methods. These data are intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and further research into the potential relationship between mitochondrial RNA regulation, neuroendocrine responses, and anxiety symptoms in the context of persistent academic stress. The findings and molecular measurements should be interpreted in light of the observational longitudinal design and the exploratory nature of the RT-qPCR subgroup analysis.
title: Mitochondrial 7S RNA Expression and Anxiety Symptoms Dataset

summary: TRANSREP — Experimental Results and Numerical Reproducibility (v1.3.0) This release provides experimental numerical data, analysis code, evaluation results, and reproducibility resources supporting the study Same Accuracy, Different Features: Checkpoint Alignment Changes Positional-Encoding Transfer Rankings in Vision Transformers . Version 1.3.0 extends the previously published v1.2.0 release with additional controlled experiments, depth- and token-resolved transfer analyses, and executable numerical verification tools. Experimental coverage Endpoint cohort E: 24 ImageNet-100 ViT-Base models across four positional-encoding configurations (Learned, Sinusoidal, 1D RoPE, and ALiBi), with six independent runs per configuration. Longitudinal cohort L: Twelve independently trained Learned and RoPE models, including upstream training trajectories, checkpoint-aligned transfer evaluations, and Oxford-IIIT Pets depth-resolved analyses. Completed-schedule cohort C: Twelve independently trained models under upstream-matched training schedules, with frozen-feature evaluations across five downstream classification tasks. Depth- and token-resolved analysis: 1,560 model-level probe scores across 13 representation depths and two token readouts (CLS and mean patch pooling). Epoch-300 evaluation: Frozen-feature readout comparisons and model-level upstream validation accuracies for twelve original endpoint models. External validation: Nine fixed public DeiT-III ImageNet-1k checkpoints comparing absolute positional embeddings with axial and mixed two-dimensional RoPE. Additional analyses: CKA representation comparisons, exploratory depth-dependent contrasts, and longitudinal late-readout comparisons. Numerical reproducibility The archive includes original numerical records, derived tables, analysis programs, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. A unified CPU-only verification procedure reproduces the supported score-level analyses, including the longitudinal and epoch-300 summaries, 65 depth-specific token-readout interaction contrasts, and 130 direct positional-encoding contrasts from archived B4-C model-level results. Verification instructions and software dependencies are provided in the root README and requirements-numerical.txt . The distribution does not include raw benchmark images, trained checkpoint weights, or large extracted feature arrays. summary: Compartment-Resolved Compatibility of MTA-Cooperative PRMT5 Inhibition and PDE4 Activation in MTAP-Deleted Glioblastoma A falsifiable dual-state hypothesis and translational research framework El Amin Bouchelit HISTAMOS — Independent R&D Decision Intelligence Initiative, Germany Correspondence: contact@histamos.com   |   https://histamos.com/ Abstract Background: Homozygous methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP) loss in cancer can create methylthioadenosine (MTA)-dependent vulnerability to protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) inhibition while also reshaping antitumor immunity. The relationship is not uniform across models: primary human MTAP-deleted glioblastomas (GBM) have sometimes lacked the predicted bulk MTA accumulation, plausibly because MTAP-competent stromal cells metabolize extracellular MTA. Separately, a November 2026 study found that pharmacological activation of cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase (PDE), using MR-L2 in MTAP-deficient GBM models, improved T-cell function and mouse outcomes. Hypothesis: A subset of MTAP-deleted GBM may simultaneously retain sufficient tumor-cell-intrinsic MTA/PRMT5 drug susceptibility and reversible immune-cell cAMP-dependent suppression. In this dual-positive state, adding a PDE4-activating intervention to an MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitor could improve durable elimination of viable tumor cells—but only if the immune benefit does not diminish tumor-specific PRMT5 target engagement or impose unacceptable normal-tissue toxicity. Proposed test: A prospective, compartment-resolved, four-arm factorial design in matched patient-derived GBM/immune/stromal systems should measure intracellular and interstitial MTA, PRMT5 pharmacodynamics, immune cAMP and cytotoxicity, host effects, and post-washout clonogenic persistence. Interpretation: The combined treatment has not been evaluated by HISTAMOS, and no clinical efficacy, synergy, novel molecule, or freedom to operate is claimed. This contribution is a conditionally falsifiable translational hypothesis that separates genotype, biochemical state, immunological reversibility, and durable tumor control. Keywords: glioblastoma; MTAP deletion; methylthioadenosine; PRMT5; phosphodiesterase-4; cAMP; tumor microenvironment; synthetic lethality; immune suppression; treatment interaction 1. Clinical and biological problem Glioblastoma is an aggressive, spatially heterogeneous malignancy in which relapse-capable cells, stromal interactions, and local immune dysfunction complicate the translation of target engagement into durable benefit. MTAP commonly resides within the chromosome 9p21 deletion region alongside CDKN2A/B. MTAP deletion is an established molecular finding, but it should not be treated as equivalent to a measured metabolic drug-response phenotype. Large genomic surveys confirm the frequency of MTAP loss across multiple cancers, while leaving metabolite abundance and compartment-specific function unresolved in individual tumors [1–3]. The translational problem is twofold. First, MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors require an adequately permissive biochemical state in malignant cells. Second, immune activity within the same lesion can be inhibited by MTA-associated signaling and other, non-MTA mechanisms. The question is not whether either axis exists; it is whether selective tumor pharmacology and productive immune recovery can be achieved concurrently in primary human GBM, with a safety margin and incremental reduction of residual viable cancer cells [4–9]. 2. What is already established—and what is not 2.1 MTAP loss and MTA-cooperative PRMT5 pharmacology In isogenic cell systems and transplanted tumors, MTAP loss has been associated with increased vulnerability to PRMT5 perturbation. MTA-cooperative inhibitors such as AM-9934, MRTX1719, and brain-directed candidates including TNG456 have demonstrated selective preclinical PRMT5 activity in defined contexts. These are prior discoveries, not HI

summary: This record contains the code, district-level data, and stored outputs needed to reproduce the tables and figures of “Who Pays for Disasters? Evidence from a Household Panel in Peru” (Víctor Cárdenas-Santiago and Roberto Guerrero Compeán, Inter-American Development Bank, 2026). The paper uses Peru’s national household survey panel (ENAHO, 2007 to 2024) to study who reports disasters, how reports relate to welfare, and how incorrect household linkage in a rotating panel can reverse the distributive answer. Self-reported exposure is contrasted with daily satellite rainfall (CHIRPS) and with administrative emergency records (INDECI). Contents: All programs (Stata and Python) that build the household unit, estimate every table, and produce every figure. District-level CHIRPS extreme-rain measures and INDECI district-year records. The stored outputs (coefficients, intervals, counts) behind each table and figure, so that every number in the paper can be checked without running the code. A README with the correspondence between tables, programs and outputs, the order of execution, software requirements, and a manifest with the MD5 checksum of every file. Household-level files (ENAHO microdata from INEI and the analytical bases derived from them) are published in a separate record with restricted access. Extracting both records into the same folder merges them into one tree, and the programs then re-estimate all results. With this public record alone, all results can be verified against the stored outputs but not recomputed. ENAHO microdata are distributed free of charge by INEI at https://proyectos.inei.gob.pe/microdatos/ . Software: Stata 19.5 SE (reghdfe, ftools, eventstudyinteract, csdid, boottest) and Python 3.10 (pandas, numpy, scipy, pyreadstat, matplotlib).
