summary: Autonomous agents often reason and coordinate through labels that do not reveal which external information they denote. We present Sema, a content-addressed reference system for reasoning and communication that creates hash-based verifiable words: participants encode and hash information under an agreed representation, then reuse the content address as a term, optionally with a human-readable handle. Sema can use any representation if participants agree on how content is encoded, hashed, resolved, and decoded. This paper develops one concrete realization based on canonicalized JSON-compatible objects, field-level Merkle commitments, explicit identity rules, and content-addressed references. Full-reference verification establishes identity of the resolved hashed content, while semantic equivalence, correctness, and compliance remain separate questions. As a worked application of the Sema primitive, we introduce Pattern Cards, a concrete schema for deliberate, System 2-style reasoning. They make often-skipped reasoning moves explicit through contracts for mechanisms, conditions, invariants, typed dependencies, and failure modes. Within one agent, resolving a card can make a reusable reasoning procedure explicit. Across agents, the same content-addressed definitions support coordination: agents can verify that they resolved the same definitions; in strict mode, an enforced handshake halts on mismatch. A bootstrap library of more than six hundred cards demonstrates the design. Its contract fields averaged 26.7 times the tokens of short wire references—a transmission-compression result, not an inference-token saving, because definitions were hydrated before use. Illustrative agent demonstrations examine coordination behavior. The same primitive could support a Living Taxonomy of Thought; its utility, evolution, and governance remain open questions.
title: Sema: When the Hash Is the Word

summary: Standard nanoindentation analysis suppresses the time-dependent response of a tested material, discarding the property that governs how a heritage paint film survives climatic loading: its viscoplastic dissipation potential. We recover it, together with the elastic modulus, from a single displacement-controlled relaxation indent by Bayesian inverse identification through a Gaussian-process surrogate of a finite-element contact model. The central difficulty is that the constitutive law is adequate during relaxation but structurally violated during loading, where the particulate film deforms by granular compaction. Overweighting the loading forces the optimiser to absorb this model-form discrepancy into the constitutive parameters, leaving a deceptively good global fit. We expose this failure mode through a three-way audit of weighting schemes: expert-encoded physics, Fisher-information optimality, and a data-driven Empirical Bayes filter. Information-optimal weighting under model-form error produces the most biased parameters with an equally tight posterior, an effect we term Constitutive Overfitting. A polycarbonate control, for which the model is uniformly adequate, confirms that the three schemes converge, establishing the audit as a diagnostic of model inadequacy rather than a pipeline artefact. This work has two outcomes. The first is the complete viscoplastic dissipation potential of a heritage paint film, the rate-dependent descriptor that fracture and digital-twin models require, from a single high-information indent. The second is the audit: an unaudited inversion would report a tight posterior on a biased modulus, whereas the three-way comparison separates reliable parameters from artefacts wherever constitutive fidelity varies within a single experiment. Population-level variability is deferred to a forthcoming multi-indent study.
title: Regime-Aware Bayesian Identification of the Viscoplastic Dissipation Potential in Heritage Paint Films from Nanoindentation

summary: We Are Here : a Resource-Ratio Alternative to Energy-Based Civilizational Scales   A Discussion Paper Alexandre Costa Coelho, M.Sc. [1] M.Sc., Massachusetts Institute of Technology, MIT Sloan Fellow '07 December 11, 2026 - DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24202174   Keywords: Fermi Paradox, Kardashev scale, SETI, STRATA gradients, civilizational advancement Abstract Civilizations have been ranked by how much energy they burn. That habit bundles together two questions that should never have shared one variable. What to measure, in order to find a civilization at all, and by what means. And how advanced it is, once found. Dyson raised the first in 1960. A star-enclosing energy collector radiates detectable waste heat. Kardashev, four years later, defined his civilization types by energy, inside an analysis of how much power a transmitter would need to be heard across interstellar distances. Dyson's sphere was his example of a Type II civilization. The scale grew out of a detection question and was then used as a ranking of how advanced a civilization is. The two roles were never separated, and we argue they should be. Call it the Two Stones, Two Birds Problem. One stone, energy, thrown at two birds that were never in the same tree. This paper throws both stones, one at a time. For ranking, we propose a Resource Utilization Ratio, which scores consumption against need and the ecological cost of energy, and we combine it with two defined but unmeasured dimensions, a behavioral capacity and an empathic one, in a Civilizational Advancement Index (CAI). The illustrative Earth baseline of about 13% depends on the author's hypothetical values for those two dimensions. We also propose STRATA I, II and III, bands of the CAI, as a ranking alternative to Kardashev's Types I, II and III, and the two sets of names do not mean the same thing. For detection, we propose Tunelength (TnL), a speculative signal drawn from brain-interface engineering and a peer-reviewed, if contested, theory of consciousness. [1] Faculty, Assistant Professor of Instruction, McCombs School of Business, The University of Texas at Austin, USA . The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent the position of the University of Texas at Austin or the McCombs School of Business. Email: alexandre.coelho@mccombs.utexas.edu.

summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π (x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Version 1.0. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p² is treated as the first level of a ladder where the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. The formula turned out to be the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses. The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof and claims this approach as his own; the missing step is named.     Работа продолжает геометрическую модель распределения простых чисел [2] и работу «Числовая стрела и прямая 1/2» [1]. Геометрическая формула числа нечётных составных до p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, рассматривается как первый уровень лестницы, в которой масштаб на каждой ступени возводится в квадрат: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. Показано, что эта формула — наилучшая квадратичная формула уровня до 5⁴: она точна везде, кроме одной компенсирующей пары промахов (p = 15 и p = 17). Квадратичная решётка уровня держится до базиса 7 включительно и разрушается сразу после него. Ошибка формулы раскладывается на две наложенные таблицы: плавную поправку уровня и колебание, которое в явной формуле есть сумма косинусов по нулям дзета-функции. summary: Unconventional superconductivity in rhombohedral $n$-layer graphene exhibits a rich phase diagram with multiple distinct superconducting regions, whose microscopic origins remain unclear. Here, we investigate the competition between charge-density-wave (CDW) and pair-density-wave (PDW) instabilities near the inner van Hove singularities (VHSs), using a patch renormalization-group approach with the realistic band structures incorporated. We identify two key findings. First, we find an effective attractive interaction emerging from purely repulsive interactions through RG flow in the presence of $C_3$ symmetry breaking. The resulting interaction structure, with two repulsive couplings and one attractive coupling, gives rise to competing CDW and PDW instabilities. Second, the competition is controlled by the detuning from the VHS. While CDW dominates near the VHS filling and at higher temperatures, PDW becomes the leading instability on either side of the VHS and at lower temperatures. This mechanism naturally produces two superconducting regions separated by a CDW-dominated regime, providing a possible qualitative explanation for the experimentally observed separation between SC1 and SC2.
title: Emergent Attraction and Competing Orders near the Van Hove Singularity in Rhombohedral $n$-layer Graphene

summary: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $φ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.
title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution

summary: Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.
title: Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler

summary: Unequal couplings to a common emergent gauge field provide a continuous way to tune competing magnetic instabilities in an effective description of $U(1)$ spin-liquid mixtures. We study this mechanism in quantum electrodynamics in 2+1 dimensions with two families of four-component Dirac fermions. Combining a leading large-$N$ treatment with Schwinger--Dyson equations, we obtain chiral condensates representing Néel order in the two sectors. At fixed fermion number, the coupling ratio $κ=e_2^2/e_1^2$ controls which condensates develop. Depending on $N$, the phases with a single condensate are connected through either coexistence or a finite interval in which both fermion families remain gapless. The mass-generation thresholds are reciprocal, and the fermion gaps close with Miransky essential singularities. The renormalization group flow has a circular line of fixed points parametrized by the invariant ratio $κ$. At the calculated order, gauge-invariant staggered magnetization correlations have continuously varying exponents in the gapless regime, while the exponent for correlations between the two sectors is independent of $κ$. These results connect the competition between magnetic orders to a continuous family of critical theories and identify magnetic correlation signatures of the intervening gapless regime.
title: Competing Magnetic Orders and Continuously Varying Exponents in $U(1)$ Spin Liquids

summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π (x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The similarity with the construction of the Birth of Dimensions model is shown. Section 8 shows that the accumulated mismatch over the seams is Euler's sine at one half ( π ), while accumulation over the primes gives γ (Mertens); that the error of the prime count at a step is of the order of the square root of the mismatch of the frame; and that the transfer of the observer changes nothing if and only if all zeros lie on the axis 1/2 — this is the Hilbert — Pólya programme. Each seam is a right triangle in a circle: the centre along the line is the radius, the centre on the circle the cosine, the hole the sine, and sin² + cos² = 1. The author believes that this work can become a proof of the Riemann hypothesis; the missing step is to show that the unity of the process makes the transfer of the observer a symmetry. The work is laid out as a programme of proof: the missing step is formulated as a target statement, and the Davenport — Heilbronn function serves as a test that it rests on the birth of the arrow. The missing step is also written as a statement about positivity: from Mertens' square 2(1 + cos θ )², which pushes the zeros away from 1, to the square of Weil's energy, which must hold them on ½ and forbid pairs of zeros on opposite sides of the circle. Version 10. Section 8 gains the item “Three directions — three projections of the sphere” with Table 8. On the circle z = 1 − 1/s, one becomes the centre-balance, the axis ½ the equator at distance 1 from it, s = 2 goes to z = ½, and zero to the opposite pole. The Riemann hypothesis in this form: all zeros are at one and the same distance 1 from the point of balance. The arrow is a meridian of the Riemann sphere, and the axis ½ its equator. The centre of a seam (n(n + 1))^½ and the axis x^½ ar
title: The Fractal Ladder of Prime Density: Quadratic Scale and Linear Error

summary: This research archive presents a detailed continuum-model derivation of the electron anomalous magnetic moment g−2 within the electron sector of a broader common-continuum theoretical framework. It consolidates the historical Paper02 construction with the current Model113 formulation through A3.8328 and provides a complete derivational record of the intrinsic anomaly, second-normal residual dynamics, mechanical magnetic-current correction, gradient contribution, and the subsequently developed propagated electromagnetic-return channel. The current construction begins from the fixed electron structural parameter N2, the tangent-sector magnetic-current source, and the second-normal residual inventory Delta_infinity = 1 / [12 N2^2 (N2 - 1)]. The previously frozen mechanical magnetic correction is retained without modification. A distinct electromagnetic-return contribution is constructed through four separately typed factors: the electromagnetic-to-strong support ratio 1/N2, two-dimensional transverse spreading 1/(2 pi), the three-dimensional-to-two-dimensional ring-plane projection sqrt(2/3), and the inherited gradient enhancement 1 + 2/(pi N2). The resulting electromagnetic-return contribution is delta a_EM = Delta_infinity × (1/N2) × (1/2pi) × sqrt(2/3) × [1 + 2/(pi N2)]. Combining the inherited mechanical operator and the newly closed electromagnetic-return operator gives a_e = 0.0011596521805908756337882909101487… The archive explicitly preserves the earlier Paper02 precision-test failure rather than retrospectively rewriting the historical operator. The electromagnetic-return term was developed subsequently and is therefore reported as a new model-internal operator. Its close numerical agreement with the measured electron anomaly is treated as a retrospective consistency test rather than as a blind prediction. Particular attention is given to the provenance and physical identity of every factor, the separation of mechanical and electromagnetic readout channels, source-field-receiver typing, amplitude-versus-inventory distinctions, NoAlias constraints, NoDoubleCount constraints, and high-precision numerical reproducibility. summary: How many photons are needed to reach an optical entropy limit, and how accurately must that limit be approached to identify the full input state? This article determines both for finite products of one-mode Gaussian channels, with exact total input entropy and a mean-photon budget imposed in the laboratory frame. The comparison includes arbitrary non-Gaussian, entangled and infinite-support normal inputs. Exact entropy and photon allocation. For a channel product \(\Phi\), the full frontier is \[M_\Phi(T,E)=\min_{\rho:\,S(\rho)=T,\,\operatorname{Tr}(N\rho)\le E}S(\Phi\rho).\] An exact finite convex allocation gives this value, physically budgeted Gaussian optimizers and the least photon budget at which the entropy-only limit is attained. Moving a squeezed bath between two links can change that threshold even when their pure-input frontiers and entropy-only limits coincide. Singular limits requiring unbounded squeezing have sharp inverse-energy or logarithmically enhanced photon costs, including leading coefficients, matched corrections, inverse error budgets, joint low-entropy crossovers and actual finite-budget allocations. For a given set of links, specify \(T\) and \(E\) in laboratory coordinates and compare \(E\) with this threshold. Below it, the finite-budget allocation gives the correct benchmark for evaluating an observed output entropy (Sections 2–5). Complete limiting recovery curves. For a fixed singular channel product, let \(\sigma_E\) be its finite-budget optimizer, \(\lambda_E\) the actual photon support price, and \(\eta_E(\rho)=S(\Phi\rho)-M_\Phi(T,E)\). Define the worst-case full trace-norm error by \[\omega_E(x)=\sup_{\substack{S(\rho)=T(E),\ \operatorname{Tr}(N\rho)\le E\\ \eta_E(\rho)\le x\lambda_E/E}}\|\rho-\sigma_E\|_1.\] Along every path \(T(E)\to0\), including zero entropy, and for each fixed finite \(x\ge0\), the article proves \[\lim_{E\to\infty}\omega_E(x)=2\sqrt{1-e^{-4\alpha_{\max}x}},\] where \(\alpha_{\max}\) is the largest leading photon share. This determines the whole limiting error curve, not only the scale at which recovery becomes possible. For fixed positive input entropy, when the dominant modes retain positive thermal occupations, the corresponding curve is a trace-norm optimization over displaced thermal states. The displacement ellipsoid is paid for within the original photon cap while preserving the exact input entropy. Thus approaching the optimal output value can require much less accuracy than identifying its source. To read the curve in reverse, choose a target full trace-norm error \(0<d<2\). Any fixed \(x<-\log(1-d^2/4)/(4\alpha_{\max})\) places the limiting worst error strictly below \(d\); the corresponding output-entropy tolerance is \(x\lambda_E/E\) (Section 8). Local optimality and global guarantees can differ. At a fixed strictly active interior budget, the input optimizer is unique and the optimal local square-root stability coefficient is characterized by one joint thermal and coherence price. Nevertheless, a finite feasible disturbance can have a larger ratio \(\|\rho-\sigma_E\|_1/\sqrt{\eta_E(\rho)}\) than every infinitesimal disturbance at the same channel, entropy and photon budget. An explicit replacement–unitary family proves this strict separation and has a sharp Poisson variational limit. The local comparison already includes all quantum-state perturbations; the separation is not an artefact of restricting it to Gaussian states. Other specified mixed-reference instances have the exact common coefficient \(2/\sqrt{\lambda}\). For a given excess \(u\), first check that it lies in the range certified for the local estimate with the desired slack. A guarantee over a finite interval requires a bound valid on that whole interval (Sections 6–10). Recovery to an optimizer set and changing channel families. Above an attainable regular entropy plateau, the geometry of the original photon cap yields matching square-root, quarter-power and logarit
title: Photon costs and input rigidity at Gaussian entropy limits

summary: Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics (with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution) with a minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and limits on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex. Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.
title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots

summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.
title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration

summary: Coordinating a team of heterogeneous agents to complete tasks with unknown requirements is a challenging multi-agent planning problem. Agents differ in their ability to discover task requirements and in their ability to engage tasks, so the planner must coordinate task discovery, execution, and staging. This paper introduces a hierarchical planner that uses a graph neural network policy to assign actions to agents, then finds a path to the action's location using a shortest-path algorithm. The central part of our approach is the CAAT graph, which is a graph representation of the planning context consisting of the agents, tasks, capabilities, and actions. We demonstrate that our learned planner can jointly coordinate a heterogeneous team to simultaneously discover task requirements and complete tasks in a shorter time compared to baselines that optimize task discovery and task engagement independently. Furthermore, we show that our policy can zero-shot plan on out-of-distribution settings by training only on an outdoor map then transferring without finetuning to an indoor map with more agents, tasks, and capabilities than seen during training.
title: Coordination of Heterogeneous Teams with Uncertain Task Requirements

summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.
title: Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models

summary: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.
title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators

summary: Latent variable models are popularly used to characterize dependence among many observed variables through underlying latent variables. Recent advances in statistics and machine learning methods have encouraged growing interest in studying latent variable models with flexible latent distributions that capture complex latent structures. This flexibility, however, raises a fundamental question of whether model parameters can be identified when the latent distribution is unknown and must itself be learned. In this paper, we show that exact identifiability fails almost everywhere, in the sense that distinct but arbitrarily close pairs of model parameters and latent distributions can yield exactly the same distribution for the observed variables. Nonetheless, the resulting identification ambiguity is small. In particular, we prove that the identification ambiguity, measured by the diameter of the set of parameters inducing the same marginal distribution, vanishes at a superpolynomial rate of $\exp\{-c(\log p)^2\}$ as the number of observed variables $p$ grows. Building on this result, we show that the failure of exact identifiability need not preclude consistent estimation or valid inference of the model parameters and latent distribution. These results suggest that, when many variables are observed, the identifiability issue is far less of an obstacle to estimation and inference in latent variable models than is commonly expected.
title: Identifiability of latent variable models with flexible latent distributions

summary: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.
title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation

summary: We investigate the use of an artificial-intelligence (AI) coding agent, supervised by human physicists, for collider physics analyses using CMS Open Data. OpenAI Codex performs dimuon event selection, two-dimensional invariant-mass and decay-length fits, Monte Carlo detector simulations, and systematic uncertainty evaluation after acquiring physics and experimental knowledge from published studies and external references, with human review at each stage. The workflow is tested on two CMS datasets, with custom full-detector simulations used to determine acceptance and reconstruction efficiencies. In proton-proton collisions at sqrt(s) = 7 TeV, prompt J/psi differential cross sections are measured versus transverse momentum and rapidity. The ratios of remeasured to published CMS cross sections have a mean of 1.000 and an RMS spread of 0.215 across 39 bins. In peripheral (50-100% centrality) PbPb collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV, the corresponding prompt J/psi fiducial cross-section ratios have a mean of 1.158 and an RMS spread of 0.225 across six intervals. We identify agent failure modes and demonstrate the importance of structured human review in ensuring reliable results.
title: AI-Assisted Analysis of CMS Open Data: Prompt J/psi Cross-Section Measurements in pp and Peripheral PbPb Collisions at sqrt(S)= 7 TeV and sqrt(sNN) = 2.76 TeV

summary: Refreshable tactile displays can make graphics accessible to blind and low-vision people, but high-resolution actuator arrays remain expensive. We study whether a low-cost vibrotactile surface can convey simple figures, and how they are read. Nine participants (four blind; five sighted, tested blindfolded then open-eyed) identified seven figures by touch, with video and timing analysis of their exploration. Blind and blindfolded-sighted readers achieved comparable accuracy, but blind participants were about three times faster, using a continuous, rhythmic "gliding" strategy-reading through motion, whereas sighted participants searched in halting, pause-heavy passes; among the sighted, more pausing accompanied errors. Recognition failures were concentrated in specific figures (a diagonal was misread even with vision), locating the bottleneck in representation rather than resolution. We contribute an empirical characterization of tactile reading strategies and design implications for low-cost refreshable tactile displays and affordable tactile representation.
title: An Affordable Vibrotactile Surface for Tactile Figure Recognition: Exploration Strategies of Blind and Sighted Users

summary: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.
title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows

summary: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PRUDENT.
title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.
title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models

summary: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://towzeur.github.io/RCR/.
title: When Neural Collapse Fails to Route: Routing Drift in Continual Learning

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.
title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation

summary: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.
title: FailureGen: Scalable Robot Failure Data Generation with World Models

summary: Whether a foundation model succeeds as an autonomous agent depends as much on its runtime software as on its weights. This runtime, the agent harness, manages context and memory, steers multi-turn control, executes tool actions in sandboxes, and verifies work before stopping. Because models differ in how they use tools and how they fail, a static harness tuned for one model or task often stalls, wastes tokens, or regresses on another. This bottleneck has driven a shift from prompt tuning to self-improving agent harnesses: systems that inspect their own execution traces, separate runtime bugs from model limits, and rewrite their own code. We present a unifying architectural and design framework for self-improving agent harnesses. The framework pairs four editable runtime components (context and state, agent control, action interfaces, and verification and recovery) with a four-stage loop that diagnoses failures, proposes code patches, validates candidates, and deploys updates. Using this framework, we show how optimizers trace errors across long trajectories and discover reusable runtime mechanisms such as pre-stop verifiers, loop breakers, and persistent memory. We further show why full-harness rewrites overfit or break across modules, and how modular updates with validation gates generalize across models while bounding token cost. To keep self-modification safe, we establish practical defenses against recurring failure modes including prompt bloat, benchmark gaming, and evaluator tampering. Finally, experiments on SWE-bench Lite validate this framework, showing that gated modular evolution outperforms prompt reflection and full-harness rewrites across models and repositories at a fraction of the token cost.
title: Harnesses That Improve Themselves: A Unifying Framework for Self-Improving Agent Harnesses

summary: Choosing features is difficult with few labeled molecules, even for a tabular foundation model that learns in context. We study this problem with TabPFN for low-data molecular property prediction, separating input width, feature meaning, and predictive usefulness while keeping contexts, query molecules, and predictor settings matched. On ADME/Tox assays from Therapeutics Data Commons, endpoint-matched assay predictions improve a compact RDKit descriptor baseline, and a provenance audit shows that most audited query molecules already occur in the predictors' training sources. Across 77 FS-Mol development tasks and 157 held-out test assays drawn from ChEMBL, broad RDKit descriptor and fingerprint families provide a strong default, rank-averaging TabPFN with support-fitted fingerprint forests improves upon both models, and learned weighting of family predictions adds further gains at a larger prediction budget. A utility-trained selector builds a traceable 16-column input from 238 sourceassay predictors, improving upon the baseline while trailing wider representations and equalwidth structural SVD coordinates. Named outputs identify what each feature predicts and where it comes from. Their usefulness for a new assay is assessed alongside the other input features, and paired removal and replacement tests measure what each selected output contributes. Together, these studies offer a protocol for evaluating feature selection, representation choice, and data provenance with a fixed tabular foundation model for few-shot molecular property prediction.
title: Feature Selection for Tabular Foundation Models: Exploring Feature Utility in Low-Data Molecular Prediction

summary: Energy smells are inefficient implementations that waste energy. Once code reaches production, these smells become costlier and riskier to fix, so energy efficiency checks should shift left, i.e., move earlier in the development lifecycle, to where code is written. Existing energy smell tools rely on fixed static rules and do not measure energy savings, whereas LLM-based optimizers mostly target execution time and rarely ground their changes in concrete smell definitions. To address both limitations, we present DR. GREENS, an agent skill that detects and repairs energy smells in Python code within the developer's coding environment. The skill grounds the coding agent in our taxonomy of 12 energy smells and 65 root causes, augmented with repair guidance drawn from 230 measured cases. The skill also encapsulates a static analyzer and an independent verifier to confirm behavior preservation and energy saving for each attempted repair. We evaluated DR. GREENS in 18 sessions on three open-source repositories, with two models and three skill configurations. Of the 258 measured repairs, 68.6% saved energy, with a median saving of 24.9%. Compared with a baseline skill that lacks the taxonomy, the full skill found more energy smells with verified savings in all three repositories with both models. DR. GREENS helps developers detect energy hotspots and fix them reliably without altering program behavior, which makes energy-efficient development more feasible.
title: Identifying and Repairing Energy Smells with Agent Skills

summary: Carrier self-trapping is a fundamental relaxation pathway in strongly correlated quantum materials, yet the microscopic lattice motions that drive it have remained largely inaccessible to direct observation. Here we investigate the van der Waals antiferromagnet NiPS$_3$ upon excitation across its ligand-to-metal charge-transfer gap, and reveal a nonequilibrium pathway that initially generates unbound carriers before they evolve into correlated excitonic states. Using ultrabroadband optical-pump terahertz-probe spectroscopy, we simultaneously track carrier localization and the associated lattice dynamics in real time. The transient conductive response quenches with a time constant of $\sim$109 fs and evolves into a localized exciton state, accompanied by pronounced renormalization of Ni-S optical phonons and the emergence of a transient 2.7 THz vibrational mode. Temperature-dependent measurements, together with mode-resolved dielectric dynamics and symmetry analysis, identify the 2.7 and 8.0 THz responses as spectroscopic indicators of exciton self-trapping and point to a cooperative two-phonon mechanism. These findings establish the excitation pathway as a key parameter controlling carrier localization and many-body relaxation in strongly coupled quantum materials.
title: Charge-transfer excitation drives cooperative phonon-assisted exciton self-trapping in NiPS$_3$

summary: Advection-diffusion priors are a common way to make neural sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts physics-informed. We test where such a prior must enter a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM to help, using daily NOAA OISST v2.1 for the Bay of Bengal (1982-2024) and a synthetic benchmark on the same grid with known currents of controlled strength. (i) On real data, a soft advection-diffusion residual with a learned velocity gives no reliable benefit (lead-15 CRPS -0.007 degrees C, 95% interval [-0.022, +0.008]); a plain temporal-smoothness penalty matches it, and equivalence within 3% is not established either. (ii) Learned velocities do not recover the currents, whether placed in the loss, in an explicit transport step, or in a transport step without neural correction: they correlate with the reference no better than a shuffled-date null, even on synthetic data where knowing the currents would improve day-15 forecasts by 16-23%. (iii) Supplied currents help on synthetic data, but mostly as information: giving them to the network as input channels, without transport, recovers 92% of the transport design's lead-5 gain, and a frozen-current numerical forecast does as well as either. (iv) With GLORYS12 reanalysis currents on real data, the transport design is 6% and 4% worse at leads 1 and 5; reanalysis advection explains essentially none of the daily OISST change (correlation 0.02), and frozen-current transport is worse than persistence. (v) The defect that matters is lead-dependent miscalibration shared by every model. One variance multiplier per lead, fitted on validation data, brings 90% coverage to 0.85-0.91 at all leads and lowers day-1 CRPS by 13-21%; fine-tuning on 15-day rollouts fixes long-lead coverage but costs short-lead skill. This version withdraws an earlier claim of an 81% CRPS reduction that came from an uncontrolled comparison.
title: Where Should Physics Enter? Information, Identifiability and Calibration in Probabilistic Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting

summary: Identifying whom a person looks at is central to understanding multi-party conversations, yet gaze geometry alone becomes ambiguous as more people appear. Conversations offer cues that geometry lacks, such as who is speaking and what is said, but no gaze dataset provides them for many multi-party scenes. We introduce SORBET, a benchmark of 3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended person labels, covering more multi-party scenes than existing gaze datasets. Prior gaze models struggle to use these cues, which come in different forms, must be linked to the right person, and can conflict with gaze geometry. We propose Nunchi, a framework that constructs a text prompt from the transcript and the outputs of gaze and speaker models, links every cue to the candidates with shared labels, and lets a vision-language model (VLM) weigh gaze geometry against conversational cues to identify the attended person. Nunchi outperforms the strongest existing method by 4.8 percentage points. On SORBET, conversational cues help whereas additional visual cues do not, and the gains hold across three VLMs, with automatic transcripts, and on two existing datasets.
title: Nunchi: Ears Help Eyes in Multi-Party Conversations

summary: Conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) provide a principled framework for assessing treatment-effect heterogeneity and identifying patients who may benefit from an intervention. For survival outcomes, CATEs may also evolve over time and pose challenges for estimation and inference. Existing methods can accommodate complex covariate heterogeneity but often fail to exploit shared temporal structure or provide valid inference for time-varying treatment effects and their contrasts. We propose a deep survival learning framework that combines neural networks for nonparametric covariate effects with a shared spline representation of temporal variation, enabling joint estimation of CATE trajectories. Using doubly robust pseudo-outcomes and sample splitting, we establish nonasymptotic oracle bounds accounting for network and temporal approximation, nuisance estimation, and optimization errors. Our theory shows that exploiting shared temporal structure yields sharper error bounds for temporal contrasts than those derived from separate time-specific estimators. For inference, we develop a subsampled ensemble procedure and establish asymptotic normality for pointwise CATEs, temporal contrasts, and covariate contrasts, including temporal contrasts over shrinking time intervals. Under suitable regularity and bias-control conditions, consistent infinitesimal jackknife variance estimators yield asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Simulations evaluate estimation accuracy, interval coverage, and sensitivity to temporal dimension and basis mismatch. An application to lung cancer survival data illustrates the framework's ability to characterize heterogeneous treatment benefits over time.
title: Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Deep Survival Learners

summary: Blind source separation (BSS) is increasingly needed in sensing architectures where mixtures are acquired by multiple remote devices but the inference itself is carried out centrally. In such systems, the sensors often cannot transmit their raw observations since the communication links are rate-limited, energy-limited, or both. The fusion center therefore must recover the latent sources from compressed versions of the mixtures. This setting raises questions that classical BSS models do not address directly: whether source identifiability survives compression, how separation accuracy changes under a specified compression model, and how the separation procedure should be modified to account for the statistical model induced by the compression stage. In this work, we develop a framework for distributed BSS from compressed mixtures that addresses these issues at three levels. First, we formalize identifiability under compression and establish a data-processing viewpoint showing that compression cannot introduce distinguishability that is absent before compression. Second, for mixtures of Gaussian sources with general covariance structures, we derive an idealized Gaussian rate-distortion-based Cramér-Rao lower bound benchmark for the interference-to-source ratio. Third, we develop practical compression-aware separation schemes based on subtractively dithered quantization together with debiasing at the fusion center for both fourth-order-cumulant-based and second-order-statistics-based methods. Simulation experiments demonstrate the resulting tradeoffs between communication rate and separation performance and the gains obtained by compression-aware separation in representative distributed sensing scenarios.
title: Distributed Blind Source Separation from Compressed Mixtures

summary: Dark matter may consist of multiple components with distinct particle-physics origins. We investigate a scenario in which a universal axion couples to both visible and twin QCD, with twin baryons providing a possible dominant dark-matter component. The presence of a second strongly interacting sector can substantially enhance the axion mass while preserving its role in resolving the strong-CP problem, provided the physical vacuum angles are appropriately aligned. For a representative uniformly rescaled twin spectrum with a confinement scale five times that of ordinary QCD, the axion mass is enhanced by approximately a factor of 25. Using lattice-informed QCD results and a two-temperature description of the early universe, we investigate the cosmological evolution and relative abundances of the dark-sector components. In a representative conditional numerical benchmark, axions account for a small percentage of the observed dark matter, while twin baryons could constitute the remainder for a suitable primordial baryon asymmetry. We also examine the implications for additional relativistic species, strong-CP alignment, and the interactions of stable twin matter. Our results provide a quantitative framework for exploring mixed axion--twin-baryon dark matter and identify the particle-physics and cosmological conditions necessary for a viable realization, including constraints from the thermal history and formation of cosmic structure.
title: A Universal Axion in a Twin-QCD Sector

summary: Most AI-generated video detectors analyze decoded pixels and overlook how videos are produced. We show that causal video autoencoders leave an architecture-specific rhythm in compressed bitstreams: their temporal stride concentrates unpredictable content at latent-chunk boundaries, so rate-distortion optimized encoders allocate bits periodically. Without decoding pixels, we observe four-frame pulses in CogVideoX and Wan2.2 and eight-frame pulses in LTX-Video, which are absent from content-matched camera footage. Passing camera footage through a generator's autoencoder alone induces the pulse, supporting its proposed origin. A training-free peak-ratio statistic separates generated from camera video (AUC 0.84-0.94) and persists across tested quantization settings and H.264/H.265 encoding. Frame-size traces also identify four commercial generators, with 89.2%, 84.1%, and 83.0% accuracy under H.264, H.265, and AV1, beating the pixel-based UnivFD baseline (72.7-73.6%). Our results directly link generative architecture to measurable coding demand.
title: The Rhythm of Generated Video: Latent Chunking Leaves Periodic Traces in Compressed Bitstreams

summary: Ontology matching remains a fundamental challenge in biomedical data integration, since independently developed ontologies, such as the Mouse Anatomy (MA) and the National Cancer Institute Thesaurus (NCI), adopt different terminologies, granulari-ties and conceptual structures. This work presents ViewEntanglement, a revised version of the View_Entanglement_7 pipeline, which combines sentence-level em-beddings (SBERT), explicit latent-space entanglement simulated through random orthogonal transformations, a ridge-regression codec to align the entangled spaces, and a supervised re-ranker based on Random Forest. We formalize the orthogona-lity property of the true cross-referential transformation, analyze the computational complexity of each stage, and evaluate the pipeline on the Anatomy benchmark. Reference results indicate that the learned codec almost fully reverses the simulated entanglement (relative Frobenius error ≈ 0,12) and that the Random Forest re-ranker raises the F1-Score by approximately 3 percentage points over the cosine baseline.
title: ViewEntanglement: Latent-Space Alignment and Supervised Re-ranking for Biomedical Ontology Matching

summary: Replication code and derived data for electronics journal
title: Replication code and derived data for electronics journal

summary: Today's Warning: AI Is Becoming an Operational Cyber Actor — Taiwan's August 13 Attack and the Case for Execution-Finality Today's (13th August 2026, Reuters) reported AI-assisted cyberattack targeting Taiwan's government agencies highlights an important shift: AI does not need to "go rogue" to create danger — it can simply execute a malicious operator's objective faster, in parallel, and adapt when one route fails. The proposed execution-finality architecture addresses a different layer of this problem: it does not attempt to control the attacker's AI. Instead, it seeks to ensure that, within defender-controlled infrastructure, a machine-generated request, valid credential, available tool, or technically possible action cannot automatically become an externally effective consequence without independent pre-effectuation authorization at the protected consequence boundary. In short: the attacker may control the AI, but the defender should still control what its own systems are allowed to make real. The Shift This Incident Reveals Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs confirmed that government agencies were targeted during July by an overseas campaign combining conventional cyber techniques with AI agents. The agencies detected the abnormal activity and successfully handled the incident. The significance of this is not the attack itself — automated intrusion attempts are routine — but what it signals about the trajectory of offensive capability: AI agents can now perform reconnaissance, target analysis, vulnerability research, tool selection, execution, observation, and adaptive re-planning with progressively less human intervention at each step. This produces an offensive chain that looks fundamentally different from scripted automation: Human Objective → AI-Agent Planning → Machine-Generated Actions → Tools → Target Infrastructure → Attempted Consequence The defender cannot interrupt this chain by making the attacker's AI safer, because the defender does not control that AI, its infrastructure, its guardrails, or its instructions. A hostile operator can strip safety measures, supply unrestricted tools, use stolen credentials, and instruct multiple agents to keep searching until something works. Reframing the Defensive Question This is why the article's central move is to discard the question "how do we force the attacker's AI to behave safely?" as unanswerable, replacing it with: "Even if a hostile AI successfully generates an attack, what determines whether our protected infrastructure is allowed to turn that request into an unauthorized consequence?" This reframing relocates the defensive objective. It is no longer about predicting or constraining the attacker's reasoning process — it is about independently governing the transition point inside the defender's own infrastructure where a request becomes a real-world effect: a database release, a network transmission, a financial settlement, a privileged API call, an industrial actuator command. Why Existing Controls Are Necessary but Insufficient Modern security stacks — authentication, IAM/RBAC, OAuth scopes, sandboxing, firewalls, IDS/IPS, EDR, zero trust, and model guardrails — remain essential and are not being replaced. But each answers a narrower question than the one that matters most for high-consequence actions: Authentication confirms a credential is valid — not that a specific resulting operation is authorized. IAM/RBAC confirms an identity can access a resource — not that a specific export, quantity, or destination is sanctioned. OAuth/API tokens confirm scoped access to a function — not final authority over every consequence that function can produce. Sandboxing confines where software runs — but legitimate environments often expose network access, database access, and privileged APIs that don't require any "escape" to misuse. Model guardrails are the weakest link against a d
title: Cyberattack on Taiwan Exposes the Execution-Finality Gap: The AI Didn't Go Rogue — It Followed Orders

summary: This record contains reproducibility software, exact and interval certificates, fixed certificate data, figure source data, environment files, and validation documentation supporting the manuscript “Activation Thresholds for Noisy-Reference Quantum Metrology.” It includes the certificate-generation and independent-verification workflow for the benchmark results at N=3 and y=11/20, the general-survival interval cover, the rank-two activation window, and finite endpoint-witness upper bounds. The manuscript and its supplementary information are separate outputs and are not included in this deposit or covered by its licenses. summary: Replication code for Vergili, A. and Hafalır, İ., "Expertise, signaling and learning in fish auctions", Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization (2026), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2026.107814.
