See the README for software requirements, the mapping from scripts to tables and figures, and information on data access.
title: Replication package for: Expertise, signaling and learning in fish auctions

summary: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.
title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization

summary: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.
title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents

summary: Analytic continual learning replaces iterative gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pre-trained representations, summarizing all past sessions in two running sufficient statistics: the feature autocorrelation matrix $Σ_t$ and the class cross-correlation matrix $Γ_t$. Lifting backbone features into a wide random code of dimension $M \gg D$ substantially improves linear separability across tasks, but forces $Σ_t$ to grow quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Under a fixed persistent memory envelope $\Bcal$, a learner faces a fundamental structural trade-off: store exact pairwise co-activations inside a narrower feature code, or expand to a wide code while compressing cross-coordinate interactions. We observe that the coordinate self-variances $v_t = \diag(Σ_t)$ and class statistics $Γ_t$ grow only linearly with $M$, whereas off-diagonal interactions dominate memory. We introduce \method (\textbf{Co}ordinate-\textbf{Re}stored \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning), which retains $(v_t, Γ_t)$ exactly, maintains off-diagonal co-activations through a streaming rank-$q$ factor $F_t$, restores exact diagonal variances via $\Sighat_t = F_t^\top F_t + \Diag(v_t - \diag(F_t^\top F_t))$, and solves the full $M\times C$ normal equations via the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, \method matches dense full-covariance readouts within $0.09$ points while cutting persistent state by $90.7\%$ ($35.9$ vs.\ $385.3$ MiB). Under equal memory envelopes of $16$--$80$ MiB, prioritizing expansion width $M$ over covariance rank $q$ outperforms exact narrow readouts in $17$ of $18$ configurations by up to $+2.19$ points.
title: Variance Restoration over Covariance Rank: Memory-Budgeted Analytic Continual Learning

summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.
title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory

summary: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.
title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model

summary: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026
title: The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale

summary: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.
title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops

summary: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at https://bit.ly/reachypi.
title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots

summary: Looped diffusion Transformers reuse shared blocks to deepen computation and match larger models with fewer parameters, reducing storage and deployment burdens. Yet repeated attention and MLP computations remain costly. Pruning reduces storage and computation by removing redundant parameters or units. Training-free methods struggle to resolve recurrent contributions, while training-based methods lack explicit constraints on position-specific errors affecting later inputs and final outputs. We propose LoopPrune, a pruning and recovery framework addressing these requirements. Recurrent importance estimation combines shared-removal effects and position variation to select a shared structure; shared reconstruction pools recurrent input statistics to compensate weights. Loop-position recovery compares complete denoising predictions at identical student states and matches text guidance, updating all student parameters against a fixed dense teacher. Extensive experiments across four open-source models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms demonstrate effectiveness. At 30% structured parameter pruning, Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense six-benchmark average accuracy, exceeding the best baseline by 9.49%. Across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion, pruned SDXSv3 reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x over dense models.
title: LoopPrune: Recurrent Pruning for Looped Diffusion Transformers

summary: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen computation by reusing shared layers, approaching larger models' capabilities with fewer parameters and easing the storage and deployment burden of stacking independent layers. However, repeatedly processing long visual sequences still incurs substantial compute and GPU memory costs. Visual token compression reduces these costs by shortening sequences. Existing methods mainly select original tokens directly or combine selection with aggregation. In looped models, the former may overlook changing token importance across calls and discard information needed later; the latter lack joint consideration of output changes across calls, limiting information preservation. We propose LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm addressing both issues. Visual aggregation builds a compact candidate pool before the looped backbone, and cross-invocation selection averages instruction attention from the first two existing calls of the same shared attention layer to retain tokens needed by both states. Weight-tied value correction then jointly fits shared visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs, reducing output deviations across states. To validate LoopZip's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments covering two open-source looped VLMs, eleven benchmarks, and three pruning ratios. On LoopVL-1B, LoopZip retains 97.16% of the original model's performance at 50% pruning ratio and exceeds the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning ratio. Across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, LoopVL-1B with LoopZip reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups over the original model.
title: LoopZip: Visual Token Compression for Efficient Looped Vision-Language Models

summary: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.
title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information

summary: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.
title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling

summary: Flow matching models, ODE-based generative models, generate samples by gradually morphing a simple source distribution into a target distribution. However, these models still face challenges in optimally balancing computational efficiency with generation fidelity. While predictor-corrector schemes have been proven to help address this issue in diffusion models effectively, their application to flow matching models remains under-explored. In this work we present a novel training-based predictor-corrector framework for flow matching, which exploits the fact that the ODE can be easily reversed. Our key idea, termed Marginal Matching, is to correct samples at a particular time step in the forward ODE towards a matching marginal distribution of the backward ODE. This scheme proves to reduce a bound on the distance between the data distribution and the learned distribution, motivating two different implementations for the correction function. We show that our proposed method improves sample quality on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, with minimal overhead in computation time.
title: Correcting Flows with Marginal Matching

summary: This article addresses the coefficient identification inverse problem for a coupled nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation with cubic nonlinearity. More precisely, we consider a coupled nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation in a bounded cylinder contained in $\mathbb{R}^{1+\ell}$, where $ \ell\geq 2$, and establish the unique recovery of the time-independent coefficients appearing in both the zeroth-order perturbation and nonlinearity term from both full and partial boundary measurements of the solution. The unique recovery of zeroth-order coefficients is obtained via first-order linearization; however, the nonlinearity coefficients are recovered using the higher-order linearization. Finally using the unique continuation principle, we establish the unique identification of the coefficients from the partial boundary measurements of the solution.
title: Inverse Boundary Value Problems for a Coupled Semilinear Klein-Gordon System

summary: Chiral molecular adsorption can modify the spin and orbital character of metal surface states, providing an electronic-structure basis for interpreting spin-dependent interfacial phenomena. Using first-principles calculations with spin-orbit coupling, band unfolding, and an atom-projected orbital angular momentum (OAM) analysis, we investigate spin and OAM textures at chiral heptahelicene/Au(111) interfaces and compare them with clean Au (111) and an achiral coronene/Au system. Adsorption changes the orientations of the spin and OAM vectors and reduces the sampled OAM magnitudes of Au-derived surface states near the Fermi level. The two heptahelicene enantiomers exhibit textures related by mirror and time-reversal symmetries, whereas the comparison with coronene identifies changes that also occur without molecular chirality. These results clarify how molecular adsorption modifies interfacial spin and orbital character and establish symmetry constraints relevant to chirality-dependent photoemission.
title: Spin and Orbital Angular Momentum Textures at Chiral Molecule-Metal Interfaces

summary: In this paper, we employ a combination of several first-principles-based approaches to systematically scan chains of several types of magnetic atoms in different chain geometries on top of various overlayers on the Nb(110) surface, to develop a pathway to engineer topological Majorana edge states. Using atomistic spin-model calculations, we first identify a rich variety of magnetic configurations, including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-spiral, and exotic up-up-down-down states stabilized solely within a second-order Heisenberg model. In the next step, we solve the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations using a band-theoretical method. Depending on the magnetic structure and atomic configuration, the superconducting spectra may exhibit topologically trivial minigaps, broad overlapping Shiba bands, or localized zero-energy edge states accompanied by sizable topological minigaps. In particular, Fe chains on Ag/Nb(110) are found to display pronounced signatures associated with topological superconductivity, including strongly localized zero-energy edge states and indications of Shiba band inversion. We further demonstrate that changes in the spin structure or a small amount of spatial relaxation can substantially modify the superconducting band structure and the localization properties of the edge states.
title: Ab initio Engineering of Topological Superconductivity in Substrate-Supported Magnetic Chains

summary: Strange metals display a linear-in-temperature resistivity, $ρ_{xx}\sim T$, and a quadratic inverse Hall angle, $\cotΘ_H\sim T^2$. These seemingly universal laws are often attributed to quantum criticality, yet no controlled theory realizes both at an asymptotic zero-temperature fixed point, and experimentally they persist only over finite temperature windows. Here, we show that these properties can arise from an intermediate critical regime that does not govern the ground state. Using a minimal class of holographic models, we construct a fully backreacted realization of both scalings, which appear within a finite temperature window controlled by an emergent intermediate scaling geometry. The window is bounded by relevant deformations of the corresponding fixed point: momentum relaxation sets the upper edge, while the magnetic field $B$ closes it from below at $T_{\min}\sim B^{2/3}$, up to logarithmic corrections. At $T_{\min}$, strange-metal transport, the scaling geometry, and critical thermodynamics break down together. Our results point to intermediate criticality as a distinct route to strange-metal transport, and suggest that it can be identified by the simultaneous breakdown of transport and thermodynamic scaling under a magnetic field.
title: Strange-Metal Magnetotransport without a Strange-Metal Ground State

summary: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schrödinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.
title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus

summary: Hydroxide at neutral-to-alkaline pH and halides inhibit fungal laccases and limit their use in wastewater treatment. From GFN2-xTB cluster models of Trametes versicolor laccase (PDB 1GYC) we build a four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction of the trinuclear copper cluster and execute its charge-transfer dynamics on the Euro-Q-Exa quantum computer (IQM, 8 qubits, Trotterized circuits with Pauli twirling; 726 jobs). The charge-transfer frequency is measured to 3-5 meV, reproducibly over nine days and across changes of the device qubit map: hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy of the crystal-geometry model by 92.0 +/- 2.2 meV (exact 87) and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 +/- 1.8 meV. A screen of charged probes in three dielectric models identifies Y116E; in the probe model the hardware resolves a reduction of the hydroxide penalty by 74 +/- 7 meV and of the halide penalty by 64 +/- 5 meV, acting on the site-energy gap rather than on the coupling. A real Glu116 (five conformers) with PROPKA protonation states and the coupled Asp456 gives a realistic reduction of 10-30 meV, with the same sign in 28 of 28 model combinations; the direction and ordering are the prediction, rate factors only an illustration. Scanning the on-site repulsion reverses the sign of the hydroxide effect, and a one-electron Hartree model reproduces the reversal: the measured dynamics is effectively single-particle. On a Fermi-Hubbard benchmark the hardware does not resolve electron correlation; it would need a contrast loss below 0.13 percent per CZ gate instead of the measured 0.34-0.54 percent.
title: Countering Anion Inhibition of Laccase Electron Transfer: Electrostatic Design, Charge-Transfer Dynamics on a Superconducting Quantum Processor, and Its Limits

summary: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.
title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering

summary: Using a high-resolution GRMHD simulation of a magnetically arrested disk, we investigate the physical mechanism driving magnetic-flux eruption. The horizon-threading magnetic flux declines mainly in off-equatorial regions, whereas localized hot spots associated with magnetic reconnection appear near the equatorial plane around the onset of flux decline. A non-axisymmetric, magnetically supported low-density structure, which we identify as a magnetic bubble, expands radially and azimuthally within a pre-existing low-density channel in the filamentary accretion flow. Based on these findings, we propose a physical picture linking reconnection, bubble expansion, and horizon magnetic flux decline. The reconnection occurs in the pre-existing low-density channel, and may reconfigure the field and promote bubble expansion. Magnetic-pressure gradients provide broadly distributed outward support for the expansion, while magnetic tension contributes a localized outward force near the equator. Bubble expansion may limit gas replenishment, helping to maintain the low-density region and reduce the total pressure near the equator. This pressure reduction may facilitate equatorward electromagnetic energy transport. In the simulation, the polar electromagnetic energy flux reverses from poleward to equatorward near the onset of the horizon-flux decline. The equatorward transport is concentrated in the bubble sector and carries electromagnetic energy from the off-equatorial magnetosphere to the equatorial region. This energy supply may sustain localized reconnection and plasma heating as the eruption develops.
title: Magnetic Flux Eruptions in Magnetically Arrested Disks: Magnetic Reconnection and Bubble Expansion

summary: Analysis code, the rainfall-only reconstruction and derived data supporting a manuscript currently under peer review. Files are restricted until publication; editors and referees receive access through a private link.
title: Code and data for a manuscript under peer review (dryland albedo)

summary: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.
title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail

summary: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.
title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control

summary: When processor implementation details are unavailable, black-box microarchitectural reverse engineering helps security researchers identify hardware conditions related to security vulnerabilities. However, this process requires substantial manual effort to design experiments, develop test programs, and analyze results for each processor. We present ProcReverser, a multi-agent system that automates this process. ProcReverser uses execution feedback to improve experimental plans and test programs and identifies microarchitectural properties from measurements. We develop a comprehensive suite of property identification tasks focused on hardware mechanisms relevant to Spectre-class attacks, covering speculative execution, branch prediction, memory dependence, and cache behavior. We evaluate ProcReverser on the XuanTie C910, the gem5 RISC-V O3 CPU model, and the SiFive P550. ProcReverser achieves Pass@1 and Pass@5 scores of 81.3% and 93.8%, respectively, on C910, and 83.0% and 100.0% on gem5 O3. On the SiFive P550, ProcReverser further characterizes microarchitectural properties covered by the proposed task suite. These findings highlight the potential of automated microarchitectural reverse engineering to support processor vulnerability analysis and defense evaluation.
title: ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis

summary: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.
title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents

summary: An agent-neutral research workflow that coordinates seven specialized roles to plan experiments, implement methods, verify results, and preserve reproducible evidence.
title: Shakthi-Bala/DevResearchFlow

summary: Lipophilic steroid and thyroid hormones circulate in human blood predominantly bound to high-affinity hepatic transport glycoproteins, leaving only a minute unbound fraction available for immediate cellular entry and receptor activation. According to the free hormone hypothesis, biological activity is governed primarily by this free hormone fraction rather than total circulating hormone concentrations. This structured IMRAD literature review, prepared at the Department of Biological Chemistry of Andijan State Medical Institute, examines the molecular biochemistry of the three principal specific transport proteins—thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), and corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG, or transcortin)—and analyzes how pathological states alter the ratio of free to bound hormone fractions. TBG and CBG belong to the serpin superfamily and utilize allosteric reactive center loop conformational transitions to regulate ligand release, whereas homodimeric SHBG binds testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, and estradiol with nanomolar affinity stabilized by divalent cations. Pathological conditions profoundly distort these carrier levels: hyperestrogenism and pregnancy elevate TBG and SHBG via sialylation and HNF-4α upregulation; insulin resistance, obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and polycystic ovary syndrome suppress SHBG, elevating bioavailable free androgens; and hepatic failure, nephrotic syndrome, and critical illness reduce TBG and CBG, raising free cortisol and altering total hormone diagnostics. Evaluating free hormone indices alongside carrier protein biochemistry prevents diagnostic misinterpretation and clarifies tissue-level endocrine bioavailability.
tags: thyroxine-binding globulin, sex hormone-binding globulin, transcortin, free hormone hypothesis, bioavailability, insulin resistance, polycystic ovary syndrome, hepatic dysfunction.
title: BIOCHEMISTRY OF HORMONE-BINDING PROTEINS (TBG, SHBG, TRANSCORTIN): ALTERATIONS IN THE RATIO OF FREE AND BOUND HORMONE FRACTIONS ACROSS PATHOLOGIES AND THEIR IMPACT ON BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY

summary: This dataset provides total column water vapor, vertical profiles, retrieval uncertainties, and averaging kernels derived from the mid-wave infrared (MWIR) channels of FengYun-4B/GIIRS using the Optimal Sequential Physical Retrieval System (OSPRS). FY-4B/GIIRS is the world’s first operational hyperspectral thermal infrared sounder in geostationary orbit, with the unique advantage of continuously scanning the atmosphere over East Asia on two hours basis during both daytime and nighttime. OSPRS is a full physical retrieval method based on the optimal estimation; it employs a sequential, multi-step retrieval strategy to reduce the non-linearity of the inverse problem at each step and to reduce the interference of non-target species on the primary retrieval targets (H2O, CO, and O3). The OSPRS algorithm is described in: Liang, Z., Gu, D., Li, X., Xu, Z., Cao, X., Bai, H., ... & Lau, A. K. (2025). An optimal sequential physical retrieval system for retrieving high-accuracy diurnal atmospheric gases from FY-4B/GIIRS: Theory, algorithm and evaluation. Remote Sensing of Environment, 328, 114901.  The full text is also available on the team’s webpage (http://dasagu.people.ust.hk/?page_id=108). The OSPRS water vapor products have been evaluated against ERA5 reanalysis, the TROPESS water vapor product retrieved from the polar-orbiting JPSS-1/CrIS instrument, and measurements from IGRA radiosondes and AERONET sun photometers. These evaluations demonstrate the utility of the products for characterizing spatial, temporal, and vertical variations in atmospheric water vapor and for monitoring extreme events, while identifying areas for further improvement. The detailed evaluation is provided in: Li, C., Liang, Z., Cao, X., Li, X., Xu, Z., Chan, W., ... & Gu, D. (2026). Comprehensive evaluation of atmospheric water vapor products retrieved from FY‐4B/GIIRS using the OSPRS algorithm. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 131(12), e2025JD046022. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025JD046022. The full text is also available on the team’s webpage (http://dasagu.people.ust.hk/?page_id=108). The current dataset covers four representative months: April, July, and October 2023, and January 2024. Retrieval results covering longer time series will be released upon request or following further algorithmic improvements. Cloud screening was applied during preprocessing. It's also suggested implementing post-filtering based on "Number of iterations at convergence", "RMSE of the spectral fit residuals", and the "reduced cost function." It should be noted, however, that the definition of the "reduced cost function" in the current version is a subject of debate: some literature defines it as the cost function value at convergence divided by the number of spectral channels minus the number of variables in the state vector, whereas other sources suggest dividing it simply by the number of spectral channels. The current version of the product adopts the former approach, which may result in a higher calculated value for the reduced cost function. If you have any questions regarding the OSPRS algorithm or products, please contact Zhenxing Liang (zhxliang@ust.hk); if you have questions concerning the details of the water vapor evaluation in JGR-Atmospheres, please contact Cheng Li (clieo@connect.ust.hk).
title: FengYun-4B/GIIRS OSPRS Water Vapor (H2O) Products:Columns, Profiles, Uncertainties, Averaging kernels

summary: In The Architectural Wall, I mapped how physical control systems hit an engineering ceiling across four epochs—from cast-iron lugs at the Tay Bridge (1879), to software bypass switches at Chernobyl (1986), to digital MUX bus latency at Deepwater Horizon (2010), culminating in probabilistic cross-syntax AI models "smoothing over" analog anomalies until kinetic failure occurs (Epoch IV)—and resolved it with The Minos Gate™ (a hardware-level 0V physical cutoff outside the compute loop). This sequel demonstrates what happens when that exact same failure mode scales from industrial hardware to sovereign statecraft and critical national infrastructure.
title: The Geopolitical Wall

summary: Radar image restoration is often challenged by system blur and speckle noise, which degrade target visibility and structural fidelity. In this work, we evaluate three restoration approaches—Richardson–Lucy deconvolution with total variation regularization (RL+TV), Deep Image Prior (DIP), and a new attentionenhanced framework combining DIP with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (DIP+CBAM). A point-spread function (PSF) was extracted from a measured corner reflector and used to simulate realistic degraded radar images. Experimental results show that RL+TV provides limited recovery of fine details, achieving a PSNR of 14.66 dB and SSIM of 0.4969. DIP substantially improves reconstruction quality (PSNR 19.39 dB, SSIM 0.5267), benefiting from the implicit prior of untrained networks. The proposed DIP+CBAM method further enhances performance, reaching the highest PSNR (19.54 dB) and SSIM (0.5361). These findings demonstrate that integrating attention mechanisms into DIP offers a more effective prior for radar image restoration and leads to clearer, more structurally accurate reconstructions
title: Attention-Driven Deep Image Prior for Radar Restoration with Known PSF

summary: We reassess selected neutral oxygen–gallium-vacancy configurations in GaN using archived CP2K/PBE calculations and new endpoint evaluations. Five components comprise a 72-atom host, substitutional oxygen, a gallium vacancy and separately selected two- and three-oxygen vacancy complexes, C2 and C3. Although the original static energies are reconstructable, fixed-coordinate energy-and-force evaluations using one recorded executable reveal failures of the retained force criteria for the vacancy, C2 and C3. Small total-energy changes therefore do not establish acceptable endpoints. Bounded C2/C3 optimizations followed by separate complete energy-and-force evaluations now support selected-protocol endpoints. Explicit combined review of original geometry criteria and current force/electronic evidence also admits the host and substitutional-oxygen endpoints. Direct subtraction of these four raw energies gives b3 = 1.76504 eV for the selected host-balanced C2/C3 comparison. The vacancy repair fails its first updated-geometry SCF after 300 iterations, producing no qualified new endpoint; cumulative A2/A3 results remain unaccepted. The evidence preserves a C2 interruption after its complete converged step, a C3 wavefunction overwrite resolved through its documented backup, and a corrected provenance error in an excluded one-oxygen complex. This is a traceable numerical case and a restricted association descriptor, not a new discovery of oxygen–vacancy binding. Global structural/electronic minima, calibrated numerical uncertainty, capture kinetics and an oxygen-removal process are not established.\n\nThis technical report is accompanied by supplementary evidence and a metadata-redacted analysis dataset with scripts to reconstruct core tables and figures from saved CP2K outputs. It is not a complete DFT rerun environment. External peer review has not been completed. The selected result is a limited numerical case, not a novelty claim about oxygen–vacancy binding.
title: Selected neutral oxygen gallium-vacancy association in GaN: a technical report with reconstructable data

summary: Scholarship on cultural assets typically treats legal protection as a single condition that an instrument either achieves or fails to achieve. This study evaluates that premise by analyzing a corpus of twenty-three publications against a two-axis framework: an evidentiary axis, evaluating whether transactional facts can be documented and verified, and a recognition axis, evaluating whether a forum's substantive property law treats established facts as sufficient to resolve a claim. Applying this classification, combined with a jurisdictional instantiation test and an econometric reanalysis of repeat-sales art returns, demonstrates that documentary standardization improves evidentiary consistency without reconciling divergent national recognition rules. A comparison of identical, documented provenance records under Swiss and New York law yields opposing title determinations. Furthermore, adjusting repeat-sales return indices for selection bias reduces estimated risk-adjusted performance by approximately half. These findings indicate that transaction security depends on coordinating technical verification frameworks with international choice-of-law agreements.
title: FROM INVESTMENT RISK TO INTERNATIONAL PROTECTION: A LEGAL MODEL FOR CULTURAL ASSETS

It specifies typed evidence states, an explicit transition decision procedure, provenance and policy bindings, and independently verifiable receipts. The design prevents integrity checks, structural conformance, or matching scientific invariants from being silently promoted into scientific truth, independent reproduction, or institutional authority. The term "constitutional law" denotes internal, machine-checkable governance constraints; this proposal does not create state law, legal rights, institutional authority, scientific certification, or IETF consensus. It is an individual Informational Internet-Draft intended to support interoperable, falsifiable research workflows. summary: The RISE Humanities Data Benchmark, maintained by RISE (Research and Infrastructure Support) at the University of Basel, evaluates large language models on tasks from humanities research: transcribing, interpreting and extracting structured data from historical documents such as letters, library cards, newspaper advertisements and medieval manuscripts, scored against ground truths defined by domain experts, with the cost and runtime of every request. summary: The complete computational record behind two studies of the catalytic zinc of the bacterial deacetylase LpxC: a crystallographic survey of its first coordination shell across the 75 deposited LpxC–inhibitor complexes with a resolved catalytic zinc, and a docking benchmark in which every pose is scored three ways — by heavy-atom RMSD, by the number of ligand donor atoms placed on the metal, and by the identity of those atoms. The main archive lpxc_makale2_veri_TAM.tgz contains the input coordinate files, the prepared receptors and ligands in neutral and anionic form, the docking poses from every run configuration, the grid maps and AD4Zn parameter files, the SLURM job scripts, the analysis scripts, the summary result tables and the recorded computing environment. It is unchanged from version 1. Version 2 adds the entry-level inventory of all 102 candidate Protein Data Bank records with the ground for each of the 27 exclusions, which both manuscripts cite as Supplementary Table S1, together with a self-contained script that rebuilds that inventory from the RCSB search and data APIs. README_v2_additions.md describes both files, the four selection criteria, and the precedence under which entries failing more than one criterion are counted. The contact-level coordination dataset in this deposit is the primary source for the reference geometry used in the docking study and can be consulted independently of either manuscript. Version 3 adds the GM-DockZn comparison requested in revision. The file gmdockzn_zenodo.tgz contains the scripts that prepare GM-DockZn inputs, run the docking and score its poses under the donor-identity criterion, together with the per-method comparison table (Table S4) and the comparison figure (Figure 4). GM-DockZn itself is not redistributed; it is obtained from the authors (www.qmclab.com). Of the 75 inhibitors, 60 could be parameterised; the 15 that could not (nitrile, alkyne, bromine or fused-heteroaromatic groups) are listed in Table S5. Version 4 adds two tables that support the revised crystallographic survey. TableS6_checkmymetal_validation_74_sites.csv holds the metal-site validation metrics returned by the CheckMyMetal server for 74 of the 75 structures; 7PHN could not be processed by the server. For each catalytic zinc the table gives the geometry class assigned by the server, the elemental composition of its contact list, the bond valence sum, the normalised vector sum, the angular deviation from the assigned ideal polyhedron and the vacancy, together with the coordination number counted here at 2.2, 2.5 and 2.6 Å and a flag recording whether the server's contact list matches that enumeration at each threshold. The server's list agrees with the enumeration for all 74 sites at 2.6 Å, for 71 at 2.5 Å and for 28 at 2.2 Å, which places the server's own distance criterion inside the interval the survey shows to be decisive. TableS7_aspartate_geometry_by_organism_75_structures.csv holds the per-structure breakdown of aspartate geometry by source organism for all 75 structures: organism, resolution, the two aspartate oxygen distances, whether the aspartate presents both oxygens within 2.5 Å, and the coordination number at that threshold. The three organism groups differ in the second aspartate oxygen but not in the histidine nitrogens or the first aspartate oxygen.
title: LpxC catalytic-zinc coordination: structures, docking outputs and analysis code for 75 inhibitor complexes

summary: This document proposes an experimental, evidence-bound governance profile for research workflows involving artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It specifies procedural invariants governing claims, evidence, provenance, authority, disagreement, independent replication, and research release decisions. It distinguishes observable AI value expression from computational architecture and from unverified assertions of subjective consciousness. The term "constitutional law" denotes a voluntary set of research-governance constraints, not positive law, a legally enforceable constitution, an IETF policy, or a scientific theory proved by this document. This proposal neither modifies existing Internet protocols nor establishes AI consciousness. summary: Plant genomics with a hybrid classical-quantum model Artificial intelligence and quantum computing for the digital design of plant genomes Italian patent application no. 102026000034324 , filed on 18 November 2026. Inventor, applicant and sole rights holder: Paolo Ciccolella . This invention proposes combining artificial intelligence and quantum computing to explore possible combinations of plant DNA and identify those worth investigating further. For businesses interested in plant genomics, the idea is to provide early guidance for computational design: turning a vast number of possibilities into selected, evaluated and documented digital candidates . The challenge is easy to picture. If DNA is a large instruction book, studying alternative versions of some passages means comparing many combinations. Three alternatives for each of twenty regions already produce more than three billion possibilities . The method tackles this complexity by dividing the work between a classical computer, two AI models and a quantum search component. HOW THE HYBRID MODEL WORKS The idea is to choose one alternative for each DNA region being studied , put the choices together and evaluate the resulting combination. Everything happens on a computer. The process follows six steps . •     Prepare the data. The computer starts with a digital version of the plant’s DNA, called a reference genome . It identifies the regions to study and organises the available alternative sequences for each one, recording where they come from. •     Give each alternative an initial score. The first AI model examines each alternative separately. Having learned from other cases, it can provide guidance before any complete combination in the new case has been evaluated . The computer also measures similarity between the ends of sequences that will be placed next to one another. These scores and measurements define the selection problem. [B12] •     Search for combinations. The quantum component receives this problem expressed in numbers. It uses QAOA , an algorithm whose role is to propose combinations while seeking to favour those with better scores. Qubits represent the possible choices ; the DNA sequences remain on the classical computer, which sets and updates the algorithm’s parameters. [B11] •     Evaluate the whole combination. The computer checks that each combination selects exactly one alternative per region and assembles valid choices into a digital candidate. The second AI model evaluates the complete candidate , including relationships between its parts that the first AI model could not observe when examining them separately. •     Guide the next search. The system compares the overall evaluation with the score predicted at the start and uses the difference to update the search . When only a few results are available, it limits the correction’s influence to avoid relying too heavily on sparse information. •     Return verifiable proposals. For each selected candidate, the system retains the chosen sequences, their provenance and the evaluations performed. It also records a digital fingerprint , a code used to check the content. Researchers can reconstruct the proposal and understand how it was selected. If necessary data are missing, the system flags this. A concrete example: the patent uses the digital reference for Micro-Tom tomato and considers three regions, each with three alternatives created for the test. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible combinations. The search uses a nine-qubit quantum circuit simulated on a classical computer . This tests the computational method without producing plants. [B14] INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS The patent describes the production of verifiable digital representations of candidate genomes. Its industrial role lies in designing and selecting hypotheses

summary: Phishing detectors are often judged by random-split accuracy on public benchmarks, against weak baselines or none. Using the Hannousse and Yahiouche dataset (11,430 URLs, 87 features), we examine how much machine learning (ML) improves on simple rule-based baselines, how much of that accuracy survives when related URLs are kept apart, and which feature groups carry it. We compare a six-rule URL heuristic, a domain blacklist, a one-split decision stump and shallow decision trees with Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, using repeated 5-fold cross-validation (15 folds) with random folds and with class-balanced folds grouped by registered domain. XGBoost on all features reached 97.08 ± 0.32% accuracy with random folds and 95.17 ± 1.06% with domain-grouped folds, against 64.3% for the rule heuristic and 78.1% for the blacklist (random folds only; zero recall by construction in grouped folds). The strongest simple baseline, a one-split stump on the external feature google_index, reached 86.5%. Domain grouping lowered tree-model accuracy by 1.6 to 1.9 points with all features and by 3.9 to 4.2 points with URL-only features, and reduced XGBoost's true-positive rate at 1% false positives from 92.7% to 83.1%. External-service features were the most informative group, and URL-only XGBoost (87.5% on grouped folds) was not significantly better than the stump. A dataset audit shows sampling artifacts. ML clearly helps, but part of the apparent gain reflects baseline choice, dataset sampling and external lookups
title: Machine Learning versus Simple Rule-Based Baselines for Phishing Website Detection: Effects of Domain-Grouped Evaluation and Feature Sources

summary: This dataset contains the experimental data and Data Dictionary supporting the manuscript titled "Interactive Effects of  Warning Type and Pre-drive Trust on Takeover Performance in Conditionally Automated Driving: An Information Processing Perspective". The data were generated from a 2×2 within-subjects driving simulator experiment investigating the effects of warning type (single-stage vs. two-stage) and pre-drive trust (low vs. high) on takeover performance, eye-tracking measures, and subjective evaluations in conditionally automated driving. The dataset is structured within a single multi-sheet .xlsx file, comprising data from 24 valid participants. It explicitly focuses on the 288 Type C critical takeover events extracted for the core statistical analyses (24 participants × 4 blocks × 3 events per block). The workbook is organized into five specific sheets: 1. Data_Dictionary: Comprehensive operational definitions, value labels, and units for all variables. 2. Main_Dataset: The consolidated event-level data matrix encompassing Demographics, Takeover Performance (Takeover Success, TRT, Min TTC), and phase-divided Eye-tracking Measures (TTFF_Post, PFD_Baseline, PFD_Pre, PFD_Post, Delta_PD_Pre, Delta_PD_Post). 3-5. Pre_Trust_Score, Post_Trust_Score, and Workload_TLX: Three detailed sheets containing the full item-level data and sub-dimensional scores for the subjective evaluations. Access Note: To ensure participant privacy and adhere to the ethical guidelines approved by the Ethics Committee of Beihang University, the raw datasets containing individual eye-tracking and human factors data are under restricted access. De-identified data are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request strictly for academic verification or replication purposes.
title: Dataset for: Interactive Effects of Warning Type and Pre-Drive Trust on Takeover Performance in Conditionally Automated Driving: An Information Processing Perspective

summary: Changed Switched from openalexR to the openalexPro ecosystem ( openalexPro , openalexSnowball ). The snowball search is now done with openalexSnowball::pro_snowball() and stored as Parquet in data/snowball/ (replaces data/snowball.rds and data/snowball_supplemented.rds ). DOIs are passed directly to the snowball search; the conversion to OpenAlex ids with oa_fetch() is not needed anymore. The supplemented citation network uses the extended edges returned by the snowball search instead of being computed from referenced_works . Plotting code is in two functions used for both networks. Static PNG figures are saved at 300 instead of 600 dpi. Re-ran the snowball search (2026-11-18); results and figures updated. R packages are referred to as links of the form {package} ; external links open in a new tab. Author affiliation updated to SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics. Section "Supplementing the citation network" renamed to "The extended citation network"; unfinished draft section at the end removed. CI caches the installed R packages. Added Sections on the OpenAlex API key, the structure of the results (node roles, edge types, provenance) and the offline snowball search against an OpenAlex snapshot. Reproducibility as point 7 in "Things to keep in mind". Table with the provenance of the snowball search (date, key papers, package versions) and a note on citing the packages. The interactive graphs are published to GitHub Pages, so the "Open in new window" links work. Download links for the PDF and PNG versions of the static network graphs (also published to GitHub Pages). Saving as SVG is shown but commented out, as the files are very large. The OpenAlex API key can be provided to CI as the repository secret OPENALEX_API_KEY . Example of a snowball search using OpenAlex ids instead of DOIs. Fixed Node size in the interactive graphs used a hard-coded year (2024), giving negative or infinite sizes for works published later. Point 2 in "Things to keep in mind": works neither cited by nor citing the key papers are missing.

summary: For vectors a, b ∈ R n, b ̸= 0, we study a matrix-valued quotient that maps b to a and a compatible bilinear matrix-valued product. The quotient is E(a, b) = ∥b∥ −2 [(a · b)I + abT − baT]; the associated product is M(a, b) = ∥b∥ 2E(a, b). We establish transport and covariance identities, derive a unique vector inverse from the matrix identity M(a, x) = I, and characterize the product by orthogonal equivariance, transport, and either a scalar symmetric-part normalization or a diagonal normalization. A constrained Frobenius-norm principle characterizes the quotient. Its spectral decomposition gives exact criteria for invertibility and shows why matrix reciprocity fails in dimensions greater than two. The construction is placed in the context of complex multiplication and exterior and Clifford algebra, without claiming historical priority for its constituent formulas.
tags: matrix-valued quotient; bilinear map; orthogonal equivariance; skew-symmetric operator; isotropic tensor; exterior algebra
title: A Matrix-Valued Quotient and a Compatible Bilinear Product on Euclidean Vector Spaces

summary: ABSTRACT Encrustation and eventual stone formation over the tip of the catheter may be the cause of a retained Suprapubic Foley catheter. Though this is not unusual in developing countries like ours but more worrisome is the ignorance feigned by the patients with regards to the instructions to attend the clinic regularly to have their catheter s changed while awaiting definitive surgical intervention often delayed due to financial constraints. This article seeks to proffer recommendations to urologists who manage patients on long-term suprapubic catheterisation with a view to shortening its duration and possibly enhance regular change of the catheter with a view at speedy surgical intervention. Case Report: The patient, Mr. DA, a 34-year-old male referred to our facility as a case of an incomplete post-inflammatory urethral stricture and had been on suprapubic catheter for more than a year despite the availability of a sponsor for his investigations and surgical intervention. He presented with retained and leaking suprapubic three-way catheter following a severance of the irrigation, balloon channels and per urethral leakage of offensive urine and scrotal excoriation. The patient denied any information as regards the need for regular change of the catheter or the need for follow-up with regards to investigations to plan the definitive management of the underlying condition. Patient had an emergency suprapubic cystostomy which revealed a small capacity bladder, infected, foul-smelling urine and stone adherent to the tip of the retained suprapubic catheter. Conclusion: Encrustation of suprapubic catheters and the consequent failure of the balloon to deflate remains the commonest cause of retained suprapubic catheter therefore the need to educate patients on catheter hygiene and a mandatory suprapubic catheter change.
title: A Retained Suprapubic Foley Catheter: Who Takes the Blame for this? – A Case Report and Review of Literature

summary: Astronomy education in secondary schools faces limitations imposed by the prioritization of traditional content and the reduction of Physics course loads, compromising its formative potential. This textbook is the result of the development and classroom implementation of an educational resource aimed at the structured integration of Astronomy, with a focus on both science olympiad preparation and students’ engagement with contemporary Astrophysics research through cooperative learning. In this method, students assume specific roles within small groups, solve topic-specific problems individually, share their understanding with peers, and collaboratively tackle complex challenges. Across its multi-year implementation in a public school, this textbook and pedagogical approach led to significant outcomes, including a substantial increase in Brazilian Astronomy and Astronautics Olympiad (OBA) medalists, yielding the school’s first gold medals and qualifying multiple students for international selection stages.
title: Iniciação à Astronomia: Para disciplinas eletivas, olimpíadas e mentes curiosas

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Forty-nine entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature, among them: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7; a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients; a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset; a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten; a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998); a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation; a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight; a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. Light through a Jerlov water type. The package: computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963); converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors; gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m, and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers; integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth; gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two; and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent; ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum; carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models; converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient. Measurements it carries. Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type, against which the depth profile is checked; Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille; the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures; Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters; five published spectra of the absorption of pure water, Pope & Fry (1997), Smith & Baker (1981), Mason, Cone & Fry (2016), Lee et al. (2015) and Morel et al. (2007), for the caller to choose from; the eight stations of the clearest ocean water measured, Morel et al. (2007); the measured reflectance of ten materials found in and around water, from the USGS Spectral Library Version 7, for reference images of how they look through each water type. Without a water type. It gives: Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001, and the earlier edition of Morel 1988), or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013); the attenuation of the visible and of the whole shortwave from the surface to a depth, and the depth where a given fraction of the visible light is left, the euphotic depth among them, from the absorption and backscattering coefficients at 490 nm and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2007); from chlorophyll, the absorption by phytoplankton (Bricaud et al. 1995) and
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: This dataset and code release supports the manuscript “What evidence resolves a renewable-energy choice? A request-conditioned framework and a held-out regional replay”, with the analysis files frozen on 18 November 2026. The archive implements a request-conditioned evidence-to-decision layer built on real amply soft sets (RASS). Request and native-model dependencies generate active evidence obligations, which govern the admissible numerical domain, policy-relative authorization, stopping and acquisition of the next evidence packet. The files include frozen normalized inputs and executable code for the U.S. wind–photovoltaic held-out replay, a retrospective temporal extension, target-supported precision checks, same-value evidence-role controls, the Türkiye cost–emissions request, and a retrospective Australian four-alternative source-table operation check. These analyses have different evaluation roles; the temporal repeats and Australian development check are not independent blinded replications. The reproducibility archive includes reproduction commands, registered protocols, source provenance and hashes, decision traces, result summaries, and an embedded SHA-256 manifest. Original derived data and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0, and original code is licensed under MIT. Third-party materials retain their source-specific terms and attributions, as documented in LICENSE.md. Version 2.0 updates the deposit from the earlier national-ranking-portability release to the request-conditioned decision layer and its current reproducibility files. Previous record versions remain available.
title: Reproducibility data and code for "What evidence resolves a renewable-energy choice? A request-conditioned framework and a held-out regional replay"

summary: This repository provides the computational data, source code, trained models, validation partitions, predictions, and reproducibility materials supporting a study on leakage-aware ensemble learning and inverse molecular screening of protic organic salts for phase-change thermal energy storage.   The study evaluates 69 experimentally characterized salts and a fixed library of 182 cation–anion combinations. The archive includes comparisons of regression and ensemble methods, molecular descriptors, ionic-liquid transfer representations, conditional denoising experiments, uncertainty analyses, and inverse screening at target melting temperatures of 120, 150, 180, and 210 °C.   The repository contains reproducible computational workflows, model checkpoints, individual predictions, candidate rankings, scientific figures, and documentation. Experimental measurements are attributed to their original sources. The prioritized candidates have not undergone new experimental validation.   Reproduction instructions, software dependencies, dataset provenance, and reuse conditions are provided in the accompanying README and documentation files.
title: Leakage-aware ensemble learning and inverse screening of protic organic salts for phase-change thermal storage: reproducibility archive

It contains the Qualtrics export ( collected-data-excel-format.xlsx ), the survey instrument ( questionnaire.pdf ), and four PDFs with the full pattern descriptions.
