summary: ABSTRACT Background: Haemorrhage is a common complication of transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), contributing to impaired endoscopic visibility, prolonged operative time, increased irrigation requirements, blood transfusion and postoperative morbidity. Tranexamic acid (TXA), an antifibrinolytic agent, has demonstrated efficacy in reducing blood loss in several operative specialties, but evidence regarding its routine use during TURP remains inconsistent. Objective: To evaluate the effect of intravenous tranexamic acid on perioperative blood loss and related outcomes during monopolar TURP. Methods: This prospective randomized double-blind controlled trial was conducted at University of Benin Teaching Hospital, Nigeria, between August 2022 and August 2023. Sixty men with symptomatic BPH scheduled for TURP were randomized equally to receive either intravenous TXA (1 g at induction followed by two additional 1 g doses at 8-hour intervals) or placebo. The primary outcome was peri-operative blood loss assessed by postoperative haemoglobin reduction and haemoglobin loss per gram of resected prostate tissue. Secondary outcomes included blood transfusion, clot retention, irrigation fluid volume, duration of postoperative irrigation and adverse events. Results: Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were comparable between both groups. Mean postoperative haemoglobin loss, haemoglobin loss per gram resected tissue were consistently lower in the TXA group but differences were not statistically significant at 1 hour, 24 hours or 72 hours after surgery (all P > 0.05). Blood transfusion was required in 13.3% of control group compared with 3.3% TXA group; clot retention occurred in 20.0% and 6.7%, respectively; neither difference reached statistical significance. Patients receiving TXA required significantly lower intra-operative irrigation volumes (34.3 ± 5.2 L vs 44.9 ± 2.3 L; P < 0.001), lower postoperative irrigation volumes (15.2 ± 6.0 L vs 22.6 ± 2.6 L; P < 0.001) and shorter postoperative irrigation duration (29.4 ± 5.5 hours vs 36.1 ± 8.8 hours; P < 0.001). No adverse drug-related events were observed. Conclusion: Intravenous TXA significantly reduced peri-operative irrigation requirements and postoperative irrigation duration during TURP. Although reductions in haemoglobin loss, blood transusion and clot retention were observed, differences were not statistically significant. Larger adequately powered randomized trials are required to determine whether TXA should be recommended routinely during TURP.
title: Intravenous Tranexamic Acid During Transurethral Resection of the Prostate for Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: A Prospective Randomized Double-Blind Controlled Trial

summary: This record contains the data, code and SCAPS-1D device files for the manuscript "Diagnosing degradation mechanisms in lead-free RbSn0.5Ge0.5I3 perovskite solar cells from temperature- and light-dependent open-circuit voltage with interpretable machine learning" by Nabanita Sarker and Hafiz Imtiaz (Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology), submitted to RSC Advances. The study uses 42,238 SCAPS-1D simulations of an FTO/TiO2/RbSn0.5Ge0.5I3/CuI/Au solar cell. It trains a multi-label classifier that identifies six modeled degradation mechanisms from temperature- and light-dependent open-circuit-voltage data, and it compares surrogate models trained on factorial grids and on Latin hypercube designs. The Electronic Supplementary Information (ESI) repeats the sampling analysis for four further absorbers, using 29,584 additional simulations. Contents: data/: all datasets and result tables (CSV/JSON) and trained models (.joblib). scaps_run_ledger.csv lists every simulation batch and its run count. code/: the Python scripts that generate every dataset, figure and number in the manuscript. scaps_def/: SCAPS-1D device definition files, including the baseline device (RbSnGeI3_CuI_IF.def) and the four ESI absorbers. digitized/: values digitized from published measurement figures, used in the measured-device section. The sources are cited in the manuscript. Requirements: SCAPS-1D 3.3.x (free from ELIS, Ghent University) and Python 3.10+ with numpy, pandas, scikit-learn, xgboost, shap, scipy, matplotlib and joblib. See README.md for setup.
title: Data and code: interpretable machine learning diagnosis of degradation mechanisms in RbSn0.5Ge0.5I3 perovskite solar cells

summary: Abstract Background: Benign ureteric strictures represent a clinically significant cause of upper urinary tract obstruction, frequently arising from endourological procedures such as ureteroscopy and retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS). While endoscopic management remains the initial approach for short, non-ischemic strictures, its efficacy is limited in fibrotic, ischemic, or long-segment disease. Buccal mucosal graft (BMG) ureteroplasty has emerged as a tissue-sparing reconstructive alternative that maintains ureteral continuity while augmenting luminal diameter. Methods: We report a retrospective case series of five consecutive patients who underwent laparoscopic ventral onlay BMG ureteroplasty for benign ureteric strictures at a tertiary care center between January 2024 and December 2025. Preoperative evaluation included contrast-enhanced CT urography and retrograde pyelography. Data on operative parameters, perioperative course, donor site morbidity, and follow-up were collected. Surgical success was defined as symptomatic improvement with radiological evidence of unobstructed drainage and stable renal function (eGFR decline <25% from baseline). Results: Five patients (3 female, 2 male) with a mean age of 44.6 years (range 39–52) and mean BMI of 30.8 kg/m² underwent the procedure. The primary etiology was iatrogenic injury following stone management (4/5; 80%); one patient had IgG4-related disease. Mean stricture length was 3.2 cm (range 2.5–4.0 cm). Mean operative time was 168 minutes (range 155–180 min) with a mean blood loss of 80 ml (range 60–100 ml). No intraoperative complications or conversion to open surgery occurred. Minor donor-site oral discomfort was noted in two patients (40%), resolving within one week without intervention. At a median follow-up of 19 months (range 18–24 months), all five patients demonstrated complete symptom resolution, radiological absence of obstruction, and stable renal function, yielding an overall success rate of 100%.
title: Outcomes of Laparoscopic Ventral Onlay Buccal Mucosal Graft Ureteroplasty for Complex Benign Mid and Proximal Ureteric Strictures: A Single-Center Case Series

summary: A 2x2 Tiny Tapeout analog tile (SKY26c, sky130A) implementing a chain of two EML cells, each computing exp(u) - ln(v) in current mode using translinear NPN loops, together with the simulation code and SPICE decks behind the paper. Snapshot of the repository as used for revision 1 of "Composability rather than computation sets the cost of an analog EML hardware fabric" (npj Unconventional Computing, in revision; submitted version at arXiv:2609.17903). The repository holds the SkyWater 130 nm 2x2 tile layout of a analog two-cell EML chain submitted to a Tiny Tapeout shuttle (SKY26c, sky130A), the SPICE characterization and extraction decks, the differentiable network model and benchmark harness, the energy analysis, and the scripts that draw the paper's figures (paper/figures/). The design implements a chain of EML cells, each computing exp(u) - ln(v) in current mode using translinear NPN loops. Relative to the submitted version this release adds the wake-up and gating decks with waveforms, the exact (400-digit) grammar enumerator, the training-density check on sin(2πx₁x₂), and the scripts for Figs. 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 of the revised paper. All current results are from circuit simulation of the layout or from the network model that uses its parameters.
title: tt-eml-fabric: code and simulation decks behind "Composability rather than computation sets the cost of an analog EML hardware fabric"

summary: This dataset records the research data and artificial intelligence (AI) policies of 25 paleontology journals, selected as the top 25 by number of papers in the Paleontology category of the Open Observatory of Indexed Research (OOIR) rankings (Crossref data, October 2022 to October 2026). For each journal, it records publisher, society affiliation, open access model, and codes for eight data policy variables (data availability statements, public availability, repository deposition, reviewer access, phylogenetic matrices, character descriptions, data provenance, and data peer review) and nine AI policy variables (disclosure requirements, location, tool reporting, research use, verification responsibility, oversight reporting, and research images). Journal pages were captured on 6 October 2026, two journal pages were recaptured on 5 November 2026, and publisher AI policies were captured on 5 November 2026. This dataset supports Long-Fox and Young, “AI risks exacerbating paleontology’s reproducibility problem,” submitted to Paleobiology. See README for variable definitions and coding.
title: Data and AI policies of 25 paleontology journals: audit dataset

summary: Woody Crown Hydraulic Network (WCHN): corrected empirical crown networks, recalculated ecological analyses, and reproducible principal component analyses This updated dataset version (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24353093) contains 99 field woody crown hydraulic networks (WCHNs): 75 from the Cerrado and 24 from the Caatinga, including the documented reconstruction and correction of 20 existing Cerrado networks. The original source workbooks, six recalculated ecological comparison tables, corrected-topology audit workbook, and practical crown-reconstruction toolkit are preserved. The mathematical definitions, algebraic relationships, and derivations are maintained in a separate, independently citable Zenodo record (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24181915). New in this version Reduced principal component analyses (PCAs) of five properties (NAV, revised VUL, LAT, BAS, and PTP) now incorporate the 20 corrected Cerrado WCHNs. The first two principal components explain 89.8% of variance in the 74 complete Cerrado WCHNs and 91.1% in the 24 Caatinga WCHNs. Network-size-adjusted analyses use ordinary least-squares regressions of ln(property) on ln(total node count, ΣNO), followed by correlation-matrix PCAs of standardized residuals. The first two adjusted components account for 97.5% of residual standardized variance in Cerrado and 98.9% in Caatinga. Six pairwise partial correlations among NAV, BAS, PTP, and VUL are reported for each biome, together with Holm-adjusted significance tests. The deposit includes two explicit input CSV files, updated Excel workbooks, PCA figures, machine-readable JSON results, a reproducible Python analysis script, technical documentation, and a changelog. These materials enable independent reproduction and examination of the recalculated results. Data provenance and interpretive limitations The original Caatinga observations and the 55 Cerrado networks not redigitized in the correction exercise retain their previously stored numerical precision. One Cerrado WCHN with undefined BAS is excluded from the main PCA but remains documented in the input dataset and sensitivity analysis. The results characterize mathematical and topological relationships among WCHN properties. They do not independently demonstrate causal effects of crown topology on hydraulic safety or attainable tree height. Citation and versioning For analyses and files introduced in this update, cite the version-specific DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24353093 . The concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22849807 identifies the complete version history of this dataset. The preceding published version is available at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24197048 .
title: Recalculated woody crown hydraulic network properties and reduced principal component analyses of Caatinga and Cerrado trees

summary: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.
title: Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks

summary: A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.
title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D

summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.
title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI

summary: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.
title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels

summary: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.
title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving

summary: This deposit accompanies the article "Not Flawless, but Good Enough: Vision-Language Models and the Invisible Errors of Machine Transcription" (Wouter Haverals and Andrew Janco, Computational Humanities Research 2027). It holds what ten transcription systems returned for the 10,373 line images of the IAM handwriting database, the scored records behind Table 1 of the article, and the code that builds the table from them. The ten systems are Tesseract, Kraken with the McCATMuS model, PyLaia with and without a language model, GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, Qwen3-VL and Chandra. The records were scored with Misnomer , our framework for classifying the differences between a transcription and a verified reference. Contents : - README.md : what each file is, how the columns of Table 1 are defined, and how to rebuild the table - table1.csv : Table 1 as printed, unrounded, with 95 percent intervals and the counts behind each cell - table1_sensitivity.csv : the same rates under the other choices that the article quotes in its footnotes and its section on limitations - left_out_pairs.json : the 595 word pairs left out of the counts because five or more systems agree against the reference - prompts.md and systems.md: the instruction each system received, and the model, software, settings and date of each run - data_model_outputs.zip : the output of each system for every line, including the second pass of GPT-5 - data_scored.zip : the scored records, the run manifests, and a list of all substitutions - code.zip : the script that builds Table 1, the scripts that ran the systems, and the source of Misnomer at the tag table1-camera-ready - checks.zip : three smaller checks quoted in the article -  fig1_vinegar_chr_Haverals_Janco.pdf :Figure 1 - second_auditor.txt : the result of repeating the analysis with a second auditor The IAM line images are not included. They are available as Teklia/IAM-line on Hugging Face, and a line number in this deposit is a row index in that distribution. The reference transcriptions of the lines are included in the output files; the terms of the IAM database apply to them. Version 2.0.0 replaces version 1.0.0, the anonymous deposit made for review in August 2026.

summary: Aggregate result tables underlying version 2 of the technical report Constructing newcomer cohorts from Wikimedia logs. Two archives and a README: twelve CSV files covering accounts registered in the Polish, Czech, Hungarian and Danish Wikipedias during calendar year 2024, and ten CSV files for the Catalan Wikipedia, added in November 2026 as a contrast case under the same queries and design and not pooled with the four. All accounts are observed for six months from each account’s own registration. What is new in version 2. Version 1 counted only edits that remain visible in the revision table. Contributions to pages that were later deleted move to archive and were not counted. These tables count both. Between 261 and 1,095 accounts per edition that version 1 recorded as never having edited had in fact edited, and all their edits had been deleted. Deletion is reported here as a second measured channel alongside reverting. Contents. Cohort states; the classification of each account counting live revisions only against counting live and archived revisions; the distribution of edit counts and the risk of stopping at each count; the fall from one edit to two under three cohort definitions; raw contingency counts for first-edit outcome against abandonment, with and without the observation window; odds ratios with confidence intervals, p values, pooled estimates and a heterogeneity test; the share of single-edit abandonment occurring without friction; a version 1 against version 2 comparison; and an index of the thirty-six Quarry executions behind both versions, with permanent links. The Catalan files follow the same structure, without the pooled estimates, the heterogeneity test or the version comparison, and with their own index of seven executions. Warnings. Deletion is not always friction from the community. Some deleted pages are spam or self-promotion, and some are deleted at the author’s own request; the archive does not record which, so these figures are an upper bound on deletion as rejection. Revert tag identifiers are assigned per wiki and cannot be carried between editions. No individual-level data are included. Every file holds counts or statistics aggregated over accounts. Extracted from the public Wikimedia database replicas via Quarry. Column descriptions and provenance are in the README. The version 1 tables remain available and unchanged at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23141235 .
title: Newcomer cohorts in four Wikipedia language editions. Aggregate dataset (version 2)

summary: PhageLysClass v1.0 — Evidence-Aware Machine Learning for Phage Lytic Enzyme Classification PhageLysClass is an evidence-aware machine learning framework for the identification and functional classification of bacteriophage-associated lytic proteins from amino acid sequences. It integrates curated biological evidence, sequence redundancy control, homology-aware data partitioning, numerical protein representations, and supervised and positive–unlabeled (PU) learning to support reproducible model development and systematic evaluation. The framework addresses two complementary prediction problems: distinguishing putative phage lytic enzymes from a defined non-lytic protein background and assigning lytic candidates to three functional categories: endolysins, depolymerases, and virion-associated lytic enzymes (VALs). Dataset and scientific contents This Zenodo release provides the frozen research datasets, computational results, and trained models supporting the PhageLysClass study, including: Biological evidence and classification tasks: curated PhageLysData-derived records, UniProtKB phage-protein backgrounds, evidence-state annotations, and datasets distinguishing known positives (P), candidate negatives (N), and unlabeled sequences (U). Redundancy and homology-aware partitions: nonredundant sequence collections and 144 factorial task–partition configurations spanning four redundancy regimes (R90–R30) and four homology-aware splitting regimes (S90–S30), together with training, validation, and test assignments. Numerical protein representations: Roxy physicochemical descriptors, sparse one-hot encodings, and pretrained ESM2-T6 and ESM2-T30 protein language model embeddings, with associated sequence identifiers and metadata. Predictive benchmarking: aggregated evaluation results and individual held-out predictions from 2,240 supervised and 768 positive–unlabeled experimental configurations, including model-selection metadata, diagnostic scores, and comparative analyses of representations, algorithms, and experimental regimes. Pretrained predictive models: the frozen PhageLysClass v1 model bundle comprising five predictive components and ten fitted estimators, supporting hierarchical lytic-enzyme recognition and subtype classification. External sequence applications: predictions and supporting physicochemical and representation-space analyses for PhageLysData prediction-extension proteins, ZymCTRL-generated sequences, and structurally ambiguous phage proteins. Exploratory characterization: machine-readable results describing sequence composition, physicochemical properties, representation geometry, and relationships among the biological evidence-defined populations. Reproducibility and reuse The release preserves the original computational outputs, experimental assignments, numerical representations, prediction scores, and model metadata to facilitate independent analysis, methodological comparisons, and downstream research. PhageLysClass explicitly distinguishes experimentally supported biological annotations from candidate negative and unlabeled examples. In particular, PU-learning results are evaluated against observed labels and must not be interpreted as performance estimates against experimentally verified negative proteins. The pretrained classifiers and external sequence applications provide computational functional predictions, not experimental confirmation of enzymatic activity or biological efficacy. The associated PhageLysClass GitHub repository contains the source code, computational workflows, documentation, and FASTA-based inference interface. This Zenodo record serves as the complementary archive of research data, benchmark outputs, and trained model artifacts. These resources provide a reusable foundation for studying bacteriophage lytic protein diversity and developing evidence-aware protein function prediction methods.
title: PhageLysClass: Evidence-aware classification of phage lytic proteins using protein language models

summary: Replication package for a study of whether the adoption of autonomous coding agents spreads through open-source collaboration networks. The package rebuilds every number, table and figure in the paper from two public sources: the AIDev dataset of agent-authored pull requests (Hugging Face, hao-li/AIDev) and GH Archive (Google BigQuery public dataset). Neither source is redistributed here. Contents: the BigQuery query used to extract weekly developer-repository activity; Python scripts for adoption-event extraction, dynamic co-activity network construction, person-week panel building, discrete-time hazard models, five identification tests (within-week comparison, propensity matching, timing permutation, future-tie placebos, and exposure split by agent), a calibrated agent-based seeding simulation, and figure generation; and the resulting tables as CSV and JSON. Study scope: 282,626 developers across 17,353 repositories over 30 weeks of 2025, with 2,250 first-adoption events. Requires Python 3.10+ with pandas, pyarrow, numpy, scipy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, igraph, matplotlib and pillow, plus a Google Cloud project with BigQuery access. See README.md for the run order. Version 2 (November 2026) — peer-review revision.   Adds revision_2026/, containing the diagnostics produced in response to peer review: per-cell event counts and Firth penalized estimates for the cause-specific hazards, Benjamini-Hochberg q-values, propensity-matching balance and common-support diagnostics, a re-matching cluster bootstrap, the reconciliation of the no-Codex robustness specification, a sensitivity analysis restricting the outcome to the sampled repositories, and the scripts that audit every reported number against its source.   Also adds requirements-pinned.txt and documents a reproducibility issue: the propensity model in 05_identification.py inherits scikit-learn's default L2 penalty, so the matched rate ratio is not bit-reproducible across library versions. A current environment gives rho = 1.48 rather than the published 1.38, and the ratio ranges from 1.345 to 1.482 across propensity specifications and calipers. All variants exceed 1 and lie well below the within-week ratio of 1.81, so no conclusion in the paper changes. See revision_2026/README.md.   No files from version 1 were removed or altered except README.md.

summary: In this paper, we establish the structural verifications for the symbolic navigation associated with the Tribonacci substitution via its projection onto the complex internal space and the corresponding Rauzy subtiles. We formulate the directed graph of geometric transitions, its $5$-adic encoding in $\mathbb{Z}_{5}$, and the geometric projection of infinite paths. Finally, we prove general compatibility criteria for families of inverse branches and deduce the exact disjointness condition that guarantees the existence and uniqueness of a global geometric transformation on the union of the subtiles.
title: Structural Verifications for Symbolic Navigation in the Tribonacci System

summary: Contemporary methodologies exist for assessing the nationwide impacts of geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), such as the Coupled Space Weather Impact Model (C-SWIM), which links power grid vulnerability with economic losses. Yet regional mitigation requires adapting the national model to the local transmission network so operators and planners can identify substations at risk and evaluate economic and population consequences and protective actions. We present the first adaptation of C-SWIM to Virginia, modeling the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnection, which includes Dominion Energy Virginia and Appalachian Power. Its extra high voltage network was assessed under the May 2024 Gannon, October 2003 Halloween, and March 2015 St. Patrick's Day storms in addition to nine return period scenarios derived from statistical fits to 92 historical events. Using the Leontief consumption and production input-output model, we estimated daily losses of USD 145.5M for a 100-year storm and USD 230.6M for a 250-year storm, with 339,000-535,000 people and up to 12,000 businesses at risk of power outage. The Ghosh input-output model was used to evaluate three island selection algorithms for protective islanding, which temporarily disconnects parts of the grid to reduce transformer damage. Only one algorithm yielded benefits exceeding costs across all twelve scenarios, with avoided losses up to USD 9.69M per day and a cost of USD 0.204M per intervention. However, these islanding benefits assume disconnection for 6 hours and transformer replacement after 365 days. Moreover, the analysis uses national economic relationships and models only transformer thermal failure, excluding voltage collapse, cascading failures, and restoration. Transmission operators and state energy policymakers can use this statewide assessment to prioritize regional monitoring and appraise protective islanding.
title: A State-Level Assessment of Space Weather Impact on the Virginia Power Grid: From Vulnerability to Mitigation Strategies

summary: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.
title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models

summary: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per snapshot. JITAtlas further identifies 15 new bugs across five failure classes, each with a reproducible proof of concept.
title: JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime and Protection Obligations in Compiler Rewrites

summary: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.
title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII

summary: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.
title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics

summary: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models

summary: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.
title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution

summary: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.
title: ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation

summary: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.
title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old

summary: Solid-state synthesis still relies on heuristics to choose reaction temperatures. The most widely used, Tammann's rule, places reaction onset at two-thirds of the lowest precursor melting point, but has never been systematically tested. Using an automated laboratory, we heated 1,035 pairwise combinations of 46 common precursors at their Tammann temperatures and identified the products by x-ray diffraction. Only 25% of pairs formed products containing both precursors. Combining these outcomes with text-mined literature syntheses, we trained log-normal accelerated failure time models that treat each fixed-temperature experiment as a bound on the unknown onset temperature. On 26 reactions with onset temperatures measured by in situ x-ray diffraction, a three-descriptor model reduced the mean absolute error from 131°C (Tammann's rule) to 88°C; adding 29 further physicochemical descriptors did not improve the model. Reaction onset can therefore be predicted from routine pass/fail synthesis outcomes, and predictions will improve as such data accumulates.
title: Predicting solid-state reaction onset temperatures from high-throughput pairwise synthesis

summary: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.
title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem

summary: STARLI | F131–F140 / 300 旗艦13 裂變 · 第二卷 · 人工智慧引導的微/奈米系統、採樣和驗證 作者:33 | 非臨床研究設計工作版 v1.1 / Gate 註 v1.2 | Zenodo 十卷本英文概述 title: STARLI | F131–F140 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · AI-Guided Micro/Nanosystems, Sampling and Validation Author: 33 | Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.1 / Gate Annotation v1.2 | English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview These ten STARLI flagship monographs form an AI, nanosystems and microfluidic research-design collection in the second volume of the Flagship 13 Fission atlas. The studies connect adaptive sampling, counterfactual inference, autonomous calibration, hybrid physical-learning models, failure prediction, interpretable quantum sensing, closed-loop latency, multi-agent coordination, external digital-twin validation and biological signal drift. Each volume defines a prospective measurement target and competing explanation. No result is claimed to be experimentally demonstrated. The collection contains ten separately authored 777-page English working editions: 300 prospective mathematical plates, 820 chapter openers, 4,100 separately paginated study positions, 2,000 Research Gates with six annotation fields per Gate, and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. These counts describe the publication structure, not validated scientific novelty. A companion publication ZIP includes the ten original PDFs and ten per-book Zenodo introductions. The Ten Research Directions F131 AI-Driven Microfluidic Sampling Strategy Optimization At The Limit — Examines recoverable analyte as a fraction of input under fixed sampling resources. Expert tuning with equal trials is the comparator; hidden human intervention is the rival. Blind recovery audits and out-of-distribution refusal test whether AI planning adds genuine value. F132 Nano-Quantum System Counterfactual Inference At The Limit — Tests held-out, intervention-specific counterfactual prediction error while retaining constraint-violation safeguards. Frozen open-loop policies anchor comparison; training-test leakage and nonreplayable observation-to-action chains can invalidate apparent autonomy. F133 AI-Driven Microrobotic Autonomous Calibration At The Limit — Uses blind-standard calibration bias after autonomous correction as a physical measurement target. Preregistered experimental design is the baseline. Extra experimental trials and any action outside the authority envelope defeat a claimed improvement. F134 Microscale Physical Model and Neural Network Coupling At The Limit — Challenges coupled learning and physical models against independently measured conservation residuals under withheld shifts. Matched expert tuning and hidden manual intervention are alternative explanations; unsafe confidence outside the tested domain is a stop condition. F135 AI-Driven Nanoscale Sampling Failure Prediction At The Limit — Proposes prospective fault warning lead time, in seconds, at a fixed false-alarm rate. Frozen open-loop policies and unselected failure cases distinguish early warning from hindsight leakage. Recovery outcomes and complete action replay remain necessary. F136 Quantum Sensor Interpretable AI At The Limit — Asks whether AI explanations agree with mechanism-specific physical ablations, rather than merely producing plausible narratives. The proposed witness is an agreement fraction, with counterfactual error and calibrated sensing as safeguards. More experimental trials are a competing account. F137 Microrobotic Closed-Loop Control Latency At The Limit — Measures the full sensor-to-physical-action delay, in seconds, inside a declared operating envelope. Expert-tuned controls under matched resources establish the comparison. Hidden human intervention and high-confidence out-of-domain action must be ruled out. F138 AI Multi-Agent Sampling Mission Coordination At The Limit — Evaluates calibration-adjusted joint sampling mission completion as a fraction under fairness and safety vetoes. Frozen open-loop coordination and identical observation budgets serve as controls; training-test leakage and missing action provenance are rival explanations. F139 Nano-Quantum Digital Twin External Validation At The Limit — Freezes a digital twin before evaluating out-of-site prediction error against independent measurements. Preregistered experimental design is the reference; additional experiments, leakage or operating outside the authorized action envelope cannot be counted as predictive success. F140 AI Biological Signal Concept Drift Identification At The Limit — Measures detection delay, in seconds, at a fixed false-alarm rate, separating biological-state drift from sensor and calibration changes. Equal-trial expert tuning and hidden manual correction are comparators. Confident action on unsupported states triggers a hard stop. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All volumes are prospective nonclinical research designs for traceable samples, authorized ex-vivo, simulated or closed-bench settings; no laboratory results, clinical efficacy or quantum advantage are reported. Principal comparisons include equal-budget expert tuning, frozen open-loop control and preregistered experimental design. Preserved sample identity, independent measurement, held-out blind challenges, negative-run reporting and hard safety stops are required. The source QA marks structural checks as passed, but physical derivation review, causal distinctness, claim-level DOI matching and exhaustive visual inspection as partial or unfinished. Selected Established Methodological References Degen, Reinhard & Cappellaro (2017) · Quantum sensing · DOI 10.1103/RevModPhys.89.035002 | Koscher et al. (2023) · Autonomous molecular discovery · DOI 10.1126/science.adi1407 | Seo, Paik & Yim (2019) · Modular reconfigurable robotics · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-053018-023834 These references support established methods, not the untested STARLI-specific hypotheses. Individual flagship source-to-claim DOI mappings remain to be independently verified. We only hope that when they open it, they will find a little light to guide their way.

summary: Code, data and simulation outputs for the paper "Fractional Order or False Memory: Identifiability of Caputo SIR Models from Incidence Data" by Md Babul Hossain and Mohammad Shah Alam (2026). The package contains the Python code for all simulations, figures and real-data fits in the paper, the daily COVID-19 case data for Bangladesh and the United States, and the raw per-replicate outputs of every Monte Carlo study, so each table can be re-summarized without re-running the simulations. title: Fractional Order or False Memory: code and data"

summary: A person and a language model work on a project together, in one long session. The person says what they want, the model reads and changes the code, and between them the work is talked into shape. That conversation is where they meet, and it is finite. When it outgrows the model's context, the harness cuts it, and a summary takes its place. The session that goes on meets the same person and the same work, holding only a model's retelling of what was said. That second meeting, at the cut, is where continuity holds or is lost. We describe a model of continuity across such cuts, and Crossings, an implementation of it for Claude Code that is limited on purpose to a project's memory. What was said is kept word for word on the person's own disk. As the work goes, the session writes short retellings of it, each resting by id on the messages it is about. At each cut a bounded frame crosses to the session that wakes, made by fixed rules from plain files: those retellings, and the person's own sentences with what was told of each beneath. What the session declined crosses with its reason, and a door lets that session reach back to the words. The contribution is both architectural and methodological: a bounded, provenance-preserving mechanism for continuity across context cuts, and an examination of the ways its instructions and retellings can themselves steer the continuity they are meant to preserve. We give the mechanisms, their costs, and the safeguards with what holds each. We report six cases from our own use. Five are the system's failures: a frame that carried only the work, a session placed in a history it had not been part of, three sound sentences that leaned together, a sentence that said more than the plugin knows, and sentences of the person's that no retelling rested on. The sixth is a sense of convergence that we cannot yet tell apart from them. Nothing here is measured: the cases are observations, and we say how another could test what they suggest. Last, we follow what the system opens: whether convergence is the pair's or the frame's; whose memory it is, and who settles a dispute over it; what consent would rest on for each side; and what such a memory could become. We close on a recommendation to those who make harnesses. Version 2 adds what the software has gained since version 1, at its release 0.4.0, and the two cases behind it.
title: For What Purpose? A Model for Human–AI Continuity Through Conversational Convergence
