summary: This deposit contains synthetic benchmark inputs, mathematical specifications, computational artifacts, saved results, and validation materials supporting the manuscript “Evaluating Delivery-Fee Policies in Omnichannel Retailing with Integrated Fulfillment and Last-Mile Routing.” The materials are organized into two distinct evidence streams. The expected-demand stream contains the five-group benchmark inputs and the archived computational materials used for the fixed-price operational model and the separate descriptive ALNS-LP/Hybrid comparison on generated instances. The realized-order stream documents Construction A, in which customer choices are frozen as indivisible 0.5-order-equivalent orders and vehicle routes are represented over physical address–slot visits. It compares only tariff policies B and C across baseline and low-Store-inventory scenarios using 500 paired replications (2,000 MILP solves in total). All benchmark data are synthetic. No real customer records, personally identifiable information, or confidential retailer data are included. The expected-demand and realized-order formulations are complementary but are not algebraically equivalent. The 52-policy finite comparison belongs to the expected-demand formulation; the realized-order experiment compares only B and C and does not re-evaluate all 52 policies. Net delivery contribution (NDC) excludes merchandise margins and should not be interpreted as total retailer profit. The archived computational outputs and validation materials are preserved as saved evidence. Their inclusion does not mean that the historical experiments were rerun during deposit preparation. Title clarification: The current manuscript supported by this deposit is titled “Evaluating Delivery-Fee Policies in Omnichannel Retailing with Integrated Fulfillment and Last-Mile Routing.” The legacy expected-demand package contains a historical manuscript-context file bearing an earlier working title (version v0.3, dated 13 November 2026, explicitly marked “Not for submission”). This file is retained solely as historical provenance for the earlier computational evidence and does not represent the current manuscript or its title.
title: Research Data and Computational Materials for: Evaluating Delivery-Fee Policies in Omnichannel Retailing with Integrated Fulfillment and Last-Mile Routing

summary: AQUA-PRITHVI v2 expands the previously published metadata-only aquatic Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) corpus into a reusable multispectral research dataset, accompanied by harmonized in situ water-quality observations and reproducibility tools. The aquatic HLS corpus comprises 29,079 original compressed NPZ microshards containing 169,907 materialized patch-period samples. A quality-controlled catalog identifies 169,429 approved observations from 2,389 spatial patches across eight global regions during 2018–2024. Each approved observation references six HLS reflectance bands (blue, green, red, narrow NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2), 224 × 224 pixels at 30 m spatial resolution, together with valid-pixel and water masks. Spatially independent train, validation and test partitions are provided. The original NPZ archives may also contain excluded observations; only records identified as approved in the accompanying catalog should be treated as quality-controlled samples. The companion water-quality dataset integrates 2,107,785 harmonized observations from CONAGUA RENAMECA (Mexico) and AquaMatch (United States and territories), covering chlorophyll-a, total suspended solids, turbidity and water transparency where available. Source provenance, measurement units, censoring information and quality indicators are preserved. The release also provides Python tools for reading HLS tensors, preparing candidate water-quality labels and planning satellite-scene searches. These tools support the future construction of reproducible HLS–in situ matchup datasets. Important limitation: The harmonized in situ observations are not yet paired with satellite scenes. The monthly HLS composites used for aquatic domain-adaptive pretraining must not be interpreted as same-day satellite matchups. Valid supervised matchups require independent scene-level temporal matching, radiometric quality control and spatially independent evaluation. This resource is intended to support aquatic remote sensing, self-supervised representation learning, reproducible geospatial machine learning and research on satellite-based water-quality assessment. Original datasets retain their respective provenance, attribution and reuse conditions. Related Research Resources This dataset is part of the AQUA-PRITHVI research ecosystem , which integrates aquatic satellite observations, domain-adapted geospatial foundation models and reproducible scientific workflows. Trained foundation model — Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/freddyvillota/AQUA-PRITHVI-EO-2.0-300M-TL The repository provides the aquatic-domain-adapted Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL model weights, model documentation and loading instructions for aquatic multispectral representation learning and spectral reconstruction. Source code and scientific documentation — GitHub: https://github.com/FreddyHVG/AQUA-PRITHVI-DAPT-V2 The repository contains methodological documentation, preprocessing workflows, quality-control procedures, experimental results and reproducibility resources. Together, these resources enable researchers to access the aquatic HLS dataset, reuse the adapted foundation model, and reproduce or extend the associated scientific workflows. Note: The adapted model has been evaluated for aquatic spectral reconstruction. Its availability does not imply validated predictive performance for chlorophyll-a, suspended solids or other water-quality variables. summary: In 1513 the Castilian Crown began directing its conquistadors to read aloud the Requerimiento, a legal demand that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas submit at once to the authority of the Pope and the Spanish monarch. Composed by the jurist Juan López de Palacios Rubios, it was recited in Spanish or Latin, often out of earshot and to communities with no means of grasping its terms, and yet refusal, or the mere inability to consent, was treated as lawful grounds for war and enslavement. For the Taíno of the Caribbean it was the purest instrument of weaponized information asymmetry: a choice demanded under conditions that made informed choice impossible. This article formalizes the structural inverse of that instrument. It proposes a formal model of a peer-recognition currency in which the unit of account is perceived contribution value, issuance is fully endogenous, no sovereign intermediary exists, and the exchange space is structured by context-tagged domains rather than a flat signal architecture. The model's central claim is that when a boundedly rational agent simultaneously optimizes for accumulation, because a high balance signals competence and influence, and for expenditure, because high spending signals piety, humility, and reciprocal embeddedness, the resulting equilibrium is altruistic in the behavioral sense, not because altruism is designed into the incentive structure but because it is the only stable solution to the dual-motive optimization problem in a peer network with an observable ledger. A novel institutional role is defined: the epistemic witness, which informs without judging and without suggesting, preserving full independent agency while eliminating the information asymmetry between a participant and their own recognized contribution record. Where the Requerimiento compelled assent to terms that could not be read, the witness makes the terms of recognition fully legible to the participant before they act. The model is situated within the intersecting literatures of mechanism design, social epistemology, signaling theory, gift economy, commons governance, social compact theory, and cognitive behavioral economics. A candidate validation architecture is identified in which the model's predictions are falsifiable, and a formal appendix establishes the equilibrium result as a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium under perfect public monitoring. The paper concludes that the architecture described represents a distinct class of social exchange institution whose properties cannot be derived from any existing system and whose emergence of altruism as a structural rather than moral outcome has implications beyond the design of digital platforms.
title: E-Karma: A Formal Model of Peer-Recognition Currency, Cross-Domain Enforcement, and Structural Altruism

summary: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.
title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video

summary: Multimodal trajectory forecasting must cover diverse future behaviors without sacrificing dynamical coherence. Most generative forecasters evolve frame-wise positions directly, leaving the relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration implicit. We present SpecFlow, a conditional flow-matching framework that treats the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients of future accelerations as its generative state. SpecFlow learns a transport from Gaussian noise to acceleration spectra and reconstructs velocity and position through fixed analytical integration initialized by the last observed state. A joint phase-space objective supervises all three kinematic levels. To represent destination uncertainty without future information, an endpoint predictor produces candidate destinations and confidence scores solely from observed context, and the highest-confidence candidate conditions the spectral denoiser. Alternating attention over trajectory hypotheses and agents captures multimodality and interaction. Under best-of-20 evaluation, SpecFlow achieves average minADE/minFDE of 0.15/0.22 on ETH/UCY, 0.69/0.86 at four seconds on NBA, and 7.38/11.57 on SDD. It establishes state-of-the-art results across all five ETH/UCY scenes and achieves the lowest four-second ADE on NBA with a tied-best FDE, while remaining competitive on SDD. Together, these results demonstrate that acceleration-spectrum flow matching provides an effective structured generative state across smooth pedestrian motion, coordinated multi-agent sports dynamics, and heterogeneous outdoor trajectories. Code will be made publicly available.
title: SpecFlow: Flow Matching in the Acceleration Spectrum for Multi-Agent Trajectory Forecasting

summary: The increasing demand for intelligent, low-latency services in edge-cloud continuum systems poses new challenges for dynamic and efficient task offloading. We propose a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework for distributed task offloading under partial observability, where each device offloads only a portion of its computation to a target edge server while executing the remaining portion locally (partial offloading). The problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where each device independently learns an optimal policy under partially observable system states. To address the non-convexity, high-dimensional state space, and continuous action space, we develop a multi-agent Advantage-Weighted Actor-Critic (AWAC)-enhanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based computation offloading algorithm. The proposed method combines the stable policy updates of PPO with an advantage-weighting mechanism inspired by AWAC to emphasize higher-quality actions during training. To encourage cooperation without inter-device communication, a shared global reward aligned with system cost is employed. Extensive simulations demonstrate rapid convergence and significant improvement in overall system cost compared with baselines, e.g., Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Deep Q-Network (DQN).
title: Coordinated Offloading: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for the Edge-Cloud Continuum

summary: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/nimashaklaa/TravelPlanner_Research
title: LM-based Personalized Travel Planner

summary: Following AFTD's negative answer dated November 5, 2026, to Hausmann's Question 5.4 in Weighted Max Cut in Subcubic Graphs (arXiv:2611.05178v1, Section 5), we give a different counterexample with an exact residual-order calculation: the generalized Petersen graph GP(7,2) has odd girth five, but deleting any independent set leaves a component with at least four vertices. We prove this by classifying its maximal independent sets into five symmetry classes. The bound four is attained on this graph. The same classification gives an obstruction to the nonempty-independent-side version of Question 5.3; its printed quantifiers admit an empty-side solution.
title: Residual order four in GP(7,2): an alternative proof for Hausmann's Question 5.4 (arXiv:2611.05178v1, Section 5), after AFTD (2026)

summary: Written analysis plan for the study "Choosing a Donor Feeder: Sector Direction and the Cost of Zero-Shot Load-Forecast Transfer", submitted to GECOST 2027. The study measures the day-ahead forecast error of a model trained on one Moroccan distribution feeder and applied without retraining to another, across all 272 ordered pairs of 17 smart-metered feeders in four cities. This document records, for each of 15 analyses, the procedure and the reading rules that decide how its outcome is interpreted. Each section was written before the analysis it governs was run, so that outcomes could not be chosen after seeing the results. The plan covers: the replication gate; the transfer-ratio estimand and dyadic bootstrap; the seasonal-naive baseline; the donor-selection experiment; pooled same-sector models; alternative feeder labels; shape descriptors; the tuned local reference; weather covariates and two discriminating tests of weather sensitivity; second and summer evaluation blocks; few-shot local references; an additive feeder-identity comparison; a permutation test of sector labels; a partition analysis of where pooled transfer beats the naive; a second learner; and a zero-shot foundation-model baseline. Several pre-registered rules returned negative or inconclusive outcomes, and all are reported in the paper, including the finding that no donor-transfer configuration beats a seasonal naive and that a pretrained model outperforms every configuration measured. Data: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/malaklahmidi1/moroccan-feeder-load-time-series-30-min-cleaned
title: Analysis plan for "Choosing a Donor Feeder: Sector Direction and the Cost of Zero-Shot Load-Forecast Transfer"

summary: Abstract Purpose: Glioblastoma immunotherapy trials routinely assess tumor immunity based on a single surgical biopsy. We wanted to know how often biopsy location would reverse a relatively immune-rich or immune-poor classification. We also wanted to know whether CD8 T cell expression correlated with antigen-presenting gene expression and which immune programs remain consistent across regions after accounting for overall leukocyte infiltration. Methods: We scored 14 predefined immune expression programs across 75 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)–localized, nonnecrotic biopsies from 19 patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)–wild-type glioblastoma, alongside 122 microdissected samples from 10 glioblastomas and two multiregion hepatocellular carcinoma cohorts. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) measured regional agreement relative to between-patient differences before and after adjusting for a 12-gene leukocyte score. Results: Regional scores fell on both sides of the fixed 141-biopsy reference mean in 7 of 19 patients (37%) for CD8 expression and 7 of 19 for leukocytes; only two crossed both. Within tumors, CD8 tracked supportive and inhibitory programs equally (mean r = 0.37 and 0.36) but barely tracked major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) transcripts (r = 0.06). Leukocyte adjustment lowered median program ICC from 0.56 to 0.34. Interferon-associated expression retained the highest adjusted point estimate (0.70), though separation from MHC-I (0.47) remained uncertain; additional tumor-purity adjustment yielded similar ICCs (0.66 and 0.62). Conclusion: Biopsy location alone can reverse a glioblastoma’s relative immune-abundance classification. Measuring CD8, interferon, antigen-presentation, and inhibitory programs together across anatomically documented regions separates shared tumor-level features from local variation.
tags: Glioblastoma; Tumor microenvironment; Intratumoral heterogeneity; Tissue biomarkers; CD8 T lymphocytes; Interferon signaling
title: What a single biopsy reveals and misses about the glioblastoma immune microenvironment: Regional reproducibility of immune expression programs

summary: We extend Su's (2026) proof of Peter Bala's conjectures in OEIS A281428, COMMENTS, items 1–2 (displayed March 3, 2026), with factorial bounds and sharp onsets for the two accompanying examples. For a(n)=(2n)![x^(2n)]C(x), we prove v_p(a(n)) >= v_p((2n)!) for every prime p >= 5. The proof combines integral exponential coefficients with ordinary coefficients in Z[1/6], using the inverse cubic u-u^3/3=x. The exact eventual-zero onset modulo 385 is 6; modulo 27, the least eventual period is 18 and its earliest onset is 2. The same argument gives factorial bounds for every polynomial in the two differential-system solutions, including the companion A281427 and A052502.
title: Factorial bounds and sharp onsets for A281428: extending Su (2026) on Bala's COMMENTS, items 1–2

summary: Reconstructing a fragmentary manuscript of a known text rests on prior knowledge that editors apply implicitly and never evaluate. We formalise this knowledge as four priors (the reference text, the scribe's orthography and letter metrics, the physical geometry of the roll, and a rule for reading ambiguous ink) and combine them with large language model (LLM) agents and a constrained alignment model in a three-stage pipeline: reading, placement and layout. We evaluate it on the Greek Deuteronomy roll P. Fouad 266b (Rahlfs 848), which survives in some 140 fragments. An LLM agent, tuned by reflective prompt evolution, transcribes the plates and restores them against the reference text, missing 1 of 943 present letters on held-out plates. Fragments are placed by a banded, information-weighted edit distance with scribal substitution costs, chained across rows by a line-advance model and committed only above a confidence threshold. On a two-fold, plate-level split the placement model places 88% of held-out units (110 of 125) with no false placement (95% upper bound on the error rate about 3%). A deterministic constraint solver then rebuilds 85 columns that keep all 6,736 inked letters at their text positions. Unplaced units are mostly too short to place; the four that no setting places depart in wording from both reference texts, so the model's failures locate textual variants rather than errors. Transferred unchanged to a second roll, P. Fouad 266c (847), it places one unidentified fragment.
title: Reconstructing a Fragmentary Text from Priors: Language-Model Agents and Learned Alignment for P. Fouad 266b (848)

summary: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection on the NASA CMAPSS FD001 turbofan dataset. An LSTM autoencoder trained on healthy sliding windows is compared on 20 held-out engines with a cycle-count score, PCA reconstruction, an Isolation Forest and a one-class SVM, with bootstrap intervals over engines, paired comparisons of warning time at equal false-alarm rates and a causal alarm rule. The model is served through a typed FastAPI service and a Streamlit demo in a multi-stage Docker stack.
title: Anomaly Detection API: Autoencoder + FastAPI + Docker

ONE FAMILY, FIVE INCOMMENSURATE EVIDENCE STREAMS The first temptation in an integrated research civilization is to take five measurements and make one score. This is dangerous when their physical units have different meanings. A response in micrometers per kilopascal cannot be added meaningfully to a cell speed in micrometers per hour. Neither can be averaged with a degradation half-life in days or a pore oxygen flux in moles per unit surface and time. Even a dimensionless stability index requires an operational definition and a prespecified acceptable region. A scientifically defensible integration records the full vector and permits a hard stop when any essential component fails. Suppose a matrix allows quicker cell movement while the frequency of adverse changes in cell identity rises. An averaged numerical improvement might hide this problem. A research contract instead keeps separate thresholds for structural fidelity, independent physiology, matrix compatibility, calibrated uncertainty and process safety. The cross-family interface can share measured quantities and evidence packages while refusing to transfer conclusions that have not been independently established. That refusal is itself a form of technological maturity. THIRTY MATHEMATICAL PLATES AND FORTY-TWO RECONSTRUCTABLE SURFACES A formula becomes valuable when its domain of validity is written beside it. The third family preserves the source atlas's thirty candidate formula positions and distinguishes generic test-logic equations from specific physical companion interpretations. For a quasi-elastic response, strain is the ratio of stress to modulus under a declared small-strain regime. That is not enough to describe a hydrogel that relaxes, erodes and remodels while cells exert force. Migration tracking must remove moving substrate landmarks; degradation kinetics must separate dry polymer mass from swollen water; oxygen flux must connect gradient, diffusivity, tortuosity and the actual pore network; remodeling stability must declare how long a bounded trajectory is monitored. Forty-two synthetic three-dimensional models make sensitivities visible across registered parameter ranges. Each saved graph belongs to a CSV numeric grid and a reproducible Python reconstruction program, with units for all axes. They are proposed model objects, not measured cells. Their purpose is to help another investigator find a discontinuity, a nonidentifiable parameter combination or a wrong prediction before undertaking a biological assay. When a future experimental series disagrees with a curve, that discrepancy should be welcomed as evidence, not repaired away by changing the axis limits. TWO HUNDRED RESEARCH GATES AS A LIBRARY OF DISAGREEMENT The 200 Research Gates are not decorative questions. Each door begins with a distinct local investigation and asks why that problem matters, how the most serious competing explanation could account for the visible pattern, and what a successor could do with a simple independent witness. Across gel stiffness, migration, degradation, pore transport and remodeling, the language and scale change. Some doors begin from an intriguing contour, others from a physical contradiction or a failed denominator. Some describe a world in which swelling accounts for everything. Others imagine a pore network that is beautiful but disconnected, an apparently motile cell that is actually being carried by its gel, or a stable feedback trace that conceals tissue identity loss. Their future plans ask for blind sample exchange, matched budget controls, withheld perturbations, new batches, sealed negative specimens and automatic refusal. A Gate has done its work when it leaves a person outside the current research group with enough information to prove the attractive explanation wrong. The failure scenario is therefore not an embarrassment; it is an inheritance. The archive should preserve it with the same care as the favored result. THIRTY-THREE PHOENIX EMBRYOS AND A CIVILIZATION THAT CAN STOP The Phoenix possibilities develop small prototypes rather than claiming completed machines. Their names suggest instrument exchanges, counterfactual matrix libraries, pore-network tomography challenges, mechanical memory loops, independent material reference standards and new methods for storing negative outcomes. Each idea includes a minimum test and a reason to retire it. In a mature autonomous experimental environment, this has consequences beyond documentation. Controllers must abstain when calibration disappears. Hardware or material intervention cannot proceed merely because a prediction model is confident. Human permission, biological source provenance and contamination controls remain external authority constraints. A system that pauses when its assumptions collapse is often more useful than one that always returns an answer. The same principle applies to writing and publication: a research program can be inspirational without presenting synthetic models as achieved biological capabilities. The open scientific record grows stronger when authors state what has not yet been built, measured or validated. THE SCIENTIFIC INHERITANCE The supplied STARLI F18 organ-on-chip monograph reminds this family of a central distinction: geometric precision is not physiological function. In a material-focused family, the same argument has multiple forms. An excellent modulus map is not morphogenesis. A migrating centroid is not necessarily a migrating cell. A fall in wet weight is not always polymer cleavage. A large apparent flux is not necessarily oxygen supply to living tissue. And a stable material signal is not proof of organ-specific homeostasis. Published work on organoid hydrogels, synthetic matrices, viscoelasticity and dynamic mechanics offers methodological precedents. Those sources do not experimentally verify the five new STARLI couplings. This research family offers a plan for making such claims testable, including measurements, strong baselines, uncertainty accounting, data reconstruction and stopping conditions. The long-term goal is not to build a library of conclusions that cannot be questioned, but an open architecture of precise experimental doors. Each generation should be free to improve the questions, reject a mistaken mechanism and keep whatever remains genuinely useful. Let beauty have the ability to continue happening. summary: Reproducibility companion for a powder X-ray diffraction reference-library holdout audit. The package includes Python scripts, checksum-verified source provenance, nominal-label crosswalks, per-query and aggregate results, and figures. It compares the minimum total-variation error for selection of an eligible label with that for a convex blend, using scan/sample-ID, whole-recipe and (where applicable) filename-series holdouts. The nested Archive A bundle includes unchanged files from the Bickmore–Terry–Eberl archive (CC BY 4.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23692859). Archive B patterns are obtained separately from the Pabst et al. archive (CC BY 4.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.18235708) and checksum-verified by the scripts. These are analyses of public measurements against nominal labels; no new measurements were collected. See README.txt and SOURCE-ATTRIBUTION.txt for reproduction and attribution.

summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π (x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The similarity with the construction of the Birth of Dimensions model is shown. Section 8 shows that the accumulated mismatch over the seams is Euler's sine at one half ( π ), while accumulation over the primes gives γ (Mertens); that the error of the prime count at a step is of the order of the square root of the mismatch of the frame; and that the transfer of the observer changes nothing if and only if all zeros lie on the axis 1/2 — this is the Hilbert — Pólya programme. Each seam is a right triangle in a circle: the centre along the line is the radius, the centre on the circle the cosine, the hole the sine, and sin² + cos² = 1. The author believes that this work can become a proof of the Riemann hypothesis; the missing step is to show that the unity of the process makes the transfer of the observer a symmetry. The work is laid out as a programme of proof: the missing step is formulated as a target statement resting on the birth of the arrow — a pure projection from one unit, the product over the primes. The missing step is also written as a statement about positivity: from Mertens' square 2(1 + cos θ )², which pushes the zeros away from 1, to the square of Weil's energy, which must hold them on ½ and forbid pairs of zeros on opposite sides of the circle. The work rests on classical results — Pell–Lagrange, Legendre's sieve, the explicit formula of Riemann and von Mangoldt — and proposes a new linking of them: the geometry of the seam as a model of the process linking the primes. summary: Version v6.0-jbi accompanies the submission of the article to the Journal of Biomedical Informatics (Elsevier). It adds manuscript_jbi/, which builds the shortened journal version (body of about 5,980 words, two figures, six tables) and its supplementary material from the v5.0 manuscript, a graphical abstract (figures/Graphical_abstract_JBI_DNFR.png), and check_numbers.py, which verifies that every number in the journal version occurs in the v5.0 manuscript or supplement generated from the result files. It also adds the ratings of a second, blinded clinical rater (a physician; results/expert_review2_filled.xlsx with the rater’s name withheld, and the agreement and discrimination statistics in results/expert_review2.json). Models, data and the main results are unchanged from v5.0. Code, derived data and result files for Differentiable Neuro-Fuzzy Reasoning (DNFR), a path-based link predictor that learns degree-aware edge memberships, a Schweizer–Sklar t-norm per metapath and metapath reliabilities, and aggregates paths by noisy-OR, used as an instrument for a controlled component analysis on medical knowledge graphs. Tasks: drug repurposing in Hetionet v1.0 and PrimeKG, disease–symptom prediction in Hetionet and in the graded health knowledge graph of Rotmensch et al. (2017), and a secondary test on a NHANES fuzzy relation, under leave-dyad-out random and disease-centred splits. Comparators: fixed t-norms, component ablations, restarts of the t-norm parameter, DWPC with logistic regression (with and without degree and prior features), a degree-preserving edge prior, popularity, AnyBURL, truncated and soft-thresholded SVD and knowledge graph embeddings. Version v4.0 (fourth revision) completes 10 leave-dyad-out splits on Hetionet compound–treats–disease for the fixed Hamacher product, fixed degree terms, annealing, frozen memberships, DNFR 2.0, the shared and fixed t-norm parameters and AnyBURL; adds an ablation without metapaths that contain the target relation, a fact-level attribution of DWPC-LR next to DNFR's, the evidence share by metapath class, an information-content check with matched spread, a profile of the t-norm parameter extended to p > 0 and run on Hetionet disease–symptom, a tuning grid for NBFNet, a script that re-runs a key result from a clean checkout (scripts/verify_clean.sh), and the sheet for a clinical assessment of the explanations (dnfr/expert_sheet.py, dnfr/expert_summary.py). The secondary NHANES test was removed from the article. Version v3.0-rev3 (third revision) added DNFR 2.0, four refinements tested one at a time and in combination (overlap-aware aggregation, Gumbel-softmax operator choice, an information-content hub discount and membership annealing), a fixed t-norm selected on validation data, a converged L-BFGS profile of the t-norm parameter, an unbounded parameterisation, a compact NBFNet baseline, an exact edge-level Shapley attribution of the explanations, a mechanistic classification of the drug-repurposing explanations, a sparsity variant that keeps the target relation, and 10 leave-dyad-out splits for the main comparisons on Hetionet compound–treats–disease, Hetionet disease–symptom and the graded health knowledge graph. summary: Electrons can change subband in quantum transport, holes can be solved by it too, the package makes quality triangle meshes, the quantum channel on meshes keeps band steps where the mesh puts them, and scattering lifetimes and mobility of a 2D gas are computed from its own wavefunction. The examples print what they printed before, except example 58 (the quantum channel on a mesh, now closer to the tensor grid); examples 62 to 65 are new. Added Device.negf(..., coupled_modes=M) : NEGF in coupled mode space, the lowest M states of every column joined by their overlaps, so electrons change subband where the channel's profile across it changes; with all modes it is the full 2D problem (ballistic only). kpenvelope.negf adds Slab , slab_transport and lead_surface_green (leads by decimation). Device.negf(..., carrier="holes") : the holes of a QuantumChannel with holes=(m_z, m_inplane, ...) , with or without scattering, uncoupled or coupled; Slab(mass_x=) for a mass along x of its own. kpenvelope.mesh.quality_mesh(regions, h, min_angle) : quality meshes of polygon regions by Delaunay refinement (every boundary and interface an edge, no node in a segment's diametral circle, smallest angle up to 34 degrees, a size field). kpenvelope.scattering.Subband : transport and quantum lifetimes and the mobility of one subband from acoustic phonons, alloy disorder, interface roughness (Gaussian or exponential correlation) and screened charged impurities (sheets or profiles), with your material numbers. Changed The quantum channel on meshes: the material on each sample of a line is the mean over its share of the line. Before, a node on a band step took its whole share from the one region it belongs to, which moved the step by up to half a spacing, differently on each line: on a quality mesh the confined sheet was 1.6 to 2.0 percent off a fine tensor grid at every mesh size; now 0.54, 0.20 and 0.10 percent at 1, 0.5 and 0.25 nm. On a mesh made from a tensor grid with a band step inside the window, the result now differs from the tensor grid's by that half-spacing effect of the tensor grid. Device(grid=...) refuses nodes closer than 1e-6 nm with a clear message (a near-duplicate node made the Poisson solve fail). Not included (see docs/limits.md) Scattering in coupled mode space; phonon self-energies in NEGF; NEGF on triangle meshes; both carriers in NEGF at once. Polar optical phonon and intersubband scattering in the lifetimes. The hot-electron model's limit at zero relaxation time with velocity saturation, the plasma's own chemistry, oxide shapes that follow the flow, elasticity, electronic stopping beyond Lindhard-Scharff, tunneling paths that bend with the field, tunneling and heat inside one Newton solve, and the Peltier heat in Fermi-Dirac form are as in 0.26.0. The app does not have the new features yet. Checks (tests) 15 new tests (372 in all; docs/checks.md has the tolerances): the leads by decimation against the exact chain lead; coupled mode space against the dense real-space inverse, mode counting, the sum of chains without mixing, and the uncoupled device; holes against the mirror image of electrons and the QuantumChannel's holes; a slab with a mass along x of its own; the quality mesh's angles, areas, conformity and diametral circles, and a ring resistor converging at second order; the quantum channel on a quality mesh against a fine tensor grid; the scattering rates against closed forms (Fang-Howard and square-well overlaps, Price's acoustic rate, the alloy rate), an independent integral with the closed-form Fang-Howard form factors, the far-away-charge limits, the Hellmann-Feynman shift of a level, and the thermal average. All 65 documented examples were rerun.
title: kpenvelope: interface charges, misfit-dislocation charge, two-dimensional electron and hole gases and device curves of wurtzite nitride stacks, with a self-consistent six-band k.p solver

summary: A finite record can leave equally many states possible after each observation and still resolve one question perfectly while giving little information about another. For a specified answer map, the nonempty cells of its joint table with the record characterize exact recovery. If a state law is given, the largest cell mass in each row determines optimal one-guess accuracy. If only the record law and a statewise loss are given, row minima and maxima give attainable bounds on the mean loss. We prove the relations between fiber size, mass and conditional diversity, including their dependence on uniform input, and give finite witnesses to their limits. For composition and updates, we determine when a count or a next record follows from the retained information. Two dice give records of the same diversity but accuracies of one and one sixth for the same question. In an office occupancy series, an added sensor bit lowers training error, yet a fixed decoder incurs more errors in both test periods. Declaration of AI Use ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic) assisted in preparing and checking the materials used for this work. AI was used for drafting, mathematical cross-checks, and preparation of figures and verification code. The author retains responsibility for the manuscript and its conclusions. These checks do not constitute independent peer review.
title: Re-Phase Vol.4.7: Records for Required Answers — Effective Diversity, Exact Recovery, and Sharp Loss Bounds

summary: 中文摘要 空间旋转、观察者涡度、内部规范场的旋转结构以及时空挠率往往被放在同一概念框架中,但它们在对称性、规范变换和动力学上并不等价。本文综合一系列关于 “ 真实旋转自由度能否构成普通质量引力之必要动力学来源 ” 的模型检验,首先指出球对称单一时间类矢量场满足 ,因而其投影涡度为零;特定平直空间切片上的纯环向差分旋转度规还受到弱能量条件与零能量条件的限制。其次,以已知 Einstein–Yang–Mills 和 Einstein–Yang–Mills–Higgs 模型为对照,说明内部规范旋转能够形成正则、球对称的自引力构型,但并未导出独立的度规引力动力学。本文的主要技术焦点是固定空间三标架下三支 Abelian 横向矢量场的静态交换:当源仅由标量密度线性、局域解析地构成,并同时满足守恒及对角   不变性时,源顶点在零动量至少含一阶导数,树级源 — 源核不具有非零系数的   牛顿红外极点。与此对照,非局域横向投影   可在正的自由场能量下产生吸引性   静态核;带质量 Proca 空间源也可产生吸引的 Yukawa 势,但伴随非守恒源、优选切片或奇异的无质量极限。这些结果排除或限定了若干最小模型,却没有构造出局域、协变、健康且满足红移、光偏折、等效原理与引力波要求的完整旋转起源引力理论。 Abstract   — We critically synthesize a sequence of model-level investigations into whether a genuine rotational degree of freedom can be a necessary dynamical origin of ordinary gravity. Spatial coordinate rotation, the vorticity of a chosen timelike congruence, internal gauge curvature and spacetime torsion are treated as distinct objects. A spherically symmetric single timelike one-form is hypersurface orthogonal, whereas familiar Einstein–Yang–Mills–Higgs solutions demonstrate that non-Abelian internal structure can coexist with regular, positive-energy self-gravitating configurations without establishing a new origin of metric dynamics. Our central conditional result concerns a static triplet of positive-kinetic Abelian vector fields on a fixed spatial slice. If their conserved sources are linear in a scalar mass density, analytic near zero momentum and invariant under a diagonal , the tree-level source–source kernel has no Newtonian  infrared pole. A spatially nonlocal transverse-projection source provides an explicit counterexample to any broader impossibility claim: it produces an attractive static interaction, but presupposes an inverse Laplacian and a preferred slicing. Massive Proca couplings admit additional attractive Yukawa examples while raising different consistency issues. None of these constructions establishes a complete local, covariant and observationally viable theory in which spatial rotation necessarily generates all gravitational phenomena.

title: 空间旋转能否成为引力的动力学起源?——从球对称涡度约束到多场交换核的条件性障碍与反例

summary: M2-US: A Large-scale Multi-domain and Multi-task Ultrasound Image Dataset Ultrasound imaging is widely used across various clinical applications due to its real-time imaging capabilities, portability, and cost-effectiveness. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated considerable potential in ultrasound image analysis. However, the development of generalizable AI models remains challenging due to variations in imaging devices, acquisition protocols, anatomical structures, and clinical tasks. Most existing ultrasound datasets focus on specific anatomical regions or individual prediction tasks, limiting their applicability to multi-domain and multi-task learning. To address these limitations, we introduce M2-US , a large-scale, multi-domain and multi-task ultrasound image dataset comprising 67,620 ultrasound images collected from publicly available datasets and retrospective clinical cohorts. The dataset covers more than 30 anatomical structures and pathological targets across diverse clinical applications, including maternal–fetal, cardiac, vascular, abdominal, pulmonary, breast, thyroid, and gynecological ultrasound imaging. The images originate from multiple countries and were acquired using approximately 24 ultrasound scanner models from more than 10 manufacturers, providing substantial diversity in imaging conditions and clinical settings. M2-US supports 26 subtasks across four major ultrasound image analysis tasks : segmentation (12 subtasks), classification (9 subtasks), object detection (2 subtasks), and landmark-based regression (3 subtasks). The dataset provides task-specific annotations, including pixel-wise segmentation masks, image-level classification labels, object bounding boxes, and anatomical landmark coordinates. All data are organized into predefined training, validation, and testing partitions, accompanied by standardized CSV metadata files to facilitate reproducible model development and evaluation. M2-US is designed to support research on task-specific deep learning models, multi-task learning, transfer learning, foundation model adaptation, and cross-domain generalization in ultrasound image analysis. By integrating diverse anatomical targets, imaging conditions, and annotation types within a unified benchmark, M2-US aims to facilitate the development and systematic evaluation of more robust and generalizable ultrasound AI methods. Dataset website: https://m2-us.github.io/ GitHub repository: https://github.com/m2-us/m2-us Baseline experiments: https://github.com/m2-us/experiments License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
title: A Large-scale Multi-domain and Multi-task Ultrasound Image Dataset

summary: This dataset record contains seven curated microscopy image segmentation datasets with image files, corresponding mask annotation files, and predefined train, validation, and test splits. The datasets are derived from public or previously published sources cited in the associated manuscript: Grain (Warren et al., 2024), EMPS (Yildirim and Cole, 2021), Aachen-Heerlen (Iren et al., 2021), UHCS (DeCost et al., 2017), MetalDAM (Luengo et al., 2022), and Super/EBC (Stuckner et al., 2022). The files were reorganized for a unified benchmark, split into train, validation, and test subsets, and subjected to annotation review, supplementary annotation, and quality control. The depositor has confirmed that the curated files can be redistributed for research use. The deposit includes 3,625 image files, 3,625 mask label files, and 163,901 mask instances counted as 8-connected non-zero connected components within the label images. The datasets included are Aachen-Heerlen, EBC, EMPS, Grain, MetalDAM, Super, and UHCS. File-level checksums, dataset statistics, class-wise mask-instance counts, source mapping, and documentation are provided to support reuse and reproducibility.
title: Microscopy image segmentation datasets with mask annotations

summary: the zipped file is a self-contained replication package for the paper "The Cost of Restricting Access to Natural Areas: African Swine Fever Containment Zones and Local Income". The execution requires locally installed recent versions of both Stata and R and the download of a package of external data from official websites of the Government of Italy. All steps are documented in the readme file and discussed in the paper. ABSTRACT The spread of African Swine Fever in the European Union since 2014 has triggered a policy response that, in several cases, included severe restrictions on access to forests and other natural areas. In most cases, pig farming and, to a lesser degree, the agricultural sector were compensated for the costs incurred as a consequence of the disease and its containment measures. The indirect costs borne by outdoor-based local economies, on the contrary, have been typically excluded from compensation schemes and, for the most part, remain unmeasured. This paper estimates these costs in the context of the African Swine Fever outbreak that affected North-West Italy from 2022 onward. Using municipal-level taxable income data and a difference-in-differences design, we estimate the effect of access restrictions on local income. We find a decline of self-employment income per taxpayer of about 18–23 percent relative to control municipalities. The effect is weaker and below statistical significance for small business income and absent for wage income and pension income. The result is also unaffected by pre-outbreak pig-farming intensity in the municipality, indicating that the impact of direct costs is negligible. These findings suggest that the portion of containment policies that restricted access to natural areas shifted a significant part of the economic burden of disease control on sectors unrelated to pig farming and on municipalities where pig farming has a very limited presence. They also raise a compensation-design issue: containment policies generate broad public benefits, but also appropriable benefits for pig producers outside the outbreak zone. In those circumstances, when indirect costs remain uncompensated and sector-specific benefits from containment measures are not internalized by the beneficiaries we should expect distorted incentives and sub-optimal policy responses. The paper discusses policy options to improve both the efficiency and fairness of compensation for disease-containment measures that restrict access to natural areas.
title: Full, self-contained replication package for "The Cost of Restricting Access to Natural Areas: African Swine Fever Containment Zones and Local Income"

summary: An open educational engineering module on hypersonic waverider aerodynamic design, cone-derived shock capture, and lift-to-drag maximization. Covers inverse design from conical shock flowfields, shock-riding leading edges, and zero-spillage lower-surface pressure capture; the osculating cones method for non-axisymmetric planforms and scramjet inlet integration; hypersonic drag polars, lift-to-drag (L/D) maximization, the Küchemann barrier, and leading-edge bluntness versus aerothermal heating trade-offs; worked numerical calculations for caret-waverider pressure lift, wave drag, and polar L/D; an interactive waverider L/D and shock-capture explorer; and conventional delta wing versus waverider comparisons. Aligned with Washington Accord graduate attributes (WA1–WA3) and published on Prep4Uni.Online.
title: Waverider Aerodynamic Design Explained: Cone-Derived Leading Edges & L/D Maximization

summary: This dataset contains the complete experimental sequencing data generated for the study "Thermodynamically Constrained Encoding Improves Reliability in DNA Data Storage" . The study investigates the impact of thermodynamic constraints, based on Gibbs free energy (ΔG), on the reliability and efficiency of DNA-based digital data storage. Two encoding strategies are compared: the reference JPEG DNA encoding and a thermodynamically constrained version designed to improve the representation and recovery of encoded information during DNA sequencing. DNA oligonucleotide pools were synthesized by three independent providers: Agilent SurePrint, Dynegene, and GenScript. The synthesized DNA was amplified and sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) PromethION sequencing. Dataset contents The dataset comprises experimental data, including: Raw sequencing reads in FASTQ format from the three DNA synthesis providers. Sequencing data corresponding to both reference and thermodynamically constrained JPEG DNA encoding configurations. These data enable further investigation of sequence-dependent coverage biases, decoding efficiency, and the effects of thermodynamic constraints on the reliable reconstruction of digitally encoded images from synthetic DNA. Related resources A smaller subset of the FASTQ files, sufficient to decode the images synthesized by each provider, is also available on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22712282
title: JPEG DNA Thermodynamically Constrained Encoding Dataset

summary: STARLI | F051–F060 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Quantum Sensing, Reference Integrity and Trustworthy Biosensor Qualification Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection joins two five-theme research units from the STARLI 300-theme atlas. Research Unit I (F051–F055) examines long-term quantum-sensor stability, magnetic readout–motion decoupling, optical interface loss, autonomous fault diagnosis and multisite calibration. Research Unit II (F056–F060) develops common-mode failure identification, biological ground-truth validation, low-photodamage operation, trustworthy metrology and full-lifecycle qualification. The common challenge is whether a measured improvement survives independent references, hidden nuisance variables and resource-matched classical controls. The ten English working editions contain 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 one-page investigations, 2,000 separate Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Version 1.3 revises the six notes beneath each Gate question: causal mechanism, independent witness, blinded falsifier, competing explanation, stop rule and successor interface. These numbers describe editorial architecture and proposed research designs, not experimentally established originality or quantum advantage. The Ten Research Directions F051  Microscale Quantum Sensor Long-Term Stability At The Limit — Studies whether sensitivity remains stable across prolonged acquisition, replacement references and biological-matrix changes. Compares a quantum channel with identical-optics quantum-off ablation; tracks detection limit, calibration drift and interval coverage. Hidden reference drift or undercoverage of blinded truth defeats the proposed advantage. F052  Quantum Magnetic-Field Sensing And Microrobotic Motion Decoupling At The Limit — Separates quantum magnetic-field readout from motion-induced field changes in microrobotic experiments. Tracks Allan deviation, field sensitivity and photon budget against a strong classical sensor. Equal-photon comparisons test whether an apparent gain comes from photon count rather than quantum coherence. F053  Quantum Optical Microfluidic Interface Loss At The Limit — Examines losses and nuisance coupling at an optical quantum-sensing interface within microfluidic systems. Uses recorded photon budgets, contrast, drift and a locked reference instrument to test end-to-end readout integrity. Post-selection and loss of reference identity are explicit rival or stopping conditions. F054  Quantum Biosensor Autonomous Fault Diagnosis At The Limit — Designs autonomous detection of biosensor failure states without equating a model alert with an independently verified fault. Hidden reference-drift challenges, quantum-off ablations and withheld measurements interrogate field sensitivity, contrast and coherence-time estimates. Uncalibrated uncertainty intervals must trigger abstention. F055  Multisite Quantum Sensing Network Calibration At The Limit — Proposes traceable calibration transfer between quantum sensing sites, including independent references and shared-drift injection. Compares sensitivity, Allan deviation and cross-site reproducibility with classical optical or magnetic sensors. A site-consistent improvement is insufficient if extra photons explain the difference. F056  Quantum Sensor Common-Mode Failure Identification At The Limit — Investigates common-mode faults that can make multiple quantum sensors agree while all are wrong. A locked reference instrument, masked reference substitution and covariance-aware uncertainty audits separate shared errors from true agreement. Missing reference identity or selective retention of good readings invalidates release. F057  Biological Sample Quantum Readout Truth

summary: Observable forms are frequently used to identify, classify, and evaluate systems. However, an observable form does not necessarily provide a complete account of the internal processes that produce or govern the system. In some situations, the external representation becomes the dominant basis for interpretation, replacing a more direct examination of the system's internal structure, functional relationships, and causal processes. The Surface-Process Inference Paradox (SPIP) is proposed as a general theoretical framework for examining this problem across different classes of observable systems. Its central question is whether what is externally observed adequately represents the system's actual internal processes, or whether the observer becomes restricted by the external form and consequently fails to understand what is occurring within the system. The framework distinguishes two principal pathways. The first is structural observational ambiguity, in which different internal processes can produce indistinguishable observable forms. The second is observer-mediated surface capture, in which the observer gives excessive interpretive importance to an external category or representation despite the availability of relevant process evidence. A primary case study, the Genre-Bound Musical Evaluation Case (GBMEC), is used to preserve the original observation concerning music genre and internal musical structure. The framework is then generalized to human behaviour, visual art, literature, social practices, institutions, software, artificial intelligence, biological systems, and physical systems. Mathematical formalization is developed through state-space models, observation functions, observer representations, process-inference errors, mutual information, observability, and controlled category interventions. Eight theoretical propositions, boundary conditions, hypotheses, and falsification criteria are established. SPIP is presented as a testable and potentially cross-disciplinary framework, not as a completed universal law. Its scientific contribution will depend on whether its mechanisms can be operationalized, distinguished from existing explanations, and independently reproduced across relevant domains.
tags: Surface Representation; Internal Process; Observer; Process Inference; Category Capture; Surface-Process Relationship; Observability; Information Loss; System Interpretation; Cross-Domain Generalization.
title: THE SURFACE-PROCESS INFERENCE PARADOX

summary: Processing code, derived maps and result tables for a study of urban expansion, summer land surface temperature (LST) and residents' potential surface-heat exposure in Baghdad, Basra and Erbil, Iraq, from 2000 to 2025. All files are derived from open datasets (Landsat, MODIS, GLC_FCS30D, GHSL, WSF Evolution, WorldPop, JRC Global Surface Water, SRTM, ERA5-Land). See 00_README.md for file contents, raster codes, limitations, run order and source citations.

summary: THE DEVICE MUST EARN ITS RELEASE An Integrated Technical Guide to Trustworthy Autonomous Neural Nanomanufacturing STARLI / YULI | Research Family 16 | Flagships F151–F160 of 200 | Author: 33 / STARLI–YULI | Research Design and Technical Integration Edition | 7 November 2026 The central question of autonomous neural nanomanufacturing is not whether an intelligent manufacturing line can produce a visually convincing neural electrode. It is whether the line can demonstrate, by evidence accessible to an independent examiner, that the fabricated object meets its declared physical and functional criteria, that its apparent efficiency was not created by quietly excluding unsuccessful attempts, that its defect assessment is not dependent on a shared mistake, and that the machine would refuse an unsafe or unqualified decision even when the optimization algorithm prefers to continue. Neural nanomanufacturing brings a remarkable variety of engineering disciplines into contact. Lithography controls geometry; material preparation establishes the initial chemical state; microscopy and electrochemical measurements create partial views of a device; statistical models infer hidden quality; control systems change recipes; safety interlocks restrict what the equipment may do; and qualified people determine whether the resulting evidence is sufficient for release. Each discipline can work well in isolation while the complete manufacturing claim remains false. This guide proposes a way to make the interfaces between them scientifically accountable. The basis for this essay is a set of ten prospective STARLI / YULI research introductions, F151 through F160. Their research questions concern autonomous recipe selection, closed-loop nanoelectrode fabrication, intelligent nanomaterial quality control, adaptive microstructure formation, AI-based defect detection, process digital twins, cross-batch electrochemical stability, energy efficiency, autonomous stopping, and trustworthy release authority. Those ten investigations are treated here as interacting duties within one nonclinical experimental program, not as ten completed demonstrations and not as proof that an integrated factory already exists. Their common physical perimeter is a controlled neural nanoelectrode manufacturing bench, with coded material lots, instrument-calibration records, machine event logs, independent inspection, and hardware-level ability to stop. Their common scientific demand is falsifiability. A device receives no special status because its manufacturer calls the controller intelligent, autonomous, quantum, or advanced. Its status comes from comparisons with an appropriate conventional line, independent measurement and a complete record of the attempts that failed. A newcomer can enter the topic through a simple thought experiment. Imagine two production benches that receive nominally similar precursor materials and seek to produce a defined pattern of neural electrodes. The first follows a fixed qualified recipe and relies on manual inspection. The second can alter processing settings when a sensor reports a deviation. After a week, the adaptive line displays more attractive device images and announces lower production energy. Have we learned that it is better? Not until we know the denominator of attempted devices, the calibration condition of the metrology, the origin of its defect labels, whether defective parts were discarded before counting, whether the energy calculation included idling and rework, and whether a safety stop would still work if the optimizing software failed. The appropriate research object is therefore not a single successful coupon. It is the documented manufacturing episode, from material receipt to independent release or justified refusal. This episode becomes the basic unit that connects the ten flagships. 1. summary: Flight safety and the reliability of aircraft operations under the extremely low temperatures of the Arctic Zone depend directly on the stability of the low-temperature properties of aviation fuels. The critical parameter determining the cold-flow properties and uninterrupted pumpability of fuel is the freezing point (the onset of crystallization, TNK); exceeding it leads to the precipitation of a solid phase and the risk of fuel filter blockage. This article presents a comparative analysis of the freezing point of TS-1 aviation kerosene produced by four leading Russian oil refineries (coded as A, B, V, and G). The tests were conducted in a certified laboratory using the GOST 5066 method with the "KRISTALL-20" automatic analyzer. Significant differences in coldflow properties depending on the manufacturer were revealed. Samples from manufacturers A, B, and V demonstrated high phase stability (freezing points from −62.3 °C to −66.8 °C), ensuring a reliable safety margin relative to GOST 10227 requirements (not higher than −60 °C) for polar aviation. The product from manufacturer G showed a freezing point of −58.7 °C, which meets the baseline standard but imposes operational limitations according to GOST 16350. Additionally, an analysis was conducted on the impact of seasonal temperature fluctuations in Arctic regions on the permissible storage duration of fuel at airfields without loss of low-temperature characteristics. Typical operational scenarios in remote airports, where the possibility of prompt replacement of a fuel batch is absent, were considered: under such conditions, even a slight deviation of the freezing point from optimal values can lead to a critical reduction in fuel system throughput. It was concluded that the manufacturer factor must be taken into account during the incoming quality control of aviation fuels for Arctic regions. It is recommended to include in acceptance procedures not only verification of compliance with baseline standards but also an assessment of the freezing point margin, taking into account forecast minimum temperatures in the area of operation. This approach will minimize the risk of fuel system failures and enhance the overall reliability of aviation equipment under extreme climatic conditions.
title: Comparative Analysis of the Onset Crystallization Temperature of TS-1 Aviation Fuel from Different Manufacturers.

summary: This paper examines the emerging possibility of organised data marauders and data warriors for hire as a structural feature of the liquid order. These actors operate across strategic, infrastructural, algorithmic and cognitive domains, exploiting the inverse law of sovereign accountability. The paper connects this development to the rise of independent security constructors who offer Dual-Core compatible, contestable services rather than pure extraction. Within the Flow Sovereignty and Reserve of Humanity framework, such constructors can be integrated as peripheral agents whose morphisms remain auditable, while unconstrained data marauders constitute a cohomology threat. The analysis closes with architectural propositions for containing the former and constraining the latter under Permanent Systemic Instability. KSCCN article (3 pages).
title: Data Marauders and Organised Data Warriors for Hire in the Liquid Order: From Historical Private Force to Algorithmic Neo-Contractors and the Rise of Contestable Security Constructors

summary: This paper addresses the fundamental question of the precise extent to which spectral bounds for fractional Schrödinger operators transfer to their magnetic counterparts, and delivers five major results that together form a complete map of what survives, what fails, and what must be proved to close the remaining gaps. The central objects are the magnetic Laplacian H_A = (−i∇ + A)² defined as a Friedrichs form extension from the quadratic form q_A[u] = ∫ |(−i∇ + A)u|² dx for A ∈ L²_loc(ℝᵈ; ℝᵈ), its fractional powers H_{s,A} = (H_A)^s defined via the spectral theorem, and the Aharonov–Bohm potential A_α = (α/ρ)ê_θ with flux parameter α in the cylindrical coordinates of ℝᵈ = ℝ² × ℝ^{d−2}. The negative eigenvalue counting function is denoted N(K) = Tr 1_{(−∞,0)}(K), the Riesz means are Tr(K)^−_γ = Σ |λ_j|^γ for γ > 0 with the convention Tr(K)^−_0 = N(K), and the abbreviated notation T^γ_α = Tr(H_{s,α} + V)^−_γ and N_α = T^0_α is used throughout. The semiclassical constants are L^{cl}_{0,d} = (2π)^{−d}|B_d| and L^{cl}_{γ,d,s} = (2π)^{−d} ∫(1 − |ξ|^{2s})^γ_+ dξ, where |B_d| is the volume of the unit ball in ℝᵈ. The first and most striking result is a definitive negative one: the diamagnetic inequality, which states that |e^{−tH_A}(x,y)| ≤ e^{tΔ}(x,y) for almost every x, y and all t > 0, implies no comparison whatsoever of eigenvalue counting functions or of Riesz means between magnetic and non-magnetic operators. The physical intuition that a magnetic field, which raises the ground-state energy, should also decrease the number of bound states and the sums of powers of negative eigenvalues, is shown to be false by explicit counterexamples. The mechanism of failure is a flux-induced change of degeneracy: at half a flux quantum, the lowest angular channel of an axially symmetric system becomes doubly degenerate, so that two shallow magnetic bound states may replace a single deeper non-magnetic one. The ground-state energy still increases in accordance with the diamagnetic inequality, but the count and even the sum of binding energies may increase. The primary counterexample is constructed in three dimensions with s = 1, R = 1, and V = −8·1_{|x|<1}, a spherical square well of bounded, compactly supported potential belonging to L^∞_c(ℝ³) ⊂ L^{3/2}(ℝ³), the natural CLR class. The channel with angular parameter l ≥ 0 possesses a negative eigenvalue if and only if √λ R exceeds the first positive zero of the spherical Bessel function j_{l−1}, and the number of negative eigenvalues in that channel equals the number of positive zeros of j_{l−1} below √λ R. This follows from matching logarithmic derivatives at r = R between the interior solution u = r j_l(kr) with k = (λ − κ²)^{1/2} and the exterior decaying solution u = r^{1/2} K_{l+1/2}(κr), and taking the limit κ ↓ 0 where the exterior solution behaves like r^{−l}, reducing the threshold condition to j_{l−1}(√λ R) = 0. The relevant thresholds in the variable λR² are: for l = 0, the first threshold is π²/4 ≈ 2.467401 governed by j_{−1}(x) = cos x/x; for l = 1/2, the first threshold is j²_{0,1} ≈ 5.783186 governed by j_{−1/2} ∝ J₀; for l = 1, the first threshold is π² ≈ 9.869604 governed by j₀(x) = sin x/x; for l = 3/2, the first threshold is j²_{1,1} ≈ 14.681971 governed by j_{1/2} ∝ J₁. At α = 0 the channels are l ∈ ℕ₀ with multiplicity 2l + 1, and since 2.467401 < 8 < 9.869604, only l = 0 is active, carrying exactly one eigenvalue since 8 < 22.206610, giving N(H₀ + V) = 1. At &al
title: Aharonov–Bohm Flux and Magnetic Eigenvalue Bounds: Failure of the Diamagnetic Comparison, a Sharp Factor-Two Substitute, and Magnetic Lifting of Lieb–Thirring Constants

summary: This dataset contains two types of files: Replication Package Benchmark Logs (.zip) Below, we explain each file. 1) Replication Package: This Excel file documents the framework selection process and presents the benchmark results and their analysis. It includes five sheets that describe the framework selection process, benchmark results, and analysis used in the study. Sheet 1: Search_String This sheet provides the search strings used to identify candidate frameworks from GitHub, along with the inclusion and exclusion criteria applied during the framework selection process. Sheet 2: Initial_Frameworks_Extraction This sheet contains the initially extracted 164 repos, followed by the refined set of 55 frameworks shortlisted from the original pool. Sheet 3: Final_Frameworks This sheet presents the final set of frameworks selected for the experimental evaluation. It also includes the selection criteria used to finalize these frameworks for further benchmarking. Sheet 4: Benchmark_Results (RQ1–RQ3) This sheet reports the benchmark results for each agentic framework across the three reasoning benchmarks: BBH, GSM8K, and ARC. It includes the accuracy of each framework, the time taken per task, the total execution time per framework, and token consumption at both the task and framework levels for each benchmark. Sheet 5: Analysis This sheet contains the analysis of the benchmark results and summarizes the comparative performance of the evaluated frameworks. 2) Benchmark Logs (.zip): This ZIP file contains the benchmark execution logs for all 22 evaluated agentic frameworks across two reasoning benchmarks: BBH and ARC. The file is organized into separate folders for each benchmark, containing the execution logs of all frameworks, including those that failed to complete the evaluation. These logs provide detailed task-level information, including accuracy, token consumption, and execution time. However, for four frameworks, token consumption was not recorded in the logs and was instead obtained from the OpenAI usage dashboard. Across both benchmarks, the dataset covers 9,881 tasks, and the total ZIP file size is 19.1 MB.
title: Agentic Frameworks for Reasoning Tasks: An Empirical Study

summary: Every LLM request SWAN AI-SQL (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWAN-AISQL) and the baselines issue on SemBench MOVIE/ECOMM/MMQA, the 30-query hybrid bench of the PLOP paper and the SWAN 2.0 benchmark (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWANBench), with the provider's answer, its measured latency and its cost, as a DuckDB file (gzip-compressed, 1.02 GB; 4.8 GB unpacked; 2,541,389 recorded calls) for the repository's cache proxy (serve/ai_cache_server.py). It holds SWAN AI-SQL, LOTUS 1.2.4, PLOP (the public Morrila fork, DP cost-model mode), BlendSQL 0.1.27, ThalamusDB 0.1.15 (exact mode) and Palimpzest 1.5.3 (Abacus optimizer) on every benchmark each of them runs. Each prompt is kept with its most recent recording; this version is the one behind the tables of both repositories as of 2026-11-21, every row a replay on one machine. Always use the latest version: the concept DOI and serve/fetch_cache.sh resolve to it. Every table in the repositories replays without a provider key: run serve/fetch_cache.sh (it downloads, checks and unpacks the latest version), then the benchmark harnesses; the proxy replays each recorded answer with its recorded latency and cost. Model: gpt-5.6-luna, temperature 0, each system's default prompts (zero-shot). Replay matches requests byte for byte; an edited query, another model, or a client library that renders the request differently is a fresh request. The systems' may have their own run-to-run variance (LOTUS's ranking order, result assembly in BlendSQL and Palimpzest, ThalamusDB's sampler, PLOP's parallel operator order).
title: SWAN AI-SQL replay cache: recorded gpt-5.6-luna answers of SWAN, LOTUS, BlendSQL, Palimpzest, ThalamusDB and PLOP on SemBench, the PLOP hybrid bench and SWAN 2.0
