summary: Postoperative complications remain an important concern in the surgical treatment of cicatricial esophageal strictures. Identifying risk factors before surgery is clinically relevant for treatment planning and for correcting potentially modifiable factors. To identify factors associated with the development of postoperative complications in patients with cicatricial esophageal strictures. A retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with cicatricial esophageal strictures treated at three surgical institutions in the Kyrgyz Republic between 2015 and 2025. The overall study cohort comprised 194 patients; the analysis of postoperative complications included 154 patients who underwent surgical treatment: minimally invasive surgery (n=143) or open surgery (n=11). Postoperative complications were recorded according to the Esophagectomy Complications Consensus Group criteria and graded using the Clavien–Dindo classification. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with postoperative complications. Postoperative complications occurred in 55 of 154 surgically treated patients (35.7%). In univariate analysis, open surgery (OR=5.45; 95% CI 1.38–21.48; p=0.015) and the presence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (OR=2.19; 95% CI 1.02–4.68; p=0.043) were associated with postoperative complications, whereas higher serum albumin levels (OR=0.85; 95% CI 0.76–0.96; p=0.010) and a higher prognostic nutritional index (OR=0.88; 95% CI 0.80–0.96; p=0.005) were associated with lower odds of complications. In the multivariable model, ASA class III–IV (OR=3.14; 95% CI 1.44–6.85; p=0.004) and serum albumin level (OR=0.85 per 1 g/L increase; 95% CI 0.74–0.97; p=0.014) remained independent predictors. After adjustment for baseline characteristics, open surgery was not independently associated with postoperative complications (OR=3.36; 95% CI 0.74–15.15; p=0.115). The risk of postoperative complications in patients with cicatricial esophageal strictures was independently associated with higher ASA physical status and serum albumin level. These findings highlight the importance of preoperative assessment of the patient’s general condition and nutritional status when planning surgical treatment. The association between open surgery and complications observed in the unadjusted analysis was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for baseline characteristics; therefore, differences between surgical approaches should not be interpreted as an independent effect of the operative technique.
title: Risk Factors for Postoperative Complications in Patients with Cicatricial Esophageal Strictures: A Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: This preprint presents an existence and local uniqueness certificate for a family of collision-free periodic choreographies in the planar, equal-mass Newton–Yukawa three-body model. In dimensionless units, the pair potential is Vα(r) = −[1 + α exp(−r)]/r, with the gravitational constant, individual masses, and inverse screening length set to one. The certificate covers every coupling value in the closed interval α ∈ [0.00997, 0.01003] at the specified fixed initial separation. The construction starts from a symmetric collinear configuration and imposes three endpoint equations at one-sixth of the period. Reversing symmetries and cyclic relabeling extend a collision-free shooting solution into a periodic choreography in which all three bodies traverse the same closed path one-third of a period apart. The numerical argument combines outward-rounded enclosures of the flow and its first derivatives, collision exclusion over the fundamental arc, and a strict uniform Krawczyk inclusion. Subject to the correctness of the interval implementation and its rounding guarantees, these bounds imply exactly one shooting root in the stated box for each coupling. The manuscript documents the original MPFR Taylor–Picard calculation. A subsequent CAPD 6.0.0 implementation, using a different validated ODE solver, reports strict inclusion in all three shooting coordinates, a contraction bound below 0.495687, and pairwise separation above 0.688548 throughout the fundamental arc. The manuscript and source audit record the earlier stage of the work, when the CAPD run had yet to be executed. Independent technical review of the CAPD implementation and rounding remains open. The result concerns the specified orbit family and coupling interval. A certified connection to the Newtonian orbit at α = 0, geometric figure-eight topology, and orbital stability remain open for this family.
title: Collision-Free Three-Body Choreographies in Newton–Yukawa Gravity: A Uniform AI-Verified Certificate

summary: HYOWON v0.1.1 — Maintenance Release HYOWON v0.1.1 is a maintenance update to v0.1.0. It changes numerical support code, checkpoint reading, MPI error handling, source provenance capture and documentation. The release does not introduce a new physical model or gravity solver. Paper 0 provenance: The Paper 0 manuscript identifies HYOWON v0.1.0 as its simulation source. Version 0.1.1 was not used to generate those results and should not replace v0.1.0 in their software citation. Changes CIC geometry: Reuse validated mesh geometry and the upper coordinate bound within a deposition or interpolation operation. The per-particle wrapping, division, clamping and interpolation-weight calculations retain their existing order. Exact sums: Partition non-negative segment sums among host workers and combine exact integer accumulators before rounding the result to binary64. SHA-256: Process complete input blocks without copying them byte by byte into a staging buffer, and encode hexadecimal digests without a formatting stream. The hash algorithm and persisted identity encoding are unchanged. Checkpoint loading: Decode particle state, timestep and associated provenance into temporary state before publication. Distributed reads require agreement on the manifest digest and successful validation of each rank's checkpoint shard before publishing the loaded state. The manifest is hashed while reading the opened stream, and bound HDF5 descriptors are rewound before descriptor-backed opening and hashing. MPI failure handling: Synchronise errors in force-storage preparation and acceleration publication. Unrecoverable MPI startup or communication failures use an abort path rather than allowing a rank to unwind independently. Text and build provenance: Use the classic locale for machine-readable text and Linux memory observations. Refresh Git source information before executable builds. The reported commit and tree describe Git HEAD, not uncommitted contents or the resulting executable. Documentation and metadata: Update build and usage guidance and the version information in CITATION.cff . Numerical scope and verification The tagged changes leave the gravity and FFT solver implementations, initial-condition generators, cosmological drift/kick calculations and native snapshot/restart schema definitions unchanged. Changes to CIC support routines and force-preparation error paths do not guarantee identical results in every execution environment. The [ v0.1.1 changelog ](https://github.com/youngjinphys/HYOWON/blob/v0.1.1/CHANGELOG.md) records Linux Release builds with and without MPI, the existing smoke test, and matched-input 64-particle comparisons. These are bounded software checks, not evidence of cosmological convergence. Bitwise agreement across arbitrary FFTW plans, thread counts or MPI decompositions is not claimed. The HDF5 descriptor-offset correction was not exercised on macOS. Source and citation Version: 0.1.1 Source commit: 1d9ed3448d36a57e723d63618eca556c7cc8cdde Licence: GPL-3.0-or-later Author: Youngjin Yeom See the [ README ](https://github.com/youngjinphys/HYOWON/blob/v0.1.1/README.md) for build and usage instructions and [ CITATION.cff ](https://github.com/youngjinphys/HYOWON/blob/v0.1.1/CITATION.cff) for citation metadata. Full changelog: https://github.com/youngjinphys/HYOWON/compare/v0.1.0...v0.1.1 Full Changelog : https://github.com/youngjinphys/HYOWON/compare/v0.1.0...v0.1.1

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Fifty entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature, among them: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7; a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients; a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset; a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten; a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998); a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation; a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight; a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. Light through a Jerlov water type. The package: computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963); converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors; gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m, and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers; integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth; gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two; and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent; ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum; carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models; converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient. summary: Source code and experimental result data accompanying the paper "A bi-objective optimization of multi-robot inspection planning and charging infrastructure design under energy constraints" (Avossevou, Guenounou, Nait Chabane, Beddiar; submitted to Transactions of the Institute of Measurement and Control). This repository implements a bi-objective optimization framework for multi-robot industrial inspection, jointly deciding robot routing and task allocation, partial recharge scheduling, and the placement and technology of charging stations. The problem is solved exactly via a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (weighted-sum and epsilon-constraint scalarization) and approximately via three tailored multi-objective metaheuristics: NSGA-II, a Multi-Objective Ant Colony Optimization approach (MOACO), and a Decomposition-Based Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithm (MOEA/D). See the included README.md for repository structure and reproduction instructions.
title: Code and data for: A bi-objective optimization of multi-robot inspection planning and charging infrastructure design under energy constraints

summary: Background: Introduction: basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant skin neoplasm. Its nasal location poses a challenge for surgical oncology and reconstructive plastic surgery, particularly in recurrent lesions with infiltrative histologic patterns and involvement of multiple anatomical subunits. Case report: We present a case report of a 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and systemic arterial hypertension, with a history of previously excised basal cell carcinoma of the right nasal ala. She subsequently developed recurrence with growth toward the contralateral ala. Preoperative biopsy revealed infiltrative basal cell carcinoma with an adamantinoid component. Wide oncologic excision was performed under general anesthesia, with a planned clinical margin of 1 cm. The excision included skin and subcutaneous tissue, with documented operative dimensions of 10 × 2 cm. Immediate reconstruction was performed using a frontonasal rotation flap designed through a t-shaped incision. Definitive histopathologic examination demonstrated tumor-free margins. No intraoperative complications were documented. Conclusion: the management of recurrent nasal basal cell carcinomas requires integration of oncologic and reconstructive principles. Negative histopathologic margins represent a favorable initial result. Long-term follow-up is essential to assess recurrence, nasal function, and reconstructive outcomes.   Keywords: basal cell carcinoma; nasal neoplasms; tumor recurrence; oncologic excision; frontonasal flap; reconstructive surgery.
title: Recurrent infiltrative basal cell carcinoma involving both nasal alae: wide oncologic excision and reconstruction using a frontonasal rotation flap. A case report

Here the alternative explanation matters just as much: optical focus drift, scaffold swelling, magnetic substrate distortion or selective imaging of successful placements can mimic improved assembly precision. A second example, glucose consumption coupling, challenges the possibility that apparent shifts in glucose consumption coupling may alter measured neural niche oxygen heterogeneity, yet sensor bias, culture stress or geometry confounding could mimic an improvement.. Its proposed test is to audit the glucose consumption coupling contribution and contrast an orthogonal assay with the favored readout under equal budgets. The laboratory witness should be external to the favored model. For this flagship it is blinded confocal fiducial metrology and independent stage encoder before and after tool withdrawal. This section therefore links to Research Gate G014: Can a second blinded laboratory reproduce the effect of metabolic demand boundary on neural niche oxygen heterogeneity [umol/L] without private calibration or discarded failures? The hard stop is any device escape, material contamination, uncontrolled mechanical load, untraceable failed placement or unauthorized actuation. 03 F161: NEURAL OXYGEN GRADIENTS AND MICROFLUIDIC TRANSPORT This section begins by distinguishing two physical accounts: more detected spikes may reflect a better electrode contact rather than better neural viability or repair. The preregistered physical endpoint is neural activity retention [%], and its physical rationale is electrode-tissue coupling, network maturation, glial support and metabolic stress jointly determine extracellular network activity and its detectability. Here the alternative explanation matters just as much: electrode contact, impedance, detection threshold, filtering or survival selection can inflate apparent neural network retention without a biological gain. It cannot manipulate physical time. A first reconstructable example concerns spatial sensor-registration error. A credible laboratory study would attempt to isolate the spatial sensor-registration error contribution and challenge a cross-material or cross-geometry transfer without hidden recalibration before interpreting the estimated difference as support for a model-based hypothesis. A second example, longitudinal niche heterogeneity, challenges the possibility that apparent shifts in longitudinal niche heterogeneity may alter measured neural niche oxygen heterogeneity, yet sensor bias, culture stress or geometry confounding could mimic an improvement.. Its proposed test is to register the longitudinal niche heterogeneity contribution and compare a reference physical measurement with a simulated trajectory. The laboratory witness should be external to the favored model. For this flagship it is independent MEA acquisition plus orthogonal live/dead or identity assays using frozen spike-detection thresholds. This section therefore links to Research Gate G027: If the assumed role of stagnant interface pocket were reversed, which independent observation would distinguish actual change in neural niche oxygen heterogeneity [umol/L] from its rival? The hard stop is electrode quality invalidates comparisons, apoptosis or tissue identity is unaccounted for, unsafe stimuli are required, or holdout labels leak. 04 OXYGEN CONSERVATION, CORE GRADIENTS AND INDEPENDENT PROBES This section begins by distinguishing two physical accounts: a model that interpolates its own training samples cannot be called an external twin of neural repair. The preregistered physical endpoint is neural twin external validation error [1], and its physical rationale is coupled conservation-based oxygen diffusion, scaffold deformation and bounded neural state-space dynamics produce predictions under independently observed boundary conditions. Here the alternative explanation matters just as much: data leakage, hidden batch recalibration, tuned boundary parameters or shared sensor bias may produce a false numerical agreement between twin and neural tissue. It cannot manipulate physical time. A first reconstructable example concerns core-to-surface exposure matching. The laboratory witness should be external to the favored model. For this flagship it is externally timed oxygen mapping and blind MEA holdout with independent feature extraction. The hard stop is holdout leakage, unidentified parameters, broken conservation, unbounded prediction uncertainty or unsupported control actuation. 05 F162: BOUNDED ROBOTIC PLACEMENT IS NOT TISSUE ALIGNMENT This section begins by distinguishing two physical accounts: a successful chip surrogate is not evidence of in-vivo nerve repair or clinical recovery. summary: Reproducibility package (v6, final submission with structural revalidation and updated Fig. 6C/Fig. 10) for the manuscript The single Rho GTPase of Trypanosoma cruzi signals to actin through a non-catalytic OCRL-family RhoGAP . Contents: 01_figuras.zip — all 23 submission figures exactly as embedded in the manuscript (10 main-text figures Fig1–Fig10, 12 supplementary figures FigS1–FigS12, and GraphicalAbstract.png); 02_dados_de_origem.zip — 78 standardised source tables and sequence files (including per-figure datasets, invariant-set microarray re-normalisation tables, ex vivo midgut adhesion totals, and GenBank QB139547 TcOCRL sequences); 03_proveniencia.zip — 61 per-result provenance records tracing each figure and table to its laboratory source file, plus the numbering crosswalk; 04_scripts.zip — 124 analysis and figure-generation scripts; 05_reconstrucao_3d.zip — autonomous 3D confocal reconstruction package for GFP-TcOCRL epimastigotes (raw confocal z-stacks of Series019, isotropic volumes for 16 cells, silhouettes, STL meshes, and localisation classification); 06_codigo_de_analise.zip — 259 files preserving the directory layout cited in Methods and Data Availability ( pipeline_reanalise/ , in_silico/ , tools/ , and raw_data/14_Tabela1_insilico_toolkit/ ). Linked public accessions: Polysomal microarray data are deposited in NCBI GEO under accession GSE354409 (platform GPL1061). The corrected full-length TcOCRL mRNA sequence from T. cruzi Dm28c (2,537 bp; 5′ UTR isoforms of 191 and 10 nt; 781 aa) is deposited in GenBank under accession QB139547 . summary: Most installed machines watch themselves only with fixed limit alarms. We propose agentising: an AI check layer, learned from healthy operation, added beside those alarms, plus an agent that would turn warnings into actions for a person to approve. Only the detection layer is tested here. We tested it on five public machine datasets that map onto Germany’s largest manufacturing sectors: CNC milling (AI4I 2020), a hydraulic rig (ZeMA), the Tennessee Eastman chemical plant, NASA C-MAPSS turbofans and the SKAB pump test bed. Thresholds were set for 1% false alarms on healthy calibration data; measured test false-alarm rates were 0.85–4.0% on the milling, hydraulic and chemical-plant data and up to 31% on the pump test bed. Adding the AI check to a simulated per-sensor limit baseline at least doubled caught milling failures (14% to 30% with a random split, 8% to 20% with a row-order-preserving split), raised mean detection over 18 observable chemical-plant faults from 82% to 91% while halving detection delay, and warned on every held-out engine with median leads of 50 to 76 cycles depending on the split. Hydraulic valve and pump faults stayed invisible without pressure sensors. Fresh GitHub-hosted runs reproduced the five- machine benchmark outputs and the split-sensitivity outputs exactly. A separate camera-inspection demonstration was run in a browser app and is not part of that automated reproduction.
title: Agentising Existing Machines: An AI Check Layer for Current Machinery, Tested on Five Industrial Simulations and Test Rigs

summary: Data, code, result tables and figures for: El-Samra, R., El-Fadel, M. “A Combined Hydro-Climatic Stress Index for the Jordan River Basin: Observed Stress 1981–2020, SPEI Benchmark and CMIP6 Projections to 2050”, submitted to Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies (manuscript EJRH-D-26-04528, revised version R1). The Combined Hydro-Climatic Stress Index (CHSI) is the difference between standardized annual precipitation and temperature anomalies, rescaled to unit variance over 1981–2010. It is computed from NASA POWER data for 11 grid cells (0.5° × 0.625°) covering the Jordan River Basin, grouped into three hydro-climatic zones, for 1981–2020. The decade 2011–2020 is withheld from standardization and used for evaluation. CHSI is benchmarked against SPEI-12 with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith reference evapotranspiration. It is projected to 2050 with 30 NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, each standardized against its own 1981–2010 historical run. This version accompanies the revised manuscript. It adds the sensitivity of the projections to the standardization, the reference period, the threshold and the weight given to temperature; seasonal CHSI; CHSI for each grid cell and on a 0.1° grid (ERA5-Land temperature, CHIRPS precipitation); significance tests and effect sizes; and a comparison with soil moisture and runoff from MERRA-2 and ERA5-Land. It also contains the Word files of Supplementary Tables S1–S14. Only this version matches the revised manuscript. Contents: raw extracts (data_raw/), configuration of cells and weights (config/), Python scripts (scripts/), and derived series, tables and figures (outputs/). See README.md for the folder structure, how to reproduce each table and figure, and data sources and licences. ERA5-Land extracts contain modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information; neither the European Commission nor ECMWF is responsible for any use of this information.
title: Combined Hydro-Climatic Stress Index (CHSI) for the Jordan River Basin: data, scripts and results

summary: AquaTrajectories is an open-source R and Python research-software toolkit for aquatic animal 2D and 3D movement analysis, video-based fish-tracking interfaces, multiview reconstruction, camera geometry, behavioural methods, conditional uncertainty assessment and reproducible scientific visualization. Version 0.2.0 adds evidence safeguards for estimator sensitivity, mixed coordinate units, independent-unit interpretation, spatial support, measurement-geometry associations and descriptive falsification checks. Its synthetic numerical oracles and cross-platform qualification do not certify biological identity, real-video tracking generalization, physical underwater XYZ metrology, causal feeding responses, fish welfare outcomes or hardware safety.
title: AquaTrajectories: Aquatic Animal Movement and Multiview Trajectories

A competing account holds that shared vendor software, batch selection, forgiving score normalization or device-specific hidden patches can falsely inflate reproducibility. The future archive must preserve both refusals and the possibility of better tests. Independent measurements require external blind replay of raw sensor traces, independent device-reference phantoms and between-device variance audit against controlled laboratory-to-laboratory replication with frozen manual standard operating procedures and equally calibrated instruments. Neither automation throughput nor a clean dashboard proves living biological function. The complete failed-attempt record remains part of the evidence. Consider legacy controller interface: unsupported operations may silently degrade into approximations. An independent trial should run capability negotiation and refuse non-equivalent action. Contrast inter-site authority mapping, where permissions may not carry lawfully across institutions; a different test would require explicit local human approval before activating robots. These two investigations must retain calibration and sample identities. The future biological laboratory must obtain appropriate authority before work with living samples; present examples are synthetic or inert. Two future gates ask about clock synchronization transfer and inter-site authority mapping. Freeze the reference and the comparator before changing the suspected cause, then transfer the protocol unseen to an external reviewer. Stop if hidden device-specific tuning is required, inter-lab variance exceeds tolerance, authorization metadata are absent or independent scores disagree. Preserve dissent as a source of better experiments. THE CROSS-FLAGSHIP VERIFICATION CONTRACT F151 may pass traceable batch identity, robot operation timing and status of independent qualification to F152, but it may not pass a presumed biological quality claim. F152 may share physical sensor status and external fault labels with F153, but a low alarm count is not permission to run the next experiment. F153 may propose new tests while an authorized human panel retains control of approval and veto. F154 receives only commands within its pre-authorized local hardware envelope; independent emergency-stop circuits cannot be overridden by an AI policy. F155 receives the typed protocol, calibration provenance and failed execution records, and tests whether another vendor device produces equivalent physical actions without privileged tuning. Every inter-flagship signal carries its unit, confidence bounds, timestamp, data lineage, authority and invalidity conditions. The thirty candidate mathematical relations in the PDF include accounting identities, sensor-performance ratios, timing budgets, review queue measures, dimensionless transfer loss and uncertainty-sensitive reproducibility scores. Each states its assumptions and dimensions. The forty-two three-dimensional models are explicitly synthetic and independently recalculable from raw numerical formulas and stored CSV triples. They are visualization and software-reconstruction exercises, not material validation. The eighty-two research chapters repeat a six-phase logic with different physical questions: physical identity and authorization, fair competing explanation, recomputed three-dimensional sensitivity, blinded independent measurement, benign counterfactual fault challenge, external transfer and permission to refuse. Their three literary and scientific voices are mechanism, measurement and refutation. A reader should find genuine scientific disagreement and a feasible negative answer, not merely an impressive number of pages. The two hundred Research Gates are planned future investigations with a distinct origin, an extreme counterworld and an independent research plan. They do not promise that robotic laboratories will be more accurate, biological samples more mature or quantum and AI computations magically faster than physical constraints permit. The thirty-three Phoenix prototypes are nonclinical and predominantly inert apparatus concepts: batch-accounting ledgers, blind sensor fault chambers, human veto interfaces, safe-state clocks and cross-device reference artifacts. Their purpose is to be built, modified, contradicted or retired by future engineers. An honest boundary is a durable scientific inheritance. summary: This archive contains the occurrence datasets, environmental predictor sets, projected habitat-suitability rasters, derived tables and analysis code supporting the study "Climate-driven shifts in the potential distributions and spatial overlap of pear (Pyrus spp.) and the oriental fruit moth (Grapholita molesta) in China" (Geng et al.). Contents 01_occurrences/ - Spatially filtered occurrence records used for modelling: Pyrus_spp_occurrences.csv (n = 1063) and G_molesta_occurrences.csv (n = 108), with fields record_id, taxon, longitude, latitude, source (GBIF / iNaturalist / literature) and year. Derived from 2327 Pyrus and 139 G. molesta raw records by removing duplicates and applying 5 x 5 km spatial filtering in ENMTools. 02_environmental_variables/ - The 40 candidate variables (19 bioclimatic, 3 topographic, 18 soil) with their provenance, the sets retained after Pearson (|r| < 0.8) and VIF (< 5) screening, and the final predictor sets at 2.5 arc-min: Pyrus spp. = Bio2, Bio4, Bio6, Elevation, Aspect, Slope, T-CaCO3, T-CaSO4; G. molesta = Bio1, Bio4, Bio19, Elevation, Aspect, Slope, T-CaCO3, T-pH-H2O. 03_kuenm_optimisation/ - kuenm calibration output: 600 candidate parameter sets (regularization multiplier 0.1-4.0 crossed with 15 feature-class combinations) ranked by delta AICc. Selected settings: RM = 0.8, FC = LPT for Pyrus spp.; RM = 3.7, FC = QT for G. molesta. 04_suitability_rasters/ - Projected habitat suitability (GeoTIFF, 2.5 arc-min, China extent) for the current baseline (1970-2000, WorldClim) and the 2050s, 2070s and 2090s under SSP126, SSP245 and SSP585 (BCC-CSM2-MR), for both taxa, from the optimised MaxEnt models and the Biomod2 committee-averaging (EMca) ensembles, together with the species-level MaxEnt models for P. pyrifolia, P. ussuriensis and P. bretschneideri. 05_area_overlap/ - Suitable area by suitability class (threshold >= 0.2), change rates relative to current, spatial overlap extent, Jaccard indices among species-level models, and centroid displacements for each period and scenario. 06_scripts/ - R and shell scripts for MaxEnt and kuenm calibration, Biomod2 ensemble modelling (10 algorithms, 10 replicates, pseudo-absence to presence ratio 10:1 with a 5 km minimum distance), MESS extrapolation diagnostics, thresholding, area and centroid calculation and overlap analysis. Run order and required package versions are given in README.txt. 07_tables/ - Manuscript Tables 4-7 as csv: variable percent contribution and permutation importance, projected suitable areas and species-level model performance. Methods summary MaxEnt 3.4.4 was run with kuenm-optimised settings; ensemble models were built in Biomod2 with the six top-performing algorithms and integrated by committee averaging; calibration and evaluation followed a 75/25 split, and performance was assessed with AUC, TSS and Kappa. All layers were standardized to 2.5 arc-min. Notes The Pyrus occurrence set comprises genus-level records rather than verified commercial orchard locations, so the projections represent climatic suitability for the sampled Pyrus occurrences and not cultivated pear production area. Raw records originate from GBIF (https://www.gbif.org) and iNaturalist (https://www.inaturalist.org) and remain under their original licences; this archive provides the filtered, modelling-ready derivatives. Author contributions are given in the additional description. Contact: gengqf@sdau.edu.cn

summary: Overview This versioned reproducibility archive supports the manuscript Earthquake Waiting Times Adjusted for Seismicity Rate: Implications for Short-Term Forecasting . The study evaluates whether adjusting earthquake waiting times for the seismicity rate estimated by an epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) model can improve short-term earthquake forecasts. The proposed model (M2) is compared with temporal ETAS (N0), a constant-weight two-component model (M1), and a model using ordinary waiting times with a fixed reference rate (D1). Synthetic experiments also consider a magnitude-weighted alternative (N1). What's New in Version 1.1 Version 1.1 preserves the original version 1.0 archive and adds: Available protocols and results from additional historical earthquake sequences, including exploratory Cohort B and the 18-sequence geographically stratified Cohort C. Event catalogs, forecast scores, model-fitting outputs, and diagnostic analyses. Profile-likelihood investigations of practical parameter identifiability. Parameter-boundary sensitivity experiments involving the Omori decay exponent and exponential triggering timescale. Detailed analyses of the 2011 Tohoku, 2012 Haida Gwaii, and 2017 Iran–Iraq earthquake sequences. Reproducibility documentation, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks. Main Scientific Findings Forecast performance varies across earthquake sequences. Although rate-adjusted waiting times improve retrospective forecast scores in some cases, the results do not demonstrate consistent superiority over ETAS or matched ordinary-waiting-time alternatives. Some apparent improvements depend on the fitted model parameters and their allowable bounds. Nearly equivalent calibration fits can produce substantially different forecasts, including reversals in model ranking. Scope and Limitations The additional global evaluations are retrospective hindcasts, not independently issued prospective forecasts. The available Cohort A component contains the study protocol but not complete final scored results. The Vanuatu audit addendum does not establish verified prospective forecast skill. The parameter-sensitivity analyses are diagnostic and do not establish structural parameter identifiability. Reproducibility The archive contains source code, available input catalogs, fitting outputs, forecast scores, documentation, and checksum manifests. Users should consult README_START_HERE.md , RELEASE_NOTES_v1.1.md , and CLAIM_TO_ARCHIVE_MAP.csv before reproducing individual experiments. The original version 1.0 archive is preserved unchanged within the version 1.1 package.
title: Earthquake Waiting Times Adjusted for Seismicity Rate: Reproducibility Data, Code, and Forecast Evaluation

summary: Description This repository provides the data and Python code supporting an extended triple collocation (ETC)-based fusion of daily transpiration-to-evapotranspiration ratios (T/ET) across 47 sites of the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON).  Four categories of T/ET estimates are included: HFT: High-frequency Turbulence RSA: Remote Sensing Model GSP: Gridded Land Surface Product BIO: Biogeophysical Process Model ETC-based fusion framework The accompanying Python code implements an ETC framework to estimate the time-varying random errors of the four T/ET methods and combine them into a dynamically weighted fused product. The ETC system is reconstructed independently for each target day using a centered 30-day moving window, with at least 15 fully collocated daily observations required for estimation. This moving-window approach allows method-specific error variances, error covariance, fusion weights, fused T/ET, and fused uncertainty to vary with phenological and environmental conditions. HFT defines the common reference scale to which the other three estimates are rescaled, but it is not assumed to be error-free. The default ETC configuration permits correlated errors between HFT and BIO because both methods are derived partly from tower eddy-covariance observations and may share footprint and energy-balance-closure effects. The identifiability of the specified error-correlation structure is checked before the fusion is performed. For each valid moving window, the ETC equations are assembled as an overdetermined linear system and solved by ordinary least squares. If an ETC solution cannot be obtained, the program attempts a standard triple collocation solution without correlated errors. Method weights are subsequently calculated using best linear unbiased estimation based on the full error covariance matrix. Complete fusion dataset The principal file, NEON_TET_Fusion_47sites.csv , is a long-format dataset containing 85,654 daily site records and 16 variables. It includes: Daily fused T/ET; Estimated uncertainty of the fused T/ET; Daily T/ET estimates from HFT, RSA, GSP, and BIO; Dynamic fusion weights assigned to the four methods; and Method-specific random error variances. T/ET values, fusion weights, and fused uncertainties are dimensionless. Method-specific error variances have units of ((T/ET)^2). The four method weights sum to one within floating-point precision. Missing observations are represented by empty fields and were not filled during conversion of the fusion workbook to CSV. Figure-specific datasets Figure-specific tables Figures 2 and 3: Figure2_Figure3_NEON_Site_Data_Aligned.csv contains site coordinates, error variances, error standard deviations, and mean fusion weights. Error standard deviation is the square root of the temporal mean error variance. Figure2c_Figure3c_Statistics_Check.csv lists the plotted summaries alongside values recomputed from the 47 site records. Figure 4: Figure4_NEON_Fusion_Weights_by_Site_and_Vegetation.csv contains site and display coordinates, vegetation classes, and site-level mean fusion weights. Figure 5: Figure5_Plot_Data.csv documents the displayed trends, correlations, variance inflation factors, regression coefficients, and explained-variance contributions for the environmental-driver analysis. Figure 6: Figure6_TET_Consistency_and_Distributions.csv contains the daily category-level and fused T/ET series, with 68,047 valid pairs per comparison. contains the displayed density grids, histograms, curves, and statistical annotations, with recomputed metrics identified separately. Figure 7: contains site–comparator records for the error-reduction maps and Taylor diagram, including error reductions, correlations, normalized standard deviations, and centered root-mean-square differences. Figure 10: Figure10_Data.csv contains daily trajectories, centered seven-day means, a non-drought baseline, and peak-season summaries for SOAP, TEAK, and SJER. Figure 11: docum
title: Continental-Scale Benchmark Transpiration Ratios Derived from Multi-Method Data Fusion across the NEON Network

summary: Examines timbral divergence as a pedagogical problem in the professional preparation of wind-instrument students for ensemble performance. Timbral heterogeneity is an inherent quality of a wind ensemble, since instruments with different sound-production mechanisms, registers and dynamic capacities form its distinctive sonic palette. In an educational ensemble, however, natural timbral differences are intensified by students’ individual performing habits, different types of attack, tone production, dynamics, intonation and breathing. The study distinguishes artistically productive timbral differentiation from timbral divergence understood as a pedagogically significant inconsistency of individual sound-production patterns that prevents the formation of an integrated ensemble sonority. The empirical basis of the study was an experimental project conducted at Shandong University of Arts in 2024–2026 with 16 wind-instrument students. Pedagogical observation, expert assessment, the Soundcorset digital tuner and spectral analysis using Sonic Visualiser were applied. At the initial diagnostic stage, 68% of participants demonstrated a low level of intonational and timbral-intonational balance, while only 6% achieved a high level. Following the implementation of the author’s training programme, the proportion of students at the low level decreased to 25%, whereas 25% reached the high level. The findings make it possible to interpret timbral divergence not merely as an acoustic deficiency but as an integrative indicator of insufficient ensemble hearing, performing flexibility and the ability to consciously modify one’s individual sound within a shared sonic space. The pedagogical objective is therefore not to erase timbral individuality, but to transform it into a flexible element of collective artistic expression.
title: Timbral Divergence as a Pedagogical Problem in Preparing WindInstrument Students for Ensemble Performance.

summary: What does it mean to say that looking at an atom changes it? A detector can register the same initial average light signal for two proposed measurement processes, even when the processes disturb a trapped ion in different ways. This preprint asks whether a second measurement of the ion’s motion can tell them apart. In a protected three-level calcium-ion benchmark, moving the beam inward at equal calibrated optical gain reduces the initial two-quantum excitation rate by 7.09% under a least-energy-exchange rule and increases it by 23.47% under an energy-frame rule. A scalar optical channel gives zero direct excitation at the inner position. A separate test allows the ion to leave the three levels. Twelve equally sampled preparations give a pooled return probability of exactly one half for original positive rank-one detector events ending within the measured levels. The calibrated scalar model gives 0.999082 at the outer position. Both tests await a matched physical experiment. Published Maryland and Innsbruck apparatus parameters delimit the necessary optical calibration and motional readout. A successful blinded replication would establish which specified rule predicts the disturbance across settings on that instrument. Ordinary quantum measurement theory accommodates the alternatives. The ERU kernel supplies no positive event rate with the probe switched off. This preprint extends An Operator Formulation of the Equation of Relational Unity (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24382197). The deposit includes the experimental protocols, editable manuscript source and reproducibility files.
title: ERU and Wavefunction Collapse: Relational Dynamics, Definite Outcomes and Falsifiable Predictions

summary: We establish a deterministic algorithm that computes the exact closed meandric number M_n from the order n in 2^{O(sqrt(n) log n)} bit operations. The main construction splits each crossing into two points and gives a bijection between closed plane meanders and a prescribed class of straight-line Hamilton cycles on a rational point set of size 4n. A polynomial-size system of local annotations selects exactly one constrained Delaunay triangulation for each cycle. Applying the annotated-triangulation counting theorem of Marx and Miltzow then yields the subexponential bound. We make the geometric construction, the uniqueness of every annotation and the integer-arithmetic cost explicit. A technical appendix gives a periodic-depth realization with canonical rooted-path states and the same asymptotic bound. As a separate consequence, an interval decomposition and formal Lagrange inversion give an exact coefficient formula and a subexponential algorithm for an associated core count; these cores are exponentially rare among all meanders. Reproducible finite checks are reported separately from the proof and from larger reference counts. Version 2.0 (22 November 2026): revised and simplified proof of the main reduction, with an explicit c*N^15 bound for the essential annotation catalogue; clearer attribution to the general Marx--Miltzow counting framework; the depth-augmented realization moved to a technical appendix; removal of the former core-coverage theorem section; expanded bibliography and precise reference-count provenance; and reproducible positive, negative and rank-feasibility diagnostics. The accompanying source archive contains editable LaTeX, BibTeX, vector figures, standard-library Python checks and raw records. It does not implement or benchmark the full subexponential counting engine at large orders. This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.
title: Exact Subexponential Counting of Closed Plane Meanders

summary: This paper proposes the Theory of Asymmetric Resource Dissipation and Nullification (ARDN), a general systems-level framework for examining the relationship between internal resource expenditure, local functional returns, and additional value obtained by entities outside an operational system boundary. The central observation is that resource expenditure within a system does not necessarily produce a proportionate functional benefit for that system. Under specified conditions, internal agents may consume time, energy, attention, information, computational capacity, labour, or other measurable resources while failing to produce sufficient net functional output relative to their defined objective. At the same time, some result of their activity may pass through an identifiable transfer pathway and create measurable additional value for an external beneficiary. The framework distinguishes the internal system, the external reference, the transfer pathway, and the external beneficiary. It formulates a conditional resource-output-gain relationship and separates four possible systemic outcomes: decision dilemma, functional divergence, structural contradiction, and local functional nullification. The primary case is the Friends Celebrity Quarrel Case (FCQC), in which two friends expend conversational and cognitive resources while arguing about a celebrity who may be unaware of their existence. The case is used as a recurring human illustration rather than as the definition of the general mechanism. The distinction between the celebrity as an external reference and a digital platform as a possible external beneficiary is made explicit. The paper develops a fourteen-layer architecture, twelve principal disciplinary domains, operational definitions, a mathematical notation system, conditional scaling models, falsifiable propositions, counterexamples, and a proposed computational and empirical research programme. ARDN is presented as a theoretical proposal, not as an established universal law. Numerical parameter estimation, empirical replication, and cross-domain validation remain necessary before its broader claims can be accepted. summary: The Default Relative Domination Principle (DRDP) is a proposed human psychological framework concerned with the possibility that an individual may experience an unearned sense of relative self-elevation after observing the decline, failure, or downward movement of another person. The central proposition is that an observer may experience a favorable comparative shift without making a corresponding objective improvement, acquisition, or additional effort. The proposed framework includes familiar and unfamiliar individuals, relationship-independent activation, spontaneous self-other comparison, relative-gap perception, latent ego-related activation, conscious and unconscious processing, and possible affective gratification, relief, stability, and perceived security. The framework preserves a five-stage human mechanism: observed decline, spontaneous comparison, relative-gap perception, ego-related activation, and possible affective gratification. It further distinguishes conscious ego-gratification from unconscious ego-gratification and both from the possible activation of a latent ego-related tendency. DRDP does not assert that every human being experiences pleasure whenever another person declines. Rather, it proposes a potentially recurring human tendency whose activation may depend on comparability, perceived relevance, relationship conditions, empathy, self-evaluation, and other contextual factors. The manuscript distinguishes the proposed construct from social comparison, schadenfreude, downward comparison, self-evaluation maintenance, and related psychological explanations. A formal mathematical architecture is developed to separate objective position, subjective relative position, latent ego-related activation, self-elevation, gratification, and perceived security. Sixteen theoretical layers, multidisciplinary research domains, ten hypotheses, boundary conditions, alternative explanations, operational definitions, and an empirical validation roadmap are specified. No new participant data or experimental findings are reported. The present work is a theoretical formulation whose distinctiveness, reliability, causal structure, and generalizability require independent testing. summary: Abstract This document gives a technical and functional description of Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints (ALF): a way to verify that an AI model or algorithm in production still makes the decisions that were reviewed and approved, and to stop its output from taking effect if it does not. The problem. Current AI trust mechanisms prove identity and origin, not behaviour: Model signing (OpenSSF Model Signing, led by Google, NVIDIA and HiddenLayer; NVIDIA NGC signed models) proves which file a model is. Attestation and transparency logs (for example Apple Private Cloud Compute) prove which software a server runs. Neither shows what the model actually decides. A model can be fine-tuned, quantised, wrapped in a prompt or proxy layer, or replaced behind the same name or signature, and an AI agent can act on its output before anyone notices. How it works. Fingerprint generation. A compact cryptographic fingerprint of decision behaviour is created without access to source code, model weights or training data. For machine-learning models it is built by sampling decision boundaries. For rule-based or traditional code it is built from normalised control-flow and decision structure. Sealed-probe verification. In the highest-assurance mode, the model is tested with a sealed set of inputs that the computing system cannot see in advance. Four views must match together: decision boundaries, monotonicity and consistency, constraint activation, and constraint topology. A different model wrapped to imitate the approved one cannot pass all four. Approved-fingerprint registry. Each approved model or algorithm version has a reference fingerprint that can be checked at any time. Run-time check at the point of effect. Inside a trusted execution environment (for example a confidential VM or a confidential GPU), the live fingerprint is compared with the approved one after computation finishes and before the output is used. Fail-closed enforcement. If the fingerprint does not match, approval is automatically invalidated and the output is withheld. The capability needed to act (send, pay, move, transmit) is not released. Validation receipts. Each decision produces a tamper-evident receipt anchored in a ledger, for audit and incident analysis. Where it applies. The same mechanism applies to AI agents and model-serving platforms, payment and digital-currency systems (including offline wallets), vehicles and robots, and satellites. It complements existing technology rather than replacing it: model signing and model registries (NVIDIA NGC, Google Kaggle); verifiable and confidential AI clouds (Apple Private Cloud Compute, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS, and NVIDIA, Intel and AMD confidential hardware); agent platforms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services); payment flows (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Ant Group); vehicle software governance under UN Regulation 156; Chinese AI platforms (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Tencent, Huawei, Zhipu AI). It also gives a technical signal for the EU AI Act's substantial-modification rule and for China's generative AI filing regime, both of which depend on knowing whether the deployed system is the one that was assessed. summary: The Boundary-Coupled Threat-Transduction Framework (BCTTF) is proposed as a cross-domain theoretical architecture for examining how an element initially external to a system can become incorporated into the system's effective or identity-related boundary, and how a threat to that element may subsequently be processed as a threat to the system itself. The framework retains two principal branches: a subjective-agent branch, centred on identity-related defence in human systems, and a mechanical and automated branch, centred on operational dependency and fault response. Its central question concerns why a system may defend a deeply connected external element even when the system has no immediate direct material or physical-survival requirement to protect that element. The framework formalizes a twelve-stage default mechanism, eighteen analytical layers, two primary case studies, branch-specific mathematical models, parameter-estimation procedures, operational definitions, falsifiability conditions, and a computational simulation design. A supplied Python implementation was executed using synthetic data only. Its parameter-recovery and held-out prediction results demonstrate numerical consistency under the script's own data-generating assumptions; they do not establish empirical validity, universality, or originality. The manuscript therefore distinguishes the proposed general mechanism from branch-specific implementations and distinguishes synthetic model verification from empirical validation. boundary incorporation; threat transduction; identity-related defence; operational coupling; homeostasis; fault response; parameter estimation; system dynamics; computational simulation; cross-domain modelling

summary: Abstract Introduction: The polymeric product obtained in the presence of microheterogeneous catalytic systems is characterized by a fairly reasonable molecular weight distribution (MWD), resulting from kinetically non-equivalent active centers (ACs) in the system that initiates the polymerization process. The nature and composition of the ACs are determined by defining and solving an inverse problem in MWD formation. This problem is acute because revealing the nature of the kinetic heterogeneity explains the changes in molecular parameters and product consumption for different catalyst compositions and propagation modes in polymerizations. Objective: This study aimed to develop methods and algorithms for interpreting gel chromatograms to analyze the kinetic heterogeneity of an industrially obtained polymeric product in microheterogeneous catalytic systems. Methods: The solution method assumes that the MWD formed is a superposition of distributions inherent to each type of AC. Since the problem in the final formulation refers to Fredholm integral equations of the first type, the regularization method of A. N. Tikhonov is used for its numerical solution, with the original problem being preliminarily discretized. This methodology and the developed software algorithms were used to determine the kinetic heterogeneity of catalytic systems containing titanium and neodymium. Results and discussion: MWD analysis revealed two types of CAs with an average molecular weight of A̅T1 - lnM = 11.3 and B̅T1 - lnM = 13.2 in the titanium catalyst, and three types of A̅Nd - lnM = 11.1, B̅Nd - lnM = 12.7 and C̅Nd - lnM = 14 for the neodymium catalyst, respectively. Conclusions: Repeated computational experiments under different polymerization conditions and requirements for the preparation of a catalytic system allow us to reveal a relationship with the resulting heterogeneity of CAs. It allows us to define and solve problems related to controlling the molecular characteristics of the resulting polymer product. Resumo Introdução: o produto polimérico obtido na presença de sistemas catalíticos microheterogêneos é caracterizado por uma distribuição de peso molecular bastante razoável (MWD), resultante de centros ativos cineticamente não equivalentes (ACs) no sistema que inicia o processo de polimerização. A natureza e a composição dos ACs são determinadas definindo e resolvendo um problema inverso na formação de MWD. Este problema é agudo porque revelar a natureza da heterogeneidade cinética explica as mudanças nos parâmetros moleculares e de consumo do produto para diferentes composições de catalisador e modos de propagação em polimerizações. Objetivo: o presente estudo teve como objetivo desenvolver métodos e algoritmos de interpretação de cromatogramas em gel para analisar a heterogeneidade cinética de um produto polimérico obtido industrialmente em sistemas catalíticos microheterogêneos. Métodos: o método de solução parte do pressuposto de que o MWD formado é uma superposição de distribuições inerentes a cada tipo de ACs. Como o problema na formulação final se refere às equações integrais de Fredholm do primeiro tipo, o método de regularização de A. N. Tikhonov é usado para sua solução numérica, com o problema original sendo preliminarmente discretizado. Esta metodologia e os algoritmos de software desenvolvidos foram usados para determinar a heterogeneidade cinética de sistemas catalíticos contendo titânio e neodímio. Resultados e discussão: a análise MWD revelou dois tipos de ACs com um peso molecular médio de A̅T1 - lnM = 11.3 e B̅T1 - lnM = 13.2 no catalisador de titânio, e três tipos de A̅Nd - lnM = 11.1, B̅Nd - lnM = 12.7 e C̅Nd - lnM = 14 para o catalisador de neodímio, respectivamente. Conclusões: experimentos computacionais repetidos sob diferentes condições de polimerização e requisitos para a preparação de um sistema catalítico permitem revelar uma relação com a heterogeneidade resultante de ACs. summary: Reproducible by Seed? Not on GPUs: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models Text-to-image models are often assumed to be reproducible when the prompt and the random seed are fixed. The paper shows that this does not hold on GPUs. The same prompt and seed can produce a different image when the request is processed inside a batch instead of alone (batch size 1), and the result also changes across GPU models. Replaying exactly the same call is bit-exact, so the differences come from the execution setting (batch shape, numerical precision, GPU) and not from random sampling. This record provides every image used in the image-level analysis of the paper: 3,536 PNG images from 5 models (Qwen-Image-2.1, FLUX 3 Klein, HiDream-O1, Emu3.5 and Janus-Pro-7B), organized into 10 runs. For each prompt: solo images (batch 1, generated twice), batched images and verbatim replays. A static web viewer that shows these images side by side. For each image it tells you whether it is bit-identical to the batch-1 reference and, if not, gives its pixel MAE. Contents t2i_viewer.zip (~73 MB): the viewer, with a small sample (prompts 0, 4 and 8 of every run, 224 images). dataset_test.zip (~1 GB): the full dataset: all 3,536 images, run metadata ( run.json per run), the viewer data file ( manifest.js ) and the original provenance records ( _source/ ). How to view the images No installation is needed, only a web browser. Unzip t2i_viewer.zip and open t2i_viewer/index.html . It shows the sample. To see all the images, unzip dataset_test.zip , copy the resulting dataset_test folder inside t2i_viewer/ (replacing the sample) and reload index.html . The viewer lets you choose a run (model + GPU), a cross-GPU comparison (Janus-Pro-7B on RTX 6000 Ada vs RTX A6000) and, for Janus-Pro-7B, the decoding mode. The amplified difference map in the comparison view needs the folder to be served over HTTP (e.g. python3 -m http.server 8000 inside t2i_viewer/ ). Runs Ten runs, all in bf16: Qwen-Image-2.1 (RTX 6000 Ada, 10 and 100 prompts), FLUX 3 Klein (RTX 6000 Ada, 10 and 100 prompts), HiDream-O1 (RTX 6000 Ada, 100 prompts), Emu3.5 (H100 NVL, 10 prompts) and Janus-Pro-7B (RTX 6000 Ada and RTX A6000, 10 and 100 prompts each). Prompt ids are shared across models. File names (arms) A0.png : solo generation, batch size 1 (the reference). A1.png : solo rerun with the same configuration (bit-identical to A0 in all runs). B_<tag>.png : the same prompt and seed generated inside a batch (e.g. b16-r00-s11 = batch size 16, round 0, slot 11). R_<tag>.png , C_<tag>.png : verbatim replay of a batched call (bit-identical to its batched image in all runs). Janus-Pro-7B file names have a decoding-mode prefix ( sampled- or greedy- ), each with its own A0 reference. Metrics Computed on decoded RGB pixels. Exact means bit-identical RGB data. MAE is the mean absolute pixel difference (0–255 scale) against the A0 of the same prompt and decoding mode. The values are stored in manifest.js and reproduce the paper. Provenance The images were collected from the experiment servers into two dumps ( T2I_v12_images_full_janus_20261121 and T2I_v12_images_full_nonjanus_20261121_b ) and renamed into this layout without modifying their content. The original manifests (with SHA-256 for every image; all 3,536 images match), the collection journal and contact sheets are kept in dataset_test/_source/ . The SDXL images and the fp8/int8 variants discussed in the paper are not included. The images were generated with third-party models; the terms of use of each model may also apply to its outputs.
title: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models: Images and Viewer

summary: NovaFabric is self-hosted, open-source replay and evidence infrastructure for AI agents and agentic systems. It captures agent executions as portable, secret-scanned Run Capsules and provides replay, behavioral and structural diff, lineage, cryptographic provenance, assurance, and audit around those executions. The same capture layer can wrap general commands and runs entirely in the user's own infrastructure, from local environments through Kubernetes to SLURM/HPC, with no accounts and no telemetry. It is built around five primitives — Asset Registry, Run Capsule, Replay, Lineage, and Evidence Bundle — and five explicit replay modes (forensic, mocked, semantic, exact, and the experimental intervention mode). Run Capsules can be sealed with the user’s own key; sealing is opt-in. Evidence bundles verify offline using only sha256sum and an ed25519 verifier, with no NovaFabric installation required. Interoperates with established specifications rather than inventing formats: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, in-toto/DSSE, RFC 3161 timestamping, W3C PROV, OpenLineage, and CycloneDX.
title: NovaFabric: replayable, verifiable execution evidence for AI agents

summary: A pre-registrable experimental protocol for testing whether the apparent "self" of an LLM agent behaves as a localised, persistent substrate ( ātman ), as a process assembled from the five aggregates with no fixed substrate ( anattā ), or as a surface regularity with no internal organisation (null). summary: The analytical modeling of a plasma wakefield driven by a relativistic proton beam is an element in optimizing advanced plasma-based acceleration schemes. In this work, we present a 1D nonlinear fluid framework under the quasi-static approximation to describe the wake potential excited by a positively charged proton driver which attracts background electrons into a density compression rather than expelling them. We extend the classical 1D nonlinear relativistic plasma wakefield paradigm to evaluate the fluid profiles driven by intense relativistic proton trains under the comoving coordinate approximation. Using a two-bunch scheme, our piecewise-event integration model is validated to high numerical accuracy ($\sim 10^{-11}~\mathrm{GV/m}$) against independent phase-space quadrature of cold-fluid solutions, confirming that interface boundary corners represent physical step discontinuities in the second potential derivative. Scaling to an $N=100$ ramped micro-bunch train with fixed $2\pi$ spacing, we resolve macroscopic phase-accumulation and subsequent nonlinear detuning by deriving a piecewise analytical scaling model. This formulation maps the initial unattenuated quadratic coherent growth alongside the flat asymptotic post-train residual wake plateau, which is determined exactly by the conserved vacuum Hamiltonian invariant evaluated at the final bunch-train exit state. Furthermore, the framework estimates the onset of nonlinear phase-slippage that arrests growth and causes the transient wakefield overshoot to decay toward the residual horizon. Providing immediate 1D analytical benchmarks, this computationally inexpensive tool offers a reproducible baseline for verifying 1D fluid and multi-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) codes. It also provides a tractable starting point for exploring asymmetric, custom-shaped driver profiles relevant to transformer-ratio optimization. --- This repository contains the UPDATED VERSION of supplementary materials for the preprint manuscript, including: - fig1.py: The Python script used to produce Fig. 1. - requirements.txt and README.md: The package dependencies and step-by-step instructions required to run the code and replicate the results. This work is submitted for publication. Preprint is available at arXive:  http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06458
title: Exact 1D Nonlinear Solutions for Proton-Driven Plasma Wakefields

summary: (PT) Este artigo, primeiro de uma trilogia dedicada ao prolongamento do Itinerário Complementar 6 (IC6) e ao futuro da Região Metropolitana de Coimbra (RMC), discute a relação entre a melhoria das acessibilidades e a construção de um projeto de desenvolvimento territorial à escala regional. Partindo da urgência de concluir a ligação rodoviária no eixo Tábua–Oliveira do Hospital–Seia, o texto defende que a concretização da infraestrutura não deve depender da definição prévia de uma estratégia regional, mas que ambas as questões devem ser discutidas no presente. O IC6 permitirá reduzir obstáculos à mobilidade quotidiana, facilitar o acesso a serviços e diminuir custos para famílias e empresas, respondendo a necessidades de territórios onde já existem atividades, relações e oportunidades que importa reforçar. O artigo questiona, contudo, a ideia de que a melhoria das acessibilidades, por si só, assegura o desenvolvimento territorial ou contraria a perda de população. Defende que a consolidação da Região Metropolitana de Coimbra depende da capacidade de transformar a proximidade física em relações de trabalho, formação, cooperação e acesso a serviços, valorizando os diferentes centros urbanos e os lugares que estruturam a região. A reflexão propõe, assim, que a reivindicação do IC6 seja acompanhada por uma discussão mais ampla sobre a urbanidade que se pretende construir, entendendo a região metropolitana não apenas como um território de distâncias mais curtas, mas como um sistema de relações e oportunidades partilhadas. Publicado no Diário As Beiras , em 2 de novembro de 2026, p. 20, na rubrica urbanidadeS . (EN) This article, the first in a trilogy devoted to the extension of the IC6 road and the future of the Coimbra Metropolitan Region (RMC), examines the relationship between improved accessibility and the development of a territorial project at the regional scale. Starting from the urgent need to complete the road connection along the Tábua–Oliveira do Hospital–Seia corridor, the article argues that the construction of this infrastructure should not depend on the prior definition of a regional strategy, but that both issues must be addressed in the present. The IC6 will help reduce obstacles to everyday mobility, improve access to services and lower costs for households and businesses, responding to the needs of territories where activities, relationships and opportunities already exist. The article nevertheless challenges the assumption that improved accessibility alone can ensure territorial development or reverse population decline. It argues that consolidating the Coimbra Metropolitan Region depends on the ability to transform physical proximity into opportunities for employment, education, cooperation and access to services, while strengthening the different urban centres and settlements that structure the region. The discussion therefore proposes that the demand for the IC6 should be accompanied by a broader debate on the kind of urbanity to be developed, understanding the metropolitan region not merely as a territory of shorter distances, but as a system of interconnected places, relationships and shared opportunities. Originally published in Diário As Beiras , 2 November 2026, p. 20, in the urbanidadeS column.
title: IC6: um itinerário para consolidar uma região metropolitana?

summary: Effective Worlds: Objects, Laws, and Changes of Description belongs to the Emergence Calculus series. This free electronic edition is released under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), as a PDF with page numbers matching the print edition and as a reflowable EPUB. What makes a description a useful theory, and what survives when we change it? Six Birds Theory organizes this work around six primitive roles: descent, representability, route mismatch, staging, packaging and audit. Here they help test whether a coarser description still supports a law, compare what different descriptions retain, and check what supports a chosen world. The book opens with a description that cannot predict and a law gained by forgetting, at the cost of a question the description can no longer answer. Readers build states from the questions they must answer, classify descriptions as equivalent, refining, coarsening or incomparable, and separate repairing a description from changing the question. Later units ask what admitted operations require of a state, carry a public theory across representations, choose descriptions that support a joint operation, and show why a readout does not determine a reconstruction. A unit on averaging builds exact ensembles in which evolving and then averaging differs from averaging and then evolving, the structural question physicists call backreaction, without modeling general relativity or cosmology. Readers then construct the best prediction a description allows for a declared target and loss, and carry checked error bounds through changing descriptions. The final unit chooses and defends an effective world for a stated purpose. Scientific conditions, available operations, access assumptions and competing interpretations stay explicit, so each comparison shows what it relies on. For scientists, engineers and philosophers interested in scientific modeling, coarse graining, effective theories, prediction and the philosophy of science. Prose, monochrome figures, worked examples and answered checks carry a complete route; optional mathematics adds precision. The book builds on the introductory Emergence Calculus course; no other specialist volume is required. More about the series: www.emergencecalculus.com
title: Effective Worlds: Objects, Laws, and Changes of Description

F136 separates true conformer search quality and incomplete reference minima. F137 demands a consistent VQE Hamiltonian, active space, electron spin and shot budget before calculating errors. F138 requires blind externally authenticated aroma spectra, instrument holdouts, honest class imbalance and a capable classical kernel classifier. F139 converts quantum and conventional computational overhead into a declared equivalent core-hour ledger. The five main endpoints have different units and do not combine into one score. Forty-two deliberately synthetic 25-by-25 surfaces propose experimental questions rather than actual device runs. A classical success must remain visible; no human aromatherapy or experimental quantum advantage is claimed. summary: STARLI · WHITE RAINBOW ERA · FAMILY 27 · F131-F135 GENERATIVE COMPUTATIONAL DESIGN OF AROMA MOLECULES RESEARCH ESSENCE · PROSPECTIVE / NONCLINICAL / FALSIFIABLE / REPRODUCIBLE FAMILY RESEARCH CONTRACT This family studies five complementary but scientifically distinct aspects of computational design for plant-derived odorants. The central claim is not that a machine can create a beneficial scent. It is a prospectively falsifiable proposal that molecular graph candidates, predicted odour descriptors, volatility-constrained Pareto sets, oxidation-stability models and abstract synthesis-route plausibility can be compared fairly against competent classical baselines. Each flagship uses its own denominator, measurement unit, external witness, negative-case ledger and stopping authority. Computational syntax does not establish real molecular identity; a predicted odour attribute does not verify a human perception; a feasible Pareto set is not a safety certificate; a stable simulation is not an aging experiment; and a synthetic route diagram is not a synthesized compound. The response surfaces throughout the 819-page PDF are synthetic 25-by-25 numerical illustrations intended to illuminate hypothetical shape, sensitivity and non-identifiability. They are not model outputs obtained from new molecular-generation runs. Future groups should preregister sample inclusion, chemical identity, strong nulls, risk exclusions and uncertainty before examining results. Classical models should be allowed to win. FLAGSHIP F131 · Generative Design of Candidate Aroma Molecular Structures at the Limit Scientific object: chemical-graph generation under valence, stereochemistry, scaffold holdout and provenance constraints. Physical basis: SMILES parsing, valence and aromaticity sanitization, canonical graph uniqueness, stereoisomer assignment, charge conservation and training scaffold leakage. Primary endpoint: Chemical validity of generated molecules [%]. Comparator: expert-curated terpene analogues, fragment recombination and a tuned classical SMILES generator at the same proposal budget. Strong rival: memorized scaffolds, duplicate canonical graphs, invalid stereochemistry, biased molecular-size filtering or generator reward hacking. Withheld intervention: sealed scaffold-family holdout with stereochemical and charge-state swaps. Independent observation: independent canonicalization and chemistry-rule audit plus blinded scaffold-novelty registry. summary: This replication package accompanies the study of Norgespris, Norway's voluntary fixed-price electricity scheme. The paper compares electricity meters that entered the scheme early with meters classified as non-adopters in three southern Norwegian bidding zones (NO1, NO2 and NO5) from October 2023 to April 2026. It examines who stood to gain from fixed-price protection, how the cohorts responded to daily electricity prices before and after adoption, and how their relative consumption changed. The archive includes aggregate hourly consumption and meter counts from Elhub, ERA5 temperature data obtained through Open-Meteo, and the Python and R code used to generate the tables, figures and numerical results in the paper and its supplement. The README gives the software versions, the command for running the analysis, and a guide to the files behind each exhibit. The included retrieval script obtains the hourly electricity prices from Hva koster strømmen and checks all 2,829 supplier responses against their archived SHA-256 digests.
title: Who Gives Up the Price Signal? Selection, Price Responsiveness and Demand under Norway's Voluntary Fixed Electricity Price

summary: STARLI · WHITE RAINBOW ERA · FAMILY 26 / F126-F130 QUANTUM AROMA SIMULATION AND EXPERIMENTAL BENCHMARKS · FIVE THOUSAND WORD RESEARCH ESSENCE Prospective / Nonclinical / Falsifiable / Reproducible / All numerical 3D surfaces are synthetic RESEARCH POSITION This scientific working edition specifies separate tests for nanomaterial adsorption-energy calculations, quantum molecular-simulation benchmarks against strong classical methods, blind botanical-isomer spectral identification, solvent/interface free-energy transfer, and uncertainty calibration against experimental aroma analysis. The five outcomes use incompatible denominators: energy mean absolute error in kilojoules per mole, isomer identification accuracy in percent, and externally observed uncertainty coverage in percent. Surface geometries, molecular identities, gas-phase and condensed-phase reference states, classical compute cost, isomer standards, and prediction interval widths cannot be silently exchanged. The forty-two plotted meshes are deterministic synthetic illustrations rather than actual quantum calculations or experiments. Nothing in these figures establishes a materials improvement, neurological effect, human benefit or special quantum healing property. Research inheritance depends on explicit null comparisons, falsifiers, negative cases, working code and externally held evidence. FIVE INDEPENDENT FLAGSHIP CONTRACTS F126 · Calculation of Aroma Adsorption Energies on Nanomaterials at the Limit Research object: adsorption-energy predictions for traceable botanical volatiles on characterized nanomaterial surfaces. Primary endpoint: Adsorption energy MAE [kJ/mol]. Principal physical uncertainty: surface-site heterogeneity, adsorbate orientation, surface coverage, dispersion, substrate relaxation, basis-set superposition error and solvent competition. Strong classical comparator: matched-geometry periodic DFT or established dispersion-corrected classical reference with independently measured desorption if available. Independent scientific witness: independent adsorption reference table with surface identity, adsorption site, coverage, energy conventions and uncertainty. Concealed adversarial perturbation: blind swap of adsorption-site geometry, surface hydroxylation and reference molecule orientation. A rival interpretation is coverage-dependent aggregation, omitted surface hydroxylation, ghost-basis correction or a shifted adsorption reference rather than true improvement. Stop if unknown surface chemistry, missing adsorption reference state, energy sign inconsistency, uncontrolled basis or incomplete mass accounting. This is a prospective design rather than a verified result. F127 · Quantum-Computing Benchmarks for Aroma Molecular Simulation at the Limit Research object: equal-budget quantum-circuit and classical molecule-simulation benchmarking. Primary endpoint: Equal-resource quantum simulation error [kJ/mol]. Principal physical uncertainty: active-space selection, fermion-to-qubit mapping, variational ansatz expressivity, measurement shots, circuit depth, gate noise, error mitigation and total wall-time cost. Strong classical comparator: strong classical electronic-structure baseline and noiseless quantum simulator at the same molecule and explicit wall-time, energy and precision budget. Independent scientific witness: independent reference energy and auditable device/simulator circuit, shot, calibration, compiler and runtime ledger. Concealed adversarial perturbation: withheld spin/active-space perturbation combined with a noisy-shot and calibration-day reversal. A rival interpretation is reference leakage, noise mitigation bias, inconsistent active space, cherry-picked molecule or ignored overhead. Stop if absence of matched classical resource ledger, unreproducible measurement statistics, unstable optimizer or unreported hardware calibration. This is a prospective design rather than a verified result. F128 · Sp
