summary: This release provides crystal structures, thermal-conductivity data, pretrained DANA-$\kappa$ models, and computational workflows for high-throughput discovery of low-conductivity materials. It includes DANA-$\kappa$ predictions for 1,953,259 structures from Materials Project and Crystoria, 4,724 GRACE-based thermal-conductivity results, and CIF files for the 1,712 GRACE records satisfying $0<\kappa_{\mathrm L}<2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The DFT dataset contains 60 completed calculations with corresponding relaxed structures, including 58 phases below $2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and 29 below $0.5~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The lowest DFT value is approximately $0.1826~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{CsKAu_2}$. Conductivity values refer to 300 K and represent the diagonal average of the population-plus-coherence lattice thermal-conductivity tensor, excluding electronic conductivity. Additional resources include second- and third-order DFT force constants and reference transport outputs for the 58 low-conductivity phases, three split-specific DANA-$\kappa$ checkpoints, and scripts for inference, physical-property filtering, computational-cost estimation, structural deduplication, GRACE calculations, and VASP validation. Structure provenance, calculation settings, and quality annotations accompany the data to support reproducible analysis and subsequent model development.
title: Accelerated Discovery of Ultralow-Thermal-Conductivity Materials via Structure-to-Property and Machine-Learning Potential Models

summary: A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.
title: PRC4D: Physical Relation-Constrained Persistent 4D Reconstruction

summary: Diffusion models are increasingly used for medical image reconstruction and super-resolution, but their samples may contain plausible fine-scale hallucinations that are difficult to identify from the reconstructed image alone. We propose Med-PODiff, a patch-wise proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) diffusion framework for brain MRI super-resolution that performs generative reconstruction in compact and interpretable local coefficient spaces. Unlike pixel-space or learned-latent diffusion models, Med-PODiff uses the POD structure to separate low-rank anatomical variation from fine-detail residual variation, enabling predictive uncertainty to be decomposed into total, coarse, and fine components. Building on this decomposition, we define a pixel-wise hallucination-risk score, $H_p$, that emphasizes regions where fine-detail uncertainty dominates coarse structural uncertainty. On brain MRI, Med-PODiff outperforms representative diffusion baselines in reconstruction quality while producing well-calibrated predictive intervals, with total uncertainty detecting high-error regions at AUROC 0.954. More importantly, the decomposed uncertainty is scale-selective: coarse and fine uncertainty preferentially predict errors at the corresponding scales, with $H_p$ localizing fine error at AUROC $0.906$. Controlled injections and retrospective Cartesian $k$-space undersampling further support fine-detail localization and degradation robustness. The discarded POD tail is only $3.8\%$ of the retained fine-error magnitude, and Med-PODiff improves downstream segmentation consistency while requiring substantially less inference time than pixel-space diffusion.
title: Interpretable Orthogonal Latent Diffusion with Scale-Selective Uncertainty for Medical Image Super-Resolution

summary: This paper proposes a method for identifying a control-oriented model of a stable continuous-time linear system from aperiodically sampled input-output data. Rather than recovering the continuous-time matrices, the method directly identifies a discrete-time linear parameter-varying (LPV) state-space model that depends affinely on the measured normalized sampling-interval variation, a structure obtained from the first-order expansion of the zero-order-hold discretization. The resulting model is directly usable in control design for aperiodic sampled-data systems. An initial LPV estimate, including approximate first-order terms, is derived from a standard LTI subspace model through sampled-data relations. The method then iteratively alternates state-sequence reconstruction and LPV parameter refitting. Numerical examples show that the identified model retains high validation accuracy over a wide range of sampling-interval variations where a fixed LTI model degrades. Already at initialization, the state-space LPV structure substantially outperforms an LPV-ARX regression with the same scheduling variable, and the iterative refinement brings the model close to a state-measured benchmark, a practical upper-bound reference.
title: Iterative Identification of Aperiodic Sampled-Data Systems via Affine LPV Models Scheduled by the Sampling Interval

summary: We study scalar-field models in 1+1 dimensions with field-dependent kinetic coefficients, motivated by self-dual Yang-Mills (SDYM) theory as a generator of integrable equations. We derive the Euler-Lagrange equation, traveling-wave reduction, and first integral, and solve the inverse problem: given a kinetic structure and a prescribed tanh kink, which potential makes it exact? A quadratic spatial deformation with a canonical temporal sector yields a sextic potential. We obtain: (i) a closed-form kink energy with a Bogomolny-type formulation, independent of the odd parameter, which nonetheless shapes the energy density asymmetrically; (ii) vacuum curvature relations tying the spectrum to the kinetic function at the vacua; (iii) two propositions on speed families, plus a lemma showing single-speed data probe only one combination of the kinetic functions; (iv) a unified admissibility analysis in which positivity of the spatial kinetic function controls hyperbolicity, the potential bound along the kink, and the vacuum masses; (v) a self-adjoint fluctuation operator with a closed-form potential whose asymptotes are the vacuum masses, an exact translation zero mode, and numerical spectra with no negative mode on the admissible region, evidence for spectral stability. Exact SDYM reductions yield integrable equations, whereas the deformed model is generically non-integrable and cannot be an exact reduction. The correct bridge is the moduli-space route: SDYM reduces to the Bogomolny equations, whose BPS monopole and dyon dynamics produce field-dependent kinetic terms; any smooth one-dimensional moduli metric expands, to second order, to the quadratic model studied here, and the Taub-NUT metric of well-separated dyons gives an explicit realization. Full identification of the sextic potential within a specific gauge-theory moduli dynamics remains open and is formulated as a research program.
title: Field-Dependent Kinetics, Exact Kinks, and a Moduli-Space Route from Self-Dual Yang-Mills Theory

summary: We investigate the linear stability of energetic-particle (EP) driven Alfvén eigenmodes and the wave-particle interaction in phase space, using the newly implemented energetic-particle module in the electromagnetic global full-f gyrokinetic code GYSELA. The coupled gyrokinetic-Maxwell system self-consistently evolves the EP species alongside thermal ions and kinetic electrons, retaining finite-orbit-width and global profile effects. To mitigate the relaxation of the initial distribution in global full-f models, a canonical Maxwellian initialisation is employed, which strongly reduces this relaxation and the associated change of the drive. The framework is verified against the ITPA-TAE and the reversed-shear NLED-AUG cases, including scans in EP temperature and density. The agreement with published multi-code results is quantitative for the ITPA-TAE case and qualitative for the NLED-AUG case, where a reversed-shear Alfvén eigenmode (RSAE) is found near $q_{\rm min}$. Beyond verification, we use a constants-of-motion (CoM) diagnostic to project the gyrocentre distribution and the local wave-particle power exchange ($P = -\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}$) onto invariant space. This identifies the orbit classes and resonances that interact with the mode. For the ITPA-TAE, deeply co-passing orbits dominate the drive. For the NLED-AUG RSAE, counter-passing orbits drive the mode and co-passing orbits damp it, and the sign of the exchange follows that of the linear EP drive. These results provide a basis for future global full-f studies of nonlinear energetic-particle transport and mode saturation.
title: Global full-f gyrokinetic analysis of energetic-particle-driven Alfvén eigenmodes and their phase-space drive with GYSELA

summary: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) for Bayesian inverse problems is expensive: the unknown is high-dimensional, every likelihood evaluation requires a forward solve, and gradients are often unavailable. The posterior typically differs from the prior in a few directions and is often approximately Gaussian in most of them but strongly non-Gaussian in a few. We propose the NQU sampler, a gradient-free MCMC method that splits the parameter space into non-Gaussian (N), approximately quadratic (Q) and uninformative (U) directions. The split is learned once, before sampling, from likelihood values, and each block is updated by a kernel suited to it; a collapsed update handles a global prior scale. Because the learned structure only shapes the proposals, every update leaves the exact posterior invariant, at the cost of one likelihood evaluation. We give a condition under which the blocks can be learned and show that, for likelihoods with exactly the learned structure, the spectral gap of the sampler does not depend on the dimension, whereas updating the scale given all coordinates can have a gap of order $1/d$. On the posterior axes, the NQU sampler, learning included, needed the fewest evaluations in four of five synthetic examples with $d=200$, among nine baselines including gradient-based ones; in those with non-Gaussian directions, gradient-free baselines needed at least ten times as many. On a methane ignition problem with 219 uncertain rate constants, it gave consistent estimates, whereas full-space robust adaptive Metropolis needed about 300 times as many evaluations and an ensemble sampler degenerated.
title: Gradient-free MCMC exploiting low-dimensional Gaussian and nonGaussian posterior structure

summary: Calibrating a spatiotemporal mechanistic model to field data is a Bayesian inverse problem in which every likelihood evaluation needs a simulator run. The R package *spDBL* replaces the simulator with a dynamic emulator, a matrix-variate dynamic linear model with a closed-form posterior that evolves the field in discrete time and processes large grids in spatial blocks. It then calibrates the parameters without further simulator runs, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (implemented in the Stan programming environment) conditionally on emulator draws. In benchmarks on epidemic fields, with every method tuned alike, *spDBL*'s predictions at untried inputs were the only ones with near-nominal interval coverage, though a tuned *RobustGaSP* was more accurate, and *spDBL*'s calibrations matched the accuracy of *RobustCalibration* with higher, though below nominal, interval coverage (80% against 67-76%) and over 50 times more effective samples per CPU second.
title: Dynamic Emulation for Bayesian Inverse Problems in Spatiotemporal Mechanistic Models

summary: This paper proposes a framework for sequential Bayesian updating in probabilistic digital twins using data from multiple sources collected over time. The framework distinguishes between property data and behavior data, according to how observations relate to the digital state. Property data directly inform a subset of the uncertain model parameters and can therefore be incorporated using efficient dedicated Bayesian updating methods. Behavior data provide indirect information through the prediction model and require the solution of a Bayesian inverse problem. To reduce the associated computational cost, an active-learning-based surrogate strategy is introduced that evolves with the digital state and adaptively refines the prediction model in regions relevant to posterior inference. The framework is evaluated using an idealized cantilever beam example and a geotechnical case study of a canal wall subject to varying water levels and corrosion. The examples show how complementary data sources, including both equality observations and inequality information from observed system survival, can inform uncertain parameters and system reliability. The proposed surrogate-based updating scheme yields posterior estimates and prediction accuracy comparable to those of physics-based updating while requiring substantially fewer model evaluations. The proposed framework thus supports multi-source updating and reliability assessment in probabilistic digital twins of engineering systems.
title: Bayesian Data Integration and Model Updating in Probabilistic Digital Twins

summary: Diffusion models provide effective generative priors for solving noisy linear inverse problems. However, existing posterior sampling methods may require singular value decomposition (SVD) of the measurement operator or prior knowledge of the measurement noise variance, while guidance based on local gradients provides only a limited view of posterior geometry. We propose progressive posterior sampling (PPS) with manifold projection, which automatically estimates the measurement noise variance and avoids SVD. During reverse diffusion, PPS constructs a Gaussian approximation to the posterior distribution in closed form and guides a sample drawn from the local prior toward the approximate posterior mean. We then project the guided sample onto a spherical level set that approximates the local noisy image manifold, promoting consistency with the local geometry of the diffusion prior. Experiments on FFHQ and ImageNet across four restoration tasks and three measurement noise levels demonstrate competitive reconstruction accuracy and perceptual quality by PPS.
title: Denoising Diffusion with Progressive Posterior Sampling

summary: The electrical degradation and time-dependent current behavior of vertical $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Schottky barrier diodes (SBDs) subjected to energetic Au-ion irradiation were systematically investigated. Two successive irradiation exposures were conducted under a constant reverse bias of $-100$ V to evaluate the effects of heavy-ion irradiation on device performance and transient current response. Following irradiation, the devices exhibited degraded forward conduction, increased specific on-resistance, enhanced reverse leakage current, and reduced apparent carrier concentration. During irradiation, pronounced increases in leakage current and transient current spikes were observed. Following each beam termination, the leakage current exhibited an initial rapid decay followed by a slower relaxation process. Single-exponential fitting identified distinct fast and slow relaxation components, while a double-exponential model provided a more comprehensive description of the overall current decay. After the second irradiation exposure, the characteristic time constants of the fast and slow relaxation processes increased from 33.50 to 40.64 s and from 190.35 to 282.29 s, respectively, indicating prolonged recovery dynamics under repeated irradiation. A charge-trapping-based model is proposed to explain the irradiation-induced current enhancement and subsequent fast and slow relaxation processes through modulation and gradual recovery of the effective Schottky tunneling barrier. These findings provide insights into the relationship between heavy-ion-induced electrical degradation and time-dependent current relaxation in $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ SBDs.
title: Electrical Degradation of Vertical $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Schottky Barrier Diodes Under Au-Ion Irradiation to a Fluence of $1.3 \times 10^7$ cm$^{-2}$

title: The Burst-Modified Cosmological Expansion Model: A Parameterized Framework for Testing Transient Structure in the Late-Time Expansion History

summary: Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.
title: AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction

summary: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $β\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\geβ$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.
title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs

summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.
title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation

summary: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.
title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules

summary: Solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) over long time horizons is computationally expensive using traditional numerical methods. While neural operators provide an efficient alternative, they suffer from the accumulation of approximation errors along the predicted trajectory, typically caused by the failure to capture fine-scale details. In this work, we design a Commutator Memory Neural Operator that identifies fine-scale dynamical details by commuting two operations and leverages these details to enhance the neural operator's capability in capturing fine-scale features over long time horizons. Specifically, we identify a performance gap between two operations: downsampling the high-resolution field before rollout prediction versus performing rollout prediction before downsampling. We observe that fine-scale dynamical details are often encoded in this gap. By commuting these two operations, the fine-scale details removed during downsampling can be captured. Furthermore, we employ a memory module to store these fine-scale features along the trajectory and retrieve them during rollout, generating spatially adaptive corrections that enhance long-horizon fidelity. Empirical results across five systems demonstrate that CoMNO improves prediction accuracy and long-horizon rollout stability.
title: CoMNO: Commutator Memory Neural Operators for Long-Horizon PDE Prediction

summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are advancing in physical reasoning, but whether they can understand external physical drivers from internal observations remains an open question. Existing benchmarks have not specifically targeted this setting. To this end, we introduce CaveBench, a benchmark for abductive physical reasoning from internal observations. Models receive apparatus descriptions and internal images while the external controls remain hidden, and must infer the operations responsible for the observed responses. CaveBench spans 20 apparatus scenes in five physical domains and contains 10,200 simulated episodes, split into 9,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 200 test episodes. Questions span one to six events and require the complete control set at every event, testing whether an explanation accounts for the entire process. Synchronized observations and control records provide the inputs and reference answers. Evaluating 27 VLM configurations yields six-event exact-match accuracies of 68.0% for the strongest closed-source model and 12.5% for the strongest open-weight model. Seven adaptation baselines show that single-event gains need not improve complete sequences. Error analysis identifies failures in visual identification, physical inference, evidence integration, and action composition, specifying where current models struggle to connect internal phenomena with their external causes.
title: CaveBench: Benchmarking Abductive Physical Reasoning from Internal Observations

summary: Kidney transplantation is the optimal treatment for life-threatening end-stage renal disease, providing significant survival advantages over dialysis. Given the severe shortage of donor organs, accurately predicting the time to premature graft failure is an essential clinical task for optimizing organ allocation and tailoring individualized immunosuppressive therapies. This study is motivated by a comprehensive United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS) dataset containing 243,443 kidney transplant records with complex multi-region structures and high right-censoring rates. We propose EnSurv (survival engression), a deep generative survival framework designed to capture complex, non-linear clinical covariate interactions for modeling time to graft failure. Within a pre-additive noise model (pre-ANM) family, EnSurv optimizes an energy score augmented with pooled Kaplan-Meier tail completion to handle right-censoring. We identify the pooled-completion target of the objective, establish consistency for its best approximation within the pre-ANM family, and give conditions and error bounds for its relation to true conditional graft survival. EnSurv also provides global explainability through summaries of fitted feature weights and incorporates domain constraints through established clinical directions using a soft gradient penalty. Extensive simulation experiments were conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method in comparison with existing methods. Application to the UNOS cohort demonstrates that EnSurv effectively models individual and region-level effects, consistently outperforming baselines across evaluation metrics encompassing discrimination, calibration, and accuracy.
title: EnSurv: Deep Generative Survival Modeling with Application to Kidney Graft Outcomes

summary: Robot-programming agents improve executable control policies through repeated testing and repair, yet binary success saturates while execution risk persists across unseen scenes. We introduce MARGIN, a risk-aware agent that converts successful robot rollouts into actionable evidence for program refinement. Its near-miss margin measures the fraction of the execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout. The agent uses this signal to prioritize fragile programs, guide targeted repairs, and select revisions that preserve development success while increasing execution headroom. An exact safe-racing rule accelerates success-based candidate evaluation. We evaluate MARGIN across LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-90, and Robosuite. In our 80-task LIBERO-Pro reproduction, 78 programs attain perfect development success while accounting for substantial failures on unseen seeds. The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774, and low-margin programs exhibit 2.97 times higher failure risk. Across two independent evaluation rounds spanning 37 unique LIBERO-Pro tasks, MARGIN reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0%, with reductions of 18.0-20.0% on LIBERO-90 and Robosuite. Safe racing reduces fixed-sequence candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% while retaining identical selections, and paired execution probes improve acceptance decisions by identifying hidden regressions. Together, these results establish near-miss evidence as an effective basis for risk-aware, budget-efficient robot program refinement.
title: MARGIN: A Risk-Aware Agent for Robot Program Refinement

summary: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.
title: From Memory Access to Evidence Sufficiency: Diagnosing and Addressing Demand--Evidence Misalignment

summary: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.
title: ExpGuard: Guarding Long-Horizon LLM Agents against Corrupted Experience

summary: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement. Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.
title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes

summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promise in RTL debugging, yet accurately localizing functional errors and generating reliable repairs remain challenging. We propose RTLDetective, a multi-agent framework that integrates signal dependency analysis, simulation-guided fault localization, and knowledge-based reasoning for automated RTL debugging and repair. RTLDetective constructs signal dependency graphs from RTL code and extracts failure information from waveform traces. A lightweight localizer agent predicts expected intermediate signal values and evaluates them through targeted simulation interventions, iteratively probing signal dependencies to isolate suspicious logic and identify potential fault locations. A debug agent combines this evidence with static analysis, a curated knowledge base of hardware design principles and RTL bug patterns, and reasoning to generate corrected RTL. To reduce inference overhead, the framework reuses cached context across debugging iterations. We evaluate RTLDetective on the MEIC benchmark, achieving an 86.1% fix rate, 13.9 percentage points above the best baseline, while making fewer LLM calls.
title: RTLDetective: Agentic RTL Debugging through Dataflow Analysis and Simulation-Guided Fault Localization

summary: Stopping criteria have become a crucial component of probabilistic and statistical methods in structural reliability analysis, helping prevent structural defects and failures, as well as inaccurate evaluations of existing structures. Over time, these rules have evolved in both concept and application, whereas their treatment in the literature remains fragmented. They are often developed and presented in connection with specific models or analytical frameworks, obscuring their broader applicability across diverse models and methodologies. On this basis, the aim of this article is twofold. First, it overviews a wide range of stopping rules, drawing on concepts from applied probability and statistics. These strategies include classical methods based on error estimates or variance, and stability detection. While many of these ideas were developed in other fields, they have the potential to offer useful tools for structural reliability tasks like managing sampling, improving surrogate models, and checking for convergence. Second, this article introduces a structured framework to organize past and recent developments in this area. It brings together various stopping criteria, clarifies their conceptual roles, explains their theoretical foundations, and compares their practical strengths and limitations. By relating these methods to common modeling and methodological practices, and by incorporating a systematic comparison of performance aspects such as accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, we aim to identify dominant strategies, highlight shared challenges, and point to directions for further progress.
title: Stopping criteria in structural reliability analysis: An overview

summary: This book is a  reproducible, grade-by-domain assessment of frontier AI capability in mid-2026.  Across  six reasoning domains  — math, code, planning, social reasoning, language, and scientific reasoning — the book assigns each domain a letter grade (A through F) and documents the  reproducible benchmark evidence  behind the grade. Every claim is anchored on  publicly available benchmarks  and on  models released on or before 2026-06-18 , the book's deliberate 4-month model-release cutoff. The grading system is  defensible, reproducible, and intentionally future-proof : it is designed to last longer than any specific benchmark or model.  The book is a snapshot of the mid-2026 frontier, not a verdict on AI's long-term trajectory. The book argues a single central claim:  frontier AI in 2026 is best understood as a very high-fidelity compression of the prior distribution of human problem-solving , with  selective generalization to nearby problems  but  reproducible failure on out-of-distribution, underspecified, or long-horizon tasks . The compression thesis is supported by three pieces of evidence: the  saturating benchmarks  (AIME 2026, LiveCodeBench, ARC-AGI-2) where frontier models now score at-or-above human level, the  emerging frontier benchmarks  (Riemann-Bench, CritPt, Senior SWE-Bench, Long-Horizon-TB, ARC-AGI-3) where the same models drop into the single digits, and the  CoT smoking gun  — the persistent gap between explicit Theory of Mind (near-perfect) and applied Theory of Mind (49.5% without CoT, jumping to 93.5% with CoT) on SimpleToM.  The book's contribution is the framework, the grades, and the evidence trail — not a verdict on whether the model is "intelligent" in any contested sense. The 4-month cutoff, the contamination audit, and the openly cited sources are the book's commitment to honesty.
title: The Grade Book: A Grade-by-Domain Assessment of Frontier AI Capability in 2026

summary: The rapid expansion of virtual laboratories and online learning in engineering education, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has created an urgent need for clearer pedagogical guidance on how digital laboratory modalities should be used. This review addresses the unresolved educational problem of ensuring that virtual and remote laboratory environments support not only conceptual understanding but also practical laboratory skills and broader professional competencies. Using a structured review of recent empirical studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses, the paper synthesizes evidence on simulation-based laboratories, remote laboratories, immersive environments, and the wider online learning conditions that shape their effectiveness. The review finds that virtual laboratories are consistently effective for conceptual learning, visualization, flexibility, and access, while remote and immersive environments can strengthen authenticity and practical skill development when combined with active learning, multimodal assessment, and strong instructional support. However, persistent limitations remain in psychomotor skill development, assessment validity, accessibility, and institutional readiness. The review concludes that no single modality is sufficient on its own; rather, a hybrid model that pedagogically integrates virtual, remote, immersive, and physical laboratory experiences offers the most defensible pathway for meaningful and sustainable engineering laboratory education.
title: Virtual laboratories and online learning in engineering education: a review

summary: Speculo  is an open-source  persistent data structure  for managing  speculative context states  in  long-context LLM serving . The library treats speculative context slices as a  probability distribution  (a  superposition ) and provides seven persistent operations:  add_candidate ,  measure ,  error_correct ,  refresh ,  evict_stale ,  collapse_to , and  branch . Speculo is a  classical analogue  of quantum superposition — not a quantum computer — and a  persistent state  for the LLM context, not a streaming  KV cache . The book documents the design, the  Python reference implementation  (2,185 LOC, 71 tests passing in 2.5s), the verified  arXiv-cited  competing systems (SpeContext, PRR, LongSpec, Superposition Prompting, SpecPV), and the user-facing API. The book is  honest about what is and isn't contributed : novel data structure, not a novel speculation algorithm. Speculo is the  third book  in a three-book series on persistent data structures for LLM systems, alongside  The Persistent Rope  (KV cache, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23241292) and  Anduril (agent state, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23265187). The three books together cover every persistent state in an LLM system. Apache 2.0. Source at github.com/lordxmen2k/speculo-context-processing
title: Speculo: Superposition and Measurement for Long-Context LLMs

summary: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
title: ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models

summary: Mechanisms recur across the sciences: the equation for heat in a solid also describes molecular diffusion or a Brownian particle. A mechanism is rarely written in one equation; its operation, boundaries, parameters and closures are stated at different steps of a derivation, where methods that read text or fit formulas miss it. We built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, and show that mechanisms can be compiled from them and constructed by deterministic calculation. A constructor detaches, transfers, unfolds, composes and joins their parts across disciplines; where parts do not fit, the failure is an equation for the missing term. Constructions turn a threshold reactor into a memory that a weak signal writes, an oscillator into a switch through two changes that each fail alone, and a rhythm into the regulator of a chemical amount, each with conditions for an experimental test.
title: Constructing physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence

summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.
title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries

summary: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.
title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics

summary: Multi-omics studies are becoming more and more frequent, and are especially suited to decrypt the complexity of dysregulation happening in cancer. In this context, improving prognostication through interpretable methods could provide better patient stratification and help identify new prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Multi-omics data are however very often high-dimensional (few patients/high number of variables). A possible solution to high-dimensionality is Joint Dimension Reduction (JDR) methods, which compute a low-dimensional latent space from multi-omics data. In this work, we benchmark 12 JDR methods on 18 different TCGA cancer datasets. Survival prediction is achieved through a two-step process: the estimation of a low-dimensional multi-omics latent space followed by survival prediction with or without additional clinical data. We had to equip 4 methods with the ability to predict the survival of new patients. Results reveal that JDR methods can improve survival prediction with clinical data, and match the predictive performance of clinical data alone, with a high variability between different cancers. Among JDR methods, JIVE and RGCCA show superior performance. In a subsequent bootstrap analysis, JDR methods identify reliable prognostic biomarkers across cancers. We propose a clinically relevant interpretation of such markers on Low-Grade Glioma. Reproducible codes are available on https://github.com/vlegoff/MultiOBenchmark.
title: Cancer multi-omics joint dimension reduction leads to reliable and interpretable survival predictions

summary: An agent can spend almost as much deciding what to do as doing it. In our documentation workflow, control-flow routing accounts for 42.5% of baseline reference cost on the initial task. Lower token prices alone do not solve this control-flow tax: inexpensive general-purpose routers can trigger additional calls to the expensive generator. We evaluate a heterogeneous architecture in which Jev, a specialized System 1 decision model, controls finite actions while Sol generates documents. Across four software tasks, 480 valid runs comprise 470 completions and ten request-limit endpoints. Jev full routing achieves the lowest mean cost and elapsed time on every task, completing all 40 specialist-controlled runs along the shortest trajectory. On the initial task, mean cost falls by 49.6% (95% paired-bootstrap interval: 42.9% to 56.3%) and elapsed time by 33.2% (19.6% to 46.7%). Across three further tasks, cost reductions are 40.5% to 42.9% and concurrent elapsed-time reductions are 12.9% to 14.4%. Existence-only specialization saves just 1.8% on the initial task. Separately, Sol and Jev each select accepted actions on 100/100 reviewed retail states, with Jev using 97.88% less reference cost and 72.30% less mean request time. The results identify two requirements for efficient agent control: inexpensive decisions and trajectories that preserve those savings.
title: The Control-Flow Tax: Specialized Decision Routing for LLM Agent Workflows

summary: Sharing brain imaging data supports secondary analysis and reproducibility, but privacy risks and differing legal and governance requirements can make unrestricted release inappropriate. The PublicnEUro repository was developed to support discovery and reuse under diverse legal requirements. Here, PublicnEUro's governance, architecture, BIDS-based deposition and curation, metadata and identifier services as well as open and controlled retrieval workflows are described. We then assess the repository published datasets against FAIR subprinciples and the repository public information against TRUST principles. The FAIR assessment shows strong findability and public metadata accessibility. The TRUST assessment documents governance, stewardship, continuity provisions and technical safeguards. Together this demonstrates that PublicnEUro, by separating open discovery from governed data retrieval, supports FAIR-aligned and trustworthy reuse of sensitive brain imaging data without requiring unrestricted disclosure.
title: PublicnEUro: A FAIR and TRUSTworthy infrastructure for controlled access to human neuroimaging data

summary: Guidelines on the anonymity of neuroimaging data help manage research data, inform institutional legal and governance frameworks, and support data-sharing workflows. The question of identifiability is particularly salient in human brain imaging because such data are not only potentially personal (i.e., related to an identifiable person) but also sensitive and thus require extra precautionary and protective processes. The identifiability of brain imaging data is also salient for emerging legal and ethical frameworks regarding rights that emphasise the special status of brain data as closely linked to personal identity, mental privacy, and autonomy. Using a combined nominal group technique and Delphi process, we obtained expert consensus ratings of re-identification and singling-out likelihood across 34 neuroimaging data types, spanning multiple imaging modalities and processing levels, from curated research data to maps, matrices, and summary tables. Expert ratings suggest that 38-67% of the assessed neuroimaging data types could be shared with minimal restrictions based on their intrinsic re-identification likelihood, subject to contextual safeguards. The resulting classification enables researchers to engage with relevant legal teams to guide the appropriate and safe release of data, and to determine the appropriate level of protection (licensing, access controls, governance) in line with domestic and international legal requirements, with the ultimate goal of facilitating international data exchange. A website (https://brainimagingprivacy.github.io/) has been created to facilitate the dissemination of these findings and related evidence among relevant parties.
title: An expert consensus on identification likelihood in NeuroImaging data

summary: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) commonly uses cropped or zoomed-in image regions as teacher-side privileged information to improve fine-grained perception in small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, local pixel-level cues are insufficient for complex visual reasoning that requires global structure, spatial relationships, and high-level semantics. We propose Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation (VC-OPD), which extends teacher-side privileged information beyond local image regions to question-conditioned visual cues. Advanced MLLMs generate cues capturing key visual details, structural relationships, and semantic evidence needed to answer each question. A multi-stage quality filtering process selects reliable cues, which are provided only to the teacher during training. This enables informative token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, helping the student learn to identify and reason over critical evidence directly from the original image. No additional information is required at inference time. Since advanced MLLMs are used only for visual cue generation, VC-OPD is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary black-box models. Experiments on STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements across model scales over reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation baselines. Notably, a 4B model trained with VC-OPD outperforms many baselines with 8B or more parameters, demonstrating effective capability transfer through question-conditioned visual cues.
title: VC-OPD: Learning to See What Matters via Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation

summary: In fitness and sports training, timely action quality assessment (AQA) is essential for learners to identify and correct technical errors during movement execution. However, most AQA methods assess completed performances, limiting their ability to provide timely feedback. Streaming methods alleviate this latency, but limited reasoning hinders their use of subtle movement cues and sport-specific knowledge. Moreover, their fragmented feedback focuses on one body part at a time, overlooking movement details of other body parts and transitions between action phases. To address these limitations, we propose StreamCoach, a streaming AQA framework under the OnCueCoaching paradigm that couples continuous chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with proactive, evidence-gated coaching. Technique-Aware Reasoning tracks body-part movements and action-phase transitions against sport-specific criteria, while Holistic Coaching integrates accumulated evidence to deliver timely, comprehensive feedback on strengths and technical errors. To support training and benchmarking, we construct EE4D-Stream from 1,213 sports video sequences in Ego-Exo4D through LLM-assisted reannotation and manual review of selected claims, pairing dense CoT annotations with evidence-gated speech content. Building on this dataset, we train StreamCoach using Temporal-Semantic Alignment Reinforcement Learning to jointly optimize feedback timing and content. We benchmark 11 offline and streaming baselines on EE4D-Stream, including three proprietary models. StreamCoach achieves state-of-the-art results across intervention timing, action assessment, and coaching quality, surpassing both GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5.
title: StreamCoach: Proactive Sports Coaching via Continuous Visual Reasoning

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Add up the distances between every pair of points in a tree-shaped network with n vertices: this is the Wiener index, introduced by Wiener in 1947 to predict boiling points of paraffins and now a standard measure of how spread out a network is. If the diameter d (the longest distance) is prescribed, every distance is at most d, so the total lies below d times the number of pairs. How far below the largest possible total must fall is settled here to second order. Context. Plesník determined the least sum of distances for given order and diameter and remarked that upper bounds seem much more difficult; the maximum has since been called Plesník's problem (Cambie; Knor, Škrekovski and Tepeh, Problem 28). For trees, the maximum M d (n) lies just below (d/2 − ε/4)n 2 , ε the parity of d. Exact maximisers were known for d ≤ 4 and d ≥ n − 3, with sharp expansions for d ≤ 6 by Mukwembi and Vetrík. Cambie (2020) showed that the shortfall has order (dn) 3/2 and placed its coefficient between √2/3 ≈ 0.4714 and 29/60 ≈ 0.4833, in iterated limits; his lower construction already used branches forking into two at geometrically spaced heights (ratio about 0.38), and his lemma that every leaf of a maximiser lies at full depth is used in the proofs here. Main results. (1) Whenever d → ∞ and d/n → 0, with no order of limits imposed, the shortfall is (κ + o(1))(dn) 3/2 with κ = √((175 − √7)/756) ≈ 0.47747. (2) For each fixed d ≥ 4, M d (n) = (r + ε/4)n 2 − 2√c h n 3/2 − (zr + β h )n + O d (√n), with rational constants computed from the effective resistance of small rooted trees and tabulated for h ≤ 8; for example M 8 (n) = 4n 2 − √70 n 3/2 − n + O(√n). (3) For large n every maximiser is built from a finite catalogue of branch shapes, so for each fixed d an exact algorithm running in time polynomial in log n exists. (4) An explicit formula for M 5 (n) and all its maximisers for every n ≥ 6. (5) Exact maxima for 6 ≤ d ≤ 11 and n ≤ 3000 locate where the catalogue takes over in the tested range. Method. An exact distance identity writes the shortfall as a sum over branches of a depth cost and the squared subtree sizes. Treating the leaves as an electric current from the centre, the squared sizes are the energy of the current, so each branch costs its depth cost times an effective resistance. For large diameter this becomes a continuum problem (mass flowing down, splitting for free), solved by the calibration V = τ 2 /2 + τx 2 − x 4 /7, whose splitting excess is a sum of two squares: equality only for equal binary splits at heights τ = x 2 /2, so the remaining height shrinks by the factor 1/4 at each split. Limits. Trees only: for odd d graphs beat the tree leading term, and for even d the constant answers Plesník's problem for graphs only if Cambie's question (are the graph maximisers trees for large n?) has a positive answer. The constant κ is the leading coefficient; lower-order terms in the joint regime are open, as is the regime d/n → ρ > 0. The thresholds of the fixed-diameter and shape theorems are effective but not computed, and the fast algorithm is proved to exist but is not implemented. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); nine Python scripts with their recorded outputs: the coefficient table, the diameter-five formula against exhaustive enumeration up to 19 vertices, an independent recursion and the order-249 example (M 8 (249) = 215016), the large-height constructions, an exact symbolic certificate of every Section 5 constant, a claims check and the exact maxima for diameters 6 to 11 up to 3000 vertices; the bibliography, a machine-readable index, a research-gate record, a review summary, a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Every check fails explicitly, also under python
title: The maximum Wiener index of trees with prescribed diameter: the sharp second-order constant

summary: Write-ahead preregistered benchmark ( OSIRIS-BT2T-001-FEZ , Card A ; independent gate G1 signed off prior to submission) of exact non-abelian group inversion g -> g^-1 in the 24-element binary tetrahedral group 2T = Q_8 |x Z_3 embedded in a 5-qubit register (frozen encoding bt2t-enc-1 ) on a five-transmon heavy-hex T-junction [21, 22, 23, 16, 24] of the 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processor ibm_fez (job dc2ee3uq4uuc73a56o6g ; HARDWARE_ATTESTED , 288 ISA circuits, 27,648 equal-shot physical measurements across 3 interleaved randomized blocks, 11 s QPU, N_windows = 1 ). Coset-parity Boolean factoring over 2T = Q_8 |x Z_3 compresses heavy-hex CZ count 10.04x from 723 CZ (1,560 sqrt(X) , unitary depth 2,073) in the generic 11-transposition reference to 72 CZ (151 sqrt(X) , unitary depth 218) for the identical 32x32 permutation unitary, and compresses local pytket H2 -native compilation from 400 to 47 ZZPhase gates (8.51x). Uniform valid-24 raw inversion accuracy rises from 0.0661 +/- 0.0030 to 0.5337 +/- 0.0059 (0.6104 readout-mitigated, cond(M_32) = 1.4524 ), yielding Delta P_valid24 = +0.4676 (paired block t = 73.23, one-sided p = 9.32e-5; 24/24 elementwise wins, Wilcoxon p = 1.19e-7; H1 = SUPPORTED ) and 32/32 exact modal majority-vote recovery. Unused-codeword fixed-point preservation rises by +0.4818 (0.5595 vs 0.0777) while valid-to-unused subspace leakage drops to 0.0940 < 0.15 below the 0.25 uniform random baseline ( H2 = SUPPORTED ). The interleaved 0- CZ SPAM control achieves 0.9076 ≥ 0.90 on unused-8 but 0.8643 < 0.90 on valid-24, honestly refuting H3 ( REFUTED ) and isolating an unflagged 14.91x live readout staleness excursion on leaf transmon q24 (0.33% published vs 4.92% live) and a 2.70x excursion on q21 (2.34% vs 6.33%).
title: Exact Binary Tetrahedral Group Inversion on a 5-Qubit Heavy-Hex Superconducting Register: Coset-Parity Synthesis Compression and Unflagged Readout Staleness (OSIRIS-BT2T-001-FEZ)

summary: This deposit holds the spectrogram images and audio of the 7,530 items in the synthetic set of BioSpecQA, a benchmark of questions about call properties in bioacoustics. The 7,020 multi-step questions reuse these clips. Together with the code, the answers of every evaluated model and the scripts that reproduce the results. The real set is built from published recordings and is not included here. Files - synthetic_<task>.zip: seven files, one per task. Each holds the spectrogram image (<task>/<id>.png) and the audio (<task>/<id>.wav) of every item of the task. The tasks are peak frequency, harmonic count, contour shape, pulse rate, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), number of calls and call density. - items.jsonl: one line per item with its question, the allowed categories for categorical questions, the correct answer, the answer format, the tolerance, the values set by the generator and the paths of its image and audio. - checksums.jsonl.gz: a SHA-256 checksum of the decoded pixels and of the decoded samples of every item. - README.md: the contents of the deposit and how to check a copy. Formats - Images: PNG, 768 × 768 pixels, linear frequency axis, viridis colour scale over the 80 dB below the image maximum. - Audio: WAV, 22,050 Hz, 32-bit float, mono. Checking a copy pipeline/check_build.py in the code repository compares a downloaded copy, or a set rebuilt with the code, against these checksums.
title: BioSpecQA synthetic set: spectrogram images and audio

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [CONTROL]
summary: In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.
title: Unjamming Deferrals: Supporting Students Through JAMN Bot, a Mobile RAG-Grounded Policy Assistant

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [CONTROL]
summary: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and distinguishing demonstrated interoperability from stronger conformance claims.
title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [CONTROL]
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.
title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation

summary: Original paper authored by Kaswey Philyaw, Judith Covey, and Daniel T. Smith. DOI: 10.1080/10413200.2024.2428649 . That paper's replication repository, "Matching hypothesis in sport DATA and SCRIPTS for OSF.zip", is obtained from Daniel T.
